notes: Guidance records were drafted by AI agents working to AUTHORING.md, reviewed adversarially and revised; see reports/adversarial-review.md.
Activities are research-informed proposals, not empirically validated interventions. A citation supports the rationale or principle, not necessarily the specific activity.
Citation keys resolve in references.json, which records each reference’s verification status.

records.summary: Nation's analyses show that the most frequent word families supply most of the coverage of any text, so securing this base is the highest-return vocabulary investment for learners below upper-intermediate level. Instruction should combine deliberate learning of unknown high-frequency items with large amounts of meaning-focused input, such as graded extensive reading, to build fluent recognition, consistent with Schmitt's review of instructed vocabulary learning. Diagnostic testing should identify learners who already have this base so that class time is not spent on it unnecessarily.

activities.title: Band diagnosis and targeting
learnerActions: Take a vocabulary levels test
Identify the first frequency band where your score falls below mastery
Make word cards for unknown items in that band from a frequency-graded list
Retest after four weeks and compare
activities.intendedInsight: Vocabulary study is most efficient when aimed at the first incomplete frequency band.
activities.rationale: Frequency-based coverage figures imply that unknown high-frequency words repay study far more than rarer words.

activities.title: Graded extensive reading
learnerActions: Choose graded readers in which you know almost every word
Read an agreed number of pages each week
Note words met repeatedly that you still do not recognise instantly
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated meetings in easy texts build fast, automatic recognition.
activities.rationale: Webb and Nation describe extensive reading at an appropriate level as a key source of the repeated encounters needed to consolidate frequent vocabulary.

difficulties.pattern: 'I already know the basic words; I need academic words.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners study AWL lists while still failing items in the 2,000–3,000 bands; reading stays slow despite academic vocabulary study.
difficulties.response: Share test results and coverage figures to show where the gaps are. Do not dismiss learners' academic goals; present the high-frequency base as the platform for them.

difficulties.pattern: Only the most common sense of polysemous high-frequency words is known.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misreadings such as 'state' understood only as a political unit, or 'account' only as a bank account.
difficulties.response: Teach the common alternative senses that appear in academic texts ('state that', 'take into account', 'in this case').

diagnostic.task: Give a 150-word general-academic text and ask the learner to underline unknown words and summarise it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Few unknown words, mostly low-frequency; an accurate summary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Several unknown high-frequency items, but the gist is understood.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Many high-frequency items unknown; cannot summarise.

records.contextNotes: Core at foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals, particularly for learners entering at B1 or below. On PG-entry pre-sessionals, test rather than assume, and target only identified gaps; most of these learners revisit rather than relearn the base.
reviewNotes: Word-family counts depend on how a 'family' is defined (e.g. Bauer and Nation's levels versus lemmas) and on the list used; all figures are approximate.

Review response: R1-02 and R1-03 — teaching-time bands, assessed-task anchors and course templates are a project-level pathways layer outside the topic schema and are not added here. This record now supports that layer: it is core at foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals and only revisited (after testing) on PG-entry pre-sessionals.

records.summary: Hu and Nation's study suggested that about 98% coverage is needed for adequate unassisted comprehension of a fiction text; Laufer and Ravenhorst-Kalovski proposed 95% as a minimal and 98% as an optimal threshold; and Schmitt, Jiang and Grabe found a roughly linear relationship between coverage and comprehension rather than a sharp cut-off. Nation estimates that 98% coverage of written text requires around 8,000–9,000 word families, while van Zeeland and Schmitt suggest listening may tolerate somewhat lower coverage. Teach these as approximate planning tools, not exact cut-offs.

activities.title: Count and calculate
learnerActions: Choose three texts: a graded reader, a textbook page and a journal article
Mark unknown words in a 200-word sample of each
Calculate the percentage of known words
Compare your comprehension of the three and discuss the relationship
activities.intendedInsight: Small differences in coverage produce large differences in experienced difficulty.
activities.rationale: Coverage studies relate the percentage of known words to comprehension; experiencing the relationship directly makes the research meaningful and its approximate nature visible.

activities.title: From size to goals
learnerActions: Take a vocabulary size test
Compare your estimate with the sizes associated with roughly 95% and 98% coverage
Set a realistic weekly learning target and decide which texts to read extensively and which intensively
activities.intendedInsight: Vocabulary goals should be realistic and connected to reading strategy.
activities.rationale: Nation's estimates of vocabulary needed for reading and listening, and Laufer and Ravenhorst-Kalovski's thresholds, let learners translate test results into goals.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I know 95% of the words, I should understand everything.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Frustration with texts that are lexically accessible but conceptually or syntactically hard.
difficulties.response: Explain that comprehension rises gradually with coverage and that background knowledge and sentence complexity also matter.

difficulties.pattern: Discouragement at the size of the gap.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who find they are thousands of families short of a target lose motivation.
difficulties.response: Emphasise the large coverage gains from high-frequency and academic words, the role of strategies and glossaries, and long-term goals. Do not present the targets as pass/fail thresholds.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'If you know 19 out of every 20 words in an article, will you understand it? What would you do?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that one unknown word in 20 is roughly 95% coverage, enough for partial understanding with effort, and proposes strategies (pre-learning key terms, glossing, rereading) or easier texts for extensive reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises that comprehension will be incomplete but proposes no strategy.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes full comprehension, or has no sense of the relationship.

records.contextNotes: At foundation, keep to counting and text choice. On pre-sessional courses, link coverage to set readings and to planning independent study between the course and the degree; on PG-entry courses, include the denser vocabulary load of research articles in the learner's field. For teachers, coverage estimates inform text selection and glossing at every stage.
reviewNotes: Coverage studies differ in text type, comprehension measures and participants; 95% and 98% should be presented as approximations.

records.summary: Bauer and Nation's word-family levels rank affixes by frequency, regularity and productivity, implying that a limited set of regular, frequent affixes is the efficient place to start explicit teaching. Learners often know a word's meaning without knowing its derivatives, so recognising and producing forms should be practised separately. Hinkel identifies word-form errors as common in the academic writing of students using English as an additional language; linking forms to sentence slots makes the grammatical dimension explicit.

activities.title: Word family tables
learnerActions: Complete noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms for ten key words from a reading
Mark which forms appeared in the text
Write sentences using two different forms of each word
activities.intendedInsight: One word learned well can yield several usable forms.
activities.rationale: Bauer and Nation's framework assumes that once regular affixes are known, word families can be learned as sets.

activities.title: Slot detective
learnerActions: Identify the word class required by each gap in a set of sentences from the surrounding words
Choose the correct form
Correct word-form errors in an anonymised student text and explain each correction
activities.intendedInsight: The sentence slot dictates the form.
activities.rationale: Hinkel recommends explicit attention to word class in context because word-form errors are frequent in the student texts she analysed.

difficulties.pattern: Wrong word class in nominal contexts ('the analyse', 'a significance increase').
difficulties.revealedBy: Word-form errors clustering in noun phrases.
difficulties.response: Practise slot identification and keep an error log of recurrent forms. Do not treat these as careless slips if the learner cannot name the required class.

difficulties.pattern: One form used across several word classes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Base forms in adjective or noun slots, especially from learners whose L1 can use one form in several word classes without a change of suffix.
difficulties.response: Make suffix–word class associations explicit (-tion, -ity for nouns; -al, -ive for adjectives) and practise them with known words.

difficulties.pattern: Non-existent family members coined by analogy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Forms such as 'analysation' or 'investigatement'.
difficulties.response: Show that families have gaps and teach checking in a learner dictionary.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to complete 'This study provides a detailed ___ (analyse) of ___ (economy) change and is ___ (significance) for policy.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'analysis', 'economic', 'significant', with a correct explanation of each slot.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One or two correct, or correct forms without being able to explain the slots.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Base forms used throughout.

records.contextNotes: Core at foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals, emphasising frequent suffixes, conversion pairs and slot identification. PG-entry learners usually need targeted work on persistent word-form errors. In UG in-sessional work, revisit it through the learner's own drafts.

records.summary: Nation recommends teaching the most frequent and regular affixes and using word-part analysis both as an inferencing strategy and as a memory aid, always combined with checking against context. Bauer and Nation's affix levels provide a sequence from regular, frequent affixes to less transparent ones. Greco-Latin roots and combining forms are especially productive in science, medicine and social-science terminology, but meanings have shifted historically, so the strategy should end in verification.

activities.title: Word part builder
learnerActions: Learn ten high-frequency affixes and ten roots relevant to your field
Build as many real words as you can and check each in a dictionary
Use the parts to guess the meaning of five new words from your reading, then check
activities.intendedInsight: A small set of parts unlocks many words.
activities.rationale: Teaching frequent, regular affixes gives high returns because they recur across many families.

activities.title: When word parts mislead
learnerActions: Analyse 'inflammable', 'discursive', 'invaluable' and 'prevent' by their parts
Compare your guesses with dictionary meanings
Write a rule of thumb for when to trust a word-part guess
activities.intendedInsight: Word-part analysis produces a hypothesis, not a proof.
activities.rationale: Nation stresses that word-part strategies work best combined with context and checking, because historical meanings can diverge from present ones.

difficulties.pattern: Overconfident meanings inferred from word parts alone.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Discursive' read as 'disruptive'; 'inflammable' read as 'not flammable'.
difficulties.response: Build checking into every word-part task; praise accurate checking as much as accurate guessing.

difficulties.pattern: Segmenting words where no affix exists.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Interest' split as 'inter' + 'est'; 'reason' as 're' + 'ason'.
difficulties.response: Teach that removing a genuine affix leaves a recognisable stem with a related meaning.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to work out 'intergenerational' and 'deregulation' from their parts and say how they would check.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Segments correctly, gives plausible meanings ('between generations'; 'removal of rules') and proposes checking in context or a dictionary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Segments one correctly or gives meanings without proposing checking.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot segment or guesses without reference to parts.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, focus on frequent affixes. In UG in-sessional work, and for PG-entry learners heading for science or health programmes, add the roots and combining forms that dominate the field (e.g. medical and life-science terms).

records.summary: Coxhead's AWL (570 word families beyond the General Service List) and Gardner and Davies's lemma-based AVL both identify vocabulary with broad academic range and each covers a meaningful share of academic text (about 10% of Coxhead's Academic Corpus for the AWL and about 14% of academic text for the AVL, figures not directly comparable because they use different units and corpora). Hyland and Tse argued that AWL items differ in frequency, meaning and collocation across disciplines, and Durrant found substantial disciplinary variation in how relevant AVL items are to student writing. Lists are therefore best used as a menu for selection, cross-checked against the learner's field, and taught with collocation and grammar rather than as isolated definitions.

activities.title: List meets discipline
learnerActions: Take one sublist of an academic word list
Search a set of readings from your field for each item
Classify the items as frequent, rare or absent in your field
Prioritise the frequent items for productive learning
activities.intendedInsight: General academic lists need disciplinary filtering.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse and Durrant show that the value of 'general' academic items differs by discipline.

activities.title: Depth for selected items
learnerActions: For eight priority items, record the meaning in context, word family, collocates and an example from your reading
Use each in a short paragraph about your field
Peer-check meaning, form and collocation
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing an academic word means knowing how it behaves, not just what it means.
activities.rationale: Academic word lists identify candidate words; Nation's framework of word knowledge explains what else must be learned for productive use.

difficulties.pattern: List items learned as L1 translations and then misused.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'This phenomenon is very significance'; 'the data establishes a role'.
difficulties.response: Teach items in context with collocation and word form. Do not test lists only by translation.

difficulties.pattern: 'Using more AWL words makes my writing better.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Academic words inserted where they do not fit, producing inflated or unclear prose.
difficulties.response: Focus on appropriate use and compare with expert texts, where general academic words are used precisely rather than densely.

difficulties.pattern: Belief that a single list defines 'academic English' for every field.
difficulties.revealedBy: Surprise that common list items are rare in the learner's discipline, or that key discipline words are missing from the list.
difficulties.response: Explain how lists are built and why disciplines differ; teach learners to supplement lists from their own readings.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to use 'establish', 'significant' and 'factor' in sentences about their field and to say whether each is common there.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate sentences with suitable collocates and grammar, plus a reasoned estimate of frequency in the field.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly accurate meaning but collocation or word-form errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Meanings unclear or misused.

records.contextNotes: Core at foundation and on both pre-sessional routes. At foundation, emphasise receptive knowledge. On UG-entry pre-sessionals, develop productive use from list-informed selections; on PG-entry courses, filter lists against texts from the learner's target field. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, filter lists against the student's discipline and its texts.
reviewNotes: Whether a single general academic vocabulary exists remains contested (Hyland and Tse versus list developers); this topic presents lists as tools rather than definitive inventories.
The AWL depends on the GSL and on word families; the AVL uses lemmas from a US-based corpus. Neither is universally preferable.

records.summary: Hinkel recommends explicit teaching of a core set of academic verbs with their patterns because developing writers, including the multilingual student writers in Hinkel's data, often rely on a narrower range of general verbs than expert writers. Corpus grammar shows that complementation is verb-specific, so patterns must be learned with each verb. The strength of commitment a verb conveys should be taught alongside its meaning, linking this topic to hedging and to reporting verbs.

activities.title: Verb strength continuum
learnerActions: Order 'suggest', 'indicate', 'show', 'demonstrate', 'prove' and 'establish' by strength of claim
Match each to a type of evidence
Revise a set of overclaimed sentences from student writing
activities.intendedInsight: Verb choice signals how strongly the writer commits to a claim.
activities.rationale: Hinkel notes that a restricted verb range limits a writer's ability to express degrees of certainty; a graded set makes the choice explicit.

activities.title: Pattern hunt
learnerActions: Find eight research-process verbs in an article from your field
Copy the pattern that follows each (that-clause, noun + preposition, wh-clause)
Write a sentence of your own with each verb using the same pattern
activities.intendedInsight: Each verb carries its own pattern.
activities.rationale: Corpus grammar shows that complementation patterns are lexically specific and must be learned with the verb.

difficulties.pattern: 'Prove' and 'show' used for any finding.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'This survey proves that…' for small or correlational studies.
difficulties.response: Link verb strength to the evidence and to hedging. Avoid banning 'prove', which is appropriate in mathematics and logic.

difficulties.pattern: Pattern errors with research verbs.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Attribute to that', 'consist from', 'emphasise on', 'account the result'.
difficulties.response: Record verbs with their patterns and practise them in context.

difficulties.pattern: Verbs of cognition used with inanimate subjects.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'This essay believes…', 'the data thinks…'.
difficulties.response: Distinguish verbs that conventionally take text or data subjects (show, indicate, examine, argue in many fields) from those that require human agents (believe, feel).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to complete: 'The increase can be ___ to changes in policy' and 'These results ___ that further research is needed', and to justify the verbs chosen.
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'attributed (to)'; 'suggest/indicate', with a justification about strength of evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Appropriate meanings but pattern errors, or overly strong verbs.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Inappropriate verbs or patterns.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, focus on a core set with patterns; PG-entry learners also need verbs for describing research methods and findings. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, tie verb choice to calibration of claims in the learner's discipline.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with src.reporting-verbs; this topic focuses on verbs describing research processes and findings, while reporting verbs attribute others' work.

records.summary: Schmid's corpus study of shell nouns shows how they characterise, temporarily conceptualise and link stretches of discourse, and Flowerdew's work on signalling nouns highlights their cohesive role in academic texts. Because the choice of noun encodes the writer's stance (fact versus claim versus assumption), shell nouns link vocabulary, cohesion and stance. Teach their typical patterns (N that, N to, this N, the N is that) with authentic examples.

activities.title: Label the idea
learnerActions: Find each 'this/these + noun' in a paragraph
Underline the stretch of text it refers to
Replace the noun with an alternative and discuss how meaning or stance changes
activities.intendedInsight: Shell nouns characterise the content they point to, as well as referring to it.
activities.rationale: Flowerdew shows that signalling nouns gain specific meaning from co-text and do cohesive work across sentences.

activities.title: Pattern practice
learnerActions: Group shell nouns by pattern (the fact that…, the aim is to…, the problem is that…)
Write sentences about your field using each pattern
activities.intendedInsight: Shell nouns come with characteristic grammatical patterns.
activities.rationale: Schmid identifies recurrent lexicogrammatical patterns for shell nouns, which give learners usable frames.

difficulties.pattern: 'This' used alone where the referent is unclear.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentences beginning 'This shows…' after a paragraph with several possible referents.
difficulties.response: Add a characterising noun where the referent could be misread. Unattended 'this' is not always wrong; teach it as a clarity judgement.

difficulties.pattern: A label that misrepresents the preceding content.
difficulties.revealedBy: A contested claim referred to as 'this fact'; a hypothesis called 'this finding'.
difficulties.response: Discuss the stance carried by different shell nouns and how readers interpret them.

difficulties.pattern: Vague abstract nouns used as fillers.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'This aspect', 'this issue', 'various factors' without specification.
difficulties.response: Ask 'which aspect?' and replace with a specific noun or specify the factors.

diagnostic.task: Give: 'Some researchers have argued that social media use causes anxiety in adolescents. ___ has been questioned by longitudinal studies.' Ask the learner to fill the gap and explain.
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'This claim/view/argument', explaining that 'fact' or 'finding' would wrongly endorse it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: 'This' alone or a neutral noun ('this idea') without explaining stance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: An inappropriate noun ('this fact') or cannot complete.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, introduce 'this + noun' for cohesion. In UG and PGT work, add stance-bearing choices in source-based writing. PGR writers revisit shell nouns mainly when refining literature reviews and discussion sections.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with coh.signalling-nouns. Suggested division: this topic covers the lexical set and its patterns; coh.signalling-nouns covers cohesive deployment and could take this topic as a prerequisite.
Review response: R6-11 — the IELTS criterion link was removed because this topic is taught up to postgraduate or doctoral level and is not primarily test preparation; CEFR links are kept.

records.summary: Chung and Nation found that technical vocabulary accounts for a substantial share of running words in specialised texts and proposed ways of identifying it; Woodward-Kron argues that specialist language is 'more than jargon': learning terms is learning concepts and how they relate. EAP teachers rarely have content expertise, so the most productive approach is to equip learners with methods (concept-mapped glossaries, attention to definitions in texts) and to collaborate with subject staff.

activities.title: Concept-mapped glossary
learnerActions: Extract technical terms from a chapter
Map their relationships (is a type of, is part of, causes, contrasts with)
Write a definition of each in the pattern term – class – distinguishing features
Check definitions against a textbook glossary or with a subject tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Technical terms make sense within a network of concepts.
activities.rationale: Woodward-Kron shows that technical language encodes disciplinary knowledge structures, so learning terms relationally supports learning content.

activities.title: Technical or not?
learnerActions: Rate words in a specialised text from 'general' to 'highly technical'
Compare ratings with a partner and discuss disagreements
Check doubtful items in a specialist dictionary
activities.intendedInsight: Technicality is a continuum, not a yes/no category.
activities.rationale: Chung and Nation used a rating scale to identify technical vocabulary; this activity adapts the approach for learners.

difficulties.pattern: An L1 equivalent term with different scope is assumed to match the English term.
difficulties.revealedBy: Terms used with a broader or narrower meaning than the field intends, often where the L1 term covers a different conceptual range.
difficulties.response: Compare definitions explicitly and use specialist bilingual glossaries with caution, checking English definitions.

difficulties.pattern: Varying technical terms to avoid repetition.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Participants', 'subjects', 'respondents' and 'students' alternating for one group.
difficulties.response: Explain that in academic writing changing a term signals a change of referent; keep key terms constant.

difficulties.pattern: Definitions memorised without conceptual understanding.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate textbook definitions recited, but terms misapplied in new examples.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to apply terms to new cases and explain relations between terms.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to define a key term from their field and explain how it differs from a closely related term.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate definition with class and distinguishing features, and a clear contrast with the neighbouring term.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate definition but a weak or confused contrast.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot define or confuses the terms.

records.contextNotes: At foundation, terminology is met in subject-content modules and benefits from joint planning with content tutors. Pre-sessional courses with ESAP strands, more common on PG-entry routes, can build glossaries from departmental texts. In UG, PGT and PGR settings, work is best embedded with subject staff; PGR writers may also need to define or coin terms in their own research.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with coh.terminological-consistency (consistent use across a text) and fun.defining (definition structures); both could take this topic as a prerequisite.

records.summary: Hyland and Tse demonstrate that items on general academic word lists often have different meanings and collocations in different disciplines, which challenges the idea that a single meaning can be taught for each. Because learners believe they know these words, misinterpretations go unnoticed; quick paraphrase tasks are an efficient way to surface them. Nation's account of specialised vocabulary supports anchoring teaching in disciplinary texts, ideally with input from subject staff.

activities.title: Familiar words, special meanings
learnerActions: Read sentences from texts in your field containing familiar words (e.g. significant, culture, power, normal)
Paraphrase each sentence
Compare your paraphrases with the disciplinary meaning given by a glossary or tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Words I think I know may carry a different meaning in my field.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse's evidence of discipline-specific meanings shows why familiar-looking words need checking in context.

activities.title: Two-sense sentences
learnerActions: Write two sentences for each target word, one with the everyday sense and one with the disciplinary sense
Swap with a partner, who identifies which is which
Discuss contexts where a reader could misinterpret the word
activities.intendedInsight: Context determines sense, and ambiguity can be avoided by wording.
activities.rationale: Producing both senses contrastively makes the distinction explicit, supporting the recognition of specialised senses that Nation describes.

difficulties.pattern: 'I know this word', so the everyday meaning is applied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that give the everyday sense of 'significant', 'culture' or 'consistent'.
difficulties.response: Use short paraphrase checks on set readings to surface misreadings, and keep a list of discipline-specific senses.

difficulties.pattern: 'Significant' used to mean 'important' in quantitative reports.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'There was a significant difference' with no statistical test reported.
difficulties.response: Teach alternatives ('substantial', 'notable', 'important') and reserve 'significant' for statistical significance in quantitative fields.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what 'The effect was not significant' means in a psychology results section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the result did not reach statistical significance at the chosen level, not that it was unimportant.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions statistics vaguely but also equates it with 'not important'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Interprets it as 'not important'.

records.contextNotes: At foundation, raise awareness through subject-content modules (science, law and statistics examples). On pre-sessional courses, use cross-disciplinary examples; PG-entry learners can build lists from their target field. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, build discipline-specific lists from set readings, ideally with subject staff.
reviewNotes: Classified as ESAP because the specialised senses are discipline-bound, though the awareness itself can be taught generically.
The skeleton's own example of statistical 'significant' overlaps with num.statistical-vocabulary.

records.summary: Corpus comparison of near-synonyms reveals differences in collocation, grammar and evaluative connotation that dictionaries may not capture, as Hunston shows. Hinkel describes multilingual student writers drawing on a narrower range of general vocabulary than expert prose, which can blur precision. Teach in contrastive sets drawn from learners' own texts, using learner dictionaries and concordances as evidence. Swales and Feak's attention to precise word choice in graduate writing offers models.

activities.title: Near-synonym investigation
learnerActions: Choose a set such as affect/influence/impact
Compare 20 concordance lines for each
Record differences in grammar (verb or noun), collocates and typical subjects
Write a short usage guide for classmates
activities.intendedInsight: Near-synonyms differ systematically in grammar and collocation.
activities.rationale: Hunston shows how corpus comparison reveals usage differences between near-synonyms.

activities.title: Thesaurus trap
learnerActions: Run a paragraph through a thesaurus or paraphrasing tool
Identify substitutions that change meaning, strength or register
Restore or improve each with a justified choice
activities.intendedInsight: Synonyms are rarely interchangeable in context.
activities.rationale: Hinkel's work on vocabulary in multilingual student writing highlights restricted range and imprecise substitution relative to expert prose; examining tool output makes the risks concrete.

difficulties.pattern: Synonyms treated as interchangeable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Thesaurus or paraphrasing-tool substitutions that distort meaning ('the study proves' changed to 'the study confirms').
difficulties.response: Require a justification for each substitution and check it in a learner dictionary or corpus.

difficulties.pattern: Strength miscalibrated through verb or adjective choice.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Prove' for suggestive evidence; 'huge' for modest differences.
difficulties.response: Link word choice to the evidence and teach graded sets.

difficulties.pattern: Confusion of similar forms (affect/effect, principal/principle).
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in fluent writing that the learner can correct when prompted.
difficulties.response: Add the pairs to a proofreading checklist. Do not reteach the distinction if the learner can already explain it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain the difference between 'method' and 'methodology', and between 'affect' and 'impact', with examples.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes procedure from rationale/study of methods, and explains grammatical and collocational differences between 'affect' (verb) and 'impact' (mainly a noun; its verb use is common in British and American English but disliked by some editors).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains one pair accurately.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats both pairs as equivalent.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, target common confusion sets; PG-entry learners also need near-synonyms for reporting research (show, suggest, indicate). In UG and PGT settings, work from the learner's own drafts and disciplinary near-synonym sets; PGR writers revisit it during editing.
reviewNotes: Review response: R6-11 — the IELTS criterion link was removed because this topic is taught up to postgraduate or doctoral level and is not primarily test preparation; CEFR links are kept.

records.summary: Hunston and Thompson's work on evaluation shows that evaluative meaning is spread across lexis and grammar, and Martin and White's Appraisal framework offers categories — affect (feelings), judgement of people's behaviour, appreciation of things and texts, and graduation (force: degree; focus: sharpness of category membership) — that help learners organise evaluative vocabulary. Novice writers often evaluate with a narrow range of general words (good, bad, interesting) or avoid evaluation. Build graded sets organised by what is evaluated (evidence, method, argument) and always pair evaluation with reasons.

activities.title: Evaluation ladders
learnerActions: Build graded sets of evaluative words for evidence (e.g. inconclusive, limited, adequate, strong, compelling)
Do the same for methods and arguments
Use the ladders to evaluate two studies you have read, giving a reason for each judgement
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluation is graded, and strength should match the reasons given.
activities.rationale: The graduation and attitude categories of the Appraisal framework provide a principled way to organise evaluative vocabulary.

activities.title: Evaluation in reviews
learnerActions: Highlight evaluative words in a published book review or article critique
Classify each as positive or negative and note how criticism is softened
Write a short critique of a reading using similar resources
activities.intendedInsight: Expert evaluation is specific, justified and often mitigated.
activities.rationale: Hunston and Thompson show evaluation is pervasive in academic texts and realised through varied lexical resources.

difficulties.pattern: Generic evaluation ('good', 'bad', 'interesting').
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques built on a handful of general adjectives.
difficulties.response: Build graded, object-specific sets and model their use.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluative words chosen for force rather than precision ('a terrible study', 'a perfect method').
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques that swing between unqualified praise and blanket condemnation, with no criterion named.
difficulties.response: Teach graded evaluative sets (for example limited, partial, robust, compelling) and ask learners to name the criterion behind each choice.

difficulties.pattern: Strong evaluation without justification.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'This study is useless', 'a perfect theory'.
difficulties.response: Require a reason for each evaluation and calibrate strength to it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to evaluate a study that used a sample of 20 volunteers from one university.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses precise, calibrated evaluation (e.g. 'the small, self-selected sample limits generalisability') with a reason and possibly mitigation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the problem but uses general or over-strong language ('bad sample').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the study without evaluating it.

records.contextNotes: Core on PG-entry pre-sessionals, where critical reading and source-based projects require evaluation of research. UG-entry pre-sessionals build core evaluative sets for essays. In UG and PGT settings, apply them to critiques and literature reviews. PGR writers revisit evaluation of others' work in literature reviews, peer reviews and responses to reviewers.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with sta.attitude-markers and sta.evaluating-others-language; this topic is the lexical repertoire, which those topics could take as a prerequisite.
Review response: R6-11 — the IELTS criterion link was removed because this topic is taught up to postgraduate or doctoral level and is not primarily test preparation; CEFR links are kept.

records.summary: Corpus grammar shows that phrasal verbs are far more frequent in conversation and fiction than in academic prose, but Biber's study of university registers shows they are pervasive in classroom teaching, so learners need them receptively. Gardner and Davies show that a relatively small number of lexical verbs and particles account for a large share of phrasal-verb use, supporting a prioritised list. In writing, the teaching point is judgement: some multi-word verbs are entirely standard in academic prose.

activities.title: Lecture phrasal verb log
learnerActions: Note phrasal verbs heard in two lectures or recorded talks
Check meanings in a learner dictionary
Mark which you would use in writing and which only in speech
activities.intendedInsight: Phrasal verbs are common in academic speech even when less common in academic writing.
activities.rationale: Biber's corpus of university registers shows classroom teaching shares many lexical features with conversation, including multi-word verbs.

activities.title: Keep, change or check
learnerActions: Highlight multi-word verbs in your draft
Label each 'keep', 'change' or 'check'
Check doubtful items in an academic corpus or learner dictionary register labels
Revise and justify each change
activities.intendedInsight: Some multi-word verbs belong in academic writing; others have more conventional single-word alternatives.
activities.rationale: Corpus evidence on register distribution lets learners make item-by-item decisions instead of applying a blanket rule.

difficulties.pattern: 'All phrasal verbs are informal.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Contorted replacements ('executed the experiment', 'the problem was eliminated from consideration' for 'ruled out') and avoidance of standard verbs such as 'carry out'.
difficulties.response: Show corpus evidence that some multi-word verbs are normal in academic prose. Do not teach a blanket replacement list.

difficulties.pattern: Particle meanings opaque, so phrasal verbs are avoided in listening and speaking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension breakdowns in lectures, especially for learners whose L1 typically expresses such meanings with single verbs rather than verb + particle combinations.
difficulties.response: Teach frequent particles' core meanings (e.g. 'out' as completion or revealing) and high-frequency combinations in context.

difficulties.pattern: Particle placement errors with pronoun objects.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'They pointed out it', 'we will carry out them'.
difficulties.response: Teach the separable pattern with pronouns as a word-grammar rule.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to revise 'We found out that prices went up a lot after the policy was brought in' for a report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'We found that prices rose substantially after the policy was introduced', changing colloquial items while keeping clarity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Changes some items but leaves others or over-formalises.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No changes or meaning distorted.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals, emphasise recognition in lectures and basic register judgement. PG-entry and UG in-sessional learners usually revisit it through their own drafts and disciplinary genres.

records.summary: Nassaji found that the ESL learners' lexical inferences in his study were often unsuccessful and that success was associated with the quality of strategy use — especially evaluating and verifying hypotheses — and with drawing on appropriate knowledge sources, rather than with the sheer frequency of strategy use. Coverage research (Hu and Nation) suggests that inferencing is more reliable when unknown words are sparse. Teach a short explicit procedure (look for clues, hypothesise, check) and practise with texts at suitable coverage.

activities.title: Clue types
learnerActions: Find unfamiliar words in a short academic text
Classify the clue that helps with each (definition, example, contrast, apposition, word parts, topic knowledge)
Infer each meaning and check it in a dictionary
activities.intendedInsight: Different clues give different kinds and strengths of evidence.
activities.rationale: Nation describes the clue types and steps of guessing from context as a teachable strategy.

activities.title: Think-aloud inferencing
learnerActions: In pairs, read a paragraph and take turns thinking aloud about one unknown word
Name the knowledge source used and the hypothesis
Verify the hypothesis against the next sentences or a dictionary and discuss what worked
activities.intendedInsight: Checking a guess is as important as making it.
activities.rationale: Nassaji found that verifying and evaluating inferences was associated with greater success than simply generating guesses.

difficulties.pattern: Wild guesses from a single clue, never checked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident but wrong meanings that persist into notes and summaries.
difficulties.response: Require a stated clue and a check for important words.

difficulties.pattern: Every unknown word looked up, so reading is slow and fragmented.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who read with a translation tool open and stop at every unfamiliar word.
difficulties.response: Teach decisions about which words matter for the reading purpose; practise skipping and inferring on texts at high coverage.

difficulties.pattern: 'I should be able to guess everything from context.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Frustration and failure with texts containing many unknown words.
difficulties.response: Explain the link between coverage and inferencing success and recommend pre-learning key terms for dense texts.

diagnostic.task: Give: 'Unlike earlier, more ephemeral studies, this project followed participants for twenty years.' Ask what 'ephemeral' probably means and how the learner knows.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Infers 'short-lived' from the contrast with 'twenty years' and 'unlike', and suggests checking.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vaguely negative meaning without using the contrast.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot infer or guesses at random.

records.contextNotes: Core at foundation, where reading assessments often test the strategy directly; practise with graded or accessible texts. Pre-sessional courses apply it to longer academic texts, and PG-entry courses to research articles in the learner's field. In UG in-sessional work, revisit it with disciplinary readings, combined with glossary use for technical terms.

records.summary: Nation treats dictionary use as a skill to be taught, including choosing the right sense and using dictionaries for production as well as comprehension. Bilingual dictionaries are valuable for speed and comprehension, but production benefits from monolingual entries with grammar information and examples. Machine translation and AI tools now serve as de facto dictionaries, so learners need strategies to check their output against reliable entries.

activities.title: Right sense
learnerActions: Look up polysemous words from a reading (e.g. 'state', 'case', 'issue')
Choose the sense that fits the context and explain your choice
Write a new sentence using the same sense
activities.intendedInsight: The first sense listed is often not the one needed.
activities.rationale: Nation identifies sense selection as a core, teachable dictionary skill.

activities.title: Bilingual to monolingual cross-check
learnerActions: Find an English equivalent for an L1 word you need for an assignment
Check the equivalent in a monolingual learner dictionary and a collocation dictionary
Write a sentence that follows the grammar and collocations shown, then compare with your first attempt
activities.intendedInsight: A translation equivalent is a starting point, not a guarantee of correct use.
activities.rationale: Webb and Nation describe dictionaries as tools for learning use information, not only meaning.

difficulties.pattern: The first sense listed is taken regardless of context.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpretations of polysemous words in notes and summaries.
difficulties.response: Practise reading all senses and matching them to context.

difficulties.pattern: Bilingual equivalents used in writing with L1 grammar and collocation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct word, wrong pattern ('discuss about', 'make research') traceable to the L1 equivalent's behaviour.
difficulties.response: Teach the cross-check routine and the use of example sentences before production.

difficulties.pattern: Grammar codes and examples ignored.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who use dictionaries only for translation and cannot interpret [U] or 'V that' codes.
difficulties.response: Teach the codes explicitly using the learners' own dictionary.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to use a learner dictionary to decide whether 'advice' can be plural and which preposition follows 'emphasis'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds that 'advice' is uncountable ('a piece of advice') and that 'emphasis' takes 'on', citing the entry.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds one answer or cannot locate the grammar information.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Relies on intuition or translation only.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, teach learner-dictionary features explicitly; PG-entry learners also need specialist glossaries and collocation resources for their field. In UG in-sessional settings, revisit it through discipline-specific resources and the use of machine translation and AI tools as dictionaries.
reviewNotes: No listed source reports recent empirical work on learners' use of online dictionaries, machine translation or AI tools as dictionaries; claims about these are practitioner judgement.

records.summary: Nation and Webb and Nation argue that deliberate learning with word cards or software is an efficient way to establish form–meaning links, provided it involves retrieval and spacing. Two separate findings support this: Roediger and Karpicke found that retrieval practice produced better delayed retention than restudying, and Cepeda et al.'s synthesis found spaced (distributed) practice better than massed practice, with the best gap depending on how long material must be retained. Whether expanding schedules beat equally spaced ones is not settled, so expanding intervals are an acceptable software default rather than a requirement. Deliberate learning should be balanced with meaning-focused input and output so that words learned on cards are also met and used in context.

activities.title: Build your deck
learnerActions: Choose 20 priority words from your reading using frequency and relevance
Make cards with the word on one side and meaning, collocates and an example on the other
Review by recalling before turning over, at spaced intervals over two weeks (for example after one, three and seven days)
activities.intendedInsight: Recalling words at spaced intervals helps me keep them.
activities.rationale: Webb and Nation describe word-card learning with retrieval and spacing as an efficient deliberate learning technique.

activities.title: Retrieval versus rereading
learnerActions: Split ten new words into two sets
Study one set by rereading and the other by self-testing
Test yourself on both sets a week later and compare results
activities.intendedInsight: Self-testing can feel harder than rereading yet often leads to better retention.
activities.rationale: Roediger and Karpicke found that retrieval practice improved delayed retention more than restudying, and Cepeda et al.'s synthesis found spaced practice better than massed practice; a small personal experiment lets learners check the retrieval finding for themselves.

difficulties.pattern: Long lists reread rather than retrieved.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report hours of 'learning' with little retention.
difficulties.response: Demonstrate retrieval practice and track results.

difficulties.pattern: Too many words collected, then the system is abandoned.
difficulties.revealedBy: Decks of hundreds of cards with overdue reviews.
difficulties.response: Set realistic daily limits and prioritise by frequency and relevance.

difficulties.pattern: Only the L1 translation is recorded.
difficulties.revealedBy: Cards without collocates or examples; known words misused in writing.
difficulties.response: Add collocation and example fields for words intended for productive use.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe exactly what they did the last time they studied vocabulary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes selection, retrieval-based practice and a review schedule.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses cards or an app but rereads or reviews irregularly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Rereads lists or has no system.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, set up systems explicitly and check them; PG-entry learners should select words from texts in their field. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, revisit it by maintaining systems alongside heavy reading loads.
reviewNotes: The cited retrieval and spacing studies are not all vocabulary-specific; their application to L2 word learning is supported by vocabulary researchers but effect sizes may differ.

Review response: R2-08 and R4-03 — the text now says 'spaced' rather than 'expanding', separates the retrieval finding (Roediger and Karpicke) from the spacing finding (Cepeda et al.), and states that evidence on schedule shape is mixed. A direct comparison of expanding and equal spacing (Karpicke and Roediger, 2007) was not added, because a citation is not needed once no schedule claim is made.

records.summary: Nation's framework of word knowledge distinguishes receptive and productive knowledge of form, meaning and use, and Schmitt's review shows that productive knowledge typically lags behind receptive knowledge and needs additional, targeted practice. Paquot's analysis of learner academic writing shows that even advanced learners underuse or misuse academic vocabulary in production. Activating vocabulary requires gathering use information and trialling words with feedback, not just more exposure.

activities.title: Activate five
learnerActions: Choose five words you recognise but have never used
Collect two authentic examples of each from your reading
Use each in speech (a seminar or study group) and in a paragraph
Ask for feedback and note corrections
activities.intendedInsight: Productive use needs deliberate trialling and feedback.
activities.rationale: Nation's distinction between receptive and productive knowledge implies that production requires additional, use-focused learning.

activities.title: Use-information profile
learnerActions: For a target word, record its patterns, collocates, register and any restrictions from dictionary and corpus evidence
Write three sentences that test different patterns
Peer-check and revise
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing a word productively means knowing how it behaves.
activities.rationale: Schmitt's review stresses multiple dimensions of word knowledge and the need for explicit attention to them.

difficulties.pattern: A newly met word is used in an essay before its behaviour is known.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambitious vocabulary with pattern or collocation errors.
difficulties.response: Encourage trialling in low-stakes writing first and checking patterns. Do not discourage risk-taking itself.

difficulties.pattern: Reliance on a small set of safe, familiar words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive vocabulary in writing despite good reading comprehension.
difficulties.response: Set small activation goals and reward accurate new use.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to use 'constitute' and 'attribute' in sentences about their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate sentences with correct patterns ('X constitutes Y'; 'attribute X to Y').
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct meaning, pattern errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot use the words, or meaning errors.

records.contextNotes: Foundation courses can start by recycling vocabulary from content modules, and pre-sessional courses can build activation routines, linked on PG-entry courses to vocabulary from the learner's field. In UG in-sessional settings, focus on discipline-relevant vocabulary in the learner's own assignments; PGT learners revisit it as needed.

records.summary: Pattern grammar (Hunston and Francis) shows that words have characteristic patterns and that words sharing a pattern often share aspects of meaning, which offers an efficient way to teach and learn them in groups. Corpus grammar documents verb complementation and preposition choice in detail. Treat pattern errors as gaps in lexical knowledge, recorded word by word, rather than as general grammar errors.

activities.title: Pattern families
learnerActions: Group academic verbs by pattern (V that: argue, suggest, indicate; V to-inf: aim, attempt, fail; V n to n: attribute, relate)
Notice meaning similarities within each group
Write sentences using two verbs from each group
activities.intendedInsight: Patterns and meanings go together, so words can be learned in groups.
activities.rationale: Hunston and Francis show that words sharing a pattern tend to share meaning, making pattern-based grouping efficient.

activities.title: Concordance pattern check
learnerActions: Choose three words you are unsure about (e.g. impact, consistent, emphasis)
Look at 20 concordance lines for each
Record the dominant pattern and correct your draft
activities.intendedInsight: Corpus evidence resolves pattern doubts quickly.
activities.rationale: Hunston describes how concordances reveal lexically specific patterns.

difficulties.pattern: Prepositions carried over from the L1 equivalent ('discuss about', 'emphasise on').
difficulties.revealedBy: Pattern errors where the L1 equivalent verb takes a preposition or particle.
difficulties.response: Record words with patterns and use contrastive noticing of high-risk items.

difficulties.pattern: Pattern borrowed from a related word ('emphasise on' from 'emphasis on'; 'discuss about' from 'talk about').
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors that mirror a related word's pattern.
difficulties.response: Contrast related forms explicitly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to correct 'This essay will discuss about the impact to employment and emphasise on the need for policy.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'discuss the impact on employment and emphasise the need for policy', with explanation of each pattern.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects one or two.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no errors.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, focus on high-frequency patterns. In UG in-sessional work, target persistent errors in the learner's own writing; PGT learners revisit it through editing.

records.summary: Countability in English is partly conceptual and partly lexical convention, so academic nouns whose equivalents are countable in other languages cause persistent errors. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman describe the count/non-count distinction and its interaction with articles and quantifiers, and corpus grammar shows how countability interacts with determiners. Teach the small set of high-frequency academic uncountables explicitly, with their quantifiers and countable alternatives ('studies', 'findings', 'a piece of evidence').

activities.title: Uncountable alternatives
learnerActions: List the uncountable academic nouns you use most (research, evidence, information, knowledge, feedback)
For each, find a countable alternative or a quantifier phrase (studies, findings, a piece of evidence)
Rewrite sentences from your draft using them
activities.intendedInsight: Countable alternatives let me count what an uncountable noun cannot.
activities.rationale: Hinkel recommends explicit work on the high-frequency academic nouns whose countability differs from their equivalents in many other languages.

activities.title: The 'data' decision
learnerActions: Check how your required style guide treats 'data'
Count 'data is' and 'data are' in five articles from your field
Decide on one treatment and apply it consistently in your draft
activities.intendedInsight: Some countability questions are style choices requiring consistency rather than errors.
activities.rationale: Style guides differ on 'data' (APA treats it as plural), so learners need to apply a consistent, field-appropriate choice.

difficulties.pattern: Plural or indefinite forms of uncountable nouns ('researches', 'an evidence', 'informations').
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors concentrated in nouns whose equivalents are countable in the learner's L1.
difficulties.response: Teach countable alternatives and quantifiers; check nouns with dictionary codes.

difficulties.pattern: Greco-Latin plurals used as singular ('a criteria', 'this phenomena').
difficulties.revealedBy: Agreement errors with these nouns.
difficulties.response: Teach singular/plural pairs explicitly and practise agreement.

difficulties.pattern: 'Data is' and 'data are' mixed within one text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistency the learner can fix when it is pointed out.
difficulties.response: Add the item to a proofreading checklist.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to correct 'Many researches has shown that this criteria provide an useful evidence.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'Much research has shown / Many studies have shown that these criteria provide useful evidence', with explanations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects some errors but not agreement or articles.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees few or no errors.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, target the core uncountables and plurals. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, revisit persistent errors and the 'data' convention in the learner's field.
reviewNotes: Use of 'data' as a singular mass noun is widespread and accepted in many contexts; present it as a style choice to be applied consistently.

records.summary: Nation includes written form as one aspect of knowing a word; the spelling of academic words, including derived forms, deserves explicit attention. Consistency often matters more to markers than which variety is chosen: APA style follows American spelling, many institutions in the UK and elsewhere accept either variety if it is used consistently, and some journals, departments and branch campuses specify one. Spell-checkers help but miss real-word errors such as 'principle' for 'principal'.

activities.title: Variety consistency check
learnerActions: Set your word processor's language to the required variety
Search your draft for -ize/-ise, -or/-our and -er/-re forms
Make all instances consistent with your chosen variety or style guide
activities.intendedInsight: Consistency is checkable and mostly mechanical.
activities.rationale: Style guides specify spelling conventions; a targeted search makes consistency manageable.

activities.title: Personal confusables list
learnerActions: Collect spelling and confusable-word errors from your marked work
Group them (suffix changes, confusable pairs, variety mixing)
Search for these items before submitting your next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: My spelling errors are patterned and predictable.
activities.rationale: Treating written form as part of word knowledge supports targeted practice on known weak points.

difficulties.pattern: Varieties mixed because sources and tools use different conventions.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Analyse' and 'analyze', 'behaviour' and 'behavior' in one text.
difficulties.response: Set tools correctly and run a final consistency search.

difficulties.pattern: Real-word errors that spell-checkers do not flag.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Principle investigator', 'it's findings', 'dependant variable' in some fields.
difficulties.response: Add a personal confusables list to proofreading.

difficulties.pattern: Spelling by sound, with errors in vowels, double consonants and silent letters.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors that reflect pronunciation, especially for learners whose L1 has a more transparent sound–spelling relationship or a different writing system.
difficulties.response: Teach morphological spelling patterns (refer/referred, necessary) and frequent irregular forms.

diagnostic.task: Give a sentence with 'analyze', 'behaviour', 'principle investigator' and 'it's results' and ask the learner to correct it for an assignment that requires British spelling.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Makes the spellings consistently British ('analyse', 'behaviour'), corrects 'principal' and 'its', and explains each change, noting that the same check would apply to American spelling if that were required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Fixes variety or confusables, not both.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problems.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals, establish the habit of consistency and checking. PG-entry and UG in-sessional learners usually revisit it by aligning with departmental, journal or style-guide requirements, which vary between institutions and countries. Persistent spelling difficulty that does not respond to teaching may reflect dyslexia or another specific learning difference in any language; refer sensitively to disability or learning-support services and allow assistive tools (spell-checkers, text-to-speech) rather than treating it as carelessness.
reviewNotes: Few listed sources address spelling in EAP specifically; guidance draws on general vocabulary research and style-guide practice.

records.summary: Institutional vocabulary is part of the tacit knowledge that students new to an education system must acquire. Language socialisation research (Duff) treats such learning as part of joining an academic community, and Wingate argues that academic expectations should be made explicit for all students rather than left to be absorbed. Terminology differs between institutions and countries, so teaching should use learners' own institutional documents.

activities.title: Handbook treasure hunt
learnerActions: Use your programme or module handbook to find the meaning of ten key terms
For each, write what you would need to do (e.g. how to apply for an extension)
Compare with a partner and list remaining questions for your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Institutional terms have practical consequences that I can find out about.
activities.rationale: Making institutional expectations explicit through authentic documents supports inclusive access, as Wingate argues.

activities.title: Who do I ask?
learnerActions: Read short scenarios (illness before a deadline, a question about a mark, a timetable clash)
Identify the relevant procedure and role (module leader, personal tutor, student services)
Draft the first sentence of an email using the correct terms
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing roles and procedures helps me act appropriately.
activities.rationale: Socialisation into an academic community includes learning its roles and practices through participation and explicit guidance.

difficulties.pattern: Terms assumed to mean what they meant in a previous system ('tutorial', 'course', 'college', 'assignment').
difficulties.revealedBy: Misunderstanding of what a tutorial involves or of what 'course' refers to.
difficulties.response: Contrast meanings explicitly with the learners' previous systems, treating both as valid in context, and pair the terms with a brief look at the teaching formats they name (acu.teaching-formats) where these are unfamiliar.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to ask about unfamiliar administrative terms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missed procedures (e.g. extenuating circumstances deadlines) discovered too late.
difficulties.response: Normalise asking and show where answers can be found.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what they would do if they were ill the week an assignment was due, using their institution's terms.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the correct procedure (extension or extenuating/mitigating circumstances), whom to contact and the evidence needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows to contact someone but uses vague or incorrect terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know the procedure exists.

records.contextNotes: Core at foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals, which prepare learners for a new education system. PG-entry learners need the subset for taught master's study (dissertation regulations, supervision, credit). In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, revisit it at key points (first assessments, extenuating circumstances deadlines, dissertation regulations). Terms differ between countries and institutions, and on EMI programmes and branch campuses local and home-institution terms may both be in use, so teach from the learner's own institutional documents.
reviewNotes: Listed sources support the socialisation and explicitness framing, but no listed study examines institutional vocabulary directly.

Review response: R1-25 — the soft edge from acu.teaching-formats was removed so that orientation does not gate a language topic; the two are best taught side by side, and the difficulty response still points teachers to the formats topic.

records.summary: Command words index cognitive processes comparable to those in Anderson and Krathwohl's revised taxonomy, and Horowitz's analysis of actual university assignments showed the range of tasks students must interpret. Moore and Morton found university writing tasks more often require evaluation of others' ideas than test-style opinion essays, so learners from test-focused preparation may misread commands. Teach command words as indicators, not guarantees, and always alongside criteria and exemplars, because tutors use them inconsistently.

activities.title: Command word continuum
learnerActions: Order command words (describe, outline, explain, analyse, compare, evaluate, critically assess) by cognitive demand
For each, note what the answer would contain
Compare your order with marking criteria from your course
activities.intendedInsight: Command words signal different kinds of thinking and text.
activities.rationale: The revised taxonomy offers a shared vocabulary for cognitive processes that command words point to.

activities.title: Same topic, different command
learnerActions: Take one topic and three questions with different commands
Plan an answer to each
Compare plans and identify what changes in structure and content
activities.intendedInsight: The command, not just the topic, determines the answer.
activities.rationale: Horowitz's survey of authentic assignments shows that tasks vary in what they ask students to do, not only in topic.

difficulties.pattern: 'Discuss' means 'give my opinion' or 'write everything I know'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion essays or descriptive overviews in response to 'discuss' questions.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars and criteria that reward balanced, evidence-based discussion leading to a judgement, and make the description–analysis–evaluation distinction explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Commands interpreted from a generic definition list without reading the criteria.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that match a glossary definition but miss what this tutor expects.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to read command, criteria and exemplars together and to ask when unclear.

difficulties.pattern: Secondary commands in multi-part questions overlooked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers addressing only the first part of 'Explain X and evaluate its effectiveness'.
difficulties.response: Teach systematic question annotation (underline each command and its object).

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is the difference between “describe” and “evaluate”? Give an example question for each.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that describing reports features while evaluating judges value or effectiveness against criteria, with suitable examples.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Distinguishes them vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats them as equivalent.

records.contextNotes: Core at foundation and on UG-entry pre-sessionals, taught explicitly with institutional exemplars and applied through wpr.task-analysis. PG-entry learners need fewer definitions and more work on command words in coursework briefs and research-oriented tasks. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, revisit it with real module questions and criteria, and discuss variation between tutors.
reviewNotes: Meanings of command words are not standardised across institutions or disciplines; any list of 'definitions' should be presented as typical expectations.

Review response: R1-13 — this topic is kept as the lexical resource (what command words typically demand). The procedure of unpacking a whole brief or exam question, including topic, limits and criteria, now belongs to wpr.task-analysis, which takes this topic as a hard prerequisite; mastery evidence here was narrowed accordingly.

records.summary: Style guides differ on abbreviations: APA, for instance, restricts Latin abbreviations such as 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' to parenthetical material and sets rules for 'et al.', while Chicago has its own conventions. Teach the meaning distinctions (especially e.g. versus i.e.) and then direct learners to their required guide for form and punctuation. The acronym routine — define at first mention, then use consistently — transfers across genres.

activities.title: e.g. or i.e.?
learnerActions: Sort sentences by whether the bracketed material gives examples or restates
Insert 'e.g.' or 'i.e.' accordingly
Check punctuation against your required style guide
activities.intendedInsight: 'e.g.' introduces examples; 'i.e.' restates or specifies.
activities.rationale: Style guides give explicit rules for these abbreviations that learners can apply consistently.

activities.title: Acronym audit
learnerActions: Highlight every acronym in your draft
Check that each is written out in full at first mention
Remove acronyms used only once or twice
activities.intendedInsight: Acronyms help readers only when introduced and used consistently.
activities.rationale: Major style guides require acronyms to be defined at first use.

difficulties.pattern: 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' confused.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'i.e.' followed by one example among many.
difficulties.response: Teach the expansions (for example; that is) and practise.

difficulties.pattern: Acronyms familiar to the writer are left undefined.
difficulties.revealedBy: Undefined field or institutional acronyms in assignments.
difficulties.response: Teach the reader's perspective and the define-at-first-use rule.

difficulties.pattern: Latin abbreviations overused to sound academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'viz.', 'cf.' and 'etc.' scattered through running text.
difficulties.response: Show style-guide restrictions and plain English alternatives.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to complete 'Several factors (___ cost and access) affect uptake' and 'The main factor (___ cost) was…' and explain.
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'e.g.' for the first and 'i.e.' for the second, with a correct explanation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One correct.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Both wrong or cannot explain.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional courses, teach core forms with the referencing style in use. In UG in-sessional settings, revisit it by aligning with departmental style requirements.
reviewNotes: Conventions are style-guide and edition specific; teachers should check the edition in use.

records.summary: Collocation awareness is a precondition for learning phraseology because learners tend to attend to individual words; Schmidt's noticing hypothesis implies that combinations not noticed are unlikely to be learned. Nesselhauf's analysis of advanced learner writing shows frequent collocation errors, especially with restricted combinations, so awareness is worth building early. Concordance lines make co-occurrence patterns visible efficiently, and Nation's treatment of multiword units supports recording vocabulary in chunks.

activities.title: Chunk hunt
learnerActions: Highlight every combination of two or more words in an academic paragraph that seem to 'go together'
With a partner, agree which are fixed, which are strong preferences and which are free combinations
Add five combinations to your vocabulary record, each with an example sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Many meanings are carried by combinations rather than single words.
activities.rationale: Explicit noticing directs attention to multi-word form–meaning pairings that learners might otherwise process word by word.

activities.title: Concordance noticing
learnerActions: Read 20 concordance lines for a node word such as 'research' or 'evidence'
List the verbs and adjectives that occur with it
Note combinations you expected but did not find (e.g. 'make research') and discuss why
activities.intendedInsight: Collocational preference is conventional, probabilistic and observable in data.
activities.rationale: Concordance displays make recurrent co-occurrence salient, as Hunston describes for corpus-informed language teaching.

difficulties.pattern: 'If each word is correct and the grammar is correct, the phrase must be correct.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Combinations such as 'make research', 'strong rain' or 'big importance' defended as logical.
difficulties.response: Show corpus frequency evidence and explain that collocation is conventional rather than logical. Avoid presenting it as an inaccessible 'native-speaker intuition'; evidence is available to every learner.

difficulties.pattern: Vocabulary recorded as single-word translation pairs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Word lists with only L1 equivalents and no collocates or examples.
difficulties.response: Model records that include collocates and example sentences, and set notebook tasks that require them.

diagnostic.task: Ask which verb goes with each noun: ___ a conclusion, ___ research, ___ a question, ___ a role.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives 'draw/reach', 'conduct/carry out/do', 'raise/pose/address' and 'play', and notes that more than one verb can be possible with different meanings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct for some nouns, with transferred choices for others (e.g. 'make research').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses 'make' or 'do' throughout and sees no difference.

records.contextNotes: Groundwork at foundation, where collocation is introduced through high-frequency nouns in course texts and simple recording formats; UG-entry pre-sessionals extend it with collocation dictionaries and short concordance lines. PG-entry pre-sessional and UG in-sessional learners usually revisit it only as the frame for phr.academic-collocations work or when miscollocation persists.

records.summary: Ackermann and Chen's Academic Collocation List offers a corpus-derived, expert-judged inventory of academic collocations that can serve as a syllabus starting point. Durrant and Schmitt's comparison of writing by first-language and additional-language users of English suggests that the latter rely more on frequent, general combinations and use fewer strongly associated but less frequent ones (a comparison with first-language student writing, not with an ideal), so teaching should extend range, not just correct errors. As with single-word lists, disciplinary relevance should be checked against field texts.

activities.title: Collocation grids
learnerActions: Choose eight nouns central to your field
Use an academic collocation list or corpus to find common verbs and adjectives for each
Build a grid showing which combinations occur and tick those you have met in your reading
Write a short paragraph using six of the combinations
activities.intendedInsight: Each academic noun brings a limited set of conventional verbs and adjectives.
activities.rationale: The ACL was designed as a pedagogical inventory of academic collocations; grids turn it into a production resource tied to the learner's field.

activities.title: Upgrade the collocation
learnerActions: Highlight adjective–noun and verb–noun combinations in your draft
For each very general combination ('big problem', 'get results'), find a more precise academic alternative
Check each alternative in a corpus or collocation dictionary before using it
activities.intendedInsight: Collocational range adds precision and makes writing easier for expert readers to process.
activities.rationale: Durrant and Schmitt found that the essays of their non-native group (the study's category) relied more on frequent collocations and used fewer strongly associated ones than their native group; the activity extends range towards expert disciplinary use rather than treating frequent combinations as errors.

difficulties.pattern: Overuse of a few safe combinations ('play an important role', 'have a big impact').
difficulties.revealedBy: The same small set of collocations repeated across texts.
difficulties.response: Extend range by recording alternatives and their meaning differences. Do not ban frequent collocations; they are correct and useful.

difficulties.pattern: List items used without regard to meaning or field.
difficulties.revealedBy: Combinations such as 'conduct a conclusion' or 'empirical opinion'.
difficulties.response: Teach collocations in context with examples and have learners check items in disciplinary texts.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to complete 'The study ___ a significant ___ between the two groups' and give alternatives.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives 'found/revealed/identified … difference' with alternatives and notes any restrictions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct core collocation but few alternatives, or one miscollocation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses inappropriate verbs and nouns ('made a significant change').
