learnerActions: Revise a learner-style paragraph that contains ambiguous it/they and a drifting synonym chain
Justify each change to a partner by stating what the reader would otherwise have assumed
activities.intendedInsight: Changing the word for a referent is a meaning choice, not a stylistic decoration.
activities.rationale: Working on plausible learner text targets the repair skill needed for self-editing and links reference choices to reader inference.

difficulties.pattern: 'I was taught never to repeat a word, so I change it every time.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Synonym cycling (participants, subjects, people, individuals) that leads readers to wonder whether different groups are meant.
difficulties.response: Show textbook or corpus evidence of repetition of key nouns; distinguish variation in non-technical wording from fixed reference to key participants. Avoid replacing one blanket rule with another ('always repeat').

difficulties.pattern: Second mention with 'a' or no article, or omitted subject pronouns, so that chains break down.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'A participant… A participant said…' for the same person; missing 'it' as subject; readers unsure whether a new entity is introduced.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages lack articles or allow null subjects benefit from focused work on first versus subsequent mention, using the learner's own texts as data.

difficulties.pattern: 'It' or 'they' placed after several intervening nouns in long sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers cannot resolve the pronoun without rereading; peer readers propose different antecedents.
difficulties.response: Teach a simple check: if two candidate antecedents exist, repeat the noun or use a precise general noun.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes three linked sentences about a process or study in their field and underlines every expression referring to the main participant.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The chain mixes repetition, pronoun and a general noun; every reference is resolvable; articles shift appropriately from first to second mention.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The chain is resolvable but relies on a single device (only pronouns or only repetition), or contains one article slip.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The referent shifts or is ambiguous; synonyms imply different entities.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on pronoun and article reference and simple repetition in textbook paragraphs. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work extends to general nouns and the risks of synonym substitution in source-based writing. For taught postgraduates the emphasis moves to longer chains across sections and to disciplinary expectations about repeating technical terms.
reviewNotes: The claim that expert prose repeats key nouns more than learners expect is a teaching generalisation consistent with corpus descriptions; it is not quantified here for particular disciplines.

records.summary: Biber et al. describe the semantic categories of linking adverbials and show that a relatively small set accounts for most uses in academic prose, and Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman treat connectors by both semantic relation and grammatical type, the combination learners need to choose precisely. Learner-corpus studies measure difference from a reference corpus rather than error: Granger and Tyson compared French-speaking learners' essays with essays by English-L1 students (the study's 'native' category) and found overuse of some connectors and underuse of others rather than overall overuse, Altenberg and Tapper's chapter in Granger's collection reports overall underuse by Swedish learners, and Hinkel documents reliance on sentence-level transitions across several L1 groups. Because these comparisons use student reference corpora, expert disciplinary writing is the better model for teaching. Teach connectors by relation, with evidence of expert frequency and position and with minimal pairs that make the change in claim visible, aiming for fewer, better-chosen links rather than long lists of supposed equivalents.

activities.title: Frequency reality check
learnerActions: Count linking adverbials per 100 words in a paragraph of your own and in a published paragraph from your field
Note their positions (initial, medial) and the relations they signal
Delete connectors from your paragraph wherever the relation is already clear, and reread
activities.intendedInsight: Expert prose uses fewer connectors, places some medially and relies on content to carry many relations.
activities.rationale: Comparison with expert texts in the learner's own field targets the sentence-initial stacking reported in some learner-corpus studies, while taking expert writing rather than other students' essays as the model.

activities.title: Relation first, connector second
learnerActions: For each of ten sentence pairs, decide the relation (addition, contrast, concession, result, exemplification) before choosing any connector
Choose a connector or decide that none is needed
Discuss pairs where the group chose no connector
activities.intendedInsight: A connector should follow from a judged relation, and sometimes the best choice is none.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Hasan's grouping of conjunctive relations into additive, adversative, causal and temporal gives learners a manageable framework for the prior judgement.

activities.title: Minimal pairs
learnerActions: Read two versions of a sentence pair that differ only in the connector (however versus on the contrary; whereas versus although; therefore versus thus)
Paraphrase the claim each version makes
Decide which version the writer most plausibly intended, given the surrounding text, and justify the choice by naming the relation
activities.intendedInsight: Connectors change propositions, not just style.
activities.rationale: Contrasting forms in controlled pairs is intended to focus attention on meaning differences that are easily blurred in lists of 'linking words'; Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman's treatment by relation and grammatical type supplies the contrasts.

difficulties.pattern: 'Every sentence should start with a linking word to show cohesion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Chains such as Firstly… Secondly… Moreover… Furthermore… In addition… with a connector before most sentences.
difficulties.response: Show expert density and ask learners to justify each connector by naming the relation. Do not ban connectors or impose an arbitrary quota.

difficulties.pattern: Treating connectors from a list as interchangeable: 'X is expensive. On the contrary, Y is cheap', or 'On the other hand' used to add a point.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'On the contrary' for simple contrast between two items; 'On the other hand' with no preceding contrast; 'Besides' as a neutral additive in formal writing.
difficulties.response: Teach connectors grouped by relation and register with authentic examples: 'on the contrary' rejects a preceding (often negated) proposition, whereas 'in contrast' compares two items. Return to mismatches in the learner's own text rather than issuing longer lists.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'however' like 'but' to join two clauses with a comma.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comma splices of the form '…, however, …' between independent clauses.
difficulties.response: Contrast 'but' (coordinator), 'although' (subordinator) and 'however' (adverbial) with the same content, and show the punctuation each requires.

difficulties.pattern: 'Therefore' introducing a conclusion that the preceding sentences do not support.
difficulties.revealedBy: A list of facts followed by 'Therefore,…' with no step connecting them to the claim.
difficulties.response: Ask 'why does this follow?' and have the learner write the missing step; treat each connector as a promise that the content must keep.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites a 100-word paragraph in which five of six sentences begin with a connector, keeping only the links a reader needs, and then explains the difference between 'Sales fell. However, profits rose.' and 'Sales did not fall. On the contrary, they rose.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Keeps two or three connectors that mark genuine contrast or result, removes additive stacking, moves at least one connector medially and punctuates correctly; explains that the second pair corrects a negated claim rather than contrasting two facts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Removes some connectors but keeps mismatched ones or sentence-initial positioning throughout, or senses that the two pairs differ without naming the relation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Replaces connectors with other connectors at the same density, and treats however and on the contrary as interchangeable.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the core semantic categories, punctuation and the distinction between coordinators, subordinators and adverbials. Undergraduate pre-sessional courses should explicitly address test-preparation habits of connector stacking; postgraduate pre-sessional courses can add precision among concessive and inferential connectors in argument and source-based writing. In-sessional support is most productive on students' own assignments, where connector overuse often masks problems of argument structure, and can tie precision to disciplinary reasoning, such as inference in quantitative fields or concession in humanities argument.
reviewNotes: Hinkel (2002) reports frequencies for specific L1 groups and essay prompts; teachers quoting figures should state those groups and prompts.

Review response (R1-15): coh.connector-precision has been merged into this topic. Its relation distinctions (contrast, concession, correction; inference and consequence), minimal-pair activity and 'unsupported therefore' difficulty are now part of this record. The range stays B1–C1 with B1+ as the core band (R1-09); precision among near-equivalent connectors is the C1 end of the range. The absorbed topic's 'although… but' double-marking difficulty is handled in sta.concession-language, which depends on this topic.

records.summary: Systemic functional accounts distinguish theme–rheme (the clause's point of departure) from given–new (what the reader is assumed to know), which typically but not always coincide. For EAP, Swales and Feak's advice on old-to-new information flow offers a practical entry point, and Thompson explains the systems accessibly. The passive is best taught here as a tool for arranging information rather than as a marker of objectivity, and work should use sentence pairs so that 'given' is always relative to preceding text.

activities.title: Which version follows?
learnerActions: Read sentence 1 of a short passage, then choose between an active and a passive version of sentence 2
Explain your choice by pointing to what sentence 1 has already introduced
Repeat with a different sentence 1 that reverses the best choice
activities.intendedInsight: Voice and subject choice depend on context; neither active nor passive is better in itself.
activities.rationale: Directly counters the myth that the passive is inherently more objective or academic, and shows information flow as the reason for the choice.

activities.title: Old-to-new audit
learnerActions: Underline the first noun phrase of each sentence in your own paragraph
Check whether it links back to something already mentioned
Rewrite any sentence that opens with brand-new information
activities.intendedInsight: Many 'choppy' paragraphs open sentences with new information.
activities.rationale: Applying the principle to one's own text is intended to build a self-editing routine rather than abstract knowledge.

difficulties.pattern: 'The passive is more academic, so I use it whenever I can.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Passive sentences that place new information first and push given information to the end.
difficulties.response: Show pairs where the active is the better choice because of what precedes it. Do not replace this with 'avoid the passive'.

difficulties.pattern: Fronting a topic and then repeating it with a pronoun: 'This problem, researchers have studied it for decades.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dislocated topics with resumptive pronouns; unusual word order at the start of clauses.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages mark topic through word order or particles benefit from seeing the English resources for the same purpose: passive, a different subject, existential there or a summarising noun phrase.

difficulties.pattern: Very long subjects carrying new information before the main verb.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers wait a long time for the verb; heavy noun phrases at the start of clauses.
difficulties.response: Show how moving the heavy, new element to the end (end-weight) improves processing; link to sentence-level editing.

diagnostic.task: The learner improves the flow of: 'Rising sea levels threaten coastal cities. Large-scale relocation programmes may be required by this threat.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Rewrites so that 'This threat' opens sentence two (This threat may require…) and explains that it links back to the previous sentence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves the sentence but cannot explain why the new version reads better.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the order unchanged or makes only lexical changes.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce the principle through sentence pairs and short paragraphs. In undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support it becomes a revision tool for students' own drafts. Doctoral writers benefit from applying it to dense methods and discussion prose, where long subjects are common.

records.summary: Daneš's typology of thematic progression gives a compact model learners can apply to their own drafts, and Thompson's functional grammar explains theme without heavy terminology. Halliday and Martin show how scientific writing nominalises the rheme of one clause so that it can serve as the theme of the next, building chains of reasoning — a pattern worth making explicit to writers in all fields. Present the patterns as diagnostic tools rather than templates: expert paragraphs mix them.

activities.title: Theme arrows on your own draft
learnerActions: Mark the theme of each sentence in a paragraph you have written
Draw an arrow from each theme to the earlier theme or rheme it picks up
Revise any sentence whose theme has no arrow
activities.intendedInsight: Disjointed paragraphs often contain themes that do not connect to anything earlier.
activities.rationale: Daneš's patterns become a practical revision check when applied to learners' own writing rather than only to model texts.

activities.title: Nominalise to move on
learnerActions: For each sentence pair, turn the process described in sentence 1 into a noun phrase that can open sentence 2 (Temperatures rose → This rise…)
Compare the result with a version that uses bare 'This' or 'It'
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalisation lets a writer carry a whole process forward as the starting point of the next step.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Martin identify this rheme-to-theme nominalisation as central to how scientific argument is built.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study… The study… It… The study…' — the same theme throughout a paragraph that should develop an argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: List-like paragraphs in which each sentence adds a fact about the same participant without building a line of reasoning.
difficulties.response: Show how linear progression lets each sentence build on the last. Do not tell learners to vary the subject with synonyms, which damages reference.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing theme with topic, or treating a fronted adverbial as the whole theme.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent analysis of themes in exercises; uncertainty about what counts as the theme.
difficulties.response: Use an operational teaching definition (everything up to and including the subject) and acknowledge it as a simplification of the grammatical account.

difficulties.pattern: Nominalising every process to create linear progression, producing dense, opaque sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of abstract nouns with weak verbs (the implementation of the improvement of…).
difficulties.response: Treat nominalisation as a resource with costs for clarity; use it at the point of linkage, not throughout.

diagnostic.task: The learner analyses the themes in a five-sentence published paragraph, names the dominant pattern and identifies one sentence that would be harder to follow if its theme were changed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels themes accurately, recognises a mix of linear and derived progression and explains the link that a changed theme would break.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Labels most themes but cannot relate them to the progression patterns or explain their effect.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify themes consistently or sees no connection between successive sentence openings.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses keep terminology light and focus on arrows and linking. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support can use the patterns to diagnose paragraphs in assignments and dissertations. Doctoral writers often respond well to the full model when revising dense theoretical or methods prose.

records.summary: Flowerdew's work on signalling nouns shows how nouns such as problem, process and aspect take specific meaning from co-text, both anaphorically and cataphorically. Swales and Feak's 'this + summary word' advice gives a teachable rule of thumb, while corpus work on this and these in published prose suggests that bare 'this' also occurs, so the issue is reader clarity rather than an absolute ban. Teach labels as choices that categorise and evaluate as well as link.

activities.title: Label the shell
learnerActions: Find every this/these/such + noun in a research article extract
Bracket the stretch of text each one encapsulates
Decide whether the noun also evaluates (claim, assertion, problem) and how
activities.intendedInsight: Signalling nouns both summarise and classify what came before, often with an evaluative angle.
activities.rationale: Flowerdew's analysis shows that the meaning of these nouns is realised in co-text, so learners need to see the stretch being encapsulated.

activities.title: Upgrade the bare 'this'
learnerActions: Search your draft for sentence-initial This and It
Decide for each whether a reader could misidentify the referent
Add a precise noun where needed and compare two alternative labels for their effect
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a noun clarifies reference and lets the writer characterise the previous content.
activities.rationale: A search-and-revise routine converts a known rule of thumb into a self-editing habit.

difficulties.pattern: 'This shows that…' where 'this' could refer to several preceding ideas.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers ask 'this what?'; peers bracket different antecedents.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to name what 'this' refers to; if it takes more than a word or two to say, add a signalling noun.

difficulties.pattern: A narrow repertoire: 'this issue', 'this problem', 'this thing' for every kind of content.
difficulties.revealedBy: The same two or three labels used for findings, arguments, methods and proposals alike.
difficulties.response: Build a sorted bank of signalling nouns from reading in the learner's field (finding, trend, assumption, limitation, distinction).

difficulties.pattern: Inadvertent evaluation, such as calling a well-supported result 'this claim' or 'this assumption'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Labels that undercut the writer's own or a source's position without the writer intending it.
difficulties.response: Compare the effect of finding, claim, assertion and assumption on the same content and discuss the stance each implies.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads two sentences reporting a study's result and continues with a sentence beginning 'This ___ suggests…'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Supplies an accurate label (result, finding, pattern) and can explain why 'claim' or 'assumption' would change the stance.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Supplies a plausible but vague label (issue, situation).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves 'This' bare or chooses a label that misrepresents the content.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce 'this + noun' as a high-yield revision habit. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support should extend to cataphoric uses and evaluative labelling in literature reviews. Doctoral writers benefit from attention to how labelling positions others' work.

records.summary: Hoey's accounts of culturally popular text patterns, building on Winter's clause relations, show that readers recognise patterns through lexical signals and that patterns can be recursive, as when a negatively evaluated response creates a new problem. Carrell found that explicit training in top-level rhetorical structure improved ESL readers' recall, supporting the teaching of patterns for reading as well as writing. Swales and Feak's units on general–specific and problem–process–solution texts provide graduate-level writing models.

activities.title: Signal hunt
learnerActions: Highlight the problem, response and evaluation vocabulary in a problem–solution passage
Map the passage onto situation–problem–response–evaluation boxes
Find any point where a negative evaluation triggers a further problem and response
activities.intendedInsight: Patterns are signalled lexically and can repeat within one text.
activities.rationale: Hoey shows that readers rely on lexical signals to recognise pattern elements; making signals explicit is intended to build this recognition.

activities.title: Predict the next paragraph
learnerActions: Read a text paragraph by paragraph with the remainder covered
Before uncovering each paragraph, predict its function from the pattern so far
Compare predictions with the original and discuss the signals that helped
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing the pattern lets readers anticipate content and read more efficiently.
activities.rationale: Carrell's study of ESL readers found that training in text structure improved recall, which suggests pattern awareness supports comprehension.

difficulties.pattern: Treating patterns as fixed templates and forcing every task into problem–solution.
difficulties.revealedBy: A compare-and-contrast task answered as a problem–solution essay; artificial 'problems' invented to fit the frame.
difficulties.response: Present patterns as reader expectations that the task and content select, and practise matching tasks to patterns.

difficulties.pattern: Responses listed without any evaluation, so the pattern stops short.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that describe several solutions but never assess whether they work.
difficulties.response: Show that evaluation is an expected element; ask 'did it work, and how do we know?' after each response.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a reported view in a claim–counterclaim structure as the writer's own position.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that attribute to the writer a view the writer goes on to reject.
difficulties.response: Teach the signals of the hypothetical element (it is often claimed, many assume) and the real element (in fact, however, the evidence suggests).

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a 200-word passage and labels its pattern elements, then writes one sentence that would continue the pattern.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels elements correctly with reference to signals, and the continuation fits the next expected element (for example an evaluation of the response).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the overall pattern but mislabels one element or writes a continuation that repeats an earlier element.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the content without recognising any organising pattern.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, use simple problem–solution and general–specific texts from subject textbooks for both reading and writing. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses can add claim–counterclaim structures, which are important for following argument. Taught postgraduates benefit from using patterns to read research articles and policy documents efficiently.
reviewNotes: Carrell (1985) used Meyer's top-level structures rather than Hoey's patterns; the two frameworks overlap but are not identical, so the evidence supports pattern awareness in general rather than Hoey's taxonomy specifically.

records.summary: In Hyland's interpersonal model, frame markers are one category of interactive metadiscourse; Hyland and Tse's study of postgraduate dissertations shows metadiscourse use varying by discipline and by degree level. Bunton's analysis of PhD thesis introductions identifies outlining the structure of the thesis as a regular element. Teach density relative to genre and length: roadmaps that suit a thesis can read as mechanical in a short essay, and propositional signposting (what a section shows) is more useful than procedural announcement (what it talks about).

activities.title: Roadmap scaling
learnerActions: Compare roadmap sentences from a short essay, a dissertation chapter and a research article
Note how much each previews and how it is worded
Write a roadmap for your current assignment at the appropriate scale
activities.intendedInsight: The amount and form of signposting should match the length and genre of the text.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse's evidence of variation across disciplines and levels supports teaching metadiscourse as genre-sensitive rather than as a fixed formula.

activities.title: Metatext audit
learnerActions: Highlight all metatext in your draft
Delete any that does not help a reader navigate
Rewrite procedural metatext as propositional signposting
activities.intendedInsight: Useful frame markers tell readers what a part of the text establishes, not only what it is about.
activities.rationale: Treating frame markers as reader-oriented metadiscourse focuses revision on their function for the reader.

difficulties.pattern: 'This essay will discuss X, Y and Z' followed by 'In this paragraph I will…' at the start of every paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic roadmaps and paragraph-level announcements in short essays.
difficulties.response: Show propositional roadmaps that preview the argument; reserve paragraph-level metatext for long texts. Do not ban 'This essay will', which is acceptable in many contexts.

difficulties.pattern: A roadmap that no longer matches the body after revision.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sections appear in a different order from the one promised, or a promised section is missing.
difficulties.response: Encourage writing or revising the roadmap last and checking it against a reverse outline.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly as the only structure for a complex argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Enumerated points of unequal weight with no indication of how they relate.
difficulties.response: Show how stage labels and topic shifts can signal relations (more importantly, a further complication) as well as order.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites the sentence 'This essay will talk about the causes, effects and solutions of urban flooding.' as a roadmap for a 2,500-word argumentative essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a roadmap that previews the argument and its stages (for example, argues that drainage policy matters more than climate factors, first by…), at an appropriate length.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves register but still lists topics without signalling the argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Retains a topic list or adds paragraph-by-paragraph announcements.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need simple, accurate roadmaps for short essays and reports. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work should address scaling for dissertations. Doctoral writers need chapter-level metatext across a thesis, which links to thesis macrostructure.

records.summary: Transitions are where coherence at text level becomes visible to the reader. Wingate's work on students' understanding of argument identifies the coherent presentation of a position across a text as a component many students do not recognise, and Hoey's view of text as interaction suggests that a paragraph opening should answer the reader's question 'how does this relate to what I just read?'. Teach transitions through reverse outlining of paragraph relations and through encapsulation with signalling nouns, rather than through inventories of 'transition words'.

activities.title: Relation map
learnerActions: Write a one-line summary of each paragraph in your draft
Label the relation between each pair of consecutive paragraphs (extends, contrasts, qualifies, applies, results from)
Rewrite each paragraph opening so that it expresses that relation
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraph relations should be stated where the reader needs them — at the opening of the new paragraph.
activities.rationale: Making the argument's structure explicit addresses the component of argument Wingate found students often overlook.

activities.title: Bridge building
learnerActions: Read pairs of paragraph endings and beginnings joined only by 'Furthermore'
Replace each with a bridging sentence that encapsulates the previous point and introduces the new one
Compare versions and discuss which shows the argument more clearly
activities.intendedInsight: A summarising noun phrase plus the new point does more work than a bare connector.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak's advice on linking ideas with summary words gives a concrete technique for bridging.

difficulties.pattern: 'Another reason is… Another reason is… Another reason is…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs added in sequence with no indication of how they relate or build.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to rank the points and decide which depends on which, then write openings that reflect that structure.

difficulties.pattern: Paragraph-initial 'Furthermore' or 'Moreover' used as the transition regardless of relation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Additive connectors opening paragraphs that actually contrast with or qualify the previous one.
difficulties.response: Show encapsulating openings and ask learners to state the relation in words before choosing any connector.

difficulties.pattern: Transitions written before paragraphs were reordered, so bridges no longer fit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Openings that refer back to points that now come later or have been cut.
difficulties.response: Add a final check of every paragraph opening after any structural revision.

diagnostic.task: The learner is given two consecutive paragraph summaries (Paragraph A: cost explains part of a decline; Paragraph B: changing consumer attitudes) and writes the opening of Paragraph B.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a bridging sentence that encapsulates A and positions B in relation to it (While cost explains part of the decline, it cannot account for…).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Introduces B clearly but links to A only with a connector (In addition, attitudes…).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Begins B with no reference to A.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should introduce relational transitions in extended essays. Undergraduate in-sessional work can use students' assignments for reverse outlining. Taught postgraduate support extends to transitions between dissertation sections and chapters.

records.summary: Halliday and Martin show that technical terms in science form taxonomies, so a change of term can imply a different place in the taxonomy; Hyland and Tse show that apparently general academic words take discipline-specific meanings. Both point to the same teaching message: in academic writing, lexical variation carries meaning. Address the prior-schooling expectation that repetition is poor style, and give learners a concrete self-editing routine.

activities.title: Term inventory
learnerActions: List the five most important concepts in your draft
Use find-all to locate every expression you used for each
Standardise wherever variants refer to the same concept, and add an explicit note where a distinct term is intended
activities.intendedInsight: Many apparent synonyms in one's own text turn out to be unintended variation.
activities.rationale: Repetition is itself a cohesive device; a mechanical search turns this principle into a reliable editing habit.

activities.title: Same or different?
learnerActions: In discipline groups, judge pairs of terms from your field (for example sex and gender; effect and impact; learner autonomy and self-directed learning)
Check how glossaries or key sources in the field distinguish them
Report one pair that the field treats as distinct and one it treats as interchangeable
activities.intendedInsight: Whether two terms are interchangeable is a disciplinary question, not a dictionary one.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse's evidence on discipline-specific meaning and Halliday and Martin's account of technical taxonomies both support discipline-based judgement.

difficulties.pattern: 'Repeating the same word is boring, so I use synonyms.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Key concepts referred to by three or four different terms; readers or markers asking whether a new concept has been introduced.
difficulties.response: Show published texts that repeat key terms; distinguish variation in everyday wording from fixed technical reference.

difficulties.pattern: One concept rendered by different English terms in different sections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent English equivalents for one source-language term, especially when drafting through the first language or machine translation.
difficulties.response: Encourage a personal bilingual term list for each project and a final find-all consistency check.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding pronouns and general nouns altogether to stay 'consistent'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mechanical repetition of long noun phrases where a pronoun or 'this approach' would be clear.
difficulties.response: Clarify that consistency applies to the naming of concepts, not to banning reference devices.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a 200-word paragraph that uses 'motivation', 'drive', 'willingness' and 'engagement' for the same construct, and comments on it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the variation, explains that a reader in the field might take these as distinct constructs, and standardises with a justification.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices variation but considers it acceptable style, or standardises without explaining why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no issue, or praises the variety of vocabulary.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, introduce the principle with extended source-based writing. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support should link it to disciplinary terminology and dissertation editing. Doctoral writers need consistency across chapters, publications and figures, often for a large set of defined constructs.

records.summary: Making reasoning explicit is a reader-oriented decision: writers judge which connections their intended reader needs stated and which can be left to inference. Hyland's account of interactive metadiscourse describes the resources writers use to guide readers through a text, and Lea and Street show that tutors' comments such as 'unclear' or 'argument' often rest on tacit expectations that students are not told, so teaching should make those expectations explicit rather than present them as common sense. Biber and Gray's evidence that academic prose leaves many relations implicit within compressed noun phrases is a useful counterweight: explicitness is selective even in English. Cross-cultural typologies of reader and writer responsibility are discussed critically in idn.intercultural-rhetoric and are not needed to teach this skill.

activities.title: Where would a reader stop?
learnerActions: Read a partner's paragraph aloud and pause wherever you have to infer a connection
The writer notes each pause and decides whether to state the connection
Discuss which inferences an expert reader in the field could reasonably be expected to make
activities.intendedInsight: How much to make explicit depends on the reader, but many markers expect the links that carry the argument to be stated.
activities.rationale: Turns the reader's need for explicit links into a concrete judgement about a specific text and reader, using the interactive resources Hyland describes.

activities.title: Same content, different readers
learnerActions: Take a paragraph you have written for your tutor
Rewrite it for a non-specialist reader, adding the links and definitions that reader needs
Then cut any statement an expert examiner would take for granted, and compare the three versions
activities.intendedInsight: Explicitness is about the links that matter to a particular reader, not about stating everything.
activities.rationale: Biber and Gray show that expert academic prose leaves many relations implicit, so learners need to judge explicitness by reader rather than maximise it.

activities.title: Comparing explicitness across disciplines and genres
learnerActions: Bring two short academic texts from different disciplines or genres, or one from another language you know
Identify where each makes its main point and key links explicit (title, opening, headings, topic sentences, conclusion)
Discuss the variation you find within each language and discipline as well as between them
activities.intendedInsight: Explicitness conventions vary by genre and discipline as well as by language, and no tradition is uniform.
activities.rationale: Draws on learners' plurilingual resources while reflecting the intercultural-rhetoric view that conventions vary within as well as across languages and contexts.

difficulties.pattern: 'I build up to my main point so that the conclusion has more impact.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Main claims withheld until the conclusion or left implicit; feedback such as 'what is your argument?'.
difficulties.response: This is a rationale many novice writers hold in any language, and some school and examination genres reward it. Show the expectation of the target genre and ask the learner to compare the effect of an early and a delayed statement on the intended reader, without implying that the earlier practice was wrong.

difficulties.pattern: 'Changing how I write means my previous writing was bad.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Resistance to feedback on explicitness; discomfort when discussing other writing traditions.
difficulties.response: Frame the topic as expanding a repertoire for different readers rather than replacing a deficient habit.

difficulties.pattern: Over-explicitness after instruction: stating the obvious and narrating every step.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy metatext and explanations of points an expert reader would take for granted.
difficulties.response: Return to the intended reader: explicitness is about the links that matter to the argument, not about everything.

difficulties.pattern: Feedback such as 'unclear', 'flow' or 'make it explicit' with no indication of which link is missing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who revise vocabulary or grammar in response to comments about clarity, or who ask what the comment means.
difficulties.response: Teachers and markers can point to the specific passage and name the missing link or reader question; programmes can share annotated exemplars that make the expectation visible. Learners can be taught to ask 'which connection was missing here?' in tutorials.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains in their own words why a tutor in their target programme might write 'make your argument explicit' on an essay whose main point appears only in the conclusion, and says what they would change.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains the expectation that the writer states the position and key links early and clearly for this reader, proposes a specific change, and notes that this is a convention of the context and genre rather than a universal rule.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains the expectation but presents it as the only logical way to write, or cannot say what to change.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot connect the comment to explicitness, or interprets it as a grammar issue.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and undergraduate pre-sessional level the skill supports introductions, topic sentences and the interpretation of feedback. Postgraduate pre-sessional courses extend it to linking evidence to claims in longer source-based projects and to writing for readers outside the writer's specialism. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support revisits it in tutorials when students are puzzled by comments on clarity. Expectations of explicitness can differ across disciplines and in EMI and transnational programmes, so take the intended reader in the learner's target context, not a national norm, as the reference point.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-21): the topic is named and framed around the skill of making reasoning explicit for a given reader. The discussion of Hinds's reader/writer responsibility typology and its critiques (Connor; Kubota and Lehner) has been removed from this record and belongs in idn.intercultural-rhetoric, which already cites Hinds; the ID is kept as fixed by the skeleton. The R5-11 difficulty is re-voiced as a rationale held by novice writers in any language and recoded as conceptual.

records.summary: Hyland's interpersonal model of metadiscourse, refined in Hyland and Tse, is the most widely used pedagogical framework, although its boundaries (for example whether transitions are propositional or metadiscursive) are debated, so present it as a heuristic. Teach the concept after learners have met concrete resources such as signposting and hedging, so that it organises what they already know. Cross-disciplinary comparison then shows that metadiscourse norms belong to communities rather than to 'good writing' in general.

activities.title: Two-colour metadiscourse highlight
learnerActions: Highlight interactive metadiscourse in one colour and interactional metadiscourse in another in a published discussion section
Read a version of the same text with all metadiscourse removed
Discuss what the reader loses in the stripped version
activities.intendedInsight: Metadiscourse does not add propositional content but shapes how readers process and evaluate it.
activities.rationale: Hyland's model is designed to show writing as interaction; comparing texts with and without metadiscourse makes that interaction tangible.

activities.title: Discipline comparison
learnerActions: Count the metadiscourse categories in two short extracts from contrasting disciplines
Hypothesise why the patterns differ
Check your hypotheses against a third extract from your own field
activities.intendedInsight: Metadiscourse use reflects disciplinary values about argument, evidence and the reader.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse document disciplinary variation in metadiscourse in postgraduate writing, supporting discipline-aware teaching.

difficulties.pattern: Treating metadiscourse as a fixed list of words that always have the same function.
difficulties.revealedBy: Classifying 'clearly' as a booster in 'the results are clearly presented', or 'however' as metadiscourse wherever it appears.
difficulties.response: Insist on functional analysis in context; discuss borderline cases openly as part of the model's acknowledged fuzziness.

difficulties.pattern: After learning the concept, adding metadiscourse everywhere to appear reader-friendly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense signposting and reader address in short texts; feedback that the writing 'talks about itself'.
difficulties.response: Return to genre and length: compare metadiscourse density in exemplars of the target genre.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains, with examples from a provided text, what metadiscourse is and why a writer would use it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines metadiscourse as language that organises the text or expresses the writer's stance towards content and reader, gives correctly classified examples of both kinds and links them to reader needs.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives correct examples of one kind (usually signposting) but does not recognise stance devices as metadiscourse.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates metadiscourse with linking words or cannot give examples.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, introduce the concept as a way of drawing together signposting and hedging. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work can use it for disciplinary text analysis. Doctoral writers benefit from the full model when analysing target journals.
reviewNotes: Alternative, narrower reflexive models of metadiscourse exist; none is in the current bibliography, so the guidance presents Hyland's model as one influential heuristic rather than the only account.

records.summary: Hyland's study of hedging in science research articles distinguishes hedges that concern the accuracy of claims from those that concern the writer's relationship with readers, and Salager-Meyer's taxonomy (shields, approximators, expressions of doubt, compound hedges) gives a practical classification that includes the approximators of quantity, frequency and degree used to bound generalisations. Hyland and Milton compared examination scripts by Cantonese-speaking Hong Kong school leavers with those of British school leavers and found a narrower range of devices and stronger certainty in the first group; as a difference from one comparison corpus, this suggests prioritising range and placement, with expert writing in the learner's field as the model. Hinkel provides form-focused exercises on hedges, quantifiers and tendency expressions. Teach hedges and limiters together with the evidence they respond to, not as politeness formulae, and treat precise scope as often a better remedy for overgeneralisation than an added modal.

activities.title: Hedge the claim to the evidence
learnerActions: Read short study summaries that specify design and sample
Write one claim for each, hedged to match the evidence
Compare with a partner and justify any difference in hedge choice
activities.intendedInsight: Hedges express the writer's judgement of evidence, not general politeness.
activities.rationale: Hyland's account links hedging in research writing to the epistemic status of claims; tying each hedge to evidence reflects that function.

activities.title: Sweeping to bounded
learnerActions: Rewrite sweeping statements from typical essay openings as bounded claims
Label what you changed: quantity, frequency, degree, context or certainty
Check which rewrites need a source to support them
activities.intendedInsight: Bounding a claim usually means specifying who, how many, how often or where, not just adding 'may'.
activities.rationale: Hinkel's techniques for teaching hedging and qualification in L2 writing support explicit, form-focused practice; the labelling step is intended to show that scope and certainty are separate choices.

activities.title: Section map of hedging
learnerActions: Mark all hedges in a research article from your field
Count them by section (introduction, methods, results, discussion)
Explain the distribution you find
activities.intendedInsight: Hedging clusters where writers interpret and generalise, and is sparse where they describe procedures.
activities.rationale: Salager-Meyer reported that hedging in medical articles varied across rhetorical sections, which learners can test in their own field.

difficulties.pattern: 'Hedging makes me sound unsure; strong statements show confidence.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged interpretations and sweeping openings ('Since the dawn of time, humans have always…'), often modelled on test-preparation essay formats that reward forceful, unqualified positions; resistance to feedback asking for qualification.
difficulties.response: Show expert texts in the learner's field in which hedging accompanies authoritative claims, and frame hedging and bounded scope as precision. Explain that markers in the target context often read unsupported sweep as weak use of evidence, while acknowledging that the earlier format had its own purpose.

difficulties.pattern: 'It may possibly be suggested that this could perhaps indicate…', or qualifying established facts ('In most cases, water tends to boil at 100°C at sea level').
difficulties.revealedBy: Several hedges stacked on single claims after instruction; definitions and well-established facts qualified; feedback that the argument is unclear.
difficulties.response: Teach one hedge per source of uncertainty and ask the learner to state what exactly is uncertain; qualify empirical generalisations, not definitions or established facts. Do not react by discouraging hedging altogether.

difficulties.pattern: 'This can be the reason for the decline.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Can' used for epistemic possibility where 'could' or 'may' is expected.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages use one modal for both ability and possibility need to see that 'can' expresses general possibility (This can be problematic) but not, in positive statements, an inference about a specific case, where 'may', 'might' or 'could' is used (This could be the reason).

difficulties.pattern: 'Most of people tend to using…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors with quantifier + of, tend + to-infinitive and agreement after 'the majority of'.
difficulties.response: Give focused form practice on the grammar of quantifiers and tendency expressions using the learner's own sentences. Do not let these form errors displace feedback on whether the scope of the claim fits the evidence.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Social media causes depression in teenagers' as a claim based on one cross-sectional survey of 200 students.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a claim that is hedged for causation and scoped to the sample (for example 'use of social media was associated with higher depression scores among the students surveyed'), and explains both changes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds a modal ('may cause') but leaves the causal claim and the scope unchanged.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the claim unchanged or adds an intensifier.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a core set of devices beyond modals and the habit of bounding generalisations in essay openings and topic sentences. Undergraduate pre-sessional courses link hedging and scope to evidence and sources in argument essays; postgraduate pre-sessional courses add the hedging of interpretations of data and studies, leading into claim calibration. Undergraduate in-sessional support connects hedging to disciplinary conventions in students' own assignments, while taught postgraduate and doctoral writers mainly revisit it within claim calibration, reader-oriented hedging and the need to claim contribution.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-15, R1-09): sta.generalisation-qualification has been merged into this topic, which now covers quantifiers, frequency and tendency expressions and scope limiters alongside hedging devices; its 'sweeping to bounded' activity and quantifier-grammar difficulty are included here. The range stays B1+–C2 with B2 as the core band: bounding generalisations is taught from B1+, and reader-oriented hedging in research writing continues to C2.

Hyland and Milton (1997) compared school leavers' examination scripts, not university writing; use it to motivate attention to range and placement, not as a description of any group's academic writing.

records.summary: Toulmin's qualifier makes explicit that claim strength is part of argument structure, and Hyland shows how hedges in research articles respond to the epistemic status of claims. Swales and Feak's graduate-level material on qualification and strength of claim offers practical exercises. Teach calibration from the evidence outward: first decide what the design and data license, then choose wording; avoid fixed 'hedging quotas'.

activities.title: Evidence-to-claim ladder
learnerActions: Place candidate claims about a finding on a ladder from weakest to strongest
Decide which rung the evidence supports and write the claim
State what further evidence would justify the next rung
activities.intendedInsight: Each level of claim strength corresponds to a level of evidence.
activities.rationale: Toulmin's model treats the qualifier as tied to the grounds of an argument; the ladder operationalises that link.

activities.title: Calibration-only peer review
learnerActions: Review a peer's draft for claim strength only
Mark each miscalibrated claim as over-claimed or over-hedged and note the evidence issue
Discuss disagreements about the marks
activities.intendedInsight: Calibration judgements can be argued and refined with reference to evidence.
activities.rationale: Focused peer review isolates one feature so that attention is not diluted; Hyland's account of hedging as negotiated with readers supports discussing such judgements.

difficulties.pattern: 'The data show a correlation, so X causes Y.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Causal language for correlational findings; general claims from one sample.
difficulties.response: Return to what different designs can and cannot establish before working on wording.

difficulties.pattern: Hedging every claim to the same degree regardless of evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniform 'may' or 'it seems that' across strong and weak findings.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to rank their claims by strength of evidence and to make the language reflect the ranking.

difficulties.pattern: Under-claiming one's own findings for fear of appearing arrogant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Doctoral or master's writing that presents clear results as barely suggestive; supervisors asking 'what is your contribution?'.
difficulties.response: Discuss expectations of contribution in the field; practise firm but bounded statements of what the study shows.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a summary of a randomised trial and of a single interview study on related topics and writes one claim based on each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Calibrates differently: firmer causal language for the trial (still scoped), exploratory and context-bound language for the interview study, with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Hedges both claims but to the same degree.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Makes unqualified or general claims from both.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses introduce calibration with short summaries and data. Undergraduate in-sessional work links it to discussion of sources. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers apply it to their own findings and to claiming contribution, where both over- and under-claiming are risks.

records.summary: Hyland treats boosters as the counterpart of hedges in projecting commitment and solidarity. Lorenz's chapter in Granger's learner-corpus collection on adjective intensification in advanced learners' essays, and Hyland and Milton's comparison of Hong Kong and British school leavers' examination scripts, report more overstatement and speech-like intensification in the learner corpora than in the comparison corpora, while Aull and Lancaster report differences in stance markers between first-year and more advanced writers. Because these are differences from particular reference corpora, expert writing in the learner's field is the better model. Teach boosters with hedges as a single certainty continuum, and treat intensifiers as a register issue.

activities.title: Certainty cline
learnerActions: Arrange verbs and adverbs (suggest, indicate, show, demonstrate, prove; possibly, probably, clearly, undoubtedly) on a cline of certainty
Check a few disputed items in concordance lines from an academic corpus
Decide which items are appropriate for empirical findings in your field
activities.intendedInsight: Certainty is graded, and some strong items (prove) are rarely appropriate for empirical claims.
activities.rationale: Hyland's stance model positions boosters and hedges on one dimension of commitment; a cline makes that dimension visible.

activities.title: Justify your certainty
learnerActions: Annotate every booster in your draft with the evidence that justifies it
Remove or replace any booster for which you cannot state evidence
Keep boosters where evidence is strong and explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Boosters are earned by evidence and should be used deliberately.
activities.rationale: Developmental differences in stance marking reported by Aull and Lancaster suggest that conscious attention to certainty markers is worthwhile for novice academic writers.

difficulties.pattern: 'The experiment proves that the treatment works.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Prove' and 'demonstrate' used for single empirical studies or correlational findings.
difficulties.response: Contrast the near-synonymous verbs by strength and connect them to the evidence each implies.

difficulties.pattern: 'This is a very, very important issue that is extremely relevant.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent general intensifiers (very, really, extremely, totally) in written assignments.
difficulties.response: Replace intensifiers with precise statements of degree or significance and with evidence; treat this as register development.

difficulties.pattern: After hedging instruction, removing every booster so that the main claim lacks commitment.
difficulties.revealedBy: Central arguments and well-established facts heavily hedged.
difficulties.response: Show that expert writers commit firmly to well-supported and central claims; practise deciding where to boost.

diagnostic.task: The learner sorts six sentences into 'certainty justified' and 'certainty not justified' given brief evidence descriptions, then revises one.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sorts accurately, retains boosters for robust or well-established findings and downgrades others with precise alternatives.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies overstatement but downgrades every booster, including justified ones.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats all boosters as acceptable or cannot link certainty to evidence.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on intensifiers and on the difference between show and prove. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses link boosters to evidence. Taught postgraduate writers work on committing firmly to their own findings where warranted.
reviewNotes: The adjective-intensification findings come from Lorenz's chapter in the Granger (1998) collection; name the chapter author when the collection is cited in teacher materials.

records.summary: Hyland treats attitude markers as one stance resource, and Martin and White's attitude system (affect, judgement, appreciation) offers a finer lens for analysing what is being evaluated. Hunston and Thompson's collection frames evaluation as both expressing opinion and organising discourse, for example by marking what matters most. Teach that evaluation is expected in academic writing but must be anchored in evidence and expressed with disciplinary lexis; the aim is purposeful evaluation, not removal of the writer's view.

activities.title: Appraisal sort
learnerActions: Collect evaluative expressions from a book review and a discussion section
Sort them into affect (feelings), judgement (people's behaviour) and appreciation (things, ideas, texts)
Discuss which category dominates and why
activities.intendedInsight: Academic evaluation mostly appraises ideas, evidence and texts rather than expressing personal feeling.
activities.rationale: Martin and White's attitude categories give learners a principled way to see what kind of evaluation academic genres favour.

activities.title: Signalling significance
learnerActions: Revise a results or discussion paragraph you have written so that one attitude marker identifies the most important finding
Ask a partner to identify the key finding without being told
Adjust the marker if the partner chose a different finding
activities.intendedInsight: A well-placed attitude marker guides readers to what the writer considers significant.
activities.rationale: Hyland's stance model emphasises evaluation as a means of guiding readers' interpretation.

difficulties.pattern: 'I must never show my opinion in academic writing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Purely descriptive results and literature summaries; feedback asking for more evaluation or significance.
difficulties.response: Show attitude markers in expert texts from the learner's field and distinguish evidence-based evaluation from unsupported opinion.

difficulties.pattern: 'The results were shocking and amazing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Emotive or conversational affect in written assignments.
difficulties.response: Replace affect with appreciation tied to evidence (an unexpected finding, a notably large effect).

difficulties.pattern: 'Interesting' and 'important' used for every evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated general evaluative adjectives that do not tell the reader why something matters.
difficulties.response: Ask 'interesting or important in what way?' and build a bank of more precise evaluative lexis from reading.

diagnostic.task: The learner evaluates a finding described in two sentences, in one sentence suitable for a discussion section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses precise evaluative lexis anchored in the data (a notably larger effect than previously reported) and makes the significance explicit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Evaluates with general adjectives (important, interesting) without saying why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the finding without evaluation, or uses emotive language.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can link attitude markers to moving beyond description. In undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work, the focus is evaluating sources and results in the discipline. Doctoral writers attend to how evaluation positions their work relative to others.

records.summary: Tang and John's typology of first-person roles shows that 'I' ranges from the low-risk guide or architect to the high-risk opinion-holder and originator. Hyland found self-mention more frequent in humanities and social science research articles than in science and engineering, and found that undergraduate writers in his study tended to avoid authoritative uses of 'I'. Hyland and Jiang's diachronic study suggests that some informal features, including first-person pronouns, have increased in certain fields. Teach with discipline-specific evidence and explicitly challenge 'never use I' as an absolute rule.

activities.title: Role spotting
learnerActions: Find every first-person pronoun in extracts from two disciplines
Classify each by Tang and John's roles
Compare which roles each discipline uses and which are absent
activities.intendedInsight: Disciplines differ not only in how often writers use 'I' but in which authorial roles they allow it to perform.
activities.rationale: Combining Tang and John's typology with Hyland's evidence of disciplinary variation makes the choice evidence-based.

activities.title: Who is responsible?
learnerActions: Rewrite three impersonal sentences from your draft using self-mention and three first-person sentences impersonally
Discuss how responsibility for each claim changes
Decide which version suits your discipline and genre
activities.intendedInsight: Self-mention makes the writer accountable for a claim; impersonal forms shift attention to processes or data.
activities.rationale: Hyland's work on authorial identity shows that student writers often avoid authoritative self-representation; explicit comparison makes the trade-off visible.

difficulties.pattern: 'I was told never to use I in academic writing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Convoluted agentless passives and 'the author' or 'the researcher' for the writer, even in reflective genres where 'I' is expected.
difficulties.response: Present field evidence and genre expectations; distinguish module guidance (which should be followed) from a universal rule.

difficulties.pattern: After learning that 'I' is acceptable, overusing 'I think' and 'I will talk about'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion-holder 'I think' on most claims; procedural 'I' announcing each paragraph.
difficulties.response: Show that expert self-mention is concentrated in particular roles and moves, such as stating contribution or methodological choice.

difficulties.pattern: 'The researcher believes that…', or 'we' for a single author, used to avoid 'I'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Third-person self-reference or exclusive 'we' in single-authored assignments, sometimes switching between forms within one text.
difficulties.response: Discuss the options and their effect on the reader, and check discipline and module guidance: exclusive 'we' for one author is conventional in some fields, such as mathematics, but reads oddly in others. Ask the learner to choose one form deliberately and use it consistently.

diagnostic.task: The learner states whether 'In this study we argue that…' would be acceptable in a dissertation in their field, and explains why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a field-specific answer based on observed practice, distinguishes 'we' for single authors, and notes genre and supervisor expectations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a general answer (yes/no) without reference to field or genre.
diagnostic.gapResponse: States an absolute rule ('never use I or we').

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses address myths and introduce the role typology. Undergraduate in-sessional support connects self-mention to module guidance and reflective genres. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers need discipline-specific evidence, especially for stating contribution and methodological decisions in theses and articles.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-01): a student-status ('I have no right to argue') difficulty was replaced with a self-mention-specific pattern so that the deference figure does not recur across topics.

records.summary: Hyland's stance-and-engagement model identifies reader pronouns, directives, questions, appeals to shared knowledge and personal asides as ways writers acknowledge and position readers, with distributions varying across disciplines. His study of addressee features in research articles develops this account, and Chang and Swales discuss informal elements such as direct questions and imperatives as both risks and opportunities for advanced L2 writers. Teach engagement as calibrated to readership through comparative genre analysis rather than through rules. Note that Hyland's 'engagement' (reader-oriented features) differs from 'engagement' in Martin and White's appraisal framework (dialogic positioning; see sta.dialogic-positioning).

activities.title: Textbook versus article
learnerActions: Find all engagement markers in a textbook introduction and a research article introduction on related topics
Classify them and compare their density
Explain the differences in terms of the intended reader
activities.intendedInsight: Engagement density and type depend on who the reader is and what the writer assumes they know.
activities.rationale: Hyland's model links engagement to writers' projections of readers, which genre comparison makes visible.

activities.title: Question or claim?
learnerActions: Find the questions in your own draft
For each, decide whether it frames a genuine problem or replaces a claim you should state
Rewrite those that replace claims
activities.intendedInsight: Questions can frame inquiry but cannot substitute for the writer's position.
activities.rationale: Chang and Swales present informal elements such as questions as features advanced writers can use deliberately rather than avoid or overuse.

difficulties.pattern: 'Have you ever wondered why…?' as an essay opening.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rhetorical questions addressed to a general reader at the start of essays and paragraphs.
difficulties.response: Show research article and essay openings in the field; reserve questions for framing a genuine problem or research focus.

difficulties.pattern: 'As we all know, obviously…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Appeals to shared knowledge for contested or specialised claims.
difficulties.response: Ask whether the intended reader genuinely shares the knowledge; if not, provide evidence instead.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing author 'we' and reader-inclusive 'we' in the same paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguity about whether 'we found' and 'we can see' refer to the same people.
difficulties.response: Make the distinction explicit and check each instance in the learner's draft.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Everybody knows that exercise is good. So why don't people do it?' as the opening of a public health essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Replaces the appeal to shared knowledge with evidence and turns the question into a framed problem (Despite well-documented benefits, participation remains low, raising the question of…).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Removes informality but loses the problem framing, or keeps an unsupported appeal.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the opening unchanged or only changes vocabulary.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduate in-sessional support targets questions and shared-knowledge appeals in essays. Taught postgraduate writers work on directives and reader reference in reports and dissertations. Doctoral writers attend to how engagement varies in their target journals and in public-facing writing.

records.summary: Martin and White's engagement system models how texts acknowledge or suppress alternative voices. Chang and Schleppegrell made these resources explicit for L2 social-science writers and argue that explicit metalanguage helps advanced learners take effective stances; Lancaster found that higher-graded upper-level student papers more often combined acknowledging and countering alternative views. Introduce a reduced metalanguage ('opening up' and 'closing down' the discussion) before the full system, and analyse disciplinary exemplars rather than invented sentences. Note that 'engagement' in appraisal theory differs from Hyland's 'engagement' (reader pronouns, directives, questions; see sta.engagement-markers), and this topic's name avoids the term to prevent confusion.

activities.title: Open or close?
learnerActions: Label each clause of an exemplar paragraph as opening up or closing down the discussion
Trace the sequence across the paragraph
Explain how the sequence leads the reader to the writer's conclusion
activities.intendedInsight: Persuasive academic paragraphs often open the dialogue before narrowing it towards the writer's position.
activities.rationale: Chang and Schleppegrell's work shows the value of making engagement resources explicit for L2 writers using authentic disciplinary texts.

activities.title: Rewriting bare assertion
learnerActions: Take a paragraph of your own that consists mostly of unqualified statements
Add moves that acknowledge an alternative view or attribute a position
Close the paragraph with a contracting move that states your position
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledging alternatives and then countering them can make a position more persuasive than bare assertion.
activities.rationale: Lancaster's comparison of higher- and lower-graded papers suggests readers in the disciplines value this pattern.

difficulties.pattern: 'Stating my opinion directly is enough to show I have a position.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of bare assertions that ignore known debates; feedback such as 'engage with the literature'.
difficulties.response: Show how expert writers position claims relative to others and practise attributing and countering specific views.

difficulties.pattern: Opening the dialogue but never closing it: balanced texts that do not conclude.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussions that list views with equal weight and end without a position.
difficulties.response: Show that contracting moves (countering, pronouncing) are needed to state a position; practise the final move of a paragraph.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains the difference in stance between 'Some researchers claim that X' and 'Research has shown that X', and writes a sentence that acknowledges X but limits it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the first distances the writer and the second endorses, and writes an acknowledging-then-limiting sentence with appropriate resources.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a difference in certainty but cannot relate it to the writer's position.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees the sentences as equivalent.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduate in-sessional work can introduce the reduced metalanguage in upper-level assignments. Taught postgraduate support applies it to literature reviews and discussion sections. Doctoral writers benefit from the full system when positioning their work in articles and theses.
reviewNotes: Lancaster (2014) studied a limited set of disciplines and assignments; the association between concede-and-counter patterns and grades should not be generalised to all fields without caution.

records.summary: The distinction between averred and attributed propositions, introduced by Sinclair and developed by Hunston in Hunston and Thompson's collection, underpins both critical reading and transparent source use: readers assume unattributed statements are the writer's own. Thompson and Ye show how the choice of reporting verb signals whether the writer accepts an attributed proposition, and Hyland documents how disciplines differ in attribution practices. Teach the concept explicitly before reporting-verb lists, using colour-coding of authentic and student texts.

activities.title: Whose voice?
learnerActions: Colour-code each clause of a literature-review paragraph as averred or attributed
Underline the words that signal each attribution
Mark any clause where you cannot tell, and discuss how the writer could make it clear
activities.intendedInsight: Attribution must be signalled; anything unsignalled is read as the writer's own claim.
activities.rationale: Making the averral–attribution distinction visible addresses a source of both weak argument and unintentional misattribution.

activities.title: Endorse, neutral or distance?
learnerActions: Read the same proposition framed with shows, argues, claims, according to and as X notes
Rate how far the writer appears to accept the proposition in each version
Choose the framing that matches your own stance towards a source you are using
activities.intendedInsight: Attribution frames carry the writer's stance towards the attributed claim.
activities.rationale: Thompson and Ye's analysis of evaluation in reporting verbs shows how such choices encode writer stance.

difficulties.pattern: 'One citation at the end of the paragraph covers everything in it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs mixing source content and the writer's comment with a single citation at the end; markers unable to tell which ideas are the student's.
difficulties.response: Show how readers interpret unsignalled sentences, and practise re-signalling attribution (The authors further note…) and marking the writer's comment (This suggests…).

difficulties.pattern: 'Motivation is the most important factor in language learning', where this is one source's claim written as established fact.
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims from a single study stated without attribution, especially where the learner's earlier study relied on textbooks that present knowledge as settled and unattributed; textbook-style prose in literature reviews.
difficulties.response: Distinguish established knowledge from claims made by particular studies; ask 'who says so, and on what basis?', and compare how a textbook and a research article attribute the same idea.

difficulties.pattern: Losing track of which source a claim belongs to in multi-source sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reporting clauses whose complement mixes the views of two sources, or a that-clause that runs on into the writer's comment.
difficulties.response: Practise one source per reporting clause and a clear end to each attributed that-clause before adding comment.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads: 'Smith (2019) found that bilingual children outperformed monolinguals on attention tasks. This advantage disappears in adulthood.' and says who is responsible for the second sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the second sentence reads as the writer's own claim and that, if it comes from Smith or another source, attribution is needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Assumes it is Smith's claim but cannot explain why a reader might think otherwise.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not see any ambiguity.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should introduce the distinction early in source-based writing. Undergraduate in-sessional work links it to integrity and to marker feedback on unclear sources. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers apply it to literature reviews and to positioning their own studies.

records.summary: Hyland's analysis of book reviews shows that academic criticism is typically mitigated, for example through praise–criticism pairs, hedging and specific rather than global targets. Thompson and Ye's analysis of evaluation in reporting verbs, and Petrić's finding that higher-rated master's theses used citations more for functions beyond simple attribution, point to evaluation as a marker of quality. Feak and Swales's literature-review materials provide graduate-level models. Teach critique through genre exemplars and practise varying the strength of evaluation for different readers.

activities.title: Anatomy of praise and criticism
learnerActions: Identify praise and criticism in extracts from published book reviews
Note how criticism is softened (pairing, hedging, specific target)
Write a praise–criticism pair about a text you have read this week
activities.intendedInsight: Academic criticism is usually specific and mitigated, and often paired with acknowledgement of strengths.
activities.rationale: Hyland's analysis of book reviews documents these interactional strategies in expert practice.

activities.title: Strength dial
learnerActions: Write the same critique of a study at three strengths
Decide which version suits a literature review, a critique assignment and a peer review report
Justify your choices to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate strength of critique depends on genre, audience and the writer's purpose.
activities.rationale: Thompson and Ye's account of evaluative reporting and Feak and Swales's literature-review guidance support teaching evaluation as graded choice.

difficulties.pattern: 'This study is perhaps maybe slightly limited in some ways.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Criticism so heavily mitigated and so vague that the reader cannot tell what the problem is or whether it matters, often after instruction on politeness and hedging.
difficulties.response: Teach mitigation as one device per criticism, attached to a specific target and its consequence (The small sample limits how far these findings generalise).
