Contrast it with the unmitigated version in the next difficulty, so that directness is seen as a scale rather than a choice between rude and polite.

difficulties.pattern: 'This study is wrong and useless.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Global, unmitigated evaluations without reasons or specific targets.
difficulties.response: Ask what exactly is weak and why, and rebuild the critique with a specific target, a reason and appropriate mitigation.

difficulties.pattern: Listing what studies did as if this were evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of 'X studied… Y found… Z examined…' with no judgement of relevance or quality.
difficulties.response: Return to evaluation criteria and practise adding a judgement to each report.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a 100-word summary of a study with a small, convenience sample and writes one evaluative sentence for a literature review.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a specific, mitigated critique that acknowledges a contribution and names the sampling limitation and its consequence for generalisation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the limitation but in global or unmitigated terms, or acknowledges the study without critiquing it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the study without evaluation.

records.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessional courses introduce critique of single articles. Undergraduate in-sessional work focuses on evaluating sources in assignments. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers need graded evaluation for literature reviews, gap statements and peer review.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-01): the earlier 'Who am I to criticise…?' difficulty has been replaced with a topic-specific pattern. Hesitancy to critique published work is kept in the anchor topics crt.concept, ess.criticality and res.literature-review, where it is framed as common among novice writers of all backgrounds.

records.summary: Ivanič's account of writer identity (autobiographical self, discoursal self, self as author) frames voice as constructed in and through discourse. Hyland's research on authorial identity found that student writers often avoid authoritative roles, and Wingate identifies the writer's position and its relation to others' views as core components of argument that many students do not grasp. Teaching should make the linguistic resources of voice visible while respecting that adopting a new academic voice involves negotiating identity.

activities.title: Whose paragraph is it?
learnerActions: Compare two paragraphs that use the same sources: one led by the sources, one led by the writer's claim
Identify the features that make the writer visible in the second
Revise a source-led paragraph of your own to be claim-led
activities.intendedInsight: Voice is created by structure and stance choices, not only by using 'I'.
activities.rationale: Wingate's analysis of what students miss about argument points to the writer's position as the organising principle of source-based paragraphs.

activities.title: Voice reflection
learnerActions: Compare your voice in an earlier text (in any language) with your current academic draft
Note what feels comfortable and what feels borrowed
Set one specific change to try in your next draft
activities.intendedInsight: Academic voice develops through deliberate choices that can draw on, rather than erase, existing identities.
activities.rationale: Ivanič's account of the discoursal self supports reflective work on identity alongside linguistic analysis.

difficulties.pattern: 'Having a voice means writing I think.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion statements added to otherwise source-led paragraphs; voice equated with personal opinion.
difficulties.response: Show the range of resources that construct voice (evaluation, framing of sources, structure) and analyse texts with strong voice and little self-mention.

difficulties.pattern: 'When I write academically, it doesn't feel like me.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to adopt academic stance features; heavy reliance on source wording.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge identity negotiation as normal, discuss voice as a repertoire that can be extended, and avoid deficit framings of the learner's other writing.

difficulties.pattern: Paragraphs structured as a sequence of source summaries.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Smith says… Jones says… Brown says…' with the writer's view, if present, only at the end.
difficulties.response: Teach claim-led paragraph openings and the explicit marking of the writer's comment on each source.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains what a tutor means by the comment 'Where is your voice?' on a source-heavy paragraph, and proposes a revision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the writer's own position and evaluation are not visible, and proposes a claim-led opening, evaluative framing of sources and a concluding comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Suggests adding 'I think' or a personal opinion without restructuring.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Interprets the comment as being about speaking or grammar.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses introduce voice through source-based paragraphs. Undergraduate in-sessional support responds to feedback about voice and criticality. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers work on voice in literature reviews and discussions, and on identity as emerging researchers.

records.summary: Biber et al. describe concessive subordinators and concessive and contrastive linking adverbials and their distribution across registers. In Martin and White's engagement system, concession forms part of a counter move that acknowledges and then supplants an expectation. Lancaster's analysis of upper-level student writing associates acknowledging-and-countering patterns with higher-graded work. Teach the grammar together with its argumentative function, and assess whether concessions are followed through.

activities.title: Objection–response chains
learnerActions: One partner writes the strongest objection to the other's thesis
The other writes a concessive response that acknowledges and then limits the objection
Swap roles and compare the strength of the responses
activities.intendedInsight: A good concession states the objection fairly and then shows precisely how far it limits the claim.
activities.rationale: Lancaster's findings on valued stance patterns suggest that concede-and-counter moves are worth explicit practice.

activities.title: Concession or contrast?
learnerActions: Sort sentences into contrast (comparing two items) and concession (acknowledging a point and then limiting it)
Rewrite two contrast sentences as concessions and note the change in argument
activities.intendedInsight: Concession is an argumentative move, not just a contrastive link.
activities.rationale: Combining the grammatical description in Biber et al. with the counter category in Martin and White links form to function.

difficulties.pattern: 'Although the policy is costly, but it is effective.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Double marking of concession across both clauses.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages pair concessive markers across clauses need to see that English marks one clause only; practise both English options with the same content.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I mention the other side, my argument will look weak.'
difficulties.revealedBy: One-sided essays with no acknowledgement of counter-arguments; feedback asking for consideration of alternative views.
difficulties.response: This is a common rationale among novice writers of any background. Show high-rated exemplars that concede and counter, and discuss how acknowledging objections can strengthen credibility with an academic reader.

difficulties.pattern: Concession with no counter, leaving the writer's position unclear.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'It could be argued that X.' followed by a new topic; markers unsure what the writer thinks.
difficulties.response: Teach concession as a two-part move and check that every concession is followed by a response.

diagnostic.task: The learner responds in two sentences to the objection 'Online learning reduces social interaction' in an essay arguing for expanded online provision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Concedes the point accurately and limits it (While online learning can reduce informal interaction, well-designed collaborative tasks can…), with correct grammar.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Concedes but the counter merely contradicts, or there is a grammatical slip such as although…but.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores or dismisses the objection without engaging with it.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses introduce concession in argumentative and discussion essays. Undergraduate in-sessional support applies it to disciplinary argument. Taught postgraduate writers use it to handle competing positions in literature reviews and to discuss limitations.

records.summary: Hyland's model treats code glosses as interactive metadiscourse through which writers anticipate readers' needs, and his study of exemplifying and reformulating shows that these markers vary by discipline. Teach code glosses as reader-oriented decisions — what does this reader need clarified? — together with the precise differences between i.e., e.g., namely and such as.

activities.title: Reader swap
learnerActions: Take a paragraph written for experts in your field
Add glosses for a non-specialist reader, then remove those an expert would not need
Compare the two versions with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Glossing decisions depend on the intended reader.
activities.rationale: Hyland's account of code glosses as anticipating readers' knowledge supports practising adjustment for different readerships.

activities.title: i.e. or e.g.?
learnerActions: Correct sentences that confuse i.e. and e.g. or namely and such as
Check usage in authentic examples
Write one sentence of each type about your own topic
activities.intendedInsight: Reformulation specifies or restates; exemplification gives non-exhaustive instances.
activities.rationale: Hyland distinguishes reformulation from exemplification as functions of code glosses, which this contrast targets.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study used three methods, i.e. interviews' where the list is incomplete.
difficulties.revealedBy: i.e. and e.g. used interchangeably; namely used before partial lists.
difficulties.response: Contrast the abbreviations by meaning (that is versus for example) with minimal pairs.

difficulties.pattern: 'In other words' followed by a different claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reformulations that strengthen, narrow or change the original statement.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to check that the reformulation could replace the original without changing its meaning.

difficulties.pattern: Glossing basic field terms for an expert reader.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dissertations that define terms every reader in the field would know, while leaving novel terms unexplained.
difficulties.response: Return to the intended reader and decide which terms need glossing for that reader.

diagnostic.task: The learner adds one reformulation and one example to: 'The intervention targeted metacognitive strategies.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Adds an accurate reformulation (that is, strategies for planning and monitoring learning) and an example with correct marker and punctuation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds suitable content but confuses i.e. and e.g. or punctuates incorrectly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the sentence or adds unrelated information.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on accurate exemplification and the basic abbreviations. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses add reformulation and reader-oriented decisions. Taught postgraduate writers adapt glossing to expert and mixed readerships, for example in interdisciplinary dissertations.

records.summary: Biber's analysis of university registers shows that stance is expressed more densely, and through different devices, in spoken registers such as classroom teaching than in academic writing. Basturkmen's work on seminar discussion shows that ideas are negotiated over several turns, so stance is often co-constructed rather than delivered as a single opinion. Teach spoken stance through recorded authentic or semi-authentic interaction, attending to prosody and turn sequences, not phrase lists alone.

activities.title: Stance in the transcript
learnerActions: Read and listen to a seminar extract
Highlight every expression of opinion, agreement, disagreement or doubt
Note how participants soften disagreement and build on each other's positions over several turns
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken stance is negotiated across turns and is often softened through hedging and vague language.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen's analysis of seminar discussion shows that meanings are negotiated collaboratively rather than stated once.

activities.title: Disagree three ways
learnerActions: Respond to a contestable statement with mild, moderate and strong disagreement
Record your responses and listen for intonation as well as words
Decide which response suits a peer seminar, a supervision and a conference question session
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken stance combines word choice and prosody, and its appropriate strength depends on the setting.
activities.rationale: Biber's evidence that spoken university registers rely heavily on stance expressions supports explicit practice of spoken stance resources.

difficulties.pattern: 'I think…' as the only way of signalling a view, or agreeing aloud despite reservations.
difficulties.revealedBy: A narrow range of opinion frames; silence or agreement in discussion followed by reservations expressed later in writing or private conversation.
difficulties.response: Build a repertoire of mitigated agreement and disagreement frames and rehearse them in low-stakes discussion. Do not treat reticence as a lack of ideas, and where the assessment allows, accept prepared points or written and online contributions as alternative modes of participation.

difficulties.pattern: Using written hedges in speech: 'It may be suggested that this is not correct.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Spoken contributions that sound read aloud or overly formal.
difficulties.response: Contrast spoken and written stance resources with transcripts and model natural spoken alternatives.

difficulties.pattern: Missing a lecturer's sceptical or ironic stance.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes that record a view the lecturer was signalling doubt about; confusion when the lecturer later rejects it.
difficulties.response: Recognising irony and scepticism from the voice is demanding for most L2 listeners and depends on cultural familiarity; focused listening to prosodic stance cues may help, particularly for listeners whose other languages carry such meanings mainly through particles or word choice.

diagnostic.task: In a short role-play, the learner disagrees with a peer's interpretation of a reading and states an alternative.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses a mitigated but clear disagreement frame, gives a reason and states an alternative position, with appropriate prosody.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Disagrees clearly but bluntly, or mitigates so heavily that the position is unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not express disagreement or relies on a single frame.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses build a basic repertoire for seminars and presentations. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work focuses on assessed discussion and group work. Doctoral learners need stance resources for supervisions, conference questions and the viva.

records.summary: Trimble identifies definition as a core rhetorical function of scientific and technical discourse, distinguishing formal and less formal definitions and ways of expanding them. Swales and Feak show how graduate writers use definitions to display knowledge and position themselves, including by engaging with contested definitions, and Halliday and Martin show that technical definitions build taxonomies in science. Teach the formal definition frame early, then move quickly to definitions in authentic disciplinary use.

activities.title: Class and difference
learnerActions: Write formal definitions of three terms from your field (term, class, distinguishing features)
Test each by asking whether another term from the same class would also fit the definition
Add or sharpen distinguishing features until only your term fits
activities.intendedInsight: A definition works only if its distinguishing features exclude other members of the class.
activities.rationale: Trimble's account of formal definition gives a clear structure; the substitution test makes its logic operational.

activities.title: Whose definition?
learnerActions: Collect two or three definitions of a contested term from sources in your field
Note what each includes and excludes
Write a short paragraph presenting the definitions and stating which one you adopt and why
activities.intendedInsight: In many fields definition is an argument, and choosing a definition is part of the writer's position.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak's treatment of definitions in graduate writing emphasises their role in positioning the writer.

difficulties.pattern: 'Globalisation is the process of globalising the world.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Circular definitions or definitions with no class word; relative clauses that do not attach to a class.
difficulties.response: Practise the term–class–features frame with the defining relative clause, using the learner's own terms.

difficulties.pattern: 'The Oxford Dictionary defines culture as…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays opening with general-dictionary definitions where a disciplinary definition is expected.
difficulties.response: Show how sources in the field define the term and discuss why a general dictionary rarely captures disciplinary meaning.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a contested term as having one correct definition.
difficulties.revealedBy: A single definition presented without attribution for terms such as 'identity' or 'sustainability'.
difficulties.response: Present competing definitions and require an explicit adoption statement.

diagnostic.task: The learner defines 'renewable energy' (or a key term in their field) in one sentence and then states whether the term is contested.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a formal definition with class and distinguishing features and recognises where definitions in the field differ.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a usable definition without a clear class word, or does not recognise contestation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a circular or example-only definition.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on formal definitions of subject terms in textbooks and short-answer questions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses add extended and source-based definitions. Taught postgraduate students need operational and contested definitions in dissertations.

records.summary: Trimble treats classification as a core function of scientific and technical discourse, and Mohan's knowledge framework places classification among the knowledge structures that link language and content. In Rose and Martin's genre map, classifying reports are a recognised factual genre. Teach classification through visual organisers (tree diagrams) and then prose, and push beyond formulae to the criterion and its limits, which is where academic value lies.

activities.title: Tree to text and back
learnerActions: Describe a classification tree diagram in a paragraph
Give your paragraph to a partner who redraws the tree without seeing the original
Compare the trees and revise the paragraph where they differ
activities.intendedInsight: Clear classification prose lets a reader reconstruct the scheme exactly.
activities.rationale: Mohan's knowledge framework links knowledge structures to graphic organisers and to language, supporting movement between diagram and text.

activities.title: Spot the faulty scheme
learnerActions: Examine classifications that mix criteria or leave out categories
Identify the problem in each
Repair one scheme and state its basis explicitly
activities.intendedInsight: Classification depends on a single, explicit criterion.
activities.rationale: Trimble's treatment of classification stresses the basis of classification as part of the function.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing criteria within one scheme (vehicles divided into cars, electric vehicles and red vehicles).
difficulties.revealedBy: Overlapping categories; items that fit more than one category.
difficulties.response: Require learners to state the criterion before listing categories and to test each category against it.

difficulties.pattern: 'The system is consisted of three parts' or 'comprises of three parts'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Passive forms of consist of; comprise followed by of.
difficulties.response: Contrast consist of (active only), comprise (without 'of') and be composed of (passive), with corpus examples. Note that 'is comprised of' is common but contested and avoided by some style guides, so 'consists of' or 'comprises' is the safer choice.

difficulties.pattern: Listing members without naming the categories or the scheme.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lists of examples with no superordinate terms.
difficulties.response: Return to class words and practise naming categories before giving members.

diagnostic.task: The learner classifies a list of ten items from their field and writes two sentences describing the classification.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Groups items by one stated criterion, names the categories and uses classification verbs accurately.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Groups items sensibly but does not state the criterion or makes a verb error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Groups inconsistently or lists items without categories.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes use classification extensively in science, engineering and business content. Pre-sessional courses use it as a component of reports and essays. Undergraduate in-sessional work addresses discipline-specific classification schemes and their limits.

records.summary: Trimble lists process description among the core functions of scientific and technical discourse, and Rose and Martin distinguish procedures (how to do something) from sequential explanations (how something happens), which maps onto the difference between a methods section and an explanation of a phenomenon. Teach with discipline-relevant diagrams and authentic methods paragraphs, and treat voice as a choice about agency rather than an automatic marker of science.

activities.title: Diagram to prose and back
learnerActions: Work in pairs: one learner has a process diagram, the other a blank template
Describe the process so your partner can complete the diagram
Swap roles with a different process and compare accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Clear process description depends on sequencing, purpose and precise verbs.
activities.rationale: Trimble's discourse approach links process description to visual–verbal relationships typical of technical texts.

activities.title: Procedure, method or explanation?
learnerActions: Sort short texts into instructions, methods recounts and explanations of natural processes
Note the tense, voice and mood of each
Rewrite one text as another type
activities.intendedInsight: The same sequence of steps is expressed differently depending on whether it instructs, recounts or explains.
activities.rationale: Rose and Martin's distinction between procedures and sequential explanations clarifies the genres in which process description appears.

difficulties.pattern: 'Then… then… after that… then…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive sequencing with one or two devices.
difficulties.response: Introduce time clauses (once, after X has been…), participle clauses and varied sequencers.

difficulties.pattern: Agentless passives where the agent matters, such as who conducted the interviews.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods sections in which it is unclear who did what; feedback asking 'by whom?'.
difficulties.response: Discuss when agency matters for credibility and replicability, and show methods sections that use active voice. Do not replace this with 'avoid the passive'.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing purpose and result ('The sample was heated so it melts').
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatch between purpose and result expressions; tense errors after so that.
difficulties.response: Contrast to + infinitive and in order to (purpose) with so and so that, using steps from the learner's field.

diagnostic.task: The learner describes a four-step diagram of a familiar process (for example making paper) in a short paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the steps in order with varied sequencing, appropriate passives, at least one purpose expression and consistent present tense.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the sequence correctly but with repetitive sequencing or inconsistent voice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Omits steps, confuses order or cannot sustain the passive.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes emphasise process description in science and engineering content. Pre-sessional courses link it to methods sections and data commentary. Undergraduate in-sessional support targets laboratory reports and technical writing.

records.summary: Trimble's discourse approach to English for science and technology distinguishes physical, functional and process description, and Rose and Martin's compositional reports describe the parts of an entity. Mohan's knowledge framework links such description to graphic representation. Information-gap tasks in which a partner reconstructs a diagram from a description give learners immediate feedback on precision and suit foundation science and engineering cohorts in particular.

activities.title: Describe and draw
learnerActions: Describe a labelled diagram from your field to a partner who cannot see it
Your partner draws it from your description
Compare the drawing with the original and revise your description
activities.intendedInsight: Precise spatial and part–whole language is what allows a reader to reconstruct a structure.
activities.rationale: Physical description is a core EST function in Trimble's account; the information gap tests precision directly.

activities.title: Structure plus function
learnerActions: Make a table of an object's or organisation's components and the function of each
Turn the table into a paragraph that moves from whole to parts
Add function language for each component
activities.intendedInsight: Academic description often combines what something consists of with what each part does.
activities.rationale: Mohan's link between knowledge structures and graphic organisers, and Rose and Martin's compositional reports, support moving from table to text.

difficulties.pattern: 'The heart is consist from four chambers.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in the form and complementation of part–whole verbs.
difficulties.response: Teach consist of, comprise, contain and be made up of as patterns, with examples from the learner's field.

difficulties.pattern: Spatial prepositions mapped from another language (on the corner of the diagram, in the left).
difficulties.revealedBy: Prepositional errors in spatial description; partners drawing components in the wrong place.
difficulties.response: Languages divide spatial relations differently, so teach spatial prepositions in chunks (at the top of, on the left, adjacent to) with diagrams.

difficulties.pattern: Describing parts in random order.
difficulties.revealedBy: Descriptions that jump between components with no spatial or hierarchical logic.
difficulties.response: Teach whole-to-part and spatial ordering strategies (top to bottom, outside to inside) and plan the order before writing.

diagnostic.task: The learner describes a simple labelled diagram of a familiar object (for example a bicycle) in four sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Moves from whole to parts, uses part–whole verbs and spatial prepositions accurately and states at least one function.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names parts accurately but with weak ordering or prepositional errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists parts without relations.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach structural description within science, engineering and business content. Pre-sessional courses use it in technical reports and for describing organisations. Undergraduate in-sessional support addresses discipline-specific descriptive writing, such as design reports and anatomy.

records.summary: Trimble treats comparison and contrast as a rhetorical technique that supports many functions in technical discourse. Carrell's study suggests that awareness of top-level structures, including comparison, supports L2 readers' recall, so comparison can be taught for reading as well as writing. The Academic Formulas List includes formulas for contrast and comparison, which gives a corpus-based starting point for phraseology. Emphasise criteria first, then organisation, then a concluding point.

activities.title: Criteria grid first
learnerActions: Build a grid of criteria for comparing two items before writing
Decide whether point-by-point or block organisation suits the purpose
Write the comparison and finish with a judgement based on the grid
activities.intendedInsight: Academic comparison is led by criteria and should lead to a point.
activities.rationale: Trimble's account of comparison as a rhetorical technique places it in the service of a larger function such as evaluation or recommendation.

activities.title: Comparison formula hunt
learnerActions: Find comparison formulas in texts from your field
Group them by meaning (similarity, difference, degree)
Choose three to use in your next comparison
activities.intendedInsight: Comparison relies on recurrent multi-word formulas, some of which signal degree.
activities.rationale: Simpson-Vlach and Ellis identify contrast and comparison formulas in academic speech and writing, providing a frequency-informed basis for selection.

difficulties.pattern: 'The GDP of China is higher than Japan.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Comparisons between non-equivalent items; missing 'that of' or 'those of'.
difficulties.response: Show the logic of comparing like with like and practise that of and those of.

difficulties.pattern: Listing similarities and differences without a conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comparisons that end after the last difference; feedback asking 'so what?'.
difficulties.response: Require a final sentence that states what the comparison shows in relation to the task.

difficulties.pattern: 'On the other hand' used in every sentence of a comparison.
difficulties.revealedBy: One contrastive connector used repeatedly, sometimes for similarity.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of comparison resources, including within-sentence structures (whereas, unlike X, Y…).

diagnostic.task: The learner compares two study methods (for example interviews and questionnaires) in four sentences for a methods justification.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Compares on explicit criteria, uses accurate comparative structures and ends with a justified choice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Compares accurately but without criteria or a conclusion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes each method separately with no comparison.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes use comparison with data and subject content. Pre-sessional courses link it to expository essays organised by comparison and data commentary. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work applies it to comparing theories, methods and findings.

records.summary: Halliday and Martin show that scientific English often realises causal relations within the clause, as verbs (leads to, causes) or nouns (the cause of), rather than between clauses with conjunctions. Schleppegrell describes this shift as a key feature of the language of schooling that learners need explicit help with. Teach the full range of realisations, and connect language to reasoning so that 'leads to' is not used for associations.

activities.title: Four ways to say because
learnerActions: Express one causal relation from your field as a conjunction, a preposition, a verb and a noun phrase
Compare the four versions for emphasis and formality
Decide which version best links to the previous sentence in a given paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Causation can be packaged in different grammatical forms, and academic writing often favours verbs and nouns.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Martin's account of grammatical metaphor shows how causal relations move into the clause in scientific discourse.

activities.title: Correlation or cause?
learnerActions: Read short descriptions of findings from different study designs
Decide whether each supports a causal or an associational claim
Write each claim with suitable verbs (causes, leads to, is associated with, is linked to)
activities.intendedInsight: The strength of causal language must follow the evidence.
activities.rationale: Schleppegrell's emphasis on making the linguistic demands of reasoning explicit supports connecting causal language to the reasoning behind it.

difficulties.pattern: 'Smoking results from cancer' or 'Due to prices rose, demand fell.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reversed result in/result from; due to used as a conjunction before a clause.
difficulties.response: Teach causal verbs and prepositions as patterns with direction arrows, using the learner's own sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Causal verbs for correlational findings ('Social media use leads to anxiety').
difficulties.revealedBy: Causal claims from surveys or correlations.
difficulties.response: Link causal verbs to design and practise associational alternatives.

difficulties.pattern: Relying only on because and so, producing chains of short clauses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Spoken-style causal chains in writing; few causal verbs or nouns.
difficulties.response: Show nominalised alternatives and practise combining clauses into causal noun-phrase structures where appropriate.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Because the temperature increased, the ice melted faster' in two other ways, one beginning with 'The increase'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces accurate verb and noun versions (The increase in temperature caused the ice to melt faster; The faster melting was due to…).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces one accurate alternative with an error in the other.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot move beyond because and so.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach cause and effect with subject content and data. Pre-sessional courses connect it to expository essays organised by cause and effect and data commentary. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work focuses on calibrating causal claims in discussions of evidence.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography directly addresses learner difficulties with causal claim strength; the guidance draws on general research-literacy principles and on the treatment of correlation and causation in crt.correlation-causation.

records.summary: Trimble lists exemplification among the rhetorical techniques that support functions in technical texts, and Hyland treats exemplification as one form of code gloss, a reader-oriented elaboration whose frequency varies by discipline. Two teaching priorities follow: grammatical control of the main markers, and the argumentative judgement of which example is representative and how it links back to the claim.

activities.title: Representative or exceptional?
learnerActions: Read a general claim and four candidate examples
Decide which examples best represent the claim and which are exceptional
Write a sentence using the best example and linking it back to the claim
activities.intendedInsight: Good examples are typical of the claim, and their relevance should be stated.
activities.rationale: Trimble's treatment of exemplification as serving a larger rhetorical purpose highlights selection, not just markers.

activities.title: Marker grammar sort
learnerActions: Correct sentences that misuse for example, such as and e.g.
Classify the markers as sentence-level or phrase-level
Write one sentence of each type about your own topic
activities.intendedInsight: Exemplification markers differ in grammar: some introduce a sentence, others a noun phrase.
activities.rationale: Hyland's analysis of code glosses provides a functional frame; grammatical sorting addresses persistent form errors.

difficulties.pattern: 'Many countries such as China has increased spending' or 'such as the government should…'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Such as followed by a clause; agreement errors with the head noun.
difficulties.response: Show such as as part of a noun phrase and practise for example for sentence-level examples.

difficulties.pattern: An anecdote presented as proof of a general claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: A single personal example used as the main support for a broad claim.
difficulties.response: Distinguish illustration from evidence, and show how examples complement rather than replace evidence.

difficulties.pattern: Strings of examples with no link back to the point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that list several examples and end without stating what they show.
difficulties.response: Require a linking sentence after each extended example (This illustrates…).

diagnostic.task: The learner supports the claim 'Some renewable energy sources are intermittent' with one example and explains how it supports the claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a representative example (for example solar power at night) with correct marker grammar and links it explicitly to intermittency.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an appropriate example but does not link it back, or makes a marker error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives an irrelevant or unrepresentative example.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes focus on marker grammar and on selecting relevant examples. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work emphasises representativeness and the difference between illustration and evidence.

records.summary: Hoey's analyses show the situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern to be widespread across text types, signalled by recognisable lexis and often recursive. Swales and Feak's problem–process–solution texts provide graduate-level models. Teach the pattern with authentic texts from learners' fields and give particular attention to the evaluation element, which learners often omit.

activities.title: Pattern chain
learnerActions: Reorder jumbled sentences from a problem–solution text
Label each sentence as situation, problem, response or evaluation
Identify the words that helped you decide
activities.intendedInsight: Problem–solution texts follow a recognisable sequence signalled by specific vocabulary.
activities.rationale: Hoey's description of the pattern and its lexical signals makes the sequence teachable and recognisable.

activities.title: Evaluate the response
learnerActions: Choose criteria (effectiveness, cost, feasibility, side effects) for evaluating responses to a problem in your field
Write an evaluation sentence for each response
Where a response is evaluated negatively, propose a further response
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluation completes the pattern and can lead to a new cycle.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak's problem–solution texts and Hoey's account of recursion both treat evaluation as integral to the pattern.

difficulties.pattern: Listing several solutions without saying whether they work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end after describing responses; feedback asking for evaluation.
difficulties.response: Require one evaluation sentence for each response, using explicit criteria.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing the causes of a problem with its effects or symptoms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses that address symptoms rather than causes; mixed-up cause and consequence statements.
difficulties.response: Map causes and consequences visually before writing, then check that responses target causes where appropriate.

difficulties.pattern: Forcing every task into a problem–solution frame.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion or comparison tasks answered as problem–solution essays.
difficulties.response: Analyse task wording to select the relevant pattern; problem–solution is one pattern among several.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes four sentences on a familiar campus problem (for example a shortage of study space) using the full pattern.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Includes situation, problem, response and a criterion-based evaluation, with precise problem and response vocabulary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes the elements but evaluates only vaguely (this is a good solution).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the problem only, or lists solutions without structure.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach the pattern in short essays and business or engineering content. Pre-sessional courses apply it to expository essays organised by problem and solution and case studies. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support connects it to case analyses, reports and research introductions.

records.summary: Rose and Martin distinguish sequential, causal, factorial and consequential explanations, a useful map of what explaining can involve. Nesi and Gardner identify explanation as a genre family across disciplines in UK student writing. Basturkmen's comparison of commenting on results found that published articles offered and evaluated alternative explanations more fully than master's dissertations, which suggests that weighing explanations deserves explicit teaching.

activities.title: Description to explanation
learnerActions: Take three descriptive sentences from your own draft
Add the mechanism or reason behind each
Compare the revised sentences with the originals and discuss what was added
activities.intendedInsight: Explanation answers 'how' and 'why', not just 'what'.
activities.rationale: Rose and Martin's explanation genres show the stages explanation adds beyond description.

activities.title: Rival explanations
learnerActions: Generate at least two explanations for an unexpected result
Weigh them using evidence and plausibility
Write a short paragraph presenting and evaluating the alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Considering alternative explanations strengthens the analysis.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen's finding that expert writers develop and evaluate alternative explanations more than novice writers supports this practice.

difficulties.pattern: 'My feedback says I am too descriptive, but I explained everything.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Detailed descriptions of what happened with little account of why; feedback asking for more analysis.
difficulties.response: Show explicit contrasts between description and explanation in the learner's own texts and practise adding mechanisms.

difficulties.pattern: 'The reason is because…'; chains of 'this is why'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Informal or redundant explanatory structures.
difficulties.response: Teach formal explanatory structures (The reason for X is that…; …, which explains why…).

difficulties.pattern: A single explanation presented as certain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion sections that offer one account of a result without considering others.
difficulties.response: Require at least one alternative explanation and a reason for preferring one.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains why a survey had a low response rate (data provided) in three sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives plausible mechanisms, considers more than one explanation and links each to the data.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Offers a single plausible explanation without weighing alternatives.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the low response rate without explaining it.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach explanation through science and social science content. Pre-sessional courses link it to expository essays and data commentary. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work focuses on explanation genres and on explaining results.

records.summary: Hopkins and Dudley-Evans identify hypothesis among the moves of discussion sections, alongside explanation and deduction, and Hyland's work on hedging shows how speculation about results is carefully modalised. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman provide a teachable account of conditional meanings. Teach prediction and hypothesis through research questions and data from learners' own fields, contrasting 'will' (confident prediction), 'would' (hypothetical) and 'is likely to' (probabilistic).

activities.title: From question to testable hypothesis
learnerActions: Take a research question from your field
Write a hypothesis that names the variables and the expected relation
Ask a partner what result would count against it, and revise if they cannot say
activities.intendedInsight: A hypothesis must predict something that could turn out to be wrong.
activities.rationale: Linking form (conditionals, modals) to the logic of testing makes hypothesis language purposeful; the conditional forms follow the account in Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman.

activities.title: Speculation in discussions
learnerActions: Find the sentences in discussion sections where writers speculate about causes or implications
Note the modal and hedging devices used
Write one speculative sentence about a finding from your own reading
activities.intendedInsight: Expert speculation is explicitly marked as tentative.
activities.rationale: Hopkins and Dudley-Evans identify hypothesis moves in discussions, and Hyland shows how such claims are hedged.

difficulties.pattern: 'If the temperature will increase, the reaction will speed up.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'will' in the if-clause of real conditionals; tense errors in unreal conditionals.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages mark future or hypothetical meaning in both clauses benefit from contrasting the English pattern explicitly, using predictions from their own field.

difficulties.pattern: 'This study will prove that…' or a hypothesis that merely restates the research question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypotheses that are untestable or framed as certainties.
difficulties.response: Distinguish questions, hypotheses and predictions, and discuss testability.

difficulties.pattern: 'Would' used for confident predictions ('The results would show a clear increase').
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypothetical 'would' where 'will' or 'is expected to' is meant, making predictions sound unreal.
difficulties.response: Contrast will, would and is likely to in pairs of sentences.

diagnostic.task: The learner turns 'Does sleep affect exam performance?' into a hypothesis and a prediction.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a testable hypothesis naming variables and direction, and a correctly formed conditional prediction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes a hypothesis without a clear direction or with a conditional error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the question or makes a certain claim.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach prediction with simple data and science content. Pre-sessional and in-sessional courses link it to research proposals and discussions. Doctoral writers apply it to hypotheses, research questions and implications in theses and articles.

records.summary: Recommendations are central to the case study and proposal genre families described by Nesi and Gardner and to the conclusion sections of research articles, where Yang and Allison identify recommendations for further research as a regular move. Moore and Morton found that IELTS writing tasks elicit statements about what ought to be done more than university assignments do, which may encourage sweeping recommendations unsupported by analysis. Teach recommending as the end point of analysis rather than an expression of opinion.

activities.title: Finding-to-recommendation chain
learnerActions: List the key findings of a case or report
Write a recommendation that follows from each finding, naming who should act and how
Rank the recommendations by strength of evidence and feasibility
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations should be traceable to findings and prioritised.
activities.rationale: Nesi and Gardner's genre families show recommendations embedded in case studies and proposals, where they must follow from analysis.

activities.title: Directness for the reader
learnerActions: Rewrite one recommendation for a client report, a policy brief and a research article's implications section
Compare how directness and the named actor change
activities.intendedInsight: The form of a recommendation depends on the reader's role and the genre.
activities.rationale: Yang and Allison's analysis of research article conclusions shows recommendations framed for researchers, which contrasts with practice-oriented genres.

difficulties.pattern: 'Governments should ban all cars' with no supporting analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sweeping, unsupported recommendations, especially in essays influenced by test preparation.
difficulties.response: Show how recommendations follow from analysis; ask the learner to trace each recommendation back to evidence.

difficulties.pattern: 'It is recommended that the company changes / to change its policy.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in mandative structures.
difficulties.response: Teach the mandative subjunctive and the should-alternative as patterns, noting variation in British usage.

difficulties.pattern: 'More research is needed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Vague recommendations that specify no actor, action or focus.
difficulties.response: Require recommendations to state who, what and why, and model specific future-research recommendations.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes two recommendations based on a finding that students rarely use the library's online chat service.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes specific recommendations naming actors and actions, linked to the finding and accurately formed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes relevant recommendations that are vague or contain a mandative error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes general opinions unrelated to the finding.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach recommendation language in business and engineering contexts. Pre-sessional courses focus on reports and expository essays organised by problem and solution. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support addresses case studies, business reports and dissertation conclusions.
reviewNotes: British usage often accepts should + infinitive or an indicative verb after mandative expressions as alternatives to the subjunctive; teachers should present the options rather than a single correct form.

records.summary: Yang and Allison's analysis of research articles separates summarising the study, evaluating it and drawing deductions in concluding sections, a useful way to show learners that concluding is more than restating. In Hyland's model, stage labels such as 'in sum' are frame markers whose use should be proportionate to the text's length. Teach synthesis-based conclusions at paragraph and section level, linked to hedged inference.

activities.title: List or synthesis?
learnerActions: Compare two conclusions to the same set of findings: one that lists them and one that synthesises them
Identify the language that achieves synthesis (taken together, these findings, overall pattern)
Rewrite a listing conclusion of your own as a synthesis
activities.intendedInsight: A conclusion should say what the findings add up to, not repeat them.
activities.rationale: Yang and Allison's distinction between summarising and deducing in concluding moves shows the step from restatement to inference.

activities.title: Taken together
learnerActions: Encapsulate three related findings in one noun phrase (These three findings…)
Add an inference with an appropriate hedge
Compare the strength of inferences across the group
activities.intendedInsight: Encapsulation plus calibrated inference is a compact concluding pattern.
activities.rationale: Hyland's treatment of frame markers and stance resources supports teaching the concluding move as a combination of organisation and stance.

difficulties.pattern: 'In conclusion,' followed by a restatement of the introduction.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions that repeat the introduction or the paragraph topics without synthesis or implication.
difficulties.response: Show conclusions that synthesise and draw implications; ask what the reader now knows that they did not know at the start.

difficulties.pattern: 'To sum up' at the end of every paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent summative markers in short texts.
difficulties.response: Reserve summative markers for section and text endings, and use concluding sentences without markers elsewhere.

difficulties.pattern: Conclusions that over-claim or introduce new evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Stronger claims in the conclusion than in the body; new sources or data introduced at the end.
difficulties.response: Check conclusions against the body and calibrate inferences to what has been shown.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes a two-sentence conclusion to three short paragraphs showing that a programme improved attendance, grades and satisfaction.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Synthesises (the programme had consistently positive effects across measures) and draws a hedged inference about its value.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Synthesises partially or draws an unhedged inference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists the three findings again.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach concluding sentences and short conclusions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses address essay and report conclusions. Taught postgraduate writers apply the function to dissertation chapters and discussion sections.

records.summary: Rose and Martin trace a progression from recounts to historical accounts and explanations, in which time shifts from simply ordering events to organising an argument through periodisation and causal accounts. Nesi and Gardner identify narrative recounts and methodology recounts among university genre families. Teach chronology as both a resource and a risk: learners need control of time expressions and tense, but they also need to move from recount to interpretation.

activities.title: Timeline to account
learnerActions: Group events on a timeline into phases and label each phase
Write a paragraph that moves through the phases using time expressions and tense shifts
State the basis of your periodisation in one sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Periodisation turns a list of events into an interpretive account.
activities.rationale: Rose and Martin show how historical genres use time to build an argument rather than a simple sequence.

activities.title: Recount to account
learnerActions: Take a narrative paragraph (for example a case history or methodology recount)
Add a sentence after each phase that interprets its significance
Compare the effect on the reader
activities.intendedInsight: Academic narration usually needs interpretation as well as sequence.
activities.rationale: Nesi and Gardner's genre families show that recount genres in university writing serve purposes beyond narrating events.

difficulties.pattern: 'In 1990 the theory has been developed by…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Present perfect with specific past time expressions; past simple for developments continuing to the present.
difficulties.response: Learners whose other languages do not distinguish perfect aspect in the same way benefit from timeline-based contrasts of past simple and present perfect.

difficulties.pattern: Narrating events when analysis was required.
difficulties.revealedBy: History or case essays that tell what happened without explaining why it matters; feedback asking for analysis.
difficulties.response: Practise adding interpretive sentences and organising by theme or argument where the task requires it.

difficulties.pattern: 'Then… after that… then…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Monotonous sequencing with a small set of time words.
difficulties.response: Introduce time clauses and periodising expressions (By the late 1990s, Over the following decade).

diagnostic.task: The learner writes a four-sentence account of the development of a technology or idea in their field from a given timeline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses varied time expressions, correct tense and aspect, groups events into phases and ends with a comment on significance.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sequences accurately but with tense errors or no interpretation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists dates and events with errors in sequence or tense.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach narration with history, business and science content. Pre-sessional courses link it to methodology recounts and case histories. Undergraduate in-sessional support targets history, law and health case writing, where moving from narration to analysis is a frequent issue.

records.summary: Mohan's knowledge framework places evaluation alongside classification and principles as a knowledge structure with characteristic language. Nesi and Gardner's critique genre family shows evaluation as an assessed purpose in its own right across disciplines, and Hunston and Thompson treat evaluation as pervasive in academic discourse rather than confined to explicitly evaluative genres. Teach criteria first, then language, then weighing.

activities.title: Criteria before judgement
learnerActions: Agree in groups on criteria for evaluating a policy, method or text
Rate the item against each criterion
Write an evaluation that weighs the ratings to reach an overall judgement
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluation is more convincing when its criteria are explicit.
activities.rationale: Mohan's framework treats evaluation as a knowledge structure that can be taught through explicit criteria and graphic organisers.

activities.title: Description or evaluation?
learnerActions: Highlight descriptive and evaluative sentences in a sample critique
Convert three descriptive sentences into evaluations
Check your own draft for the balance between the two
activities.intendedInsight: Many 'descriptive' texts can be improved by adding judgement of value or significance.
activities.rationale: Nesi and Gardner's critique genre family provides authentic models of evaluative writing across disciplines.

difficulties.pattern: 'I described the study in detail, so I have evaluated it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques and reviews that summarise without judging; feedback asking for critical evaluation.
difficulties.response: Make the description–evaluation distinction explicit using the learner's own text and practise adding judgements.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study is good and interesting.'
difficulties.revealedBy: General evaluative words without criteria or precision.
difficulties.response: Build a bank of evaluative lexis by criterion (robust, representative, limited, compelling) from reading in the field.

difficulties.pattern: 'Evaluating means finding what is wrong' or 'it is just my opinion'.
difficulties.revealedBy: One-sided criticism, or evaluation presented as personal preference.
difficulties.response: Present evaluation as balanced, criterion-based judgement that recognises strengths as well as weaknesses, and show how stating the criterion turns a preference into a supported judgement.

diagnostic.task: The learner evaluates a short description of an online survey of 50 volunteers in two sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a criterion (for example representativeness), states a strength and a weakness and gives an overall judgement in precise language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a weakness but without criteria or balance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the survey without judging it.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes introduce evaluation with simple criteria and familiar topics. Pre-sessional courses link it to critiques and discussion essays. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support applies evaluation to sources, methods and theories in the discipline.

records.summary: Introduce the interactive model through learners' own reading experiences rather than as theory for its own sake; the goal is diagnostic self-awareness. Grabe's (2009) synthesis shows that efficient lower-level processing is a precondition for higher-level comprehension, and meta-analytic evidence indicates that L2 vocabulary and grammar knowledge correlate more strongly with L2 reading comprehension than L1 reading ability or strategy knowledge do (Jeon & Yamashita, 2014), consistent with Alderson's (1984) language-threshold argument. Keep the model simple (words, sentences, what the text says, what the reader understands) and return to it whenever learners report difficulty.

activities.title: Reading breakdown log
learnerActions: Read a short academic text at your own pace and mark every point where understanding faltered
For each mark, decide whether the cause was an unknown word, a sentence you could not untangle, a missing link between ideas or unfamiliar subject matter
Compare logs in pairs and agree one remedy for each cause type
activities.intendedInsight: Different breakdowns have different causes and need different responses; reading strategies cannot compensate for every problem.
activities.rationale: Making lower- and higher-level processes visible helps learners locate problems instead of attributing all difficulty to the text or to themselves; the cause categories mirror the component-skills view in Grabe (2009).

activities.title: Same text, more knowledge
learnerActions: Read a specialist paragraph once with no preparation and write a two-sentence summary
Read a short accessible introduction to the same topic
Reread the paragraph, summarise again and compare what the background reading made possible
activities.intendedInsight: What the reader brings to the text changes what they can take from it, even when the language is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Demonstrates the knowledge-based contribution to comprehension that construction–integration models describe (Kintsch, 1998) and that Grabe and Stoller (2011) build into reading pedagogy.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I learn the right strategies, I will be able to understand any text.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners apply previewing or skimming routines to texts whose vocabulary is far beyond them and still cannot answer basic questions.
difficulties.response: Show, using an estimate of unknown-word density in the learner's own text, that strategies operate on language that is already largely understood, and redirect effort towards vocabulary and fluency alongside strategy work. Do not abandon strategy teaching; present it as dependent on a language base.

difficulties.pattern: 'I understood every word but I don't know what it means.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate word-level glosses but summaries that list details without a central point.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a problem of integration rather than vocabulary: work on main ideas, text structure and background knowledge rather than more glossing.

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to translate every sentence to understand it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Very slow reading, with written L1 glosses above most lines of the text.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that intensive translation is a familiar and sometimes useful study practice, then contrast it with tasks requiring overall meaning, and build fluency with easy texts where translation is unnecessary. Do not ban L1 use.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Why might a student who knows many reading strategies still fail to understand a journal article in English?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that strategies depend on recognising words and parsing sentences efficiently and that an unfamiliar topic also limits comprehension, and proposes different remedies for each.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions vocabulary or topic knowledge but treats difficulty as a single undifferentiated factor.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attributes failure to not trying hard enough or to using strategies incorrectly.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, present the model concretely through activities rather than terminology. On pre-sessional courses, use it to explain the course's balance of vocabulary, fluency and strategy work; the topic is also a teacher-facing principle for planning that balance. For postgraduates, a brief explicit treatment helps them understand why reading in a new discipline feels slow despite high general proficiency.
reviewNotes: The construct of a reader's situation model derives from van Dijk and Kintsch (1983) and Kintsch (1998); Kintsch (1998) is cited as the fuller statement of the construction–integration model.

records.summary: Word recognition is the main bottleneck for reading rate and is built chiefly through exposure and practice with known words, not through strategy teaching; skilled reading speed reflects the efficiency of word identification (Rayner et al., 2016) and the quality of stored lexical knowledge (Perfetti, 2007). Koda (2005) shows that processing routines developed for the L1 writing system transfer to L2 reading, so learners whose L1 uses a non-alphabetic or non-Roman script may need more orthographic practice. Teach through high-volume easy reading, timed recognition activities and attention to word-family morphology.

activities.title: Timed word-family recognition
learnerActions: Scan rows of words and circle every form of a target family (analyse, analysis, analytical) against the clock
Repeat with new rows over several sessions and plot your time and accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Recognition of known words speeds up with focused repetition, and morphology helps group forms quickly.
activities.rationale: Fluency-oriented practice with known material builds automaticity (Nation, 2009); attention to derivational morphology supports recognition of academic word families.

activities.title: Easy-text repeated reading
learnerActions: Read a 300-word passage with almost no unknown words and record your time
Reread it twice more, timing each reading
Read a new passage using the same vocabulary and compare the time
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated encounters with known words make recognition faster, and some of the gain carries over to new texts with familiar vocabulary.
activities.rationale: Repeated reading is a widely recommended fluency activity (Grabe, 2009); including a new passage tests transfer rather than memory of one text.

difficulties.pattern: Misreads visually similar words such as casual/causal or adopt/adapt, especially when reading quickly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension errors traceable to a single misrecognised word; misreadings during reading aloud.
difficulties.response: Explain that word-processing routines developed for the L1 writing system carry over into English (Koda, 2005), and give targeted contrastive practice with such pairs in context. Do not treat the errors as carelessness.

difficulties.pattern: 'I know this word' — but recognising it still takes noticeable effort.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate but slow completion of timed tasks; fatigue and declining comprehension in long texts.
difficulties.response: Provide large amounts of easy reading and timed practice with known words. Do not respond only by teaching more new vocabulary: knowing a word and recognising it automatically are different stages.

difficulties.pattern: Gaps in high-frequency vocabulary disrupt reading of otherwise accessible texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low scores on a vocabulary size test at the 2,000–3,000 family levels; frequent stops at common words such as whereas, despite or tend.
difficulties.response: Return to systematic high-frequency vocabulary learning supported by graded reading; academic word lists add little while the high-frequency base is incomplete.

diagnostic.task: A two-minute sentence-verification task built from high-frequency vocabulary, followed by a short vocabulary-size check.
diagnostic.strongResponse: High accuracy and a completion rate comparable to proficient peers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: High accuracy but noticeably slow completion, indicating that known words are not yet recognised automatically.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Low accuracy on items built from common words, indicating gaps in the high-frequency vocabulary base.

records.contextNotes: Most relevant at foundation and pre-sessional level, where gains in automaticity pay off most. In-sessional undergraduates who read slowly may be better served by self-access fluency programmes than by class time. Postgraduates rarely need explicit work here except with unfamiliar technical vocabulary. Persistent difficulty with word recognition despite practice may reflect a specific learning difference such as dyslexia, which affects reading in all of a learner's languages; refer the learner for support rather than prescribing more timed drills.

records.summary: Treat fluency as rate plus comprehension and build it through a dedicated fluency strand of timed reading of easy texts, repeated reading and extensive reading (Nation, 2009; Grabe, 2009). Rayner et al. (2016) review eye-movement and comprehension research and conclude that speed-reading techniques claiming very high rates trade away comprehension, and that the sustainable route to faster reading is practice and a larger vocabulary. Set targets from each learner's own baseline, keep comprehension checks low-stakes, and use L1 adult norms (Brysbaert, 2019) only as a rough orientation.

activities.title: Timed reading programme
learnerActions: Read a short passage written well within your vocabulary level and note your time
Answer a few comprehension questions without looking back
Record words per minute and your score on a progress chart
Repeat two or three times a week across the course
activities.intendedInsight: Rate can increase on easy text without loss of comprehension, and progress becomes visible.
activities.rationale: Speed-reading courses built on easy, controlled-vocabulary texts are a recommended fluency activity (Nation, 2009); the comprehension check prevents rate gains being bought by skimming.

activities.title: Speed-reading claims check
learnerActions: Read a short advertisement or blog post promising very high reading speeds
Read a teacher-prepared summary of what eye-movement research says about word identification and comprehension
In pairs, explain why the promised rates are implausible and what realistic improvement looks like
activities.intendedInsight: Faster reading comes from more efficient word recognition and practice; very fast 'reading' is skimming with reduced comprehension.
activities.rationale: Confronts a persistent myth with the evidence reviewed by Rayner et al. (2016) and redirects motivation towards practice with a stronger evidence base.

difficulties.pattern: 'Good readers read every text at the same high speed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners rush dense methodological or theoretical sections and then misreport them.
difficulties.response: Teach rate flexibility: faster on familiar or low-priority text, slower on dense argument. Do not set a single words-per-minute target for all text types.

difficulties.pattern: Rereads lines habitually, even when nothing was misunderstood, for fear of missing something.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow rates on easy texts; learners report anxiety about missing details.
difficulties.response: Use easy texts and timed practice to build trust in first-pass comprehension, and normalise purposeful looking back at genuinely difficult sentences. Do not forbid regressions; some are functional.

difficulties.pattern: Rate stays low because recognising common words is still effortful.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow rates even on graded texts, combined with good untimed comprehension.
difficulties.response: Return to automatic word-recognition work and extensive reading before timed practice with academic passages.

diagnostic.task: Timed silent reading of a 400–500-word easy text followed by five comprehension questions answered without looking back.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A rate approaching the learner's target for easy text with most questions answered correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Good comprehension at a markedly slow rate, or a fast rate with weak comprehension.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Slow rate and weak comprehension even on easy text, suggesting vocabulary or word-recognition gaps rather than a fluency problem.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes can timetable a regular fluency strand. In-sessional learners benefit from self-access timed reading with progress charts. For postgraduates the focus shifts to rate flexibility across specialist text types and to realistic planning; very high rates are not a goal. Adapt timed reading for learners with dyslexia, visual impairment or other access needs, for example with text-to-speech or untimed versions.
reviewNotes: Published rate norms come mainly from L1 English adult readers; L2 academic readers will usually read more slowly, and no norm should be used as a pass mark.

records.summary: Day and Bamford (1998) set out widely adopted principles: easy material, wide choice, learner selection, large quantity, reading for meaning and pleasure, and the teacher as role model. A meta-analysis indicates a positive overall effect of extensive reading on reading proficiency, with effects varying by learner and programme characteristics (Jeon & Day, 2016), and Beglar et al. (2012) found reading-rate gains among university EFL learners reading for pleasure, larger for those who read more simplified text. In EAP, extensive reading can be bridged towards academic content through popular science and narrow reading on one topic, but ease must be preserved.

activities.title: Self-selected reading with a level check
learnerActions: Choose a graded reader or accessible non-fiction text from a class or online library
Read one page and count unknown words; move down a level if there are more than a few
Read for 20–30 minutes a day and log pages, time and a one-line response
activities.intendedInsight: Volume of reading at an easy level is what builds fluency and confidence.
activities.rationale: Applies core extensive reading principles and the high-coverage condition for unassisted reading (Day & Bamford, 1998; Nation, 2009).

activities.title: Narrow reading bridge
learnerActions: Choose a topic linked to your future discipline
Read several accessible texts on it in sequence, such as popular-science articles, magazine features and introductory chapters
Note which terms and ideas become easier with each new text
activities.intendedInsight: Reading many texts on one topic recycles vocabulary and knowledge, so later texts become easier.
activities.rationale: Narrow reading increases repeated encounters with topic vocabulary, supporting incidental learning (Nation, 2013), while extending extensive reading towards academic content.

difficulties.pattern: 'Easy books are for children; I should be reading academic texts.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners choose texts far above their level and soon abandon reading, especially where earlier reading lessons used difficult texts for intensive study.
difficulties.response: Explain that fluency is built only on text that is easy for the reader and that graded readers for adults exist. Offer graded non-fiction and accessible academic topics rather than insisting on fiction.

difficulties.pattern: Turns extensive reading into intensive study, looking up every unknown word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low page counts in logs; dictionary-annotated pages.
difficulties.response: Show why extensive reading needs very high coverage, set a minimal-dictionary rule and move to an easier level. Do not attach comprehension tests to every book.

difficulties.pattern: Reading lapses after the first few weeks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Irregular entries in reading logs and no change in rate.
difficulties.response: Build reading time into class, use brief book talks and peer recommendations, and treat the log as a record rather than a test.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to summarise the last few pages of their current extensive reading text and note unknown words on one page.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Few or no unknown words and an easy, accurate summary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Several unknown words but an adequate summary; the level could be lowered.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Many unknown words and no clear summary; the text is not functioning as extensive reading.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes can run sustained extensive reading throughout the year. Short pre-sessionals are unlikely to show measurable gains on their own, so extensive reading should be framed as a habit to continue into the degree. In-sessional learners can bridge to popular-science and disciplinary magazines; postgraduates may use narrow reading in their field for fluency and background knowledge.
reviewNotes: Evidence for measurable extensive reading gains on short (6–12-week) pre-sessional courses is limited; most positive findings come from longer programmes.

records.summary: Grabe and Stoller (2011) distinguish reading purposes such as searching for information, reading quickly for gist, reading to learn, reading to integrate information, reading to write and reading to critique, each implying different processing. Teach purpose-setting as the first decision in any reading task and require learners to articulate it. Metacognitive inventories such as MARSI include setting a purpose as a global strategy (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002), but reported awareness does not guarantee use, so observe what learners actually do.

activities.title: One text, three purposes
learnerActions: Receive one article with three different task cards (find a statistic, summarise the argument, evaluate the method)
Plan how you would read for each card: which sections, what speed, what notes
Carry out one plan and compare with peers who had different cards
activities.intendedInsight: How you should read depends on why you are reading; one text can legitimately be read in several ways.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the purpose categories in Grabe and Stoller (2011) and shows that selective reading can be principled.

activities.title: Purpose statements with a stopping rule
learnerActions: Before each assigned reading, write a one-sentence purpose and a 'done when…' criterion
After reading, check whether the criterion was met and what you would do differently
activities.intendedInsight: An explicit purpose gives a stopping rule and makes reading more efficient.
activities.rationale: Goal-setting and self-evaluation are core phases of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, 2002), and purpose-setting is a global reading strategy (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'I must read every word from beginning to end or I am not really reading.' Intensive-reading exercises in which every detail is tested can reinforce this view.
