difficulties.revealedBy: Uniformly slow reading of all texts regardless of task; weekly reading left unfinished.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that careful reading is often right, then show tasks where lecturers expect partial reading. Do not replace careful reading with skimming across the board.

difficulties.pattern: States a vague purpose such as 'to understand the text'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Purpose statements that could apply to any text.
difficulties.response: Model task-specific purpose statements tied to an assignment or seminar question and give feedback on their specificity.

diagnostic.task: Give two different tasks for one text and ask the learner to describe their reading plan for each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Two clearly different plans tied to the tasks, covering sections, speed and notes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some differentiation, such as speed, but the same sequence and scope for both.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The same plan for both tasks.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need explicit modelling with short texts. Pre-sessional courses should tie purpose to assessed tasks. In-sessional undergraduates and postgraduates benefit most from linking purpose to seminar preparation and assignment questions, since over-careful reading of everything is a common cause of overload.

records.summary: Academic written English compresses meaning into noun phrases with extensive pre- and post-modification and nominalisation, leaving logical relations implicit (Biber & Gray, 2010, 2016). Readers used to clausal, conversational English often take a noun inside a modifier for the subject, or a participle for the main verb. Teach parsing explicitly with authentic sentences from learners' disciplines, using guided detailed reading that moves from the main clause outwards (Rose & Martin, 2012), and fade support as learners internalise the routine.

activities.title: Find the core
learnerActions: Take a 40-word sentence from a textbook or article in your field
Bracket prepositional phrases and relative or participle clauses
Underline the main verb and the head noun of its subject
Write the core proposition in under ten words, then add back one qualification at a time
activities.intendedInsight: Long academic sentences have a short core; most of the length is modification.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the phrasal compression that distinguishes academic writing from conversation (Biber & Gray, 2010).

activities.title: Guided detailed reading
learnerActions: Listen as the teacher paraphrases a sentence's meaning in everyday language
Locate, prompted by teacher cues, the wording that carries each part of that meaning
Highlight the nominalisations and say what process each stands for
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalised wording can be unpacked into who did what to whom.
activities.rationale: Adapted from the detailed-reading cycle of Reading to Learn pedagogy, which supports access to dense written text through guided sentence-level work (Rose & Martin, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Takes the first noun of a premodified noun phrase as its head (reading 'student writing assessment criteria' as being about students).
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that misidentify what a noun phrase refers to; wrong answers to questions about the subject of a sentence.
difficulties.response: Teach that the head of an English noun phrase is normally its final noun and that preceding nouns classify it; practise rewriting premodifier strings as postmodified phrases (criteria for assessing student writing).

difficulties.pattern: Takes the noun nearest the verb as its subject, or reads a past participle as the main verb (the method used in the study showed…).
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries attributing actions to the wrong entity; garden-path misreadings of reduced relative clauses.
difficulties.response: Locate the head noun before any postmodifying phrase or clause, use subject–verb agreement as a check, and reconstruct reduced relatives in full (that was used) while looking for a second finite verb.

difficulties.pattern: Can gloss every word of a nominalisation but cannot say what process it refers to.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct translation of 'the reduction of' with no idea of what was reduced, by whom or why.
difficulties.response: Unpack nominalisations into clauses and repack them, using examples from the learners' disciplines.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to reduce a 45-word sentence from an article in their field to its core claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct subject, verb and claim, with the key qualification noted.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct topic but the wrong relation, or the claim without its qualification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A noun from a modifying phrase is treated as the subject, producing a different claim.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from intensive guided practice with textbook sentences. Pre-sessional and in-sessional work should use texts from target disciplines, since compression patterns vary (heavy premodification in science, long nominal groups in social theory). Postgraduates may need this mainly for dense theoretical, legal or policy prose.

records.summary: Schema-theoretic research established that readers' content knowledge and knowledge of text organisation strongly affect L2 comprehension (Carrell & Eisterhold, 1983; Carrell, 1985). Grabe (2009) treats background knowledge as one of several interacting resources that becomes more important as texts become more specialised. Teach learners to activate what they know, to build knowledge deliberately through accessible sources before specialist texts, and to check that prior beliefs are not overriding what the text actually says.

activities.title: Know, expect, check
learnerActions: Before reading, list what you know and what you expect the text to say
Read and mark where the text confirmed, extended or contradicted your expectations
Revise your list and highlight any expectation you nearly attributed to the author
activities.intendedInsight: Prior knowledge helps prediction but can also distort recall of what the text said.
activities.rationale: Activating prior knowledge is a widely recommended pre-reading practice (Grabe, 2009); the final step trains readers to separate the text from their expectations.

activities.title: Build before you read
learnerActions: Before a specialist article, read an encyclopaedia entry, textbook section or review on the same topic
Note five key concepts and their relationships in a simple diagram
Read the article and add to the diagram
activities.intendedInsight: Reading an accessible overview first is an efficient, legitimate strategy, not a shortcut.
activities.rationale: Building content schemata reduces the knowledge load of specialist reading (Carrell & Eisterhold, 1983).

difficulties.pattern: 'If I don't understand, my English must be the problem.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Proficient learners report low confidence when reading in a new discipline.
difficulties.response: Help learners separate language problems from knowledge problems, and normalise background-building reading for anyone entering a new field.

difficulties.pattern: Reports what they believe about the topic rather than what the author argued.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries containing claims absent from the text.
difficulties.response: Require a line reference for each summary point and compare summaries with the text. Do not discourage the use of prior knowledge; teach checking it.

difficulties.pattern: Misreads texts that assume local institutional or national knowledge, such as references to a particular health system, legal precedent or policy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension failures concentrated on context-dependent references.
difficulties.response: Provide brief contextual glosses and teach learners to identify and look up assumed knowledge, treating this as a feature of texts written for a local readership rather than as a learner deficit.

diagnostic.task: Give a short specialist text on a topic unfamiliar to the learner with an accessible overview available, and observe whether and how they use it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses the overview strategically and can explain how it helped with the specialist text.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reads the overview but does not connect it to the specialist text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores the available background material and struggles with the specialist text.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners often meet unfamiliar subject content in content modules taught alongside EAP; integrate background-building with those modules. On pre-sessionals, choose texts linked to learners' future fields where possible. PGT students changing discipline and PGR students reading across fields benefit most from explicit background-building routines.
reviewNotes: Schema theory has been criticised as underspecified as a cognitive model; it is used here as a practical framing, with Grabe (2009) and construction–integration models as the more current theoretical basis.

records.summary: University reading lists are often longer than students can read closely, and lecturers frequently expect selective reading; Leki's (2007) case studies show L2 undergraduates developing their own ways of coping with reading demands, not all of them productive. Teach triage as a purpose-driven judgement linked to module documents and assessments, combined with realistic time estimates from learners' own reading rates, within a plan–monitor–reflect cycle (Zimmerman, 2002). Be explicit that faster reading alone will not solve overload (Rayner et al., 2016).

activities.title: Reading-list triage
learnerActions: Take an authentic module reading list and the module's assessment brief
Label each item essential, useful or optional and justify the label
Estimate how long each essential item will take using your measured reading rate
Compare your plan with a lecturer's or a more experienced student's view
activities.intendedInsight: Not everything on a list is meant to be read in full; priorities follow from teaching and assessment.
activities.rationale: Makes tacit expectations about reading lists explicit and links reading choices to purpose (Grabe & Stoller, 2011).

activities.title: Plan, monitor, review
learnerActions: Draft a weekly reading schedule
Record the time actually spent and what was read
At the end of the week, compare plan and reality and adjust the next plan
activities.intendedInsight: Reading plans become realistic when they are tested against one's actual pace.
activities.rationale: Applies the forethought, performance and self-reflection phases of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'I'm behind because I read too slowly, so I'll learn speed reading.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Interest in speed-reading apps; plans that assume unrealistic rates.
difficulties.response: Explain the evidence on speed reading and shift the solution to prioritising and planned partial reading. Do not promise rate gains that would remove the need to select.

difficulties.pattern: Reads optional items closely and skips essential ones.
difficulties.revealedBy: Seminar contributions based on peripheral reading; assignments missing core sources.
difficulties.response: Teach the reading-list conventions of the target context (for example essential and further reading in many UK programmes, or required and recommended readings and a course reader elsewhere) and how they relate to assessment, and require a purpose statement for each item read.

difficulties.pattern: Stops reading altogether after falling behind.
difficulties.revealedBy: A sudden drop in preparation and avoidance of seminars.
difficulties.response: Help the learner reprioritise to the minimum viable reading for the next session, and refer to support services where workload is affecting wellbeing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they decided what to read for last week's seminar and how long it took.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes clear priorities linked to the seminar question and accurate use of time.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has priorities but unrealistic time estimates.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Read in list order or not at all, with no basis for choice.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need guidance on what reading lists are and how they relate to modules. Pre-sessional courses can simulate realistic loads. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT students face the sharpest overload, PGT timelines being especially compressed. PGR researchers need longer-term strategies for sustaining reading of a literature alongside writing.
reviewNotes: Expectations about how much of a reading list students should read vary by discipline and lecturer; teachers should gather local evidence rather than generalise.

records.summary: A meta-analysis found a modest comprehension advantage for paper over screen for expository texts, especially under time constraints (Delgado et al., 2018), which suggests that the risk lies in faster, shallower processing habits rather than in technology itself. Teach learners to match medium to purpose, to use PDF tools for purposeful annotation rather than mass highlighting, which is a low-utility technique (Dunlosky et al., 2013), and to check unfamiliar web sources by reading laterally as professional fact-checkers do (Wineburg & McGrew, 2019). Do not present screen reading as inherently inferior: most university reading is now digital.

activities.title: Screen versus paper reflection
learnerActions: Read one short article on screen and a comparable one on paper, each with the same type of question
Write an unaided three-sentence summary after each
Compare the summaries and reflect on how you read in each medium (speed, distraction, annotation)
activities.intendedInsight: Felt understanding can exceed actual understanding, particularly after fast screen reading.
activities.rationale: Invites learners to test against their own experience the screen disadvantage for expository text under time pressure reported by Delgado et al. (2018).

activities.title: Purposeful PDF annotation
learnerActions: Set a reading purpose for a PDF article
Use at most two highlight colours with defined meanings and add margin comments in your own words
List your comments and check whether they answer your purpose
activities.intendedInsight: Annotation helps when it records your thinking, not when it marks most of the page.
activities.rationale: Highlighting alone has low utility for learning (Dunlosky et al., 2013); writing comments requires generative processing.

difficulties.pattern: Highlights large parts of a PDF and treats the text as read.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavily coloured PDFs combined with weak recall.
difficulties.response: Limit highlighting and require margin comments in the learner's own words. Do not ban highlighting.

difficulties.pattern: Follows hyperlinks or switches tabs and loses the thread of the main text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fragmented notes and long reading sessions with little progress.
difficulties.response: Agree a link policy (note links to follow later) and use focus modes, downloaded copies or print for close reading.

difficulties.pattern: 'I read it, so I understood it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident self-ratings alongside weak unaided summaries after screen reading.
difficulties.response: Build closed-file summaries into screen-reading tasks so that learners calibrate their judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their annotated PDF of a recent reading and to state, without looking, the author's main argument.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sparse, purposeful annotations and an accurate account of the argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate account, but annotations unrelated to any purpose.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Extensive highlighting and a vague or inaccurate account.

records.contextNotes: Learners at every stage read mainly on screen. Foundation and pre-sessional learners may need basic PDF and e-book skills; in-sessional learners benefit from discussing medium choice for heavy reading; postgraduate researchers need workflows that link PDF annotation to reference managers and notes. Text-to-speech, screen readers and adjustable display settings are legitimate ways of reading on screen, particularly for learners with dyslexia or visual impairment.
reviewNotes: Screen-reading research changes quickly with technology and reading habits; Delgado et al. (2018) should be read alongside more recent syntheses as they appear.

records.summary: L2 reading draws on reading ability and conceptual knowledge developed in other languages (Koda, 2005; Cummins, 2008), and L2 readers report frequent use of support strategies such as translating (Sheorey & Mokhtari, 2001). A translanguaging perspective treats this as a resource rather than a deficit (García & Li Wei, 2014). The teaching task is to make L1 and machine-translation use strategic and checked: used to unblock rather than replace English reading, with verification of technical terms, hedges, negation and attribution, and with awareness of institutional rules.

activities.title: Machine-translation fidelity check
learnerActions: Machine-translate a short hedged paragraph from an article in your field into a language you know well
Compare the translation with the original, marking changes in certainty, negation, attribution and technical terms
Explain to a partner, in English, one change that would mislead a reader
activities.intendedInsight: Machine translation can help with gist but may alter the precise claims that academic reading depends on.
activities.rationale: Uses the learner's plurilingual repertoire as a resource (García & Li Wei, 2014) while building verification habits; translation quality varies by language pair and domain.

activities.title: Bilingual concept glossary
learnerActions: While reading a set of texts, record key disciplinary terms with the English definition from the text, an L1 equivalent and an example
Flag terms whose L1 equivalent has a different scope or connotation
Review the glossary before seminars
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalents across languages are often partial; noticing differences sharpens understanding in both languages.
activities.rationale: Builds on cross-linguistic transfer of conceptual knowledge (Cummins, 2008) while attending to mismatches.

difficulties.pattern: Translates the whole text before reading any of the English.
difficulties.revealedBy: Machine-translation output used as the reading text; inability to locate claims in the original.
difficulties.response: Set tasks that require line references to the English text and limit translation to passages the reader has flagged as blocking comprehension. Do not prohibit machine translation, which is unenforceable and removes a legitimate support.

difficulties.pattern: Accepts an L1 equivalent that does not match the disciplinary meaning, for example taking 'significant' in a statistical report to mean simply 'important'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misreadings of sub-technical terms in otherwise accurate summaries.
difficulties.response: Teach checking key terms against English glossaries and their use in context, and collect common false equivalents in the learners' languages.

difficulties.pattern: 'Using my own language is cheating or unacademic.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners hide L1 use or avoid useful L1 resources while understanding little.
difficulties.response: Discuss legitimate uses and institutional policy openly, distinguishing support for reading from submitting translated writing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they handled the hardest part of their last reading and whether they used another language or a translation tool.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes selective, checked use of L1 or machine translation and knows the local rules.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses L1 or machine translation but does not check terms or hedges.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Either relies entirely on translation or avoids all L1 resources while understanding little.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit discussion and practice. In EMI and transnational settings, bilingual reading is often the norm and should be planned for. Postgraduate researchers may read substantial literature in other languages and need conventions for citing translated sources.
reviewNotes: Institutional policies on machine translation in reading and in submitted work differ and change frequently; local rules should be checked.

records.summary: Previewing is a global strategy in metacognitive reading inventories (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002) and is widely recommended for academic reading because it is quick and can support both relevance decisions and later careful reading (Grabe & Stoller, 2011). Teach it with authentic articles and chapters, always followed by a check of predictions against the text, and link it explicitly to purpose and source selection. As with all strategies, its benefit depends on learners being able to read the preview features themselves.

activities.title: Three-minute preview and check
learnerActions: Preview an article for three minutes using only the title, abstract, headings, figures and conclusion
Write predictions about its topic, type, main claim and structure
Read the article and score your predictions
activities.intendedInsight: A short, systematic preview gives a reliable framework, and checking predictions sharpens it.
activities.rationale: Prediction followed by verification turns previewing into active comprehension rather than a ritual (Grabe & Stoller, 2011).

activities.title: Relevance sort
learnerActions: Receive eight abstracts or first pages on a topic, together with an essay question
Preview each and sort them into read closely, read in part and not needed
Justify each decision to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Previewing is a decision tool for managing reading, not only a comprehension aid.
activities.rationale: Links previewing to source selection and the source-based writing demands of university study (Alexander et al., 2019).

difficulties.pattern: Treats previewing as wasted time and starts reading at the first line, a habit suited to the short texts read in full for detailed questions in many reading courses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot describe a text's structure until they have finished reading it.
difficulties.response: Demonstrate the time saved on a realistic task and make previewing a required first step in early tasks, always tied to a purpose. Do not assess previewing as a ritual detached from purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Relies on the abstract and treats it as the whole argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that reproduce the abstract's claims without the qualifications found in the discussion.
difficulties.response: Compare abstracts with discussion sections to show what abstracts leave out, such as limitations and qualifications.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to preview an unfamiliar article for three minutes and predict its main claim and structure.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate predictions drawing on several preview features.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate topic but a vague or inaccurate claim and structure.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Begins reading linearly, or makes predictions unrelated to the text.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners should practise with textbook chapters and short articles. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply previewing to source selection for assignments. Postgraduates use rapid previewing to screen large numbers of search results, often alongside reference management software.

records.summary: Skimming has a legitimate role in orientation and relevance decisions, but Rayner et al. (2016) show that it trades comprehension for speed: readers lose information in what they skip, so skimming serves gist and relevance decisions only when readers can identify the important parts. Materials shaped by test formats often over-teach skimming and scanning relative to careful reading for learning and argument, which Grabe (2009) and Grabe and Stoller (2011) identify as central academic reading purposes. Teach skimming as a bounded, purposeful technique and always pair it with decisions about which parts to read carefully.

activities.title: Skim, then decide
learnerActions: Skim an article in four minutes and write its gist and a section outline
Mark two sections you would need to read carefully for a given essay question
Read those sections and check whether the skim led you to the right places
activities.intendedInsight: Skimming is a route to careful reading of the right parts, not a substitute for it.
activities.rationale: Positions skimming within purposeful reading (Grabe & Stoller, 2011) while keeping its limits visible (Rayner et al., 2016).

activities.title: What did the skim miss?
learnerActions: Skim a text and answer gist and detail questions
Read the text carefully and answer the same questions
Compare your answers and list the kinds of information skimming lost
activities.intendedInsight: Skimming preserves structure and gist but loses qualifications, evidence and detail.
activities.rationale: Lets learners experience directly the speed–comprehension trade-off documented by Rayner et al. (2016).

difficulties.pattern: 'Skimming is how fast readers read everything.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners skim texts they are required to critique and then misrepresent the argument.
difficulties.response: Teach skimming as one reading mode chosen for a purpose. Do not set skimming as the default first and only reading of every text.

difficulties.pattern: Reads only the first sentence of each paragraph and assumes it states the paragraph's point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gist statements that miss delayed or implicit main points.
difficulties.response: Show paragraphs whose point is delayed or implicit, and teach sampling of paragraph endings and evaluative language as well as openings.

difficulties.pattern: Matches question words to text words without reading for meaning, a habit formed in timed test preparation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fast, keyword-driven answers that fail when the text paraphrases the question.
difficulties.response: Use tasks with paraphrased questions and require justification of answers. Acknowledge that the habit was rational in the test context in which it was learned.

diagnostic.task: A four-minute skim of a 1,500-word article followed by a gist statement and a question about a qualification within one paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate gist and outline, and recognition that the qualification requires careful reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate gist, but an inaccurate answer about the qualification given with confidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: An inaccurate gist or a list of topics with no overall point.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners often arrive with test-driven skimming habits that need repositioning within purposeful reading. In-sessional learners use skimming mainly for relevance decisions and seminar preparation under time pressure; for postgraduates it is chiefly a literature-screening tool. Timed skimming tasks can disadvantage readers with dyslexia or visual impairment; allow extra time or text-to-speech and assess the relevance decisions rather than speed alone.
reviewNotes: The claim that skimming and scanning are over-taught relative to careful reading reflects practitioner analysis and reading researchers' emphasis on reading to learn; systematic evidence on the content of EAP materials is not in the closed bibliography.

records.summary: Scanning is a simple skill whose teaching value in EAP lies less in speed drills than in two habits: anticipating the form of the target, including paraphrases and word-family variants, and verifying the context once something is found. Grabe and Stoller (2011) treat searching for information as a distinct reading purpose. In digital documents, search functions do much of the mechanical work, so predicting search terms and checking context become the key skills.

activities.title: Paraphrase hunt
learnerActions: Receive questions whose key words are paraphrased in the text
Brainstorm possible wordings of each target before scanning
Scan, locate the information and read the surrounding sentence to confirm it
activities.intendedInsight: Scanning for meaning requires anticipating varied wordings and checking context.
activities.rationale: Counters the keyword-matching habit and connects scanning to vocabulary knowledge and purpose (Grabe & Stoller, 2011).

activities.title: Digital search versus print scan
learnerActions: Find specified information in a long PDF report using the search function
Find comparable information using a printed index or contents page
Discuss which search terms failed and why
activities.intendedInsight: Digital search is fast but only as good as the search terms; synonyms and word families matter.
activities.rationale: Reflects the digital format of most university reading and the dependence of locating information on lexical knowledge (Alexander et al., 2019).

difficulties.pattern: Stops at the first occurrence of a keyword without checking that it answers the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Wrong answers taken from sentences that mention the keyword in another context.
difficulties.response: Require learners to quote the full sentence and explain why it answers the question.

difficulties.pattern: Cannot find information worded differently from the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Success on verbatim items and failure on paraphrased ones.
difficulties.response: Teach prediction of synonyms and word-family variants before scanning, and connect the task to vocabulary development.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to find three paraphrased items in a long report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates all three quickly and confirms each in context.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Locates only items worded as in the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reads linearly from the start, or gives keyword-matched wrong answers.

records.contextNotes: Mainly a foundation and pre-sessional focus, often already familiar from test preparation, so little class time is needed beyond the verification habit. At later stages scanning is embedded in work with databases, tables and reference lists. Allow extra time or digital search for readers with visual impairment or dyslexia, since locating information is the skill being assessed, not visual search speed.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-08 lowered the range to A2–B2, which is applied. Scanning is kept as 'develop' rather than 'core' at foundation, and as 'revisit' on pre-sessionals, because it is usually familiar from test preparation and digital search does much of the work; the teachable content is anticipating wording and verifying context.

Merging rds.skimming and rds.scanning into one 'selective reading' topic was considered and not adopted, because the two serve different purposes (gist versus a located target) and fail in different ways.

records.summary: Main-idea identification corresponds to the macro-processes of comprehension models, in which readers delete, generalise and construct propositions to form a gist (Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978); Brown and Day (1983) found that the harder operations of generalising and inventing an implicit topic sentence develop late. Teach with authentic paragraphs in which main ideas are not always stated first, using sentence-function labelling and hierarchical outlining, and connect the skill explicitly to summarising and note-making.

activities.title: Sentence function labelling
learnerActions: Label each sentence of a paragraph as claim, explanation, example, evidence or qualification
Identify the claim that the other sentences support
Write the main idea in one sentence of your own
activities.intendedInsight: A main idea is identified by what the other sentences do in relation to it.
activities.rationale: Makes the functional hierarchy of propositions explicit, approximating the macro-operations described by Kintsch and van Dijk (1978).

activities.title: Constructing an implicit topic sentence
learnerActions: Read a paragraph that has no explicit topic sentence
Delete trivial and repeated information
Replace lists with a superordinate term and construct a topic sentence
Compare with peers and with how the writer uses the paragraph in the wider text
activities.intendedInsight: Sometimes the reader must construct the main idea rather than find it.
activities.rationale: Targets the generalisation and invention operations that Brown and Day (1983) found to be the latest to develop.

difficulties.pattern: 'The main idea is always the first sentence.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Main-idea answers copied from first sentences even when these are background or transitional.
difficulties.response: Present paragraphs with delayed and implicit main ideas and ask for evidence from the rest of the paragraph.

difficulties.pattern: Selects the most vivid example or statistic as the main idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Main-idea statements that restate an example.
difficulties.response: Ask what the example is an example of, and practise generalising from specific to general.

difficulties.pattern: Copies a long sentence rather than stating the idea in their own words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Verbatim main-idea statements that include irrelevant modifiers.
difficulties.response: Require own-word statements of a fixed short length; if the learner cannot shorten the sentence, check whether they have parsed it. Treat copying here as a comprehension signal, not as an integrity issue.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with an implicit main idea and a vivid opening example and ask for the main idea in one sentence of the learner's own.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate generalisation covering the whole paragraph.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A partly accurate statement that is too narrow or too broad.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the example or copies the first sentence.

records.contextNotes: Central at foundation and on undergraduate pre-sessionals, where it underpins summary and note-making; on postgraduate pre-sessionals it is usually reviewed within summary and source-reading tasks. In-sessional work applies it to longer disciplinary texts and sections. Postgraduates usually manage paragraph-level main ideas but may need work at whole-article level, where the contribution can be stated subtly.

records.summary: Knowledge of how paragraphs are organised is part of the discourse-structure awareness that Grabe (2009) identifies as important for L2 comprehension, and Carrell's (1985) training study showed that explicit teaching of text structure improved ESL readers' recall. Teach paragraph patterns as probabilistic cues, using authentic paragraphs that include delayed and implicit points, and connect reading to learners' own paragraph writing. Avoid presenting the topic-sentence model taught for writing as a universal description of expert paragraphs.

activities.title: Paragraph reconstruction
learnerActions: Reorder the jumbled sentences of an academic paragraph
Identify the controlling sentence, the development pattern and any linking sentence
Explain which signals helped you
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraphs have an internal logic signalled by reference, connectors and general-to-specific movement.
activities.rationale: Reordering requires attention to coherence signals and structure, building the discourse awareness Grabe (2009) describes.

activities.title: Predict the paragraph
learnerActions: Read only the first sentence of several paragraphs
Predict each paragraph's development pattern and likely content
Read the paragraphs and evaluate your predictions
activities.intendedInsight: Opening sentences often set up expectations, but not always; checking predictions builds flexible use of structure.
activities.rationale: Prediction from structural cues engages readers with organisation, in line with structure-training approaches (Carrell, 1985).

difficulties.pattern: Expects every paragraph to follow the topic sentence–support–conclusion model taught for writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion with expert paragraphs that open with a counter-view, data or a question.
difficulties.response: Show the range of expert paragraph structures and distinguish a writing scaffold from a description of all paragraphs.

difficulties.pattern: Ignores connectors and treats each sentence as independent.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reordering completed by topic guesswork; contrastive sentences read as additive.
difficulties.response: Highlight connectors and the relations they express before reordering and prediction tasks.

diagnostic.task: A jumbled-paragraph reordering task that includes one paragraph with a delayed main point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct order with signals explained and the delayed main point recognised.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct order explained only by topic, without reference to signals.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Incorrect order, with the first sentence assumed to be the main point.

records.contextNotes: Mainly a foundation and pre-sessional focus, linked to paragraph writing. In-sessional, it is better integrated into main-idea and text-organisation work with disciplinary texts than taught separately.

records.summary: Carrell (1985) found that explicitly teaching top-level rhetorical structures improved ESL readers' recall, and Hoey (1983, 2001) shows how patterns such as problem–solution and claim–counterclaim are signalled lexically and how readers use those signals to anticipate what comes next. Teach a small number of high-frequency patterns with graphic organisers, focus on signalling vocabulary, and move quickly to authentic disciplinary texts in which patterns are embedded and combined.

activities.title: Graphic organiser mapping
learnerActions: Identify the overall pattern of an article
Complete a graphic organiser for that pattern, for example situation–problem–response–evaluation
Underline the signalling words for each element
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the overall pattern makes long texts easier to follow and remember.
activities.rationale: Reproduces the core of Carrell's (1985) structure training, with signalling vocabulary drawn from Hoey's (1983) pattern analysis.

activities.title: Signal and predict
learnerActions: Read a text section by section, stopping at signals such as 'however, this approach' or 'a further problem'
Predict what the next section will do
Check and discuss your predictions
activities.intendedInsight: Writers signal their plans, and readers who notice the signals can anticipate.
activities.rationale: Draws on Hoey's (2001) account of reading as interaction in which the writer answers questions the reader is led to ask.

difficulties.pattern: Identifies a pattern from a single signal and forces the content to fit it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rigid organiser completion with content placed in the wrong slots.
difficulties.response: Use texts that combine patterns and require justification of each slot assignment from the text.

difficulties.pattern: Overlooks headings and frame markers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines that miss section-level structure.
difficulties.response: Begin outlining from headings and frame markers before reading for detail.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to outline a 700-word problem–solution text and name its signals.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate pattern mapping supported by signals.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct pattern identified, but elements incomplete or misplaced.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A linear list of content with no pattern.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses can teach patterns explicitly with accessible texts. In-sessional and PGT teaching should focus on how patterns appear in disciplinary genres, such as problem–solution in engineering and business reports and claim–counterclaim in humanities argument.

records.summary: Research articles follow conventional macrostructures and move patterns described in genre analysis (Swales, 1990, 2004), which readers can exploit to read non-linearly according to purpose. Wallace and Wray (2016) encourage postgraduates to read with a clear question and to be selective rather than reading everything from start to finish. Teach the functions of each section, practise purpose-driven routes through articles from learners' fields, and highlight disciplinary variation, including qualitative, theoretical and review articles that do not follow IMRaD.

activities.title: Article grid race
learnerActions: Receive an article from your field and a grid (question, design, sample or data, main finding, limitation)
Complete the grid in ten minutes, noting section and page for each entry
Compare the routes you took with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing where information usually sits makes articles navigable without reading every word.
activities.rationale: Applies genre knowledge of research-article sections (Swales, 1990) to efficient reading.

activities.title: Purpose routes
learnerActions: For three purposes (relevance check, finding a method to adapt, evaluating a claim), plan a route through an article
Carry out one route and judge whether it was sufficient
Note where the article departed from IMRaD and how you adapted
activities.intendedInsight: Different purposes call for different routes through the same article.
activities.rationale: Combines purpose-driven reading with awareness of genre variation (Swales, 2004; Wallace & Wray, 2016).

difficulties.pattern: Reads every article from start to finish, including long methods sections, whatever the purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long reading times; notes dominated by methodological detail irrelevant to the task.
difficulties.response: Model expert reading routes and set timed, purpose-specific tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Assumes every article follows IMRaD.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion with theoretical, review or qualitative articles.
difficulties.response: Include varied article types and practise identifying structure from headings and introductions.

difficulties.pattern: Reads the abstract and discussion and reports findings without their conditions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-generalised reporting of findings in the learner's writing.
difficulties.response: Require one methodological condition (sample, setting, design) to accompany each finding the learner reports.

diagnostic.task: A ten-minute grid completion with an unfamiliar empirical article.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate grid with page references, reached by a non-linear route.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A mostly accurate grid reached by slow linear reading.
diagnostic.gapResponse: An inaccurate grid, or methods information not located.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses for postgraduates should introduce article navigation with articles from learners' fields. Undergraduates meet research articles increasingly in later years. PGT and PGR readers need it most; PGR researchers also benefit from discussing how experienced readers in their field read.
reviewNotes: Empirical studies of how expert readers navigate research articles are not represented in the closed bibliography; a suitable source could be added.
Review response: following R1-04, the topic is tagged for postgraduate pre-sessionals only, not undergraduate ones; undergraduates meet research articles during the degree (in-sessional).

records.summary: Comprehension models treat inferencing as central: readers generate bridging inferences to connect propositions and knowledge-based inferences to build a coherent situation model (Kintsch, 1998; Grabe, 2009). Academic writing's phrasal compression leaves many logical relations implicit (Biber & Gray, 2010), increasing inferential demands on readers of English as an additional language. Teach inference as reasoning from textual evidence, distinguishing warranted inferences from speculation, and support it by building the background knowledge on which inferencing depends.

activities.title: Stated, inferable or unsupported?
learnerActions: Classify a set of statements about a passage as stated, validly inferable or unsupported
Underline the words that justify each decision
Discuss borderline cases with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Good inferences are anchored in the text; plausible ideas without textual support are not inferences from the text.
activities.rationale: Builds the distinction between text-based inference and free elaboration that comprehension research describes (Grabe, 2009).

activities.title: Making implicit relations explicit
learnerActions: Find a sentence in which a nominalised phrase hides a causal or contrastive relation
Rewrite it with an explicit connector or clause
Check whether your rewrite fits the rest of the text
activities.intendedInsight: Compressed academic phrasing often leaves the reader to infer how ideas are related.
activities.rationale: Targets the implicitness of phrasally compressed academic prose (Biber & Gray, 2010).

difficulties.pattern: Adds personal knowledge or opinion as if the text had stated it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident answers that go beyond the text.
difficulties.response: Require textual justification for every inference and distinguish inference from personal response. Do not discourage elaboration; label it as such.

difficulties.pattern: Reads literally and misses implied evaluation or causation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that lose implied relations, or no answer to 'why does the writer mention this?'.
difficulties.response: Practise purpose questions about sentences and the unpacking of implicit relations.

difficulties.pattern: Builds an inference on a wrongly resolved pronoun or 'this'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inferences that rest on an incorrect antecedent.
difficulties.response: When an inference is wrong, check reference resolution first.

diagnostic.task: Three statements (stated, inferable, unsupported) about a short passage, with justification required.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct classification supported by textual evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct classification without evidence, or confusion between the inferable and the unsupported.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unsupported statements treated as true.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need inference work with accessible texts and explicit modelling. In-sessional and PGT learners meet heavy inferential demands in dense disciplinary prose and in reading writers' implied positions, which connects this topic to stance and critical reading.

records.summary: Reference is a core cohesive resource (Halliday & Hasan, 1976), and academic writing makes heavy use of signalling nouns that encapsulate and evaluate stretches of preceding text (Flowerdew, 2003). For readers of English as an additional language, unresolved or wrongly resolved reference often goes unnoticed and undermines comprehension (Grabe, 2009), so teach it explicitly through reference-chain tasks, with particular attention to 'this/these + noun' and to reference to whole clauses and paragraphs.

activities.title: Reference chain arrows
learnerActions: Draw arrows from each pronoun, demonstrative and signalling noun in a paragraph to what it refers to
Mark items that refer to a whole clause or paragraph
Compare with a partner and resolve disagreements
activities.intendedInsight: Some references point to ideas, not single words.
activities.rationale: Makes cohesive ties visible (Halliday & Hasan, 1976).

activities.title: What is 'this'?
learnerActions: Find signalling nouns such as 'this problem' or 'these findings' in an article
Write a one-sentence summary of what each encapsulates
Check each summary against the preceding text
activities.intendedInsight: Signalling nouns summarise and label earlier text, steering the reader's interpretation.
activities.rationale: Based on Flowerdew's (2003) analysis of signalling nouns as text-organising and evaluative devices.

difficulties.pattern: Links 'it' or 'this' to the nearest noun.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpretations where the referent is a clause or a more distant noun.
difficulties.response: Practise extended reference with explicit marking, testing candidate antecedents for agreement and sense.

difficulties.pattern: Treats synonyms and general nouns in a reference chain as different entities.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that count one study or concept as several.
difficulties.response: Trace lexical chains explicitly and discuss how writers vary wording for the same referent.

difficulties.pattern: Reads signalling nouns as neutral labels and misses their evaluation, for example treating 'this claim' as endorsement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that present as established what the writer labelled a claim or assumption.
difficulties.response: Discuss how the choice of signalling noun can evaluate as well as refer, using contrasting examples.

diagnostic.task: Five numbered reference items in a 200-word passage; the learner states each referent.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All referents correct, including extended reference.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Pronouns correct, but encapsulating items resolved vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Several referents wrong, with a nearest-noun strategy evident.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit teaching. In-sessional work can focus on dense disciplinary prose and on links to the learners' own use of reference in writing.

records.summary: Academic texts present claims of varying certainty, supported by evidence and marked by hedges, boosters and attribution (Hyland, 1998). Kuhn (1991) found that many people do not reliably distinguish evidence from theory or explanation, which suggests that the distinction needs explicit teaching. Replace the fact/opinion binary with a richer set of categories and use hedging and attribution as linguistic cues to status.

activities.title: Status labelling
learnerActions: Label sentences in an academic paragraph as background, claim, evidence, evaluation or speculation
Circle the hedges, boosters and attribution that helped you decide
Discuss sentences whose labels are debatable
activities.intendedInsight: Academic statements differ in status, and language signals that status.
activities.rationale: Uses hedging research (Hyland, 1998) to link linguistic form to epistemic status.

activities.title: Evidence or claim?
learnerActions: Separate what a short argument claims from what it offers as evidence
Ask whether the evidence would convince a sceptical reader
Rewrite the claim so that its strength matches the evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Claims and evidence are different, and claims can be stronger or weaker than the evidence warrants.
activities.rationale: Targets the evidence–theory distinction that Kuhn (1991) found many reasoners blur.

difficulties.pattern: 'Facts are true and opinions are just personal.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Anything in a published source treated as fact; evaluative statements dismissed as 'just opinion'.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that the fact/opinion binary is common in school reading curricula and test items, then present academic knowledge as claims supported by evidence and open to revision. Do not simply swap the labels 'fact' and 'opinion' for new ones without changing the underlying view.

difficulties.pattern: Ignores hedges and reports a tentative finding as certain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that drop 'may', 'suggests' or 'in this sample'.
difficulties.response: Teach hedges as meaning-bearing and check every summary for preserved certainty; where learners do not recognise the devices themselves, return to explicit work on hedging.

diagnostic.task: A four-sentence paragraph labelling task with cue words to be identified.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate labels, cues identified, and nuance on debatable items.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly accurate labels but reasoning in fact/opinion terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: All published statements treated as fact.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need explicit work beyond the binary. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners should connect it to argument identification and to preserving claim strength in their own source use.
reviewNotes: What counts as established fact differs across disciplines (for example in physics and in history); examples should come from learners' fields where possible.

Review response: the name was sharpened from 'Distinguishing fact, opinion, claim and evidence' to 'Distinguishing claims, evidence and their status' so that it no longer presents the school fact/opinion binary that the topic replaces; the ID and scope are unchanged. The soft edge from sta.hedging was removed (R3-02); hedging is now reached in the guidance text rather than as a prerequisite.

records.summary: Writers construct stance through hedges, boosters, attitude markers and self-mention (Hyland, 2005) and manage other voices through attribution and reporting verbs whose evaluative force signals endorsement or distance (Thompson & Ye, 1991; Hyland, 1999). Appraisal theory's engagement system describes how writers acknowledge, distance themselves from, counter or endorse other voices (Martin & White, 2005). Teach readers to track voices sentence by sentence and to read concessive structures carefully, since these are where misattribution most often occurs.

activities.title: Voice colouring
learnerActions: Colour each clause of a literature-review paragraph by voice: the writer, Source A, Source B
Circle reporting verbs and evaluative words
State the writer's position and the evidence for it
activities.intendedInsight: Academic texts are multi-voiced, and the writer's position emerges from how other voices are framed.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the distinction between averral and attribution and the evaluative role of reporting verbs (Hyland, 1999; Thompson & Ye, 1991).

activities.title: Decoding concession
learnerActions: Find sentences built on patterns such as 'Although X has argued…, …' or 'X is right that…, but…'
Identify which part the writer concedes and which part they assert
Paraphrase the writer's view accurately
activities.intendedInsight: In concessive structures, the writer's own position usually follows the concession.
activities.rationale: Draws on the engagement resources of concession and counter-expectation in Martin and White (2005).

difficulties.pattern: Attributes a cited view to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries stating 'the author argues X' when the author reported X in order to reject it.
difficulties.response: Practise voice colouring and require the source of every idea to be identified in summaries.

difficulties.pattern: Reads all reporting verbs as neutral equivalents of 'says'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that turn 'claims' into 'shows'.
difficulties.response: Teach the evaluative range of reporting verbs with contrasting examples from the same text.

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic writers are neutral, so the writer has no opinion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report that a text expresses no position despite evaluative framing.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that school writing advice often presents academic writing as impersonal or objective, then show how stance is expressed through lexical and grammatical choices in academic writing, and why tracking it matters for accurate source use.

diagnostic.task: A literature-review paragraph reporting three sources and critiquing one; ask whose view is endorsed and how the learner knows.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct attribution, with evidence from reporting verbs, concession and evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct overall position, but one cited view misattributed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cited views equated with the writer's own.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduate pre-sessional learners meet it through simple reporting and concession; postgraduate pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners need it to avoid misrepresenting sources in assessed writing. PGT and PGR readers need finer interpretation of stance in literature reviews and discussion sections, including disciplinary variation in how stance is signalled.

records.summary: Metacognitive monitoring is a hallmark of skilled reading (Flavell, 1979), and strategy inventories such as MARSI (Mokhtari & Reichard, 2002) and SORS (Sheorey & Mokhtari, 2001) indicate that more able readers report greater use of monitoring and problem-solving strategies. Reciprocal teaching combines predicting, questioning, clarifying and summarising with modelling and gradual handover (Palincsar & Brown, 1984). Teach monitoring through think-alouds and inconsistency-detection tasks, and be candid that self-report inventories measure awareness rather than use and that the effects of strategy instruction are variable (Plonsky, 2011) and are likely to depend on adequate language knowledge.

activities.title: Reciprocal teaching groups
learnerActions: In groups of four, take the roles of predictor, questioner, clarifier and summariser
Read a section, then perform your role aloud for the group
Rotate roles for the next section
activities.intendedInsight: Comprehension can be checked and repaired collaboratively, and the routine can then be internalised.
activities.rationale: Adapts reciprocal teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984), which was developed with younger L1 readers; use with adult L2 readers is an adaptation rather than a tested intervention.

activities.title: Spot the contradiction and calibrate
learnerActions: Read a text containing an inserted inconsistency and note anything that does not make sense
Rate your understanding from 1 to 5
Answer comprehension questions and compare your score with your rating
activities.intendedInsight: Feeling that you have understood is not the same as understanding, and monitoring can be trained.
activities.rationale: Targets the cognitive monitoring described by Flavell (1979) and builds calibration of self-judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Keeps reading after losing the thread, hoping it will become clear.
difficulties.revealedBy: Think-alouds with no pauses or repairs; vague summaries.
difficulties.response: Introduce stop-and-check points after each section with a quick self-question.

difficulties.pattern: Uses the same repair, usually rereading, for every problem.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated rereading of sentences whose difficulty lies in an unknown key word or missing background knowledge.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to match repairs to causes: a dictionary for a key unknown word, parsing for a tangled sentence, background reading for a missing concept.

difficulties.pattern: Overestimates their understanding of difficult texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: High self-ratings alongside low comprehension scores.
difficulties.response: Use calibration activities regularly. Do not rely on asking 'Do you understand?'.

diagnostic.task: A text with an inserted inconsistency, followed by a self-rating and four questions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Detects the inconsistency, and the self-rating matches the score.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices confusion but cannot locate it; moderate calibration.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No detection and an overconfident rating.

records.contextNotes: Relevant at all stages. At foundation level, reciprocal teaching can be adapted for short texts. On pre-sessional and in-sessional courses, embed monitoring in authentic reading tasks. Postgraduates more often need to detect subtle misunderstanding of specialist arguments than outright breakdown.
reviewNotes: Evidence for reciprocal teaching comes predominantly from school-age L1 readers; its use with adult L2 academic readers is a reasonable extrapolation, not an intervention tested in this context.

records.summary: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate highlighting and underlining as low-utility study techniques, largely because they require little processing. Annotation adds value when readers summarise, question and connect in their own words, in line with Kiewra's (1985) depth-of-processing account of note-taking, although his review found the benefits of reviewing notes more consistent than the encoding benefits of taking them. Teach a small, purposeful annotation system linked to the reading task and to later note-making, and make the separation of author's and reader's ideas a routine part of it.

activities.title: Annotation audit
learnerActions: Compare two annotated copies of a text: one heavily highlighted, one with sparse highlights and margin notes
Use each copy to answer a question about the text without rereading
Decide which annotation was more useful and why
activities.intendedInsight: What matters is the thinking that annotations record, not how much of the page is marked.
activities.rationale: Shows learners the limits of highlighting as a study technique (Dunlosky et al., 2013).

activities.title: Margin summaries and questions
learnerActions: Write a three-to-six-word summary beside each paragraph
Add a question or response mark where you disagree or want evidence
Use the margin summaries to write a short summary of the text
activities.intendedInsight: Own-word annotations can make later use of a text much easier.
activities.rationale: Own-word summaries require the deeper processing that Kiewra (1985) proposed as the source of encoding benefits, although his review found those benefits less consistent than the benefits of reviewing notes; the summaries are also intended to make later review easier.

difficulties.pattern: Highlights most of the page.
difficulties.revealedBy: Annotated texts with most lines highlighted and no comments.
difficulties.response: Limit highlighting and require margin comments; return to distinguishing main claims from detail. Do not ban highlighting entirely.

difficulties.pattern: Annotations mix the reader's own ideas with the author's without distinguishing them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Later writing that blurs the boundary between source ideas and the writer's own.
difficulties.response: Use distinct symbols for the author's claims, views the author reports and the reader's responses, and link this explicitly to good source use.

difficulties.pattern: Annotates without a purpose, so the annotations do not help with the task.
difficulties.revealedBy: Annotations unrelated to the assignment question.
difficulties.response: Set the purpose first and annotate against it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer a question about a text using only their annotations.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sufficient own-word annotations that allow an accurate answer.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Annotations partly useful, with reliance on highlighted source wording.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Annotations unusable without rereading the text.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit annotation systems. In-sessional and PGT learners benefit from linking annotation to note-making and synthesis. Digital tools change the practicalities but not the principle.
reviewNotes: Research specifically on annotation in L2 academic reading is not represented in the closed bibliography; claims draw on general learning research.

records.summary: Textbooks construct disciplinary knowledge through dense technical vocabulary, taxonomies and nominalised explanation (Halliday & Martin, 1993; Schleppegrell, 2004), which makes them demanding for readers of English as an additional language despite their pedagogical apparatus. Teach learners to use that apparatus and to study actively: building glossaries and concept maps, explaining processes in their own words and self-testing with review questions, in line with the high utility of practice testing (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006). On foundation programmes, coordinate with content teachers where possible.

activities.title: Chapter study cycle
learnerActions: Preview a chapter using its objectives, headings and summary
Read one section and build a glossary of the terms it defines
Close the book, answer the review questions, then check and note errors
activities.intendedInsight: Textbooks are designed to be studied actively, and self-testing reveals what was actually learned.
activities.rationale: Self-testing exploits the testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).

activities.title: Unpacking a technical definition
learnerActions: Find a technical definition or classification in a chapter
Identify the term, the class it belongs to and its distinguishing features
Restate it in everyday language and give an example of your own
activities.intendedInsight: Technical definitions compress knowledge into a predictable structure that can be unpacked.
activities.rationale: Addresses technicality and taxonomy as defining features of disciplinary language (Halliday & Martin, 1993).

difficulties.pattern: Reads the textbook once, like a story, and relies on rereading before tests, a pattern that recognition-based tests can reward.
difficulties.revealedBy: Good familiarity with the material but poor recall under test conditions.
difficulties.response: Teach study cycles built on retrieval practice. Do not recommend rereading or highlighting as the main study method.

difficulties.pattern: Copies definitions into a glossary without understanding them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Verbatim glossary entries and inability to give examples or non-examples.
difficulties.response: Unpack definitions and classifications explicitly and require an own example for each term.

diagnostic.task: Closed-book recall of three definitions and one application question after reading a section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate definitions and a correct application.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Definitions recalled verbatim, but application weak.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Inaccurate definitions.

records.contextNotes: Most relevant on foundation programmes and in first-year undergraduate study, especially in sciences, business and economics. Undergraduate pre-sessional courses can include a textbook unit for students going to textbook-heavy programmes. It is less relevant to postgraduate study.

records.summary: Graph comprehension depends on the reader's knowledge of the display type and of the content as well as on visual features, and novices tend to describe surface features rather than interpret relationships (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002). Friel et al. (2001) distinguish reading the data, reading between the data and reading beyond the data. Multimodal texts make meaning through the interplay of image and words (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006). Teach learners to move deliberately between prose and visuals and to check claims against the data.

activities.title: Text–visual cross-check
learnerActions: Read a results paragraph and its figure
List each claim the text makes about the figure
Check each claim against the figure and mark it accurate, overstated or omitted
activities.intendedInsight: Writers' descriptions of data can overstate or omit, and the visual is evidence to check.
activities.rationale: Develops interpretation beyond surface description (Shah & Hoeffner, 2002; Friel et al., 2001).

activities.title: Reading beyond the data
learnerActions: Identify one pattern in a visual that the text does not mention
Suggest an implication or question it raises
Compare your idea with the writer's discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Visuals often contain more than the text reports.
activities.rationale: Targets the 'reading beyond the data' level described by Friel et al. (2001).

difficulties.pattern: Skips figures and tables altogether.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries omitting key data; inability to answer questions about the data.
difficulties.response: Set tasks that can only be completed using the visuals, and teach readers to pause at each in-text reference to a figure.

difficulties.pattern: Describes visual features ('the blue line goes up') without interpreting the relationship shown.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts of figures that never name the variables or their relationship.
difficulties.response: Practise moving from description of marks to statements about variables and relationships.

difficulties.pattern: Misreads tables with several variables, units or notes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors with row and column headings, units or footnoted exclusions.
difficulties.response: Practise systematic table reading: title, headings, units, notes, then cells.

diagnostic.task: A results paragraph with one overstated claim about an accompanying graph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the overstatement and cites the relevant data.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a mismatch but cannot specify it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the text's claim without consulting the graph.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need basic integration practice. In-sessional and PGT learners in quantitative disciplines need close checking of claims against data; in qualitative and theoretical fields, conceptual models and framework diagrams are more common.

records.summary: Moore (2013) found that academics in history, philosophy and cultural studies understand critical thinking in at least seven different ways, from judgement and scepticism to sensitive reading and self-reflexivity, and Atkinson (1997) questioned whether it can be taught as a culture-free, generic skill. Wallace and Wray (2016) present critical reading as evaluating texts in relation to the reader's own purpose, with constructive as well as sceptical engagement. Teach critical reading as discipline-situated questioning and evaluation, model it with texts from learners' fields, and make explicit that being critical includes recognising strengths.

activities.title: Description versus evaluation sort
learnerActions: Sort statements about a text into descriptive and evaluative
Rewrite two descriptive statements as evaluations with reasons
Discuss what makes an evaluation 'critical' in your discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Critical reading adds a reasoned judgement to an accurate account of the text.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the distinction between describing and evaluating that underpins critical reading for postgraduates in Wallace and Wray (2016).

activities.title: What does 'critical' mean here?
learnerActions: Read short extracts of assessment criteria or feedback from different departments that use the word 'critical'
Identify what each seems to mean by it
Compare your findings with the range of meanings academics report
activities.intendedInsight: 'Critical' has different emphases in different disciplines.
activities.rationale: Draws on Moore's (2013) finding of multiple disciplinary meanings to avoid a one-size-fits-all model.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means finding what is wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques that list only weaknesses, often minor ones.
difficulties.response: Model balanced evaluation that includes strengths, and ask what a text does well for a given purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Criticises what they assume the text says rather than what it says.
difficulties.revealedBy: Criticisms of claims the author did not make.
difficulties.response: Require an accurate summary before evaluation, and check comprehension first.

difficulties.pattern: Applies the same short list of criticisms ('the sample is small', 'the author is biased', 'the source is old') to every text, whatever its discipline or purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques that could be attached to any text; the same criticisms recur across responses to very different readings.
difficulties.response: Ask which strengths and weaknesses matter for this text and this purpose, and model what counts as a significant criticism in the learner's discipline, with input from subject staff where possible. Accept that a well-argued text may warrant a mainly positive evaluation.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is critical reading, and what would it involve for an article in your subject?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes questioning claims, evidence and assumptions relative to a purpose, including strengths, with a discipline-specific example.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes evaluation, but only as finding faults.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates critical reading with careful reading or summary.

records.contextNotes: Introduce at foundation level through accessible argumentative texts. Undergraduate pre-sessionals should link the concept to assessed summary–response and essay tasks; postgraduate pre-sessionals should also show how criticality differs in learners' target disciplines. In-sessional and postgraduate teaching should model discipline-specific criticality, ideally with input from subject staff.
reviewNotes: Whether critical thinking should be taught as a generic skill or only within disciplines is contested; this topic takes a disciplinarily situated position.

records.summary: Toulmin's (2003) model offers a vocabulary of claim, grounds and warrant that helps readers reconstruct arguments, and Walton (2006) shows how argument structure can be diagrammed and evaluated. Wallace and Wray (2016) stress identifying what an author is claiming and how the claims are supported before judging them. Teach reconstruction through outlines and argument maps, using authentic texts in which arguments are embedded in description and literature review, and check reconstructions for fairness to the author.

activities.title: Claim–reasons–evidence outline
learnerActions: Find the main claim of a text and write it as a contestable statement
List the reasons offered and the evidence for each
Check whether the author would accept your outline as fair
activities.intendedInsight: Arguments have a structure that can be reconstructed and checked.
activities.rationale: Uses the claim–grounds structure from Toulmin (2003) as a reading tool.

activities.title: Argument mapping
learnerActions: Draw a box-and-arrow map of a short argumentative text
Mark co-premises, objections and rebuttals
Compare maps with peers and resolve differences by returning to the text
activities.intendedInsight: Mapping exposes the logical structure of an argument and its gaps.
activities.rationale: Diagramming argument structure is set out in Walton (2006), and van Gelder (2005) argues that practice with argument maps supports critical thinking.

difficulties.pattern: Gives the topic as the claim ('The main claim is climate change').
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines whose 'claim' cannot be agreed or disagreed with.
difficulties.response: Teach that a claim is a statement that could be disputed, and practise turning topics into claims.

difficulties.pattern: Lists evidence as if it were the reasons.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines in which statistics appear as reasons without a stated point.
difficulties.response: Distinguish claim, reason and evidence with labelled examples from the same text.

difficulties.pattern: Misses the argumentative force of connectors such as thus, however and nevertheless.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions misidentified; counter-arguments read as the author's position.
difficulties.response: Highlight conclusion indicators and contrastive signals before mapping.

diagnostic.task: A claim–reasons–evidence outline of a 500-word argumentative text.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate, complete and fair reconstruction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The correct claim, but reasons and evidence mixed together.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic given as the claim, followed by a list of content.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners work with accessible argumentative texts. In-sessional and PGT learners apply the skill to disciplinary articles, where arguments are embedded in the reporting of research and in literature reviews.

records.summary: Kuhn (1991) found that many people struggle to distinguish evidence from theory and to judge how well evidence supports a claim, which suggests that evidence evaluation must be taught explicitly. Gal (2002) argues that statistical literacy includes asking critical questions about where data come from, how they were produced and how they are interpreted. Teach evaluation through explicit criteria (relevance, sufficiency, quality) applied to authentic texts, and aim for calibrated judgements rather than wholesale acceptance or dismissal (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Evidence audit
learnerActions: For each main claim in a text, identify the type of evidence offered
Rate its relevance, sufficiency and quality, giving a reason for each rating
Write a one-sentence judgement of how well the claim is supported overall
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence can be strong for one claim and weak for another in the same text.
activities.rationale: Applies explicit criteria to make evaluation systematic (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Questions for a statistical claim
learnerActions: Read a news report of a study
Ask who collected the data, how, from whom, and whether the headline claim follows
Compare the report with the study's abstract
activities.intendedInsight: Reported statistics need checking against their source and the design behind them.
activities.rationale: Uses the critical questions about data that Gal (2002) treats as part of statistical literacy.

difficulties.pattern: Treats any statistic or citation as strong evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations that cite the presence of numbers or references as proof.
difficulties.response: Teach evidence types and their typical limits with contrasting examples.

difficulties.pattern: Dismisses evidence as 'biased' or 'not enough' without specific reasons.
difficulties.revealedBy: Blanket scepticism applied equally to all sources.
difficulties.response: Require a specific reason for every negative judgement and a statement of what evidence would be adequate.

difficulties.pattern: Accepts causal claims based on correlational data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical acceptance of 'X leads to Y' drawn from cross-sectional survey data.
difficulties.response: Teach the correlation–causation distinction with field-relevant examples.

diagnostic.task: A short text making a general claim supported by one statistic and one anecdote; ask how well the claim is supported.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes the mismatch in scope and the limits of each evidence type, and reaches a calibrated judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes one weakness without connecting it to the scope of the claim.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts or dismisses the claim without specific reasons.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduate pre-sessional learners meet general criteria with accessible texts; postgraduate pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners apply them to the sources of assessed source-based writing. PGT and PGR learners apply the evidential standards of their disciplines, which differ, for example, between experimental sciences, social research and the humanities.
