records.summary: Toulmin's (2003) warrant names the often unstated principle that licenses the step from evidence to claim, and Walton (2006) treats the reconstruction of missing premises and the critical questions attached to common argument schemes. Teach learners to ask what must be true for a conclusion to follow and to distinguish a missing premise from an objection. Value and framing assumptions deserve explicit attention because they are often naturalised in disciplinary and policy texts (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Find the missing premise
learnerActions: Read a short argument with a gap between its evidence and its conclusion
Write the premise that would close the gap
Judge whether that premise is acceptable
activities.intendedInsight: Many arguments rest on unstated premises, which may be their weakest part.
activities.rationale: Applies the warrant concept (Toulmin, 2003) and missing-premise reconstruction (Walton, 2006).

activities.title: Reframing an issue
learnerActions: Identify how a text frames an issue, for example as an economic, health or rights question
Rewrite the opening paragraph under a different frame
Discuss how the frame changes what counts as relevant evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Framings carry value assumptions that shape the whole argument.
activities.rationale: Makes value assumptions visible as part of critical reading (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

difficulties.pattern: Offers an objection instead of an assumption ('The assumption is that it might not work').
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Assumptions' that are criticisms rather than premises the author relies on.
difficulties.response: Contrast what the author takes for granted with what could go wrong, using the warrant as a model.

difficulties.pattern: Restates the conclusion as the assumption.
difficulties.revealedBy: Circular 'assumptions' that repeat the claim.
difficulties.response: Test each proposed assumption by asking whether the argument fails without it, starting from a clear reconstruction of the argument.

difficulties.pattern: Finds assumptions only in texts they disagree with.
difficulties.revealedBy: Detailed analysis of uncongenial texts and none of congenial ones.
difficulties.response: Deliberately set texts aligned with learners' own views and use peer questioning.

diagnostic.task: A short argument with an implicit premise; the learner states the premise.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a genuine missing premise and evaluates its acceptability.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Points towards the premise but states it vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the claim or raises an objection.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners practise with accessible policy and argumentative texts. PGT and PGR learners extend the skill to theoretical and paradigmatic assumptions in research.

records.summary: All texts are written from a position, so the aim is not to label texts 'biased' but to understand how perspective shapes selection, framing and language and to judge the consequences for reliability. Wineburg and McGrew (2019) show that professional fact-checkers establish who is behind an unfamiliar source before reading it closely, and Nickerson (1998) reviews how confirmation bias shapes readers' own evaluations. Teach both directions: perspective in the text and bias in the reader.

activities.title: Same issue, two sources
learnerActions: Read two texts on one issue from organisations with different interests
Compare their terminology, the evidence each selects and what each omits
Write a balanced account noting how each perspective shapes the text
activities.intendedInsight: Perspective shows in concrete choices that can be identified without dismissing a source.
activities.rationale: Develops analysis of framing and selection as part of critical reading (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Who is behind this?
learnerActions: Before reading an unfamiliar web source closely, search for information about its author or organisation
Note funding, mission and affiliations
Read the source and discuss how this information affects your evaluation
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing who produced a text helps interpret its perspective.
activities.rationale: Based on the lateral reading practices of professional fact-checkers (Wineburg & McGrew, 2019).

difficulties.pattern: 'This text is biased, so it is useless.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources dismissed on the basis of affiliation alone.
difficulties.response: Distinguish perspective from distortion and evaluate the evidence on its merits.

difficulties.pattern: Recognises bias only in texts they disagree with.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical acceptance of congenial sources.
difficulties.response: Discuss confirmation bias explicitly and ask learners to evaluate a text they agree with.

difficulties.pattern: Misses perspective expressed through framing rather than explicit opinion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that a text is neutral because it never says 'I think'.
difficulties.response: Analyse framing, lexical choice and the treatment of other voices.

diagnostic.task: Two texts on one issue; ask about framing, evidence selection and omissions in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies specific framing, selection and omissions in both texts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies perspective in only one text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Labels one text biased without evidence.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners focus on public, media and policy texts. PGT learners extend the analysis to research funding, researcher positionality and paradigms.

records.summary: Methods critique asks whether a study's design can support its conclusions. Creswell and Creswell (2018) set out the logic of quantitative, qualitative and mixed designs, Gal (2002) frames statistical literacy as asking critical questions about data, and Wasserstein and Lazar (2016) caution against equating statistical significance with importance or truth. Teach a consumer-level set of questions adapted separately to quantitative and qualitative studies, practise with studies from learners' fields, and involve subject specialists where possible.

activities.title: Design–claim match
learnerActions: Read a study's abstract and methods section
Identify the design, sample and measures
Judge whether the conclusion matches what the design can show and suggest a better-calibrated conclusion
activities.intendedInsight: Conclusions should not go beyond what the design can support.
activities.rationale: Applies the logic of research design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018) to reading.

activities.title: Significance versus importance
learnerActions: Read a results paragraph reporting p-values and effect sizes
Explain in plain words what the numbers indicate
Discuss whether the finding matters in practice
activities.intendedInsight: A statistically significant result may be small or unimportant, and a non-significant one is not proof of no effect.
activities.rationale: Draws on the principles in the ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

difficulties.pattern: Applies quantitative criteria to qualitative studies ('the sample is too small to be valid').
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques of qualitative studies focused solely on sample size and generalisability.
difficulties.response: Teach criteria appropriate to qualitative research and discuss the different aims of the two traditions.

difficulties.pattern: Bases critique on the abstract because methods information cannot be found.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic critiques that could apply to any study.
difficulties.response: Practise locating design information in methods sections and appendices.

difficulties.pattern: Equates statistical significance with importance or proof.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'the study proves…' based on p < .05.
difficulties.response: Teach basic interpretation of significance, effect size and confidence intervals.

diagnostic.task: The abstract and methods of a study whose conclusion over-generalises; ask whether the conclusion is justified.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Connects specific design features to the scope of the claim and proposes a calibrated conclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes a limitation but does not connect it to the conclusion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the conclusion as stated.

records.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessionals can introduce it with short empirical studies from learners' fields. Undergraduates in empirical disciplines meet it in later years. PGT learners need it for literature reviews and dissertations. PGR learners need discipline-specific critique; EAP input should complement, not replace, research methods training.
reviewNotes: EAP practitioners may lack expertise in specific research methods; collaboration with subject staff is advisable. The EGAP classification reflects consumer-level critique; specialist appraisal is discipline-specific.

records.summary: Multiple-text comprehension involves constructing a representation of both the content of several documents and the sources themselves and their relationships (Perfetti et al., 1999). Bråten et al. (2009) found that students' trust in and evaluation of sources related to how well they understood an issue across multiple texts, and Spivey (1990) describes discourse synthesis as selecting, organising and connecting content from several sources. Teach sourcing explicitly, use sets of texts that genuinely conflict, and require attributed integration rather than serial summaries.

activities.title: Source-tagged comparison grid
learnerActions: Read three texts on an issue
Complete a grid of claims, each tagged with its source details
Mark agreement, conflict or difference of focus across the texts
activities.intendedInsight: Integrating texts requires tracking who said what, not only what was said.
activities.rationale: Supports construction of a representation that links content to sources (Perfetti et al., 1999) and attention to sources (Bråten et al., 2009).

activities.title: Explaining disagreement
learnerActions: Identify a conflict between two sources
Investigate possible reasons: method, sample, definitions, date, perspective
Write an account that explains the conflict rather than merely reporting it
activities.intendedInsight: Conflicts between sources often have explanations that matter for synthesis.
activities.rationale: Develops the connecting operations of discourse synthesis (Spivey, 1990).

difficulties.pattern: Ignores source information and treats all texts as equally reliable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Integrated accounts that never mention authors, dates or publication venues.
difficulties.response: Require sourcing notes for every text and discuss how source features affect trust.

difficulties.pattern: Summarises each text separately without comparing them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Serial summaries with no cross-reference.
difficulties.response: Use comparison grids and integration prompts that require each point to draw on at least two sources.

difficulties.pattern: Assumes that if sources disagree, one of them must simply be wrong.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts that declare a winner without considering method or scope.
difficulties.response: Explore legitimate reasons for disagreement and discuss knowledge as constructed and contested.

diagnostic.task: Three partly conflicting texts; ask for a brief integrated account.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An attributed integration that explains the conflicts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A comparison that identifies conflicts but does not explain them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Serial summaries without attribution or comparison.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduate pre-sessionals can introduce multiple-text reading with sets of short texts; postgraduate pre-sessionals should make it central to the extended source-based project. Undergraduate in-sessional learners apply it to assignments. PGT and PGR learners need it at scale for literature reviews.

records.summary: Feak and Swales (2009) treat the literature review as a research story in which writers position their work; mapping the literature is its reading counterpart. Kwan (2006) describes the thematic organisation of doctoral literature reviews, and the ACRL (2016) frame of scholarship as conversation captures the idea that sources respond to one another over time. Teach mapping as iterative, visual and conceptual, using concept maps or matrices and citation networks.

activities.title: Concept map of a literature
learnerActions: Write each source on a card or digital note
Group the cards by theme or position and draw the relationships between groups
Mark debates and areas with little research
activities.intendedInsight: A literature has a structure beyond the list of its sources.
activities.rationale: Constructing concept maps is associated with better learning than studying text alone (Nesbit & Adesope, 2006), and the map makes the scholarly conversation visible (ACRL, 2016).

activities.title: Following the conversation
learnerActions: Take an influential article and find works that cite it
Note how later works build on, extend or challenge it
Add these relationships to your map
activities.intendedInsight: Fields develop through dialogue between texts over time.
activities.rationale: Links mapping to positioning one's own work within a research story (Feak & Swales, 2009).

difficulties.pattern: Organises the map source by source rather than by theme or position.
difficulties.revealedBy: Maps that are annotated lists.
difficulties.response: Prompt grouping by theme or position and require at least one relationship between groups.

difficulties.pattern: Feels overwhelmed by the volume of literature and keeps searching without mapping.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ever-growing reference lists with no organising structure.
difficulties.response: Set boundaries for the search, start from review articles and map early.

difficulties.pattern: Misses the influential works on which a field builds.
difficulties.revealedBy: Maps containing only recent articles.
difficulties.response: Use backward and forward citation chaining to identify frequently cited works.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to map ten sources on their topic.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Conceptual grouping with debates, relationships and gaps visible.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Thematic grouping without relationships between groups.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of sources.

records.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessionals can introduce mapping on a small scale in the extended project. Final-year undergraduates use mapping for dissertations. PGT learners need it for literature reviews; PGR researchers use it continuously to position their research and update their understanding of the field.

records.summary: Maton's (2013) concepts of semantic gravity and semantic density describe how theoretical texts operate at high abstraction and condensation, and how understanding involves moving between abstract concepts and concrete cases ('semantic waves'). Meyer and Land (2005) describe threshold concepts as potentially troublesome knowledge that learners may grasp only after a period of confusion. Teach the reading of theory through concept glossaries, plain-language reconstructions and example generation, and normalise multiple readings.

activities.title: Riding the semantic wave
learnerActions: Identify an abstract claim in a theoretical extract
Find or create a concrete example of it
Restate the claim in plain language and link it back to the theory's terms
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding theory involves moving back and forth between the abstract and the concrete.
activities.rationale: Based on the concept of semantic waves (Maton, 2013).

activities.title: Theory glossary
learnerActions: List key terms with the author's own definition of each
Note how each differs from everyday use
Compare with another theorist's use of the same term
activities.intendedInsight: Theory-specific meanings of familiar words need explicit attention.
activities.rationale: Addresses the troublesome character of threshold concepts (Meyer & Land, 2005).

difficulties.pattern: Reads theoretical terms such as discourse, capital or structure in their everyday sense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpretations that make sense only with the everyday meaning.
difficulties.response: Build theory glossaries and contrast everyday and theoretical senses explicitly.

difficulties.pattern: Gets lost in long, abstract, nominalised sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inability to restate the claim of a key sentence.
difficulties.response: Parse key sentences together and unpack nominalisations.

difficulties.pattern: Cannot see what the text is arguing against.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that present the theory without its position in a debate.
difficulties.response: Identify the opposing position the author constructs and how the argument responds to it.

diagnostic.task: A theoretical extract; ask for definitions of two concepts, a restatement of the argument and an example.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Faithful definitions, an accurate argument and an apt example.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate definitions but a vague account of the argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Everyday definitions and no identifiable argument.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduates in the humanities, social sciences and education meet theoretical texts early, and postgraduate pre-sessionals for these fields can include a short theoretical reading. PGT and PGR learners face extended theoretical reading, often of works translated from other languages, where translators' terminological choices add a further layer.

records.summary: A critical response draws on an evaluativist view of knowledge, in which claims are weighed by evidence and argument rather than accepted as certain or dismissed as mere opinion (Hofer & Pintrich, 1997). Wallace and Wray (2016) and Swales and Feak (2012) treat critique as reasoned evaluation grounded in analysis of the text. Teach critical response through structured tasks that move from summary to analysis to evaluation, with models of qualified evaluative language.

activities.title: Summary–analysis–evaluation ladder
learnerActions: Write a two-sentence summary of the text
Identify two features of its argument or evidence
Evaluate each feature with a reason
Combine these into a short response that takes a position
activities.intendedInsight: A critical response is built on an accurate summary and specific analysis.
activities.rationale: Structures the move from comprehension to evaluation (Wallace & Wray, 2016).

activities.title: Test your response in discussion
learnerActions: Prepare a position on a reading for a seminar
Present it with reasons and respond to challenges from peers
Revise your position in writing afterwards
activities.intendedInsight: Critical responses are tested and refined through dialogue.
activities.rationale: Evaluativist thinking involves weighing and revising views in light of argument and evidence (Hofer & Pintrich, 1997).

difficulties.pattern: Gives a personal opinion unconnected to the text ('I agree because it is important').
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses whose reasons do not refer to the text's argument or evidence.
difficulties.response: Require each reason to be linked to a specific feature of the text.

difficulties.pattern: Summarises at length and adds a one-line evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses dominated by summary.
difficulties.response: Limit the summary to a fixed length and scaffold the evaluation with critical questions.

difficulties.pattern: 'Everyone has their own opinion, so all views are equally valid.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Refusal to take a position, or conclusions that simply list views.
difficulties.response: Discuss how academic judgements weigh evidence and argument, and model qualified positions.

diagnostic.task: A 150-word response to a short argumentative article.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A qualified position supported by text-linked reasons, acknowledging strengths and limitations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A position supported by general rather than text-specific reasons.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A summary, or an unsupported opinion.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners practise through short summary–response tasks; on undergraduate and postgraduate pre-sessionals the critical response is usually an assessed reading-into-writing task. In-sessional learners write critiques and reviews of articles. Doctoral researchers apply the skill in literature reviews and peer review.

records.summary: Field (2008) argues that the conventional comprehension approach (listen, answer questions, check answers) tests listening without teaching it, and proposes diagnosing which processes fail. Vandergrift and Goh (2012) similarly treat listening as interacting bottom-up and top-down processes managed by metacognition. For EAP learners the payoff is practical: once they can name where listening breaks down, they can choose targeted practice rather than simply 'more listening'. Keep the model light and anchored in learners' own listening data rather than presented as theory.

activities.title: Transcribe, then explain
learnerActions: Listen twice to a 20–30-second unscripted extract and write down exactly what the speaker said, leaving gaps where unsure
Compare the transcript with the original and mark each mismatch
Sort each mismatch: a known word not recognised, an unknown word, or words heard but the meaning missed
Discuss which category dominated and what that implies for practice
activities.intendedInsight: Many failures happen at word recognition even when the vocabulary is known, and comprehension questions alone hide this.
activities.rationale: Field's process approach uses short transcription and error analysis to expose decoding breakdowns that answer-checking conceals; Goh's diary study found learners frequently reported not recognising words they knew.

activities.title: Listening problem log
learnerActions: After each lecture or practice task, note one moment where understanding broke down and what seemed to happen
Classify each entry as a decoding or a meaning-building problem using a short checklist
Review the log fortnightly with a peer and choose one targeted practice activity
activities.intendedInsight: Listening problems are specific and patterned, so practice can be chosen rather than left to general exposure.
activities.rationale: Vandergrift and Goh's metacognitive approach uses reflection on listening problems to build person and task knowledge; a log makes that reflection routine.

difficulties.pattern: 'My only problem is vocabulary — if I knew more words I would understand.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners can read the transcript of an extract fluently but could not follow it aurally, yet attribute every failure to unknown words.
difficulties.response: Show the transcript after listening and ask learners to underline words they knew but did not catch; the gap between known and recognised words makes the decoding problem visible. Do not dismiss vocabulary size, which does constrain listening, but separate it from speed and accuracy of recognition.

difficulties.pattern: Learners build a plausible interpretation from a few recognised words and topic expectations, and are confident in it even when it is wrong.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that are coherent but contradict the extract, often reflecting what the learner expected the speaker to say.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to verify each prediction against specific words heard on a second listening, and praise checking rather than fluent guessing. Do not teach 'guess from context' as a stand-alone remedy for weak decoders; Field cautions that compensatory strategies cannot substitute for accurate decoding.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe the last time they failed to understand part of a lecture and why. Then play a 20-second extract and ask them to point to where they lost track and whether they heard the words at that point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates specific moments, distinguishes not catching words from not understanding the point, and suggests different remedies for each.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies breakdown points but attributes all of them to vocabulary or speed without distinguishing processes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reports global failure ('it was too fast', 'I understood nothing') and cannot locate or characterise breakdowns.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, present the model through concrete examples and learners' own transcripts rather than terminology. On pre-sessional courses it can frame the whole listening syllabus and justify the balance of short decoding work and extended lecture listening. In-sessionally it is most useful in one-to-one or small-group diagnosis with students who report persistent difficulty in lectures. Persistent difficulty that does not respond to decoding practice may reflect a hearing or auditory processing difference rather than a language problem; refer the student to disability or learning support services and offer captions or transcripts in the meantime.

records.summary: Learners often know a word in writing but fail to recognise its reduced spoken form; Goh (2000) found that not recognising known words was among the problems learners most often reported. Field (2008) recommends short, intensive decoding exercises with authentic or semi-scripted speech, attending to the forms words take in context rather than in isolation, and Rost (2011) describes reduction, assimilation and elision as regular processes that can be taught. Prioritise recognition before production, focus on the high-frequency function words and phrases where most reduction occurs, and keep extracts short enough for close attention.

activities.title: Gapped transcription of function words
learnerActions: Listen to a 10–15-second lecture extract with a transcript from which the function words have been removed
Fill each gap, replaying as needed
Compare with the full transcript and note which weak forms were missed
Repeat with a new extract that features the same forms
activities.intendedInsight: The words that are hardest to hear are often the shortest and most familiar.
activities.rationale: Field's process approach targets the specific forms that cause recognition failure; gapping function words directs attention to weak forms rather than to content words, which learners already prioritise.

activities.title: Citation form versus connected form
learnerActions: Hear a phrase spoken word by word and then in natural connected speech
Write down what changed: sounds lost, merged or linked
Find two further examples of the same pattern in a lecture recording
activities.intendedInsight: Connected-speech changes are systematic, so a small number of patterns explains many recognition problems.
activities.rationale: Rost (2011) presents reduction, assimilation and elision as regular features of spoken English; contrasting the two forms makes the regularities noticeable.

difficulties.pattern: 'Lecturers swallow their words — they don't speak clearly.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners attribute recognition failure to the speaker and expect every word to be fully articulated, as in scripted course-book audio.
difficulties.response: Explain that reduction is normal in fluent speech in every language, including learners' own, and that unstressed words carry little acoustic information because listeners are expected to predict them. Use L1 examples where the group can supply them. Do not present asking lecturers to 'speak clearly' as the main solution.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language gives syllables similar prominence and reduces vowels little expect every syllable to be equally clear and do not register reduced vowels.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcriptions omit or misidentify unstressed function words, and learners insert full vowels when repeating reduced phrases.
difficulties.response: Contrast stressed and unstressed syllables explicitly, using the schwa as a focal point, and practise recognising strings containing several weak forms. Production work can follow, but prioritise recognition first.

difficulties.pattern: Learners have practised mainly with scripted, slowly delivered recordings, so their first authentic lectures feel unintelligible.
difficulties.revealedBy: A large gap between scores on course-book listening and comprehension of authentic lecture extracts.
difficulties.response: Introduce short authentic or semi-scripted extracts early, with transcripts, so that exposure to connected speech is gradual but real.

diagnostic.task: Play a 15-second lecture extract twice and ask for a word-for-word transcription.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Content and function words are largely restored, including weak forms and reduced sequences; errors are minor and do not affect parsing.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Content words are mostly captured but many function words are missing or wrong, and some reduced sequences are misanalysed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Only isolated content words are captured; the transcript cannot be parsed as sentences.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and early pre-sessional level, short intensive decoding work should feature in most listening lessons. Later it is best used diagnostically: when in-sessional students report not being able to follow a particular lecturer, close transcription of a short extract often shows reduction rather than vocabulary to be the barrier.

records.summary: Listeners to English exploit the tendency for content words to begin with a strong syllable (one with a full, unreduced vowel) when hypothesising where words start; Field (2003, 2008) reviews this research and proposes explicit segmentation training for L2 listeners, whose first languages may use different boundary cues. Teaching should combine noticing of strong syllables with lexical and grammatical checking, because a segmentation hypothesis is confirmed or revised as more of the utterance arrives. Short extracts, replay and comparison with transcripts suit this kind of close work.

activities.title: Find the strong syllables first
learnerActions: Listen to a short sentence and mark each strong (clearly pronounced, often stressed) syllable on a line
Predict where content words begin, using the strong syllables
Replay and write the full sentence, checking the predictions
activities.intendedInsight: Strong syllables are useful landmarks for finding content words, although not infallible ones.
activities.rationale: Field (2003) proposes training L2 listeners to use strong syllables as segmentation cues, as listeners to English do.

activities.title: Mishearing repair
learnerActions: Read pairs of plausible mishearings collected from learner transcripts
Listen to the original and decide which version was said
Explain which cue (stress, linking, grammar, context) resolves the ambiguity
activities.intendedInsight: Segmentation is a hypothesis to be checked against grammar and context, not a one-off decision.
activities.rationale: Field (2008) treats word recognition as tentative and revised as listening proceeds; repairing plausible errors rehearses this checking.

difficulties.pattern: Learners may transfer the segmentation routines of their first language (for example syllable-based segmentation in French or mora-based segmentation in Japanese) or expect stress at a fixed position in the word, so English strong syllables are not used, or are misused, as onset cues. The effect is not uniform: listeners whose first language has fixed initial stress may already treat a stressed onset as a likely word boundary.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boundary errors cluster around words that begin with an unstressed syllable (economy, consider, analysis), which are attached to or split from neighbouring words.
difficulties.response: Teach explicitly that weak-initial words are the main exception to the strong-onset tendency and therefore the main source of boundary errors; practise prefix-initial academic words (con-, de-, re-) in context, linked to word-stress work. Diagnose from transcripts rather than assuming a problem from the learner's first language.

difficulties.pattern: Learners commit to the first segmentation they make and interpret the rest of the sentence to fit it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcripts with an early mis-segmentation followed by a forced or ungrammatical reading of the rest of the sentence.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to flag uncertain words during a first listening and revisit them at the end of the sentence; model revision aloud. Accept tentative transcriptions with marked alternatives rather than penalising them.

diagnostic.task: Play a 10-second extract that includes a word beginning with a weak syllable and a linked sequence; ask for a transcription and then ask the learner to explain any revisions they made.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Places boundaries correctly, or corrects an initial error on replay and gives a reason (stress, grammar, context).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Places most boundaries correctly but does not notice errors around weak-initial words.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes non-words or merges and splits words without noticing that the result is ungrammatical.

records.contextNotes: Most important at foundation and pre-sessional level, particularly for learners who have learnt English mainly through reading. In-sessionally, segmentation problems resurface with new technical vocabulary, where learners lack the lexical knowledge to check a hypothesis; pairing listening with pre-taught terminology may help.
reviewNotes: Review response (R2-06): terminology now distinguishes strong (full-vowel) syllables from stressed syllables, and the L1 mechanism is restated as transfer of segmentation routines. The primary sources the reviewer suggested (Cutler & Carter, 1987; Cutler, 2012) are not in the closed bibliography; the claim is cited through Field (2003), which reviews that research, and they could be added if the bibliography is extended.

records.summary: Speed is the problem learners most often name (Graham, 2006), and slower delivery can improve comprehension (Griffiths, 1992). Slowed input is a scaffold rather than a solution, however: Field (2008) attributes much of the sense of speed to decoding that is not yet automatic, so the longer-term remedy is extensive and repeated listening that builds fast word recognition. In the short term, teach learners to keep pace by letting go of missed words and using the restatement and redundancy typical of lecture discourse.

activities.title: Graduated speed replay
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract at reduced speed with a transcript
Listen again at reduced speed without the transcript
Listen at natural speed and summarise
Record which sections still caused problems and why
activities.intendedInsight: Recognition at natural speed tends to improve with repeated exposure to the same speaker and material.
activities.rationale: Griffiths (1992) found slower rates aided comprehension; here rate reduction is used as a scaffold that is withdrawn within the task, moving learners towards natural rates rather than dependence on slow input.

activities.title: Keep going
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section and tick a box each time a word or phrase is lost, but keep listening
After listening, note what was later recovered through restatement, examples or summary
Compare with a partner which missed points were recovered and how
activities.intendedInsight: Lectures repeat and reformulate key content, so missing a word is rarely fatal if attention stays on the stream.
activities.rationale: Goh (2000) found that learners lose subsequent input while dwelling on an earlier problem; practising the decision to move on targets that pattern.

difficulties.pattern: 'Everyone speaks too fast — I need them to slow down.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners rate all authentic material as too fast regardless of actual rate, report low confidence and avoid authentic listening.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the experience, then make progress visible by tracking improvement on the same speaker across repeated listenings; Graham (2006) found learners tend to attribute listening failure to low ability, which undermines persistence. Do not rely only on slowed or scripted material, which delays adaptation to real lectures.

difficulties.pattern: Learners stop to translate or work out a missed word and lose the next segment.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries capture the first part of an extract well and little or nothing after a difficult word.
difficulties.response: Practise continuing past gaps and show that later restatement often resolves them. Avoid pausing recordings after every sentence for comprehension checks, which reinforces word-by-word processing.

difficulties.pattern: Recognition of frequent words is not yet automatic, so even moderate rates overload the learner.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcriptions show missing frequent words even in slower speech.
difficulties.response: Increase the volume of comprehensible listening (graded podcasts, repeated listening to the same recording) and continue decoding work. Strategy instruction alone will not solve this.

diagnostic.task: Play two comparable 60-second extracts by the same speaker, one at 0.8 and one at natural speed, and ask for the key points after each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Captures the main points at natural speed, with only minor additional detail at reduced speed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures main points only at reduced speed but continues to follow the thread at natural speed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Loses the thread at natural speed after the first difficulty and recovers little even at reduced speed.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, slowed or semi-scripted material can bridge to authentic rates but should not replace them. Pre-sessional courses should include unscripted lecture extracts from the outset. In-sessional students facing a fast lecturer benefit most from repeated listening to recordings of that lecturer, which builds speaker-specific familiarity.
reviewNotes: Lecture speech rates vary widely by speaker, discipline and phase; this record deliberately avoids giving a words-per-minute threshold.

records.summary: Accent familiarity affects listening: Major et al. (2002) found that listening test scores could be lower when lectures were delivered by speakers the study classed as non-native, and a shared first language did not consistently help. Perceptual research indicates that listeners adapt to an unfamiliar accent with exposure, and that exposure to several speakers of an accent supports generalisation to new speakers (Bradlow & Bent, 2008). Jenkins (2014) argues that international universities are lingua franca settings in which native-speaker accents should not be treated as the default. Teaching should broaden exposure, build adaptation, and address listener attitudes as well as perception.

activities.title: Accent exposure ladder
learnerActions: Listen two or three times each to short academic talks by several speakers who share an accent
Transcribe a short section from each and note recurring features that caused errors
Listen to a new speaker with the same accent and compare accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptation generalises better when exposure includes several speakers rather than one.
activities.rationale: Bradlow and Bent (2008) report that multi-talker exposure supported talker-independent adaptation to foreign-accented speech; the activity applies this to academic listening as a proposal, not as a tested EAP intervention.

activities.title: Whose accent counts as standard?
learnerActions: Map the accents of lecturers and classmates they will meet, for example from departmental video introductions
Discuss which they find easier and why (familiarity, rate, signposting)
Agree listening and clarification strategies that do not assume one variety is correct
activities.intendedInsight: Difficulty depends on the listener's familiarity and expectations as well as on the speaker.
activities.rationale: Jenkins (2014) documents the dominance of native-speaker norms in university language policy and argues for a lingua franca perspective; making expectations explicit addresses the attitudinal side of accent comprehension.

difficulties.pattern: 'I can only understand British (or American) English; other accents are wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong preference for one prestige variety, reflecting materials used in previous study; dismissive comments about lecturers' or peers' accents.
difficulties.response: Broaden exposure deliberately and discuss the international make-up of staff and students. Rubin (1992) found that listeners' expectations about a speaker affected their comprehension of identical speech, which helps frame accent comprehension as partly the listener's responsibility.

difficulties.pattern: Learners give up on an unfamiliar speaker within the first minute.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension of the opening of a talk is low and does not improve, because attention has been withdrawn.
difficulties.response: Show improvement curves from repeated exposure and set short, achievable goals for new speakers. Avoid restricting early-level learners to 'easy' accents, which delays adaptation.

difficulties.pattern: Words are misrecognised when a speaker places lexical stress differently from the pattern the learner expects.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcription errors cluster on multi-syllable words with shifted stress.
difficulties.response: Use transcription comparison to identify the feature, then practise with that speaker. Field (2005) found that misplaced stress disrupted recognition for both the native and the non-native listeners in his study, so this is a normal listener difficulty rather than a learner deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Listening materials and tests draw almost entirely on a narrow set of prestige accents, so learners first meet the range of accents used at their university in their lectures.
difficulties.revealedBy: Course audio and practice tests feature one or two varieties; learners who score well on them report being unable to follow particular lecturers or peers.
difficulties.response: Course teams should audit listening materials for the range of accents they include and add recordings of lecturers and students from the target institution, with permission. Learners can be shown how to find varied recordings for independent listening.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to listen to a 90-second extract by a speaker whose accent they find difficult and summarise it, then listen to a further 2 minutes by the same speaker and summarise a new section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The second summary is markedly more accurate, and the learner can name what caused the initial difficulty.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some improvement, but the learner cannot identify the cause of difficulty.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No improvement; the learner disengages or dismisses the accent as 'bad English'.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes often rely on a narrow range of audio sources; widen these early. In-sessionally, the key accents are those of the student's own lecturers and peers, and lecture recordings allow targeted exposure. For PGR students, conferences and research seminars bring the widest range of accents, often with less signposting.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-18): topic text now avoids the native/non-native binary except when reporting the categories used by Major et al. (2002) and Field (2005).

records.summary: Young (1994) identified recurring phases in university lectures — discourse structuring, conclusion and evaluation, alongside content, exemplification and interaction — and showed that they interweave rather than occurring in a fixed order, so a lecturer may return to structuring talk many times. Teaching these phases gives learners a top-down frame for meaning-building, but the frame should be presented as a set of expectations, not a template: lectures vary by discipline and lecturer, and interactive formats have become more common (Lynch, 2011).

activities.title: Phase mapping
learnerActions: Listen to a 10-minute lecture extract
Mark each phase on a timeline using colour codes (structuring, content, example, evaluation, interaction)
Compare timelines in groups and replay disputed sections
Identify which phases contained the information they would note
activities.intendedInsight: Lectures repeatedly signal their own structure, and those signals are chances to reorient.
activities.rationale: Applies Young's (1994) phase model; comparing maps shows how phases interleave.

activities.title: Two lecture styles
learnerActions: Watch extracts from a closely scripted lecture and an interactive one on related content
Note where structure is signalled and where it must be inferred
Discuss what each style demands of the listener
activities.intendedInsight: How explicitly structure is signalled varies, so listeners sometimes have to build the structure themselves.
activities.rationale: Lynch (2011) reviews changes in lecture formats towards greater interactivity; contrasting styles prepares learners for variation rather than a single model.

difficulties.pattern: 'The introduction is just the lecturer talking; the real lecture starts later.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners miss or do not note the preview and later cannot see how sections relate.
difficulties.response: Show how the preview predicts the lecture's sections, use it to set up a note frame, and return to it at the end of the lecture.

difficulties.pattern: Learners expect lectures to follow the tidy linear structure of course-book recordings and are disoriented by recursion, asides and interaction.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion when a lecturer returns to an earlier point or opens questions mid-lecture.
difficulties.response: Use authentic lectures early and treat phase switching as normal; Young's (1994) finding that phases interweave is a useful framing to share with learners.

diagnostic.task: Play the first 3 minutes of a lecture and ask the learner to predict the sections of the rest; then play two later 1-minute segments and ask which section and which phase each belongs to.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Predicts sections accurately from the preview, identifies phases correctly and explains the cues used.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Predicts sections but misclassifies evaluation or example phases as content.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot use the preview to predict, and experiences the lecture as undifferentiated.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from explicit phase labels applied to short, well-structured lectures on familiar topics. Pre-sessional courses should use full-length authentic lectures and link phases to note frames. In-sessionally, analysing a recording from a student's own module reveals discipline- and lecturer-specific patterns.

records.summary: Chaudron and Richards (1986) found that macro-markers aided recall of a lecture whereas micro-markers did not, while Flowerdew and Tauroza (1995) found that micro-markers did aid comprehension; the effect of markers is therefore not uniform and probably depends on listeners and materials. Thompson (2003) showed that lecturers signal organisation through intonation as well as words, and that listening materials tend to under-represent this. Teach a working inventory of macro-markers drawn from authentic lecture language, such as the discourse-organising bundles Biber et al. (2004) found in classroom teaching, and draw attention to prosodic boundaries.

activities.title: Marker hunt and prediction
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section and pause after each macro-marker
Predict what will come next (new topic, example, summary, return)
Continue listening to check the prediction
Add the marker to a personal list organised by function
activities.intendedInsight: Markers are cues for prediction, not just phrases to recognise.
activities.rationale: Uses macro-markers, which Chaudron and Richards (1986) found aided recall, as triggers for top-down prediction.

activities.title: Hearing structure without words
learnerActions: Listen to an extract in which a topic shift is signalled by a pause and pitch reset with little lexical signalling
Mark where they think a new section begins
Compare with a transcript and discuss which cues they used
activities.intendedInsight: Lecturers signal structure through the voice as well as through words.
activities.rationale: Thompson (2003) found intonation working alongside text-structuring metadiscourse in lectures; this targets a cue that materials under-represent.

difficulties.pattern: Learners listen for formal written connectors (firstly, in conclusion) and miss the informal markers lecturers actually use (so, right, OK, what we're going to look at now).
difficulties.revealedBy: Topic transitions marked by informal or reduced markers go unnoticed; notes run sections together.
difficulties.response: Build the marker inventory from lecture corpora and recordings rather than from written connector lists; Biber et al. (2004) show that classroom teaching uses many discourse-organising bundles that differ from written ones.

difficulties.pattern: Short micro-markers are not perceived because they are unstressed and run into the following words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcriptions omit so, now, right, and learners do not notice the shift these words signal.
difficulties.response: Include marker-plus-clause sequences in short decoding exercises, treating recognition of markers as a decoding goal as well as a discourse one.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a transcript of a 2-minute lecture extract with the markers removed; ask them to listen, insert the markers they hear and label each one's function.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Inserts most markers, including informal ones, with correct functions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures formal macro-markers but misses or mislabels informal or reduced micro-markers.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Captures few markers and cannot identify their functions.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners need explicit inventories and recognition practice; later pre-sessional work should shift to prediction and to lecturers who signal less explicitly. In-sessionally, the focus moves to discipline- and lecturer-specific signalling habits, including transitions led by slides rather than by speech.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-18): coh.spoken-signposting has been merged into prs.signposting (production). This topic is the reception counterpart. The former soft edge from prs.signposting has been removed so that the PRS strand can make prs.signposting depend on this topic (recognition before production) without creating a cycle.

records.summary: Deroey and Taverniers (2012) catalogued the lexicogrammatical patterns lecturers use to mark relevance and showed that these markers both highlight content and manage what students should attend to, including what will be assessed. Because importance is also marked prosodically (Thompson, 2003), teaching should combine an inventory of verbal markers with attention to stress, pausing and repetition. Learners should practise acting on markers — starring, boxing, prioritising in review — not just recognising them.

activities.title: Relevance marker log
learnerActions: Listen to an authentic lecture and pause each time the lecturer marks something as important or unimportant
Write down the marker and the point it flags
Group the markers by form (verb, noun, adjective or adverb, reference to assessment, voice only)
Compare the flagged points with the lecture's slides and note any that appeared only in speech
activities.intendedInsight: Lecturers repeatedly tell students what matters, and the signals can be learnt.
activities.rationale: Builds on the types of lexicogrammatical relevance markers identified in lecture data by Deroey and Taverniers (2012).

activities.title: Spot the emphasis
learnerActions: Read a transcript of a lecture extract from which verbal relevance markers have been removed
Listen and mark where the speaker signals importance through voice alone
Compare with the original recording and transcript
activities.intendedInsight: Importance is signalled through the voice as well as through words.
activities.rationale: Thompson (2003) showed that intonation contributes to signalling in lectures alongside metadiscourse.

difficulties.pattern: Learners give every point equal weight and do not respond to signals of importance.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes without hierarchy; points the lecturer flagged as key are missing from recall tasks.
difficulties.response: Teach relevance markers explicitly and require visual prioritisation (stars, boxes) in notes; review notes against a list of the points the lecturer flagged.

difficulties.pattern: Learners attend mainly to lexical content and, especially when decoding load is high, do not use the speaker's voice (heavy stress, slowing, pausing, repetition) as a cue to importance.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners catch verbal relevance markers but miss points emphasised by voice alone.
difficulties.response: Contrast the same sentence delivered with and without emphatic stress and ask what changes; link to production work on prominence so that perception and production reinforce each other.

difficulties.pattern: 'If it isn't on the slides, it isn't important.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Attention drops when the lecturer moves away from slide content; points flagged orally are absent from notes.
difficulties.response: Show examples in which lecturers flag oral-only content as important or assessable, and ask learners to collect such moments from their own lectures.

diagnostic.task: After a 10-minute extract, ask: 'What three things did the lecturer most want you to remember, and how did you know?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Retrieves the flagged points and names verbal or prosodic cues for each.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Retrieves some flagged points but relies on slide content, or cannot say how importance was signalled.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists points at random or simply the first points heard, with no awareness of signalling.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit teaching with clear examples. In-sessional UG and PGT students benefit from analysing their own lecturers' relevance marking, which can be idiosyncratic and is often tied to assessment.

records.summary: Lectures share many features of conversation (Biber, 2006), including personal narrative, humour and asides, and Young's (1994) phase model shows how such material sits among structuring and content phases. Asides may carry cultural references that are opaque to newcomers, a cross-cultural dimension of listening that Flowerdew and Miller (2005) include in their model. Teach learners to recognise departure and return, to judge an aside's purpose, and to protect the main thread in their notes, recognising that anecdotes often serve as memorable illustrations of key points.

activities.title: Thread and tangent
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract and draw a line for the main thread, branching off when the lecturer digresses
Note the words or voice changes that signalled departure and return
Decide whether each branch illustrated a main point or was incidental
activities.intendedInsight: Digressions are signalled and often have a purpose.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the movement between content phases and conversational material characteristic of lecture discourse.

activities.title: Does the reference matter?
learnerActions: Listen to an aside that uses humour or a cultural reference
Discuss in groups what knowledge it assumes
Decide whether it matters for understanding the point, and how they could find out if unsure
activities.intendedInsight: Missing some references is normal; the skill is judging whether it matters.
activities.rationale: Addresses the cross-cultural dimension of lecture listening described by Flowerdew and Miller (2005) without treating it as a deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Learners record anecdotes or jokes as main content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes devote space to the anecdote and omit the point it illustrated.
difficulties.response: After each anecdote ask 'Why did the lecturer tell this story?' and note the point, not the story.

difficulties.pattern: Learners lose the thread after a digression and do not recognise the return.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes stop or become fragmented after an aside.
difficulties.response: Teach return markers explicitly and suggest leaving a visible gap in notes during a digression, resuming with a heading when the lecturer returns.

difficulties.pattern: Learners feel excluded or anxious when they miss humour or cultural references.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports of feeling lost; disengagement after jokes.
difficulties.response: Normalise the experience as something anyone new to a context meets, and avoid presenting any national style of humour as something learners lack.

diagnostic.task: Play a lecture extract with a 1-minute digression and ask for a three-sentence summary, then ask what the digression was for.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The summary keeps the main thread; the digression is identified and its function judged.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The main thread is captured but the digression is over-represented or its link is not seen.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The summary is dominated by the digression or breaks off at it.

records.contextNotes: Less a foundation priority than a pre-sessional and in-sessional one, where authentic and conversational lecturing styles are common. In discussion-led PGT modules, asides often carry disciplinary values and practitioner knowledge that are worth noticing.

records.summary: Selecting main points draws on meaning-building: listeners construct a representation of the speaker's argument and decide what is central, using discourse cues and prior knowledge (Field, 2008; Rost, 2011). It also depends on decoding fluency and vocabulary: Nation (2006) estimated that around 6,000–7,000 word families are needed for 98% coverage of spoken English, and van Zeeland and Schmitt (2013) suggest adequate listening comprehension may be possible at somewhat lower coverage, with considerable individual variation. Main-point work should therefore be paired with vocabulary development and should move from cue-supported selection towards inferring importance where cues are sparse.

activities.title: Rank and justify
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section and note up to six points
In pairs, rank the points by importance and justify the ranking with cues heard (previews, relevance markers, time spent, summaries)
Compare the ranking with the lecturer's own summary or slides
activities.intendedInsight: Importance is signalled by several converging cues that can be used deliberately.
activities.rationale: Encourages meaning-building that integrates discourse cues, as described by Field (2008).

activities.title: Claim or support?
learnerActions: Read a list of statements taken from a lecture they have just heard
Label each as main claim, example, evidence or restatement
Rebuild a hierarchy diagram of the section and check it against the recording
activities.intendedInsight: Main points and supporting material have different functions, which determines what to note and how.
activities.rationale: Making the hierarchy explicit connects listening comprehension to note-taking and summary.

difficulties.pattern: Learners treat memorable details (figures, names, vivid examples) as the main points.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries list salient details but omit the more abstract claim they supported.
difficulties.response: After each example, ask 'What was this an example of?' and practise abstracting from examples to claims. Avoid teaching 'note the numbers' as a general strategy.

difficulties.pattern: Decoding takes so much attention that little is left for following the argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners can repeat phrases verbatim but cannot say what the point was.
difficulties.response: Reduce decoding load through preparation and repeated listening, then focus a later listening on structure. Do not read this as a lack of critical or analytical ability.

difficulties.pattern: Learners expect each main point to be stated explicitly once, as in a topic sentence, and miss points developed cumulatively.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners identify explicitly announced points but not points the lecturer builds towards inductively.
difficulties.response: Use lectures with inductive structure and ask learners to formulate the point the lecturer was building towards before it is stated.

diagnostic.task: After a 5-minute extract, ask for the main point in one sentence and two supporting details.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Abstracts the main point accurately and subordinates the details correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures the main point only partly or confuses it with a detail; the details themselves are accurate.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists fragments or details without any central point.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need short, explicitly signalled lectures on accessible content. Pre-sessional work should include full lectures linked to note-taking and integrated writing tasks. For PGT students in fields where lectures argue cumulatively, practise identifying points that are built rather than announced.
reviewNotes: The coverage figures cited are estimates for general spoken English; lecture-specific coverage requirements may differ and depend on technical vocabulary.

records.summary: The planning stage of Vandergrift and Goh's (2012) metacognitive cycle — setting goals and predicting content and vocabulary — is the classroom counterpart of lecture preparation. Prior knowledge supports meaning-building, but Field (2008) cautions that strong expectations can lead listeners to hear what they predicted, so predictions must be checked rather than trusted. Slides and readings posted in advance make preparation feasible for many lectures; the teaching task is to turn them into a short, sustainable routine that includes how key terms sound.

activities.title: Twenty-minute preparation routine
learnerActions: Skim the slides and note the likely sections
List up to ten key terms and check their meaning and pronunciation
Write three questions the lecture is likely to answer
After the lecture, tick the questions answered and note anything unexpected
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation makes a lecture more predictable, but predictions must be checked against what is said.
activities.rationale: Applies the planning and verification stages of Vandergrift and Goh's (2012) pedagogical cycle to lecture listening.

activities.title: Prediction versus delivery
learnerActions: Predict the content of a lecture section from its slide
Listen and note where the lecture went beyond or departed from the slide
Discuss what would have been missed by relying on the slides alone
activities.intendedInsight: Slides outline a lecture; they do not contain it.
activities.rationale: Field (2008) notes that top-down expectation can override what is actually said; contrasting prediction with input trains checking.

difficulties.pattern: 'I don't have time to prepare for every lecture.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparation is attempted in full for a week or two and then abandoned.
difficulties.response: Teach a minimal 10-minute version (structure and key terms only) for heavy weeks, and a fuller version for the most difficult modules.

difficulties.pattern: Learners pre-learn the spelling and meaning of key terms but not their pronunciation, so do not recognise them when spoken.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners know a term in writing but report never hearing it in the lecture where it was used repeatedly.
difficulties.response: Build pronunciation checking (dictionary audio, earlier lecture recordings) into term preparation, with stress marked on the term list.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read the slides thoroughly beforehand and then stop listening attentively during the lecture.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lecture notes simply reproduce slide text.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to annotate slides during the lecture only with what is said and not shown, and review those annotations afterwards.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what they did before their last lecture, then give them a slide deck and 10 minutes to prepare while you observe.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Works systematically: identifies structure, lists terms with pronunciation, writes predictions, and explains how they will use them during the lecture.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reads the slides and checks the meaning of some vocabulary, without structure or pronunciation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does no preparation, or reads the slides without any specific focus.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, preparation can be scaffolded with teacher-provided term lists and prediction questions. Pre-sessional courses should build independence. In-sessionally, students' real module materials make the routine immediately useful, and PGT students with heavy reading loads need efficient, prioritised preparation.

records.summary: Biber (2006) found that stance expressions are frequent in university classroom teaching, so lecturers routinely signal evaluation as well as content. In speech, stance is carried jointly by lexis, the framing of reported views and prosody, and scepticism or irony may be carried largely by the voice. Flowerdew and Miller (2005) include a critical dimension in their model of second language listening. Link this topic to written stance work (Hyland, 2005), but foreground spoken-specific cues.

activities.title: Whose voice?
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section that presents several positions
Note each position and label it reported, endorsed, questioned or rejected
Underline the words, or describe the delivery, that told them
activities.intendedInsight: Lecturers often present views they do not hold, and the cues that mark distance can be subtle.
activities.rationale: Applies the distinction between the speaker's own claims and attributed claims to speech, where prosody adds cues not available in writing.

activities.title: Same words, different stance
learnerActions: Hear the same sentence delivered neutrally, approvingly and sceptically
Identify the stance each conveys and the vocal cues involved
Find a similar moment in a lecture recording and discuss it
activities.intendedInsight: Delivery can qualify or even reverse the literal meaning.
activities.rationale: Makes prosodic stance cues noticeable for learners who attend mainly to words; relates to the critical dimension of listening in Flowerdew and Miller (2005).

difficulties.pattern: Learners take every statement in a lecture as the lecturer's own view or as established fact, a pattern common among new university students of all backgrounds, especially where earlier courses presented content as settled knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes and later essays attribute to the lecturer positions the lecturer reported in order to criticise them.
difficulties.response: Teach spoken reporting frames (some people would argue…, the standard view is…) and make explicit that lecturers often present positions in order to evaluate them; this is a convention of the genre that new students need to learn.

difficulties.pattern: Ironic or sceptical delivery is missed and the literal meaning recorded.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes record ironic remarks as straightforward claims.
difficulties.response: Contrast literal and ironic delivery of the same sentence and flag irony when it occurs in class recordings.

diagnostic.task: After a 3-minute extract presenting a debate, ask: 'Which view does the lecturer favour, and what makes you think so?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the favoured view correctly and cites both lexical and prosodic cues.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the favoured view from lexical cues only, or partly confuses reported and endorsed views.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish the lecturer's view from the views reported.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG courses can introduce stance in lectures alongside written stance; on pre-sessional PG courses it is a core listening skill because lectures and seminars present contested positions from the start. PGT and PGR students in the social sciences and humanities meet lectures and seminars in which stance on contested theory is central; in STEM fields stance more often concerns the certainty of findings and evaluation of methods.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no source specifically on prosodic cues to stance or irony in L2 lecture listening; the prosodic claims are general and could be strengthened with a verified source.

records.summary: Basturkmen (2002) showed that meaning in seminar discussion is negotiated across several turns and speakers rather than in neat question–answer exchanges, and Basturkmen (2003) found that interaction patterns change when a tutor joins a student discussion. Subject lecturers also expect students to participate in class discussion (Ferris & Tagg, 1996), which requires following it first. Following such talk means tracking participants and their positions as well as content. Use authentic or realistic recordings of student discussion and link listening tasks directly to preparation for participation.

activities.title: Discussion map
learnerActions: Listen to a recorded seminar extract
Draw participants as nodes and arrows showing who responds to whom
Label each arrow (agrees, challenges, extends, asks)
Compare maps and replay disputed sections
activities.intendedInsight: Discussion has structure, built from relationships between turns.
activities.rationale: Reflects Basturkmen's (2002) finding that meaning in seminars is co-constructed across turns.

activities.title: Tutor in, tutor out
learnerActions: Compare two short recordings of a group discussion, with and without a tutor
Note differences in who speaks, turn length and how ideas are developed
Discuss what each pattern means for following and joining in
activities.intendedInsight: Discussion dynamics vary with participants and roles.
activities.rationale: Based on Basturkmen's (2003) comparison of discussion with and without the tutor present.

difficulties.pattern: Learners concentrate on decoding each speaker and lose track of how contributions relate.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report fragments of content but not who said what or how contributions connected.
difficulties.response: Use mapping tasks and set a second listening focused on relationships rather than content.

difficulties.pattern: Peers' varied accents, overlapping talk and fast exchanges lead learners to disengage.
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence in discussions; comments such as 'I couldn't follow, so I couldn't speak'.
difficulties.response: Build exposure gradually, and teach confirmation checks as legitimate participation. Avoid treating speed of response as the measure of good participation.

diagnostic.task: Play a 3-minute discussion and ask: 'What was the disagreement, and who was on each side?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the disagreement accurately and attributes positions correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the topic and some positions, with misattribution.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify any disagreement or attribute positions.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should include listening to recorded seminars before learners lead their own. In UG and PGT programmes with assessed participation this is a priority. PGR students face research group meetings and conference question sessions with faster, more specialised exchanges. Overlapping talk is particularly hard for deaf and hard-of-hearing students and for some autistic students; turn-taking ground rules, live captions and a shared written record of the discussion make following it accessible, and should be treated as normal practice rather than special treatment.

records.summary: Multimedia learning research suggests that learning from words and pictures depends on how the two are coordinated, and that on-screen text duplicating speech can compete for attention (Mayer, 2009). Rowley-Jolivet (2002) showed how central visuals are to scientific conference presentations, and the same holds for many lectures. For L2 listeners, decoding speech competes with reading slides, so teach them to use slides for orientation and speech for content, to annotate rather than copy, and to resolve spoken references to visuals.

activities.title: Slide plus
learnerActions: Receive a slide deck before a recorded lecture section
While listening, add only information that is said but not shown
Compare annotations with a partner to see what each captured
activities.intendedInsight: The value of attending a lecture lies largely in what is said beyond the slides.
activities.rationale: Directs attention to the spoken channel and away from reading text the speaker is also saying, the redundancy problem Mayer (2009) describes.

activities.title: Follow the pointer
learnerActions: Watch a lecturer explain a graph or diagram
Pause at each spoken reference (this, here, that peak) and point to the element meant
Give a short spoken explanation of the figure to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken references to visuals only work if the listener tracks both channels.
activities.rationale: Visual discourse is integral to academic presentation (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002); practising reference resolution is intended to build integration of the two channels.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read slides in full while the lecturer speaks and miss what is said.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes reproduce slide text; spoken explanations and examples are absent.
difficulties.response: Encourage reading slides before the lecture so that listening can take priority during it; annotate rather than copy.

difficulties.pattern: Learners cannot match spoken references to features of a graph because the graph type is unfamiliar.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion when the lecturer refers to axes, trends or regions of a diagram.
difficulties.response: Pre-teach the relevant graph conventions and trend vocabulary, and review the visuals before the lecture.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a slide containing a graph and play the lecturer's 1-minute explanation of it; ask them to annotate the slide with what was said about each feature.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Annotations are linked to the correct features and include spoken-only content.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some correct links, but annotations largely repeat what is already on the slide.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot link speech to the visual; annotations are absent or copied.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, integrate this with graph reading and data commentary. In-sessionally, slides from students' own modules allow practice with real materials. Disciplines differ: some lectures are equation- or board-led, others rely on image or text slides. Spoken references such as 'this curve here' exclude blind and partially sighted students; teachers can model verbal description of visuals, which can also help every listener.
reviewNotes: Mayer's principles derive largely from experiments with first-language learners; their application to L2 lecture listening is an extrapolation.

records.summary: Recordings give L2 listeners the control over pace and repetition that live lectures lack, and captions can support listening comprehension and vocabulary learning (Montero Perez et al., 2013). Recordings are also easily used for low-utility study: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate rereading as low in utility, and passive rewatching is analogous. Lynch (2011) reviews the growing role of technology in academic listening. Teach learners to mark gaps during the live lecture, replay selectively, verify automatic captions, and turn what they review into retrieval practice.

activities.title: Mark, replay, repair
learnerActions: During a live or simulated lecture, mark moments of difficulty in notes with a symbol and approximate time
Afterwards, replay only those sections, with captions if helpful
Complete the notes and write one question to test themselves on later
activities.intendedInsight: Targeted replay is quicker and more useful than rewatching everything.
activities.rationale: Combines monitoring during listening with retrieval practice afterwards, rather than passive rewatching, which resembles the low-utility rereading discussed by Dunlosky et al. (2013).

activities.title: Check the captions
learnerActions: Watch a short lecture section with automatic captions
Identify caption errors on technical terms and names using the slides or reading
Discuss when captions help and when they mislead
activities.intendedInsight: Automatic captions are a useful but fallible support.
activities.rationale: Captions can support L2 listening (Montero Perez et al., 2013), but automatic captions are often unreliable for specialist terms and names.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll watch the recording later' — and then either does not, or rewatches everything passively.
difficulties.revealedBy: A growing backlog of unwatched recordings; notes no better after rewatching.
difficulties.response: Agree a specific replay plan with time limits and targets. Avoid suggesting recordings as a remedy for every listening problem.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read captions as a text and stop listening.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension drops sharply when captions are removed.
difficulties.response: Alternate captioned and uncaptioned replays, using captions to check rather than to follow. This advice is for listening practice only: for deaf and hard-of-hearing students, and some students with auditory processing differences, captions and transcripts are an access requirement and should never be withdrawn.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how they would use the recording of a lecture they found difficult.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes targeted replay of marked sections, verification of terms and a time limit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Plans to rewatch the whole lecture, possibly with captions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no plan, or intends to rely on recordings instead of attending.

records.contextNotes: Many foundation and pre-sessional students meet lecture capture for the first time, so establish habits early. In UG and PGT programmes, recordings are most valuable for difficult lecturers and dense modules. Institutional recording policies and caption quality vary.
reviewNotes: Evidence on how lecture capture relates to attendance and attainment is mixed and not represented in the bibliography.
