records.summary: Vandergrift and Goh (2012) propose a metacognitive pedagogical sequence — planning and predicting, first verification, second verification, final verification and reflection — that embeds strategy use in repeated listening to the same text. Vandergrift and Tafaghodtari (2010) reported that learners taught in this way outperformed a comparison group, with less skilled listeners gaining most. Field (2008) cautions that strategies compensate for decoding gaps rather than remove them, so metacognitive work should run alongside decoding practice rather than replace it.

activities.title: Metacognitive listening cycle
learnerActions: Predict the content and some vocabulary of a lecture extract from its title and first slide
Listen and check predictions, noting difficulties
Compare with a partner and listen again for unresolved points
Listen once more with a transcript for final verification
Write a short reflection on what helped and what to try next time
activities.intendedInsight: Listening can be managed rather than simply endured.
activities.rationale: Follows the pedagogical sequence described by Vandergrift and Goh (2012) and examined empirically by Vandergrift and Tafaghodtari (2010).

activities.title: Listening diary
learnerActions: Record each week what they listened to, what was difficult and what they tried
Rate their confidence for each listening
Review entries monthly to identify recurring patterns and set a new goal
activities.intendedInsight: Knowledge of oneself as a listener is built through reflection over time.
activities.rationale: Goh (2000) used learner diaries to reveal listening problems; reflection develops the person, task and strategy knowledge that Flavell (1979) identifies as metacognitive knowledge.

difficulties.pattern: Learners equate 'strategy' with guessing and rely on it in place of listening closely.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident but inaccurate summaries; little change between first and second listening.
difficulties.response: Emphasise the verification stages of the cycle and make learners point to the words that support each inference. Revisit the distinction between decoding and meaning-building.

difficulties.pattern: Learners treat reflection as a task done for the teacher and write generic entries.
difficulties.revealedBy: Log entries such as 'it was difficult' or 'I need more practice' with no specific moment or action.
difficulties.response: Model specific entries, keep logs short, and link each reflection to a concrete practice choice the learner then carries out.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What do you do when you lose track during a lecture?' Then ask about the last time it happened.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific monitoring and repair actions linked to the type of problem, and some evaluation of whether they worked.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions general strategies ('I try to guess') without linking them to problem types or evaluating them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Says they stop listening, or has no strategies beyond asking a friend later.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level the cycle can be run fully with teacher guidance on short texts. On pre-sessional courses it should become a routine learners can run independently with recordings. In-sessionally, the reflective log is the most portable element and works well in self-access or tutorial settings.

records.summary: Biber (2006) found that university classroom talk contains a substantial amount of procedural and directive language, and Biber et al. (2004) identified directive bundles (for example I want you to) among those frequent in classroom teaching. Obligation is often expressed indirectly or with hedging, so learners must interpret the strength of an instruction as well as its content. Teach learners to turn spoken instructions into checklists, to query conditions and deadlines, and to verify against written sources.

activities.title: Briefing to checklist
learnerActions: Listen to an assignment briefing
Write a checklist of requirements and deadlines
Compare with the written brief and identify discrepancies or information given only orally
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken briefings often add to or clarify the written brief.
activities.rationale: Links real-time listening to an action outcome using the kind of procedural talk Biber (2006) found common in university settings.

activities.title: Must, should or might?
learnerActions: Listen to extracts containing directives of varying strength
Rank them from obligatory to optional
Discuss which indirect forms nevertheless signal obligation
activities.intendedInsight: Indirect phrasing can still carry strong obligation.
activities.rationale: Directive bundles in classroom teaching often take indirect forms (Biber et al., 2004).

difficulties.pattern: Learners interpret hedged directives (you might want to look at…) as genuinely optional suggestions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Required preparation or tasks are missed after briefings phrased indirectly.
difficulties.response: Make explicit the force of common indirect directives in academic settings and encourage checking with the lecturer when the strength is unclear.

difficulties.pattern: Learners rely on peers' messages for instructions rather than checking official sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in deadlines or formats traced to second-hand information.
difficulties.response: Teach a verification routine using the learning platform and course handbook after every briefing.

difficulties.pattern: Institutional terms in briefings (extension, extenuating or mitigating circumstances, resit or make-up examination, submission point) are misunderstood, and the terms and procedures differ between institutions and countries.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners act on a briefing but misapply a procedure, for example confusing an extension with extenuating circumstances.
difficulties.response: Pre-teach the institutional vocabulary of the learners' own programme and target context, and check it in context.

diagnostic.task: Play a 1-minute laboratory safety briefing and ask the learner to list the steps in order and any prohibitions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All steps are listed in order and all prohibitions identified.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most steps are listed, but the order or conditions are confused.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Key steps or prohibitions are missing.

records.contextNotes: Particularly important at foundation level, where students are new to institutional procedures, and for practical disciplines with laboratories, studios or fieldwork. Pre-sessional courses can use real briefings for the course's own assessments. Spoken-only briefings disadvantage deaf and hard-of-hearing students and students who process speech slowly; encourage lecturers to provide the same information in writing.

records.summary: Recorded academic media combine features of lectures and conversation and are often less explicitly structured than lectures, with interview and panel formats that require tracking several speakers. Lynch (2011) notes that technology is changing how students encounter academic listening. Treat media as sources to be evaluated and cited, not only as listening practice, and exploit the control that recordings give listeners (replay, transcripts, speed adjustment) as Rost (2011) discusses for self-directed listening.

activities.title: Podcast as source
learnerActions: Choose a podcast episode or recorded talk relevant to an assignment topic
Evaluate its credibility using a short checklist (speaker, affiliation, evidence, date)
Take timestamped notes on relevant content
Write a short paraphrase of one point with a citation that includes a timestamp
activities.intendedInsight: Audio sources can be used and cited like written ones, with the same critical scrutiny.
activities.rationale: Integrates listening with source evaluation and citation, which are usually taught only for written sources.

activities.title: Who said what on the panel?
learnerActions: Listen to a recorded academic interview or panel discussion
Note each speaker's main contribution
Identify where speakers agree or disagree and with whom
activities.intendedInsight: Recorded discussions require the same tracking of speakers and positions as live seminars.
activities.rationale: Extends work on following multi-party talk to recorded media, where the listener can replay to check attribution.

difficulties.pattern: Learners treat any podcast or video as authoritative because it sounds expert.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments cite popular or promotional audio sources without evaluation.
difficulties.response: Apply the source-evaluation criteria used for written sources, and compare an academic and a popular treatment of the same topic.

difficulties.pattern: Learners listen to whole episodes without a focus and cannot later locate relevant content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes are long and untargeted; no timestamps.
difficulties.response: Set a question before listening, use chapter markers and transcripts, and record timestamps as part of note-taking.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 10-minute section of an academic podcast and a question; ask for relevant points with timestamps and a credibility judgement.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Relevant points with accurate timestamps and a reasoned credibility judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Relevant points but no timestamps, or a credibility judgement based only on impression.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Untargeted notes and no evaluation.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce academic media as optional sources for projects. In UG and PGT programmes they are increasingly set as module materials. PGR students use recorded talks and podcasts to keep up with their field and should cite them accurately.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no source specifically on L2 learners' use of academic podcasts or recorded talks; this guidance is practice-based.

records.summary: Kiewra (1985) distinguished the encoding function of note-taking from the external-storage function and argued that reviewing notes typically contributes more to achievement than taking them. This framing helps learners see why notes must be organised and complete enough to use later, and why condensing ideas in one's own words matters. Mueller and Oppenheimer's (2014) finding that more verbatim note-taking was associated with poorer conceptual performance illustrates the encoding point, although Morehead et al. (2019) did not replicate its central claims about laptops robustly (see digital notes).

activities.title: Notes a week later
learnerActions: Take notes on a short lecture
A week later, without re-listening, use the notes to answer questions on the lecture
Identify what in the notes helped and where they failed
activities.intendedInsight: Notes must work as a record for a future self who has forgotten the lecture.
activities.rationale: Makes the external-storage function concrete (Kiewra, 1985).

activities.title: Transcribe or transform
learnerActions: Take notes on one short extract by writing down as much as possible word for word
Take notes on a second, comparable extract in own words and structure
Compare what can be recalled and explained from each
activities.intendedInsight: How notes are taken affects how deeply the content is processed.
activities.rationale: Illustrates the encoding function discussed by Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014); as a classroom demonstration it is not a controlled test, and outcomes will vary.

difficulties.pattern: 'Notes are for remembering what the lecturer said, so the more I write the better.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense, near-verbatim notes that learners themselves cannot use for revision.
difficulties.response: Use the 'notes a week later' activity to show that structure and selection matter more than volume.

difficulties.pattern: Learners take notes conscientiously but rarely look at them again until just before an examination.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes are unread between lecture and examination; learners report that notes 'don't help'.
difficulties.response: Build short review tasks into the course and link them explicitly to the storage function and to retrieval practice.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What are your notes for?' and 'When do you use them after the lecture?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions both processing during note-taking and use afterwards, and describes regular use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions keeping a record but not processing or regular use.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Takes notes out of habit with no later use, or takes no notes.

records.contextNotes: Most useful at foundation and pre-sessional level as the rationale for later note-taking work. Revisit briefly in-sessionally when students' notes are not supporting their revision.

records.summary: Selective notes in the note-taker's own words involve more processing than transcription and are more usable as a record (Kiewra, 1985), but learners need explicit criteria for selection. EAP guidance has long treated note-taking as a teachable study skill (Jordan, 1997). Link selection criteria to purpose and to signals in the input: structure, relevance markers, definitions and repetition.

activities.title: Purpose-driven notes
learnerActions: Take notes on the same text for two different stated purposes
Compare the two sets of notes
Explain why the content differs
activities.intendedInsight: There is no single correct set of notes; selection depends on purpose.
activities.rationale: Makes selection decisions explicit and connects them to the later use of notes.

activities.title: Note audit
learnerActions: Exchange notes with a peer
Highlight main ideas in one colour and detail in another
Discuss whether the balance suits the purpose and what could be cut
activities.intendedInsight: Selection can be evaluated and improved.
activities.rationale: Peer comparison makes differences in selection visible without a single model answer.

difficulties.pattern: Learners try to write everything down.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long notes with no hierarchy; key points buried among detail.
difficulties.response: Practise identifying main ideas first in reading, then transfer the criteria to listening; set word limits for notes on short inputs.

difficulties.pattern: Learners note content words but lose the relationships between ideas (cause, contrast, condition).
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes list topics, and a reconstruction from the notes misrepresents how the ideas were connected.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to reconstruct the argument from their notes; introduce arrows and relation symbols to record links.

diagnostic.task: Give a short text and a purpose; ask for notes in 5 minutes, then ask the learner to explain why they included each item.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes are selective, relevant to the purpose and hierarchically organised, with reasons for inclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes contain the main ideas but also much unnecessary detail.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Notes are near-verbatim copying or a random selection of details.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, use short, clearly structured texts and lectures. Pre-sessional courses should vary purposes and input length. In-sessionally, use students' real reading and lecture notes.

records.summary: Abbreviation saves time, but the time saved is only valuable if the notes remain usable when reviewed (Kiewra, 1985). Teaching should emphasise a small, consistent system over long symbol lists, with priority on symbols for logical relations because they preserve reasoning. Many learners already use shorthand or words from other languages in notes, which is a legitimate resource as long as notes remain decodable and key terms are recorded in the form they will need later.

activities.title: Build a personal key
learnerActions: Review a set of conventional symbols and abbreviations
Choose about ten, and add abbreviations for five frequent terms in their subject
Use the key in a note-taking task and revise it afterwards
activities.intendedInsight: A small, consistent system is more useful than many ad hoc abbreviations.
activities.rationale: Practice-based guidance on note-taking shorthand of the kind found in EAP study-skills materials (Jordan, 1997).

activities.title: Notes to prose
learnerActions: Exchange notes with a peer
Rewrite one section in full sentences
Check the rewrite against the original source
activities.intendedInsight: Shorthand must be decodable, including by one's future self.
activities.rationale: Tests the storage function of notes directly.

difficulties.pattern: Learners believe notes must be entirely in English and avoid using their first language or other shorthand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners slow down to find English wording while the lecture moves on.
difficulties.response: Treat mixed-language notes as legitimate if they are decodable, while making sure key terms are recorded in English for later use in writing.

difficulties.pattern: Learners invent abbreviations on the spot that they cannot decode later.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot reconstruct parts of their own notes after a few days.
difficulties.response: Keep a running key at the front of each notebook or file, and review notes within a day.

difficulties.pattern: Conventional abbreviations are confused, for example e.g. used where i.e. is meant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes and later writing that list an example where a restatement was intended, or vice versa.
difficulties.response: Teach the meanings of the most common Latin abbreviations with examples and check them in learners' notes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to take notes on a 2-minute extract and then, two days later, read their notes aloud as full sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reads back fluently and accurately, including logical relations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recovers content but some relations or abbreviations are unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot reconstruct significant parts of the notes.

records.contextNotes: Mainly a foundation and pre-sessional topic. In-sessionally, subject-specific abbreviations become more important and can be built into students' own keys.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography evaluates abbreviation systems empirically; this guidance is practice-based.

records.summary: Nesbit and Adesope's (2006) meta-analysis found that studying or constructing concept maps was associated with somewhat better retention and transfer than several comparison activities, with effects varying across conditions. The Cornell format (Pauk & Owens, 2014) builds review into the page through cue and summary areas. No format is universally superior; teach a small repertoire and the principle of matching format to the structure of the content and to the notes' later use.

activities.title: Same content, three formats
learnerActions: Take notes on a short lecture or text as an outline
Convert the notes into a table or concept map
Compare which relationships each format makes visible
activities.intendedInsight: Different formats foreground different relationships.
activities.rationale: Concept mapping that labels relations between ideas is associated with learning gains in Nesbit and Adesope's (2006) meta-analysis; the activity uses mapping as one option rather than a universal solution.

activities.title: Cornell review cycle
learnerActions: Take lecture notes in the main column
Within a day, write cue questions in the margin and a summary at the foot
Cover the main column and answer the cue questions from memory
activities.intendedInsight: A format can build review and self-testing into note-taking.
activities.rationale: Combines the Cornell layout with retrieval practice, which improves retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).

difficulties.pattern: 'Mind maps suit me because I'm a visual learner.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners use one format for all content regardless of its structure.
difficulties.response: Present format choice as matching content structure and purpose. Do not endorse matching formats to 'learning styles', a claim that lacks good evidential support.

difficulties.pattern: Learners spend so long on layout during a lecture that they miss content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Carefully drawn but incomplete notes.
difficulties.response: Use simple linear formats during the lecture and rework the notes into maps or tables during review.

diagnostic.task: Give a short comparison text and ask the learner to choose a format and make notes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses a table or matrix with criteria and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses an outline that captures the content but obscures the comparison.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies sentences with no organising format.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from explicit modelling of two or three formats. Pre-sessional courses can link tables and matrices to synthesis tasks. PGT students may extend matrices into literature synthesis grids.

records.summary: Lecture note-taking places heavy simultaneous demands on L2 listeners, as decoding, selecting and writing compete for attention. Kiewra (1985) emphasises that complete notes and review of them are associated with better learning, and research on L2 lecture comprehension and note-taking is collected in Flowerdew (1994). Teach note-taking with authentic lectures, linking discourse cues (previews, macro-markers, which Chaudron and Richards (1986) found aided recall, and relevance markers) to note structure, and build in post-lecture completion.

activities.title: Structure-first notes
learnerActions: Before the lecture, set up headings from the preview or slides
During the lecture, add points under the headings, starring content the lecturer flags
After the lecture, compare notes with a partner and fill gaps
activities.intendedInsight: A frame prepared in advance frees attention for content during the lecture.
activities.rationale: Uses macro-structure, which supports recall (Chaudron & Richards, 1986), as the organising frame for notes.

activities.title: Notes to summary
learnerActions: Take notes on a lecture
Write a summary using only the notes
Check the summary against the recording and identify gaps in the notes
activities.intendedInsight: The test of notes is what they let you do afterwards.
activities.rationale: Tests the storage function of notes (Kiewra, 1985) and links note-taking to summary writing.

difficulties.pattern: Learners try to write everything and lose the thread of the lecture.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes are detailed for the first minutes and then break off.
difficulties.response: Practise selecting main points in short segments before extending to full lectures; leave marked gaps rather than falling behind.

difficulties.pattern: Learners copy slide text and miss the spoken explanation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes duplicate the slides almost exactly.
difficulties.response: Provide slides in advance and ask learners to annotate them only with what is said.

difficulties.pattern: Learners stop to work out the spelling of unfamiliar terms and fall behind.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gaps in notes immediately after new terminology.
difficulties.response: Encourage approximate spelling marked with a query, checked afterwards against slides or readings.

diagnostic.task: Collect notes from a 15-minute lecture and ask the learner to explain the lecture's structure from the notes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The notes show the structure clearly and the explanation is accurate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Main points are present but the structure is unclear or flagged content is missing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Notes are fragmentary and the lecture cannot be reconstructed from them.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from guided note frames. Pre-sessional UG courses should use full-length lectures with integrated writing tasks that require the notes; pre-sessional PG courses can use denser lectures and link notes to seminar preparation. In-sessionally, review students' own notes from their modules. Some students (for example deaf students, or students with dyslexia or motor difficulties) work with a human note-taker, recordings or assistive technology; assess what they do with notes, such as selection and summary, rather than real-time handwriting speed.

records.summary: Pecorari (2003) showed that much L2 textual borrowing takes the form of patchwriting without intent to deceive, and Shi (2004) found more unattributed borrowing in summary tasks than in opinion tasks, and more among L2 than L1 writers in her sample. Reading notes are where source wording and one's own wording most easily become confused, so note-making routines are a practical point of intervention (Pecorari, 2013). Teach a layout that physically separates quotation, own-words notes and comment, with page numbers recorded at the time of writing.

activities.title: Three-column notes
learnerActions: Divide the page or file into three columns: exact words with page number, own-words notes, own comments and questions
Make notes on a short article using all three columns
Swap with a peer and check that each column contains only what it should
activities.intendedInsight: Separating source words, source ideas and one's own ideas at the note stage is intended to prevent confusion later.
activities.rationale: A practical routine reflecting Pecorari's (2013) emphasis on teaching source use rather than only policing plagiarism.

activities.title: Read, cover, write
learnerActions: Read a paragraph carefully
Cover it and write notes from memory in own words
Uncover and check for accuracy and for unintended copying
activities.intendedInsight: Writing notes away from the text is intended to reduce copying and to test understanding.
activities.rationale: Targets the close textual dependence described as patchwriting by Pecorari (2003).

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll remember which parts I copied.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments that include unmarked source wording traced to the student's own notes.
difficulties.response: Show how copied wording in notes later reappears unmarked in drafts; require quotation marks and page numbers at the moment of copying.

difficulties.pattern: Learners copy key sentences because they feel they cannot express the idea better than the author.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes consist mostly of copied sentences, some unmarked.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a developmental stage rather than a moral failing; support with read-cover-write and with paraphrasing practice, and allow marked quotation in notes.

difficulties.pattern: Learners omit source details and page numbers and cannot find them later.
difficulties.revealedBy: Time lost re-finding sources; citations without page numbers for quotations.
difficulties.response: Make a source header with full details and a page column non-negotiable features of every set of notes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show notes from a recent reading and point out which parts are quotations, which are their own words and which are their own ideas.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All three are clearly and consistently distinguished, with page numbers and source details.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some distinction is made but inconsistently, or page numbers are missing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No distinction is made, or the learner cannot tell which parts were copied.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, model and check the layout closely. Pre-sessional courses should link it to source-based writing assessments, with PG courses using longer and more numerous sources. In-sessional UG and PGT students reading for assignments and dissertations need the same separation in digital form, often within reference management software, as do PGR students managing a large literature.

records.summary: Kiewra (1985) emphasised review as a key function of notes. Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated practice testing and distributed practice as high-utility learning techniques and rereading, highlighting and summarisation as lower utility; retrieval practice improves long-term retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) and spacing helps (Cepeda et al., 2006). Reviewing notes is therefore best organised around self-testing at intervals, with summarising used to repair and consolidate notes rather than as the main review activity.

activities.title: Cover and recall
learnerActions: Write three to five questions in the margin of a set of notes
Cover the notes and answer the questions from memory
Check answers and mark items for further review
activities.intendedInsight: Retrieving information from memory strengthens learning more than rereading it.
activities.rationale: Applies retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) to notes.

activities.title: Spaced review calendar
learnerActions: Plan short reviews of each lecture's notes after one day, one week and one month
Record the result of each self-test
Adjust the schedule for topics that remain difficult
activities.intendedInsight: Spacing review over time supports retention better than cramming.
activities.rationale: Applies distributed practice (Cepeda et al., 2006; Dunlosky et al., 2013).

difficulties.pattern: Learners recopy notes neatly or reread them and feel they have learnt them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report hours of review but perform poorly on recall questions.
difficulties.response: Contrast rereading with self-testing in a short class experiment and discuss the difference between familiarity and recall.

difficulties.pattern: Self-testing feels uncomfortable because it exposes what has been forgotten.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners abandon self-testing after a few attempts.
difficulties.response: Explain that the effort of retrieval is part of what makes it effective, and keep early self-tests short and low-stakes.

difficulties.pattern: Learners leave all review until the examination period.
difficulties.revealedBy: No review activity during the term; heavy cramming before examinations.
difficulties.response: Build short weekly review into the course schedule and check it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would prepare from their notes for a test in two weeks.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes spaced self-testing from questions generated from the notes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes rereading or summarising, with some spacing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans to reread everything the night before.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses can model review with course content. In UG and PGT programmes, link review to module assessment schedules and to examination preparation.

records.summary: Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) reported that laptop note-takers wrote more verbatim notes and performed worse on conceptual questions than longhand note-takers. Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019) replicated and extended the study and did not find robust differences, concluding that the evidence does not justify strong claims for longhand superiority. Sana, Weston and Cepeda (2013) found that laptop multitasking harmed learning for users and for nearby peers. Both note-taking studies tested first-language English undergraduates watching short talks in laboratory conditions, so their transfer to L2 lecture note-taking is untested. Present this as an open debate: the defensible advice is to avoid verbatim transcription and multitasking whatever the device, and never to require handwriting where students rely on typed notes or assistive technology.

activities.title: Read the debate
learnerActions: Read the abstracts of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) and Morehead et al. (2019)
Summarise what each study claims and how they differ
Decide in groups what advice the evidence actually supports
activities.intendedInsight: Popular claims about research should be checked against the studies, including replications.
activities.rationale: Uses a live replication debate to model critical reading of evidence, while addressing the practical question directly.

activities.title: Device audit
learnerActions: For one week, record for each lecture which device was used, any distractions and how much of the notes was verbatim
Use the notes for a short self-test
Reflect on what to change
activities.intendedInsight: How a device is used matters more than which device is used.
activities.rationale: Makes multitasking and verbatim transcription visible to the learner (Sana et al., 2013).

difficulties.pattern: 'Research proves handwriting is better.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners repeat the claim from popular sources, sometimes against their own needs.
difficulties.response: Show the replication results and focus on processing rather than device.

difficulties.pattern: Learners type quickly and transcribe almost verbatim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Typed notes that read like a transcript.
difficulties.response: Set word limits per lecture section or require condensed headings and summaries.

difficulties.pattern: Notes are scattered across apps, devices and cloud services and cannot be found later.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot locate notes for a given lecture or source.
difficulties.response: Agree a simple filing system linked to modules and dates, with regular backup.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner which method they use and why, and to retrieve their notes from a specific lecture two weeks ago.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A reasoned choice that represents the evidence accurately; notes are found quickly and are processed rather than verbatim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Choice based on habit; notes found but largely verbatim.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats myths, cannot find notes, or notes are absent.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional students often arrive with established habits; address the evidence early. In UG and PGT programmes, practical organisation becomes more important as volume grows. Students with dyslexia, dyspraxia or other disabilities may rely on typed notes, dictation, recording or assistive software; guidance should never imply that handwriting is required.
reviewNotes: Review response: the laptop–longhand evidence is presented as contested (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014; Morehead et al., 2019), with the limits of laboratory and first-language samples stated; no device recommendation is made.

records.summary: Kiewra's (1985) distinction between encoding and external storage suggests that shared notes can supply the storage function but not the processing benefit of taking notes oneself, so students who rely only on others' notes miss that processing. Collaborative notes are probably most useful as a supplement to individual notes, through comparison, correction and pooling of gaps. Institutional rules on collusion (Bretag, 2016) mean students need to know where sharing notes ends and sharing assessed work begins. In multilingual groups, attention to equitable division of work matters.

activities.title: Compare, correct, combine
learnerActions: Take individual notes on a lecture
In groups, compare notes and mark disagreements
Check disagreements against the recording and produce a corrected shared version
activities.intendedInsight: Comparison exposes errors and gaps that individuals miss.
activities.rationale: Preserves individual processing while gaining the storage benefits of pooled notes, following Kiewra's (1985) distinction.

activities.title: Where is the line?
learnerActions: Read short scenarios about sharing notes and drafts
Decide whether each is permitted collaboration or collusion under the institution's policy
Discuss borderline cases
activities.intendedInsight: Sharing notes is usually acceptable; sharing assessed work usually is not.
activities.rationale: Applies institutional integrity policy to a common study practice.

difficulties.pattern: Some group members rely entirely on others' notes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Group members cannot explain content without the shared notes.
difficulties.response: Rotate responsibilities and require each member to add summaries or questions.

difficulties.pattern: Errors in shared notes spread to everyone who uses them.
difficulties.revealedBy: The same misconception appears across several students' work.
difficulties.response: Build in a checking role and verification against sources.

difficulties.pattern: Learners are unsure whether sharing notes for an assessed task is allowed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about collusion; very similar submitted work.
difficulties.response: Clarify institutional rules with concrete examples.

diagnostic.task: Ask a group to describe how they share notes and what they would do if asked to share notes for an assessed essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a structured process with checking and individual contribution, and an accurate understanding of collusion rules.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Shares notes informally without checking; vague on rules.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies others' notes wholesale; unaware of collusion risks.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can model collaborative notes with clear rules. UG and PGT students often form study groups independently; in-sessional support can address integrity and effectiveness together.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no empirical source on collaborative note-taking; guidance relies on reasoning from Kiewra's functions and on practice.

records.summary: Seminar expectations are largely tacit and vary by discipline, level, class size and tutor (Ferris & Tagg, 1996), so teaching should make them explicit through observing and analysing real or recorded seminars rather than issuing generic rules. Language socialisation research shows that newcomers learn participation through experience, feedback and negotiation of their position in a group (Duff, 2010; Morita, 2004). Basturkmen's (2003) observation that interaction changed when the tutor joined a student discussion group is a useful prompt for examining how format shapes who speaks and how.

activities.title: Seminar ethnography
learnerActions: Observe a seminar or tutorial in a target discipline (live with permission, or a recording) and note who speaks, how turns are allocated, what kinds of contributions occur and how the tutor responds
Compare notes in groups and draft a 'what counts as a contribution here' list
Check the list against the module handbook or by asking a subject tutor, and revise it
activities.intendedInsight: Participation norms are local and observable, and include questions, tentative ideas and links to readings, not only correct answers.
activities.rationale: Guided observation makes tacit expectations explicit, in line with language socialisation accounts of how newcomers learn participation (Duff, 2010) and with the disciplinary variation Ferris and Tagg (1996) report.

activities.title: Tutor present, tutor absent
learnerActions: Hold two short discussions on the same reading, one with the teacher participating and one without
Compare observer notes or transcripts: who addressed whom, how long turns were, how ideas developed
Decide which features of the student-only discussion to carry into tutor-led seminars
activities.intendedInsight: The presence and moves of a tutor change the interaction; learners can notice and adapt to these patterns.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen (2003) observed different interaction patterns in a student discussion group with and without the tutor; recreating the contrast makes the effect of format visible to learners.

difficulties.pattern: 'The seminar is where the teacher checks we did the reading, so I should only speak when I'm sure I'm right.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners answer tutor questions briefly but never volunteer, ask questions or respond to peers, and describe silence as safer than being wrong.
difficulties.response: Contrast recitation (tutor question, student answer, tutor evaluation) with exploratory discussion using short transcripts, and show tutors valuing tentative and questioning contributions. Present the seminar as a genre with its own rules; do not frame previous educational experience as deficient.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming one tutor's or module's participation norms apply everywhere.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners transfer a style (e.g. frequent interruption, or waiting to be nominated) into a setting where it does not fit, or report confusion when expectations differ.
difficulties.response: Have learners compare two settings and identify the variables (class size, assessment, tutor style, discipline) that shape norms, and encourage them to ask tutors directly about expectations.

difficulties.pattern: Equating participation solely with how much one speaks, and judging oneself or quieter peers as 'not participating'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Self-evaluations focus on talk volume; learners discount listening, note-taking, forum posts or small-group work.
difficulties.response: Discuss Morita's (2004) account of silence as shaped by positioning, power and task conditions, recognise multiple forms of participation, and still build routes into speaking.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In your next seminar, what do you think the tutor expects you to do before and during the session, and how would you know if you were participating well?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Refers to preparing readings, developing ideas with others, asking questions and the module's criteria, and recognises that expectations vary between tutors.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions reading and speaking but frames contributions as correct answers to the tutor's questions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot describe what happens in a seminar, or treats it as a lecture with occasional questions.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, emphasise the basic distinctions between lectures, seminars and tutorials and why contribution matters. Pre-sessional UG courses should model the seminar style of the receiving institution and connect it to any assessed seminar. Pre-sessional PG courses should prepare learners for PGT seminars in which contribution may be assessed from the first weeks, and PGT in-sessional support may need to revisit this in week one. In-sessional UG support can be embedded with subject staff and use real module expectations. Participation can take more than one form, including written and online contributions, and criteria should say which forms count.
reviewNotes: Ferris and Tagg (1996) surveyed instructors in US institutions; UK and other contexts differ in seminar formats and in whether participation is assessed.

records.summary: Preparation is the main lever learners control over the processing load of real-time discussion: task-based research reviewed by Skehan (1998) indicates that pre-task planning tends to benefit fluency and complexity. Morita (2000) describes multilingual graduate students investing heavily in preparation for oral academic activities. Teach preparation as reading for a discussion purpose — recording positions, links and questions with locators — rather than as summarising or scripting.

activities.title: Three-column seminar preparation sheet
learnerActions: For each set reading, record the author's key claim with a page number, a point you agree or disagree with and why, and one question
Add one link between two readings, or between the reading and a previous session
Use the sheet to make a first contribution within the opening ten minutes of the seminar
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation should produce contributions, not only comprehension.
activities.rationale: Structuring preparation around positions and questions shifts planning from comprehension to formulating contributions, the kind of planning that the studies reviewed by Skehan (1998) associate with more fluent output.

activities.title: Predict the questions
learnerActions: In pairs, predict three questions the tutor might ask from the module outline and the reading
Plan a 30-second note-form response to each
After the seminar, compare the predictions with what was actually discussed
activities.intendedInsight: Anticipating questions eases entry into discussion and reveals which aspects of readings tutors prioritise.
activities.rationale: Rehearsing likely responses in note form balances preparedness with the spontaneity seminars require, and the post-seminar comparison builds knowledge of the genre, echoing the preparation practices Morita (2000) describes.

difficulties.pattern: 'I read every word of the article twice, but in the seminar I had nothing to say.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Extensive highlighting or summary notes but no recorded positions or questions; the learner speaks only when asked directly.
difficulties.response: Model preparation for discussion by sharing an expert's notes containing claims, reactions and questions, and set preparation tasks that require a position. Do not respond by assigning more reading.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a full script and reading it aloud when invited to speak.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions are long, written in style and disconnected from what was just said; the learner loses their place if interrupted.
difficulties.response: Accept a scripted first contribution as a bridge, then reduce notes to key words and practise adapting a prepared point to link to the previous speaker. Do not ban notes outright, which can raise anxiety.

difficulties.pattern: Underestimating reading time, so preparation covers only the first part of longer texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes stop part-way through; the learner avoids discussing later sections.
difficulties.response: Teach selective reading for seminar purposes (abstract, introduction, conclusion and the section most relevant to the questions) and plan reading time across the week.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to talk you through their preparation notes for a forthcoming seminar in two minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes show claims with page references, at least one evaluative reaction and a question or cross-reading link; the learner can phrase a likely contribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate summary notes with no position, link or question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No notes, highlighted text only, or a full script.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners may need guided reading questions and shorter texts, and preparation is core there and on pre-sessional UG courses. Pre-sessional PG learners prepare from authentic readings with discussion questions, often with heavier reading loads. In-sessional UG and PGT learners face heavy reading loads, so selective preparation matters most. Learners with dyslexia or slower reading speeds may need texts in advance and in accessible formats, which is a course-design responsibility.
reviewNotes: The planning studies Skehan (1998) reviews used narrative and decision-making tasks; transfer to seminar preparation is an inference, not a tested finding.

records.summary: In student discussions, turns are largely taken by self-selection, and learners who wait to be nominated may rarely speak; Basturkmen (2003) shows that the presence of a tutor alters how turns are distributed. Morita's (2004) case studies show that difficulty entering talk is shaped by the pace of exchanges, how learners are positioned and how others respond, not only by proficiency. Teach recognition of transition points, short floor-claiming and floor-holding moves and recovery strategies, and work with tutors to vary how the floor is distributed.

activities.title: Transition-point spotting
learnerActions: Listen to a recorded seminar extract and mark each change of speaker and what signalled it (a completed point, falling intonation, a pause, a question)
Replay the extract and practise entering at each marked point with a short linking phrase
Discuss which entries felt rushed or late and why
activities.intendedInsight: Turns can be entered at recognisable points without waiting for an invitation.
activities.rationale: Explicit noticing of transition cues supports the coordination of listening and speaking that self-selected turn-taking requires.

activities.title: Holding the floor collegially
learnerActions: In groups of four, each person makes a 40-second point while the others try to come in politely
The speaker holds the floor by announcing structure ('two things here…'), using fillers or asking to finish
Swap roles and discuss where floor-holding becomes domination
activities.intendedInsight: Holding a turn while formulating is legitimate and can be done collegially.
activities.rationale: Gives learners rehearsed resources for the moments when they need formulation time, reducing the risk of losing the turn mid-idea; students in Ferris (1998) reported whole-class discussion as particularly demanding.

difficulties.pattern: 'I wait for a long enough pause to be polite, but by the time I'm ready the topic has moved on.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Late or abandoned entry attempts; prepared ideas are never voiced.
difficulties.response: Teach short floor-claiming moves that buy formulation time ('Can I come in on that?', 'Just on that point…') and encourage an early first contribution. Also adjust task design (think time, rounds). Do not simply tell learners to 'be more confident'.

difficulties.pattern: Applying one rule about interruption across all settings — never interrupting, or cutting in frequently to show engagement.
difficulties.revealedBy: No overlapping entries even in fast student-led discussion, or frequent cut-ins that peers find abrupt.
difficulties.response: Compare examples of supportive overlap and competitive interruption, discuss how acceptability depends on group, tutor and topic, and practise mitigated entry.

difficulties.pattern: Entry attempts are ignored or talked over because the learner has been positioned as less competent.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner reports trying to speak and being overlooked; observation shows peers not taking up their points.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a group and course-design issue, not the learner's problem: teachers should use structures such as rounds, nomination with notice and small-group work, and teach all students to take up others' points. Give the learner re-entry moves ('As I was starting to say…').

diagnostic.task: After a 10-minute recorded group discussion, ask the learner to identify one point where they entered and one where they wanted to but did not, and explain what happened.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Self-selects at transition points with linking moves, can name the cues used and recovers from overlaps.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Enters mainly when invited; recognises missed chances but lacks moves to take them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Little or no participation and cannot identify where entry would have been possible.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional classes can begin with structured turn allocation before moving to free discussion. In-sessional UG learners often meet fast discussions among peers who share local references. PGT and PGR settings may include tutor-dominated or strongly argumentative styles, so the emphasis shifts to entering and holding the floor under pressure. Learners who stammer, are autistic, are deaf or hard of hearing, or need more processing time may contribute through agreed routes such as a raised hand, invitation with notice, or a written or chat contribution; judge what is contributed, not conformity to one turn-taking style.
reviewNotes: The notion of transition-relevance places comes from conversation analysis; no listed reference covers it directly.

records.summary: Learners often have views but present them as summaries of readings or as unsupported assertions. A short claim–reason–support move, with explicit stance marking, gives a reliable unit for contribution, and framing argument as reasoned position-taking (Andrews, 2010) helps learners see why summary alone is not enough. Basturkmen (2002) shows that ideas in seminars are elaborated across several turns, so learners also need to extend their reasoning when asked 'why?' rather than treating the first statement as complete.

activities.title: Claim, reason, support in 45 seconds
learnerActions: Given a discussion question, note a one-sentence position, one reason and one example or source
Deliver it to a partner in 45 seconds
The partner asks 'Why?' or 'What's the evidence?', and the speaker extends with a further reason or a qualification
activities.intendedInsight: A position needs reasons and can be developed further under questioning.
activities.rationale: Makes the basic argumentative unit explicit and rehearses the elaboration across turns that Basturkmen (2002) found in seminar discussion.

activities.title: Summary or view?
learnerActions: Listen to six short, teacher-recorded seminar contributions and classify each as summary, unsupported opinion or supported view
Rewrite two of the weaker ones as supported views
Deliver the rewritten versions and compare them with the originals
activities.intendedInsight: Summary alone is not a contribution, and assertion alone is not persuasive.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples sharpens learners' sense of what tutors value in discussion.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I summarise the article accurately, that shows I have done the reading, and that is what the tutor wants.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions summarise readings without evaluation; the learner hesitates when asked what they think.
difficulties.response: Where earlier assessment rewarded accurate reproduction of texts, for example through comprehension-question exams, summary is a reasonable strategy. Make the shift explicit by showing seminar criteria that reward a position, model contributions that move from a one-sentence summary to a view, and make 'my view is… because…' a required element of practice tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Giving a view with no reasons ('I think it's a good idea').
difficulties.revealedBy: Short assertions; the learner repeats the claim when asked why.
difficulties.response: Require a reason in every practice contribution and work on extension with because, since and for example. Do not prioritise more sophisticated stance phrases before the reasoning is present.

diagnostic.task: Pose a contestable question about a recent reading, allow one minute's thought, ask for the learner's view, then ask 'Why?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear position with a reason and support, extended with a new reason or qualification when challenged.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A position with a vague reason; the claim is restated when challenged.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A summary of the reading with no position.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on clear claim–reason structures on accessible topics. Pre-sessional learners should base views on set readings and data. In-sessional UG learners work on the forms of evidence their disciplines accept for a view.

records.summary: Teaching materials often present agreeing and disagreeing as lists of interchangeable phrases, but Basturkmen (2002) shows that in seminar discussion disagreement emerges over several turns as ideas are negotiated. Politeness theory explains why disagreement is usually mitigated (Brown & Levinson, 1987), and research on pragmatic development indicates that explicit attention to pragmatic strategies can support learners (Kasper & Rose, 2002). Teach an acknowledge–locate–reason pattern, calibrated to relationship and stakes, and practise sustaining a disagreement over more than one turn.

activities.title: Disagreement continuum
learnerActions: Rank eight teacher-written responses to a claim from most to least direct
Discuss which would suit a peer, a tutor and a published author, and why
Respond to three new claims at an assigned point on the continuum
activities.intendedInsight: Mitigation is a set of choices adjusted to relationships and stakes, not a fixed formula.
activities.rationale: Explicit metapragmatic discussion is among the instructional approaches Kasper and Rose (2002) review, and the ranking draws on the face concepts of Brown and Levinson (1987).

activities.title: Negotiating over several turns
learnerActions: Read a transcript extract in which a disagreement develops over several turns
Identify where the point of difference becomes clear and how each speaker qualifies their position
Role-play a continuation that reaches a partly shared position
activities.intendedInsight: Disagreement in seminars is a process of negotiating meaning, not a single move.
activities.rationale: Reflects Basturkmen's (2002) analysis of ideas being negotiated across extended exchanges.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I disagree with my friend in the seminar, they will think I am attacking them.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners voice disagreement only privately or only with people they do not know; in class they agree, then raise the point afterwards.
difficulties.response: Separate the idea from the person explicitly: practise disagreements that credit the other speaker's point before locating the difference, and debrief how the exchange felt on both sides. This concern is common among novice participants of all backgrounds and is not a cultural trait.

difficulties.pattern: Stacking hedges until the position disappears ('Maybe, perhaps, I'm not sure, but possibly…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners cannot say whether the learner agrees or disagrees.
difficulties.response: Teach one-mitigator-plus-clear-point patterns and have listeners paraphrase the speaker's position as a check.

difficulties.pattern: Bald disagreement ('No, that's wrong') that peers hear as aggressive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Peers respond defensively and the learner is surprised by the reaction.
difficulties.response: Introduce acknowledgement and partial agreement as resources and practise reformulating direct responses. Avoid treating directness as a fault in itself; it can be appropriate in debate or among close peers.

diagnostic.task: Read aloud a claim a peer might make about a recent reading and ask the learner to respond, partly disagreeing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Acknowledges the claim, locates the specific difference, gives a reason and uses proportionate mitigation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mitigated but vague about the point of difference, or clear but bald.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Agrees by default, or says 'I disagree' with no reason.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a small set of reliable patterns. Pre-sessional learners should practise disagreeing with readings and tutors. In-sessional UG and PGT learners calibrate to their own tutors and peers. PGR researchers need to disagree with senior academics in research seminars with appropriate authority.

records.summary: Seminar talk is co-constructed: Basturkmen (2002) shows ideas developing across several speakers' turns, and Basturkmen (2003) observed more of this collaborative development among students when the tutor was absent. Teach an explicit back-reference plus a stated relation (extend, qualify, contrast, connect), and assess listening as part of speaking.

activities.title: Link-and-add chain
learnerActions: One student makes a point about a reading
Each subsequent speaker names the previous speaker, reformulates their point in a clause and states whether they are extending, qualifying or contrasting it
An observer records the relation used and flags any turn that does not link
activities.intendedInsight: Strong contributions are tied to what has just been said.
activities.rationale: Forces attention to prior turns and makes visible the co-construction of ideas described by Basturkmen (2002).

activities.title: Mapping a discussion
learnerActions: Map a seminar transcript as a diagram showing which turns build on which
Identify turns that start new threads without linking and discuss their effect
Plan two contributions that could have connected separate threads
activities.intendedInsight: Discussion has a structure that participants create through linking moves.
activities.rationale: Visualising exchange structure supports noticing of collaborative development, which Basturkmen (2003) found varied with the participation framework.

difficulties.pattern: 'I prepared three points, so I'll make them whenever I get a chance.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions do not connect to the preceding talk and peers do not take them up.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to adapt a prepared point by first linking it to the current thread; keep preparation but require the link. Do not discourage preparation itself.

difficulties.pattern: Using generic linking openers ('Following on from that…') without engaging the content of the previous point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic openings followed by unrelated points.
difficulties.response: Require a reformulation of the previous point before the new one and give feedback on its accuracy.

diagnostic.task: Play a 1-minute recorded seminar turn and ask the learner to respond by building on it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurately reformulates the point, states a relation and adds something new.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Links generically and adds content only loosely related to the turn.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Makes an unrelated point or simply agrees.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional programmes should introduce linking as a discussion skill. In-sessional UG and PGT learners need it in fast discussions where peers share background knowledge, and PGT seminar criteria often reward synthesis of peers' contributions. In PGR reading groups, building on others includes relating colleagues' points to different research projects.

records.summary: Subject instructors surveyed by Ferris and Tagg (1996) identified asking and answering questions and taking part in discussion as areas of difficulty for multilingual students, and students in Ferris (1998) reported class discussion as demanding. Questions are both a comprehension-repair strategy and a legitimate contribution that can move a discussion on (Basturkmen, 2002). Teach targeted questions that pinpoint the problem, form-focused work on direct and embedded questions, and mitigation proportionate to the relationship.

activities.title: Pinpoint the problem
learnerActions: Listen to a short lecture or seminar extract containing an unclear term and an unsupported claim
Write a question that names exactly what is unclear or unsupported
Compare the answers a pinpointed question and 'Can you repeat?' would receive
activities.intendedInsight: Specific questions get specific help and show engagement.
activities.rationale: Linking questions to comprehension monitoring supports listening as well as speaking, addressing a difficulty instructors reported in Ferris and Tagg (1996).

activities.title: Question types for discussion
learnerActions: Sort sample questions into clarification, elaboration, evidence, implication and connection types
Write one question of each type about a set reading
Use them in a seminar and note which ones generated further discussion
activities.intendedInsight: Different questions do different work in a discussion.
activities.rationale: Extends questioning beyond repair to the idea-developing exchanges observed in seminar discussion (Basturkmen, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'Asking a question shows everyone that I didn't understand.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner never asks in class but asks peers or approaches the tutor afterwards.
difficulties.response: Normalise questions by modelling expert questions and asking tutors to invite them; start with written or small-group questions. Do not require public questions before safer routes have been established.

difficulties.pattern: Retaining question word order in embedded questions ('Could you tell me what does this mean?').
difficulties.revealedBy: Inverted order in indirect questions, especially when the learner is mitigating.
difficulties.response: Give brief focused practice on embedded question order, but in live discussion prioritise getting the question asked over accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: Prefacing questions to tutors with so much apology that the question is lost.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long apologetic prefaces; the tutor has to ask what the question is.
difficulties.response: Practise one mitigator followed by a direct question, and discuss evidence that tutors generally welcome clear questions.

diagnostic.task: Play a 2-minute talk extract and ask the learner to put one question about something unclear and one about something they want to know more about.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Both questions pinpoint content, are intelligible and appropriately mitigated.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A generic clarification request, or form problems that obscure the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No question, or only 'I don't understand.'

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need question forms and routines. In-sessional learners focus on asking in large classes and lectures as well as seminars. PGR researchers ask questions after research talks, where questions also position the asker within the field.
reviewNotes: Ferris and Tagg (1996) and Ferris (1998) report US data; the reported difficulty with questions should not be generalised to all multilingual students.

records.summary: In multilingual academic groups mutual understanding cannot be assumed, because members differ in accent, proficiency and disciplinary background. Research on English as a lingua franca in international universities frames communicative success as achieved through accommodation and negotiation rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Jenkins, 2014), and Basturkmen (2002) shows seminar meaning being negotiated across turns. Teach confirmation checks, paraphrase-back and self-reformulation as normal collaborative moves.

activities.title: Paraphrase-back pairs
learnerActions: Speaker A explains a concept from their reading in one minute
Speaker B paraphrases it back and asks for confirmation
A confirms or reformulates with an example; then the pair swaps roles
activities.intendedInsight: Checking is efficient and collaborative, not an admission of failure.
activities.rationale: Practises the negotiation of meaning that supports mutual intelligibility in multilingual groups (Jenkins, 2014).

activities.title: Rescue the explanation
learnerActions: Explain a technical term from your field to a partner from a different field
The partner signals non-understanding whenever a term or step is unclear
Reformulate with a simpler term, an example or an analogy until the partner can paraphrase it
activities.intendedInsight: Reformulation is a skill speakers can plan for and practise.
activities.rationale: Builds a repair repertoire for the points at which explanations break down in cross-disciplinary groups.

difficulties.pattern: Nodding as if understanding to avoid interrupting.
difficulties.revealedBy: Apparent agreement followed by responses that miss the point.
difficulties.response: Model checks as routine in teacher talk, and reward accurate paraphrase rather than speed in tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Repeating the same words more loudly or slowly when not understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Identical wording repeated; the listener remains confused.
difficulties.response: Teach explicit reformulation strategies (a simpler synonym, an example, breaking the idea into steps).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a concept to a partner who has been told to misunderstand once.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notices the misunderstanding, reformulates with new wording or an example, and checks again.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices but repeats the original wording.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not notice the misunderstanding.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners practise basic checks and paraphrase. In-sessional UG and PGT learners use them in diverse groups and when explaining disciplinary terms to peers from other fields, where all students — including home students — benefit from the same practices.

records.summary: Seminar tutors expect discussion to engage with set readings; Morita (2000) describes graduate students' presentations and discussions in which critical engagement with assigned texts was central. Oral attribution adapts written signal phrases to speech: a brief reference to the author or text, the point, and the speaker's comment, sometimes with a page reference to direct peers. As in writing, attribution also positions the speaker in relation to the literature (Hyland, 1999).

activities.title: Source, point, comment
learnerActions: Prepare three cards, each with an author, a key point and a page number
In discussion, use each card once: state the source, paraphrase the point and add your own comment
Observers note whether the boundary between source and comment was audible
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken attribution is brief but makes clear whose idea is whose.
activities.rationale: Transfers the attribution and positioning functions of written citation (Hyland, 1999) to speech.

activities.title: Quote or paraphrase?
learnerActions: Compare a contribution that reads a long quotation aloud with one that paraphrases briefly and gives the page
Discuss which is easier to follow and which shows the speaker's view
Rework a quotation-based contribution into a brief paraphrase with a locator and comment
activities.intendedInsight: Reading long quotations aloud slows discussion and hides the speaker's own view.
activities.rationale: Listeners hear speech once, so brevity and explicit stance help discussion move.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting points from readings as if they were the learner's own knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Tutor or peers ask 'Where is that from?'
difficulties.response: Make attribution a required element of practice contributions and connect it explicitly to written attribution practices.

difficulties.pattern: Reading long passages aloud from the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions consist of extended quotation with no comment.
difficulties.response: Limit quotation to a short phrase and require a comment after every source reference; prepare paraphrases in advance.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to make a 1-minute contribution that uses one set reading to support or challenge a peer's point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Clear attribution, a brief and accurate paraphrase and an explicit comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Attribution present but no comment, or reliance on a long quotation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No attribution.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG and PG learners practise with set readings, often for an assessed seminar. In-sessional UG learners use module readings, and PGT learners, for whom critical engagement with readings is central, use disciplinary conventions for referring to authors, cases, statutes or datasets in speech. PGR researchers revisit it in reading groups and when positioning their own work.
reviewNotes: Research on oral attribution in student seminars is limited; this guidance extrapolates from written source-use research and studies of graduate oral activities.

records.summary: Student-led seminars often assess facilitation, and the CEFR Companion Volume treats facilitating collaborative interaction and managing interaction as mediation competences (Council of Europe, 2020). Morita (2000) describes graduate students leading class discussion as part of oral academic presentations. Because facilitation requires attending to participation and process, teach it as a set of identifiable moves: opening question, turn distribution, probing, redirection, time-signalling and summarising.

activities.title: Facilitator moves toolkit
learnerActions: Watch a recorded facilitated discussion and label each facilitator move (open, invite, probe, redirect, summarise, close)
Plan a 10-minute discussion with an opening question and three follow-up probes
Facilitate the discussion and receive observer feedback on the moves used
activities.intendedInsight: Facilitation consists of identifiable moves that can be planned and practised.
activities.rationale: Breaks a complex mediation skill into observable components, aligned with the Companion Volume's mediation scales (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: Participation map
learnerActions: An observer draws lines between speakers on a seating plan during the first 10 minutes
The facilitator reviews the map at a break
In the next 10 minutes the facilitator uses invitations, rounds or pair-then-share to widen participation
activities.intendedInsight: Facilitators can see and change who participates.
activities.rationale: Makes the effect of facilitation on participation visible, connecting to Basturkmen's (2003) observation that the participation framework shapes interaction.

difficulties.pattern: The facilitator gives their own view after each contribution and becomes the hub of all exchanges.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long facilitator turns; exchanges run only between facilitator and individual participants.
difficulties.response: Limit facilitator content turns and practise probes that hand the floor back. Do not forbid content altogether; brief framing and synthesis are useful.

difficulties.pattern: Working through a list of prepared questions without following up answers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Each question is answered once and the next is asked; ideas are not developed.
difficulties.response: Practise follow-up probes ('Can you say more about…?', 'How does that fit with what X said?') and listening for points to connect.

difficulties.pattern: Putting quieter participants on the spot by nominating them without warning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Nominated participants freeze or give minimal answers.
difficulties.response: Use advance notice, rounds, pair-then-share or written input before nominating.

diagnostic.task: The learner facilitates a 10-minute discussion while an observer maps participation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear opening, broad participation, follow-up probes, time management and a fair closing summary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Questions asked in sequence with little follow-up; some imbalance in participation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The facilitator dominates or the discussion stalls.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners may facilitate assessed student-led seminars. PGT learners often lead discussions of readings. PGR researchers chair reading groups, lab meetings and conference sessions, where time management and fair turn distribution among senior and junior colleagues are central.

records.summary: Summarising a discussion requires selecting and generalising across contributions rather than replaying them, a process analogous to the macro-rules identified for summarising written texts (Brown & Day, 1983). The Companion Volume includes note-taking in seminars and meetings among its mediation activities (Council of Europe, 2020). Teach listening for positions and agreements during discussion, structured note grids, and short, thematically organised report-backs.

activities.title: Positions, agreements, open questions
learnerActions: During a discussion, a note-taker uses a three-part grid: positions, points of agreement or disagreement, open questions
After the discussion, the note-taker has two minutes to prepare a 60-second report
The group rates the report for fairness and selectivity
activities.intendedInsight: A summary selects and organises; it does not replay the discussion.
activities.rationale: Applies the summarising operations of deleting, generalising and constructing (Brown & Day, 1983) to spoken discussion.

activities.title: Who said what, or what was said?
learnerActions: Compare a chronological report-back with a thematically organised one on the same discussion
Identify what the thematic version omits and why
Rewrite a chronological report-back thematically
activities.intendedInsight: Thematic organisation communicates the outcome of a discussion more clearly.
activities.rationale: Contrasting models makes the selection criteria for summarising explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Reporting every contribution in the order it was made.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, list-like report-backs that overrun.
difficulties.response: Impose a time limit and the three-part structure, and practise generalising several contributions into one position.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting one's own view as the group's conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Group members dispute the summary.
difficulties.response: Practise attributing positions and marking disagreement explicitly; have peers check the summary for fairness.

diagnostic.task: After a recorded 10-minute discussion, ask the learner for a 60-second summary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selective, thematically organised, fair, and includes an unresolved question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate but chronological and over-detailed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Major omissions, or the learner's own view presented as consensus.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners report back from group tasks. PGT learners summarise in assessed seminars. PGR researchers summarise discussions in meetings and reading groups, sometimes as written records.
reviewNotes: Brown and Day (1983) studied summarising written texts; its application to spoken discussion is an analogy.

records.summary: Foreign language classroom anxiety involves communication apprehension, test anxiety and fear of negative evaluation (Horwitz et al., 1986), and willingness to communicate is situational, shaped by enduring factors and by the immediate interlocutor, group and topic (MacIntyre et al., 1998). Morita (2004) shows reticence in graduate classrooms shaped by positioning and power relations rather than reducible to culture or personality. Teaching should therefore address both learner strategies and classroom conditions, and should avoid labelling learners as 'quiet students'.

activities.title: Mapping willingness to speak
learnerActions: List recent speaking situations and rate your willingness to speak in each
Identify what made each easier or harder (preparation, group size, topic, tutor moves, peers)
Choose one condition to change and one strategy to try in the next seminar, then review the outcome
activities.intendedInsight: Willingness to speak varies by situation, and some of the conditions can be changed.
activities.rationale: Applies MacIntyre et al.'s (1998) situational model of WTC to learners' own experience to locate actionable factors.

activities.title: Graded entry
learnerActions: Plan an early, low-risk contribution (agreeing with a reason, asking a clarification question)
Make it within the first ten minutes of the seminar
Over several sessions, move to higher-risk contributions such as disagreement or a new idea
activities.intendedInsight: An early, small contribution may lower the barrier to later ones.
activities.rationale: A graded sequence targets fear of negative evaluation (Horwitz et al., 1986) through experiences of success rather than exhortation.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'm just a shy person; I'll never speak in seminars.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Fixed-trait explanations and avoidance of speaking tasks.
