difficulties.response: Explore how willingness varied across situations, set small achievable goals and avoid labels. Refer to wellbeing services if anxiety is severe.

difficulties.pattern: Teachers or peers attributing a student's silence to their national or cultural background.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comments such as 'students from X don't participate' in staff or peer talk.
difficulties.response: Discuss evidence that silence reflects positioning, task design and processing load (Morita, 2004). Course teams should change discussion design (think time, small groups, rounds, written input) rather than attributing participation to a student's 'culture'.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe one seminar in which they spoke and one in which they did not, and what was different.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies situational factors and strategies they used or could use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies factors but proposes no strategies.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attributes the difference entirely to a fixed trait.

records.contextNotes: Anxiety may be acute on pre-sessional programmes where progression depends on assessed speaking. In-sessional UG and PGT students may face large classes and peers who share local references. PGR researchers may experience anxiety in research seminars and vivas. Across stages, coordinate with subject staff on discussion design. Not all reluctance to speak is anxiety: stammering, autism, hearing loss or processing differences may call for agreed adjustments and alternative modes of participation rather than anxiety strategies, and learners can be referred to disability services.
reviewNotes: EAP teachers are not counsellors; severe or persistent anxiety should be referred to appropriate support services.

records.summary: The CEFR Companion Volume added scales for online interaction, recognising it as a mode with distinct demands (Council of Europe, 2020). In videoconference seminars, reduced gaze and gesture cues and audio delay make turn-taking harder, while chat and reactions provide additional channels; research on videoconferencing in language education highlights the coordination of these multimodal resources (Hampel & Stickler, 2012). Teach explicit bidding, addressing and yielding, purposeful chat use and breakout-room routines.

activities.title: Platform protocol
learnerActions: Agree group conventions for raising hands, using chat and muting
Hold a 10-minute discussion following the protocol
Review a recording to find where turn-taking broke down and revise the protocol
activities.intendedInsight: Explicit, agreed conventions can make online turn-taking easier to manage.
activities.rationale: Explicit conventions compensate for the reduced non-verbal cues of online interaction, which the Companion Volume treats as a distinct mode (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: Chat as a second channel
learnerActions: During an online discussion, one member posts sources and questions in the chat
Spoken participants explicitly take up chat contributions
Afterwards, discuss when the chat supported the discussion and when it distracted
activities.intendedInsight: Chat can widen participation when it is integrated with the spoken discussion.
activities.rationale: Draws on the multimodal affordances of videoconferencing described by Hampel and Stickler (2012).

difficulties.pattern: Contributing only through chat to avoid speaking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many chat messages but no spoken turns.
difficulties.response: Value chat as a legitimate mode and judge it on content. Where speaking is itself a learning goal and no adjustment applies, plan one spoken contribution that develops a chat post.

difficulties.pattern: Talking over others because of audio delay, then both speakers stopping.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated overlaps and false starts in recordings.
difficulties.response: Use explicit addressing and handover phrases and ask a facilitator to allocate turns; confirm before continuing after disruption.

diagnostic.task: Review a recorded online seminar with the learner and ask them to comment on their participation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Appropriate bidding, explicit addressing and yielding, and purposeful chat use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Participates but with awkward turn-taking or chat that runs separately from the discussion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No contribution in any channel, and no account of what would make participation possible.

records.contextNotes: Relevant at every stage where online or hybrid teaching occurs, including pre-sessional courses delivered online and PGR supervision and research-group meetings with remote collaborators. Hybrid rooms add the challenge of including remote participants in in-room talk.
reviewNotes: Little research addresses student-led academic seminars online specifically; guidance is partly practitioner-based.

records.summary: Debate formats train rapid argument construction, rebuttal and concession under time pressure. Kuhn (1991) found that many people have difficulty generating counter-arguments and rebuttals for their own positions, which suggests these moves need explicit teaching. Andrews (2010) discusses argument in higher education as both exploration and persuasion; learners should recognise that debate rewards adversarial advocacy, which differs from the exploratory norms of most seminars.

activities.title: Strongest objection first
learnerActions: Before the debate, each side lists the three strongest arguments for the opposing side
Prepare a rebuttal or concession for each
In the debate, rebut at least one of the opposition's strongest arguments
activities.intendedInsight: Effective rebuttal targets the opposition's strongest points.
activities.rationale: Addresses the difficulty in generating counter-arguments and rebuttals identified by Kuhn (1991).

activities.title: Debate versus seminar
learnerActions: After a debate, hold a seminar discussion on the same topic
Compare the moves used in each format
Discuss when each mode is appropriate in academic settings
activities.intendedInsight: Adversarial and exploratory argument serve different purposes.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the distinction between exploratory and persuasive argument discussed by Andrews (2010).

difficulties.pattern: Restating one's own case instead of rebutting the opposition.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rebuttal speeches repeat the constructive speech.
difficulties.response: Require rebuttals to begin by restating the specific opposing point being answered.

difficulties.pattern: Carrying the adversarial debate style into seminars.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner treats seminar discussion as a contest to win and rarely builds on others.
difficulties.response: Contrast the two modes explicitly and practise switching between them on the same topic.

diagnostic.task: After an opposing speech, ask for a 90-second rebuttal with two minutes' preparation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Targets the strongest opposing point, explains why it fails and concedes where appropriate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Rebuts a minor point or asserts that the opposition is wrong without explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats own case.

records.contextNotes: Debate is often used on foundation programmes as an activity format, but the topic as a whole is placed from pre-sessional level, where its argument prerequisites are taught. In-sessional UG use depends on the discipline, for example politics; law moots are covered separately. It is rarely relevant at PGT or PGR level except in specific professional programmes.
reviewNotes: Kuhn's (1991) participants were not EAP learners; the finding is used as a general rationale for explicit teaching of rebuttal.

Review response (R1-09, R3-07): foundation is not tagged although debate is used as an activity there, because its hard prerequisites (arg.oral-argument, arg.rebuttal-concession) start at B2 and are taught from pre-sessional level. With foundation removed, the start level is set to B2 rather than the B1+ applied under R1-09, so that every hard prerequisite starts at or below the topic; foundation debate activities can draw on sem.opinions and sem.agreeing-disagreeing.

records.summary: The CEFR Companion Volume treats explaining concepts and texts to others as mediation, with strategies such as linking to previous knowledge, adapting language and breaking down complicated information (Council of Europe, 2020). Mauranen (2012) shows speakers in English as a lingua franca academic settings rephrasing and adding explicitness to secure shared understanding, and translanguaging research presents shared languages as legitimate resources for making meaning (García & Li Wei, 2014). Reciprocal teaching, originally tested with school-age readers, structures peer explanation of texts around summarising, questioning, clarifying and predicting (Palincsar & Brown, 1984). Teach explanation as planned selection combined with live monitoring of the listener.

activities.title: Jigsaw explain-and-apply
learnerActions: Read one section of a shared text, or one figure, and prepare a three-step explanation with one example of your own
Explain it to a group who have read other sections, ending with a question that asks them to apply the idea
Listeners summarise what they understood, and the explainer reformulates anything that was missed
Rotate roles so that each member explains, questions and summarises
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining well depends on choosing what matters and checking what listeners can do with it.
activities.rationale: Adapts the rotating summarise–question–clarify roles of reciprocal teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984) and the Companion Volume's mediation strategies (Council of Europe, 2020) to university readings; its effect with adult EAP learners has not been tested directly.

activities.title: Same concept, three listeners
learnerActions: Choose a key concept from your module or reading
Explain it in 90 seconds to a peer from your field, a peer from another field and, if possible, a peer who shares another language with you
Note what you changed each time: terms defined, examples, analogies and language used
Agree with your listeners which changes helped and which lost precision
activities.intendedInsight: Explanations are adjusted to the listener, and simplifying must not distort the idea.
activities.rationale: Builds the rephrasing and explicitness strategies Mauranen (2012) documents in lingua franca academic talk, while keeping attention on accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: Explaining by repeating the source's wording or the textbook definition, sometimes more slowly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners nod but cannot restate or apply the idea; the explainer reads phrases from the text.
difficulties.response: Teach a define–exemplify–link routine and require one example that the source does not give. Do not simply ask for a 'simpler' version without showing what to change: terms, sentence length, order or examples.

difficulties.pattern: Simplifying to the point of error, for example turning a contested or conditional claim into a general rule.
difficulties.revealedBy: Peers' summaries contain claims stronger or broader than the source makes.
difficulties.response: Ask the explainer to state one limitation or condition of the idea and to check the simplified version against the source; treat accuracy and accessibility as joint requirements.

difficulties.pattern: 'We are not allowed to use our own language in class, even to explain something to each other.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who share a language struggle for minutes over a point that a brief bilingual gloss would resolve, or switch covertly and feel they are breaking a rule.
difficulties.response: Teachers and course designers should state when other languages may be used, for example for planning and clarification in pairs, and how the outcome is then reported in English. Make sure group members who do not share the language are not excluded, for example by summarising in English after each switch.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a key term from a recent reading and ask them to explain it to you as if you were a first-year student from another discipline; after the explanation, misunderstand one point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines the term accessibly, gives a fitting example, links it to familiar knowledge, notices the misunderstanding and reformulates in new terms without losing accuracy.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate but tied to the source wording, or accessible but imprecise; repeats the same words when misunderstood.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reads or recites the definition and cannot adjust it.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners often learn subject content and English together, so explaining concepts to peers is both a language and a content-learning task; keep texts short and allow shared-language planning. Pre-sessional UG learners practise through jigsaw readings and seminar tasks, while pre-sessional PG learners explain data, methods and disciplinary terms to mixed-discipline groups. In-sessional UG and PGT learners use it in study groups and assessed seminars. For PGR researchers it is the basis for explaining their work to colleagues from other fields and for teaching and demonstrating. Learners who need more processing time or find live explanation stressful, including some neurodivergent learners, can explain from a short prepared written or visual aid.
reviewNotes: Rules on using languages other than English in class vary across institutions and across EMI and TNE contexts; the guidance assumes that local policy is made explicit to learners.

records.summary: Research on academic presentations shows speakers shaping their talk to the audience: conference introductions combine contextual, argumentative and interactional moves (Rowley-Jolivet & Carter-Thomas, 2005), and presenters use interpersonal resources to engage listeners (Hood & Forey, 2005). Morita (2000) shows that what counts as a successful presentation is learned through socialisation into a particular community. Teach audience analysis as a planning step that changes content and selection, not only register.

activities.title: Same study, two audiences
learnerActions: Read a short study summary from your field
Plan a 3-minute talk on it for specialists and another for students from a different discipline
Compare the two plans: what was added, omitted, defined or exemplified differently, and why
activities.intendedInsight: Audience changes what you say, not only how formally you say it.
activities.rationale: Makes concrete the audience-oriented choices that Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005) identify in conference introductions.

activities.title: Audience questions first
learnerActions: Before planning, list five questions the audience is likely to have about the topic
Check that the plan answers the most important ones and drop content that answers none
After presenting, compare the predicted questions with those actually asked
activities.intendedInsight: Content selection can be driven by audience needs rather than by everything the speaker knows.
activities.rationale: Builds understanding of audience expectations as part of learning a community's presentation norms, as Morita (2000) describes.

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to show the teacher everything I know.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Overloaded content, rapid delivery and overruns; slides crowded with detail.
difficulties.response: Make the audience and purpose explicit in the task brief and assess selection as a criterion. Show that a focused talk demonstrates understanding more convincingly than coverage.

difficulties.pattern: Treating audience adaptation as changing greetings, contractions and formality only.
difficulties.revealedBy: Specialist and non-specialist versions of a talk differ only in surface formality.
difficulties.response: Compare paired versions of a talk in which terminology, background and examples change, and ask learners to identify each change.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Who is your audience, what do they already know, and what should they remember after your talk?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the audience's knowledge specifically, states a focused purpose and links both to content decisions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the audience generally ('my classmates') and a broad topic rather than a purpose.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot say who the audience is or what they should take away.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners work with peer audiences and simple purposes. Pre-sessional UG learners address peers and assessors; pre-sessional PG learners, for whom it is core, plan for mixed-discipline audiences and adapt specialist content. In-sessional UG and PGT learners adapt to module audiences; PGR researchers revisit it when adapting the same research for specialist, interdisciplinary and public audiences.

records.summary: Listeners process a presentation once, in real time, so explicit macro-structure matters: Chaudron and Richards (1986) found that macro-markers signalling lecture organisation aided listeners' recall, and Thompson (2003) shows lecturers signalling structure through both words and intonation. Speech and writing package information differently (Halliday, 1989), so presentations built paragraph by paragraph from an essay are hard to follow. Teach fewer main points, roadmaps and internal summaries.

activities.title: Essay to talk
learnerActions: Take a short essay you have written
Reduce it to three main points, each with one key support
Add a roadmap, internal summaries and a conclusion that returns to the purpose, then deliver it in four minutes
activities.intendedInsight: A presentation is restructured for listeners, not a spoken version of an essay.
activities.rationale: Applies the difference between written and spoken packaging of information (Halliday, 1989) to a familiar text.

activities.title: The listener's map
learnerActions: Listen to a peer's talk without slides and sketch its structure
Compare your sketch with the speaker's plan
Discuss where and why the structure was lost
activities.intendedInsight: Structure exists for listeners only if it is audible.
activities.rationale: Gives speakers direct evidence of the comprehension benefit of explicit macro-structure reported by Chaudron and Richards (1986).

difficulties.pattern: Including too many main points for the time available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Eight or more 'main points', rushed endings and no internal summaries.
difficulties.response: Set a maximum number of main points and practise grouping related ideas under one point.

difficulties.pattern: Following the written essay's structure and wording verbatim.
difficulties.revealedBy: The outline mirrors essay paragraphs; there is no roadmap or summary because the essay had none.
difficulties.response: Contrast reader and listener needs explicitly and require a spoken redesign of the structure.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show the plan for their next presentation and explain how the audience will know where they are at each stage.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A focused plan with a roadmap, internal summaries and time allocations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A clear sequence of points but no roadmap or summaries.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of slides with no overall structure.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from a clear default structure. In-sessional UG and PGT learners adapt structure to disciplinary formats (e.g. case presentations, design reviews, project pitches).
reviewNotes: Chaudron and Richards (1986) and Thompson (2003) study lectures, not student presentations; the transfer to presentations rests on the shared demands of extended academic monologue.

records.summary: Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005) show that conference presentation introductions combine setting up context, establishing the argument and interacting with the audience. Hood and Forey (2005) show presenters using interpersonal resources, including evaluation and humour, to build solidarity with the audience. Teach openings as a repertoire of moves to select and order for the audience and genre, rather than a fixed formula of greeting, name and topic.

activities.title: Opening move analysis
learnerActions: Watch the first two minutes of three academic talks in your field (e.g. recorded conference or departmental talks)
Label the moves used: context, relevance, purpose or claim, preview, audience engagement
Compare the order and length of moves across the three talks
activities.intendedInsight: Openings are built from identifiable moves that expert speakers combine flexibly.
activities.rationale: Applies the context–argument–interaction framework from Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005) to authentic models.

activities.title: Three alternative openings
learnerActions: Write three openings for the same talk, starting respectively with a question, a problem and a striking finding
Deliver each to a small group
The group chooses the most engaging opening and explains why
activities.intendedInsight: Interpersonal engagement can be designed and tested.
activities.rationale: Practises the interpersonal resources Hood and Forey (2005) identify in presentation introductions.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with a long self-introduction or an apology ('Sorry for my English').
difficulties.revealedBy: The first 30–60 seconds contain no purpose; apologies lower the audience's expectations.
difficulties.response: Discuss the effect of apologies on credibility and practise starting with relevance. Acknowledge nerves rather than forbidding any reference to them.

difficulties.pattern: Adding a rhetorical question or 'hook' unrelated to the talk's purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: An attention-grabbing question that the talk never returns to.
difficulties.response: Require every engagement move to link to the purpose and be revisited in the conclusion.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to deliver the first 60 seconds of a talk, then ask a listener to state its purpose and predict its structure.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The listener can state the purpose and predict the structure; an engagement move links to the purpose.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Purpose is clear but there is no preview or engagement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The listener cannot say what the talk is for.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a reliable default opening. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners adapt openings to the task and audience. PGR researchers work with conference introductions that position the study within a field and establish rapport with specialist audiences.

records.summary: Thompson (2003) shows lecturers signalling organisation through both lexical metadiscourse and intonation, and notes that EAP listening materials do not always reflect these authentic patterns; Chaudron and Richards (1986) found that macro-markers aided listeners' recall of lectures. Biber, Conrad and Cortes (2004) found discourse-organising lexical bundles to be particularly frequent in classroom teaching, and Deroey and Taverniers (2012) describe how lecturers flag important points. Teach production from authentic or authentic-like spoken models, teach lexical and prosodic signalling together, and treat density as a choice rather than maximising the number of markers. Noticing markers in lectures, developed as a listening skill, is a useful starting point for production.

activities.title: Signpost and pause
learnerActions: Mark the section boundaries in your plan and write a spoken transition for each
Mark a pause and a pitch reset at each boundary
Record the talk and check whether a listener can hear the boundaries without seeing the slides
activities.intendedInsight: Signposting is prosodic as well as lexical.
activities.rationale: Reflects Thompson's (2003) evidence that intonation and pausing contribute to signalling organisation.

activities.title: Written-to-spoken swap
learnerActions: Take a written paragraph of your own that uses connectors such as furthermore and moreover
Turn it into a one-minute spoken explanation using spoken markers and pauses
Record it, listen back and note where a listener might get lost
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken signposting is worded and paced differently from written linking.
activities.rationale: Biber, Conrad and Cortes (2004) show that classroom teaching uses distinctive discourse-organising bundles, and Thompson (2003) highlights the role of intonation in signalling organisation.

activities.title: Marking what matters
learnerActions: Identify the single most important point in each section of your talk
Mark it with a relevance marker and prosodic emphasis
Ask listeners afterwards to recall the key point of each section
activities.intendedInsight: Listeners are more likely to remember what speakers explicitly flag as important.
activities.rationale: Draws on Deroey and Taverniers's (2012) description of relevance markers in lectures.

difficulties.pattern: Using the same memorised formula at every transition ('Now I would like to move on to my next point').
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive markers that sound mechanical; signposts outnumber content statements.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of transitions, including content-based ones that summarise and preview, and reduce density for short talks.

difficulties.pattern: Presentations that sound read aloud because they use written connectors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Furthermore, moreover and in addition in spoken presentations; listeners losing the structure.
difficulties.response: Model spoken markers and rehearse them as chunks, and draw attention to differences between spoken and written registers.

difficulties.pattern: Markers planned in advance disappear, or are delivered without pausing, under the pressure of live delivery.
difficulties.revealedBy: Clear slides but no verbal signalling between sections, or correct markers run into the surrounding speech so that listeners cannot hear the boundaries.
difficulties.response: Rehearse transitions specifically, attach them to slide changes and mark pauses in the notes. Do not respond by adding more markers; make the existing ones audible.

diagnostic.task: The learner gives a 60-second spoken preview and the first transition of a talk on a topic of their choice, without slides; a listener then states the planned sections.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The listener names the sections; the learner uses at least two spoken-style macro-markers and pauses at the boundary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The structure is announced but with written-style connectors, or the boundary is not marked by pausing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No structuring language; the listener cannot say what comes next.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional (UG and PG) courses build a core repertoire for short assessed talks and seminar contributions, often alongside recognising markers in lectures. In-sessional UG learners refine density and variety and adapt signposting to group handovers and recorded formats. PGT and PGR learners revisit it for longer research talks and, for doctoral students who teach, for structuring their own explanations and lectures.
reviewNotes: The cited studies concern lectures; the guidance assumes similar listener needs in student presentations and spoken explanations.

Review response (R1-18): coh.spoken-signposting has been absorbed here for production; reception stays with lis.lecture-discourse-markers. The recommended hard edge between the two is not added from this file because the listening strand already links lis.lecture-discourse-markers <- prs.signposting (soft), and the reverse edge would create a cycle. If a reception-first order is preferred, the listening strand should drop its edge and prs.signposting <- lis.lecture-discourse-markers (soft) should be added here.

records.summary: In scientific conference presentations, visuals are central to how the argument is made rather than decorative (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002). Principles of visual composition such as salience, framing and information value help explain how audiences read slides (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006), and Tufte's (2001) principle of minimising non-data elements in graphics applies to charts on slides. Accessible design follows recognised standards for contrast and for not relying on colour alone (W3C, 2023). Teach slides as support for speech: the speaker carries the explanation; slides carry the point, key terms and evidence.

activities.title: Slide makeover
learnerActions: Take one of your own text-heavy slides
Rewrite the heading as a statement of the slide's point and move explanatory sentences to speaker notes
Simplify any chart by removing non-essential elements and highlighting the feature you will discuss
activities.intendedInsight: A slide supports speech best when it shows the point and the evidence, not the script.
activities.rationale: Applies principles of salience (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) and of reducing non-data elements (Tufte, 2001).

activities.title: Accessibility check
learnerActions: Check text–background contrast with a contrast-checking tool and test font sizes from the back of the room
Identify any meaning carried by colour alone and add labels or patterns
Add alternative text to figures in slides that will be shared
activities.intendedInsight: Accessible slides are clearer for everyone.
activities.rationale: Applies widely used accessibility criteria (W3C, 2023) to presentation slides.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I put everything on the slide, I won't forget anything and the audience can read it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Full sentences and paragraphs on slides; the speaker reads them aloud.
difficulties.response: Move text to speaker notes and practise speaking from prompts, keeping slides for the point and evidence. Do not strip all text at once from anxious presenters.

difficulties.pattern: Decorative templates, animations and stock images that are unrelated to the content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Visual elements that compete with or do not relate to the message.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to justify every visual element by its function; remove those that have none.

difficulties.pattern: Pasting complex figures from published papers without simplification.
difficulties.revealedBy: Illegible axes, multiple panels and no indication of what the audience should look at.
difficulties.response: Teach simplifying, cropping or rebuilding figures and highlighting the relevant feature, with attribution.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to talk you through three of their slides, saying what each slide's point is and what the audience should look at.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Each slide has a clear point stated in the heading, minimal text and a focused visual.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Points are clear in speech but not on the slides, or visuals are not simplified.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Slides are pages of text that the learner reads aloud.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on basic text economy and legibility. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners add data visuals and accessibility. PGR researchers design for conference conditions and disciplinary conventions, for example dense results slides in some sciences.
reviewNotes: Popular slide 'rules' (e.g. fixed numbers of bullets or words per slide) lack a strong research base and are deliberately not presented as rules here.
W3C (2023) concerns web content; its contrast and use-of-colour criteria are applied to slides by analogy.

records.summary: Rowley-Jolivet (2002) shows that visuals carry much of the argument in scientific conference presentations, and the CEFR Companion Volume treats explaining data in graphs and diagrams as a mediation activity (Council of Europe, 2020). The written data-commentary moves of locating, highlighting and interpreting (Swales & Feak, 2012) transfer to speech, with an added need to orient listeners first and to synchronise speech with pointing.

activities.title: Orient, highlight, interpret
learnerActions: For a chart from your field, write one orienting sentence (what it shows, axes, units)
Choose the one or two features that matter and say what they mean for your argument
Deliver the explanation in 60 seconds and ask listeners what they would remember
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining a visual means selecting and interpreting, not describing everything.
activities.rationale: Adapts the data-commentary moves described by Swales and Feak (2012) for listeners.

activities.title: Point and speak
learnerActions: Rehearse explaining a complex figure while pointing to each element as you mention it
Use slide builds to reveal the figure in stages
Compare audience comprehension with and without builds
activities.intendedInsight: Synchronising speech and visual attention reduces audience effort.
activities.rationale: Responds to the central argumentative role of visuals in research presentations (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: Reading out every value in the chart.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long lists of numbers with no interpretation.
difficulties.response: Limit learners to two highlighted features and require a 'so what' statement.

difficulties.pattern: Errors saying numbers aloud (e.g. thirteen/thirty, decimals, large numbers).
difficulties.revealedBy: Listener confusion about quantities; mismatch between spoken and displayed figures.
difficulties.response: Practise saying the specific numbers in the talk and round where precision is unnecessary.

difficulties.pattern: Talking about a visual before it appears, or after moving on to the next slide.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatch between what is said and what is shown.
difficulties.response: Rehearse with the slides and plan builds; pause to let the audience look before explaining.

diagnostic.task: Show an unfamiliar chart for one minute and ask for a 60-second explanation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Orients, highlights one to three features and interprets them, with accurate numbers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate description but no interpretation, or interpretation without orientation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reads values left to right or misreads the chart.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners practise with simple charts. Pre-sessional PG learners treat it as a core skill because postgraduate presentations in most fields rely on data. In-sessional UG and PGT learners explain disciplinary visuals; PGR researchers explain their own complex results, often under time pressure.

records.summary: Intelligibility-oriented pronunciation teaching prioritises features that most affect listeners' understanding rather than native-like accent (Derwing & Munro, 2015). Hahn (2004) found that appropriate primary stress in a recorded lecture improved listeners' recall and their evaluations of the speaker, and Pickering (2001) found that international teaching assistants' tone choices shaped how engaging and comprehensible their teaching was perceived to be. Focus delivery work on thought groups, prominence, pace and intonation.

activities.title: Mark up and deliver
learnerActions: Mark thought-group boundaries and prominent words on a one-minute section of your talk
Record it and listen for whether prominence falls on new and contrastive information
Re-record after revising the marking
activities.intendedInsight: Where stress and pauses fall changes how easily listeners follow.
activities.rationale: Targets the prominence features Hahn (2004) found to affect listeners' comprehension.

activities.title: Intelligibility feedback from diverse listeners
learnerActions: Present a two-minute section to peers from different language backgrounds
Listeners note any moments where they lost track and what caused it
Revise the specific words or stretches identified, rather than the whole accent
activities.intendedInsight: Intelligibility depends on specific, fixable features, not on sounding native.
activities.rationale: Reflects the intelligibility priority argued by Derwing and Munro (2015).

difficulties.pattern: Speaking faster and faster to get through all the content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rising speech rate and fewer pauses as the talk progresses, especially near the end.
difficulties.response: Cut content rather than increasing speed; set time checkpoints. Do not simply tell the speaker to 'slow down' without reducing content.

difficulties.pattern: Distributing stress evenly across words and syllables, so key information does not stand out.
difficulties.revealedBy: Monotone or evenly stressed delivery; listeners miss contrasts and key terms. Speakers whose first languages mark emphasis through word order, particles or syllable timing rather than pitch prominence may transfer these patterns.
difficulties.response: Teach prominence explicitly with contrastive examples from the learner's own talk and practise with recordings.

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to get rid of my accent before I can present.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners focus on individual sounds unrelated to intelligibility, or avoid presenting.
difficulties.response: Discuss the distinction between accent and intelligibility and focus feedback on features that affect understanding.

diagnostic.task: Record the learner delivering one minute of their talk and ask them to mark where they paused and which words they stressed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Pauses at meaningful boundaries, prominence on key information and a sustainable pace; the learner can describe these choices.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Appropriate pace but even stress, or good prominence with pauses mid-phrase.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Rapid, unpaused delivery or pauses unrelated to meaning.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners focus on thought groups, pace and key-word stress as core assessed features; pre-sessional PG learners refine prominence on technical terms. In-sessional UG learners extend this to longer and recorded talks, and PGT and PGR learners revisit it for large rooms, longer talks and teaching. Learners who stammer should be assessed on intelligibility, organisation and content rather than on speech rate or smoothness, with agreed adjustments such as extra time.

records.summary: Non-verbal resources such as gaze, gesture, posture and use of space are part of spoken communication and are recognised as paralinguistic features in the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001). There is little EAP-specific research on teaching non-verbal presentation behaviour, so guidance should be pragmatic and non-prescriptive: help learners use gesture and gaze purposefully, especially to direct attention to visuals, and reduce distracting habits, while respecting individual differences including disability and neurodivergence. Avoid the widely repeated claim that most meaning is conveyed non-verbally, which misapplies experimental findings about conflicting cues to emotion.

activities.title: Sound-off review
learnerActions: Watch a video of yourself presenting with the sound off
Note what supports the message (pointing to visuals, open posture) and what distracts (pacing, fidgeting, back to the audience)
Set one specific goal for the next presentation
activities.intendedInsight: Non-verbal behaviour can be observed and adjusted one feature at a time.
activities.rationale: Video self-review isolates the visual channel that the CEFR identifies as part of communication (Council of Europe, 2001).

activities.title: Point, turn, talk
learnerActions: Practise pointing to a feature on a slide
Turn back to face the audience
Then explain the feature, repeating the sequence for several slides
activities.intendedInsight: Speakers can direct attention to visuals without speaking to the screen.
activities.rationale: Supports the coordination of speech and visuals that research presentations require.

difficulties.pattern: Reading from the screen with the back to the audience.
difficulties.revealedBy: Little audience gaze; the speaker faces the projection.
difficulties.response: Use speaker notes or a confidence monitor and practise the point–turn–talk sequence.

difficulties.pattern: Copying a single 'confident' model of body language that feels unnatural or conflicts with the speaker's own norms or needs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exaggerated, rehearsed gestures; discomfort; forced sustained eye contact.
difficulties.response: Focus on purposeful, non-distracting behaviour rather than conformity; allow alternatives to sustained eye contact (e.g. scanning, looking between faces) and discuss variation in norms.

diagnostic.task: Watch a two-minute video of the learner with the sound off and ask them to evaluate it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies specific supporting and distracting behaviours and sets a realistic goal.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies general impressions ('I look nervous') without specific behaviours.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify any features or focuses only on appearance.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit most from basic awareness and video review. In-sessional UG learners adapt to larger rooms, group formats and online cameras; at PGT level the topic is left to self-access. Autistic presenters and others for whom sustained eye contact is uncomfortable can use alternatives such as scanning or looking between faces, and should not be marked down for it.
reviewNotes: Evidence on non-verbal training for L2 academic presenters is thin; these recommendations are practitioner-based.
The often-quoted '7%–38%–55%' figures derive from experiments on inconsistent cues about feelings and should not be applied to presentations.

records.summary: Written language is lexically dense, whereas speech spreads information across more clauses (Halliday, 1989), and corpus research shows that spoken university registers differ systematically from academic writing (Biber, 2006). A written script read aloud is therefore hard for listeners to process and is usually delivered with flat prosody. Teach a graduated move from script to prompts, keeping short scripted segments for high-risk moments such as the opening and key definitions.

activities.title: Script-to-prompts ladder
learnerActions: Write a full script for one section of your talk
Highlight the key words, numbers and transitions, then copy only these onto a cue card
Deliver from the cue card, record it, and compare the recording with the script
activities.intendedInsight: Speaking from prompts produces more listenable language than reading a script.
activities.rationale: Makes the difference between written and spoken packaging (Halliday, 1989) audible to the learner.

activities.title: Written sentence, spoken sentence
learnerActions: Take three dense written sentences from your script
Rewrite each as two or three shorter spoken sentences
Say both versions aloud to a partner and ask which is easier to follow
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken academic language unpacks information into clauses.
activities.rationale: Draws on Biber's (2006) evidence of systematic differences between spoken and written university registers.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I don't read, I'll make grammar mistakes or forget something.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Refusal to give up the script; anxiety when notes are reduced.
difficulties.response: Allow scripted openings, definitions and transitions while the rest is delivered from prompts; reduce support gradually. Do not remove all notes at once.

difficulties.pattern: Memorising the whole script word for word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unnatural rhythm, little eye contact and breakdown if interrupted or a word is forgotten.
difficulties.response: Rehearse from prompts with deliberate variation in wording, and practise recovering from a lost place.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their notes for a forthcoming presentation and deliver one minute from them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Key-word notes; delivery uses spoken-style sentences with frequent eye contact.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Bullet-point notes that are full sentences, or near-verbatim recall.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A full script read aloud.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners often begin with scripts, so the move to prompts is core there and should be staged. Pre-sessional learners extend it to longer assessed talks. In-sessional and PGT learners revisit the same principles for recorded and online presentations, where reading from screen is tempting. Learners with dyslexia or other specific learning differences may work better from visual prompts such as mind maps, icons or large-print cue cards than from text-based notes.

records.summary: Wulff, Swales and Keller (2009) analysed the discussion sessions following talks at a specialised conference and describe them as a distinctive part-genre in which audience turns include comments and suggestions as well as questions. Morita (2000) shows that handling questions in classroom presentations is part of being socialised into a disciplinary community. Teach a listen–clarify–answer–check routine, strategies for critical questions and comments, and honest acknowledgement of limits.

activities.title: Question-type practice
learnerActions: Prepare for four turn types: clarification, challenge to evidence, out-of-scope question and comment or suggestion
Plan a response strategy for each (answer, acknowledge and defend, defer, thank and engage)
Practise in a simulated Q&A with peers playing each role
activities.intendedInsight: Not all Q&A turns are questions, and each type calls for a different response.
activities.rationale: Based on Wulff et al.'s (2009) description of the range of audience turns in discussion sessions.

activities.title: Reformulate before answering
learnerActions: A partner asks a long, multi-part question
The presenter reformulates it briefly and confirms
The presenter answers each part concisely and checks whether the question was answered
activities.intendedInsight: Reformulating buys thinking time and avoids answering the wrong question.
activities.rationale: Builds the interactive competence Morita (2000) describes as part of oral academic socialisation.

difficulties.pattern: Answering immediately, before fully understanding the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that address a different question from the one asked.
difficulties.response: Make reformulation or confirmation a routine first step and allow a short pause.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a critical question as a personal attack.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive tone, over-long justification or withdrawal.
difficulties.response: Reframe critical questions as engagement; practise acknowledging the point before responding. Prepare answers to likely challenges in advance.

difficulties.pattern: Not knowing how to say 'I don't know' without losing face.
difficulties.revealedBy: Guessing, evasion or a bare 'I don't know'.
difficulties.response: Teach hedged acknowledgements and offers to follow up, and show that experts use them.

diagnostic.task: After a short presentation, ask a clarification question, a challenge and an out-of-scope question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reformulates where needed, answers concisely, defends or concedes appropriately and acknowledges limits honestly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers relevantly but at length, or becomes defensive under challenge.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misunderstands questions or cannot respond to the challenge.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners practise short, predictable Q&A after group talks. Pre-sessional UG and PG learners handle timed Q&A in assessed presentations, with PG courses adding challenges to evidence and method. In-sessional UG and PGT learners face module Q&A and project panels. PGR researchers handle conference discussion sessions, progression panels and vivas, where questions may be expert and searching. Letting questioners repeat or write down questions, and allowing short thinking time, supports learners with hearing or processing differences.

records.summary: Leki (2001) found that multilingual undergraduates in group projects were often positioned as less competent and allocated marginal roles, with little guidance from instructors on how groups should work. Group presentations therefore combine language and collaboration demands. Teach shared planning of message and structure, handovers that link content, consistent slides and shared Q&A, using joint rehearsal to integrate the talk; the Companion Volume's goal-oriented co-operation scale describes the language of this kind of joint planning (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: One-sentence message test
learnerActions: Before dividing sections, the group writes the presentation's overall message in one sentence
Each member checks that their section supports that sentence
At the run-through, each member states the message from memory and the group resolves any differences
activities.intendedInsight: A group talk needs one message, not several.
activities.rationale: Makes shared planning concrete and exposes divided planning early.

activities.title: Handover rewriting
learnerActions: Collect the group's handovers from a rehearsal (e.g. 'Now X will talk about…')
Rewrite each to summarise the outgoing section and preview the incoming point
Rehearse the transitions only, several times
activities.intendedInsight: Handovers are signposts that connect content across speakers.
activities.rationale: Applies signposting to the multi-speaker format, where cohesion is most at risk.

difficulties.pattern: Dividing the talk by person rather than by content, so each member prepares a separate mini-presentation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated introductions, inconsistent slides and different messages across sections.
difficulties.response: Require a shared plan and a single slide deck before individual preparation begins.

difficulties.pattern: Multilingual members allocated only slide-making or the shortest speaking part on the basis of assumed language ability.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unequal speaking time; members report being sidelined.
difficulties.response: Address the whole group's assumptions rather than the sidelined member; teachers can require each member to present substantive content and check plans for balanced speaking roles, and provide support for all speakers.

difficulties.pattern: Handovers limited to names.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abrupt transitions; the audience loses the thread between speakers.
difficulties.response: Practise content-linking handovers and rehearse transitions separately.

diagnostic.task: Ask each group member separately to state the presentation's overall message and how their section contributes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Consistent messages and clear links between sections.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Similar topic descriptions but no shared message.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Members describe unrelated sections.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes often use group presentations as early assessment, and in-sessional UG modules use them widely, often with peer assessment of contribution. Pre-sessional and PGT courses use them less centrally.

records.summary: MacIntosh-Murray (2007) analyses the conference poster as a genre with its own forms, norms and values, noting the gap between advice that favours concise, visual posters and the text-heavy posters often produced, and the centrality of presenter–visitor interaction to the poster's communicative work. Kress and van Leeuwen's (2006) concepts of salience and composition help learners design reading paths deliberately, and accessibility criteria for contrast and use of colour (W3C, 2023) apply by analogy. Teach design and presentation together: the poster should be designed to support the spoken overview and the questions it will prompt.

activities.title: Poster gallery critique
learnerActions: Examine a set of real posters from a conference or departmental display in your field
Rate each for clarity of the main message at two metres, reading path and text density
Identify features shared by the most effective posters and draft design principles for your discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Effective posters prioritise one message and are designed for viewing at a distance.
activities.rationale: Uses authentic exemplars to surface genre norms, in line with MacIntosh-Murray's (2007) genre perspective.

activities.title: Word-budget redesign
learnerActions: Set a word budget for your own poster draft
Cut text to fit, converting prose results into captioned figures, and restructure along a clear reading path
Test the poster with a peer who has 30 seconds to state the main message
activities.intendedInsight: A word budget forces prioritisation of claims.
activities.rationale: Applies salience and composition (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) under a realistic constraint.

activities.title: Visitor role cards
learnerActions: Prepare a 30-second and a 2-minute overview of your poster
Visitors draw role cards (specialist, student from another field, potential collaborator, sceptic) and signal how much time they have
Open with a question to gauge each visitor and adapt the length, depth and route through the poster
Visitors give feedback on how well the explanation fitted them
activities.intendedInsight: Poster conversations are dialogues tailored to each visitor.
activities.rationale: Practises the visitor-driven interaction central to the genre (MacIntosh-Murray, 2007).

difficulties.pattern: Putting the essay or abstract on the poster.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense paragraphs in small type; the full text of an abstract or introduction. This is common where earlier assessment has rewarded complete written coverage of a topic.
difficulties.response: Use word budgets and distance testing, and model how to cut. Simply saying 'use less text' rarely helps.

difficulties.pattern: Decoration before hierarchy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Background images, many colours and fonts, and no clear entry point.
difficulties.response: Establish the hierarchy (headline, key figure, supporting sections) first and add decoration last, if at all.

difficulties.pattern: Delivering the same memorised monologue to every visitor.
difficulties.revealedBy: Visitors disengage; no questions are invited.
difficulties.response: Practise opening with a question to the visitor and adapting depth; rehearse with varied visitor roles.

difficulties.pattern: Standing silently and waiting for visitors to read the poster.
difficulties.revealedBy: Visitors pass by; few conversations begin.
difficulties.response: Prepare a friendly opening line and a one-sentence summary to offer. Presenters who find unscripted openings difficult, including some autistic presenters and people who stammer, can use a printed one-line summary or an invitation to ask questions as an alternative way in.

diagnostic.task: Show the learner's poster to a peer for 30 seconds and ask the peer to state the main finding; then ask the learner to present the poster to you as a non-specialist visitor.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The peer identifies the intended main finding, and the learner's overview is brief, adapted and uses the poster to guide attention.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The peer identifies the topic but not the finding, or the overview is accurate but not adapted.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The peer cannot identify the topic or the finding, and the learner recites a fixed speech.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional programmes sometimes assess posters as group or individual projects, more often for postgraduate entrants in science and health fields. In-sessional UG learners meet discipline posters, often produced in groups, and PGT learners present dissertation posters. PGR researchers present at conferences, where poster norms vary by field and event and the session is a common entry point to research networks.
reviewNotes: MacIntosh-Murray (2007) is a single case study of one health-services conference; generalisations about poster norms should be cautious.
W3C (2023) concerns web content; its contrast and use-of-colour criteria are applied to posters by analogy.

records.summary: Conference presentations are a key research genre: their introductions combine context, argument and audience interaction (Rowley-Jolivet & Carter-Thomas, 2005), visuals carry much of the argument (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002), and discussion sessions form a distinct part-genre (Wulff et al., 2009). Aguilar (2004) describes the peer seminar as a spoken research process genre in which work in progress is presented to colleagues. Teach researchers to select a take-home message, frame the niche and contribution early, design visuals for the argument and keep strictly to time.

activities.title: Take-home message first
learnerActions: Write the one sentence you want the audience to remember
Design the talk backwards, keeping only content that supports that sentence
Check that the introduction frames the niche and the conclusion restates the message
activities.intendedInsight: A research talk is an argument for one contribution, not a summary of a thesis.
activities.rationale: Applies the argumentative dimension of conference introductions described by Rowley-Jolivet and Carter-Thomas (2005).

activities.title: Comparing research talk formats
learnerActions: Compare a conference talk and a work-in-progress peer seminar in your field (recorded or attended)
Note differences in polish, interaction, length and purpose
Plan how your own talk would change between the two formats
activities.intendedInsight: Research presentation formats serve different purposes in the research process.
activities.rationale: Draws on Aguilar's (2004) characterisation of the peer seminar as distinct from the conference presentation.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting the research like a thesis chapter: long background and methods, little on contribution.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contribution appears only in the final minute or not at all.
difficulties.response: Require the niche and contribution within the first three minutes and cut background accordingly.

difficulties.pattern: Overrunning because all results are included.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rushed final slides; the chair has to intervene.
difficulties.response: Select results for the take-home message and rehearse with strict timing; prepare backup slides for questions.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the discussion session as an examination to survive rather than a dialogue about the research.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive or minimal answers; missed opportunities to engage with suggestions.
difficulties.response: Discuss the range of turns in discussion sessions (Wulff et al., 2009) and practise responding to comments and suggestions as well as questions.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to present the first three minutes and last minute of a research talk, then take two questions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Niche and contribution clear early, a focused take-home message and dialogic answers.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Clear content but contribution emerges late, or answers are defensive.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Background-heavy with no clear contribution; overruns.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional PG courses for research-degree entrants may introduce the genre through a presentation of a research proposal. PGT learners present dissertation projects or proposals. PGR researchers present at progression reviews, departmental seminars and conferences, where time limits are strict and audiences are specialist; disciplinary conventions (e.g. results-heavy sciences, text-heavy humanities papers read aloud) vary and should be observed locally. Short pitches for mixed audiences are treated as a separate genre.
reviewNotes: In some humanities fields conference papers are traditionally read from a script; guidance on speaking from notes should be adapted to local disciplinary norms.

records.summary: Recorded and online presentations are now common in assessment, including on pre-sessional programmes. They remove live audience feedback and allow re-recording, which can encourage reading from a script; learners need the same spoken-style principles as for live talks (Halliday, 1989), plus technical and accessibility skills such as providing accurate captions (W3C, 2023). Assessment rules on editing, length and tool use must be read carefully.

activities.title: Two-take comparison
learnerActions: Record a two-minute section reading from a full script
Record the same section from key-word prompts
Compare the two recordings for naturalness, pace and engagement with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Recorded talks also sound better when delivered from prompts.
activities.rationale: Applies the difference between written and spoken packaging (Halliday, 1989) to recorded formats.

activities.title: Caption check
learnerActions: Generate automatic captions for your recording
Correct errors, especially technical terms, names and numbers
Note which words were misrecognised and check your pronunciation of them
activities.intendedInsight: Captions improve accessibility and can reveal intelligibility issues.
activities.rationale: Applies captioning requirements for prerecorded media (W3C, 2023).

difficulties.pattern: Re-recording endlessly in pursuit of a perfect take.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many hours spent on short recordings; increasingly stilted delivery.
difficulties.response: Set a limit on takes and focus feedback on intelligibility and structure rather than perfection.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a script visible beside the camera, with eyes off the lens.
difficulties.revealedBy: Eye movement across text; written-style language.
difficulties.response: Use prompts placed near the camera and rehearse from them.

difficulties.pattern: Breaching task rules on editing, length or tools (e.g. AI voice or script generation).
difficulties.revealedBy: Submissions that exceed limits or use prohibited tools.
difficulties.response: Read the assessment brief and AI policy with learners and clarify what editing is allowed.

diagnostic.task: Review a 2-minute recorded presentation section and the learner's note on how it was produced.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Clear audio, synchronised slides, natural delivery, corrected captions and compliance with rules.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Technically sound but read from a script, or captions uncorrected.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Poor audio, script reading and rule breaches.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes, especially online ones, often assess recorded presentations. In-sessional UG and PGT modules use them for flexibility; PGR researchers produce recorded conference talks and three-minute research summaries for online events.
reviewNotes: Little published research addresses recorded EAP presentation assessments; guidance is practitioner-based.

records.summary: Speech production involves conceptualising, formulating and articulating (Levelt, 1989); rehearsal moves much of the conceptual and formulation work out of the live moment, freeing attention for the audience. Task-based research reviewed by Skehan (1998) indicates that planning tends to improve fluency. Rehearsal should be aloud, timed and section by section, with content cut in advance.

activities.title: Timed run-through with checkpoints
learnerActions: Set a target time for each section and mark checkpoints in your notes
Rehearse aloud with a timer, recording actual times
Cut or condense sections that overrun and rehearse again
activities.intendedInsight: Timing problems are solved by planning cuts, not by speaking faster.
activities.rationale: Applies findings on planning and fluency (Skehan, 1998) to presentation rehearsal.

activities.title: The emergency version
learnerActions: Prepare a version of your talk that is one third shorter
Decide in advance which sections or slides you would skip
Rehearse switching to the short version mid-talk
activities.intendedInsight: A planned short version protects the key message when time is cut.
activities.rationale: Builds flexibility for real presentation conditions, where sessions often run late.

difficulties.pattern: Rehearsing silently or by reading through the slides.
difficulties.revealedBy: First aloud delivery is in the assessment; large overruns.
difficulties.response: Require evidence of aloud, timed rehearsal (e.g. a recording).

difficulties.pattern: Planning to speak faster if time runs short.
difficulties.revealedBy: No cuts planned; rapid delivery at the end.
difficulties.response: Show that faster speech reduces intelligibility; plan section-level cuts.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what happened in their last rehearsal and what they changed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports timed, aloud rehearsals with specific changes and planned cuts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Rehearsed once without timing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has not rehearsed aloud.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need rehearsal built into lessons, with recordings as evidence. In-sessional UG and PGT learners revisit it for assessed talks; strict timing for conference slots and pitches is developed within those genres rather than taught separately at PGR level.
reviewNotes: Skehan (1998) reviews planning studies on L2 tasks rather than presentations; applying them to rehearsal is an inference.

records.summary: Hyland (2010) shows that writers addressing non-specialist readers construct proximity differently from those writing for peers, foregrounding relevance, engagement and accessible framing; the same choices shape pitches for mixed audiences. Research on conference introductions shows speakers combining context, argument and audience interaction from the outset (Rowley-Jolivet & Carter-Thomas, 2005), and short formats compress these moves into seconds. The Researcher Development Framework treats communicating with and engaging diverse audiences as part of researcher development (Vitae, 2010). Teach the pitch as one narrative built backwards from its significance, rehearsed at several lengths, and contrast it with the specialist research presentation.

activities.title: One sentence, three lengths
learnerActions: Write one sentence stating the problem, what you did or will do, and why it matters
Expand it into a 30-second and a three-minute version, keeping the same narrative spine
Deliver both to a partner from another discipline, who restates your research in their own words
Revise wherever your partner's restatement differs from what you meant
activities.intendedInsight: A pitch is a single narrative that can be lengthened or shortened, not a shortened thesis.
activities.rationale: Builds on the context, argument and interaction moves of conference introductions (Rowley-Jolivet & Carter-Thomas, 2005), compressed for short formats.

activities.title: Jargon and proximity audit
learnerActions: Record a draft pitch and transcribe it
Highlight every technical term, abstraction and acronym, and mark where you address the audience directly or relate the work to their experience
Replace or explain the highlighted terms and add one concrete example or analogy
Check that the simplified version has not changed or overstated your findings
activities.intendedInsight: Accessibility comes from relevance and concrete framing as well as from simpler words.
activities.rationale: Applies Hyland's (2010) account of how proximity to non-specialist readers is constructed to a spoken pitch.

difficulties.pattern: Compressing a conference talk or thesis chapter into three minutes: background, methods and results in miniature.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense, jargon-heavy pitches that overrun; listeners cannot say why the work matters.
difficulties.response: Build from the significance backwards, limit the pitch to one problem and one finding or aim, and test it with listeners from other fields. Do not respond by asking the presenter to speak faster.

difficulties.pattern: Overclaiming significance in pursuit of impact, especially for projects without results.
difficulties.revealedBy: Promises of outcomes that the evidence does not support; certainty stated more strongly than in the written work.
difficulties.response: Distinguish stating relevance from claiming outcomes, practise hedged significance statements for work in progress, and check each claim against what has actually been found.

difficulties.pattern: Losing the thread under a strict cut-off, especially in competitions that do not allow notes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Word-for-word scripts that break down when one phrase is forgotten; finishing well short or being stopped mid-sentence.
difficulties.response: Rehearse from a narrative spine and key phrases rather than a word-for-word script, and practise recovering mid-pitch. Where rules ban notes or set fixed formats, check what adjustments are available for presenters who stammer, are neurodivergent or have other relevant disabilities.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner for a 60-second spoken pitch of their research to you as an educated non-specialist, then ask, 'So why does that matter?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear problem–approach–significance narrative in accessible terms, a concrete hook and a significance claim calibrated to the evidence; the follow-up answer adds a new, concrete point.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A clear topic, but significance is generic ('it is important for the field') or jargon remains.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of methods or background with no stated problem or significance.

records.contextNotes: PGR researchers meet the format in three-minute thesis-style competitions, conference networking, progression events, interviews and funding contexts; it complements but differs from the specialist research presentation. PGT learners may pitch dissertation or consultancy projects, especially in business, engineering and design programmes. Formats vary in time limit, slides and props, so learners should check the rules of the event.
reviewNotes: No genre analysis of three-minute thesis or elevator pitches is in the project bibliography; the guidance extrapolates from research on popularisation and on conference introductions.

records.summary: Munro and Derwing (1995) showed that accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility are related but partly independent: speech can be strongly accented yet fully intelligible. Levis (2005) contrasted the nativeness principle with the intelligibility principle and argued that instruction should prioritise features that affect understanding, and the CEFR Companion Volume's phonological scales were redeveloped around intelligibility rather than native-speaker norms (Council of Europe, 2020). Jenkins' (2000) Lingua Franca Core proposes intelligibility priorities for lingua franca settings, though its specific inventory is contested. Teaching should begin from what listeners actually fail to understand.

activities.title: Transcribe and rate
learnerActions: Record a 1-minute explanation of a concept from their field
Ask two listeners to transcribe a section and rate how easy it was to understand
Compare the transcriptions with the script and identify where understanding failed
Choose one or two features to work on based on the failures, not on accent
activities.intendedInsight: What matters is what listeners understand, which is not the same as how accented the speech sounds.
activities.rationale: Applies the intelligibility measures used by Munro and Derwing (1995) as a diagnostic.

activities.title: Accent is not the problem
learnerActions: Listen to several speakers with different accents explaining academic concepts
Rate each for accent strength and ease of understanding
Discuss cases where a strong accent was easy to understand and why
activities.intendedInsight: Accent and ease of understanding are partly independent.
activities.rationale: Experiences the partial independence of accent and comprehensibility reported by Munro and Derwing (1995) and the intelligibility principle argued by Levis (2005).

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to lose my accent to be taken seriously.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for accent reduction; anxiety about speaking in front of peers.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that accent bias exists — Rubin (1992) found that listeners' expectations affected their comprehension of identical speech — while reframing goals around intelligibility and pointing out that listener attitudes are not the speaker's fault. Do not promise accent elimination or frame accent as a deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Learners equate good pronunciation with producing individual sounds correctly and neglect stress and prosody.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners ask only for work on particular sounds; their stress and prosody errors cause more misunderstanding than their sounds.
difficulties.response: Show evidence that stress and prominence affect intelligibility (Field, 2005; Hahn, 2004) and use listener transcription to locate actual breakdowns.

difficulties.pattern: Speaking criteria, feedback or listeners' comments reward 'native-like' pronunciation or penalise accent, so the learner is judged on accentedness rather than on how well they are understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rubrics with descriptors such as 'native-like' or 'neutral accent'; feedback that names the accent without identifying any misunderstanding; learners who are intelligible but receive low pronunciation marks.
difficulties.response: Assessment teams should review speaking criteria so that pronunciation is judged on intelligibility and comprehensibility for the intended audience, and train raters to separate accent from understanding. Learners can ask for feedback that names what a listener did not understand.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner: 'What would good pronunciation mean for you at university?' and 'Which parts of your pronunciation cause listeners problems?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines goals in terms of being understood by their audience and names specific features based on feedback.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions being understood but sets goals in terms of imitating a reference accent, or lists sounds without evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Aims to eliminate accent and has no sense of which features matter.

records.contextNotes: This concept frames all pronunciation work and should be introduced at foundation and pre-sessional level, both UG and PG. In-sessionally it is revisited when students ask for accent reduction. For PGR students who teach or present internationally, it supports a confident professional identity as a multilingual speaker.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-01): stage roles now limit this topic to develop at foundation and pre-sessional stages and revisit elsewhere; it is not core at any stage because it is a framing concept rather than a separately assessed skill.

records.summary: Field (2005) found that misplaced lexical stress reduced intelligibility for both native and non-native listeners, with shifts to a later syllable especially disruptive in his data. Because stress shifts systematically across academic word families, and a limited number of stress patterns account for much of the Academic Word List (Murphy & Kandil, 2004), stress can be taught alongside vocabulary as part of knowing a word. Compound and phrase stress matter too: noun + noun compounds, which are frequent in technical vocabulary, usually stress the first element, whereas adjective + noun phrases stress the noun. Teach stress with each new word, emphasise patterns rather than lists, and check perception as well as production (Derwing & Munro, 2015).

activities.title: Word family stress patterns
learnerActions: Sort members of academic word families (analyse, analysis, analytical; economy, economic, economics) by which syllable is stressed
Infer rules associated with particular suffixes
Test the rules on new words using dictionary audio
activities.intendedInsight: Stress shifts follow patterns that can be learnt and used to predict new words.
activities.rationale: Draws on the regularity of stress patterns in academic vocabulary described by Murphy and Kandil (2004).

activities.title: Stress in vocabulary records
learnerActions: Add stress marking to vocabulary notes or cards for every new multi-syllable word
Practise saying each word within a common collocation
Test a partner on stress placement for recently learnt words
activities.intendedInsight: Stress is part of knowing a word, not an extra.
activities.rationale: Field (2005) shows that stress is part of what listeners use to recognise words, so learners need it stored with the word.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language has fixed stress, or little lexical stress contrast, apply one stress position to all words or give syllables similar weight.
difficulties.revealedBy: Consistent stress on the first or last syllable regardless of the word; few reduced vowels.
difficulties.response: Teach English stress as variable but patterned, and practise reduced vowels in unstressed syllables alongside stress placement.

difficulties.pattern: Learners keep the stress of the base word in derived forms (ANalysis by analogy with ANalyse).
difficulties.revealedBy: Stress errors concentrated in derived forms of familiar words.
difficulties.response: Present family members together and highlight the stress shift; practise in contrast.

difficulties.pattern: Learners have met most academic vocabulary through reading and have guessed its stress from spelling.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident but consistently wrong stress on long words learnt through reading.
difficulties.response: Build checking with dictionary audio into vocabulary routines and treat stress as part of word knowledge.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud six academic words in two families and to mark the stress before saying them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Marks and produces stress correctly, including shifts, and explains the pattern.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct on base forms but errors on derived forms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify stressed syllables or produces most incorrectly.

records.contextNotes: Teach from foundation level onwards alongside vocabulary. In-sessionally and at PGR level, technical vocabulary from students' own fields provides the most useful material.

records.summary: Hahn (2004) found that when a non-native speaker's lecture had correctly placed primary stress, listeners recalled more content and evaluated the speaker more favourably than when stress was misplaced or absent. Prominence links pronunciation to information structure: it tells listeners which word in a thought group carries the new or contrastive point. Nuclear stress placement is one of the few prosodic features Jenkins (2000) retained in the Lingua Franca Core, so prominence is a priority in lingua franca settings as well as elsewhere. Gilbert's (2008) prosody pyramid offers a teachable sequence from thought group to focus word to stressed syllable.

activities.title: Shifting focus
learnerActions: Read the same sentence as an answer to different questions
Move the prominence each time to the word that answers the question
Explain to a partner why it moved
activities.intendedInsight: Prominence goes to new or contrastive information, so it moves with context.
