activities.rationale: Makes the link between prominence and information structure explicit, following Gilbert's (2008) focus-word approach.

activities.title: Contrast in explanation
learnerActions: Prepare a short explanation comparing two methods or theories from their field
Mark the contrastive words and practise them with prominence
Present to a peer, who notes which contrasts came across
activities.intendedInsight: Correct prominence makes comparisons and key points easier to follow.
activities.rationale: Applies Hahn's (2004) finding about primary stress and listener recall to academic explanation.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language marks focus mainly through word order, particles or syntax rather than pitch prominence do not use prominence to highlight new information, or stress every content word equally.
difficulties.revealedBy: Even stress across content words; contrasts not audible.
difficulties.response: Contrast versions with and without prominence in question–answer pairs and show how meaning changes; practise in short dialogues before extended speech. The spoken contrast can later be linked to given and new information in writing.

difficulties.pattern: Learners place prominence on the last word of every thought group regardless of whether it is new.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated or given words at the end of groups receive prominence.
difficulties.response: Practise de-accenting repeated words and moving focus to earlier new information.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer: 'Did the study use interviews or questionnaires?' with 'The study used questionnaires', then 'Did the first study use questionnaires?' with 'The second study used questionnaires'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Prominence moves correctly to 'questionnaires' and then to 'second'.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct in one case only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No change in prominence between the two answers.

records.contextNotes: Introduce at foundation level with short exchanges; develop in pre-sessional presentation work. For PGR students who teach, prominence is especially relevant to clear explanation.
reviewNotes: Review response (R2-10): the edge from coh.given-new is soft and reworded, and this difficulty now returns to thought groups rather than to written information structure, so the spoken given–new contrast is taught through question–answer pairs without waiting for B2 written-discourse work.

records.summary: Thought groups are the foundation of Gilbert's (2008) prosody pyramid: each group carries one focus word, and boundaries are marked by pitch change and pausing. Chunking speech at grammatical boundaries helps listeners parse it and gives speakers natural planning points, whereas pauses inside phrases make speech harder to follow. Derwing and Munro (2015) include prosodic features among those that matter for comprehensibility. Thought-group work transfers readily to presentations and to reading quotations or data aloud.

activities.title: Mark and read
learnerActions: Mark thought-group boundaries in a short academic paragraph with slashes
Read it aloud and record it
Listen back and compare the pauses with the marked boundaries
activities.intendedInsight: Planned chunks can make speech easier to follow and easier to produce.
activities.rationale: Applies Gilbert's (2008) thought-group principle to academic text.

activities.title: Chunk the dense sentence
learnerActions: Take a long academic sentence with heavy noun phrases
Divide it into thought groups for speaking
Discuss where a spoken version would need to differ from the written one
activities.intendedInsight: Dense written sentences need restructuring or careful chunking to be spoken intelligibly.
activities.rationale: Links thought groups to the difference between spoken and written academic language.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read aloud word by word, giving each word equal weight and pausing between many words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Monotonous, evenly paced reading, typical where reading aloud has been practised mainly as accurate word decoding.
difficulties.response: Model reading in thought groups and practise marking boundaries before reading; avoid correcting individual words while learners are working on chunking.

difficulties.pattern: Learners pause inside phrases while searching for the next word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mid-phrase pauses in spontaneous speech.
difficulties.response: Encourage planning in phrases rather than words, and link to formulaic chunks and fluency work.

difficulties.pattern: Learners break long academic noun phrases into single-word groups.
difficulties.revealedBy: Pauses inside noun phrases such as 'the long-term economic consequences of the policy'.
difficulties.response: Analyse the structure of noun phrases and practise saying them as units.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read a 60-word paragraph aloud without preparation, then again after marking thought groups.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Pauses at grammatical boundaries in both readings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves markedly after marking boundaries.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Pauses inconsistently or word by word in both readings.

records.contextNotes: A foundation-level priority that remains useful at all stages. For PGT and PGR presenters, thought-group planning supports reading definitions, quotations and data aloud clearly.

records.summary: Pickering (2001), using Brazil's discourse intonation framework (Brazil, 1997), found that international teaching assistants used fewer rising (referring) tones than native-speaker teaching assistants, which may have made their teaching sound less interactive and made shared and new information harder to distinguish. Thompson (2003) showed that intonation contributes to signalling lecture organisation. Teach intonation through its discourse functions — new versus shared information, continuation versus completion, topic structure — rather than through attitude labels, which are unreliable.

activities.title: New or shared?
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract and mark falling and rising tones on a transcript
Decide whether each marked point is presented as new or as shared
Practise a short explanation using the same contrast
activities.intendedInsight: Tone choices signal how information relates to what listeners already know.
activities.rationale: Applies Brazil's (1997) distinction between proclaiming and referring tones, as used by Pickering (2001).

activities.title: Lists and transitions
learnerActions: Practise saying lists with continuing tones and a final fall
Practise topic transitions with a pitch reset
Record a short presentation section and check both features
activities.intendedInsight: Intonation signals structure to listeners.
activities.rationale: Links intonation to the signalling of organisation described by Thompson (2003).

difficulties.pattern: Learners use a narrower pitch range and fewer discourse-marking pitch movements in English than proficient speakers, a tendency reported across many first-language backgrounds and linked to processing load and unfamiliarity with English tone choices.
difficulties.revealedBy: Narrow pitch range; topic shifts and contrasts not signalled prosodically.
difficulties.response: Practise exaggerated pitch range in controlled tasks and then reduce it; record and listen back.

difficulties.pattern: 'Intonation is about showing emotion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners treat intonation as optional decoration.
difficulties.response: Show its discourse functions with academic examples, where it affects how organisation and information status come across.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read a short list and a sentence that refers back to earlier content.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses continuing and final tones on the list and a referring tone on given information.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gets list intonation right but does not distinguish given and new.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses flat or uniformly falling intonation throughout.

records.contextNotes: Most relevant from pre-sessional level onwards. Particularly important for PGR students who teach, given Pickering's (2001) findings about teaching assistants' tone choices.

records.summary: Munro and Derwing (2006) found that errors in high-functional-load contrasts had a greater effect on comprehensibility than errors in low-functional-load contrasts. Jenkins (2000) proposed a Lingua Franca Core of features, including most consonant contrasts and vowel length, as priorities for intelligibility in lingua franca settings, while excluding features such as the dental fricatives, weak forms, word stress and pitch movement (nuclear stress placement is one of the few prosodic features it retains, which supports the priority given to prominence); the core has been influential but is contested, for example over its empirical base and its treatment of word stress. Derwing and Munro (2015) summarise evidence that instruction can improve pronunciation. Prioritise individually, on the basis of what listeners actually misunderstand.

activities.title: Find my priorities
learnerActions: Record a short reading and a short spontaneous talk
Ask a listener unfamiliar with their first language to transcribe both
Identify words misunderstood and the sounds involved
Choose two priority features and plan practice
activities.intendedInsight: Priorities should be based on what listeners misunderstand, not on a generic list.
activities.rationale: Applies the intelligibility-based prioritisation argued by Derwing and Munro (2015).

activities.title: Minimal pairs in academic context
learnerActions: Practise a high-functional-load contrast in academic sentences from their field
Ask a partner to identify which word was intended
Record and monitor the target in a short presentation
activities.intendedInsight: Practice is most useful on contrasts that change meaning frequently.
activities.rationale: Targets high-functional-load contrasts, which Munro and Derwing (2006) found to matter more for comprehensibility.

activities.title: Perception training with many voices
learnerActions: Choose one priority contrast identified from listener transcription
Using a free high-variability training tool or a teacher-made set, identify which word of a pair is spoken, across many different talkers and word contexts, with immediate feedback
Track accuracy over several short sessions
Move on to producing the contrast in academic sentences once identification is reliable
activities.intendedInsight: Hearing a contrast reliably across many voices is a foundation for producing it.
activities.rationale: High-variability phonetic training (identification across many talkers with feedback) is a well-researched perception technique that has been associated with gains in perception and, in many studies, production (Thomson, 2018); perception-focused instruction is among the approaches reviewed by Thomson and Derwing (2015). Its use in EAP classes is a proposal rather than a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: Learners try to fix every sound and become discouraged.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frustration and low confidence; little progress on any feature.
difficulties.response: Limit targets to two or three high-priority features and track progress on those.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language allows few word-final consonants or clusters delete final consonants or add a vowel after them, so that past tense and plural endings become inaudible.
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners mishear tense or number; final consonants missing in recordings.
difficulties.response: Practise grammatically meaningful endings in context, linking them to the next word where possible.

difficulties.pattern: Learners or previous teachers have focused on /θ/ and /ð/ at the expense of contrasts that matter more.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners request work on 'th' sounds but have more serious intelligibility issues elsewhere.
difficulties.response: Explain functional load and redirect effort, while respecting learners' own goals.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to name the sounds they think cause most misunderstanding, then compare with listener transcription.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names features that match listener evidence and explains why they matter.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names some correct features alongside low-priority ones.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Names only low-priority features or has no idea.

records.contextNotes: Most relevant at foundation and pre-sessional levels, where individual diagnosis can be built in. In-sessionally, work is usually individual and targeted at specific communicative needs.
reviewNotes: Specific contrasts named as high or low functional load are general tendencies; the exact ranking varies across studies.

Review response (R2-41): an HVPT activity has been added. Thomson (2018) is not in the closed bibliography and is listed under proposedReferences; if it is not accepted, cite the activity to thomsonderwing2015 only and soften the rationale.

records.summary: Recognising connected speech is clearly a priority for listening (Field, 2008); its value in production is more contested. Jenkins (2000) excluded weak forms from the Lingua Franca Core, arguing that they are not necessary for intelligibility in lingua franca communication and may even reduce it, whereas others argue that reducing unstressed words helps stressed information stand out for listeners accustomed to English rhythm (see Derwing & Munro, 2015, for discussion of priorities). A defensible middle course is moderate linking and reduction within thought groups, with content words kept clear.

activities.title: Script to speech
learnerActions: Mark linking and weak forms in a short presentation script
Practise reading with the marked features
Record and compare with an unmarked reading
activities.intendedInsight: Moderate linking makes speech flow without sacrificing clarity.
activities.rationale: Practice-based activity applying connected-speech features within thought groups.

activities.title: Chunk practice
learnerActions: Practise common presentation phrases as connected units
Use them in a short presentation
Peer-check that content words remain clear
activities.intendedInsight: Formulaic phrases are good candidates for connected delivery.
activities.rationale: Links connected speech to fluency through formulaic language.

difficulties.pattern: After learning about connected speech, learners over-reduce and blur content words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Key terms become hard to identify.
difficulties.response: Emphasise that reduction applies to unstressed function words; keep content words clear.

difficulties.pattern: Learners give every function word a full form and equal weight, so key words do not stand out for listeners used to English rhythm. Full forms are not in themselves an error, and many such speakers remain intelligible.
difficulties.revealedBy: Even rhythm and few reduced forms, together with listener reports of difficulty identifying the key points.
difficulties.response: Work on contrasting stressed and unstressed syllables, starting from recognition before production. Judge success by whether listeners can pick out the key words, not by how many weak forms the speaker uses.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read a 30-second presentation opening aloud.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Moderate linking and weak forms; content words clear.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Few reductions, but intelligible.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Listeners cannot pick out the key words, either because every syllable receives equal weight so that key words do not stand out or because over-reduction obscures content words.

records.contextNotes: Teach production after or alongside recognition. For presentation-focused PGT and PGR learners, emphasis should be on clarity of key terms and fluent formulaic phrases rather than maximal reduction.
reviewNotes: The production value of weak forms is contested; this record presents both positions without resolving them.

records.summary: Technical terms are often met first in reading, so learners form their pronunciation from spelling, which in English is an unreliable guide to stress. Because stress errors disrupt word recognition (Field, 2005) and key terms recur throughout an explanation, a mispronounced term can impair a whole presentation. Compound terms (CASE study, CONTROL group) follow compound stress patterns that learners can check in the same way. Teach a checking routine, prioritise the terms students will actually use, and accept that some names and terms have more than one accepted pronunciation (Derwing & Munro, 2015, on prioritising intelligibility).

activities.title: Presentation term check
learnerActions: List the ten most important terms and names in a forthcoming presentation
Check each using dictionary audio or a recording from the field
Mark stress and practise each term in a sentence
Ask a peer from the same field to confirm
activities.intendedInsight: Checking a few recurring key terms can make a noticeable difference to clarity.
activities.rationale: Applies Field's (2005) finding on stress and recognition to the terms that recur most in a talk.

activities.title: Acronym or initialism?
learnerActions: Sort a list of abbreviations from their field into those said as words and those said as letters
Check uncertain cases with a field-specific source
Practise them in context
activities.intendedInsight: Conventions for saying abbreviations vary and must be checked.
activities.rationale: Practice-based activity addressing a common source of uncertainty.

difficulties.pattern: Learners pronounce terms as spelled because they learnt them through reading.
difficulties.revealedBy: Systematic stress errors on technical terms.
difficulties.response: Build pronunciation checking into vocabulary learning from the start.

difficulties.pattern: International terms that are cognates in the learner's first language are given the first-language stress pattern.
difficulties.revealedBy: Familiar-looking terms are mispronounced more often than unfamiliar ones.
difficulties.response: Highlight cognates with different stress and practise them explicitly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to say five key terms from their field and explain how they checked them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct stress and a reliable checking method.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but without a checking method.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent errors and reliance on spelling.

records.contextNotes: Relevant at all stages. For PGR students presenting at conferences, names of theorists and specialised terms are particularly salient to expert audiences.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography addresses the pronunciation of technical terms directly; the claim relies on general findings about stress and intelligibility.

records.summary: Segalowitz (2010) distinguishes cognitive fluency (the efficiency of underlying processing), utterance fluency (measurable features such as speed, pausing and repair) and perceived fluency (listeners' judgements). Skehan (1998) showed that pre-task planning and task design affect fluency, with trade-offs against accuracy and complexity. Formulaic sequences reduce online processing load (Wood, 2010), and repetition under time pressure, as in 4/3/2 (Nation & Newton, 2009), is a well-known fluency-development activity. Practice should aim at automatisation through repetition on familiar content, not simply more speaking.

activities.title: 4/3/2 on a research topic
learnerActions: Talk for 4 minutes to a partner about a topic from their field
Repeat the same talk to a new partner in 3 minutes
Repeat again to a third partner in 2 minutes
Reflect on what changed
activities.intendedInsight: Repetition under time pressure is intended to make delivery of familiar content smoother.
activities.rationale: The 4/3/2 activity is described by Nation and Newton (2009) as a fluency-development technique.

activities.title: Formula bank for presentations
learnerActions: Collect signposting and hedging formulas from lectures and presentations
Practise them as units until automatic
Use them in a short presentation
activities.intendedInsight: Formulaic language can free attention for content.
activities.rationale: Builds on Wood's (2010) account of formulaic sequences and fluency.

difficulties.pattern: 'Fluency means speaking fast.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Rushed speech that listeners find harder to follow.
difficulties.response: Explain fluency as smooth delivery with appropriate pausing, not speed.

difficulties.pattern: Learners memorise full scripts and freeze when they lose their place.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent delivery that breaks down entirely after a disruption.
difficulties.response: Practise from notes and with formulaic chunks rather than full scripts.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety increases pausing and hesitation in front of an audience.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluency much better in pairs than in front of a group.
difficulties.response: Build up gradually from pairs to groups; use repetition to increase confidence.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to speak for 2 minutes on a familiar topic, then repeat after planning time.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Fluent in both, with pauses at boundaries.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves markedly with planning.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent mid-clause pauses even after planning.

records.contextNotes: Relevant at all stages. For PGR students, fluency in conference presentations and vivas is important; formulaic language for presenting research can be targeted. For students who stammer, fluency work should not aim at eliminating disfluency: judge communicative effectiveness, allow extra time, and follow the student's own preferences and any specialist advice.

records.summary: Levelt's (1989) model of speaking includes a monitor that checks speech before and after articulation; in L2 speech, monitoring competes for attention with formulation, so selective monitoring matters. Dörnyei and Scott (1997) catalogue communication strategies such as circumlocution, approximation and appeals for help, which can be taught as legitimate ways of maintaining interaction. In academic speaking, the key judgement is which errors need repair: those that change meaning, especially in technical content.

activities.title: Explain without the word
learnerActions: Draw a card with a technical term from their field
Explain it to a partner without using the term
The partner guesses the term and comments on the clarity of the explanation
activities.intendedInsight: Paraphrase and description can carry meaning when a word is unavailable.
activities.rationale: Practises circumlocution and approximation as described by Dörnyei and Scott (1997).

activities.title: Repair or let go?
learnerActions: Listen to a recording of their own talk
Identify errors and decide which affected meaning
Practise brief repairs for meaning-affecting errors only
activities.intendedInsight: Not all errors need repairing.
activities.rationale: Develops selective monitoring in line with Levelt's (1989) model.

difficulties.pattern: Learners stop and restart sentences repeatedly to correct minor errors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent restarts; fragmented speech, often where accuracy has been the main criterion of success.
difficulties.response: Discuss which errors affect meaning and practise continuing past minor errors.

difficulties.pattern: Learners abandon a message when they cannot find a word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages left incomplete; avoidance of topics.
difficulties.response: Teach and practise paraphrase strategies in a supportive setting.

difficulties.pattern: Learners do not notice signs that a listener has not understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Continuing with an explanation despite puzzled looks or questions.
difficulties.response: Practise recognising non-understanding signals and responding with reformulation markers.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a concept without using its key term.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Clear paraphrase with appropriate reformulation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some paraphrase with hesitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives up or relies on the term.

records.contextNotes: Relevant from foundation to in-sessional level. At foundation level, emphasise compensatory strategies; for in-sessional students, focus on meaning-affecting errors in disciplinary speech.

records.summary: Numbers, formulae and units are frequent in presentations across many disciplines, and errors can mislead listeners about findings. SI conventions (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, 2019) govern unit names and symbols, while spoken conventions for formulae vary by discipline and region. Teach common patterns, the -teen/-ty contrast (relying mainly on the final syllable, because -teen stress shifts forward before a stressed noun) and confirmation strategies, and have learners practise with figures from their own fields.

activities.title: Read the table
learnerActions: Read aloud a table of results from their field
A partner writes down the figures
Compare and identify misheard figures
activities.intendedInsight: Listeners need numbers said clearly and sometimes confirmed.
activities.rationale: Tests intelligibility of spoken numbers directly.

activities.title: Say the formula
learnerActions: Practise saying common formulae and units from their field
Check conventions with a subject source
Record a short explanation of an equation
activities.intendedInsight: Formulae have conventional spoken forms.
activities.rationale: Practice-based activity; unit names follow SI conventions.

difficulties.pattern: Learners confuse -teen and -ty numbers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners mishear figures such as 15 and 50.
difficulties.response: Practise the final-syllable contrast (/tiːn/ versus /ti/) in phrases such as fourteen students, where stress shift removes the stress cue, and confirm critical numbers (one five, fifteen).

difficulties.pattern: Learners read decimals and large numbers using conventions from their first language, for example decimal commas or different grouping of digits.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in spoken decimals and large numbers.
difficulties.response: Contrast conventions explicitly and practise English forms.

difficulties.pattern: Learners do not know how to read equations aloud.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hesitation or avoidance when explaining formulae.
difficulties.response: Teach conventional spoken forms for common operations.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud a slide with a table, a formula and a date range.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All figures accurate and intelligible.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most figures correct but some confusions or hesitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent errors or avoidance.

records.contextNotes: Relevant from foundation level, especially for STEM and business pathways. PGT students presenting data need fluent control of statistics and units.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no source on spoken number conventions; guidance is practice-based.

records.summary: Ferris and Tagg (1996) found that oral and interactive course requirements vary considerably by discipline, and Leki (2001) found group projects in courses across the curriculum but little instructor guidance on how students should collaborate. Teach learners to read assessment briefs for what is marked (product, process, individual contribution), to distinguish cooperation (division of labour) from collaboration (joint construction), and to locate rules on permitted collaboration.

activities.title: Decoding the group brief
learnerActions: Read a real group assignment brief and highlight what is assessed and how marks are split
Identify any individual components (e.g. reflections, peer evaluation) and their weighting
List questions to ask the module leader where the brief is unclear
activities.intendedInsight: Group tasks differ in what they assess, and reading the brief closely shapes how a group should work.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the variation in course requirements that Ferris and Tagg (1996) report and that students otherwise discover late.

activities.title: Cooperation or collaboration?
learnerActions: Classify six short task descriptions as needing division of labour, joint construction or both
Discuss what would go wrong if a joint-construction task were simply divided
Apply the distinction to a current or upcoming group task
activities.intendedInsight: Some tasks cannot be done well by dividing them up.
activities.rationale: Counters the 'divide and staple' approach that leaves group outputs fragmented.

difficulties.pattern: 'Group work is unfair because my mark depends on other people.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to engage; attempts to do all the work alone or to minimise involvement.
difficulties.response: Show how individual components and peer evaluation affect marks, and discuss the purposes of group work. Acknowledge that the concern can be legitimate where assessment design is weak.

difficulties.pattern: Treating every group task as a division of labour.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sections written independently and combined just before the deadline.
difficulties.response: Use the cooperation–collaboration distinction and plan joint stages (shared planning, integration edit, joint rehearsal).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, from a brief, what will be assessed and how their individual mark will be decided.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurately describes product, process and individual components and their weighting.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the product but not individual components.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes everyone gets the same mark for the final product.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners may meet assessed group work for the first time. Pre-sessional learners should be prepared for the group assessments in their target disciplines. In-sessional UG and PGT learners apply this to current module briefs.
reviewNotes: Leki (2001) and Ferris and Tagg (1996) are US-based; group assessment practices differ across institutions and countries.

records.summary: Leki's (2001) account of multilingual students being given marginal roles in group projects suggests that role allocation should be explicit and negotiated rather than left to assumptions about who is competent. The Companion Volume's goal-oriented co-operation scale describes the language of planning joint action (Council of Europe, 2020). Teach task breakdown from the brief, ground rules, role allocation by expertise and development, and milestone planning.

activities.title: Ground-rules charter
learnerActions: In the first meeting, agree rules on communication channels, response times, decision-making and what happens when deadlines are missed
Write the rules in a shared document and have every member confirm them
Review and revise the charter at the project's midpoint
activities.intendedInsight: Explicit rules give the group a neutral reference point when problems arise.
activities.rationale: Addresses the lack of collaboration guidance Leki (2001) observed by making group norms explicit.

activities.title: Backwards milestone plan
learnerActions: Start from the submission date and work backwards to set internal deadlines for drafts, integration and rehearsal
Assign an owner to each milestone
Identify the riskiest dependency and plan a buffer for it
activities.intendedInsight: Internal deadlines and integration time must be planned, not left to the end.
activities.rationale: Practises the planning language and joint decision-making described in goal-oriented co-operation scales (Council of Europe, 2020).

difficulties.pattern: Roles allocated by assumed language ability (e.g. multilingual members given formatting or slide design only).
difficulties.revealedBy: Some members have no substantive content role; they report feeling sidelined.
difficulties.response: Teachers should require negotiated role allocation in the group plan and check it early. Discuss Leki's (2001) findings with the whole group, allocate by expertise and development goals, and rotate roles where possible.

difficulties.pattern: No internal deadlines; all work converges on the final week.
difficulties.revealedBy: Last-minute integration and missing sections.
difficulties.response: Require dated milestones in the plan and check them at review points.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting a peripheral role to avoid conflict or exposure.
difficulties.revealedBy: A member volunteers only for low-visibility tasks and contributes little to content.
difficulties.response: Encourage members to state development goals in the planning meeting and give them language for negotiating roles.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their group's plan and explain how roles were decided.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A written plan with ground rules, negotiated roles and internal milestones.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Roles assigned but no ground rules or internal deadlines.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No plan; the work is divided by word count.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from templates for plans and charters. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply them to real projects; PGT learners often have little time to form groups, so a fast planning routine is valuable.

records.summary: Effective group meetings make decisions and responsibilities visible. The Companion Volume describes formal discussion in meetings and managing interaction as part of interaction and mediation competence (Council of Europe, 2020). There is little EAP research specifically on student project meetings, so teaching draws on practitioner models: agenda, chairing, decision language and action-point minutes.

activities.title: From agenda to action points
learnerActions: Draft a three-item agenda with a purpose and time for each item
Hold a 15-minute meeting with a rotating chair and timekeeper
Write minutes listing only decisions and action points with owners and deadlines
activities.intendedInsight: A meeting is productive when it ends with recorded decisions and actions.
activities.rationale: Practises the meeting functions captured in formal discussion and managing-interaction scales (Council of Europe, 2020).

activities.title: Minutes comparison
learnerActions: Compare narrative minutes ('X said… then Y said…') with action-point minutes of the same meeting
Identify which version would help a member who missed the meeting
Rewrite narrative minutes as action points
activities.intendedInsight: Minutes record outcomes, not conversation.
activities.rationale: Contrasting models makes the function of minutes explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Meetings drift without decisions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated discussion of the same issues across meetings.
difficulties.response: Assign a chair, use an agenda and practise proposing and confirming decisions.

difficulties.pattern: Minutes narrate the discussion and omit decisions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long minutes with no clear actions or owners.
difficulties.response: Provide an action-point template and practise summarising decisions.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner for the minutes of their last group meeting.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Decisions and action points with owners and deadlines.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some decisions recorded, but no owners or dates.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No minutes, or a narrative of the discussion.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and in-sessional UG learners apply meeting routines to assessed projects. PGT learners often meet online across time zones. PGR researchers attend research-team and supervisory meetings, where agendas and action points support progress.
reviewNotes: No listed EAP study focuses on student project meetings; guidance is practitioner-based.

records.summary: Group-work conflict often concerns process (deadlines, workload, communication) rather than ideas, and Leki (2001) documents tensions and unequal treatment in multilingual project groups. Politeness theory (Brown & Levinson, 1987) helps explain how face-threatening concerns can be raised with mitigation while remaining clear. Teach early, specific, ground-rule-referenced raising of concerns, negotiation and proportionate escalation.

activities.title: Observation, impact, request
learnerActions: Write a concern using three parts: a specific observation, its impact on the group, and a request or proposal
Role-play raising it in a meeting, with the other person responding
Discuss how mitigation affected clarity and the response
activities.intendedInsight: A concern can be raised clearly without being accusatory.
activities.rationale: Applies face-saving mitigation (Brown & Levinson, 1987) to a high-stakes, face-threatening act.

activities.title: Escalation ladder
learnerActions: List steps from informal conversation to involving the module leader
Decide what evidence is needed at each step
Draft a short, factual message to a tutor for the final step
activities.intendedInsight: Escalation is proportionate, evidenced and staged.
activities.rationale: Gives learners a procedure for the situations of unequal contribution and treatment that Leki (2001) documents.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding raising problems until the deadline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late complaints to tutors; the work is incomplete.
difficulties.response: Build in checkpoints where concerns are routinely raised, and practise early, low-key raising.

difficulties.pattern: Accusatory or emotional messages to group members or tutors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Escalating conflict; tutor intervention needed.
difficulties.response: Practise the observation–impact–request structure and mitigated language.

difficulties.pattern: Interpreting different communication styles (e.g. directness, response times) as rudeness or disengagement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Complaints about tone rather than substance.
difficulties.response: Discuss variation in communicative expectations and agree group norms explicitly.

diagnostic.task: Present a scenario in which a member is not contributing and ask how the learner would handle it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Early, specific, ground-rule-referenced raising, a proposed solution and staged escalation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Appropriate concern but vague or late.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Avoidance or immediate complaint to the tutor without evidence.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners practise in short projects. In-sessional UG and PGT learners face real conflicts with marks at stake. PGR researchers manage disagreements in research teams and co-authorship, where power differences are greater.

records.summary: Leki (2001) found multilingual undergraduates in group projects positioned as less capable and allocated peripheral roles, and Morita (2004) shows how positioning shapes participation in graduate classrooms. Research on English as a lingua franca in international universities reframes communicative success as mutual accommodation rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Jenkins, 2014). Inclusive collaboration is therefore a competence for all students, including home students and the most proficient English users, and is also supported by task design.

activities.title: Accommodation audit
learnerActions: Record a short group discussion
Each member identifies one moment where their own speech (speed, idiom, local reference) may have made understanding harder
Agree two accommodation practices for the group
activities.intendedInsight: Intelligibility is a shared responsibility of speakers and listeners.
activities.rationale: Applies ELF research on mutual accommodation (Jenkins, 2014) to group practice.

activities.title: Trying participation structures
learnerActions: Hold one discussion as open talk and one using rounds with written input first
Map who spoke and whose ideas were taken up in each
Decide which structures to use for which group tasks
activities.intendedInsight: Participation structures change who contributes.
activities.rationale: Addresses the positioning effects documented by Leki (2001) and Morita (2004) through design rather than exhortation.

difficulties.pattern: 'They can't contribute much because their English isn't good enough.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Peers allocate peripheral tasks or ignore suggestions from some members.
difficulties.response: Address the group and the task design, not the overlooked member: discuss evidence of positioning (Leki, 2001), separate language proficiency from expertise and allocate content roles to all. Teachers can reduce the problem by setting rotating roles and individual preparation that every member brings to the group, and by checking role allocation in group plans.

difficulties.pattern: Proficient or confident speakers dominating without realising it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Participation maps show one or two members taking most turns.
difficulties.response: Share participation data with the group and practise inviting and building on others.

difficulties.pattern: Multilingual members withdrawing to avoid exposure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Members volunteer only for invisible tasks.
difficulties.response: Create low-risk entry points (written input, pairs) and invite specific expertise.

diagnostic.task: Show a transcript of a group meeting in which one member is overlooked and ask what the learner notices and would do.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the exclusion and proposes concrete, tactful moves and structures.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices the problem but frames it as the overlooked member's language deficit.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Notices nothing problematic.

records.contextNotes: Relevant at every stage. Foundation and pre-sessional groups are often all multilingual, so practise accommodation among varied Englishes. In-sessional UG and PGT groups mix home and international students, where awareness among more proficient users is critical. PGR teams are often international. Inclusive practice also covers disabled and neurodivergent members, for example by agreeing written channels, processing time and accessible meeting formats.

records.summary: Collaborative writing requires coordinating text, not only dividing tasks; Leki (2001) shows group projects often resulting in fragmented division of labour. Classroom research on collaborative writing among L2 learners suggests that writing jointly can prompt discussion of both ideas and language (Storch, 2005). Teach agreed structures and style sheets, shared-document workflows, integrating edits and the boundary with individually assessed work.

activities.title: Group style sheet
learnerActions: Agree key terms and their definitions, tense conventions and the citation style
Record them in a one-page style sheet at the top of the shared document
Check each section against the style sheet before integration
activities.intendedInsight: Consistency across authors must be agreed, not assumed.
activities.rationale: Coordinates the text-level choices that separately drafted sections otherwise leave inconsistent.

activities.title: Integration edit
learnerActions: Each member reads the whole draft and comments on links between sections
The group meets to agree transitions and cut repetition
One member makes a final consistency pass while others check references
activities.intendedInsight: Integration is a joint revision stage that needs time in the plan.
activities.rationale: Draws on evidence that joint writing prompts collaborative attention to ideas and language (Storch, 2005).

difficulties.pattern: Sections pasted together at the last minute.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent style, repetition and no transitions.
difficulties.response: Schedule an integration milestone well before submission.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to edit peers' text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comments only, or no edits; inconsistent final text.
difficulties.response: Agree editing norms and use suggestion mode so that changes are visible and negotiable.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about whether help with individually assessed parts is allowed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Shared drafts of individual reflections; questions about collusion.
difficulties.response: Clarify the brief's rules on individual components with the module team.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe how their group will turn separate sections into a single report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a style sheet, an integration stage, shared tools and a final consistency check.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions a final proofread only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes sections will simply be combined.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners may co-write short reports. In-sessional UG learners co-write reports and proposals in many modules, especially in engineering and business, where it is commonly assessed. PGT learners co-write consultancy-style or business reports. PGR researchers co-author papers, where contributor roles and authorship conventions also matter.
reviewNotes: Storch (2005) concerns pair writing in class rather than extended group projects, so its relevance to assessed group reports is indirect.

records.summary: Evaluative judgement depends on understanding criteria and comparing work against them (Sadler, 1989). Peer evaluation of contributions can reproduce the positioning Leki (2001) documented, in which multilingual members' contributions were undervalued. Teach criterion-referenced, evidenced evaluation and accurate self-documentation.

activities.title: Rating backed by documented contributions
learnerActions: Read anonymised minutes and a version history for a group project
Rate each member against the given criteria, citing evidence for each rating
Compare ratings with peers and discuss where and why they differ
activities.intendedInsight: Fair judgements rest on criteria and evidence rather than impressions.
activities.rationale: Applies Sadler's (1989) account of evaluative judgement against criteria to peer evaluation.

activities.title: Contribution statement
learnerActions: Write a 150-word statement of your own contribution, citing evidence
Include one limitation and what you would do differently
Exchange statements with a group member and check them against shared records
activities.intendedInsight: Accurate self-reporting includes evidence and limitations.
activities.rationale: Builds the self-documentation skills individual reflective components require.

difficulties.pattern: Rating contribution by how much someone talked in meetings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low ratings for members who did substantial written or research work.
difficulties.response: Separate visibility from contribution and use evidence from task logs and version history.

difficulties.pattern: Under-reporting one's own contribution.
difficulties.revealedBy: Vague or modest self-statements that omit significant work.
difficulties.response: Model evidenced statements and give language for describing contributions accurately.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to rate two group members on given criteria and justify the ratings.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Criterion-based ratings with specific evidence, including less visible work.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Ratings with general justifications.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equal ratings with no justification, or ratings based on friendship or talk.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes introduce peer evaluation in short projects. In-sessional UG and PGT modules often use peer moderation of group marks, so fairness and evidence matter for grades.

records.summary: Flower and Hayes (1981) model composing as goal-directed sub-processes (planning, translating, reviewing) that interrupt one another; Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) add the contrast between knowledge-telling and knowledge-transforming, which maps closely onto tutors' complaints about ‘description’. Zamel's (1983) case studies suggest that skilled ESL writers, like skilled L1 writers, defer editing and revise for meaning. Teach the model through learners' own process data rather than as a diagram to memorise, and do not present it as a fixed sequence of stages.

activities.title: Process retrospective timeline
learnerActions: Reconstruct as precisely as possible how a recent short text was written, marking each episode as planning, drafting, reviewing or reading
Compare timelines in pairs and identify where each writer looped back and where they stayed linear
Annotate one point where an idea changed during drafting and say what triggered the change
activities.intendedInsight: Writing is not a pipeline; returning to planning mid-draft is normal and productive, not a sign of poor preparation.
activities.rationale: Making tacit process visible lets learners compare their behaviour with descriptions of recursive composing by skilled writers (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Zamel, 1983) without imposing a model as a rule.

activities.title: Telling versus transforming
learnerActions: Read two short responses to the same question: one listing recalled facts in the order remembered, one selecting and reordering them around a claim
Highlight the sentences in each that answer the question directly
Rewrite the opening of the first response so that its content serves a claim
activities.intendedInsight: The difference between the texts lies in what the writer did with their knowledge, not in how much they knew or how accurate the English is.
activities.rationale: Bereiter and Scardamalia's (1987) distinction gives teachers and learners shared language for the move from description to argument; contrasting texts keeps attention on observable textual consequences.

difficulties.pattern: ‘I should plan everything first and then just write it out; if I change my plan, I planned badly.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines followed rigidly even when drafting exposes a weak point; reluctance to restructure; distress when the argument shifts.
difficulties.response: Normalise plan revision by showing real draft histories (your own or published ones) and ask for a short ‘what changed since my plan’ note with each draft. Do not penalise justified departures from a submitted outline.

difficulties.pattern: Writers stop after every sentence to check grammar and vocabulary and lose the thread of their argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very slow drafting, short texts with few ideas but relatively few errors, constant dictionary or translator use mid-sentence.
difficulties.response: Teach placeholders (for example [?word]) and timed drafting with editing explicitly postponed. Do not respond with more detailed grammar correction at the drafting stage, which reinforces premature editing.

diagnostic.task: Give learners an essay question and ten minutes. Every two minutes they note what they are doing (thinking, noting, writing, rereading, correcting).
diagnostic.strongResponse: The log alternates between planning, writing and rereading; at least one reread leads to a change of content or order; correction is mostly deferred.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some planning before writing, but rereading is only for errors and the content order is fixed from the first line.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writing starts immediately with no plan, or the whole period is spent planning; reviewing consists only of spelling and grammar checks.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, use the model to legitimise drafting and redrafting within portfolio or process-based assessment. In-sessional undergraduates benefit from relating it to their own assignment habits and deadlines. For postgraduates and doctoral researchers, emphasise knowledge-transforming and writing as a way of thinking (Kamler & Thomson, 2014), including the cost of postponing writing until the reading is ‘finished’.
reviewNotes: Cognitive process models were developed mainly with L1 writers. Their application to B1 writers is supported in general terms by L2 composing studies, but the heavier language-processing load at lower levels may make recursive composing harder to sustain.

records.summary: Flower and Hayes (1981) place the writer's representation of the rhetorical problem at the start of composing, and a weak representation constrains everything that follows. In two 1986 studies Horowitz documented the coursework tasks university staff set (Horowitz, 1986) and analysed essay examination prompts (Horowitz, 1986), showing that exam questions also call for selecting and organising material for a specific purpose. Under pressure, writers may fall back on knowledge telling, writing all they know about the topic (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987), and Lea and Street (1998) show that tutors' expectations about 'answering the question' are often tacit. Teach one routine for coursework briefs and exam questions, use authentic briefs and past papers from target departments, treat command words as cues to interpret in context, and keep checking relevance after the plan is made, since relevance depends on how content is framed for the argument (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Brief deconstruction
learnerActions: Annotate a real assignment brief in four colours: instruction, topic, limits and other requirements
Rewrite the task as one sentence beginning 'My text must…'
Compare with a partner, list remaining ambiguities and draft a short message asking the tutor about one of them
activities.intendedInsight: A brief contains more instructions than the question line, and some requirements are implicit.
activities.rationale: Explicit task representation is the first planning operation in cognitive models (Flower & Hayes, 1981), and authentic briefs expose the task types learners will actually meet (Horowitz, 1986).

activities.title: Same topic, different question
learnerActions: Read three exam questions on the same topic with different command and limiting words
Mark the command, topic, focus and limiting words and write one sentence on what a good answer to each would do
For a past paper, convert marks into minutes for each question, including planning and checking time
activities.intendedInsight: The question's wording, not the topic, decides what counts as a good answer, and time should follow marks.
activities.rationale: Contrasting questions that share a topic makes the transformation demand visible that knowledge telling misses (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987); exam prompts vary in what they ask writers to do with content (Horowitz, 1986).

activities.title: Relevance audit
learnerActions: Write the question at the top of a draft
In the margin of each paragraph, write one line on how it helps answer the question
Keep, reframe or cut each paragraph, and rewrite the opening and closing sentences of one reframed paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Every paragraph has to earn its place, and relevance is often a matter of framing as well as content.
activities.rationale: Makes tacit expectations about relevance explicit (Lea & Street, 1998) and connects relevance with argument (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Writing everything known about the topic and overlooking the command word or a limiting condition such as a period or context.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate but generic essays or exam answers; tutor comments such as 'not focused on the question' or 'relevance?'.
difficulties.response: Require a one-sentence task statement before planning and a relevance audit before submission. Rather than handing out command-word definitions, have learners infer what a command word demands from higher- and lower-scoring answers. Do not tell learners to repeat the question's wording in every paragraph, which produces mechanical text without improving relevance.

difficulties.pattern: In an exam, recognising a revised topic and writing a prepared answer that does not address the specific question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers relevant to the topic but not to the question; feedback such as 'does not answer the question'.
difficulties.response: Practise with questions that deliberately twist familiar topics. Where assessment systems the learner knows rewarded reproducing model answers, make the different expectation explicit rather than criticising the habit.

difficulties.pattern: Answering one part of a multi-part question at length and neglecting the other, or spending too long on the first exam question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unbalanced texts in which the evaluative part receives one paragraph; unfinished final exam answers.
difficulties.response: Word-budget or time-budget each part at the planning stage and practise with fixed checkpoints.

difficulties.pattern: Briefs whose requirements are vague, contradictory or left to tacit departmental convention, so that learners cannot tell what is expected.
difficulties.revealedBy: Several learners misreading the same brief in the same way; questions about the brief surfacing only after marking.
difficulties.response: With learners, model clarification requests and when tutors expect them. With departments, share examples of briefs that state genre, reader, criteria and word-count rules explicitly, and feed recurring misreadings back to module leaders rather than treating them as learner error.

diagnostic.task: Give a coursework brief (question, word limit, required reading, three-criterion rubric) and an exam question on a related topic. Ask for a list of what each requires, in five minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies command, topic, limits and sub-questions in both; notes genre, sources and at least one implication of the criteria for the brief; describes the shape of the exam answer and a time allocation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies topic and command words but misses limiting conditions, sub-questions or the implications of the criteria.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the topic only, or lists generic study advice unrelated to the task.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the routine for both subject exams and short coursework, starting with adapted briefs and moving quickly to authentic ones. Undergraduate-entry pre-sessionals apply it to extended essays and to timed tasks in progression assessment; postgraduate-entry pre-sessionals, who usually control command words already, concentrate on open briefs that leave scope and angle to the writer. In-sessional work is most effective when learners bring their own module briefs and past papers. At PGT level briefs are shorter and more open, and dissertation students set their own questions, which then have to be answered consistently. Test preparation can foster a narrow view of writing tasks (Moore & Morton, 2005), which may need explicit unlearning. Brief conventions, exam formats and word-count rules vary between institutions and countries, so work from the target context's documents.
reviewNotes: Absorbs exm.question-analysis and ess.answering-question (R1-13). voc.command-words remains the lexical resource; exm.timed-writing covers pacing and planning within a timed answer.

Review response: R1-13 suggested moving time allocation by marks to exm.timed-writing. It is kept here as one exam mastery statement, because allocating time follows directly from reading the paper's questions and mark weightings; exm.timed-writing covers pacing within an answer.

records.summary: In Flower and Hayes's (1981) model, generating is a sub-process of planning that retrieves content from memory and the task environment; Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) show that novice writers tend to stop at whatever first comes to mind. Present techniques as options to try rather than a required sequence, and always follow generation with task-based selection. Freewriting (Elbow, 1973) suits writers who censor themselves; question heuristics suit those who produce little. Allow generation in any language.

activities.title: Heuristic ladder
learnerActions: Write one obvious point in answer to a question
Apply five questions to it (why, how, when does it not hold, who disagrees, so what) and note an answer to each
Mark which answers need evidence from reading
activities.intendedInsight: Interrogating a first idea is often more productive than searching for more first ideas.
activities.rationale: Structured prompts act as procedural facilitation, the kind of support Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) used to help novice writers reach beyond knowledge-telling.

activities.title: Generate, then judge
learnerActions: Freewrite for five minutes on the question without stopping or correcting
Underline phrases that could become points
Sort the points into relevant, possibly relevant and off-task, using the task statement
activities.intendedInsight: Postponing judgement produces more material; selection is a separate, task-driven step.
activities.rationale: Freewriting separates production from evaluation (Elbow, 1973); pairing it with task-based selection stops it becoming unfocused.

difficulties.pattern: ‘I have no ideas about this topic.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Blank pages, very short plans, requests for model answers.
difficulties.response: Start from talk or questions rather than writing, allow L1 notes, and give a short reading to prime content. Do not supply the ideas yourself, which builds dependence.

difficulties.pattern: Generates many ideas but keeps all of them, producing list-like plans.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans with eight or more unconnected points for a 1,000-word text.
difficulties.response: Require explicit selection against the task statement, with a reason for each discarded idea.

diagnostic.task: Give a question and ask for a three-minute brainstorm, then the three best points with a reason for each choice.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Ten or more varied ideas, including at least one non-obvious angle; choices justified by the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Several ideas but similar in kind; choices justified by preference (‘easier to write about’).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Two or three ideas that restate the question; no selection rationale.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, generation is often the main bottleneck and benefits from oral rehearsal and shared brainstorming. Pre-sessional and in-sessional writers increasingly generate from reading, so link generation to reading questions. For postgraduates, generative writing and discussing ideas with peers or supervisors are usually more useful than formal brainstorming.
reviewNotes: Mind mapping is widely recommended, but research on concept maps concerns learning from maps rather than idea generation for writing, so it is not cited here as support.

records.summary: Planning in Flower and Hayes's (1981) model includes organising and goal-setting as well as generating. Ellis and Yuan (2004) found that pre-task planning time increased the fluency and syntactic complexity of L2 writing, although their task was narrative and transfer to source-based academic writing is an inference. Teach outlines whose entries are claims, so that the plan already carries the argument, and treat every outline as provisional (Hyland, 2003).

activities.title: Topic labels to claims
learnerActions: Take an outline made of topic labels (‘1 Background, 2 Advantages, 3 Disadvantages’)
Rewrite each entry as a full-sentence claim that helps answer the question
Read the claims in sequence and check that they form an argument without the body text
activities.intendedInsight: An outline made of claims is already a draft of the argument; one made of topics is only a table of contents.
activities.rationale: Making each plan entry a claim turns topic-driven planning into goal-driven planning of the kind associated with expert writers (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987).

activities.title: Format trial
learnerActions: Plan the same question once as a linear outline and once as a map or table
Draft one paragraph from each plan
Note which format exposed missing links or evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Different formats reveal different weaknesses; there is no single correct planning format.
activities.rationale: Formats are compared by what each reveals about the plan for this task, so the choice rests on observable results rather than on a presumed personal preference or 'style'.

difficulties.pattern: Plans are lists of topics copied from lecture headings or source sections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines consisting of nouns only; essays that describe each topic in turn.
difficulties.response: Require claim-based outlines and model converting topics into claims by asking ‘so what does this section show?’ for each entry.

difficulties.pattern: ‘Planning wastes time when the deadline is close or in an exam.’
difficulties.revealedBy: No visible plan; essays that drift or end without a conclusion.
difficulties.response: Practise five-minute plans and compare the resulting texts with unplanned ones. Do not insist on elaborate plans for every task; brief plans are legitimate.

diagnostic.task: Give a question, a set of source notes and ten minutes to produce an outline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Claim-based outline with evidence attached to each point, a stated ordering logic and rough word allocations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Logical sequence with evidence attached, but entries are topics rather than claims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: List of loosely related topics, or the notes reproduced in source order.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from template outlines that are gradually withdrawn. Pre-sessional extended writing is a good place to teach outlines revised alongside drafts and submitted for feedback. At PGT and PGR level, planning extends to chapter and section maps negotiated with supervisors; in timed exams, plans become brief but remain claim-based.
reviewNotes: Ellis and Yuan (2004) used a narrative writing task; the effects of planning time on extended, source-based academic writing are extrapolated.

Review response: R4-08 suggested citing Pashler et al. (2008) for the learning-styles debunk. Declined to avoid adding an unverified proposed reference; the activity rationale has been reworded so that it makes no empirical claim about learning styles.

records.summary: Zamel (1983) observed that more skilled ESL writers deferred attention to surface form and explored ideas while drafting, and Sommers (1980) found that experienced writers used drafting and redrafting to discover what they meant. In translating ideas into language (Flower & Hayes, 1981), L2 writers carry a heavier linguistic load, so strategies that protect momentum—placeholders, L1 notes, timed drafting—are especially useful. Present drafting as producing complete, revisable text, not as careless writing.

activities.title: Placeholder drafting
learnerActions: Draft for 20 minutes from a plan, writing [REF], [WORD?] or [CHECK] instead of stopping
Count placeholders and words produced
Resolve the placeholders in a separate session and compare the time spent
activities.intendedInsight: Separating getting ideas down from getting them right is faster and produces more content.
activities.rationale: Deferring local concerns mirrors the behaviour of skilled L2 writers described by Zamel (1983) and reduces competition for attention during translating (Flower & Hayes, 1981).

activities.title: What changed while drafting?
learnerActions: Reread the plan and the draft side by side
Mark one place where the draft says something the plan did not
Decide whether the change improves the answer and update the plan
activities.intendedInsight: Drafting is a way of discovering and testing the argument, not just transcribing a plan.
activities.rationale: Sommers (1980) associates experienced writers' revision with discovering meaning through drafting; making this explicit legitimises changes to the plan.

difficulties.pattern: ‘My first sentence has to be perfect before I can go on.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Long time spent on introductions, many deleted openings, incomplete drafts.
difficulties.response: Start drafting with the easiest body paragraph and write the introduction last. Do not give detailed language feedback on early drafts, which reinforces perfectionism.

difficulties.pattern: Composing each sentence in the first language and translating it word by word carries L1 clause structure and collocation into the English text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentences that are locally grammatical but hard to parse; collocations that mirror L1 patterns; heavy translator use.
difficulties.response: Encourage other languages for notes and planning, and try drafting from those notes rather than translating sentence by sentence (see wpr.l1-in-composing); for some writers and tasks, drafting a section in another language first is a legitimate alternative where rules permit. Do not ban other languages outright, which usually drives the practice underground.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to draft 300 words in 20 minutes from a supplied outline and then write two sentences about how they worked.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Complete draft following the plan, with placeholders and at least one noted development of the argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Complete draft but with long pauses for correction, or an incomplete draft with polished early paragraphs.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Introduction only, heavily reworked; reports being unable to continue until it was right.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, scaffold with paragraph-by-paragraph drafting from detailed plans. On pre-sessional programmes, draft deadlines within extended projects make drafting visible and give an opportunity for content-focused feedback. Postgraduates often over-read before drafting; encourage early, low-stakes drafting of more descriptive sections such as methods or background. Dictation and speech-to-text drafting are legitimate ways to keep momentum, particularly for writers with dyslexia or motor difficulties (see dig.assistive-technology).

records.summary: Spivey (1990) describes writing from sources as discourse synthesis, in which writers select, organise and connect content from several texts. Studies of university tasks show that much assessed writing draws on reading (Horowitz, 1986; Leki & Carson, 1997), and Plakans (2008) and Plakans and Gebril (2012) found that reading-to-write tasks prompt interaction between reading and writing, with sources used for ideas, organisation and language. Grabe and Zhang (2013) and Hirvela (2004) argue that EAP should teach reading and writing together. Teach the process end to end on one task, from question-driven reading through notes that separate source from comment to drafting from notes, rather than as separate reading and writing lessons.

activities.title: Question-driven reading plan
learnerActions: Break an essay question into sub-questions
Map each sub-question to likely sources and sections, and decide what to skip
Read and take notes under sub-question headings, marking quotation, paraphrase and own comment differently
activities.intendedInsight: Reading for writing is organised by the question, not by the source.
activities.rationale: Integrates reading and writing instruction as Grabe and Zhang (2013) and Hirvela (2004) recommend.

activities.title: Reorganise, don't summarise in order
learnerActions: Cut notes from three sources into individual points
Regroup the points under two claims that answer the question
Write a topic sentence for each group and note which sources support it
activities.intendedInsight: Source content should be arranged by the writer's points, not by source.
activities.rationale: Organising is the operation that distinguishes synthesis from serial summary (Spivey, 1990).

activities.title: Notes to paragraph, sources closed
learnerActions: Close the sources and write a paragraph making one point from your grouped notes
Check the paragraph against the sources for accuracy and attribution only after writing
Note any gap that sends you back to reading
activities.intendedInsight: How you read and take notes determines how easily, and how honestly, you can write.
activities.rationale: Writing from notes supports transformation of source content and reflects the reading-to-write processes observed in integrated tasks (Plakans & Gebril, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Reading everything on the topic before deciding what the task requires.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large volumes of notes, many irrelevant to the question; drafting starts late.
difficulties.response: Begin with task analysis and set reading priorities before reading; review them after the first draft.

difficulties.pattern: Writing with the source open and composing sentence by sentence from it, or from notes in which copied wording is unmarked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Patchwritten passages traceable to the source or to unmarked notes; source-order organisation; little commentary.
difficulties.response: Teach note conventions that separate quotation, paraphrase and comment, and close-the-source drafting. Treat early patchwriting as a developmental stage to move beyond rather than as misconduct.

difficulties.pattern: 'The more sources I include, the more academic my essay is.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources piled up with no link to the point; reporting verbs carrying the whole argument.
difficulties.response: Ask for a one-line justification of each source's role in the paragraph, and limit sources per point in practice tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting to write from personal opinion and general knowledge, as many proficiency-test and school essay tasks require.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments with few sources and much unsupported assertion.
difficulties.response: Use source-based writing tasks from the start of the course and make the expectation of source use explicit.

diagnostic.task: Give an essay question and five sources; ask which to use, which sections to read and how to organise notes, then for one paragraph from the notes with sources closed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Question-driven selection, a note plan organised by points, and a paragraph led by the learner's point with selected, paraphrased and attributed content and a linking comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Relevant selection, but notes planned source by source or a paragraph that summarises accurately without a point of the learner's own.
diagnostic.gapResponse: All sources treated equally or selection unrelated to the question; copied or closely patchwritten sentences, or missing attribution.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and undergraduate-entry pre-sessional courses should build assessment around short reading-to-write tasks with a small, given source set, since many proficiency tests ask for writing from personal knowledge (Moore & Morton, 2005). Postgraduate-entry pre-sessionals extend the process to learner-selected research articles and a larger reading base for a project or proposal. In-sessional undergraduates apply it to longer, denser disciplinary reading, and PGT students to organising large reading loads around a focused argument in assignments and dissertations. Timed reading-into-writing test tasks are treated under syn.integrated-tasks. Learners who use text-to-speech or other reading support (see dig.assistive-technology) may make and organise notes in audio or visual formats; what matters is that source and comment remain distinguishable.
reviewNotes: Absorbs rdc.reading-for-writing (R1-14), so that selecting, reading, noting, organising and drafting are taught as one procedure. Timed integrated test tasks are covered by syn.integrated-tasks.

records.summary: Johns (1997) argues for a socioliterate approach in which learners study how texts are shaped by roles and contexts, and Hyland (2005) shows that academic writing is interactive, with writers anticipating readers' needs and objections. The assessed essay's double audience—an expert marker addressed as if an informed peer—is a tacit convention that, as Lea and Street (1998) show, is rarely explained. Make the reader explicit in every task and compare how the same content changes for different readers.

activities.title: Same content, three readers
learnerActions: Write two sentences on one topic for a younger student, an expert marker and a newspaper reader
Compare what each version explains, assumes and argues
List three features that mark the version written for the marker
activities.intendedInsight: Expert readers expect explicit reasoning and a position, not more basic explanation.
activities.rationale: Varying the reader while holding content constant isolates audience effects, in line with a socioliterate approach (Johns, 1997).

activities.title: Reader questions
learnerActions: Exchange a paragraph with a partner, who writes the question an expert reader would ask after each sentence
Revise to answer the most important unanswered question in the text
activities.intendedInsight: Academic writing anticipates and answers a reader's questions.
activities.rationale: Treating text as a dialogue with an imagined reader reflects interactional accounts of written discourse (Hoey, 2001; Hyland, 2005).

difficulties.pattern: ‘The teacher already knows this, so I don't need to explain it.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Undefined key terms, skipped reasoning steps, tutor comments such as ‘explain’ or ‘how?’.
difficulties.response: Explain the convention of writing for an informed reader who is checking the writer's understanding, and show annotated feedback on such gaps.

difficulties.pattern: 'The marker wants to see that I know the lecture content and can use advanced vocabulary.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Lecture content reproduced without a position; inflated register.
difficulties.response: Discuss what markers reward using criteria and exemplars, and reframe the task as offering a reasoned view to an informed reader.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to identify the reader and purpose of three briefs (an essay, a reflective log, a policy brief) and name one way each affects the writing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes readers and purposes and names concrete consequences for content, explicitness and register.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the readers but gives generic consequences (‘be formal’).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats all three as written for ‘the teacher’ with the same purpose of showing knowledge.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the marker-as-reader convention made explicit early. In-sessional undergraduates meet a wider range of readers through professional and public-facing genres. PGT writers increasingly write for specialist peers and practitioners, so audience analysis becomes part of choosing and shaping genres.

records.summary: Self-regulated learning models (Zimmerman, 2002) highlight forethought, performance monitoring and self-reflection, all of which extended writing demands. Thesis-writing guidance (Paltridge & Starfield, 2020) and structured writing programmes such as Belcher's (2019) recommend regular writing, staged goals and planned feedback over last-minute bursts. Teach planning tools in the context of a real project and review progress at intervals; plans that are never revisited achieve little.

activities.title: Backward plan with a word budget
learnerActions: Work back from the deadline to set dated milestones, including feedback and editing
Allocate words to each section of the project
