Share the plan with a peer who checks for unrealistic weeks and missing contingency
activities.intendedInsight: Revision and feedback need protected time that must be scheduled before drafting starts.
activities.rationale: Explicit forethought and goal-setting form the first phase of self-regulation (Zimmerman, 2002).

activities.title: Writing log
learnerActions: Record date, time spent, words or sections produced and obstacles after each writing session for three weeks
Review the log to identify productive times and conditions
Set one routine change for the following fortnight
activities.intendedInsight: Regular short sessions often produce more than occasional long ones, and patterns only become visible when recorded.
activities.rationale: Monitoring and reflection complete the self-regulation cycle (Zimmerman, 2002), and regular writing is central to structured article-writing guidance (Belcher, 2019).

difficulties.pattern: Postponing all writing until the reading feels complete.
difficulties.revealedBy: No drafts until the final weeks; long reading lists with few notes.
difficulties.response: Set early, low-stakes writing milestones, such as a summary of key sources or a draft methods section, and revisit drafting as a way of thinking (see wpr.drafting).

difficulties.pattern: Schedules that assume every week will be equally productive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated slippage; plans abandoned after the first missed milestone.
difficulties.response: Build in contingency weeks and review the plan every fortnight, treating replanning as normal rather than as failure.

diagnostic.task: Ask for a schedule and word budget for a 3,000-word assignment due in four weeks alongside two other deadlines.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Dated milestones, a word budget by section, time for feedback and editing, and explicit handling of competing deadlines.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Milestones present but no word budget, or no time reserved for revision.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A single deadline with a plan to ‘write it in the last week’.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional extended projects are often learners' first long text and a useful rehearsal. Undergraduate and PGT dissertations compress project management into a few months alongside taught modules. For PGR, management spans years and links to supervision, writing groups and publication planning (see res.writing-productivity).
reviewNotes: Overlaps with res.writing-productivity, which addresses doctoral routines; this topic covers generic project management from pre-sessional level upwards.

records.summary: Rose (1980) found that blocked student writers often held rigid rules and inflexible plans, whereas fluent writers used flexible heuristics. Freewriting (Elbow, 1973) lowers the stakes of producing text, and doctoral writing pedagogy treats writing difficulty as bound up with identity and authority as well as technique (Kamler & Thomson, 2014). Treat blocks as normal and solvable, match strategies to likely causes, and avoid framing them as purely a matter of motivation.

activities.title: Rule audit
learnerActions: List the writing rules you follow (for example ‘always write the introduction first’ or ‘never use I’)
Classify each as an absolute rule or a flexible guideline, and look for counter-examples in published writing in your field
Rewrite unhelpful absolute rules as heuristics
activities.intendedInsight: Some blocks come from rules that are not actually requirements.
activities.rationale: Rose (1980) linked blocking to rigid rules; testing rules against real texts also counters widespread style myths.

activities.title: Ten-minute starts
learnerActions: Freewrite for ten minutes, in any language, about what you want the stuck section to say
Extract one sentence that could open the section
Set a concrete goal for the next ten-minute session
activities.intendedInsight: Producing imperfect text is usually the quickest way out of a block.
activities.rationale: Freewriting removes evaluation from initial production (Elbow, 1973).

difficulties.pattern: ‘I can't start writing until I know exactly what I think.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Extended reading and note-making with no drafts.
difficulties.response: Present writing as a way of finding out what one thinks and set exploratory writing that is not assessed.

difficulties.pattern: ‘My English isn't good enough, so whatever I write will be wrong.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance, missed draft deadlines, very short drafts, apologetic notes to the tutor.
difficulties.response: Separate content feedback from language feedback on early drafts and normalise multilingual drafting. Do not respond with intensive error correction on early work, which confirms the fear.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe the last time they could not write and what they did about it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific cause and a strategy that addressed it, and identifies what they would do next time.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the feeling but uses only generic strategies (waiting, more reading).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the block as a fixed trait (‘I'm just a bad writer’) and has no strategies.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and first-year undergraduates often block on high-stakes first assignments; postgraduates and doctoral researchers more often on long, ill-defined sections. At PGR level, writing groups and retreats provide useful structures, and a persistent block may signal an unresolved conceptual problem worth raising with supervisors.
reviewNotes: Rose (1980) is a small-sample study of L1 undergraduates; its extension to L2 writers is plausible but not directly tested.

records.summary: Studies of L2 composing show that writers use the L1 for particular sub-processes, especially planning and generating ideas, and that L1 use tends to decrease as L2 proficiency rises (Wang & Wen, 2002). Cumming (1989) found that writing expertise and L2 proficiency make separate contributions to L2 writing, so composing expertise developed in another language is a resource. Kobayashi and Rinnert (1992) found that lower-proficiency Japanese EFL writers' essays written in Japanese and then translated scored higher on content and organisation than their directly composed essays, so whether to draft directly in English is a contested, task-dependent choice rather than a rule. Translanguaging perspectives (García & Li Wei, 2014) legitimise plurilingual composing. Lee (2020) reports that EFL students who used machine-translation output as a reference while revising reduced some errors, but full-text translation raises learning and integrity questions, so local rules need explicit discussion.

activities.title: Language map of my process
learnerActions: Record which language you used for each step of a recent piece of writing (reading, notes, planning, drafting, checking)
Compare with peers and discuss the benefits and risks at each step
Choose one change to try in the next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Different languages can serve different steps; the useful question is which choice helps this task, within its rules.
activities.rationale: Making language choice explicit turns habit into strategy, consistent with evidence that L1 use varies by composing activity (Wang & Wen, 2002).

activities.title: Plurilingual plan, two drafting routes
learnerActions: Plan a paragraph in your strongest language or a mixture of languages
Draft it once directly in English and, where permitted, once in another language before rendering it in English
Compare the two versions for content, organisation and naturalness, and check specific terms with a dictionary or corpus
activities.intendedInsight: Each route has costs and benefits that depend on the task, the writer's proficiency and the rules.
activities.rationale: Draws on the plurilingual repertoire as a resource (García & Li Wei, 2014) and on mixed evidence comparing translation with direct composition (Kobayashi & Rinnert, 1992).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Using my first language is cheating, or it will stop my English improving.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Difficulty generating ideas in English, thin content, guilt about L1 notes.
difficulties.response: Explain that L1 planning is common among successful L2 writers and discuss when it helps. Do not ban L1 use in planning activities.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the whole text in the L1, translating it with machine translation and lightly editing the output.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent but uneven text, unexpected term choices, a gap between in-class and take-home writing (which on its own is expected, since timed in-class writing is usually weaker, and is not evidence of translation or misconduct).
difficulties.response: Clarify local rules; discuss what the learner loses (practice, control of voice) and the integrity risks; show targeted uses of translation that are permitted.

difficulties.pattern: Translating clause by clause carries over L1 information order and clause chaining, producing very long or topic–comment sentences that are hard to parse in English.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentences that are grammatical in parts but difficult to follow; unusual sentence boundaries.
difficulties.response: Try drafting from notes rather than translating clause by clause, then edit sentence boundaries and information order. Explain the mechanism in linguistic terms rather than attributing it to a ‘culture’.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to plan aloud, in any language(s), for a short question and then write the first paragraph in English.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Plans in whichever language is efficient; the English paragraph is drafted from the plan with English syntax and appropriate terms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Plans in L1; the English paragraph closely translates plan sentences and contains awkward structures.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No plan; translates sentence by sentence or asks to use a translator for the whole paragraph.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners rely most on other languages and need explicit guidance on productive uses. Pre-sessional programmes should state rules on translation and AI tools clearly, as practice varies. Whether assessed texts may themselves be translingual (quoting and glossing sources in other languages, or bilingual submission in some EMI programmes) is contested and varies by task (see idn.translingual-writing). Doctoral researchers often read and think in several languages; plurilingual note-making and the use of non-English sources are part of research practice (see src.multilingual-sources).
reviewNotes: Institutional rules on machine translation vary widely and change quickly; guidance here is deliberately non-prescriptive.

records.summary: Word limits are task constraints that force prioritisation: under-length drafts usually lack analysis, and over-length ones usually contain description or repetition. Teach word budgeting at the planning stage and cutting as a revision decision before it becomes a sentence-level task, reflecting the distinction between global revision and local editing (Sommers, 1980). Conventions on what counts and on tolerances vary, so learners should check local regulations rather than rely on general rules.

activities.title: Word budget
learnerActions: Allocate a 2,000-word limit across the introduction, body sections and conclusion of a given plan
Justify the largest allocation
Compare the budget with the actual proportions of a high-scoring exemplar
activities.intendedInsight: Introductions and background usually need far fewer words than learners give them.
activities.rationale: Budgeting turns the limit into a planning tool and exposes over-weighted description early (Hyland, 2003).

activities.title: Cut by value
learnerActions: Rank the paragraphs of an over-length draft by their contribution to the argument
Remove or compress the lowest-ranked material
Only then tighten sentences, recording the words saved at each step
activities.intendedInsight: Structural cuts save more words and do less damage than trimming every sentence.
activities.rationale: Separating global from local cutting mirrors the distinction between revision and editing (Sommers, 1980).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Writing more shows that I know more.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Long background sections, repetition, persistently over-length drafts.
difficulties.response: Show marker comments on description and practise reducing background to one or two sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Cutting the commentary and keeping the source summaries.
difficulties.revealedBy: Shortened drafts that have become more descriptive.
difficulties.response: Highlight analysis sentences before cutting and protect them.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that references and quotations never count, or that a fixed tolerance always applies.
difficulties.revealedBy: Length penalties and queries after marking.
difficulties.response: Have learners find and quote the local rule for each assignment as part of analysing the brief (see wpr.task-analysis).

diagnostic.task: Ask for a word budget for a 1,500-word essay with three body sections, and a plan for cutting a supplied 1,800-word draft by 300 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Budget favours the argument sections; the cutting plan removes low-value content first and protects analysis.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable budget, but the cutting plan trims sentences evenly throughout.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No budget; cuts the conclusion or the analysis.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners more often struggle to reach limits and need help developing analysis. Undergraduates and PGT students more often overshoot, especially in reading-heavy assignments. Doctoral researchers deal with journal limits and thesis regulations, where cutting may mean moving material to appendices or other outputs. Conventions differ by context: some UK institutions allow a stated tolerance (often around 10%) while others treat the limit as absolute; North American courses often set page rather than word limits; some continental European programmes count characters. Learners should find the rule in their target context rather than assume one.
reviewNotes: There is little dedicated research on managing word limits; guidance is practitioner-derived, and the citations support the general framing of task constraints and revision rather than specific techniques.

records.summary: Teach formatting as compliance with conventions the reader has specified rather than as a universal standard: style guides such as APA (American Psychological Association, 2020) and MLA (Modern Language Association of America, 2021) differ, and many departments impose their own templates. Combine brief instruction with hands-on practice in word-processing styles, and keep formatting in proportion to its weight in assessment.

activities.title: Style-sheet comparison
learnerActions: Compare the formatting requirements of two style guides or departmental handbooks and list five differences
Apply one set of requirements to a short document using built-in styles
activities.intendedInsight: Formatting conventions are local choices; the skill lies in finding the right one and applying it consistently.
activities.rationale: Comparing style guides counters the belief that there is one correct academic format.

activities.title: Pre-submission checklist
learnerActions: Build a formatting checklist from an assignment brief
Check a peer's document and then one's own against it
activities.intendedInsight: A checklist makes final checks quick and systematic and keeps them at the end of the process.
activities.rationale: Separating presentation checks from content work prevents formatting from displacing revision.

difficulties.pattern: Formatting manually with spaces, tabs and typed numbers, so the layout breaks whenever the text is edited.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent headings, broken numbering, misaligned text.
difficulties.response: Teach styles and automatic numbering briefly and check them in class.

difficulties.pattern: Spending disproportionate time on appearance at the expense of content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavily designed documents with weak argument.
difficulties.response: Show how marking criteria weight presentation and schedule formatting for the end of the process.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to identify the formatting requirements for a given assignment and apply them to a one-page draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds all stated requirements and applies them consistently using styles.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Applies most requirements, but manually and with some inconsistencies.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unaware of the requirements; submits in default formatting.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners may be new to academic word processing. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners need department-specific conventions. At PGR level, thesis regulations and journal templates dominate, and document accessibility (see mmd.accessibility) becomes increasingly relevant.
reviewNotes: The scope note mentions headings; headings as a rhetorical choice in essays are covered by ess.headings.

records.summary: The one-idea paragraph is a well-established pedagogical model and a helpful default for reading and writing, but Braddock's (1974) analysis of professional expository prose found that many paragraphs did not open with an explicit topic sentence, and some had none. Present the model as a reader-friendly convention rather than a law, and use authentic academic paragraphs alongside textbook models. Swales and Feak (2012) show how paragraphs organise information (for example general–specific), which is useful for awareness-raising.

activities.title: Paragraph jigsaw
learnerActions: Sort sentences from two shuffled paragraphs on related topics into two paragraphs
State each paragraph's controlling idea in one sentence
Explain which clues (point, reference, logic) guided the sorting
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraph unity comes from a shared point, not merely shared vocabulary.
activities.rationale: Reconstruction makes unity and its signals noticeable before learners have to produce it.

activities.title: Textbook versus published paragraphs
learnerActions: Compare a textbook model paragraph with two paragraphs from published work in the learner's field
Locate the main point in each
Discuss why the published writers placed it where they did
activities.intendedInsight: The one-idea principle holds widely, but where the main point is placed varies with function.
activities.rationale: Contrasting idealised and authentic paragraphs guards against overgeneralising from textbook models (Braddock, 1974).

difficulties.pattern: Paragraphs drift because each sentence follows from the one before rather than from the controlling idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Final sentences unrelated to the first; readers unable to summarise the paragraph.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to note the paragraph's point in the margin before drafting and again after, and to compare the two.

difficulties.pattern: ‘A paragraph is five sentences’ or ‘I start a new paragraph whenever I use However’.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniform paragraph lengths; breaks at connectors rather than at changes of point.
difficulties.response: Discuss paragraphing as a decision about points, and show variation in authentic texts.

diagnostic.task: Give an unparagraphed 300-word text containing three points and ask for paragraph breaks plus a one-line label for each paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Breaks match changes of point; labels state the point (a claim), not merely the topic.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Breaks mostly correct, but labels are topics, or one break is driven by length.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Breaks at arbitrary points or before every connector.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and undergraduate-entry pre-sessional learners benefit most from explicit work on unity. Postgraduate-entry pre-sessionals usually need only a diagnostic review, and authentic disciplinary paragraphs should be used from the later stages of any pre-sessional to show legitimate variation.
reviewNotes: Braddock (1974) analysed edited professional essays, not student academic writing; it is cited to qualify the universality of the topic-sentence model, not to dismiss the model.

records.summary: Teach topic sentences as claims that make a promise the rest of the paragraph keeps; prediction tasks are a quick test of whether a topic sentence is doing this. Reading a text's topic sentences in sequence is also a powerful check on the overall argument (see edt.reverse-outlining) and connects paragraph work to Wingate's (2012) emphasis on argument. Because expert writers do not always put the main point first (Braddock, 1974), present first-sentence topic sentences as a strong default rather than a rule.

activities.title: Fact, topic or claim?
learnerActions: Classify a set of paragraph openings as facts, topic announcements or claims
Rewrite the facts and announcements as claims
Predict the content of the paragraph that would follow each claim
activities.intendedInsight: A good topic sentence lets a reader predict the paragraph.
activities.rationale: Prediction operationalises the promise function of topic sentences and exposes vague controlling ideas.

activities.title: Topic-sentence spine
learnerActions: Extract the topic sentences of a model essay and read them in sequence
Do the same with one's own draft
Revise any topic sentence that does not advance the argument
activities.intendedInsight: Together, topic sentences form the skeleton of the argument.
activities.rationale: Linking paragraph-level and text-level structure supports the shift from description to argument (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Topic sentences that are too broad (‘Technology has changed society’) or too narrow (a single statistic).
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that cannot fulfil their opening, or have nowhere to go after it.
difficulties.response: Practise scaling controlling ideas with general and shell nouns (‘two main factors’, ‘a significant limitation’) and test them with prediction.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with a source (‘Smith (2019) states that…’), so that the source rather than the writer controls the paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that summarise one source with no point of the writer's own.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to begin with their own claim and move the citation into the support.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph body without its first sentence and ask for a topic sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A claim of suitable scope that the body supports, framed with a controlling noun or phrase and linked to the wider argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate topic but no claim, or a claim somewhat broader than the content.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats a detail from the body or offers an unrelated generalisation.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, insist on explicit topic sentences as the default. In pre-sessional and in-sessional work, extend to linking topic sentences to the thesis and varying their placement. In undergraduate disciplinary writing, topic sentences increasingly carry synthesis and evaluation across sources.

records.summary: Toulmin's (2003) model makes visible what a supported claim needs: grounds, and the warrant linking them to the claim. Hoey's (1983) general–particular and matching patterns describe how support is typically organised in text, and Andrews (2010) argues that argumentation in higher education needs explicit teaching. Teach support as a repertoire—explanation, data, example, comparison, concession—chosen to fit the claim, with particular emphasis on the explanatory sentences that learners most often omit.

activities.title: Support-type audit
learnerActions: Colour-code the sentences of a model paragraph by function (claim, explanation, evidence, example, comment)
Do the same for one of your own paragraphs
Add the missing function, which is usually explanation or comment
activities.intendedInsight: Strong paragraphs mix kinds of support and state the link between evidence and claim.
activities.rationale: Functional analysis makes Toulmin-style grounds and warrants visible at sentence level (Toulmin, 2003).

activities.title: Is that enough?
learnerActions: In groups, judge whether given evidence is sufficient for three claims of different strength
Either weaken over-strong claims or add evidence
Explain each decision to another group
activities.intendedInsight: How much support is needed, and of what kind, depends on how strong the claim is.
activities.rationale: Connects paragraph development to the evaluation of arguments, which Andrews (2010) treats as central to higher-education argumentation.

difficulties.pattern: A single example is presented as if it proves a general claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: One anecdote or case per paragraph; ‘For example…’ followed by the end of the paragraph.
difficulties.response: Distinguish illustration from evidence and ask ‘how typical is this example, and how do we know?’

difficulties.pattern: Claim plus quotation, with no explanation of how the quotation supports the claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotations ending paragraphs; tutor comments such as ‘so what?’ or ‘explain’.
difficulties.response: Require at least one sentence of the writer's own explanation after each piece of evidence.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a paragraph supporting a given claim using one supplied data point and one example.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Claim, data, explanation of its significance, example with comment and, if needed, a qualification of the claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Data and example included, but the explanation is thin or merely restates them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the claim, or lists the data and the example with no link to the claim.

records.contextNotes: Foundation writers often rely on personal examples and general knowledge, which suits some tasks but needs to move towards source-based evidence. Pre-sessional programmes introduce evidence from reading. In-sessional undergraduates need a disciplinary sense of what counts as evidence (see acu.disciplinary-knowledge).

records.summary: PEEL and similar acronyms are widely used in schools and foundation programmes because they make paragraph functions explicit. Wingate (2012) argues that essay advice focused on structure can obscure the purpose of essays, which is argument, and contributors to Caplan and Johns (2019) critique formulaic templates such as the five-paragraph essay for producing text that does not transfer to university genres. Use PEEL as a scaffold that is explicitly withdrawn over time, in the spirit of the guided-to-independent sequence in Sydney School genre pedagogy (Rose & Martin, 2012), and compare scaffolded with authentic paragraphs early.

activities.title: PEEL and beyond
learnerActions: Label a PEEL model paragraph
Label two authentic paragraphs from the target discipline using the same scheme
List what the authentic paragraphs do that PEEL does not capture
activities.intendedInsight: PEEL names useful functions but not a fixed order or number of moves.
activities.rationale: Comparing a scaffold with authentic text builds genre awareness rather than template-following (Caplan & Johns, 2019).

activities.title: Fade the scaffold
learnerActions: Write one paragraph with PEEL labels in the margin
Write the next with only a margin note of the point
Write a third with no notes and ask a partner to identify the functions
activities.intendedInsight: The functions can be internalised and then used flexibly.
activities.rationale: Moving from supported to independent construction reflects the teaching–learning cycle of genre pedagogy (Rose & Martin, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Every paragraph must be PEEL, and the last sentence must link back to the question.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive link sentences (‘This shows that X is important for the question’).
difficulties.response: Show authentic paragraphs without link sentences and discuss when a link is needed. Do not ban PEEL abruptly; reframe it as one option among several.

difficulties.pattern: One piece of evidence per paragraph, whatever the claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Under-supported claims; no comparison of sources within a paragraph.
difficulties.response: Introduce paragraphs that combine several sources and relate support to claim strength.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a paragraph making one point supported by two sources that partly disagree.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Point, both sources integrated with their relationship stated, explanation and a qualified conclusion; the structure departs from PEEL where needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses PEEL rigidly, with two separate evidence–explanation blocks and a formulaic link.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot accommodate the second source or the disagreement; only one source is summarised.

records.contextNotes: PEEL is most useful at foundation and on undergraduate-entry pre-sessionals, especially for learners whose schooling used it; by the end of such a course learners should treat it as one option. On postgraduate-entry pre-sessionals it should at most be revisited diagnostically, since most learners need multi-source paragraphs rather than a single-evidence template. The acronym is common in UK schooling; other systems use similar scaffolds under different names, so ask learners what they were taught. Some learners arriving in in-sessional classes have to unlearn rigid PEEL in disciplines that value other paragraph patterns.
reviewNotes: No published study known to the author tests PEEL specifically; the critique draws on broader work on formulaic writing instruction, including the five-paragraph essay (Caplan & Johns, 2019).

records.summary: Daneš (1974) described how themes progress across sentences, and Halliday and Hasan (1976) catalogued the cohesive ties that connect them; Swales and Feak (2012) turn these ideas into practical advice on old-to-new flow. Crossley and McNamara (2012) found that measures of explicit cohesion did not predict higher proficiency ratings of L2 essays in the way often assumed, whereas lexical sophistication did, which supports teaching information flow and logic rather than connector density. Work with learners' own paragraphs and focus on sentence openings.

activities.title: Theme tracking
learnerActions: Underline the first noun phrase of each sentence in a paragraph
Draw an arrow from each to where that information first appeared
Rewrite sentences whose openings have no backward link
activities.intendedInsight: Readers follow a paragraph through what each sentence starts with.
activities.rationale: Makes thematic progression (Daneš, 1974) visible and actionable, following the old-to-new advice in Swales and Feak (2012).

activities.title: Connector diet
learnerActions: Remove all sentence-initial connectors from a paragraph
Reinsert only those that state a relation the reader could not otherwise infer
Compare readability with the original
activities.intendedInsight: Too many connectors can obscure the logic rather than clarify it.
activities.rationale: Responds to evidence that density of explicit cohesive devices is not a marker of better L2 writing (Crossley & McNamara, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Using lots of linking words makes my writing coherent.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Most sentences begin with a connector; mismatched relations (‘Moreover’ introducing a contrast).
difficulties.response: Teach logical ordering and given–new first, then precise connector choice. Do not reward connector counts in feedback or rubrics.

difficulties.pattern: Each sentence introduces a new topic in subject position, so the paragraph reads like a list.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers cannot summarise the paragraph; few backward references.
difficulties.response: Use theme tracking and rewrite sentence openings so that each starts from given information.

diagnostic.task: Give five shuffled sentences from one paragraph and ask for the original order with reasons.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct order justified by reference, given–new information and logical relations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct order justified mainly by the connectors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Order based on content guesses only; no reasons given.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need basic reference and ordering. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners benefit from given–new and theme work on their own drafts. PGT writers' coherence problems often stem from dense information packaging; link to reg.information-density.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with coh.thematic-progression and coh.given-new; this topic applies them to paragraph construction and repair.

records.summary: Closing sentences are often where writers make the analytic move markers look for: saying what the evidence means. Present them functionally (significance, qualification, transition) rather than as a required restatement, and use authentic paragraphs, which often end on evidence or comment without a separate closing formula (a practitioner observation; Swales and Feak (2012) supply model paragraphs for analysis). This links to Wingate's (2012) emphasis on keeping the argument visible throughout a text.

activities.title: So what?
learnerActions: Read paragraphs that end on a piece of evidence
Add a final sentence answering ‘so what does this show for the question?’
Compare versions and choose the one that adds most
activities.intendedInsight: The best closing sentences add interpretation, not repetition.
activities.rationale: Prompts learners to state the link between evidence and argument which Wingate (2012) treats as part of developing a position through analysis of sources.

activities.title: Close or connect?
learnerActions: For each paragraph in a three-paragraph sequence, decide whether to close it, link it forward or leave it as it is
Justify the choices in pairs
activities.intendedInsight: A closing sentence is a choice determined by the paragraph's function.
activities.rationale: Encourages functional judgement rather than formula.

difficulties.pattern: Closing sentences that repeat the topic sentence in different words (‘Therefore, X is important’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end where they began; no development of the point.
difficulties.response: Ask for one new element in the last sentence: an implication, a limitation or a link to the question.

difficulties.pattern: Overstated closings (‘This proves that…’) after limited evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boosters clustered at paragraph ends.
difficulties.response: Link to hedging and claim calibration and ask learners to match the closing claim to the evidence given.

diagnostic.task: Give two consecutive paragraphs and ask for a closing sentence for the first that also prepares for the second.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The closing states the significance of the first paragraph and sets up its relation to the next point.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The closing either summarises or links, but not both.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the topic sentence.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and undergraduate-entry pre-sessional learners can use closing sentences routinely at first. From the later stages of a pre-sessional, and on postgraduate-entry courses from the start, the emphasis moves to deciding when a closing sentence is needed and to stating significance, which connects to criticality.
reviewNotes: Research on paragraph-concluding sentences specifically is limited; this guidance is practitioner-derived.

records.summary: There is no universally correct paragraph length; Braddock's (1974) study of professional prose suggests that paragraphing in practice is more varied than textbook rules imply. Teach division as a reader-oriented decision tied to shifts in point and function, and show variation across genres (shorter paragraphs in reports and online writing, longer ones in many humanities essays). In student essays, single-sentence paragraphs usually signal undeveloped ideas, and very long paragraphs usually contain more than one point.

activities.title: Where would you break?
learnerActions: Mark possible paragraph breaks in an unparagraphed text
Compare with the original and discuss the differences
Separate breaks required by a change of point from optional breaks made for readability
activities.intendedInsight: Some breaks are required by the content; others are judgements about readability.
activities.rationale: Makes paragraphing a reasoned decision, consistent with evidence of variation in expert texts (Braddock, 1974).

activities.title: Genre comparison
learnerActions: Estimate average paragraph length in an essay, a report and a blog post on the same topic
Explain the differences in terms of reader, purpose and medium
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraph-length conventions depend on genre and medium.
activities.rationale: Links paragraphing to audience and purpose rather than to a fixed rule.

difficulties.pattern: A new single-sentence paragraph for every point, as in journalistic or online writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many very short paragraphs; points asserted without support.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to develop each short paragraph (see par.support) or merge it with a related one, and show that development is what markers reward.

difficulties.pattern: Page-long paragraphs containing several points.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of 300 words or more in which readers lose track.
difficulties.response: Reverse-outline the paragraph to locate shifts in point and divide there. Paragraphing norms vary across genres and writing traditions, so present the convention as a reader-oriented choice in the target context rather than as correcting a deficit.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to paragraph an unparagraphed 400-word text.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Breaks at shifts in point, paragraphs of workable length, and a clear justification for any optional break.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly reasonable breaks, but one is driven by length and splits a point.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Breaks at fixed sentence counts, or none at all.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional teaching establishes defaults. In-sessional undergraduates need to see disciplinary and genre variation, including reports and online genres.
reviewNotes: Numerical guidance on ‘ideal’ paragraph length is deliberately avoided because it varies across genres and disciplines.

records.summary: Bruce (2008) distinguishes social genres, such as the essay, from cognitive genres, such as explanation and discussion, which organise stretches of text within them; paragraphs are often the unit at which these shift. Teaching paragraph functions helps learners see why introductions and conclusions are organised differently from body paragraphs and why counter-argument paragraphs need a response move. Swales and Feak (2012) provide accessible analyses of how stretches of text are organised for particular purposes.

activities.title: Function sort
learnerActions: Label the paragraphs of a model essay by function
Note the typical moves within each function
Use the notes to plan a new essay
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraphs with different functions have different internal structures.
activities.rationale: Function-based analysis applies genre-based thinking at paragraph level (Bruce, 2008).

activities.title: Write the bridge
learnerActions: Read the end of one section and the start of the next in an essay from which the transition has been removed
Write a short transitional paragraph
Compare with the original writer's solution
activities.intendedInsight: Transitional paragraphs help readers follow a longer argument.
activities.rationale: Prepares learners for longer texts in which transitions between sections matter.

difficulties.pattern: Introductions that launch straight into the first argument, or conclusions that introduce new evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays without context or without synthesis at the end.
difficulties.response: Analyse the typical moves of introductory and concluding paragraphs in exemplars before learners write their own.

difficulties.pattern: Counter-argument paragraphs that present the opposing view and then stop.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that appear to undermine their own thesis.
difficulties.response: Teach the response move (concession followed by rebuttal or qualification) as part of the counter-argument function.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to label the function of six paragraphs from an essay and say what each one does.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate labels, with the typical moves of each function described.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies introduction and conclusion, but not transitional or counter-argument functions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Labels paragraphs by topic only.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on introduction, body and conclusion. Pre-sessional learners add counter-argument and transitional functions, which become more important as texts lengthen (see coh.paragraph-transitions).

records.summary: Hyland (1999) shows that citation is a rhetorical choice through which writers position themselves in a disciplinary conversation, and Petrić (2007) found that higher-rated master's theses used citations for a wider range of functions, including evaluation and linking, than lower-rated ones. Pecorari (2013) argues that good source use needs to be taught explicitly rather than policed. Teach introduce–cite–comment as a default sequence, paying particular attention to the commentary sentences learners most often omit.

activities.title: Who is speaking?
learnerActions: Highlight the sentences of a source-based paragraph by voice: writer, source, or unclear
Identify where the reader cannot tell whose view is being expressed
Revise with signal phrases and comment sentences
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to be able to track who is responsible for each claim.
activities.rationale: Builds the awareness of attribution that underpins acceptable source use (Pecorari, 2013).

activities.title: Add the comment
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that ends with a citation
Write a comment that evaluates, explains or connects the evidence
Compare comments and rank them by analytic value
activities.intendedInsight: The comment is where the writer's contribution lies.
activities.rationale: Higher-rated theses used citations for evaluation and linking more often than lower-rated ones (Petrić, 2007).

difficulties.pattern: Paragraphs that are strings of source summaries (‘A says… B says… C says…’).
difficulties.revealedBy: No claims of the writer's own; tutor comments such as ‘where is your voice?’.
difficulties.response: Require a writer's claim at the start and a comment after each piece of evidence; use short synthesis tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Not marking where a paraphrase ends, so later sentences could belong either to the writer or to the source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguous attribution; possible plagiarism concerns.
difficulties.response: Teach signal phrases at the boundaries of attributed content and the ‘who is speaking?’ check.

difficulties.pattern: Commentary that only restates the evidence in other words ('This shows that pollution is a serious problem').
difficulties.revealedBy: Comment sentences that add no interpretation, evaluation or link to the paragraph's claim.
difficulties.response: Give a menu of comment moves (explain the mechanism, evaluate the evidence, compare with another source, state the consequence for the claim) and ask learners to label which move each comment makes.

diagnostic.task: Give two short source extracts and a claim and ask for a paragraph supporting the claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Claim first; both sources paraphrased and attributed; their relationship stated; a comment links the evidence back to the claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Claim and sources present, but commentary is minimal or attribution boundaries are unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sources summarised in sequence with no claim or comment, or copied.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need basic signal phrases and paragraphs built on a single source. Pre-sessional programmes should make integration central to extended writing. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT writers need disciplinary citation practices and paragraphs that put several sources in dialogue (see syn.synthesis-paragraphs).
reviewNotes: Overlaps with src.integrating-quotations and src.voice-boundaries; this topic covers the paragraph-level organisation of sources around the writer's point.

records.summary: Wingate (2012) found that students often understood essay writing as structuring content rather than presenting an argument, and argued for explicit teaching of argument as the organising principle. The five-paragraph essay can introduce thesis-led structure, but contributors to Caplan and Johns (2019) argue that it misrepresents university writing, and Nesi and Gardner (2012) show how much essays vary across disciplines. Teach structure as argument mapping and use authentic student essays from target disciplines as models.

activities.title: Argument map of a model essay
learnerActions: Write the thesis of a high-scoring student essay in one sentence
Write one sentence per body paragraph stating its contribution to the thesis
Draw arrows showing how the points build on each other
activities.intendedInsight: An essay's structure is its argument laid out in order.
activities.rationale: Makes argument the organising principle, as Wingate (2012) recommends, rather than a sequence of content blocks.

activities.title: Template versus university essay
learnerActions: Compare a five-paragraph test-style essay with a 2,000-word university essay on a similar topic
List differences in length, sources, paragraphing and structure
Decide what from the five-paragraph model is worth keeping
activities.intendedInsight: The template teaches thesis-led organisation but not how university essays actually work.
activities.rationale: Explicit comparison helps learners keep what transfers and discard what does not (Caplan & Johns, 2019).

difficulties.pattern: ‘An essay has five paragraphs: an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Three-point essays regardless of length; padding to fit the template.
difficulties.response: Show essays of varying structure and plan from the argument. Do not simply forbid the template; explain what it gets right and where it stops being useful.

difficulties.pattern: Structure follows the order of the sources or a list of topics rather than the argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Body paragraphs that each summarise one reading or describe one topic.
difficulties.response: Use argument-mapping tasks and thesis-led planning.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to outline an essay for a ‘to what extent’ question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A thesis containing a judgement; body sections ordered to build a case, including a counter-argument and response; a conclusion that answers ‘to what extent’.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Thesis present, but the body is balanced for and against without building to the judgement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of topics with no thesis.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes and undergraduate-entry pre-sessionals may begin with structured templates and should move learners to argument-driven structure in extended essays, with explicit discussion of how university essays differ from test essays. On postgraduate-entry pre-sessionals this is usually a brief review. Essay conventions differ between, for example, UK, North American and continental European universities and between EMI contexts, so use model essays from the target context.

records.summary: A thesis is the textual realisation of a position; Wingate (2012) identifies developing and stating a position as a core component of argument that students find difficult. Andrews (2010) treats argument in higher education as a mode of thinking that needs explicit teaching rather than being left implicit. Teach thesis statements by contrast (fact, announcement, opinion, arguable claim), insist on revising the thesis after drafting, and acknowledge that some disciplines and essay types favour an exploratory or delayed thesis.

activities.title: Thesis ladder
learnerActions: Start from a topic announcement
Add a position, then reasons, then a qualification
Judge which version best suits a 1,500-word essay
activities.intendedInsight: Arguable, qualified theses are both stronger and easier to support.
activities.rationale: Stepwise transformation makes the components of a position explicit (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Thesis–essay match
learnerActions: Read a model essay with its thesis removed
Write the thesis the essay actually argues
Compare with the original thesis and with the essay question
activities.intendedInsight: The thesis must match what the essay does, which may differ from the writer's original plan.
activities.rationale: Encourages treating the thesis as a claim to be revised in the light of the argument (Andrews, 2010).

difficulties.pattern: ‘This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of X.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Announcements with no position; descriptive essays.
difficulties.response: Explain that announcements can serve as roadmaps but are not theses, and require a separate position sentence.

difficulties.pattern: 'A balanced essay is safer, so my thesis should say there are arguments on both sides.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Evenly balanced theses with no judgement; conclusions that restate both sides.
difficulties.response: Where test-preparation advice presented a 'balanced view' as the safe option, explain that most university questions require a reasoned judgement, and show theses that are clear but qualified.

difficulties.pattern: Overbroad theses that cannot be supported within the word limit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Superficial treatment of many points; sweeping generalisations.
difficulties.response: Practise scoping the thesis with qualification and limiting conditions (context, period, population).

diagnostic.task: Give a question and ask for a thesis in one or two sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear, arguable, qualified position that answers the question and is feasible in scope.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A position is present but overbroad or not quite answering the question as set.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic announcement or a statement of fact.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners can start from opinion-based theses and move to source-based ones. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners need theses that answer specific disciplinary questions. PGT writers need theses that take a position within a scholarly debate, and may meet disciplinary preferences for where and how explicitly the thesis is stated.
reviewNotes: Some disciplines and essay types favour a thesis that emerges towards the end; this topic presents an explicit early thesis as a default rather than a rule.

records.summary: Essay introductions typically move from general to specific, a pattern Swales and Feak (2012) describe for many academic texts; research-article introductions (the CARS model) are related but distinct (see res.introductions-cars). Frame markers and roadmaps help readers (Hyland, 2005), but their density should suit the length of the text and the discipline. Teach introductions as something finalised last, and analyse them in authentic student essays rather than textbook formulas.

activities.title: Introduction move analysis
learnerActions: Label the moves in three high-scoring student introductions
Estimate the proportion of words in each move
Draft an introduction for your own essay using similar proportions
activities.intendedInsight: Effective introductions spend little space on background and reach the thesis quickly.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of exemplars builds genre awareness of general–specific organisation (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Opening repair
learnerActions: Collect weak openings (sweeping generalisation, dictionary definition, rhetorical question)
Rewrite each as a specific, relevant opening
Discuss when an opening definition is justified by the question
activities.intendedInsight: A specific opening signals focus from the first sentence.
activities.rationale: Targets formulaic openings that markers frequently criticise and links to work on vague and overgeneralised language.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with sweeping generalisations (‘Nowadays, technology is very important in our lives’) or dictionary definitions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic first sentences that could introduce almost any essay.
difficulties.response: Rewrite openings to name a specific context, debate or problem (see reg.vague-overgeneralised).

difficulties.pattern: Long background that delays the thesis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Introductions taking a fifth or more of the essay; the thesis appears on the second page.
difficulties.response: Word-budget the introduction and move necessary background into the body.

difficulties.pattern: Roadmaps that promise a structure the essay does not follow.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatch between the roadmap and the order of body sections.
difficulties.response: Finalise the introduction after the body is drafted and check the roadmap against the topic sentences.

diagnostic.task: Ask for a 100–150-word introduction to a supplied essay plan.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specific context, efficient narrowing, a clear thesis and a brief roadmap consistent with the plan.
diagnostic.partialResponse: All elements present, but background is too long or the thesis is vague.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Background only, or no thesis.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use a general-to-specific template. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners should compare disciplinary variation: some fields expect definitions of key terms, others discourage roadmaps in short essays. PGT writers often need to justify their chosen focus in the introduction.

records.summary: The conclusion is where the position is stated in full; Wingate (2012) found that students' understanding of argument often stopped at presenting points rather than reaching a judgement. Teach the difference between summary and synthesis and the value of stating implications and limits, and connect conclusions to claim calibration so that they neither overclaim nor retreat into vagueness. Andrews (2010) treats reaching a reasoned conclusion as integral to argument rather than an afterthought.

activities.title: Summary versus synthesis
learnerActions: Compare two conclusions to the same essay
Identify which explains how the points relate to the answer
Rewrite the summary-style conclusion as a synthesis
activities.intendedInsight: Synthesis states what the points show together, not just what they were.
activities.rationale: Makes the argumentative function of the conclusion explicit (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Answer, qualify, extend
learnerActions: Write one sentence that answers the question directly
Write one that qualifies the answer in the light of the evidence
Write one that states an implication or a question for further work
activities.intendedInsight: A short three-move conclusion can be complete and well calibrated.
activities.rationale: Provides a flexible structure that foregrounds judgement and calibration rather than repetition.

difficulties.pattern: ‘In conclusion, there are both advantages and disadvantages.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions with no judgement; the question is never actually answered.
difficulties.response: Require a direct-answer sentence and check it against the thesis.

difficulties.pattern: Introducing new evidence or new arguments in the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: New citations or claims in the final paragraph.
difficulties.response: Check every sentence of the conclusion against the body; move new material into the body or cut it.

difficulties.pattern: Overclaiming (‘This essay has proved that…’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong boosters in the conclusion after limited or mixed evidence.
difficulties.response: Link to claim calibration and ask learners to justify the strength of the final claim.

diagnostic.task: Give a three-paragraph essay body and ask for a conclusion of about 100 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Direct, calibrated answer; synthesis of how the points combine; one implication or limitation; no new evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers the question but summarises points in sequence, or omits limitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the introduction, lists points without an answer, or introduces new material.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on summary versus synthesis and giving a direct answer. In-sessional undergraduates add implications and limitations. PGT writers increasingly use conclusions to position their argument within a wider debate.

records.summary: Hoey (1983) shows how texts are organised through recurring patterns such as problem–solution and general–particular, which offer ordering principles beyond ‘firstly, secondly, thirdly’. Spivey (1990) identifies organising as a central operation in writing from sources, and source-by-source organisation is a default for many learners. Wingate (2012) argues that organisation should be driven by the argument, so teach ordering as a decision justified by the thesis.

activities.title: Re-sort the body
learnerActions: Cut a source-by-source draft into sentence strips
Regroup the strips by theme and write a claim for each group
Order the groups and justify the order in relation to the thesis
activities.intendedInsight: Thematic organisation exposes relationships between sources and supports an argument.
activities.rationale: Physically regrouping material enacts the organising operation of discourse synthesis (Spivey, 1990).

activities.title: Pattern choice
learnerActions: Identify the organising pattern (problem–solution, comparison, cause–effect, concession–rebuttal) in three model essays
Choose a pattern for a new question and justify it
activities.intendedInsight: Different questions call for different organising patterns.
activities.rationale: Text patterns provide principled ordering options (Hoey, 1983).

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source organisation, with one paragraph per author.
difficulties.revealedBy: Body paragraphs that each summarise one reading.
difficulties.response: Use re-sorting tasks and a simple synthesis grid before drafting.

difficulties.pattern: Points appear in the order they occurred to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weak points first and strongest buried; counter-argument placed at the end without a response.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state and justify their ordering principle, and check it with a reverse outline.

diagnostic.task: Give a question and six points with their sources; ask for an ordered outline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Points grouped thematically and ordered by a stated rationale; counter-argument positioned and answered.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Logical order overall, but some grouping by source remains.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Points listed in the order given or grouped by source.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a small set of ordering principles. Pre-sessional learners should practise thematic organisation of sources in extended essays. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners meet disciplinary organising patterns and longer essays divided into sections.

records.summary: Headings are a genre convention: they are standard in reports and related genre families (Gardner & Nesi, 2013) and specified in style guides such as APA (American Psychological Association, 2020), but discouraged in some essay traditions. Teach learners to check local expectations, to write informative rather than generic headings, and to keep the prose coherent without relying on headings.

activities.title: Headings test
learnerActions: Remove the headings from a draft
Read it for coherence and add transitions where needed
Restore informative headings only if they are permitted and helpful
activities.intendedInsight: Headings support coherent prose but do not replace it.
activities.rationale: Prevents headings from substituting for topic sentences and transitions.

activities.title: Generic to informative
learnerActions: Rewrite a set of generic headings as informative headings
Compare with headings in published articles in the learner's field
activities.intendedInsight: Informative headings preview content and argument.
activities.rationale: Style guidance recommends descriptive headings in a consistent hierarchy (American Psychological Association, 2020).

difficulties.pattern: Using report-style headings in essays where the discipline discourages them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Headed essays in modules whose guidance asks for continuous prose.
difficulties.response: Have learners check local guidance or ask the tutor before deciding.

difficulties.pattern: Headings replace topic sentences and transitions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abrupt section openings; the text is hard to follow without its headings.
difficulties.response: Use the headings test and require a linking sentence at the start of each section.

diagnostic.task: Ask whether headings are appropriate for two given assignment briefs and, for one, write headings for a supplied outline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Decision based on brief and discipline; informative headings in a consistent hierarchy.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable decision, but generic headings.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses or omits headings without reference to the brief; headings inconsistent.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners meet headings first in short reports, and should learn early that essays in their target departments may not use them. Pre-sessional learners should meet both headed and unheaded essays. In-sessional undergraduates need disciplinary conventions. PGT essays are often longer and more likely to permit headings, but expectations still vary by department and institution.

records.summary: Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) describe knowledge-telling as writing down what one knows about a topic, which naturally produces breadth; knowledge-transforming involves selecting and reworking content to meet goals. Teach narrowing as a strategic choice, model explicit scope statements, and show how depth is achieved by layering analysis rather than adding points. This supports the argument-centred view of essays advocated by Wingate (2012).

activities.title: Cut to three
learnerActions: List all possible points for a question
Choose the three that best support the thesis
Plan four layers of development for one of them
activities.intendedInsight: Fewer points developed in depth usually make a stronger essay.
activities.rationale: Selecting for a goal is a hallmark of knowledge-transforming rather than knowledge-telling (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987).

activities.title: Scope statement
learnerActions: Write a sentence for the introduction stating what the essay focuses on and why
Write one acknowledging what it will not cover
activities.intendedInsight: An explicit scope shows control rather than omission.
activities.rationale: A justified focus is a visible sign of argumentative control (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘If I leave something out, the marker will think I don't know it.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Long lists of points, each treated superficially.
difficulties.response: Show exemplar feedback that rewards depth, and practise scope statements.

difficulties.pattern: Taking a very broad question literally (all countries, all periods, all theories).
difficulties.revealedBy: Generalised claims with little specific evidence.
difficulties.response: Narrow to cases or contexts and justify the choice in the introduction.

diagnostic.task: Give a broad question and ask for a one-paragraph plan stating focus, rationale and the points to be covered within 1,500 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A defensible narrowed focus with a rationale, three or four points, and an acknowledgement of what is excluded.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some narrowing, but still too many points or no rationale.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attempts to cover the whole question with many points.

records.contextNotes: Some pre-sessional learners face the opposite problem of having too little to say, which calls for work on development rather than narrowing. Undergraduates frequently need help narrowing broad questions. PGT writers need to scope essays in relation to the literature and justify their focus.

records.summary: Moore (2013) found that academics define critical thinking in several distinct ways, so ‘criticality’ should be unpacked in relation to the discipline and task rather than taught as a single generic skill; its teachability and cultural framing have also been questioned in TESOL (Atkinson, 1997). Lancaster (2014) identified stance patterns valued in high-graded upper-level student writing, such as entertaining alternatives and conceding before countering, which give criticality a recognisable linguistic form. Teach criticality by contrasting descriptive and critical versions of the same paragraph and by making the language of evaluation explicit.

activities.title: Describe, analyse, evaluate
learnerActions: Label the sentences of two paragraphs as description, analysis or evaluation
Rewrite the description-heavy paragraph to add analysis and evaluation
Compare with a high-scoring exemplar
activities.intendedInsight: Criticality is visible in specific sentence functions, not a vague quality.
activities.rationale: Operationalises an otherwise opaque criterion and links it to argument (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Concede and counter
learnerActions: Identify concession–counter patterns in an expert or high-graded essay
Write a paragraph that concedes a limitation of your own position and then responds to it
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledging alternatives strengthens rather than weakens a position.
activities.rationale: Such patterns are characteristic of valued student writing in the disciplines (Lancaster, 2014).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Being critical means criticising.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Wholly negative evaluations; strengths of sources never acknowledged.
difficulties.response: Present criticality as balanced, reasoned judgement and model praise–criticism pairs.

difficulties.pattern: Hesitating to evaluate published authors or lecturers, because it is unclear when a student is entitled to judge expert work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Neutral reporting with no evaluation even when the question asks for it.
difficulties.response: Show mitigated evaluative language and annotated exemplars of what markers reward, and make the expectation explicit. This hesitation is common among novice writers of all language backgrounds and is often reinforced by assessments that rewarded accurate reproduction, so do not attribute it to any national or cultural group.

difficulties.pattern: Criticality expressed as unsupported opinion (‘I think this theory is wrong’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations with no reasons or evidence.
difficulties.response: Require a reason and evidence for every evaluative claim, and link to evaluating evidence in reading.

diagnostic.task: Give a descriptive paragraph summarising two studies and ask the learner to make it critical in no more than 80 additional words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Adds evaluation of evidence or method, a comparison of the studies and a judgement tied to the essay's argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds evaluation, but it is generic (‘this study has limitations’) or unconnected to the argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Adds more description, or adds unsupported opinion.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional programmes typically focus on evaluating sources and making a position visible. Undergraduate in-sessional work should address disciplinary forms of criticality, which differ across fields; even within the humanities, Moore (2013) found academics in history, philosophy and cultural studies holding distinct conceptions of critical thinking. PGT writers are expected to engage critically with debates and methods.
reviewNotes: The concept of criticality is contested; this topic adopts a working, discipline-sensitive definition rather than claiming a single construct.

records.summary: Swales and Feak (2012) treat titles as a short but consequential part of academic texts that should signal the focus of the work, and style guides such as APA (American Psychological Association, 2020) specify title format and capitalisation. Teach titles as a revision task—written or confirmed last, checked against the thesis, and compared with titles in the target discipline.

activities.title: Title from thesis
learnerActions: Write three titles for an essay from its thesis: a descriptive title, an argumentative title and a colon title
Ask peers which best predicts the essay's content and position
activities.intendedInsight: A good title predicts the content, and sometimes the argument.
activities.rationale: Links the title to the thesis and to reader expectations (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Disciplinary title survey
learnerActions: Collect ten article titles from a journal in your field
Classify their structures (descriptive, question, colon, statement of finding)
Write a title for your own work in the most common style
activities.intendedInsight: Title conventions vary across fields.
activities.rationale: Small-scale genre analysis of authentic titles develops independent awareness of disciplinary norms.

difficulties.pattern: Using the essay question, the module code or a single word as the title.
difficulties.revealedBy: Titles such as ‘Essay 2’ or ‘Globalisation’.
difficulties.response: Use the title-from-thesis task.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent capitalisation of titles and headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixed sentence case and title case within one document.
difficulties.response: Teach the convention of the required style and check it during proofreading.

diagnostic.task: Give an essay abstract or thesis and ask for a title.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specific, concise title indicating topic and focus (and, where appropriate, position), correctly capitalised.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate topic but no indication of focus, or overlong.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Vague one- or two-word title, or the question copied.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners usually receive set titles. Undergraduate and PGT writers need titles for self-chosen essays, projects and dissertations. At PGR level, titles of articles, theses and conference abstracts affect discoverability and should reflect disciplinary conventions.

records.summary: Sommers (1980) found that student writers mostly revised at word level, whereas experienced writers revised argument and structure; Zamel (1983) reported similar contrasts among ESL writers. In Flower and Hayes's (1981) model, reviewing includes both evaluating and revising and can occur at any point in composing. Teach the three levels explicitly and ask learners to sequence them, because many equate ‘checking’ with grammar correction.

activities.title: Change classification
learnerActions: Compare two drafts of the same text
Classify every change as revision, editing or proofreading
Discuss which changes improved the text most
activities.intendedInsight: The changes that matter most are usually global.
activities.rationale: Draws directly on Sommers's (1980) contrast between student and experienced writers' revisions.

activities.title: Three-pass plan
learnerActions: Plan three passes through your own draft, each with a different focus
Carry out the global pass first and record what changed
activities.intendedInsight: Sequencing saves time and improves quality.
activities.rationale: Separates the reviewing sub-processes described by Flower and Hayes (1981) into manageable tasks.

difficulties.pattern: ‘Revising means correcting the grammar.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Second drafts identical in structure to the first, with surface corrections only.
difficulties.response: Require at least one documented global change per redraft.

difficulties.pattern: Editing sentences that are later cut.
difficulties.revealedBy: Time spent on polished but irrelevant paragraphs.
difficulties.response: Use the three-pass plan and postpone sentence work until structure is settled.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would use two hours to improve a complete first draft due tomorrow.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Allocates time first to argument and structure, then sentences, then surface checks, with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions content and structure but plans to start with grammar.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans only grammar, spelling and formatting checks.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, use the distinction to structure multi-draft tasks. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply it to their own assignments and feedback requests. The distinction is also the basis of institutional proofreading policies (see edt.proofreading-ethics).
reviewNotes: Sommers (1980) studied L1 writers; its application to L2 writers is supported in broad terms by Zamel (1983).

records.summary: Experienced writers revise for argument and with a reader in mind (Sommers, 1980), and the skilled ESL writers in Zamel's (1983) study behaved similarly. Hyland (2003) discusses the place of teacher and peer feedback on content in multi-draft writing classrooms. Teach global revision through structured prompts (thesis check, reverse outline, reader questions), require evidence of structural change between drafts, and give feedback on content before feedback on language.

activities.title: Thesis–body check
learnerActions: Write the thesis and the point of each paragraph on one sheet
Mark where paragraphs do not support the thesis
Decide whether to revise the thesis or the body
activities.intendedInsight: Many drafts argue something different from their stated thesis.
activities.rationale: Targets the gap between intention and text that Sommers (1980) associated with experienced writers' revision.

activities.title: Reader-questions round
learnerActions: A peer reads the draft and notes three places where they could not follow or were not convinced
The writer plans one structural change in response and explains it
activities.intendedInsight: Readers reveal problems that writers cannot see in their own texts.
activities.rationale: Reader response on content is central to multi-draft process teaching (Hyland, 2003).

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to cut or restructure text that took effort to write.
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts that only grow; deleted material reinserted later.
difficulties.response: Keep a ‘cuttings’ file so that nothing feels lost, and show examples of productive large cuts.

difficulties.pattern: Unable to see global problems in one's own text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Self-review notes that list only grammar and vocabulary.
difficulties.response: Provide structured prompts, reverse outlining and peer reading. Do not rely on ‘read it again carefully’.

diagnostic.task: Give a draft with a thesis–body mismatch and a missing counter-argument and ask for a revision plan in bullet points.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies both global problems, prioritises them and proposes specific structural changes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies one global problem but mixes the plan with sentence-level edits.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists language corrections only.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need highly structured revision prompts. Pre-sessional programmes with portfolio assessment can require revision commentaries. PGT writers often revise under severe time pressure and need efficient diagnostic routines. Doctoral writers revise chapters across many drafts in dialogue with supervisors.

records.summary: Reverse outlining applies summarisation to one's own text: reducing each paragraph to its gist uses the deletion, generalisation and construction rules described by Brown and Day (1983). It supports the whole-text revision that Sommers (1980) associated with experienced writers. Introduce the technique on a supplied draft with known problems, then transfer it to learners' own drafts; it scales well to dissertations and theses.

activities.title: Outline someone else's draft
learnerActions: Reverse-outline a supplied draft that has known structural problems
Compare outlines in pairs
Agree on the three most important revisions
activities.intendedInsight: Structural problems become visible in outline form that are hard to see in continuous prose.
activities.rationale: Practising on another writer's text reduces the familiarity that hides problems in one's own (Sommers, 1980).

activities.title: Point and function
learnerActions: Write each paragraph's point and its function (claim, evidence, counter-argument, transition)
Read the sequence of functions and look for missing or misplaced moves
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence of functions can reveal a missing counter-argument or a conclusion that arrives too early.
activities.rationale: Summarising to gist relies on the macrorules that Brown and Day (1983) identified in skilled summarising.

difficulties.pattern: Outline entries describe topics (‘about pollution’) rather than points.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines made of nouns that reveal nothing about the argument.
difficulties.response: Require each entry to be a full-sentence claim.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the outline from memory of the plan rather than from the draft.
difficulties.revealedBy: An outline that matches the plan but not the actual text.
difficulties.response: Outline one paragraph at a time from the text, with the plan put away.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to reverse-outline a five-paragraph draft in ten minutes and name one structural problem.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate point statements; identifies a real structural problem such as a repeated point or misplaced paragraph.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate statements but no problem identified, or a problem identified at sentence level.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Topic labels only, or the outline reproduces the plan.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners can use reverse outlining on extended projects. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT students use it under time pressure before submission. Doctoral researchers can apply it at chapter level, outlining sections as well as paragraphs.
reviewNotes: Reverse outlining is widely recommended in writing-centre practice but has little direct empirical research; the citations support its rationale rather than its tested efficacy.
