records.summary: Hinkel (2004) provides practical techniques for teaching the vocabulary and grammar of academic style to L2 writers, and Biber and Gray (2010) show that academic writing is compressed mainly through phrasal rather than clausal complexity, which explains both what learners aim for and why over-dense text can be hard to read. Swales and Feak (2012) offer graduate-level guidance on flow and style. Teach style editing as a set of purposeful operations with reasons, and avoid prescriptive myths such as ‘the passive is always more objective’ or ‘never use I’.

activities.title: Edit with reasons
learnerActions: Edit a paragraph
Annotate each edit with its purpose (clarity, concision, register, precision)
Compare edits in pairs and resolve differences
activities.intendedInsight: Good edits have reasons; edits without a reason often make text worse.
activities.rationale: Making the purpose of each change explicit reflects the technique-based approach to academic style in Hinkel (2004).

activities.title: Unpack and repack
learnerActions: Unpack an over-dense noun phrase into clauses
Repack a wordy clausal sentence into phrases
Decide which version suits the intended reader
activities.intendedInsight: Information density is a choice to be calibrated to the reader, not a fixed target.
activities.rationale: Builds on the description of phrasal compression in academic prose (Biber & Gray, 2010).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Academic style means long words and long sentences.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Inflated vocabulary; sentences that readers cannot parse on first reading.
difficulties.response: Show concise expert prose and edit for clarity first.

difficulties.pattern: Applying style myths as absolute rules (‘never use I’, ‘always use the passive’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward passives, dangling modifiers, contorted impersonal constructions.
difficulties.response: Check each rule against exemplars or corpus evidence from the learner's discipline.

diagnostic.task: Give a 100-word paragraph with four style problems and ask for an edited version with brief reasons.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All four problems addressed; meaning preserved; reasons accurate; no new problems introduced.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Two or three problems addressed, or edits that are correct but unexplained.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Synonym substitution with no gain in clarity, or meaning changed.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners focus on register and concision. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT writers need disciplinary style conventions. Doctoral researchers edit for publication, where concision and clarity for specialist readers are judged by reviewers and editors.

records.summary: Whether written corrective feedback improves accuracy has been debated (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999). Later work, including Bitchener and Ferris (2012) and Kang and Han's (2015) meta-analysis, suggests that feedback can improve written accuracy, with effects moderated by factors such as proficiency and instructional setting. Ferris has long argued for helping learners become independent self-editors who focus on frequent, rule-governed error patterns. Teach targeted editing passes, use error logs, and pair feedback with opportunities to revise.

activities.title: Error profile
learnerActions: Collect three recently corrected texts
Tally error types
Choose three to target and write a personal editing checklist
activities.intendedInsight: A few recurrent error types account for much of the correction a learner receives.
activities.rationale: Focusing on frequent, rule-governed patterns reflects the selective approach to error treatment discussed by Bitchener and Ferris (2012).

activities.title: One error type, one pass
learnerActions: Edit a draft for one targeted error type only
Record the number of instances found
Repeat with the next error type on the checklist
activities.intendedInsight: Focused passes find more errors than a single general reading.
activities.rationale: Supports the shift from teacher correction to learner self-editing argued for by Ferris (1999).

difficulties.pattern: Reading the whole text once for ‘all errors’ and finding few.
difficulties.revealedBy: Recurrent errors left uncorrected in final versions.
difficulties.response: Replace general rereading with separate targeted passes.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting the teacher to correct every error.
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for full correction; frustration with coded or selective feedback.
difficulties.response: Explain the rationale for selective feedback and self-editing. Do not provide comprehensive correction on every draft, which shifts responsibility away from the learner.

difficulties.pattern: Article errors persist because the learner's first language has no article system or marks definiteness through other means, such as word order or demonstratives.
difficulties.revealedBy: Omitted or overused articles, especially with generic and abstract nouns.
difficulties.response: Target a small number of high-frequency article contexts with rule-of-thumb checks and accept gradual development; do not expect elimination of article errors within a single course.

diagnostic.task: Give a 200-word paragraph containing eight errors of the learner's known types plus four others, and ask for editing in eight minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds most errors of their targeted types and some others, using a systematic approach.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds some targeted errors but works unsystematically.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Finds few errors, or introduces new ones.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need simple checklists and supported practice. Pre-sessional programmes often assess accuracy, so error logs and editing passes fit well into multi-draft cycles. Postgraduate and doctoral writers usually have fewer but more persistent error types and benefit from corpus checking. Automated grammar checkers and AI tools can support targeted passes when the learner decides what to accept (see dig.automated-feedback-tools).
reviewNotes: The written corrective feedback debate remains contested in its details; this topic does not take a position on direct versus indirect feedback.

records.summary: Writers miss surface errors in their own texts partly because they read for meaning they already know; proofreading techniques work by making the text unfamiliar. There is little dedicated research on proofreading techniques for L2 writers, so present them as practical strategies for learners to trial and evaluate. Ferris's work on self-editing (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012) supports teaching learners to monitor their own surface errors rather than relying on correction by others.

activities.title: Technique trial
learnerActions: Proofread one short text silently and another aloud or in a different font and layout
Compare how many planted errors each method found
Choose techniques for the next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Changing how the text looks or sounds reveals errors that silent rereading misses.
activities.rationale: Learners test techniques on their own performance rather than accepting them on authority.

activities.title: Personal proofreading checklist
learnerActions: Combine common surface errors and personal ones from feedback into a checklist
Use it on a final draft and note which items found errors
activities.intendedInsight: A personal checklist makes proofreading faster and more reliable.
activities.rationale: Connects proofreading to self-monitoring of personal error patterns (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Relying entirely on the spell-checker.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correctly spelt wrong words (form/from, their/there, causal/casual).
difficulties.response: Teach a homophone and near-miss check as part of proofreading, alongside the spell-checker rather than instead of it; text-to-speech read-back helps many writers hear errors the eye misses.

difficulties.pattern: Proofreading while drafting rather than at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow drafting combined with errors remaining in the final version.
difficulties.response: Separate stages explicitly and schedule a final proofreading session.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing British and American spelling within one text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent -ise/-ize, -our/-or spellings and dictionary settings.
difficulties.response: Set the word processor's language, choose one variety (or follow the required style) and check consistency as a separate pass.

diagnostic.task: Give a 250-word text with ten planted surface errors and five minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds eight or more, including homophones and consistency errors, using deliberate techniques.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds five to seven, mainly obvious misspellings.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Finds fewer than five or makes new errors.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit technique practice. In-sessional learners need to fit proofreading into tight deadlines. Doctoral researchers proofread long documents, where consistency checks (terms, abbreviations, numbers, references) become more important than isolated errors. For writers with dyslexia or other specific learning differences, which carry across languages, spell-checkers, text-to-speech read-back and screen-reading tools are legitimate core techniques rather than crutches (see dig.assistive-technology), and planted-error tasks should not be timed in ways that penalise slower reading.
reviewNotes: Evidence for specific proofreading techniques is largely practitioner-based; the single citation supports the self-editing rationale, not the techniques themselves.

records.summary: Sadler (1989) argued that learners can only improve if they hold a concept of the standard being aimed for, can compare their own work with it and can act to close the gap, and that exemplars are central to developing that concept. Andrade and Valtcheva (2009) describe rubric-referenced self-assessment as a means of promoting learning, and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) place self-assessment at the centre of good feedback practice. Teach self-assessment repeatedly, with exemplars, and calibrate learners' judgements against tutors'.

activities.title: Criteria to questions
learnerActions: Rewrite each rubric criterion as two or three questions about a text
Apply them to an exemplar and then to your own draft
Mark the evidence in the text for each answer
activities.intendedInsight: Criteria become usable when turned into questions about specific features of the text.
activities.rationale: Reflects the rubric-referenced self-assessment process described by Andrade and Valtcheva (2009).

activities.title: Calibration
learnerActions: Grade two exemplars individually against the criteria
Compare with the tutor's grades and discuss the differences
Self-grade your own draft with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Judgement of quality develops through comparison with expert judgements.
activities.rationale: Builds the concept of the standard that Sadler (1989) identified as a precondition for improvement.

difficulties.pattern: Self-assessment treated as box-ticking (‘yes, I have an introduction’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Every criterion ticked, with no evidence and no identified weakness.
difficulties.response: Require quoted evidence for each judgement and at least one identified weakness.

difficulties.pattern: Systematic over- or under-rating of one's own work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large, consistent gaps between self-assigned and tutor grades.
difficulties.response: Use calibration tasks and discuss evidence rather than grades. Do not use self-assessment grades summatively.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to assess a supplied mid-band essay against a three-criterion rubric, then their own draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Judgements close to the tutor's, supported by quoted evidence, with a prioritised revision plan.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable overall judgement but little evidence, or no prioritisation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uniformly high or low judgements with no evidence.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need simplified criteria and frequent calibration. Pre-sessional programmes can build self-assessment into each draft submission. In-sessional learners should apply the process to their departments' own criteria, which vary considerably between disciplines.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with fbk.self-peer-assessment; this topic applies self-assessment specifically to revising drafts.

records.summary: Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found that L2 students trained to give peer feedback made greater gains in their own writing than those trained only to receive it, particularly on global aspects and among lower-proficiency students. Liu and Hansen (2002) and Min (2006) emphasise training: guided peer review with explicit criteria and modelling produces more useful comments and more revision. Hyland and Hyland (2019) review the social and affective dimensions of peer feedback. Train reviewers, structure the task, and focus early peer review on global issues.

activities.title: Reviewer training with a model draft
learnerActions: Review a model draft individually using a structured guidance sheet
Compare your comments with a tutor's model feedback
Rewrite your comments to make them specific and actionable
activities.intendedInsight: Useful feedback is specific, prioritised and explains why.
activities.rationale: Training reviewers with models and criteria is associated with more useful peer comments (Liu & Hansen, 2002; Min, 2006).

activities.title: Give to get
learnerActions: Review two peers' drafts
Write a note on one thing learned for your own draft
Revise your draft using that insight
activities.intendedInsight: Reviewing others' writing improves one's own.
activities.rationale: Draws on the finding that givers of peer feedback improved their own writing (Lundstrom & Baker, 2009).

difficulties.pattern: Comments limited to grammar and general praise (‘Good essay, some grammar mistakes’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic feedback sheets with no reference to argument or organisation.
difficulties.response: Provide structured guidance focused on global issues and model specific comments.

difficulties.pattern: ‘My classmates' English is no better than mine, so their feedback is useless.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Peer comments ignored in revision.
difficulties.response: Emphasise reader response and the benefits of reviewing, and combine peer feedback with tutor feedback.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding any critical comment to protect relationships.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback consisting only of praise.
difficulties.response: Model mitigated critique (‘One thing that might strengthen this is…’) and make at least one suggestion compulsory.

diagnostic.task: Give a draft with one major global problem and ask for three written comments.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the global problem first, explains its effect on the reader and suggests a change, in a constructive tone.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Specific comments, but focused on local issues.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Generic praise or error lists.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need highly structured peer review and teacher modelling. Pre-sessional programmes can make peer review a regular part of drafting cycles. In-sessional and PGT learners may review across disciplines, focusing on clarity for non-specialist readers. Doctoral writing groups provide sustained peer review and lead into formal reviewing (see pub.peer-review-reports).

records.summary: Harwood, Austin and Macaulay (2009) found wide variation in what proofreaders of student writing at a UK university did, ranging from correcting surface errors to intervening substantially in content, which shows why clear policies and learner awareness matter. Lillis and Curry (2010) describe how ‘literacy brokers’ shape multilingual scholars' publications, making editorial help a normal part of research publication. Teach the local policy, discuss grey areas openly, and avoid implying that seeking legitimate help is itself dishonest.

activities.title: Policy sorting
learnerActions: Read a sample institutional proofreading policy
Classify a list of interventions as permitted or not
Discuss the grey areas and how to resolve them
activities.intendedInsight: Policies draw a line between surface correction and changes to content and argument.
activities.rationale: Variation in proofreaders' practices (Harwood et al., 2009) means learners must know where their own institution draws the line.

activities.title: Briefing a proofreader
learnerActions: Write a short brief specifying which changes a proofreader may make
Plan how changes will be recorded, for example using tracked changes
activities.intendedInsight: Writers are responsible for controlling and documenting the help they receive.
activities.rationale: Transparency about third-party input protects the writer and clarifies authorship.

difficulties.pattern: ‘A friend only improved my English, so it is still my work.’
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner's own account of what the helper changed; tracked changes or earlier drafts showing content-level rewriting. Style differences between supervised and submitted writing are not evidence on their own.
difficulties.response: Discuss where improving language becomes changing content and authorship, using concrete examples.

difficulties.pattern: Fear that any help is cheating, leading learners to avoid legitimate support.
difficulties.revealedBy: Non-use of writing centres and in-sessional tutorials.
difficulties.response: Show permitted routes to support and what each offers.

diagnostic.task: Give three scenarios of third-party help (a friend rewrites a paragraph, a paid proofreader corrects spelling, an AI tool restructures an essay) and ask whether each is permitted under a sample policy.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Classifies each correctly with reasons referring to the content/surface distinction and disclosure.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Classifies correctly but cannot explain the principle.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats all help as acceptable, or all as cheating.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need clear rules, especially where progression depends on assessed writing. In-sessional learners may be offered paid services under pressure. Doctoral researchers need to know thesis regulations on editorial help, which often differ from coursework rules, and norms of professional editing for publication. Policies differ widely: some UK universities publish detailed proofreading policies, whereas many North American writing centres do not proofread at all, and EMI and transnational programmes may follow either the home or the partner institution's rules. Disability-related support, such as specialist study-skills tutoring for dyslexic students, is usually governed by separate arrangements. Rules on AI tools are covered by gai.policies and dig.automated-feedback-tools.
reviewNotes: Institutional policies vary; guidance does not prescribe a single standard.

records.summary: Present scholarly publishing as a social process through which disciplinary communities check, contest and record knowledge, drawing on Swales's account of discourse communities and Hyland's of disciplinary interaction. The aim is calibrated trust: peer review filters but does not guarantee, preprints are valuable but provisional, and fields privilege different outlets. Learners use this understanding when evaluating sources, choosing which version to cite and, later, when publishing themselves.

activities.title: Follow one study through the system
learnerActions: Track a single study from preprint or conference abstract to published article using links on the preprint server and journal site
Note what changed between versions (title, sample, conclusions, strength of claims)
Decide which version to cite in an essay and justify the choice in two sentences
activities.intendedInsight: A study can exist in several versions, and the published version reflects changes made through review.
activities.rationale: Tracing a concrete case makes an abstract process visible and ties it to a practical citing decision.

activities.title: Field comparison of outlets
learnerActions: In discipline groups, list the main outlet types in the field (journals, monographs, conference proceedings, reports)
Ask a subject librarian or lecturer which outlets carry most prestige and why
Present a one-slide comparison to a group from another discipline
activities.intendedInsight: What counts as a high-status publication is discipline-specific.
activities.rationale: Disciplinary variation in genres and knowledge-making is well documented; consulting insiders makes tacit expectations explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Peer reviewed means proven to be true.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that present a single study's finding as established fact with boosters such as 'proves'
difficulties.response: Discuss what reviewers can and cannot check, show published findings that were later contested, and link to the language of claim calibration. Avoid swinging to the cynical view that research is unreliable.

difficulties.pattern: A preprint is the same as a published article.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations to preprint servers with no acknowledgement of their status
difficulties.response: Teach learners to read version labels, to check for a later published version and to signal preprint status when citing; discuss when citing preprints is reasonable, for example in fast-moving fields.

difficulties.pattern: In my previous courses, the set textbook was the only source we were assessed on.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy reliance on textbooks as evidence for current debates
difficulties.response: Value textbooks for consolidated knowledge and definitions, while showing the publication lag and the role of journals for current evidence. Present this as a change of purpose, not a correction of past practice.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'An article you want to use was published last month. A researcher on social media says its results are wrong. What do you do before citing it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions checking for published comments, corrections or replies, considering the critic's expertise, reading the methods, and citing with appropriate hedging or noting the debate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says they would check that the journal is peer reviewed but does not engage with the specific challenge, or simply avoids the article.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes that publication settles the matter, or that the social media comment does.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need the basic system and what peer review means. Undergraduates benefit from disciplinary differences in outlets. Taught postgraduates need versions and preprints, particularly in fast-moving fields; doctoral researchers move to the author's side of the process in pub.publishing-process.

records.summary: Teach classification as reasoning rather than labelling: whether a source is primary, secondary or tertiary depends on the question and discipline, and the distinction between empirical, review and theoretical work can be read from genre signals such as abstracts, methods headings and reference lists. The ACRL frame 'Information Creation as a Process' supplies the rationale: format reflects how information was produced and therefore what it can support. Wallace and Wray's distinction between theoretical, research, practice and policy literature is a useful extension for learners bound for postgraduate study.

activities.title: Source sort with a discipline switch
learnerActions: In pairs, sort ten first pages or screenshots into primary, secondary and tertiary for a history question
Re-sort the same set for a public health question and mark which items changed category
Write one sentence for each changed item explaining why its status depends on the question
activities.intendedInsight: Source type is a relation between a source and a question, not a fixed property of the document.
activities.rationale: Classifying the same set for two purposes directs attention to function rather than format, the central move in the ACRL creation-process frame.

activities.title: Genre-signal hunt
learnerActions: Skim the abstracts and headings of an empirical article, a review and a theoretical paper on the same topic
Highlight the features that reveal each type (a methods heading, a statement that the paper reviews studies, the absence of data)
Use these features to classify three new abstracts and compare decisions with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Text-internal signals show what kind of knowledge a source offers before it is read in full.
activities.rationale: Learners often rely on where a source was found; attention to the text's own features is intended to transfer to unfamiliar sources and support later reading decisions.

difficulties.pattern: If it is on the library website, it must be an academic source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists that include magazine features, trade press or newspaper items found through the discovery layer and used as scholarly evidence
difficulties.response: Show that discovery tools index many document types and have learners filter by type and check the venue. Do not ban non-scholarly sources; ask what each was used to support.

difficulties.pattern: A primary source is the main or most important source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners label a key review article 'primary' or use 'primary' to mean 'central'
difficulties.response: Contrast the everyday and disciplinary senses explicitly, with field-specific examples: a diary in history, an interview dataset in sociology, an original experiment in the sciences.

difficulties.pattern: Theoretical papers have no data, so they are just opinion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conceptual articles dismissed as 'not evidence' or treated as equivalent to blog posts
difficulties.response: Explain that theoretical work supplies the concepts and frameworks that organise evidence, and model citing such sources for definitions and frameworks rather than for findings.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a sociology journal article that includes interview extracts, a systematic review and a newspaper report of one of the reviewed studies. Ask them to classify each and say what each could support in an essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Classifies with reference to the question and discipline, notes that the interview extracts are primary data reported within a secondary article, and assigns suitable uses: the review for an overview of evidence, the news report for public framing of the issue.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Classifies correctly by format but cannot say what each could support, or treats the news report as equivalent evidence to the review.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Classifies by where the item was found or by length and treats all three as interchangeable evidence.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on scholarly versus popular and on reading genre signals in textbooks and journal articles. On undergraduate pre-sessional courses, link source types to what tutors accept in an extended essay; postgraduate pre-sessional learners need the empirical, review and theoretical distinction most. In undergraduate in-sessional work, make disciplinary variation explicit, especially in history, law and the arts, where primary sources have specific meanings (see dhu.primary-sources).

records.summary: Focusing bridges task analysis and searching, and it is iterative: learners propose a focus, run a trial search and adjust scope in response to what they find. The ACRL frame 'Research as Inquiry' supports treating the question as provisional. Concrete narrowing dimensions (context, population, period, variable, perspective) give learners a repeatable procedure, and checking the narrowed question against the original task prevents drift away from what was asked.

activities.title: Narrowing ladder
learnerActions: Write the broad topic at the top of the page
Add one limiting dimension per rung (context, population, period, aspect) to produce three progressively narrower questions
Run a quick trial search on each and note roughly how many relevant results appear
Choose the rung that fits the word limit and explain the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Scope is chosen by balancing answerability, the available literature and the word limit.
activities.rationale: Trial searches give immediate feedback on scope, reflecting the iterative view of inquiry in the ACRL framework.

activities.title: Brief-back check
learnerActions: Exchange focused questions with a partner, together with the original assignment brief
The partner checks whether the focused question still addresses the command words, scope and criteria
Revise the question in response
activities.intendedInsight: A focused question must remain a response to the set task.
activities.rationale: Narrowing can unintentionally change the task; checking against the brief makes this visible before reading begins.

difficulties.pattern: If I narrow it, I will not have enough to write about.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions kept very broad, producing descriptive surveys without analysis
difficulties.response: Show model essays that achieve depth on narrow questions and discuss how narrowing creates room for analysis. Do not force narrowing before the learner knows enough to see the sub-areas.

difficulties.pattern: I chose an interesting angle, but there is nothing published on it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Topics abandoned after one search, or narrowed so far that no literature exists
difficulties.response: Teach broadening moves (relaxing one dimension, using analogous contexts) and require some background reading before the question is fixed.

difficulties.pattern: My question changed the title, but it is more interesting this way.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that answer a different question from the one set
difficulties.response: Return to the brief: underline command words and scope words, and test the focused question against them.

diagnostic.task: Give the topic 'technology in education' and a 2,500-word limit. Ask the learner for a focused question and its search concepts.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a bounded, answerable question (naming, for example, a technology, a learner group and an outcome) with three distinct concepts suitable for search blocks.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Narrows in one dimension only, or lists concepts that overlap heavily.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the broad topic as a question, or produces a question that cannot be answered from literature, such as a personal prediction.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, focusing is usually done within a set title and benefits from the ladder scaffold. In-sessional undergraduates choosing project topics need help balancing interest and feasibility. For taught postgraduates focusing a dissertation, link forward to res.research-questions, where the question also shapes research design.
reviewNotes: Creswell and Creswell address research questions within research design rather than search-oriented narrowing; the citation supports the general principle of bounded, answerable questions only.

records.summary: Searching is a language task as well as a technical one: generating synonyms, spelling variants and broader or narrower terms draws directly on vocabulary depth and disciplinary terminology. Teach the concept-table method, Boolean logic with brackets, truncation and phrase searching, but emphasise iteration, using early results to harvest better terms. The ACRL frame 'Searching as Strategic Exploration' legitimises false starts and refinement rather than a single correct search.

activities.title: Concept table to search string
learnerActions: Split a focused question into two or three concepts in separate columns
Under each concept, list synonyms, related terms and British and American spellings, using a learner dictionary and the abstract of one relevant article
Convert the table into a search string with OR inside brackets and AND between concepts
Run it, add two terms harvested from relevant results, and compare the yield
activities.intendedInsight: Effective searches come from systematic term generation and revision based on results.
activities.rationale: Making term generation explicit addresses the vocabulary demands of searching and the iterative process the ACRL frame describes.

activities.title: Diagnose the failed search
learnerActions: Examine three failed searches: too many results, too few, and mostly irrelevant results
Identify the cause of each (missing synonyms, AND/OR confusion, over-broad truncation, a full-sentence query)
Rewrite and re-run each search
activities.intendedInsight: Search problems have identifiable causes and specific repairs.
activities.rationale: Error analysis makes the logic of operators visible and is intended to transfer to learners' own searching.

difficulties.pattern: I type my whole question into the database, as I do in a web search engine.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long natural-language queries in search histories and very few or irrelevant database results
difficulties.response: Contrast relevance-ranked web search with field-based database search by running both live. Do not say natural language never works: some discovery tools handle it, but learners need to know why many databases do not.

difficulties.pattern: There is only one word for this concept.
difficulties.revealedBy: One term per concept, sometimes a direct translation of an L1 term that is rare in English-language literature
difficulties.response: When an L1 has a single established term, learners may search with its translation equivalent and miss the variants English-language literature uses. Have them harvest terms from abstracts and subject headings of known relevant articles and check candidates in a thesaurus or corpus.

difficulties.pattern: OR gives fewer results because it is more specific.
difficulties.revealedBy: Synonyms joined with AND, producing almost no results
difficulties.response: Use Venn diagrams and live comparisons of result counts for AND and OR.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a search string for the effects of remote working on employee wellbeing, and to predict what happens if they replace OR with AND between synonyms.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces bracketed OR blocks for each concept with variants (for example remote work*, telework*, 'working from home'; wellbeing, well-being, 'mental health'), joins the blocks with AND, and correctly predicts the narrowing effect.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes some synonyms but omits spelling variants or brackets, or cannot predict the operator's effect.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes the question as a sentence or joins all terms with AND.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need keywords and simple Boolean searches in the catalogue. Undergraduate pre-sessional projects are a good point to introduce concept tables; postgraduate pre-sessional learners should build full search strings in a database for their destination discipline. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should apply strategies in their subject databases, including controlled vocabularies where they exist.
reviewNotes: No source in the closed bibliography reports research on L2 learners' generation of search terms; the L1-transfer difficulty is a practitioner observation.

records.summary: Teach tool choice by coverage: what each catalogue, discovery layer, subject database and Google Scholar indexes, and which search features each offers. Hands-on work in learners' own subject databases, ideally co-taught with subject librarians, is likely to transfer better than generic demonstrations. In terms of the ACRL strategic exploration frame, expert searchers match tools to information needs and change tools when results are poor.

activities.title: Same search, three tools
learnerActions: Run the same search string in the library discovery tool, one subject database and Google Scholar
Record result counts, the types and dates of the first ten items, and the features available (filters, subject headings, export)
Write a short recommendation on which tool suits which need
activities.intendedInsight: Tools differ in coverage and functionality, so the choice of tool affects what is found.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison makes coverage differences concrete and supports the tool-choice judgements described in the ACRL frame.

activities.title: Discovery-to-access trail
learnerActions: Locate a known book in the catalogue and note its shelf mark or e-book link
Find a peer-reviewed article in a subject database and reach the full text through the library link, on and off campus
Export both references to a reference manager or document
activities.intendedInsight: Library systems link discovery, access and record-keeping.
activities.rationale: A task chain mirrors real workflows and exposes access barriers early, before assessed work depends on them.

difficulties.pattern: Google Scholar has everything, so I do not need the databases.
difficulties.revealedBy: Searching limited to Google Scholar, with no use of subject headings or filters
difficulties.response: Acknowledge Google Scholar's strengths (breadth, citation links) and show its limitations (opaque ranking, limited filtering, mixed quality). Do not prohibit it.

difficulties.pattern: It is behind a paywall, so I cannot use it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reliance on whatever is freely available, or learners paying publishers for articles
difficulties.response: Demonstrate the library link resolver, off-campus authentication and interlibrary loan live.

difficulties.pattern: The database interface was confusing, so I gave up.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abandoned searches and reliance on one familiar tool
difficulties.response: Co-teach with subject librarians, provide a one-page guide to the main subject database and build short supported practice into class time, returning to concept blocks where the search itself is the problem.

diagnostic.task: Ask which tool the learner would use to find (a) a specific book on a reading list, (b) recent empirical studies in their field and (c) later work citing a key article, and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses the catalogue, a named subject database and a citation-linking tool respectively, with reasons based on coverage and features.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Chooses appropriately for one or two needs but defaults to a single tool for the rest.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses a general web search engine for all three.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the catalogue and discovery tool. Pre-sessional learners should practise in at least one subject database related to their destination degree. Undergraduate and postgraduate learners need discipline databases and citation indexes; doctoral researchers should also use specialist databases and alerting services.

records.summary: Checklists of authority, currency, relevance and purpose are useful prompts, but they can encourage surface judgements based on domain names or design; Wineburg and McGrew's comparison of fact-checkers with students and historians shows the limits of judging a source on its own terms. Teach evaluation as purpose-specific: what is this source being used to support, and is it adequate for that? Bråten and colleagues found that students' trust judgements about sources were associated with their comprehension across multiple texts, which suggests evaluation should be integrated with reading rather than taught as a separate library exercise. Evaluation criteria are not neutral: Canagarajah shows how material and discursive conditions limit the participation of scholars from the periphery in centre journals, so a preference for highly indexed venues can narrow whose knowledge learners meet.

activities.title: Fit for purpose
learnerActions: Receive one source and three essay purposes: illustrating public debate, supporting a causal claim, defining a concept
Decide for each purpose whether the source is adequate, and why
Compare decisions in groups and agree which criteria changed across purposes
activities.intendedInsight: A source is credible for something, not credible in general.
activities.rationale: Holding the source constant while changing the purpose shows evaluation as contextual judgement, as the ACRL authority frame describes.

activities.title: Beyond the checklist
learnerActions: Apply a standard checklist to a well-designed website from an organisation with an undeclared interest and record the verdict
Investigate the organisation laterally for five minutes
Compare the two verdicts and note what the checklist missed
activities.intendedInsight: Surface features can mislead; evidence from outside the source often decides credibility.
activities.rationale: Wineburg and McGrew observed that vertical, within-site reading led students and historians to trust sites that fact-checkers quickly identified as problematic.

difficulties.pattern: Sites ending in .org, or with a reference list, are reliable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluation justifications that cite domain, design or the mere presence of references
difficulties.response: Show counter-examples and teach checking who funds the organisation and whether the references actually support the claims. Do not replace one rule of thumb with another.

difficulties.pattern: If a source agrees with my argument, it is a good source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical use of supportive sources alongside harsh critique of opposing ones
difficulties.response: Ask learners to apply the same criteria to a source they disagree with, and link evaluation to the questioning stance of critical reading.

difficulties.pattern: Our guidance says to use only top-ranked journals, so studies from my region do not count.
difficulties.revealedBy: Relevant regional, local-language or practitioner research excluded without reasons, and reference lists drawn from a narrow set of highly indexed journals
difficulties.response: Review whether module guidance equates indexing or impact with quality, and revise it where it does. With learners, judge each source by its fit and evidence for the purpose, and discuss how indexing and metrics affect visibility (see cit.citation-politics).

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a company press release announcing that a study shows its product improves memory, and the abstract of the underlying study. Ask whether and how each could be used in an essay on cognitive enhancement.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the commercial interest, checks what the study measured and with whom, notes any gap between the abstract and the press release, and limits use accordingly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes the company's interest but uses the press release's figures without checking the study.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses the press release as evidence for the claim without comment.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, focus on scholarly versus non-scholarly sources and purpose-specific use; pre-sessional learners bound for postgraduate study should also judge the evidence base of empirical studies. In-sessional undergraduates should apply module-specific expectations. For taught postgraduates, evaluation increasingly merges with methods critique (rdc.methods-critique). At every stage, ask whose perspectives a reference list includes; cit.citation-politics develops this.
reviewNotes: Review response: R5-14 recommends linking a citation-politics topic to this one. cit.citation-politics belongs to the CIT group, which sets its prerequisites, so no edge is added from this file; the link is made in the mastery evidence and context notes.

records.summary: Wineburg and McGrew found that professional fact-checkers left unfamiliar websites quickly, read across other sources to establish who was behind them, and practised 'click restraint' when choosing search results, whereas historians and students read vertically within the site and were more often misled. Teach lateral reading as a short, habitual routine for unfamiliar web sources, organisations and statistics. It complements, rather than replaces, close reading of a source once its provenance is established.

activities.title: Vertical versus lateral
learnerActions: In pairs, one learner evaluates an unfamiliar site by reading it; the other leaves the site at once and searches for information about its publisher
After five minutes, both report a verdict and the evidence used
Swap roles on a second site and discuss which approach was faster and better informed
activities.intendedInsight: Information about a source from other sources is often more diagnostic than the source itself.
activities.rationale: The task reproduces the contrast between vertical and lateral reading documented by Wineburg and McGrew.

activities.title: Trace the statistic
learnerActions: Take a statistic quoted in a news article or social media post
Follow links and searches to its original source
Record whether the original supports the claim as reported and how it was changed
activities.intendedInsight: Claims change as they travel; checking the origin is part of evaluation.
activities.rationale: Tracing claims upstream is part of the fact-checking repertoire and is intended to build the habit of checking before citing.

difficulties.pattern: We were taught to read a text closely from start to finish before judging it, so leaving the page feels careless.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners spend all the available time reading the site itself before any external check
difficulties.response: Distinguish purposes: close reading is for understanding content; lateral reading establishes whether to trust the source first. Model and time the routine.

difficulties.pattern: I clicked the first result about the organisation, which was its own page.
difficulties.revealedBy: Search histories showing reliance on top-ranked results or on the organisation's own materials
difficulties.response: Teach click restraint: scan the results page, prefer independent coverage and reference works, and check where each result comes from.

difficulties.pattern: We were told never to use Wikipedia, so I cannot look there.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners avoid reference works entirely, even for orientation
difficulties.response: Distinguish using an encyclopaedia to find out about an organisation or topic from citing it as evidence; Wineburg and McGrew report fact-checkers using it in this way.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a link to an unfamiliar organisation's report and five minutes to decide whether to cite it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Leaves the site promptly, establishes the organisation's funding, stance and reputation from independent sources, and decides on use with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Checks the 'About' page and perhaps one external source but bases the decision mainly on the site's self-presentation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges from design, domain or tone without any external check.

records.contextNotes: Lateral reading is accessible from foundation level because searching for an organisation's name is linguistically light. It matters most when learners use web sources, policy reports and media. At postgraduate level, apply it to unfamiliar journals and publishers (see inf.problematic-publishing).
reviewNotes: Wineburg and McGrew's participants were US-based; specific checks (for example which reference sites are useful) may need adapting to other information environments.

records.summary: Learners need a small set of verification habits rather than lists of 'bad journals': verify a venue's claims about indexing, editorial board and review against independent sources, check an article's status for corrections and retractions, and trace widely repeated claims to their origin. Definitions of 'predatory' publishing are contested and no universal list is reliable, so teach indicators and verification rather than blacklists. Fabricated references produced by generative AI tools are a newer route by which non-existent work enters student writing.

activities.title: Venue verification
learnerActions: Read an unsolicited invitation from a journal and visit its website
List the claims it makes about indexing, metrics and peer review
Verify each claim with an independent source, such as the claimed index's own title list
Decide whether to cite from or submit to the journal, giving reasons
activities.intendedInsight: Venue claims must be verified independently, not accepted at face value.
activities.rationale: Applying lateral checks to journals transfers an established evaluation habit to scholarly venues, where indicators are debated.

activities.title: Retraction check
learnerActions: Look up a set of articles, including one known retracted article, in a database and on the publisher's site
Find the retraction or correction notice and summarise what it says
Discuss why the article may still be cited and what a writer should do
activities.intendedInsight: Published work can be withdrawn, so status must be checked before citing.
activities.rationale: Seeing notices in situ makes the concept concrete and is intended to build a routine check.

difficulties.pattern: The journal says it is indexed and has an impact factor, so it is fine.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations to, or planned submissions to, journals whose claims cannot be verified
difficulties.response: Show how to check claims in the indexes themselves and discuss misleading metrics, building on the evaluation routine learners already use for other sources.

difficulties.pattern: Open-access journals are all predatory.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exclusion of reputable open-access sources
difficulties.response: Separate business model from quality: show reputable open-access journals and explain that author charges are not in themselves a warning sign.

difficulties.pattern: The AI tool gave me these references, so they exist.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists containing plausible but non-existent articles
difficulties.response: Require every reference to be located in a library tool before it is cited, and connect to gai.verifying-output. Treat this first as a verification skill to be taught, while being clear about institutional rules.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a plausible-looking reference that has been retracted and a second reference in a journal with doubtful indexing claims. Ask whether they would cite each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds the retraction notice, verifies the indexing claims independently and decides not to cite either as evidence (or cites the retraction itself if discussing it), with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Detects one problem but not the other, or relies on the journal's own website for verification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites both without checking.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional and undergraduate programmes, focus on article status, misinformation and fabricated references. Taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers also need venue verification when citing and, at PGR level, when choosing where to publish (see pub.journal-selection).

records.summary: Chaining puts the ACRL frame 'Scholarship as Conversation' into practice: references point back to the conversation a source joined, and 'cited by' links show how it continued. It is particularly efficient for learners whose keyword searching is limited by vocabulary, because one relevant source leads to others regardless of terminology. Learners should chain selectively, choosing references by how the citing text uses them, and record the links to see the shape of a debate.

activities.title: Read the reference in context
learnerActions: Choose a relevant article and highlight each sentence in its introduction that cites other work
Classify what each citation is used for (key finding, method, contrasting view, background)
Select three references to follow and justify each choice by its use in the text
activities.intendedInsight: How a reference is used in the citing text shows whether it is worth following.
activities.rationale: Selecting by function rather than position in the list makes chaining purposeful and reflects the conversational view of scholarship.

activities.title: Forward from a key study
learnerActions: Find a well-known study in the field in a citation index or Google Scholar
Use 'cited by' to list citing works and filter to the last five years
Skim abstracts and classify whether each supports, extends or challenges the original
activities.intendedInsight: Forward chaining shows how a claim has fared since publication.
activities.rationale: Tracking uptake supports judgements of currency and prepares for synthesising agreement and disagreement.

difficulties.pattern: I followed every reference in the list and drowned.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large, unmanaged collections of loosely relevant sources
difficulties.response: Limit chaining to references used substantively in the citing text and to two generations, applying relevance and authority judgements at each step.

difficulties.pattern: I cannot find the cited item from the reference.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abandoned references, especially in numeric or note-based systems
difficulties.response: Model decoding entries in unfamiliar styles and searching by title in the catalogue.

difficulties.pattern: Older references are out of date and can be ignored.
difficulties.revealedBy: Foundational works rejected because of their date
difficulties.response: Distinguish foundational works that define a field from superseded findings; forward chaining shows whether a work is still cited and how.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner one relevant article and fifteen minutes. Ask for two backward and two forward sources, each with a one-line reason.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects sources from substantive citations, uses a citation index for forward chaining, and gives relevance-based reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds sources but selects arbitrarily or chains only backward.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot locate cited items or does not know that forward chaining is possible.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, chaining from a key reading supplements limited keyword searching. Undergraduates should chain from module reading lists. Taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers should chain systematically and record links, which feeds literature mapping (rdc.literature-mapping) and synthesis.

records.summary: Record-keeping has low status but high consequences: incomplete records lead to unverifiable citations, wasted repeat searching and, when the origin of a note is lost, unattributed borrowing. Teach a minimal search log and the habit of capturing complete bibliographic details and locators at the point of reading, using a reference manager where available. The ACRL strategic exploration frame includes managing searching processes and results.

activities.title: Search log replication
learnerActions: Set up a log with columns for date, tool, search string, filters and results
Log every search during a 30-minute session
Swap logs with a partner, who tries to re-run two searches from the log alone
activities.intendedInsight: A search is reproducible only if it is recorded in enough detail.
activities.rationale: Peer replication gives an immediate, concrete test of record quality.

activities.title: Note-to-source audit
learnerActions: Take five notes made in the previous week
For each, identify the exact source and page or other locator
Repair any note that cannot be traced and agree a recording routine
activities.intendedInsight: Notes that cannot be traced to a source put accurate citation at risk.
activities.rationale: Auditing real notes ties record-keeping to accurate source use rather than presenting it as administration.

difficulties.pattern: I will remember where I read it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations without page numbers or details, and time spent re-finding sources near deadlines
difficulties.response: Let learners experience the cost of re-finding a source, then introduce recording at the point of reading. Do not mandate one tool; prioritise a consistent routine.

difficulties.pattern: The reference manager does it all for me.
difficulties.revealedBy: Imported records with missing or wrong fields used without checking, for example chapters recorded as books
difficulties.response: Show common import errors and build in a check of each record against the source, attending to the fields each source type requires.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show the record of a source used last week and the search that found it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces complete bibliographic details, a locator for the note, and a log entry sufficient to re-run the search.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has bibliographic details but no locator or search record.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify where the information came from.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on recording full references and page numbers. Pre-sessional and undergraduate learners should add search logs for projects. For dissertations and doctoral work, link record-keeping to reference managers (dig.reference-managers) and systematic searching.
reviewNotes: The link between lost source records and unintentional plagiarism is widely asserted in practitioner guidance; no source in the closed bibliography is cited for it here.

records.summary: Access to scholarship is structured by publishing business models and copyright, which the ACRL frame 'Information Has Value' asks learners to understand. Practically, learners need the legitimate routes to paywalled work and the ability to identify which version they have found. Discussion of unauthorised download sites should be factual rather than moralising, acknowledging the inequities of access that many learners have experienced.

activities.title: Legal access challenge
learnerActions: Receive three references to paywalled articles
Obtain each by a legitimate route: library subscription, repository, open-access finder, interlibrary loan or author request
Record the route used and the version found
activities.intendedInsight: Most paywalled work can be obtained legitimately with the right routes.
activities.rationale: Practising the legitimate routes is intended to reduce reliance on unauthorised sources (an untested expectation) and links access to version awareness.

activities.title: Who pays?
learnerActions: Compare how a subscription journal, an open-access journal with author charges, an open-access journal without author charges and a repository are funded
Discuss who can read and who can publish under each model
Relate the discussion to access in learners' home or previous institutions
activities.intendedInsight: Access models distribute costs and opportunities unequally.
activities.rationale: Understanding the value of information is a knowledge practice in the ACRL framework and prepares learners to recognise deceptive venues.

difficulties.pattern: If it is free to read, it must be lower quality.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exclusion of open-access sources
difficulties.response: Show reputable open-access journals and explain that peer review is independent of the access model.

difficulties.pattern: Everyone uses those download sites; there is no other way.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report unauthorised download sites as their default route
difficulties.response: Acknowledge access inequities without judgement: many learners have studied where subscriptions were limited. Demonstrate the legitimate routes now available to them and explain the legal and security risks, and make sure induction shows every learner how off-campus access and interlibrary loan work. Avoid moralising.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain two legitimate ways to obtain a paywalled article and how to tell whether a free PDF is the published version.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names library access, repositories or interlibrary loan, and identifies the version from labelling, layout and comparison with the publisher's landing page.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names one route and is unsure about versions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Knows no legitimate route other than paying.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners need the basic legal routes. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates need version awareness for citing. Doctoral researchers need open-access options and funder requirements for their own publications.

records.summary: Systematic and scoping searches differ from everyday searching in their transparency and reproducibility: a protocol, explicit criteria, full strategies and a record of decisions. Reporting guidelines such as PRISMA 2020 for systematic reviews, and methodological frameworks for scoping studies, set out what must be reported. Teach the procedure with subject librarians, and make clear that many taught dissertations require a documented, structured search rather than a full systematic review.

activities.title: Protocol in miniature
learnerActions: Write a one-page protocol for a dissertation question: question, databases, concept table, search strings, criteria
Run the strategy in one database and record the results
Ask a peer to run it, compare results and revise ambiguous elements
activities.intendedInsight: Reproducibility is tested by someone else running the strategy.
activities.rationale: Peer replication puts into practice the transparency standard that reporting guidelines set.

activities.title: Screening calibration
learnerActions: Two learners independently screen the same twenty abstracts against agreed criteria
Compare decisions and discuss disagreements
Reword the criteria to reduce ambiguity
activities.intendedInsight: Criteria must be explicit enough to be applied consistently by different people.
activities.rationale: Independent screening and calibration are standard review practice and reveal where criteria are underspecified.

difficulties.pattern: Systematic just means I searched thoroughly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dissertations that claim a systematic review without strategies, criteria or a flow of records
difficulties.response: Distinguish systematic, scoping and narrative reviews and what each requires, and help learners choose an accurate label for what they did.

difficulties.pattern: I changed my criteria after reading the papers and did not note it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent inclusion and unexplained exclusions
difficulties.response: Allow principled revision but require every change and its reason to be documented.

difficulties.pattern: Writing such long strings in database syntax is overwhelming.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strategies abandoned or oversimplified
difficulties.response: Build strings incrementally from the concept table with librarian support, testing each block separately.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe how another researcher could reproduce their literature search.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes full strategies per database, dates, criteria, the screening process and records kept, and names the field's reporting guideline.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes databases and keywords but not criteria or screening records.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot describe the search beyond naming one search engine.

records.contextNotes: This topic serves mainly doctoral researchers and taught postgraduates in fields with an evidence-synthesis tradition, and final-year undergraduates in health disciplines. Match expectations to the assignment: many taught dissertations require a structured, documented search rather than a full systematic review. Writing the protocol and the review report, including flow diagrams and synthesis, is taught in res.systematic-review-writing; this topic covers designing, running and recording the search.

records.summary: Treat quotation as a deliberate choice governed by discipline-dependent norms. Hyland's cross-disciplinary analysis found direct quotation concentrated in the humanities and social sciences and very rare in the sciences, so a single rule ('quote sparingly' or 'never quote') misleads some learners. Teach criteria for when wording matters, then precision: exact reproduction, economical selection, correctly marked omissions and insertions, and locators. Pecorari argues that good source use needs explicit, repeated teaching, and quotation is an accessible starting point.

activities.title: Quote or not?
learnerActions: Read six candidate extracts from a source
Decide for each whether to quote, paraphrase or summarise, using criteria (distinctive wording, definition, object of analysis, routine information)
Justify two decisions to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Quotation is warranted when the wording itself matters.
activities.rationale: Explicit criteria are intended to counter both over-quotation and blanket avoidance, and can be tied to disciplinary norms.

activities.title: Trim and mark
learnerActions: Take a long quotation from a sample essay
Shorten it to the essential words using ellipses and square brackets
Check with a partner that the trimmed version has not changed the meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Economical quotation requires exact marking of changes without distorting the source.
activities.rationale: Practising omission and insertion conventions is intended to build accuracy and economy together.

difficulties.pattern: Quoting is safest because then nobody can accuse me of plagiarism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays composed largely of long quotations with little commentary
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the anxiety, then show how over-quotation hides the writer's understanding and voice. Do not ban quotation; agree criteria and a proportion appropriate to the discipline, returning to what each source is meant to do.

difficulties.pattern: I changed a few words inside the quotation to make it fit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotation marks around wording that differs from the source
difficulties.response: Teach that quotation marks guarantee exact wording, and show how to use square brackets or change the surrounding frame instead.

difficulties.pattern: In my previous courses, marks were given for quoting the set authorities.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy quotation in a target discipline where it is unusual, such as engineering
difficulties.response: Compare expert texts from the learner's target discipline and discuss its norms, without implying that previous practice was wrong.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a paragraph that quotes a routine statistic and paraphrases a distinctive definition. Ask whether they would change anything.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Recommends paraphrasing the statistic and quoting the definition, with reasons about whether the wording matters.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises one of the two problems.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no issue, or prefers to quote everything.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on accuracy and the mechanics of short quotations. Pre-sessional learners should practise selection criteria and economy. Undergraduates should calibrate frequency to their discipline: quotation is central in literary studies and law but rare in many sciences.

records.summary: Effective quotation needs a frame before it and commentary after it: the frame names the source and indicates its relevance or stance, and the commentary explains what the quotation shows for the writer's point. Petrić's finding that stronger theses used citations for more than attribution supports teaching the follow-up move explicitly. Grammatical integration of partial quotations is a frequent site of error and benefits from focused practice.

activities.title: Frame and follow-up repair
learnerActions: Identify dropped quotations in a sample essay
Add an introductory frame naming the source and its relevance
Add one or two sentences interpreting each quotation and linking it to the paragraph's claim
activities.intendedInsight: A quotation becomes evidence only when the writer frames and interprets it.
activities.rationale: Explicit attention to the follow-up move targets the tendency for citations to be used for attribution only.

activities.title: Make it fit
learnerActions: Combine given partial quotations with given frames
Read each combined sentence aloud without the quotation marks to check its grammar
Repair errors by changing the frame, not the quoted words
activities.intendedInsight: The writer's frame must adapt to the quotation's grammar.
activities.rationale: Reading without the quotation marks exposes syntactic mismatches that learners otherwise overlook.

difficulties.pattern: The quotation speaks for itself.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end on a quotation with no comment
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write what the quotation shows for their argument; if they cannot, revisit whether a quotation is needed at all.

difficulties.pattern: The author argues that 'the results is consistent with'... (frame and quotation do not fit).
difficulties.revealedBy: Ungrammatical sentences at the join between frame and quotation
difficulties.response: Practise reading the combined sentence without quotation marks and identifying which clause element the quotation must supply. Do not alter the quoted words to repair the sentence.

difficulties.pattern: I always write 'X says that' before a quotation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive frames that give no signal of relevance or stance
difficulties.response: Once basic framing is secure, extend the range of frames and link to reporting verbs; avoid encouraging variation for its own sake.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to integrate a given 25-word quotation into a paragraph supporting a given claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Introduces the source with a relevant frame, quotes only what is needed, integrates it grammatically and adds interpretation tied to the claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Frames and quotes correctly but adds no interpretation, or the interpretation only repeats the quotation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Drops the quotation without a frame or creates a grammatical mismatch.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need the frame–quotation–commentary pattern and grammatical integration. Undergraduates in the humanities need finer integration of short phrases within analytical sentences. For taught postgraduates the emphasis is on interpretive commentary that advances an argument.
reviewNotes: Petrić's study supports the value of citations performing functions beyond attribution; it did not test the frame-and-follow-up technique itself.

records.summary: Research suggests that L2 writers' close dependence on source wording is often developmental and tied to comprehension and available linguistic resources (Pecorari; Shi; Keck), and that learners may experience paraphrasing as a mechanical requirement rather than a way of understanding and using sources (Hirvela and Du). Teach paraphrase as comprehension-driven reformulation: understand the idea, set the source aside, write from memory or notes, then check against the source for meaning, certainty and copied strings. Treat early attempts that stay close to the source as stages to work through with formative feedback, and make local expectations explicit, since academics themselves do not fully agree on where acceptable paraphrase ends.

activities.title: Cover, write, check
learnerActions: Read a short passage until you can explain its point to a partner without looking
Cover the passage and write the idea in your own words for a stated purpose
Uncover it, underline any strings of three or more words shared with the source, and check meaning, scope and hedging
Revise and add a citation
activities.intendedInsight: Paraphrase starts from understanding, not from editing the source sentence.
activities.rationale: Writing without the source in view is widely recommended to reduce reliance on source structure, and the check makes retained wording visible. This is a proposal rather than a tested intervention.

activities.title: Why paraphrase here?
learnerActions: Choose a paraphrase in your own draft
Explain to a partner what the paraphrased idea does for your argument
Rewrite the paraphrase so that it foregrounds the aspect your paragraph will discuss
activities.intendedInsight: Paraphrase serves the writer's purpose and can be shaped to the argument.
activities.rationale: Hirvela and Du found that students who approached paraphrasing as a display requirement did not connect it to their own understanding or argument; linking paraphrase to purpose is intended to address this.

difficulties.pattern: I changed every few words, so it is in my own words now.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that keep the source's sentence structure with synonyms substituted
difficulties.response: Show source and paraphrase side by side with shared strings highlighted, and teach the cover-and-write routine. At early stages, do not treat this as misconduct; give formative feedback and repeated practice.

difficulties.pattern: I cannot paraphrase this sentence; it is too difficult.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that copy or distort the difficult part of a sentence
difficulties.response: Check comprehension first by asking the learner to identify the main clause and explain the idea orally. If comprehension is the problem, more paraphrase practice will not help until the reading difficulty is addressed.

difficulties.pattern: The source said 'may', but I wrote 'shows' because it is clearer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that increase or reduce the source's certainty
difficulties.response: Treat certainty as part of meaning: highlight hedges in the source and require them to be matched in strength.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 60-word passage containing a hedged claim and a technical term. Ask for a paraphrase written with the source covered.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Preserves meaning, certainty and scope; changes structure and vocabulary; keeps the technical term; includes a citation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Preserves meaning but keeps the source structure or several strings, or drops the hedge or the citation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies with minor substitutions, distorts the meaning or omits attribution.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, keep source texts short and accessible and expect close dependence on source wording as part of development. Pre-sessional learners paraphrase under time pressure and in assessed writing and need formative feedback before summative judgement. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates paraphrase disciplinary texts, where keeping technical terms and precise scope is critical.

records.summary: Techniques give learners concrete operations, but taught alone they can encourage the mechanical substitution that produces patchwriting. Keck's taxonomy, which classifies paraphrases by the extent of retained source wording from near copy to substantial revision, offers a shared language for feedback. Teach techniques as tools within a comprehension-first process, with explicit attention to their limits: near-synonyms shift meaning, and technical terms should be kept.

activities.title: One sentence, five ways
learnerActions: Take one source sentence
Rewrite it using a specified operation each time (word-class change, voice change, clause reordering, nominalisation, combining with the next sentence)
Judge which versions preserve the meaning and which read naturally in context
activities.intendedInsight: Each operation changes something different, and not every change preserves meaning or reads well.
activities.rationale: Isolated practice is intended to build the lexicogrammatical repertoire paraphrase requires before it is combined with comprehension-based writing; Keck's categories give a way to judge the result.

activities.title: Synonym trap
learnerActions: Look up suggested synonyms for three words in a source sentence in a learner dictionary or corpus
Test each in the sentence for meaning, strength and collocation
Identify any word that should not be replaced because it is a technical term
activities.intendedInsight: Synonyms are rarely exact, and some words should be kept.
activities.rationale: Making near-synonym differences explicit targets meaning distortion, a typical outcome when substitution is the main strategy.

difficulties.pattern: The thesaurus gives me words with the same meaning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unidiomatic or meaning-changing substitutions
difficulties.response: Teach checking candidates for collocation and register in a learner dictionary or corpus. Do not ban thesauri; show how to verify their suggestions.

difficulties.pattern: Changing it to the passive makes it different enough.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that change voice only and keep the rest of the source sentence
difficulties.response: Show that a single operation leaves the source structure recognisable, and combine operations with writing from understanding.

difficulties.pattern: I do not know the noun form of this verb.
difficulties.revealedBy: Word-form errors in attempted transformations, such as 'the analyse of'
difficulties.response: Provide focused word-family work on high-frequency academic words used in the learners' sources.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a sentence and ask for two different transformations, naming the operation used in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces two accurate transformations using different operations, preserving meaning and keeping technical terms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces transformations with minor word-form or collocation errors, or slight shifts in meaning.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Produces only one-word substitutions or ungrammatical sentences.

records.contextNotes: Techniques are most useful at foundation and early pre-sessional stages, while linguistic resources are developing. By the in-sessional stage, emphasis should move to integrated paraphrase in writing, with techniques revisited to address specific problems.

records.summary: Howard characterised patchwriting as copying from a source while deleting words, altering grammatical structures or substituting synonyms, and argued that it is a transitional strategy used when writers do not yet fully understand a text, so it calls for teaching rather than punishment. Pecorari's study of postgraduate L2 writers found extensive patchwriting without apparent intent to deceive, and Pennycook showed that notions of textual ownership are historically and culturally situated. Present patchwriting to learners as a recognisable stage with strategies for moving beyond it, while being honest that institutional policies may still classify it as plagiarism.

activities.title: Find the patches
learnerActions: Compare a source paragraph with a patchwritten version
Highlight retained strings and parallel structures in matching colours
Place the version on a simple scale (near copy, minimal revision, substantial revision)
Rewrite one sentence as a genuine paraphrase and another as a marked quotation
