activities.intendedInsight: Patchwriting is visible in shared strings and structure, and it can be repaired by paraphrasing or by quoting.
activities.rationale: Side-by-side comparison makes textual dependence visible; the scale adapts Keck's categories of paraphrase.

activities.title: Policy and practice
learnerActions: Read the institution's definition of plagiarism
Decide whether given examples of close paraphrase with citation fall within it
Discuss why Howard and Pecorari argue that patchwriting should be treated developmentally, and what that means for your own drafting
activities.intendedInsight: Patchwriting sits in a contested space between learning strategy and policy breach.
activities.rationale: Discussing the contested status makes expectations explicit and can reduce anxiety without misrepresenting institutional rules.

difficulties.pattern: I cited it, so it cannot be plagiarism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Close copying with a citation and no quotation marks
difficulties.response: Explain that a citation attributes the idea and quotation marks attribute the wording; both are needed when wording is retained. Return to what an acceptable paraphrase changes.

difficulties.pattern: I am afraid anything I write from sources will be called plagiarism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of sources, or excessive quotation
difficulties.response: Frame patchwriting as a normal stage, offer low-stakes practice with formative feedback, and clarify how the institution's definitions apply. Avoid fear-based integrity messages.

difficulties.pattern: At school we memorised model sentences and reused them; that is how I learned to write well.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memorised sentences from sources reproduced without marking
difficulties.response: Acknowledge imitation and memorisation as legitimate learning strategies, and distinguish reusing general academic phrases ('it has been argued that') from reproducing a source's specific wording. Pennycook's discussion of memory and ownership supports a non-judgemental approach.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a cited passage that closely follows its source, and ask whether it is acceptable and how to fix it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies retained strings and structure, explains that a citation alone is insufficient for borrowed wording, and revises into a paraphrase or quotation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices the similarity but cannot explain why it matters or how to fix it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges it acceptable because it is cited.

records.contextNotes: Patchwriting is expected and should be addressed developmentally at foundation and pre-sessional stages. For undergraduates and taught postgraduates, connect it to institutional policy and to similarity reports (int.similarity-reports). Pecorari's participants were postgraduates, so doctoral researchers writing in a second language may still patchwrite, especially in dense theoretical or technical prose.
reviewNotes: The status of patchwriting is contested; institutional definitions differ, and some treat it as plagiarism regardless of intent. Activities are proposals rather than tested interventions.

records.summary: Passage summary builds the main-idea identification and reformulation that whole-text summary and synthesis depend on. Johns and Mayes found that lower-proficiency university ESL students copied more directly and combined fewer idea units, and Keck found that L2 writers used more near copies than L1 writers when paraphrasing in summaries, so the language demand of summarising should not be underestimated. Teach selection first (what to keep), then condensed reformulation, then checking against the source for meaning and borrowed wording.

activities.title: Main idea in ten words
learnerActions: Read a paragraph and underline the words that carry its main idea
Cross out examples, repetition and minor details
Write the main idea in no more than ten words without looking at the paragraph
Expand it into a 25-word attributed summary, keeping any qualification that affects meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Summary starts with deciding what matters, then expressing it in new words.
activities.rationale: Separating selection from reformulation is intended to reduce the load that tends to produce copying, a pattern Johns and Mayes observed in lower-proficiency summarisers.

activities.title: Summary comparison
learnerActions: Read three summaries of the same paragraph: one copied, one distorted, one acceptable
Identify the problems in each
Agree class criteria for a good summary and use them to check your own
activities.intendedInsight: Good summaries are accurate, condensed, reformulated and attributed.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples help learners build criteria for self-assessment.

difficulties.pattern: I copy the topic sentence because it is the main idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that reproduce topic sentences verbatim
difficulties.response: Credit the correct identification, then require reformulation from memory. At foundation level, give formative feedback rather than penalising heavily.

difficulties.pattern: Everything in the paragraph seems important.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries nearly as long as the source, including examples
difficulties.response: Practise separating main ideas from support through paragraph-structure analysis before summarising.

difficulties.pattern: I forgot to say whose ideas they were.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed summaries in essays
difficulties.response: Require a signal phrase or citation in every practice summary until it becomes automatic.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 120-word paragraph and ask for a one-sentence summary written without looking back.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Captures the main idea and any key qualification in own words, with attribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures the main idea but copies phrases or omits attribution.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises a detail or example rather than the main idea, or copies a sentence.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, use short, accessible paragraphs and textbook extracts. On pre-sessional courses, practise summary within note-making and integrated tasks. For undergraduates, passage summary feeds whole-text summary and synthesis.

records.summary: Brown and Day's macrorules (deletion, superordination, selection and invention of topic statements) and Kintsch and van Dijk's model of macrostructure describe what expert summarisers do: they build a representation of the text's gist rather than shortening each paragraph in turn. Brown and Day also found that the most demanding rule, inventing a topic statement, develops late. Teach learners to identify the text's purpose and structure first, then apply macrorules section by section, and to represent the author's moves with reporting language.

activities.title: Macrorules walkthrough
learnerActions: Preview the title, abstract, headings and conclusion to identify the text's purpose and structure
For each section, delete trivial and repeated material, replace lists with superordinate terms and write one gist statement
Combine the gist statements into a summary, adjusting proportions to the text's emphasis
Add reporting verbs that show the author's moves
activities.intendedInsight: Whole-text summary is built from the text's macrostructure, not its paragraph sequence.
activities.rationale: The procedure operationalises Brown and Day's macrorules and Kintsch and van Dijk's account of macrostructure.

activities.title: Purpose-shaped summaries
learnerActions: Write a 50-word summary of an article for an annotated bibliography
Write a 100-word summary of the same article for an essay's background section, focused on one aspect
Compare what was included in each and why
activities.intendedInsight: Summaries are shaped by purpose and length.
activities.rationale: Varying the purpose shows summary as a selective, rhetorical act rather than neutral reduction.

difficulties.pattern: I summarise each paragraph in order, one sentence each.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that follow the source's paragraph order and give equal weight to minor sections
difficulties.response: Teach previewing and identification of the text's macrostructure before summarising, with a gist template (purpose, method or approach, main findings or argument, conclusion).

difficulties.pattern: I added my opinion to show I understood it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluative comments mixed into summaries without marking
difficulties.response: Clarify that a summary represents the author's view and that evaluation belongs in a separate, signalled section unless the task combines them.

difficulties.pattern: The author says… then the author says…
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated 'says' that misrepresents the author's moves
difficulties.response: Once macrostructure is secure, introduce reporting verbs for specific moves (argues, reports, proposes, concludes).

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 1,200-word article and twenty minutes to write a 120-word summary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Represents purpose, main argument or findings and conclusion proportionately, uses accurate reporting verbs, and keeps unmarked opinion out.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers the main points but follows paragraph order, over-represents detail or borrows phrasing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises only the introduction, lists details, or misrepresents the main claim.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners summarise textbook sections and short articles, and undergraduate pre-sessional learners summarise articles for extended writing. Postgraduate pre-sessional learners and taught postgraduates must summarise research articles quickly and accurately for literature reviews and critiques (ges.critique).
reviewNotes: Brown and Day's participants were L1 English-speaking school and college students; their developmental findings are applied to L2 academic summary by analogy.

records.summary: Hunston's distinction between averral and attribution explains why readers need signals: each proposition is either the writer's own or attributed to someone else, and readers rely on linguistic signals to tell which. Thompson and Ye classified reporting verbs by the kind of act reported and by the evaluation they convey, and Hyland documented disciplinary differences in reporting-verb preferences. Teach a small set of grammatically secure signal phrases and continued attribution first, then verbs in functional groups with their evaluative force, using examples from learners' own disciplines; Pecorari argues that good source use of this kind needs explicit teaching rather than being assumed. Emphasise precision over variety: the aim is to represent accurately what the source did and how far the writer accepts it.

activities.title: Whose idea is it?
learnerActions: Read a summary paragraph in which only the first sentence is attributed
Mark each sentence as 'source' or 'writer' and compare with a partner
Revise using continued attribution ('The authors further argue…', 'According to the same study…')
activities.intendedInsight: Attribution must be maintained across sentences, not only at the start.
activities.rationale: The task turns the averral–attribution distinction into a practical reading and writing problem.

activities.title: Stance continuum
learnerActions: Place given reporting verbs on a line from 'writer accepts the claim' to 'writer distances themselves' (demonstrate, show, suggest, claim, allege)
Discuss borderline cases with a partner
Report the same study three times to signal acceptance, neutrality and distance
activities.intendedInsight: Reporting verbs carry the writer's stance towards the reported claim.
activities.rationale: The task draws on Thompson and Ye's distinction between factive, non-factive and counter-factive evaluation.

activities.title: Frame and verb profile
learnerActions: Collect signal phrases and reporting verbs from three articles in your field
Sort them by grammatical pattern (according to + noun; X + verb + that-clause; as + X + verb) and by the act reported (research, cognition, discourse)
Write one sentence with each pattern about a source you are using
Compare your profile with a peer from another discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Signal phrases follow a few learnable patterns, and disciplines prefer different reporting verbs.
activities.rationale: Hyland found clear disciplinary differences in reporting-verb choice, and learner-collected examples make these visible in the learner's own field. Learning frames as patterns is intended to reduce blended frames (a practitioner proposal); Pecorari (2013) supports explicit teaching of source use, not this specific effect.

difficulties.pattern: According to Smith, he argues that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Double attribution and blended frames
difficulties.response: Contrast the two patterns and practise transforming one into the other. Treat the blend as a stage in learning the patterns, not as carelessness, and do not respond by banning one of the frames.

difficulties.pattern: After I cite once, the reader knows the rest is from the source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unclear attribution in later sentences of summaries
difficulties.response: Show that readers tend to assume unattributed sentences are the writer's own, and practise continuation devices.

difficulties.pattern: I should never repeat a reporting verb, so I use claim, state and argue in turn.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strained variation that produces inaccurate verbs or unintended stance, such as 'Smith confesses that' or 'claims' for a finding the writer accepts
difficulties.response: Explain that accuracy matters more than variety, show expert texts that repeat neutral verbs, and contrast verb pairs in context, asking what each implies about the writer's view. Avoid handing out long undifferentiated verb lists.

difficulties.pattern: The author discusses about the problem and emphasises on its causes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Prepositions added to transitive reporting verbs
difficulties.response: Learners often extend the pattern of a related noun ('a discussion about', 'an emphasis on') to the verb. Teach verbs with their complementation from corpus or dictionary examples and practise noun–verb pairs side by side.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three sentences reporting one study's finding so that a reader can tell all three come from the source, then to change one verb to show that they doubt the finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses an accurate initial frame and continuation devices, and switches to a distancing verb (such as 'claims') with correct complementation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Attributes only the first sentence, uses a blended frame, or changes the verb without a real change of stance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives no attribution or only an end citation, and uses 'says' throughout.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners should automate a small set of signal phrases, continued attribution and neutral verbs. Pre-sessional learners, especially those heading for postgraduate study, add stance contrasts. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates profile their discipline's verbs, and doctoral researchers need fine control of stance when positioning their own work. Tense choice with reporting verbs is treated in grm.tense-in-reporting, once verb and frame choice are secure.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-37 asked for the grammar topics to be linked as hard prerequisites. grm.reporting-structures is now a hard prerequisite, but grm.tense-in-reporting is not linked: it starts at B2, above this topic's B1+ start, and it already depends on src.citation-forms, which depends on this topic, so the edge would invert the CEFR order and create a cycle.

records.summary: Swales distinguished integral citations, in which the cited author is part of the sentence, from non-integral ones, and Thompson and Tribble refined these categories using a corpus of theses. Hyland showed that disciplines differ in their balance of forms, with non-integral forms more frequent in the sciences. Teach the forms as rhetorical choices about emphasis, the person or the information, rather than as formatting alternatives.

activities.title: Form spotting and effect
learnerActions: Highlight integral and non-integral citations in two expert paragraphs from different disciplines
Count each type and compare the proportions
Rewrite two citations in the other form and discuss what changed in emphasis
activities.intendedInsight: Citation form changes what the reader notices: the author or the information.
activities.rationale: Comparing disciplines and testing rewrites draws on Hyland's and Thompson and Tribble's analyses of citation form.

activities.title: Revise for emphasis
learnerActions: Revise a paragraph in which every citation is integral
Make established points information-prominent and group supporting sources in a single bracket
Keep author-prominent forms only where a specific scholar's position matters
activities.intendedInsight: Varying citation form helps a paragraph focus on ideas and reserves author prominence for positions.
activities.rationale: Paragraphs built entirely from integral citations tend to read as lists of authors rather than as an account of what is known.

difficulties.pattern: I was taught to begin each sentence about a source with the author's name.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that read 'X (2019) says… Y (2020) says…'
difficulties.response: Show how information-prominent citation foregrounds ideas and supports synthesis. Do not ban integral forms; the aim is choice.

difficulties.pattern: Putting the name in brackets makes the source look less important.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of non-integral forms
difficulties.response: Explain the difference in emphasis and show science writing in which non-integral forms dominate, including for highly cited work.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner one finding supported by three sources and one contested position held by one scholar. Ask for two sentences citing them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses a non-integral citation grouping the three sources for the finding and an integral citation for the contested position, and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses appropriate forms but cannot explain the choice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites each source separately with integral forms in a list.

records.contextNotes: Introduce this on pre-sessional courses once basic in-text citation is secure. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should analyse the balance of forms in their discipline. Doctoral researchers use citation form strategically in literature reviews and discussion sections.
reviewNotes: The claim that novice paragraphs built from integral citations read as lists of authors is a practitioner observation; no source in the closed bibliography is cited for it.

records.summary: Pecorari's linguistic analysis of source use emphasises transparency: readers should be able to tell what comes from a source and what from the writer. Hunston's averral–attribution distinction and Chang and Schleppegrell's work on making stance resources explicit for L2 writers point to teaching the specific language that marks boundaries: continued attribution, citation placement, evaluative commentary and averral markers. The aim is both integrity and a visible authorial voice.

activities.title: Colour the voices
learnerActions: Highlight source content in one colour per source and the writer's own comment in another
Identify sentences that could belong to either
Revise those sentences with attribution or averral markers so that their status is clear
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need linguistic signals to tell source content from the writer's voice.
activities.rationale: Making voices visible applies the averral–attribution distinction and supports transparent source use.

activities.title: Add your voice
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that reports two sources and contains no comment
Add one sentence that evaluates, compares or applies the sources to the paragraph's point
Check with a partner that the new sentence is clearly the writer's
activities.intendedInsight: A paragraph built from sources still needs the writer's own contribution.
activities.rationale: Chang and Schleppegrell argue that L2 writers benefit from explicit teaching of the linguistic resources for taking an authorial stance.

difficulties.pattern: My previous teachers accepted one citation at the end of each paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Single end-of-paragraph citations covering mixed content
difficulties.response: Show that an end-placed citation leaves the reader unsure what it covers, and teach citation placement and continued attribution.

difficulties.pattern: I was taught that academic writing should not contain my own opinion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs consisting entirely of reported content
difficulties.response: Show expert texts in which writers evaluate and connect sources, and distinguish argued evaluation from unsupported personal opinion, without implying the learner's previous context was wrong.

difficulties.pattern: Once I paraphrase it, it becomes my idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrased content presented as the writer's own claim
difficulties.response: Clarify that paraphrase changes the wording, not the ownership of the idea.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to highlight which sentences in a 150-word paragraph from their own draft are attributed and which are their own.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Highlights accurately, and the text itself makes each sentence's status clear to a reader.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Highlights accurately, but some sentences are ambiguous in the text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish their own claims from source content.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need basic continued attribution. Pre-sessional writing assessment often rewards a visible writer's voice, so make this expectation explicit. For undergraduates and taught postgraduates, boundaries become harder to manage in multi-source paragraphs (see syn.synthesis-paragraphs).

records.summary: Style guides permit secondary citation but discourage it where the original can be obtained, because secondary accounts may simplify or distort the original. Teach both the decision and the format: attempt to trace the original through backward chaining, and use secondary citation transparently when the original is unavailable. Learners also need to know which work appears in the reference list in their required style.

activities.title: Trace the classic
learnerActions: Find a classic study reported in a textbook
Try to locate the original from the textbook's reference using the library catalogue
Compare the textbook's account with the original and note any differences
Decide whether to cite the original or use a secondary citation
activities.intendedInsight: Secondary accounts can differ from originals, so tracing the original is worth the effort.
activities.rationale: Comparing accounts shows concretely why style guides prefer citing what was read.

activities.title: Format practice
learnerActions: Write the in-text citation and reference-list entry for a secondary citation in your required style
Check them against the style guide
Explain to a partner which work is listed and why
activities.intendedInsight: Secondary citation has specific format rules that differ between styles.
activities.rationale: Checking against the guide is intended to prevent common errors such as listing the unread original.

difficulties.pattern: I list the original because it looks better.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists including works the writer has not read
difficulties.response: Explain that citing and listing the original implies having read it, which misrepresents the writer's research.

difficulties.pattern: Everything I read is in the textbook, so I use 'cited in' for everything.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large numbers of secondary citations in an essay
difficulties.response: Teach backward chaining and set the expectation that key sources are read in the original.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You read about a well-known theory in a textbook by Smith. How do you cite it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Tries to find the original first; if using Smith, cites the theory as a secondary source and, in APA style, lists only Smith.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Formats correctly but does not mention finding the original.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites the theorist directly without having read the original.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners who rely on textbooks need this early. Pre-sessional and undergraduate learners should practise chaining to originals. Taught postgraduates should seldom need secondary citation except for unobtainable or inaccessible-language originals.
reviewNotes: Conventions differ between referencing styles; apa2020 is cited for the APA approach only.

records.summary: Multilingual learners often have access to relevant scholarship in other languages, and Lillis and Curry show how English-medium publishing privileges some knowledge over other knowledge. Using such sources well requires transparency: translations are marked as the writer's own, the original work is cited, and reference entries follow the style's rules for non-English works. Teach this as a legitimate practice, and encourage learners to check local expectations, since some modules specify English-language sources.

activities.title: Translate and signal
learnerActions: Choose a short passage from a source in another language you read
Write an English quotation of it marked as your own translation, and a separate paraphrase with citation
Write the reference-list entry following your style guide
Ask a peer who shares the language to check the accuracy of the translation
activities.intendedInsight: Non-English sources can be used openly when translation is marked and the original is cited.
activities.rationale: The task practises style-guide conventions and accuracy while treating the plurilingual repertoire as a resource.

activities.title: What does English-only miss?
learnerActions: Discuss whether research on your topic exists in other languages
Consider what perspectives it adds, for example on local contexts
Plan how to raise its use with your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Non-English scholarship can add perspectives, and its use should be discussed openly.
activities.rationale: Lillis and Curry document inequalities in English-medium publishing; reflecting on them is intended to support informed choices of sources.

difficulties.pattern: I translated it myself, so it is my own writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmarked translated passages
difficulties.response: Explain that translation changes the language but not the ownership of the ideas; quotation and paraphrase rules still apply.

difficulties.pattern: Machine translation is fine for quotations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inaccurate translated quotations
difficulties.response: Show how to check machine translation against the original and how to declare tool use where policy requires it (see dig.machine-translation). Refer to the local policy rather than banning tools outright.

difficulties.pattern: My tutor will not accept sources in my language.
difficulties.revealedBy: Relevant non-English sources avoided without asking
difficulties.response: Encourage the learner to ask and to explain the source's relevance, presenting their languages as an asset to the work.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show how they would quote and reference a sentence from a source in another language.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Quotes in English marked as their own translation (giving the original if required), cites the original work, and formats the reference with a translated title.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Translates and cites, but does not mark the translation or formats the reference incorrectly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Presents the translated wording as their own without citation.

records.contextNotes: This matters wherever learners write about their own contexts, from pre-sessional projects onward. At PGR level, non-English sources may be central to the research, and conventions for presenting originals alongside translations vary by discipline.
reviewNotes: Conventions for presenting original-language text alongside translations vary by discipline and style; local guidance should be checked.

Review response: R5-02 notes that this topic is a dead-end leaf. Its natural dependants (cit.citation-politics, pub.multilingual-scholars) belong to other groups, which can add edges from this topic; no topic in this file depends on it without forcing the sequence.

records.summary: Spivey describes discourse synthesis as a constructive process in which writers select, organise and connect content from several texts to build a new structure. Feak and Swales show the same contrast at the level of the literature review, where organisation by theme rather than by author is the expected norm. Teaching the concept through contrasting examples (serial summary versus synthesis) gives learners a clear target before they learn the tools and language of synthesis.

activities.title: Two paragraphs, same sources
learnerActions: Read two paragraphs that use the same three sources, one organised source by source and one around a point
Mark the topic sentence and each source's role in both
Discuss which better answers a given question and why
activities.intendedInsight: Synthesis is organised by the writer's idea, not by the sources.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples make the difference between reproducing and transforming source organisation concrete, reflecting Spivey's account of organising and connecting.

activities.title: Find the meeting point
learnerActions: Read three short texts on one topic
Write down one point on which all three can be brought together
Note what each text contributes to that point, including where it differs
activities.intendedInsight: Synthesis starts from a point that connects sources.
activities.rationale: Generating a connecting point is the first constructive move in discourse synthesis.

difficulties.pattern: Synthesis means summarising all the sources in one paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs with several citations that summarise each source in turn
difficulties.response: Use paired examples and ask learners to identify the controlling point; if there is none, the paragraph is a sequence of summaries.

difficulties.pattern: Synthesis means giving my opinion and adding citations at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs whose organising claim does not come from the sources, with citations attached that do not support the role given to them
difficulties.response: Show that the organising point must be accountable to what the sources say: ask learners to state, for each source, what it contributes to the point and to check that it does. Return to the functions sources perform for the writer.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in their own words and with an example from their reading, the difference between a summary and a synthesis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that synthesis organises several sources around the writer's point and shows how they relate, with a concrete example.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says synthesis uses several sources but does not mention organisation or relationships.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates synthesis with summary or with using many citations.

records.contextNotes: Introduce synthesis at foundation level with two or three short texts. Undergraduate pre-sessional extended essays require it explicitly; postgraduate pre-sessional learners meet it mainly through synthesis paragraphs and relating sources. It underpins literature review assignments for undergraduates and taught postgraduates.

records.summary: A synthesis matrix externalises the organising and connecting work that Spivey identifies in discourse synthesis: it shows each source's position on each theme and lets learners read across sources. Teacher-set columns provide scaffolding at first; independent generation of columns develops alongside thematic grouping. The matrix is a planning tool rather than an end product, so learners should be shown explicitly how columns become paragraphs.

activities.title: Guided matrix
learnerActions: Receive a matrix with teacher-set columns (for example definition, causes, evidence, limitations)
Fill each cell with brief own-words notes and locators from three sources
Read down each column and write one sentence about agreement or difference
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a matrix by column reveals relationships that reading source by source hides.
activities.rationale: Set columns reduce the organising load so that learners can concentrate on selecting and comparing content.

activities.title: From matrix to plan
learnerActions: Use a completed matrix to choose two columns that answer the question
Turn each column into a paragraph plan with a topic sentence and the sources that support or qualify it
Compare the plan with an author-by-author plan for the same sources
activities.intendedInsight: Matrix columns map onto synthesis paragraphs.
activities.rationale: Making the matrix-to-paragraph link explicit is intended to stop the matrix becoming an isolated note-making exercise and reflects the thematic organisation Feak and Swales recommend for reviews.

difficulties.pattern: I copied sentences into the cells to save time.
difficulties.revealedBy: Matrices filled with source wording that later reappears in essays
difficulties.response: Require brief own-words notes in cells, with any copied wording in quotation marks and a locator.

difficulties.pattern: I made the matrix but still wrote about each source in turn.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays organised by matrix row rather than column
difficulties.response: Model writing from a column and have learners plan paragraphs from columns before drafting.

difficulties.pattern: A matrix is too much work for a short essay.
difficulties.revealedBy: Matrices abandoned or not attempted
difficulties.response: Scale the matrix to the task: a three-by-three grid may be enough for a short essay.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to build a matrix from three given abstracts for a given question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses question-relevant columns, writes concise own-words notes and identifies a cross-source pattern.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Builds a matrix with generic columns or copied content.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes a separate summary for each source instead of a grid.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and early pre-sessional stages, provide the columns. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should generate their own and may use spreadsheets or reference-manager tags. Doctoral researchers often maintain large matrices or literature databases throughout the project.
reviewNotes: No source in the closed bibliography evaluates synthesis matrices directly; the matrix is presented as a practitioner tool consistent with research on discourse synthesis.

records.summary: Thematic grouping is the analytical core of literature reviews: Kwan's analysis of doctoral literature reviews found them organised into thematic units, and Feak and Swales present thematic organisation as an alternative to chronological or author-by-author structures. Learners need explicit criteria for grouping (by factor, position, method or finding) and should test alternative groupings before choosing the one that best serves their argument. Classification skills from rhetorical-function work transfer directly.

activities.title: Card sort and re-sort
learnerActions: Write each source's key point on a card
Sort the cards into groups and name each group
Re-sort using a different criterion and decide which grouping better serves the question
activities.intendedInsight: Themes are constructed by the writer, and different groupings suit different arguments.
activities.rationale: Physical sorting makes classification criteria visible and is intended to encourage testing alternatives before committing to a structure.

activities.title: Reverse-engineer a review
learnerActions: Read a short published literature review
Identify its themes and the sources under each
Note sources that appear under more than one theme and discuss why
activities.intendedInsight: Expert reviews organise sources by theme, and a source can contribute to several themes.
activities.rationale: Analysing expert reviews reflects genre-analytic studies of the literature review such as Kwan's.

difficulties.pattern: Each source is its own theme.
difficulties.revealedBy: Theme labels that are author names or study titles
difficulties.response: Ask what issue each source addresses, and group by those issues; a matrix with question-based columns can make shared issues visible.

difficulties.pattern: My themes are 'advantages' and 'disadvantages', as in my previous essays.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic template headings unconnected to what the literature discusses
difficulties.response: Show how themes emerge from what sources discuss and relate to the question. Do not reject simple structures where they suit the task; make the classification criterion explicit.

difficulties.pattern: A source can only go in one group.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources forced into a single group, with relevant content lost
difficulties.response: Show expert reviews in which one study is cited under several themes for different aspects.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner six source summaries and ask for a thematic grouping with a justification.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces coherent, question-related themes, allocates sources (some to several themes) and justifies the criterion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces plausible groups but with vague labels or single-source themes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Groups by author, date or source type only.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, thematic grouping is practised with small source sets for extended essays. Undergraduates need it for literature review assignments. For taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers it organises dissertation and thesis literature reviews (res.literature-review).

records.summary: Spivey's connecting operation and Petrić's finding that higher-rated theses used citations for comparison and linking more than lower-rated ones point to the same teaching target: explicit statements of how sources relate. Teach a small set of relationship types (agree, corroborate, extend, qualify, contrast, contradict) with matching language, and require learners to check whether apparent disagreement reflects differences in definition, method or context. This is where reading across texts becomes writing across texts.

activities.title: Relationship labelling
learnerActions: Read pairs of short abstracts
Label each pair's relationship (agree, extend, qualify, contrast, contradict)
Check whether any disagreement is explained by method, sample or definition
Write one sentence expressing each relationship precisely
activities.intendedInsight: Precise relationship labels lead to precise relational language.
activities.rationale: Labelling before writing focuses attention on the connecting operation in discourse synthesis.

activities.title: Upgrade the list
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that cites sources in sequence with 'also' and 'another study'
Rewrite it with explicit relational language and grouped citations
Compare the two versions for what the reader learns
activities.intendedInsight: Explicit relationships turn a list of studies into synthesis.
activities.rationale: Petrić found that higher-rated writing used citations to compare and link, not only to attribute.

difficulties.pattern: Also, another study, furthermore: that shows they are connected.
difficulties.revealedBy: Additive connectors used where the relationship is contrast or qualification
difficulties.response: Require learners to name the relationship before choosing a connector or verb.

difficulties.pattern: The two studies disagree, so one must be wrong.
difficulties.revealedBy: Binary judgements of conflicting findings
difficulties.response: Show how differences in context, sample or measure can explain divergent findings, and practise reading the studies side by side before writing.

difficulties.pattern: I do not know how to say that one study extends another.
difficulties.revealedBy: A narrow range of relational verbs, often only 'says'
difficulties.response: Teach a small set of relational reporting verbs (confirm, extend, challenge, qualify) in context.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner two abstracts with partly conflicting findings and ask for a two-sentence synthesis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the relationship precisely, suggests a reason for the difference and uses accurate relational language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes that the studies differ but does not specify how or why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises each study separately.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners practise with two or three sources. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates need the full range of relationships for essays and reviews; doctoral researchers must represent complex debates fairly and precisely.

records.summary: Swales's CARS model identifies counter-claiming, indicating a gap, raising a question and continuing a tradition as ways of establishing a niche, and Kwan found related moves in doctoral literature reviews; Feak and Swales show how reviews build towards such positions. Teach gaps as outcomes of synthesis rather than as formulae: learners should be able to point to the sources and relationships that reveal a gap, and hedge claims about the absence of research in proportion to the search actually done. Identifying significant gaps develops into expert performance, so expectations should rise across stages.

activities.title: Gap with evidence
learnerActions: Use a completed synthesis matrix to find empty cells, conflicting findings and repeated limitations
For each, write a sentence identifying the gap or tension
Annotate each sentence with the matrix evidence that supports it
activities.intendedInsight: Gaps must be grounded in evidence from the literature reviewed.
activities.rationale: Linking each claimed gap to matrix evidence is intended to discourage unsupported claims that no research exists.

activities.title: Niche moves in published introductions
learnerActions: Read three research article introductions from your field
Identify how each establishes a niche (gap, counter-claim, question, continuation)
Write a niche statement for your own topic using the most suitable type
activities.intendedInsight: There are several ways to establish a niche, and fields prefer different ones.
activities.rationale: The task applies Swales's analysis of niche establishment, which learners can test against their discipline.

difficulties.pattern: No one has ever studied this.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged absolute gap claims based on a few searches
difficulties.response: Teach hedged formulations and check the claim against a wider map of the field; discuss how expert readers react to overclaiming.

difficulties.pattern: A gap is anything that has not been studied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gaps that are trivial or not worth filling
difficulties.response: Discuss why a gap matters: link it to significance, an unresolved debate or a practical need.

difficulties.pattern: The authors say what future research should do, so that is the gap.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gap statements copied from the limitations or future-research sections of single studies, sometimes already addressed by later work
difficulties.response: Treat authors' suggestions as leads to check, not as gaps: trace later work by forward chaining and compare across the set of sources before claiming that something remains unstudied.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state a gap in the literature on their topic and show the evidence for it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a specific, hedged gap linked to identified sources and explains why it matters.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a plausible gap but with weak evidence or overclaiming.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a gap, or claims an absolute gap without evidence.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, gap statements are introduced in hedged, small-scale form: undergraduate pre-sessional learners use them to give an extended essay a direction, and postgraduate pre-sessional learners use them in project proposals. Final-year undergraduates need this for dissertations. Taught postgraduates use gaps to justify dissertation questions, and doctoral researchers must articulate gaps that position an original contribution (res.gap-niche).

records.summary: Synthesis paragraphs combine argument and source use. Wingate found that students often did not understand that essays require an argument, and Petrić's comparison of high- and low-rated theses suggests that stronger writers use citations to compare and connect rather than only to attribute. Feak and Swales provide models of text that integrates several sources under the writer's point. Teach the paragraph as a sequence of moves: the writer's claim, related sources, commentary, link.

activities.title: Build from a matrix column
learnerActions: Choose a column from a synthesis matrix
Write a topic sentence that states your point about that theme
Add sources grouped by relationship, using non-integral citation for agreement and integral citation for contrasting positions
Add commentary and a closing link to the wider argument
activities.intendedInsight: A synthesis paragraph is built from a theme and a claim, not from a source.
activities.rationale: Moving from matrix to paragraph makes the organising move explicit.

activities.title: Expert paragraph anatomy
learnerActions: Analyse a published synthesis paragraph from your field
Label the writer's claim, each source's role, the relationships and the commentary
Write a parallel paragraph on your own topic using the same structure
activities.intendedInsight: Expert synthesis paragraphs have a recognisable structure that can be adapted.
activities.rationale: Analysis of expert texts followed by parallel writing is a common genre-based approach, and it makes visible the comparing and linking functions Petrić associated with higher-rated writing.

difficulties.pattern: My paragraph starts with the first source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Topic sentences that report a source
difficulties.response: Require a topic sentence in the writer's voice before any sources are added.

difficulties.pattern: With so many sources, I cannot tell where my voice is.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguous attribution in multi-source paragraphs
difficulties.response: Teach continued attribution and explicit commentary markers, and colour-code voices in drafts.

difficulties.pattern: Lots of citations in one paragraph shows synthesis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of citations without relationships or commentary
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state what each source contributes and how the sources relate before revising.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 150-word paragraph from a given matrix column.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Opens with the writer's claim, relates sources explicitly, uses appropriate citation forms, comments and links forward.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Integrates sources but lacks commentary, or begins with a source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Produces a sequence of summaries.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, synthesis paragraphs are a key target for progression writing. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates use them in essays and reviews; doctoral researchers use them throughout the thesis.

records.summary: Plakans found that reading-to-write test tasks elicited more interactive, recursive composing processes than writing-only tasks, and Plakans and Gebril showed that writers used sources for ideas, support, organisation and language, with the selection of important source ideas and the handling of source language among the differences between performances. Grabe and Zhang argue that reading and writing should be taught together in EAP, and Hirvela treats reading-to-write connections as central to L2 writing instruction. Teach integrated tasks as one process (task analysis, purposeful reading and listening, notes organised by relationship, planning by point, transformation of source language) and then rehearse it under the time limits and format of the assessment learners face, so that test preparation and coursework preparation reinforce each other. Moore and Morton's comparison of university assignments with a writing-only test task, which found that university tasks drew far more on sources, is one reason to treat integrated tasks as preparation for study rather than only as test technique.

activities.title: Relationship notes
learnerActions: Divide a page into one column per source (a reading, a talk or a second reading)
Note the main points of each source in matching rows
Draw arrows to show how points relate (supports, qualifies, challenges, extends, illustrates)
Plan and write the response from the arrows rather than from the source texts
activities.intendedInsight: Integrated tasks usually ask about how sources relate, not about each source separately.
activities.rationale: Organising notes by relationship is intended to support the selection of important source ideas, which Plakans and Gebril (2012) link to differences in performance.

activities.title: Process walkthrough under time
learnerActions: Analyse an integrated task prompt and underline what must be done with each source
Read and listen with the task in mind, making notes in the relationship format
Plan the response by points, then write it within the time limit of the assessment you will take
Record how long each stage took and agree a time split to try on the next task
activities.intendedInsight: The same process works under time pressure if time is divided deliberately between input, planning and writing.
activities.rationale: Breaking the process into stages reflects the composing processes Plakans observed in reading-to-write tasks and the case for teaching reading and writing together; rehearsing the stages under time is a practitioner proposal rather than a tested intervention.

activities.title: Source-use audit
learnerActions: Compare your response with the sources and highlight copied strings of three or more words, paraphrases, summaries and your own comment in different colours
Decide for each copied string whether it is a technical term to keep or wording to transform
Revise one section to reduce reliance on source wording and check that each point is attributed
activities.intendedInsight: Source language can support writing, but it must be transformed and attributed.
activities.rationale: Plakans (2008) and Plakans and Gebril (2012) document how writers draw on source language in integrated tasks; making that use visible allows it to be managed rather than hidden.

difficulties.pattern: I summarise the reading, then I summarise the lecture.
difficulties.revealedBy: Two-part responses organised by source ('The reading says… The lecture says…') rather than by the relationship the task asks for
difficulties.response: Model responses organised around the relationship and plan with the relationship-notes format, which requires links between sources.

difficulties.pattern: I ran out of time, so I copied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Copied strings from the reading concentrated towards the end of responses, with little transformation
difficulties.response: Practise time allocation and condensed notes that do not reproduce full sentences, then summarise from notes. Treat copying in practice tasks as a stage in learning to use sources, not as misconduct.

difficulties.pattern: I missed the speaker's main point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses based mainly on the reading that omit or misrepresent the listening input
difficulties.response: Practise note-taking on short talks, focusing on structure and on markers of stance and contrast, and require each noted point to be linked to the reading.

difficulties.pattern: My preparation book says the talk always disagrees with the reading, so I start every answer that way.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic openings that misstate the relationship when a task asks for something else, such as agreement, extension or a combined summary
difficulties.response: Preparation materials can describe a test's former format. Teachers should check the test owner's current task list and sample tasks before teaching task-specific strategies; learners should read each prompt for the relationship it actually asks about and practise with varied relationships.

diagnostic.task: Give a short reading and a short spoken or written second source with partly different positions, and ask for a two-to-three-sentence account of how they relate, written within a set time.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the relationship accurately, includes key points from both sources and uses own wording with attribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers both sources but summarises them separately, or states the relationship with copied wording.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses only one source, misrepresents the relationship or copies extensively.

records.contextNotes: On foundation and pre-sessional programmes, integrated reading-into-writing tasks are common in assessment and progression decisions, at both undergraduate and postgraduate pre-sessional level; teach the process so that it transfers to coursework. For learners preparing for a proficiency or in-house test, check the test owner's current task list and sample materials before teaching task-specific strategies: tests have added, removed and redesigned integrated tasks in recent revisions, some are delivered on computer with adaptive sections, and preparation materials can lag behind. Undergraduates meet the same process in summary–response and source-based coursework without strict time limits, so shift the emphasis from speed to the depth of selection and transformation. Learners with access arrangements in timed assessment, such as extra time for dyslexia, should practise under the conditions they will actually have.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-14 also asks for this topic to become a named task anchor in pathways (R1-02); pathways are outside this strand file, so that part is left to the pathway authors.
The difficulty about outdated preparation materials is a practitioner observation; no source in the closed bibliography documents it.

records.summary: Learners often meet citation first as a plagiarism-avoidance rule, which encourages mechanical or defensive citing. Teaching can start instead from what citation does for readers and writers: Hyland (1999) shows citation as central to how disciplines construct knowledge and how writers align themselves with a community, and Swales (1986) argued for reading citations as discourse rather than simply counting them. Pecorari (2013) recommends making the communicative rationale explicit before the mechanics, so that later decisions have a principle behind them.

activities.title: What does this citation do?
learnerActions: Read a short expert or exemplar paragraph with its citations highlighted
For each citation, note what a reader could check or follow up because of it and whose work is credited
Reread the paragraph with the citations removed, as a sceptical marker, and mark claims that now look unsupported or appear to be the writer's own
Agree a class list of citation purposes to reuse in later units
activities.intendedInsight: Citations make claims checkable, give credit, and show the writer knows the field; without them the writer silently claims others' work and loses credibility.
activities.rationale: Moving from a rule to purposes gives learners a principle they can apply to new cases. Hyland's account of citation as knowledge construction supports this framing, and Bretag et al.'s survey, in which students asked to be taught how to do it properly, supports explicit, purpose-led teaching.

activities.title: Following a claim through the conversation
learnerActions: Take one cited claim from a recent article and find the cited source
Note what the original actually said and how the citing author used it (agreeing, extending, criticising)
Draw a simple chain showing how the claim travelled across two or three texts
Discuss what a reader could not do if the chain were broken
activities.intendedInsight: Citations link texts into a conversation that readers can enter and check; a writer's citations are a public trail others will follow.
activities.rationale: Gives concrete experience of the ACRL frame 'Scholarship as Conversation' and of verifiability, and prepares learners for later work on citation accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: 'I cite so that I don't get caught for plagiarism.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations appear only beside quotations or are added after drafting to 'cover' the text; the learner cannot say what a citation tells the reader.
difficulties.response: Reframe citation around reader needs (checking, following up, credit) with model texts. Avoid fear-based framing that equates citation with compliance, which tends to produce defensive over-citation and anxiety.

difficulties.pattern: 'Citing other people makes my work look less original.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Few citations in argumentative writing; authoritative-sounding claims left unattributed; reading presented as the writer's own knowledge.
difficulties.response: Show how expert writers make their own contribution visible against cited work; ask learners to mark which claims in an exemplar are the writer's own and how citation makes them stand out. Present this as a community expectation to be made explicit, not as a learner deficiency.

difficulties.pattern: 'Textbooks and lectures don't cite much, so I don't need to cite them either.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Ideas, figures or diagrams from lecture slides and textbooks reproduced without attribution.
difficulties.response: Contrast genres: textbooks and lectures consolidate knowledge for learners and often cite lightly, whereas assessed writing must display its sources. Show how to cite lecture material where the department permits it, or how to trace it to the original source.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Give me three reasons why academic writers cite sources, other than avoiding plagiarism, with an example of each.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives three or more distinct purposes (credit, verifiability, joining or positioning within a debate, supporting a claim, credibility with the reader) with apt examples.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives credit and support for claims but cannot explain verifiability or positioning, or lists purposes without examples.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Mentions only avoiding plagiarism or penalties, or describes citation as a formality.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, keep to credit, evidence and checking, using textbooks and short articles. On pre-sessional courses, connect the purposes directly to the source-based assignment and its marking criteria; PG pre-sessional learners can move quickly to citation as positioning. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, revisit briefly for students who did not take a preparatory course, as a bridge to the functions of citation and disciplinary variation.

records.summary: Common knowledge is the hardest boundary in citation because it depends on reader, discipline and level. Shi (2011) found that students and their instructors did not always agree about what needed citing and that students' judgements were bound up with what they had themselves just learned. Teaching should therefore build a decision procedure and practise borderline cases rather than offer a fixed list. Pecorari (2013) also stresses that ideas, data and argument structure need attribution, not only wording — a gap that appears when citation is taught mainly alongside quotation.

activities.title: Cite, don't cite, it depends
learnerActions: In pairs, sort twelve statement cards from a recently studied topic into 'cite', 'no need' and 'depends'
For each 'depends' card, write the condition that would decide it (readership, discipline, how specific or contested the claim is)
Compare with another pair and with the tutor's sorting, discussing disagreements rather than seeking a single answer
Write a personal rule of thumb for doubtful cases
activities.intendedInsight: Common knowledge is a judgement about a particular readership; specific figures, findings, frameworks and contested claims almost always need a source.
activities.rationale: Because judgements of common knowledge vary even among experienced academics, discussing borderline cases and the criteria behind them is likely to transfer better than memorising a list.

activities.title: Hidden borrowing audit
learnerActions: Highlight every idea, figure, example or line of argument in a paragraph of their own draft that came from reading or lectures
Check each highlighted item for a citation
Add missing citations or reformulate to separate their own reasoning from source content
Note which kinds of borrowing (data, examples, argument structure) they most often left uncited
activities.intendedInsight: Ideas, data and the organisation of an argument need attribution as well as copied words.
activities.rationale: Self-audit applies the criteria to the learner's own text, where the hardest decisions occur, and builds self-monitoring rather than reliance on text-matching software.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I change the words, I don't need to cite.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Competently paraphrased content with no citation; surprise when told an idea needs attribution.
difficulties.response: Contrast attribution of ideas with attribution of wording using a side-by-side example: paraphrase changes the wording, not the ownership. Return to the purposes of citation.

difficulties.pattern: 'It's on lots of websites, so it's common knowledge.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncited statistics, definitions or named theories justified because they are widely available online.
difficulties.response: Distinguish 'widely available' from 'known to the intended readers without looking it up'. Use the reader-oriented question: would my marker ask where this comes from?

difficulties.pattern: Every sentence ends in a citation, including the writer's own conclusions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations attached to evaluative or concluding sentences that are the writer's own inference, so the writer's contribution disappears.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a cautious stage, not an error to penalise. Ask the learner to mark which sentences are their own inference and to remove citations that wrongly attribute them. Do not simply say 'cite less' without showing what remains theirs.

diagnostic.task: Give five statements (a specific statistic, a historical date taught in most schools, a named theory and its core claim, a contested causal claim, and the learner's own inference from two sources) and ask which need citing and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Cites the statistic, the theory and the contested claim; treats the date as probably common knowledge for this readership; does not cite the inference but signals it as their own; reasons refer to reader and specificity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but reasons are rule-based ('statistics need citations') or the learner is unsure how to treat the inference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would cite only items that are quoted, or would cite nothing that has been paraphrased.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners need concrete categories (numbers, findings, definitions, images) and a 'cite if in doubt' default. Pre-sessional learners apply the procedure across an extended project, where uncited reading-derived ideas are a common concern. UG and PGT in-sessional work should address disciplinary common knowledge — what specialist readers take for granted — and over-citation of the writer's own synthesis.

records.summary: Learners often arrive believing there is one correct way to reference. Teaching should present the families of systems and what each foregrounds — author and date (APA 7; Chicago author–date), MLA 9's author and page, sequence (IEEE; the NLM-based Vancouver style recommended through the ICMJE Recommendations), or notes with pinpoints (Chicago notes and bibliography; OSCOLA) — and train learners to find and follow the authoritative guide for each context. 'Harvard' has no single authority: it is a family of institution-specific variants, so learners should always check which version their department prescribes.

activities.title: System spotting
learnerActions: Examine five short extracts with reference lists or notes from different disciplines
Identify each system family from the in-text form and list order
Find the official or departmental guide that governs two of them
Note one design feature of each system and what it makes easy for the reader
activities.intendedInsight: Different systems meet the same needs differently, and the governing guide decides the details.
activities.rationale: Contrasting authentic texts builds recognition and the habit of consulting the authority; linking design to reader needs reduces the sense that styles are arbitrary.

activities.title: Which Harvard?
learnerActions: Compare two universities' Harvard guides for the same three sources
List the differences in punctuation, capitalisation and element order
Identify and bookmark the version that applies to their own course
Select or adjust a reference-manager output style and check that it matches that version
activities.intendedInsight: There is no single Harvard, so consistency with the specified version matters more than memorising one model.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the belief that Harvard is a fixed standard and turns variation into a practical checking routine.

difficulties.pattern: 'My previous school taught me the right way to reference, so this department's style is wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Formats from a previous institution persist after explicit instruction; resistance to departmental guidance.
difficulties.response: Validate prior learning as a legitimate convention, then frame the task as switching systems on demand, as researchers do between journals. Provide a side-by-side comparison of the old and new styles.

difficulties.pattern: 'APA and Harvard are the same thing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: APA-specific rules used where an institutional Harvard is specified, or vice versa, producing a mixed style.
difficulties.response: Show the specific points where the two prescribed guides diverge and stress checking the brief. Do not overstate the stakes: markers mainly notice inconsistency and missing information.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your module handbook says use Harvard. Where do you find the rules, and what would you do if your reference manager's Harvard output differs from them?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the departmental or library guide as the authority, notes that Harvard varies, and would select or edit the manager's output style to match the guide.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows a guide is needed but assumes any Harvard guide or the software default will do.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Believes there is one universal Harvard or treats it as interchangeable with any author–date style.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses usually teach one author–date style but should name the others so learners recognise them in reading. UG and PGT in-sessional sessions focus on the department's prescribed style, including numeric styles in engineering and medicine and OSCOLA in law. PGR writers switch between journal styles and should treat each journal's author guidelines as the authority.
reviewNotes: Style guides are revised periodically (for example Chicago's 18th edition appeared in 2024); confirm which edition institutions currently prescribe.

records.summary: Author–date citation is usually the first system taught in EAP because most general EAP programmes use APA 7 or an institutional Harvard. Linking formatting to the integral/non-integral distinction (Swales, 1990; Thompson & Tribble, 2001) gives the mechanics a rhetorical rationale. As a practitioner proposal that has not been tested, this, together with practice in placing citations so that the scope of attribution is clear, is likely to be more useful than an isolated rule list. Learners should consult the guide for edge cases rather than memorise them; the stable core is who, when and, for quotations, where.

activities.title: Narrative or parenthetical?
learnerActions: Find six citations in a model text and sort them into narrative (author named in the sentence) and parenthetical forms
Rewrite two narrative citations as parenthetical and two parenthetical as narrative, adjusting sentence grammar
Discuss how each change shifts emphasis between the author and the information
Apply the guide's rules for two-author and three-or-more-author works to the rewritten citations
activities.intendedInsight: Format follows grammatical role, and the choice of form changes what the sentence foregrounds.
activities.rationale: Linking mechanics to the integral/non-integral distinction gives form a function and prepares learners for later rhetorical choices.

activities.title: Citation clinic and personal checklist
learnerActions: Correct ten citations containing typical errors (given names, missing year, et al. misuse, ampersand in narrative form, unordered multiple works)
Check each correction against the specified guide and record the rule
Write a checklist of the three errors they personally make most often
Apply the checklist to their current draft
activities.intendedInsight: A few recurring errors account for most citation problems, and these can be self-checked.
activities.rationale: Targeted error work with a self-made checklist builds monitoring of one's own recurring patterns rather than dependence on teacher correction.

difficulties.pattern: Citing with given names, initials or full names ('John Smith (2020)'), or citing the wrong part of a name.
difficulties.revealedBy: Given or full names in citations; author names differing between citation and reference list; compound or particle surnames split wrongly.
difficulties.response: In naming systems where the family name comes first, or where given names are the usual form of reference, learners may be unsure which name to cite. Teach the guide's surname-only rule and show how to identify the family name from the article's metadata or the author's other publications.

difficulties.pattern: One citation placed at the end of a long paragraph that mixes source content and the writer's comments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers cannot tell which sentences are attributed; markers comment that the writer's own view is unclear.
difficulties.response: Show how to mark where attributed content starts (a narrative citation or signal phrase) and ends, re-citing where necessary. Avoid insisting on a citation after every sentence, which hides the writer's own contribution.

difficulties.pattern: 'et al. means and others, so I can use it for two authors.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'et al.' for two-author works, mispunctuated forms such as 'et. al', or 'et al.' in reference-list entries.
difficulties.response: Contrast the guide's rule for two authors with three or more, and note that reference lists normally give authors in full up to the guide's limit.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite a two-author source narratively, a five-author source parenthetically, and both sources together in one parenthesis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All forms correct for the guide, including 'and' versus '&', et al. for the five-author source and correct ordering of the two works.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Basic forms correct but errors in ordering multiple works or in the two-author narrative form.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses given names, omits years, or applies et al. to the two-author source.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, teach the core forms with books and journal articles. UG pre-sessional courses should add group authors, multiple works and secondary citation, which appear in extended projects; PG pre-sessional learners often have partial control and need targeted error work rather than full reteaching. UG and PGT in-sessional sessions can focus on the department's variant and on citation placement within synthesis paragraphs.

records.summary: Numeric systems are often neglected on general EAP courses that teach only author–date, leaving engineering, computing and health students to learn them unaided. The mechanics are simple but the rhetoric differs: numbers background cited authors, consistent with Hyland's (1999) finding that the hard sciences in his corpus favoured non-integral citation, so naming an author becomes a marked choice. Teaching should combine the authoritative guide (the IEEE Reference Guide; for Vancouver, the NLM-based style recommended in the ICMJE Recommendations or the journal's own instructions) with practice in reference-manager numbering.

activities.title: Renumber after revision
learnerActions: Move one paragraph earlier in a short IEEE-style text
Renumber all citations in order of first appearance and reorder the reference list by hand
Repeat the task using a reference manager and compare time and accuracy
Note which errors the software prevents and which it cannot, such as wrong item metadata
activities.intendedInsight: Numeric systems depend on sequence, which is fragile under revision; software helps with sequence but metadata still needs checking.
activities.rationale: Simulates the main practical difficulty of numeric styles and motivates disciplined reference-manager use.

activities.title: When to name the author
learnerActions: Highlight every sentence in an engineering or medical article where an author is named alongside a citation number
Classify why the author is named (contrast between studies, credit for a method, critique)
Rewrite two non-integral citations so that the author is named and judge whether the change is justified
Agree a rule of thumb for naming authors in numeric systems
activities.intendedInsight: In numeric systems, naming an author is a marked choice used for emphasis, contrast or evaluation.
activities.rationale: Connects formatting to Hyland's observation that disciplines differ in how prominently cited authors appear.

difficulties.pattern: Numbering sources alphabetically or in the order they appear in the reference-manager library.
difficulties.revealedBy: Alphabetised reference list; citation numbers that do not ascend through the text.
difficulties.response: Restate the principle of order of first citation and give a short renumbering exercise.

difficulties.pattern: Giving a repeated source a new number each time it is cited.
difficulties.revealedBy: Duplicate entries in the reference list under different numbers.
difficulties.response: Show that a number identifies a source, not an occurrence; merge duplicates in the reference manager.

difficulties.pattern: 'Numeric styles don't use page numbers', so quotations carry only the citation number.
difficulties.revealedBy: Direct quotations with no locator.
difficulties.response: Show how the specified style adds a page or section to the citation when quoting, and note that direct quotation is itself uncommon in these fields.

diagnostic.task: Give three sources cited in the order B, A, B, C and ask the learner to write the in-text numbers and the reference-list order in IEEE style.
diagnostic.strongResponse: B is [1], A is [2], B again is [1], C is [3]; list ordered B, A, C with entries in IEEE format.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sequence correct but B given a new number on repetition, or entries not in IEEE format.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Alphabetical numbering, or author–date elements mixed in.

records.contextNotes: On foundation pathways into engineering, computing or medicine, introduce numeric citation alongside author–date so learners recognise both. Pre-sessional courses with discipline-specific strands should assess the style students will meet. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, follow the department's variant; PGR writers switch between journal-specific numeric styles and mainly need reference-manager fluency.
reviewNotes: Vancouver is a family of numeric styles derived from NLM's Citing Medicine and adapted by journals; the journal's instructions are usually the operative authority.

records.summary: Note-based systems serve fields in which pinpointing, discursive commentary and varied primary sources matter, such as history, much of the humanities and law. Chicago (18th ed.) sets out full notes, shortened notes and bibliography; OSCOLA governs much UK legal writing, where cases and legislation have their own formats and pinpoints are expected. Teaching should separate the citation function of notes from their discursive use, which learners tend either to overuse or to avoid.

activities.title: From full note to short note to bibliography
learnerActions: Write a full first note for a book and a journal article in the specified guide
Write shortened notes for later citations of the same works with different pages
Compile the bibliography entries and compare punctuation and name order with the notes
Check the guide's current rule for consecutive citations of the same source
activities.intendedInsight: Notes and bibliography entries share elements but differ in punctuation and name order, and shortened notes depend on a full first note.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison of note and bibliography forms targets the most frequent formatting confusions.

activities.title: Primary and secondary authorities (law)
learnerActions: Sort a list of authorities into primary (cases, legislation) and secondary (books, articles)
Format two cases and one statute with pinpoints in OSCOLA
Add a footnote citing a journal article with a pinpoint page
Check whether the module requires tables of cases and legislation
activities.intendedInsight: Legal citation distinguishes primary authorities from commentary and expects precise pinpoints.
activities.rationale: OSCOLA formats for primary legal sources are unfamiliar to most learners and central to legal writing assessment.

difficulties.pattern: Long explanations that belong in the argument are placed in footnotes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Key argument steps or definitions appear only in notes; the main text reads as thin.
difficulties.response: Agree a test: if the reader needs it to follow the argument, it belongs in the main text. Show expert examples of short discursive notes.

difficulties.pattern: Author–date parenthetical citations mixed into a notes system.
difficulties.revealedBy: (Author, Year) in the text alongside footnotes.
difficulties.response: Explain that the systems are alternatives, then convert one paragraph fully to notes.

difficulties.pattern: Note numbers placed inconsistently or typed manually as superscripts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Numbers before and after punctuation in the same text; notes that do not renumber after editing.
