difficulties.response: Point to the guide's placement rule and use the word processor's footnote function or a reference manager.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite the same book twice in footnotes (pages 12 and 40) and give its bibliography entry in the specified guide.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Full note then shortened note with correct pinpoints; bibliography entry with inverted name and the guide's punctuation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Repeats the full note, omits pinpoints, or copies the note format into the bibliography.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses parenthetical author–date citations or gives no locators.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses with law or humanities pathways should introduce notes before progression. In UG and PGT in-sessional teaching the department's guide is the authority; PGR writers in history and law also need control of archival, legal and non-English sources in notes.
reviewNotes: OSCOLA (5th ed., 2026) and Chicago (18th ed., 2024) have both been revised recently; departments may still prescribe earlier editions during transition, so confirm the edition specified.

records.summary: Reference-list accuracy depends less on memorising models than on identifying the source type and locating its elements in the source, a step learners skip when they copy citations from search results. APA 7, MLA 9 and Chicago all organise entries around a small set of elements (author, date, title, source or container), and MLA 9 makes this core-element logic explicit, so teaching the elements first makes new formats easier to construct. Reference managers reduce workload but generate predictable errors that learners must be trained to check.

activities.title: Element hunt
learnerActions: Label the author(s), date, title, container, editors, publisher, volume and issue, pages and DOI on a PDF article, a book's title and copyright pages, and a chapter in an edited book
Classify each source type
Build the reference entries from the labelled elements
Check the entries against the guide and a classmate's version
activities.intendedInsight: Entries are assembled from elements located in the source, and the source type decides which elements are needed and in what order.
activities.rationale: Element-first teaching is likely to transfer better to unfamiliar source types than copying model entries.

activities.title: Exported reference audit
learnerActions: Export references for five sources from a library database or reference manager
Compare each with the guide and highlight errors in capitalisation, item type, names and missing elements
Correct the entries and note which errors recur
Fix the item type or metadata fields in the reference manager so the error does not recur
activities.intendedInsight: Automatically generated references are drafts that need checking.
activities.rationale: Mirrors real practice and prepares learners for systematic accuracy checks.

difficulties.pattern: A chapter in an edited book is referenced as if it were the whole book.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chapter author given as book author; editors missing; no chapter page range.
difficulties.response: Use the title and contents pages to show the two levels of authorship and the idea of a container.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll list everything I read, including sources I didn't cite.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference list longer than the set of in-text citations.
difficulties.response: Distinguish a reference list from a bibliography and check which the brief requires.

difficulties.pattern: Capitalising every main word of article and book titles in APA.
difficulties.revealedBy: Title case for article and book titles in an APA reference list, often carried over from the source's own display or from another style.
difficulties.response: Teach sentence case versus title case explicitly in context, with proper nouns as the exception, and show where the guide requires each.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a PDF of a journal article and ask for its reference entry in the specified style within three minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All elements present and correct, including the DOI in the required form, title capitalisation, and italics for journal name and volume where required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Elements present but with formatting errors in capitalisation, italics or DOI form.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Missing elements, wrong author order, or the URL of a search page instead of a DOI.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners should control books, journal articles and web pages. UG pre-sessional courses add chapters in edited books, reports and checking of reference-manager output; PG pre-sessional learners usually need consolidation and checking routines rather than first teaching. UG and PGT in-sessional work extends to the department's style and the source types common in the discipline.

records.summary: As assignments draw on reports, datasets, software, media and AI tools, learners increasingly meet sources with no exact model in their guide. The transferable skill is to identify who is responsible, which version, when, and how a reader can retrieve it, then adapt the closest model; APA 7 and MLA 9 both encourage this reasoning. Practice should include sources the reader cannot retrieve, such as personal communications and most AI conversations, whose treatment differs between guides and institutions.

activities.title: No-model challenge
learnerActions: In groups, receive three unusual sources such as an NGO report, a dataset and a podcast episode
Identify the author, date, title, version and retrieval information for each
Find the closest model in the guide and adapt it
Explain the reasoning to the class and compare with the guide's examples or library advice
activities.intendedInsight: Citing unfamiliar sources is reasoning from elements, not finding an exact template.
activities.rationale: Builds transferable reasoning for the long tail of source types that no guide fully covers.

activities.title: Citing AI output
learnerActions: Read the current guidance for AI output from the specified style guide and the module's AI policy
Note whether the guide treats the tool or its developer as author, how the prompt is described, and whether a reference-list entry is needed
Cite a short AI output as the guide requires and write the accompanying description of its use
Compare two guides' advice and discuss why they differ
activities.intendedInsight: Guidance on AI output is recent, varies between guides and institutions, and is usually combined with a declaration of use.
activities.rationale: AI outputs are typically non-recoverable for readers, which makes them an instructive limit case; because guidance is evolving, learners need the habit of checking the current version.

difficulties.pattern: 'There's no author, so I'll write Anonymous or the website name.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Anonymous' or a domain name given as author for organisational web pages and reports.
difficulties.response: Show that organisations can be authors, and how the guide treats genuinely authorless items.

difficulties.pattern: 'Datasets and software aren't texts, so they don't need citing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Data sources and analysis software named in a methods section without citation or version.
difficulties.response: Connect to the purposes of citation: credit for data creators and reproducibility of the analysis.

difficulties.pattern: Treating an AI tool as an author whose views can be attributed ('ChatGPT argues that…').
difficulties.revealedBy: AI tools in narrative citations as if they were scholarly authorities.
difficulties.response: Explain that AI output is generated text, not an authored, accountable source; follow the guide's format for documenting use and verify any substantive claim against a scholarly source.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite an organisational report on a website, a dataset with a version number, and a lecture recording at a specific minute.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Organisation as author; dataset version and identifier included; timestamp given; formats adapted correctly from the guide.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One or two items correct; uses 'Anonymous' or omits version or timestamp.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify the elements, or gives the URL alone.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should focus on web pages, reports and lecture materials. UG and PGT in-sessional work extends to datasets, software, standards and media relevant to the discipline. PGR writers need data and software citation for reproducibility and may need to follow journal or funder data policies.
reviewNotes: Guidance on citing generative AI output is evolving and differs between style guides; check the current version of the specified guide (for example the APA Style blog post, McAdoo, 2023, may since have been updated) before teaching.

records.summary: Locators are a small skill with a large effect on verifiability and on markers' judgements of care. Guides agree that quotations need a locator but differ on paraphrase: APA 7 encourages page or paragraph numbers for paraphrases, particularly of specific passages in long works; MLA 9 builds the page number into the citation; and Chicago notes and OSCOLA expect pinpoints. Teaching should cover sources without page numbers, where learners most often omit locators altogether.

activities.title: Locator ladder
learnerActions: Quote from a paginated book, an unpaginated web article, a video and a long report with numbered sections
Choose the appropriate locator for each (page, paragraph, heading, timestamp, section)
Format each in the specified guide
Swap with a partner and test whether the quotation can be found in under a minute
activities.intendedInsight: A locator should let a reader find the material quickly, whatever the medium.
activities.rationale: A reader-oriented test is easier to apply to new cases than recalled rules.

activities.title: Pinpoint the paraphrase
learnerActions: Paraphrase one specific argument from a long chapter
Decide whether to add a page number and justify the decision
Compare the decision with the guide's recommendation
Revise the citation if needed
activities.intendedInsight: Locators for paraphrase help readers verify specific claims drawn from long works.
activities.rationale: Targets the rule that varies most between guides.

difficulties.pattern: 'Web pages have no page numbers, so no locator is needed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotations from online sources and videos without any locator.
difficulties.response: Teach paragraph numbers, headings and timestamps as alternative locators.

difficulties.pattern: Page numbers taken from the PDF viewer rather than the printed pagination.
difficulties.revealedBy: Locators such as 'p. 3' for an article printed as pages 345–367.
difficulties.response: Show the difference between viewer pages and journal pagination; use the printed page numbers.

difficulties.pattern: Quotation marks used but the locator forgotten, especially when quoting short phrases.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent locators within one text; locators present for long quotations only.
difficulties.response: Add a locator check to the learner's personal citation checklist; do not re-teach the whole rule if the learner can state it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite a quotation from page 3 of a PDF of a journal article whose printed pages are 112–130, and a quotation from a 20-minute online video.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses the printed page (for example p. 114) and a timestamp, both in the guide's format.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One locator correct; uses the PDF page or omits the timestamp.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No locators.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: quotations with page numbers from books and articles. Pre-sessional: unpaginated and audiovisual sources. UG and PGT in-sessional: disciplinary pinpoint expectations, especially in law and history.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-19 proposed merging cit.locators into cit.author-date-in-text. The topic ID is retained in the skeleton, so it stays separate; it is kept distinct because locators apply across all systems (author–date, numeric and notes) and to non-paginated and audiovisual sources, and it is not core at any stage, so it does not inflate core counts.

records.summary: Citation errors undermine verifiability and markers' trust, and automated tools have changed where errors come from. Reference managers and database exports introduce predictable metadata errors, and Walters and Wilder (2023) found that ChatGPT-generated literature reviews contained many fabricated references and frequent errors in genuine ones. Accuracy checking therefore needs two layers: formal matching (citation–reference correspondence, details, consistent style) and fidelity (the cited source actually supports the claim, at the strength claimed).

activities.title: Two-pass check
learnerActions: Pass 1: tick every in-text citation against the reference list, then check the list back against the text
Pass 2: verify the details of five references against the publisher's page or DOI record
Reopen three cited sources and confirm that each claim and its hedging match the source
Record the error types found and the time taken
activities.intendedInsight: Formal accuracy and content fidelity are different checks, and both are needed.
activities.rationale: Separating checks into passes, as in proofreading, reduces cognitive load; the fidelity pass targets misrepresentation of sources, which formatting checks miss.

activities.title: Spot the phantom reference
learnerActions: Receive a reference list mixing accurate references, references with altered details, and non-existent AI-generated references
Search each in a library database, Google Scholar or a DOI resolver
Classify each as accurate, erroneous or non-existent
Discuss why the non-existent ones looked plausible and why no surface cue is reliable on its own
activities.intendedInsight: Plausibility is not existence: references must be checked against an authoritative record.
activities.rationale: Walters and Wilder's findings on fabricated and erroneous AI-generated citations make database checking a necessary habit whenever references come from automated sources.

difficulties.pattern: 'The reference manager formatted it, so it must be right.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Title-case titles, missing editors, wrong item types or duplicate entries in otherwise automated lists.
difficulties.response: Teach the typical errors and how to correct them in the manager's fields rather than only in the document.

difficulties.pattern: Citing from memory or old notes without rechecking the source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct formats but claims that overstate or misstate the source, or wrong years.
difficulties.response: Build a final fidelity check into the writing schedule and keep page-referenced notes that separate quotation, paraphrase and own comment.

difficulties.pattern: Mixed formats after copying references from different databases and websites.
difficulties.revealedBy: Some entries in the specified style and others in a database's default format.
difficulties.response: Regenerate or retype all entries in one style and add a consistency pass to the checklist.

diagnostic.task: Give a 150-word paragraph with four citations and a five-item reference list containing a missing reference, an uncited entry, a year mismatch and a non-existent reference. Ask the learner to report all problems.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds all four, and checks the suspicious reference in a database before declaring it non-existent.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds the formal mismatches but accepts the non-existent reference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Checks formatting only.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on matching and basic details. UG pre-sessional courses build systematic pre-submission checks, including reference-manager output; PG pre-sessional courses add fidelity checks and checking of AI-supplied references in longer literature-based projects. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, fidelity checks matter most in literature-based assignments. PGR writers manage large libraries, switch journal styles and must ensure every attributed claim is supported.
reviewNotes: The fidelity check (does the source support the claim?) slightly extends the skeleton scope note; flagged in authorNotes.

Review response: R1-19 proposed merging cit.accuracy-consistency into cit.reference-list. The topic ID is retained in the skeleton, so it stays separate; it is kept distinct because it covers checking citations against sources (fidelity), metadata errors from reference managers and fabricated AI-generated references, which go beyond compiling a list. It is core only at pre-sessional PG.

records.summary: Petrić (2007) found that high-rated master's theses used citations for a wider range of rhetorical functions, notably linking sources and comparing the writer's own findings with the literature, whereas attribution dominated in low-rated theses. Hyland (1999) showed how citation is central to the way disciplines build knowledge and writers position themselves, and Thompson and Tribble (2001) showed how corpus analysis of citation types can inform teaching. Teaching function gives learners a reason for every later technique — they paraphrase, quote or summarise in order to do something — and is intended to move them from 'citation as proof that I read' to 'citation as a move in my argument'. Analysis of expert and student exemplars, followed by planning source use by function in learners' own writing, makes this concrete; Petrić's study was of one field, so the association with ratings is suggestive rather than universal.

activities.title: What is this citation doing?
learnerActions: Label each citation in an expert paragraph with a function from a given set (definition, support, example, contrast, method justification, evaluation, gap)
Compare labels in pairs and discuss citations that do more than one job, using the surrounding argument to decide
Label citations in a higher-rated and a lower-rated student text on the same task
Discuss what the higher-rated writer does with sources that the other does not
activities.intendedInsight: Citations perform different rhetorical jobs, and successful writers use them to compare, evaluate and connect, not only to attribute.
activities.rationale: Modelled on Petrić's comparison of high- and low-rated theses; analysing student exemplars alongside expert text is intended to make the difference look achievable.

activities.title: Source job plan
learnerActions: Before drafting a paragraph, write the claim it will make
Assign each planned source a job (define, support, contrast, show a gap, compare with own findings)
Draft the paragraph, choosing integral or non-integral form and a reporting verb to fit each job
After drafting, check that each source did its job and that the paragraph's claim is the writer's own
activities.intendedInsight: Planning source use by function keeps the writer's argument in control.
activities.rationale: Making function explicit at the planning stage targets the tendency Petrić observed in lower-rated theses to use citation mainly for attribution; Hyland's account of citation as positioning supports the framing. The planning routine itself is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Citation forms in a small corpus
learnerActions: Search a small corpus of discipline texts for citation patterns such as author name plus reporting verb and bracketed citations
Classify the results into integral and non-integral types
Note which forms co-occur with evaluation or comparison
Write two sentences of their own using a pattern found for comparison
activities.intendedInsight: Citation forms and functions co-vary, and certain patterns are typical for comparing or evaluating.
activities.rationale: Follows Thompson and Tribble's corpus-based approach to teaching citation; suited to PG pre-sessional and in-sessional groups.

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source reporting: 'Smith says… Jones says… Lee says…'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs organised by author with no comparison, evaluation or link to the writer's point.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a normal stage; model reorganising the paragraph around an idea and the writer's claim. Avoid simply telling learners to 'be more critical' without showing the moves.

difficulties.pattern: 'I use sources to show the marker how much I have read.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Many sources summarised one after another with no claim of the writer's own; reading lists reproduced in the text.
difficulties.response: Where previous assessments (for example exam answers or reports marked on coverage of named authorities) rewarded displaying reading, acknowledge that display has a place, then contrast a knowledge-display paragraph with an argued one and show how markers in the target context read sources as support for the writer's argument.

difficulties.pattern: 'Sources are there to prove my point, so I cite only those that agree.'
difficulties.revealedBy: No contrasting or qualifying sources in extended writing; counter-evidence absent even where the literature is divided.
difficulties.response: Introduce contrast, qualification and gap functions, and show how acknowledging and answering opposing sources strengthens an argument rather than weakening it.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluative reporting verbs used without intending evaluation, for example 'claims' or 'admits' for neutral reporting.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unintended scepticism or criticism in reporting; markers question the writer's stance.
difficulties.response: Map reporting verbs by evaluative force and have learners check whether each verb matches the function they intend for that citation.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with five citations and ask the learner to explain why the writer cited each source, then propose one revision that adds comparison or evaluation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies varied functions (defining a term, establishing consensus, contrasting a view, justifying a method, evaluating) in relation to the paragraph's claim; the revision adds a genuine comparison or evaluation in an appropriate form.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies support and attribution only; the revision changes a reporting verb but adds no new function.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Says the sources are cited 'to avoid plagiarism' or 'to show research', or cannot distinguish functions.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: support, example and definition functions in short source-based paragraphs. UG pre-sessional: add contrast and simple evaluation in the extended essay. PG pre-sessional: the full range, including linking sources and planning source use by function for a literature-based project. UG in-sessional: functions in disciplinary assignments, using departmental exemplars. PGT: dissertation literature reviews and discussion sections, especially comparing own findings with the literature. PGR: positioning a contribution and managing extensive literatures.
reviewNotes: Merged with src.source-functions after review (R1-15); the CEFR range was widened to B1+–C2 so that the foundation-level 'what sources do' scope and the postgraduate typology sit in one topic.

Review response: R5-01 asked for the deference pattern ('I can't criticise published experts') to be replaced here with a topic-specific difficulty; it has been replaced by the 'cite only sources that agree' and 'display of reading' patterns.

records.summary: Hyland's (1999; 2004) corpus studies of research articles across disciplines show systematic differences: the softer disciplines in his corpus tended to cite more densely and to use more direct quotation and integral citation, while the hard sciences and engineering favoured non-integral citation that backgrounds authors. Thompson and Tribble (2001) found differences even between two related agricultural fields in doctoral theses. Learners benefit from investigating their own discipline's practice, while recognising variation within fields and between published and student genres (Nesi & Gardner, 2012).

activities.title: Mini citation study
learnerActions: Select three recent articles from a leading journal in their field
Count citations per 1,000 words in the introductions, the proportion of integral citations and the number of direct quotations
Compare results with a classmate from another discipline
Write three citation guidelines for their own writing
activities.intendedInsight: Citation norms can be discovered empirically and differ by field.
activities.rationale: A learner-as-researcher approach builds transferable genre-analysis habits and grounds advice in the learner's own discipline.

activities.title: Rewrite for another field
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that uses quotations and integral citations
Rewrite it for a hard-science readership using non-integral citation and no direct quotation
Discuss what changes in emphasis and in the image of knowledge
Decide which version suits their own discipline and why
activities.intendedInsight: Citation choices present knowledge either as interpretation attributed to people or as accumulated findings.
activities.rationale: Transformation tasks raise awareness of how form carries disciplinary meaning.

difficulties.pattern: Heavy direct quotation in science or engineering writing because general EAP classes practised quotation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent quotations in lab, design or technical reports.
difficulties.response: Show disciplinary norms with authentic texts and practise paraphrase and non-integral citation.

difficulties.pattern: 'Science never uses integral citation.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Rigid avoidance of naming authors even when contrasting studies or crediting methods.
difficulties.response: Present findings as tendencies and supply counter-examples from the learner's field.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe citation practice in their field and support the description with one example article.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies specific features with evidence from the article and links them to how knowledge is built in the field.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate general features without evidence or explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes generic EAP norms apply everywhere.

records.contextNotes: On PG pre-sessional courses with discipline strands, introduce two or three contrasting features using texts from learners' target fields. In UG in-sessional work, compare a few features using departmental exemplars. PGT learners, often changing discipline, should analyse their new field's texts early. PGR writers analyse target journals and refine practice for publication.
reviewNotes: Hyland's disciplinary findings derive from research articles; student genres may differ, so learners should also examine discipline-specific student exemplars.

records.summary: Canagarajah (2002) analysed how the conventions and material conditions of academic publishing marginalise scholars working outside the centres of knowledge production, and Lillis and Curry (2010) documented how evaluation systems reward English-medium, highly indexed journals, shaping what multilingual scholars publish and where. The ACRL Framework (2016) asks learners to recognise that authority is constructed and contextual and that some voices are under-represented in scholarly communication. EAP teaching that tells learners to prefer indexed, high-impact sources can reinforce these patterns unless it also asks whose knowledge is missing. The approach proposed here, which has not been tested as an intervention, is to make these patterns visible in learners' own reading and reference lists and to treat broadening sources as a quality judgement about relevance and perspective, not a quota. How far individual citation choices can or should redress these imbalances is debated, and learners should meet that debate rather than a fixed position.

activities.title: Audit a reading list
learnerActions: Take a module reading list or the reference list of their own draft
Tabulate each source's language, where the research was done, where it was published and what type of publication it is
Discuss which perspectives dominate and whether that matters for the question being asked
Identify one gap that matters for the argument and plan a search to address it
activities.intendedInsight: A reference list has a shape, and that shape can reflect database coverage and habit as much as relevance.
activities.rationale: Making the patterns analysed by Canagarajah and by Lillis and Curry visible in learners' own materials connects a structural argument to an everyday choice; the activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Beyond the first page of results
learnerActions: Run the same search in a major multidisciplinary index and in a regional or subject database, repository or the website of an organisation in the context studied
Compare what each returns and note sources that appear in only one
Apply the same evaluation criteria (authority, method, relevance, currency) to a source found only outside the major index
Decide whether to cite it and write one sentence justifying the decision
activities.intendedInsight: Visibility in a search is not the same as quality or relevance; every source, wherever it is found, is judged on the same criteria.
activities.rationale: Applies the ACRL frames on constructed authority and strategic exploration to source selection, and is intended to guard against both prestige bias and token inclusion.

difficulties.pattern: 'Only high-impact international journals count as good sources.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists drawn only from the top results of one major database; relevant regional studies or reports from the context studied dismissed without being evaluated.
difficulties.response: Separate the indicators (indexing, impact factor, citation counts) from the criteria they stand in for (peer review, sound method, relevance), and show cases where the most relevant evidence comes from a regional journal or an organisation in the context studied. Do not replace one rule with another: the aim is evaluation, not a quota.

difficulties.pattern: Learners who know relevant scholarship from their own region or in another language leave it out because they think it will be seen as less academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about whether such sources are 'allowed'; reading lists, model answers and exemplars that contain no such sources.
difficulties.response: Make the expectation explicit: in many assignments relevant scholarship from any region or language is welcome if it is evaluated and cited properly. Module teams can check whether reading lists, exemplars and feedback signal otherwise. Point learners to the guide's rules for citing translated and non-English sources.

difficulties.pattern: Adding sources from under-represented regions or languages to tick a box, without reading or using them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources listed but not discussed, or cited for claims they do not make.
difficulties.response: Return to what each source does in the argument: broadening a reference list is part of answering the question better, so every added source needs a job and a fair reading.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your reference list contains only journal articles from the UK and the USA, but your essay is about primary healthcare in Vietnam. Is that a problem, and what would you do?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Says it depends on the question but that research from the context studied is likely to be relevant; names concrete ways to find it (regional databases, government or NGO reports, sources in other languages); would evaluate it with the same criteria; justifies the final selection.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises the imbalance but would add sources without saying how they would be found or evaluated, or assumes they would be of lower quality.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no issue, or treats journal prestige or indexing as the only criterion.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, keep to noticing: whose voices are in this reading list, and are any from the place the topic is about? On UG pre-sessional courses, link to source evaluation in the extended project. On PG pre-sessional courses, add how databases and rankings shape visibility and how to search beyond the major indexes. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, connect to departmental reading lists, curriculum initiatives on whose knowledge is taught where they exist, and the dissertation literature review. For PGR writers, connect to positioning within a field, centre–periphery dynamics in publishing and citing multilingual scholarship. In EMI and transnational settings, local scholarship may be central rather than peripheral, and expectations differ between institutions and countries.
reviewNotes: New topic added in response to R5-14. The bibliography has no bibliometric study of database coverage or citation inequality; claims are therefore limited to what Canagarajah (2002), Lillis and Curry (2010) and the ACRL Framework support, and should be strengthened if a verified bibliometric source is added.
Suggested edges for other groups (not added here because they belong to other files): res.literature-review <- cit.citation-politics (soft) and a related-topic link with acu.critical-eap.

records.summary: The ICAI (2021) frames academic integrity as a commitment to six fundamental values — honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage — and the Handbook of Academic Integrity (Bretag, 2016) documents a sector shift from purely punitive approaches towards education and shared responsibility. For learners entering an unfamiliar academic system, values give a rationale for conventions that can otherwise seem arbitrary. Teaching should connect values to concrete practices and realistic dilemmas rather than present them as abstract virtues.

activities.title: From values to practices
learnerActions: Match each of the six values to two concrete academic practices (for example, respect: representing other writers accurately; courage: raising a problem in a group)
Rank five integrity dilemmas by difficulty and identify the competing values in each
Discuss what a person acting with integrity would do and what support would make that easier
Write a short personal statement of integrity commitments for the course
activities.intendedInsight: Integrity is enacted through everyday choices, often under competing pressures.
activities.rationale: Follows the ICAI values model and the educative approach in the integrity literature; dilemmas move learners beyond agreeing with abstract statements.

activities.title: Who is affected?
learnerActions: Read a misconduct scenario such as falsified lab results in a group report
Map who is affected: the student, peers, the institution, future patients or clients, the field
Identify which values are breached for each
Propose the honest alternative at each decision point
activities.intendedInsight: Misconduct has consequences beyond one person's grade.
activities.rationale: Consequence mapping makes trust and fairness concrete and connects integrity to professional futures.

difficulties.pattern: 'Integrity is just the university's system for catching us.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Cynical or anxious responses; questions focus on detection and penalties.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the regulatory side honestly but lead with community purposes and available support. Avoid opening a course with sanctions and case horror stories, which raise anxiety without building understanding.

difficulties.pattern: 'Helping a friend with their assignment is the right thing to do.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Endorsing sharing of work out of loyalty or kindness in scenario discussions.
difficulties.response: Treat it as a genuine conflict between loyalty and fairness, and explore ways to help (explaining concepts, pointing to support) that do not put the friend at risk.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, with an example, how one of the six values applies to writing an essay from sources.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a value, links it to a specific practice and explains how others rely on that practice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a value with a generic example and little explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot link values to practice, or equates integrity with not getting caught.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: introduce early and positively, linked to the course's own expectations. Pre-sessional: brief, values-led framing of the course's integrity expectations. UG and PGT in-sessional: revisit through professional codes in the discipline, such as health or engineering. Research students' needs are covered by int.research-integrity rather than here.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-06 asked for pgr to be removed from this B1–B2+ topic; done, with doctoral needs covered by int.research-integrity.

records.summary: Research on second-language source use complicates simple definitions of plagiarism. Howard (1995) proposed patchwriting as a developmental strategy distinct from cheating; Pecorari (2003; 2008) showed that postgraduate L2 writers' unattributed source language typically lacked any intention to deceive; and Shi (2004) found that how much students borrowed without attribution varied with the writing task. Pennycook (1996) traced how notions of textual ownership are historically and institutionally situated, an argument that should not be turned into claims that any national or cultural group 'does not understand' plagiarism. Teaching should make the textual criteria explicit, separate development from deception, and still be clear about what institutions require.

activities.title: Continuum of source use
learnerActions: Place six versions of a source-based paragraph on a continuum from appropriate to plagiarised
Justify each placement with reference to wording, ideas, structure and acknowledgement
Compare the placements with the institution's definition
Revise the two weakest versions
activities.intendedInsight: Plagiarism concerns ideas and structure as well as wording, and a citation does not license copied language.
activities.rationale: Pecorari's analysis separates the textual features of source use from the writer's intention; a continuum makes those features visible without equating every problem with cheating.

activities.title: Why do conventions differ?
learnerActions: Read short accounts of memorisation, imitation and textual borrowing in different historical and educational settings
Discuss what purpose each practice served in its setting
Identify what the current institution expects and why
Write advice for a new student that explains these expectations without judging previous practices
activities.intendedInsight: Different conventions serve different purposes; current expectations can be learned without devaluing prior education.
activities.rationale: Pennycook's analysis supports discussing textual ownership as situated; framing differences around educational practices rather than nationality avoids essentialising learners.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I cite the source, I can use its sentences.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Cited but unquoted strings of source wording; surprise at feedback.
difficulties.response: Show the double requirement: citation for the source of ideas, quotation marks for borrowed wording. Work with the learner's own text.

difficulties.pattern: 'I changed some words, so it's my paraphrase.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Synonym substitution with the source's sentence structure retained (patchwriting).
difficulties.response: Treat this as a stage: teach reading for understanding and writing from notes with the source closed. Do not use misconduct framing or punitive language for a first developmental instance, but do state the institutional standard clearly.

difficulties.pattern: 'Plagiarism only means copying words.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncited borrowing of a source's argument structure, examples or data.
difficulties.response: Use paired examples of idea and structure borrowing with and without attribution.

diagnostic.task: Show a cited but patchwritten paragraph and ask whether it is acceptable and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies retained wording and structure despite the citation, explains the need for quotation or genuine paraphrase, and distinguishes a developmental problem from deception.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a problem but cannot specify it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges it acceptable because it is cited.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: clear, non-threatening definitions with many examples and plenty of formative practice. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific forms such as code, data and images. PGR: authorship and idea attribution in collaborative research, and the standards applied to theses and publications.
reviewNotes: Whether intention bears on whether something counts as plagiarism, as opposed to the penalty, is contested and handled differently across institutions.

records.summary: Learners are often surprised that reusing their own work can be misconduct. In coursework the issue is assessment validity — each assessment should evidence new learning — and institutions differ in what they allow. In research writing, the ICMJE Recommendations require disclosure of overlapping publications, while some reuse of text (for example methods descriptions) may be acceptable with transparency; Bretag and Mahmud (2009) argue for distinguishing self-plagiarism from appropriate textual re-use. Teaching should centre on transparency and consulting the relevant policy.

activities.title: Reuse scenarios
learnerActions: Read four reuse scenarios ranging from coursework to publication
Find the relevant rule in the programme regulations or a journal's policy for each
Decide what must be disclosed, cited or permitted
Draft the sentence that discloses or cites the earlier work
activities.intendedInsight: Reuse is judged by the purpose of the new work and by transparency, not by whose words they are.
activities.rationale: Scenario work against actual policies builds the habit of checking rules rather than relying on intuition about ownership.

activities.title: Thesis to article (PGR)
learnerActions: Identify a thesis chapter or conference paper that could become an article
Check the target journal's policy on prior dissemination, preprints and deposited theses
Draft a cover-letter disclosure of related outputs
Discuss with a supervisor what counts as substantial new contribution
activities.intendedInsight: Moving work between genres is normal but requires disclosure and policy checks.
activities.rationale: Disclosure of related publications is a standard editorial requirement, and early-career researchers often do not know how to make it.

difficulties.pattern: 'It's my work, so I can use it however I like.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs from earlier assessed work reused without acknowledgement.
difficulties.response: Explain the assessment-validity rationale: the same work cannot evidence learning twice. Show how to build on earlier work by citing it, with permission where needed.

difficulties.pattern: 'I rewrote it a bit, so it counts as new.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Lightly revised versions of earlier assignments submitted as new work.
difficulties.response: Distinguish revision of wording from new analysis or contribution; refer to the regulations.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about whether conference papers, preprints or deposited theses count as prior publication.
difficulties.revealedBy: PGR writers either over-worry or fail to disclose related outputs.
difficulties.response: Show that policies differ by journal and field, and model checking author guidelines and asking editors.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Can you use material from your previous essay in this assignment?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Says it depends on the regulations and the brief, refers to permission and self-citation, and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows there are limits but cannot say where to check.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes reuse is always acceptable because the work is their own.

records.contextNotes: PG pre-sessional: an introduction to resubmission rules before the degree. UG in-sessional: resubmission rules, especially for students repeating modules or moving from foundation or pre-sessional programmes. PGT: reuse between assignments and the dissertation. PGR: text recycling in theses by publication, articles and grant applications; the genre work of turning thesis chapters into articles is covered in pub.thesis-to-article.

records.summary: Collusion is the integrity area in which learners' intentions are most often cooperative and in which the rules vary most between assessments. Bretag et al.'s (2014) student survey points to students' wish to be taught explicitly what is expected, and the integrity literature (Bretag, 2016) emphasises clear communication of collaboration boundaries. Teaching should use the actual assessment brief, present boundary scenarios, and frame legitimate collaboration positively so that learners do not withdraw from beneficial peer learning.

activities.title: Traffic-light scenarios
learnerActions: Read an assessment brief and its collaboration rules
Classify ten scenarios as green (permitted), amber (permitted if acknowledged or limited) or red (collusion)
Discuss disagreements and identify the information that would resolve them
Compare classifications under a different brief that permits group work
activities.intendedInsight: The same behaviour can be legitimate or collusive depending on the assessment's rules.
activities.rationale: Applying rules to scenarios makes tacit boundaries explicit, as students in the integrity literature request.

activities.title: Saying no and asking
learnerActions: Draft a friendly message declining a friend's request to see a finished essay, offering an alternative form of help
Draft a short email asking a tutor whether a particular kind of collaboration is allowed
Peer-review both for tone and clarity
Role-play the conversation
activities.intendedInsight: Protecting integrity can be done kindly and without damaging relationships.
activities.rationale: Learners often know the rule but lack the language to act on it in peer relationships.

difficulties.pattern: 'Sharing my essay is just helping; my friend won't copy it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Finished work shared 'for reference', with both students subsequently implicated.
difficulties.response: Show that both parties are usually treated as involved and that intention to help does not change what is submitted.

difficulties.pattern: 'In my previous studies we did homework together and handed in the same answers.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Identical answers or code in individual submissions.
difficulties.response: Validate collaborative learning, then distinguish discussing approaches from submitting shared answers in individually assessed work.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding all discussion with peers for fear of collusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners decline study groups or peer review; isolation.
difficulties.response: Present legitimate collaboration positively and show the many permitted forms.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You and a classmate discussed the essay question together. What can you share and what must you do separately?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes discussing ideas and sources from writing or sharing text, refers to the brief, and mentions acknowledging significant input where required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a general distinction but cannot apply it to specific cases.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Believes any shared work is fine if both understand it, or that any discussion is forbidden.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introduce through course tasks, since study groups are encouraged. UG in-sessional: lab reports, problem sets and code are the most frequent risk areas. PGT: group assessments with individual components and the boundary between them.

records.summary: Survey research by Bretag et al. (2019) associated contract cheating with students' perceptions that there were many opportunities to cheat and with dissatisfaction with the teaching and learning environment, which suggests addressing conditions and support rather than blaming particular groups. Newton's (2018) systematic review suggests that self-reported rates of commercial contract cheating have risen over time. Providers market directly to students, including through social media and messaging channels, so teaching should cover how to recognise their tactics and the legitimate routes to help.

activities.title: Deconstructing an advertisement
learnerActions: Analyse a constructed advertisement for 'model essays' and its language (guarantees, urgency, reassurance)
Identify what is actually being sold and what the terms omit
List the risks to the buyer, including data misuse and blackmail
Rewrite the advert as an honest description
activities.intendedInsight: Marketing language disguises outsourcing and hides the risks to the student.
activities.rationale: Critical reading of persuasive texts is an EAP skill in its own right and inoculates learners against approaches they are likely to receive.

activities.title: Map the alternatives
learnerActions: List the support services available on their course and how to access them
Match each problem a student might have (time, language, understanding the task) to a service
Find the institution's rules on proofreading and editing support
Share the map with the class
activities.intendedInsight: Most problems that lead to outsourcing have a legitimate solution if addressed early.
activities.rationale: Associations between contract cheating and dissatisfaction with the learning environment suggest that visible, accessible support is part of prevention.

difficulties.pattern: 'A model essay is just for reference, so buying one isn't cheating.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Bought 'model' essays submitted or closely adapted.
difficulties.response: Explain that submitting or adapting outsourced work is contract cheating regardless of what the provider calls it.

difficulties.pattern: 'My cousin wrote it for free, so that's not contract cheating.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Unpaid third-party authorship, including heavy 'editing' by others.
difficulties.response: Clarify that payment is not the criterion; authorship of the submitted work is.

difficulties.pattern: Desperation close to a deadline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report receiving or considering offers when overwhelmed.
difficulties.response: Normalise asking for help and give concrete routes, including extensions. Avoid fear-only messaging, which does not address the underlying pressure.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'A website offers you a custom essay written by an expert. What are the risks, and what could you do instead?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies academic, legal or financial, and blackmail and data risks, and names specific alternatives.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies academic penalties only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problem if the essay is 'original'.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: address early, as students may be contacted by providers soon after arrival. UG and PGT in-sessional: high-stakes periods such as dissertations and resits. In England, providing or advertising contract cheating services to students was made a criminal offence by the Skills and Post-16 Education Act 2022, and several other jurisdictions have similar laws; the legal position varies by country.
reviewNotes: The blackmail and data-misuse risks are widely reported in sector guidance but are not documented by a listed source; present them as reported risks. Legislation on contract cheating services differs by jurisdiction and changes; check the current position for the teaching context.

records.summary: Text-matching tools compare submissions with indexed sources and report overlaps; they do not identify plagiarism, cannot reliably detect paraphrased, translated or outsourced work, and include many legitimate matches. Pecorari (2013) cautions against letting software define good source use, and the Handbook of Academic Integrity (Bretag, 2016) stresses academic judgement in interpreting reports. Where institutions let students see formative reports, these can support learning about source use if learners are taught to read the matches rather than chase a percentage.

activities.title: Read the report, not the number
learnerActions: Examine two sample reports, one with a high percentage made up mainly of cited quotations and references and one with a low percentage hiding an uncited patchwrite
Classify each highlighted match by type
Decide which report shows a real problem
Explain why the overall percentage is misleading
activities.intendedInsight: The percentage carries no verdict; only interpretation of specific matches does.
activities.rationale: Directly counters the belief that a threshold separates plagiarism from originality.

activities.title: Fix the source use, not the match
learnerActions: Take a flagged patchwritten passage from a formative report
Reread the source, close it, and note its main idea in their own words
Rewrite the passage from the notes and add the citation
Compare with a version produced by synonym substitution and discuss the difference in quality
activities.intendedInsight: Revising from understanding produces better writing, whereas rewording to lower a score produces worse writing and may still be plagiarism.
activities.rationale: Patchwriting is best addressed by developing reading-to-write processes rather than by surface rewording.

difficulties.pattern: 'My score is under 15%, so I'm safe.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners citing a numeric threshold; no review of individual matches.
difficulties.response: Explain that there is no universal threshold and that a low score can hide problems; review matches together.

difficulties.pattern: Changing words or using paraphrasing tools until the highlighting disappears.
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward synonym-substituted text, sometimes with distorted meaning.
difficulties.response: Show the quality cost and the integrity risk, and teach rewriting from understanding.

difficulties.pattern: Panic at any highlighted text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Anxious questions about correctly quoted and referenced material being highlighted.
difficulties.response: Show that quotations, reference entries and common phrases are expected matches.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your report says 35%. Is that plagiarism?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Says it depends on what the matches are, explains how to check them, and notes that people, not software, decide.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows a percentage is not a verdict but cannot explain how to interpret matches.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the percentage as a verdict.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: teacher-guided interpretation of sample reports. UG pre-sessional: formative use of reports on the learner's own drafts where permitted. PG pre-sessional: interpretation in longer literature-based work, and how reports are used in degree programmes. UG and PGT in-sessional: department practices and what happens when a report raises concern; a score never establishes misconduct. PGR: thesis and publication screening, including matches to the writer's own earlier outputs.
reviewNotes: Institutions differ in whether students may view reports before final submission and in how reports are used.

records.summary: Learners often discover integrity procedures only when facing a concern about their work, when anxiety and unfamiliar terminology can lead to poor decisions. Bretag et al. (2014) found variation in students' awareness of integrity policy and support and argued for educative approaches, and making the process explicit is part of that education. Multilingual students are disproportionately exposed to false positives from similarity and detection software, so knowing procedural rights matters: the institution must establish any allegation, software indicators and differences in style are not evidence on their own, and students should be able to see the evidence and respond in a usable language and format. Because procedures, terminology and outcomes vary between institutions, teaching should be built around the learner's own institution's documents and support services.

activities.title: Policy scavenger hunt
learnerActions: Locate the institution's integrity policy and a module's assessment rules

Find answers to set questions: definitions, stages, who decides and on what evidence, possible outcomes, and rights to see the evidence, respond, be accompanied, request language support or adjustments, and appeal
Summarise the process as a flowchart that marks each right and support point
Compare flowcharts in groups and correct errors
activities.intendedInsight: The process is knowable and staged, and it includes rights and support at each stage.
activities.rationale: Explicit engagement with the real policy addresses the uneven policy awareness reported in survey research.

activities.title: Responding to a meeting invitation
learnerActions: Read a constructed invitation letter
Identify the concern, the evidence referred to, the deadline and the support available
List what they are entitled to ask for: the evidence, the relevant policy, an explanation of any software indicator, an adviser, interpreting or accessible formats
Draft a short, factual reply confirming attendance and requesting the information and support they need
activities.intendedInsight: A calm, prompt and factual response, with support, is in the student's interest.
activities.rationale: Rehearsing the genre before it is needed is intended to reduce anxiety and support appropriate formality (a practitioner proposal); Bretag (2016) is cited for the educative approach to integrity, not for this effect.

difficulties.pattern: Ignoring or delaying a response out of fear.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missed deadlines in the process; reports of avoiding email.
difficulties.response: Normalise seeking advice early and show where independent advice is available.

difficulties.pattern: 'The software has already decided I'm guilty.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Belief that a similarity or AI-detection score is the verdict.
difficulties.response: Explain the role of academic judgement, that indicators and differences in style are not evidence of misconduct on their own, and the learner's right to see and respond to the evidence.

difficulties.pattern: Writing an over-apologetic admission or an aggressive denial.
difficulties.revealedBy: Draft replies with inappropriate tone or claims not supported by evidence.
difficulties.response: Model a factual, courteous register and advise seeking support before writing statements.

difficulties.pattern: Invitation letters written in dense regulatory language, with short deadlines and no mention of evidence, support, interpreting or adjustments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners unable to say what is alleged or what they may bring; requests for help decoding the letter.
difficulties.response: Institutions should state the concern, the evidence, the timeline and the learner's rights in plain language and accessible formats. Teachers can help learners decode letters and request clarification, more time or support, and should point them to independent advice.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Where would you find your institution's academic integrity policy, what are the main stages if a concern is raised, and what are you entitled to see and ask for?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the policy and summarises its stages, who must establish the case, and the rights to see the evidence, respond with support and appeal.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows the policy exists but describes the process or rights vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know where the policy is, assumes outcomes are automatic, or believes the student must prove their innocence.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: an overview of the process, rights and support, with emphasis on prevention. UG pre-sessional: the policies and rights that will apply in the degree, and how they may differ from the pre-sessional provider's. PG pre-sessional: the same, plus how integrity processes interact with AI-use declarations in extended work. UG and PGT in-sessional: module-level rules and processes. PGR: research misconduct procedures, which are usually separate from student misconduct procedures. Rights, terminology and routes vary: some systems have an external complaints body after internal procedures (for example the Office of the Independent Adjudicator for students at universities in England and Wales). Disabled learners may need adjustments to meetings, such as questions in writing in advance.
reviewNotes: Terminology (for example 'academic misconduct', 'poor academic practice') and procedures vary substantially between institutions; examples should be localised.
Review response: R5-04 procedural rights are added to the description, mastery evidence, assessment prompt, summary, activities and an institutional difficulty.

records.summary: Integrity breaches are often decisions made under acute pressure rather than planned deception. Bretag et al. (2019) associated contract cheating with perceived opportunity and dissatisfaction with the teaching and learning environment, which points to institutional conditions and support, not only individual choices, as levers for prevention. Self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002) supports the planning and monitoring that can reduce the crises in which shortcuts become tempting. Teaching should normalise asking for extensions and support and make procedures concrete before learners need them, while teachers and programme teams check that briefs are clear, deadlines are not needlessly bunched and support is easy to find.

activities.title: Deadline map
learnerActions: Map all assessment deadlines for the term on one calendar
Identify clusters and back-plan milestones
Mark the extension and extenuating-circumstances deadlines and procedures
Identify one support service to contact at each risk point
activities.intendedInsight: Many crises are predictable and can be prevented or managed through procedures.
activities.rationale: Forethought and planning are core phases of self-regulated learning.

activities.title: Write the email now
learnerActions: Draft an extension request for a realistic scenario
Peer-review for clarity, mitigation and evidence
Save it as a template
Discuss what makes requesting help difficult and how to overcome it
activities.intendedInsight: Requesting help is a normal, procedural act.
activities.rationale: Preparing the request in advance lowers the barrier to using legitimate options when pressure arrives.

difficulties.pattern: 'Asking for an extension shows weakness or will lower my grade.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners do not seek extensions even when eligible.
difficulties.response: Explain the procedures and that eligible requests are routine; share anonymised examples.

difficulties.pattern: Not knowing that extenuating-circumstances processes exist, or missing their deadlines.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late claims; surprise that support was available, especially among learners whose previous institutions had no equivalent procedure.
difficulties.response: Teach the procedures explicitly early in the course.

difficulties.pattern: Starting assignments too late and finishing under extreme time pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Work submitted at the deadline; patterns of late-night drafting.
difficulties.response: Use milestone planning and check-ins; avoid moralising, which does not change planning behaviour.

difficulties.pattern: Unclear briefs, deadlines bunched across modules, and support that is hard to find or offered only at times or in formats some learners cannot use.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many learners in a cohort asking the same clarification questions; requests for extensions clustering around the same week; low uptake of support by part-time, commuting or disabled learners.
difficulties.response: For programme teams: clarify briefs, coordinate deadlines and publicise support in accessible formats and at accessible times. For learners: name the problem and ask for clarification or adjustment early, which is a legitimate request rather than special pleading.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'If you were ill the week before a deadline, what exactly would you do and by when?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the specific procedure, evidence, deadline and contact.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Would email the tutor but does not know the formal procedure.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would try to finish somehow or does not know any options.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introduce procedures early; pre-sessional deadlines are intense and progression stakes are high, and PG pre-sessional learners often combine study with work or family responsibilities. UG and PGT in-sessional: dissertation periods, part-time work and caring responsibilities. PGR: revisit for long-term workload, supervision relationships and wellbeing. Learners with disabilities or long-term conditions may have support plans that include extensions; make sure they know how to use them.
reviewNotes: Review response: R5-04 is addressed by placing risk conditions alongside institutional responsibilities in the description, mastery evidence, summary and an institutional difficulty.

records.summary: Fanelli's (2009) meta-analysis of survey data found that about 2% of scientists admitted fabricating or falsifying data at least once and up to about a third admitted other questionable research practices, with higher rates reported for colleagues' behaviour. For research students the main risks are rarely outright fabrication but undisclosed analytic flexibility, poor record-keeping and authorship disputes. Teaching should use discipline-relevant cases, link to codes of conduct such as the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, institutional and funder codes and, in medicine, the ICMJE Recommendations, and emphasise transparent reporting.

activities.title: Grey-zone cases
learnerActions: Read four short cases from their discipline (data exclusion, image adjustment, selective citation, authorship order)
Classify each as acceptable, a questionable practice or misconduct
Identify the relevant code of conduct provision
Propose transparent alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Most integrity risks lie in grey zones where transparency is the remedy.
activities.rationale: Fanelli's findings show questionable practices are far more common than fabrication, so teaching should focus on them.

activities.title: Data trail audit
learnerActions: Map how one result in their own project moves from raw data to the reported figure
Identify where records, versions or decisions are missing
Set up a simple versioning and record-keeping system
Write a transparent methods note on any exclusions or deviations
activities.intendedInsight: Good records make results checkable and protect the researcher.
activities.rationale: Verifiability depends on documented data handling.

difficulties.pattern: 'Removing data that doesn't fit is just cleaning.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Undocumented exclusions; results that change after exclusion.
difficulties.response: Distinguish pre-specified, justified exclusion from outcome-driven exclusion, and require reporting of both.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to question a supervisor's or senior colleague's practice.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report discomfort but take no action.
difficulties.response: Discuss courage as an integrity value and identify confidential advice routes.

difficulties.pattern: 'Research integrity just means not plagiarising.'
difficulties.revealedBy: No awareness of fabrication, falsification or questionable practices.
difficulties.response: Introduce fabrication, falsification and questionable practices with field examples.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain the difference between falsification and a questionable research practice, with an example from their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate distinction with a field-specific example and a transparent alternative.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Defines falsification but cannot identify questionable practices.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates research integrity with avoiding plagiarism.

records.contextNotes: PG pre-sessional: an introduction to fabrication, falsification and questionable practices for learners entering research-based programmes. UG in-sessional: lab reports and final-year projects (honest reporting of results, including failed experiments). PGT: dissertation data and ethics. PGR: full codes of conduct, data management plans and publication ethics.

records.summary: Present critical thinking as a contested construct. Facione's Delphi consensus describes it as purposeful, self-regulatory judgement combining cognitive skills (interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, self-regulation) with dispositions such as inquisitiveness and fair-mindedness, whereas Moore's interviews with academics in history, philosophy and cultural studies found several partly incompatible understandings, from judgement and scepticism to self-reflexivity and ethical stance. Atkinson's critique — that critical thinking is a tacit social practice that is hard to teach as a generic skill — is a useful caution against decontextualised checklists, though his account of learners' cultural backgrounds has itself been challenged as over-generalising. The practical implication is to make each discipline's and task's version of criticality explicit through exemplars, never to treat it as a trait some groups lack.

activities.title: Decoding 'be more critical'
learnerActions: Collect anonymised tutor comments and marking-criteria phrases that mention 'critical' or 'criticality' from their own or sample modules
Sort them into categories such as questioning evidence, comparing views, evaluating methods, applying theory and acknowledging limitations
Compare categories across two disciplines represented in the class
Rewrite one comment as a concrete revision action for a specific paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: 'Critical' names several different moves whose mix varies by discipline and task, and each can be identified and practised.
activities.rationale: Moore's finding that academics hold several distinct conceptions of critical thinking suggests learners need to decode the local meaning rather than learn a single definition.

activities.title: Critical is not the same as criticising
learnerActions: Read three responses to the same short text: one purely negative, one descriptive, one evaluative with reasoned strengths and limitations
Rank the responses and justify the ranking in pairs
Draft a class working definition of critical engagement and test it against a new response
activities.intendedInsight: Critical engagement includes acknowledging strengths, qualifying judgements and giving reasons; negativity alone is not criticality.
activities.rationale: Facione's consensus statement places fair-mindedness and judiciousness alongside analytical skills, which counters the common equation of 'critical' with 'negative'.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means saying what is wrong with the article.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses that list only weaknesses, often with disproportionate or ungrounded criticism and no acknowledgement of strengths or scope.
difficulties.response: Model evaluative balance and require at least one supported strength and one supported limitation in early tasks; show marker comments that reward measured judgement.

difficulties.pattern: 'In my previous exams, marks came from reproducing the textbook accurately, so I'm not sure when I'm allowed to evaluate a source.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate summaries with no comment and heavy hedging whenever a published source is discussed; common among novice university writers of all backgrounds, including first-language English students, when assessment has rewarded reproduction.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a difference in assessment genres and in the licence to question, not in ability: point out the evaluation learners already do in other domains, show that evaluating published work is an expected and licensed move in the target context, and teach mitigated forms of critique. Do not frame learners' educational backgrounds as lacking critical thinking or contrast 'Western' and 'non-Western' thinkers; such framings are native-speakerist and over-generalise (Holliday, 2006).

difficulties.pattern: 'Critical thinking is a general skill, so the same checklist works for every subject.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Applying the same generic questions (e.g. 'Is the author biased?') to a proof, a lab report and a novel regardless of relevance.
difficulties.response: Compare what counts as a critical move in two disciplines using exemplars, and have learners adapt a generic question list for their own field.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in two or three sentences what 'critical' means in an assignment brief from their target discipline, and to give one example of a critical move they could make in that assignment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific, discipline-relevant move (e.g. questioning whether a case study's findings generalise) and distinguishes it from opinion or negativity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a generic formula such as 'analyse, don't describe' without a concrete example tied to the task.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates being critical with criticising the source or with giving a personal opinion.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, keep the focus on concrete, low-stakes evaluation of familiar texts and data. UG pre-sessional courses should tie the concept to progression criteria; on PG pre-sessional courses it is core because master's and research programmes weight criticality heavily. It is also core in undergraduate in-sessional work, best embedded with subject tutors using module exemplars, and for PGT learners, who need rapid recalibration from the first assignment. PGR learners revisit it as criticality shades into originality and positioning within a field.
reviewNotes: Whether critical thinking is generic or discipline-specific remains contested; this record takes the position that it has both general and discipline-specific components and should be taught with disciplinary exemplars.

records.summary: Teach the distinction with learners' own texts and disciplinary exemplars rather than as an abstract hierarchy. The revised Bloom taxonomy supplies useful verbs for each move, but its ordering is a heuristic rather than a developmental ladder, and analysis and evaluation are interdependent in practice. Bereiter and Scardamalia's contrast between knowledge telling and knowledge transforming explains why fluent description can still read as 'not answering the question', and Wingate's work shows that students are often told to be less descriptive without being shown what the alternative looks like.

activities.title: Colour-coding exemplars
learnerActions: Highlight descriptive, analytical and evaluative sentences in a higher-graded and a lower-graded exemplar paragraph from the target discipline
Estimate the rough proportion of each move in both paragraphs
Discuss how description is used in the higher-graded paragraph to set up analysis and evaluation
activities.intendedInsight: Higher-graded texts do not eliminate description; they subordinate it to analytical and evaluative points.
activities.rationale: Analysing exemplars makes tacit expectations visible; Wingate notes that students rarely receive explicit models of what tutors mean by argument or by 'less description'.

activities.title: The 'how, why, so what' ladder
learnerActions: Take a descriptive statement (e.g. a figure from a table or a source's main finding)
Add a sentence answering 'how or why?' and then one answering 'so what, and how good is it?'
Compare ladders with a partner and identify which added sentences are genuinely analytical or evaluative
activities.intendedInsight: Analysis and evaluation are produced by asking specific questions of the description, not by adding more information.
activities.rationale: The activity models the shift from knowledge telling to knowledge transforming that Bereiter and Scardamalia associate with mature composing.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I include more facts and more sources, my essay will be more analytical.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Longer redrafts with more summarised sources that receive the same 'too descriptive' feedback.
difficulties.response: Show that analysis is a relation (cause, comparison, implication) between items, not more items; set a word cap on description in practice paragraphs and require one 'because' or 'which suggests' per point.

difficulties.pattern: 'Evaluation means giving my personal opinion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'I think this is a good article' with no criteria, often carried over from test or school essays that reward stated opinion.
difficulties.response: Distinguish opinion from criterion-based judgement; give lists of discipline-relevant criteria (validity, relevance, scope, consistency) and require each evaluation to name one.

difficulties.pattern: Learners label moves accurately in others' texts but drift back into description in their own drafts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Good performance on labelling tasks alongside largely descriptive extended writing produced under time and language pressure.
difficulties.response: Have learners reverse-outline their own draft, labelling each paragraph's dominant move, and revise one paragraph at a time. Do not respond by banning description, which is needed to establish what is being analysed.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three sentences about a simple bar chart or a short source extract: one descriptive, one analytical and one evaluative.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Three clearly different moves: the analytical sentence offers a reason or relationship, and the evaluative sentence applies a stated criterion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Analysis and evaluation are blurred, or the evaluative sentence is an unsupported opinion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Three descriptive sentences differing only in the detail reported.

records.contextNotes: The topic is core at foundation and on UG and PG pre-sessional courses, where "too descriptive" feedback first appears; at foundation, use familiar topics and simple data so that language load does not mask the conceptual distinction, and on pre-sessional courses connect it to progression-task criteria. In undergraduate in-sessional settings, use module exemplars because the appropriate balance varies by genre (a results section is legitimately descriptive). PGT learners revisit it quickly because master's criteria weight evaluation heavily.
reviewNotes: The proportion of description that is acceptable varies strongly by genre and discipline; no single ratio should be taught.
