Review response: R6-13 lists the 'Reports and essays' link as decorative. It is kept, downgraded to 'related', because that scale's B2–C1 range concerns evaluating ideas and giving reasons, which is this topic's central distinction; no more specific CEFR scale covers analytical and evaluative moves in writing.

records.summary: Questioning links the dispositional side of critical thinking in Facione's consensus (inquisitiveness, open-mindedness, self-regulation) to concrete reading, writing and discussion. Compact question sets, such as Wallace and Wray's critical synopsis questions for postgraduate reading, and Walton's critical questions attached to common argument types, are useful scaffolds; reciprocal teaching illustrates the value of routines that are modelled and then handed over (Palincsar & Brown, 1984). Teach a small set, model its use on a text, and then have learners select and adapt questions to their discipline and purpose rather than run full checklists. Language support matters too: learners who can form indirect and mitigated questions are better placed to ask them aloud or in writing in seminars, supervision and peer review.

activities.title: Question storming, then pruning
learnerActions: In pairs, generate as many questions as possible about a short abstract in four minutes without evaluating them
Categorise the questions (comprehension, evidence, method, scope, assumption, implication, own position)
Prune to the three questions most useful for a given assignment and explain the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Not all questions are equally productive; the most useful critical questions target evidence, reasoning and relevance to the task.
activities.rationale: Separating generation from selection is intended to build fluency and then judgement; the categories echo the critical questions Wallace and Wray propose for postgraduate readers.

activities.title: Applying and adapting a question set
learnerActions: Apply a five-question set (purpose, claims, evidence, assumptions, usefulness) to a short text from their field and answer each question with reference to the text
Discuss which questions were most productive for this text and which needed rewording for the discipline
Rewrite the set as a personal version for their own field and test it on a second text
activities.intendedInsight: A question set makes critical reading manageable, but it is most useful when adapted to the text, the discipline and the purpose.
activities.rationale: Adapts Wallace and Wray's critical synopsis approach; handing the set over for adaptation follows the modelling-then-transfer logic of reciprocal teaching.

activities.title: Questioning my own claim
learnerActions: Write a one-sentence claim for a current assignment
Swap with a partner who asks 'How do you know? According to whom? Always? Compared with what?'
Revise the claim and note which question prompted each change
activities.intendedInsight: Turning critical questions on one's own claims anticipates readers' objections and improves calibration.
activities.rationale: Facione's consensus identifies self-regulation — applying critical skills to one's own reasoning — as a core component of critical thinking.

difficulties.pattern: 'I don't have any questions — I understood the text.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence when invited to question a reading; reading logs and question lists containing only comprehension questions that can be answered by locating information in the text.
difficulties.response: Reframe questions as contributions rather than admissions of confusion. Contrast comprehension and evaluative questions on the same text, model a tutor questioning a text they fully understand, and provide question stems.

difficulties.pattern: Questions that sound like accusations ('Why is your sample so small?') or are buried in a long preamble, so that the question is not heard.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive responses from peers or tutors, questions that go unanswered, and learners who decide to keep their questions to themselves.
difficulties.response: Teach a small set of question frames ('It is not clear how…', 'I wondered whether…', 'How would the findings change if…?') and practise them first in writing, for example in a shared document or chat, before seminars. Accept written questions as legitimate participation, which also suits learners for whom real-time oral turns are difficult (for example some autistic learners, people who stammer and anxious speakers). Do not treat spontaneous oral questioning as the only evidence of the skill.

difficulties.pattern: Applying the same full checklist, or generic questions such as 'Is the author biased?', to every text regardless of purpose.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, uniform question lists and formulaic answers across very different texts, many irrelevant to the task, with no follow-up.
difficulties.response: Require learners to choose a small number of questions for a stated purpose and discipline, adapt their wording to the text, and act on at least one.

diagnostic.task: Give a 100-word source extract and a purpose, and ask for five questions the learner would want answered before citing it, followed by answers to two of them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Questions target evidence, scope, assumptions or implications and are relevant to the stated purpose; the answers are grounded in the text.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A mixture of comprehension questions and generic ones such as 'Is the author biased?' with little link to this text, or evaluative questions answered from opinion rather than the text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Only vocabulary or comprehension questions, or none.

records.contextNotes: At foundation, where the topic is core, use question stems and short, accessible texts on familiar topics. On UG pre-sessional courses, link questioning to reading-into-writing tasks and seminar preparation; on PG pre-sessional courses, extend the question set to research articles (design, sample, generalisability) and to critical synopses. Undergraduate in-sessional learners apply it to module readings and seminars; PGT learners to research designs and methods; PGR learners are assumed to question habitually and mainly adapt question sets to the norms of their field and to self-questioning before supervision.
reviewNotes: Reciprocal teaching was developed and tested with younger readers; it is cited here as a model of modelling and handing over questioning routines, not as evidence of outcomes for adult EAP learners.

records.summary: Teach evidence as fit-for-claim rather than as a fixed ranking. Sackett and colleagues' account of evidence-based medicine is useful precisely because it rejects 'cookbook' reliance on any one design and integrates research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values; Walton's treatment of argument from expert opinion shows that testimony is defeasible and can be tested with critical questions. Becher and Trowler's account of disciplinary cultures explains why historians, engineers and clinicians weight textual, experimental and clinical evidence differently, so examples should come from learners' target fields.

activities.title: Matching evidence to claims
learnerActions: Match eight evidence cards (anecdote, survey, trial, interview study, archival document, expert statement, etc.) to four claims of different types
Explain each match and identify mismatches
Discuss which matches would change in a different discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Evidential strength depends on the claim being made, not on a universal ranking of evidence types.
activities.rationale: Sackett and colleagues stress that the best evidence depends on the question asked, which counters rigid hierarchy thinking.

activities.title: Testing an expert
learnerActions: Read a media article that quotes an expert
Apply questions about the expert's field, consistency with other experts and the evidence behind the statement
Decide how much weight the quotation could carry in an essay
activities.intendedInsight: Authority is not the same as evidence; expert testimony is only as strong as the answers to these questions.
activities.rationale: Walton presents argument from expert opinion as a presumptive scheme with critical questions that can defeat it.

difficulties.pattern: 'It was published in a top journal by a well-known expert, so it must be strong evidence for my claim.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims justified by the prestige of the source or author rather than by what the source reports; quotations from authorities used in place of data.
difficulties.response: Use the critical questions for arguments from expert opinion and have learners state what evidence the cited source actually reports; distinguish the standing of a source from the strength of the evidence it provides for this particular claim.

difficulties.pattern: 'Numbers are always stronger than interviews.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissing qualitative studies as 'just opinions'; preferring any statistic regardless of design.
difficulties.response: Use claim-type matching and qualitative exemplars from learners' fields to show what each evidence type can establish.

difficulties.pattern: Reporting a source's conclusion as if it were the evidence ('Smith (2019) proves that…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations used as bare assertions, with no indication of what data the source reported.
difficulties.response: Have learners trace one cited claim back to the data reported in the source and rewrite the sentence to show the evidence.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What would count as good evidence that recorded lectures reduce attendance? What would not count?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names comparative attendance data and design issues (comparison groups, timing) and explains why anecdote or opinion is insufficient.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names relevant data but cannot explain why anecdote is weak or overlooks the need for comparison.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Offers opinions or a single example as evidence.

records.contextNotes: The topic is core at foundation, where learners work with everyday and news claims, and on PG pre-sessional courses, where research evidence and design first become central. UG pre-sessional learners develop it in source-based writing. Undergraduate in-sessional work should use disciplinary norms; PGT learners engage with research designs and, in health fields, formal evidence hierarchies; PGR learners revisit it when justifying the evidence their own designs produce.
reviewNotes: Evidence hierarchies are field-specific; teachers outside health sciences should not present an evidence-based medicine pyramid as universal.

records.summary: Introduce inference types through disciplinary examples — a legal syllogism, a generalisation from a survey, a diagnostic or historical explanation — rather than formal notation. Walton's account of presumptive, defeasible reasoning shows that most everyday and academic arguments are not deductively valid yet can still be reasonable, and Toulmin's critique of the formal-logic ideal makes the same point from a different direction. The practical pay-off in EAP is calibration: the type of inference determines how strongly a conclusion can be worded.

activities.title: Same scenario, three inferences
learnerActions: Take a scenario such as falling library visits
Write a deductive, an inductive and an abductive argument about it
Compare how certain each conclusion can be and adjust the wording accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: The inference pattern sets the ceiling on how confidently a conclusion can be stated.
activities.rationale: Walton distinguishes deductive, inductive and presumptive reasoning by the kind of support each provides, which maps directly onto hedging choices.

activities.title: Rival explanations
learnerActions: In groups, generate at least three explanations for a reported research finding
Identify what evidence would help decide between them
Write a conclusion that states the preferred explanation and acknowledges the alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Inference to the best explanation requires considering and eliminating alternatives, not just finding one plausible story.
activities.rationale: Toulmin's account of qualifiers and rebuttals frames conclusions as holding unless specific conditions apply, which this activity makes concrete.

difficulties.pattern: 'Inductive conclusions are weak because they are not proven.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissing empirical findings as 'just a theory'; demanding proof where only probable support is possible.
difficulties.response: Discuss probabilistic strength and how empirical disciplines rely on induction and abduction; contrast 'not certain' with 'not supported'.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'prove' or 'deduce' for any inference ('This proves that…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Overclaiming verbs in reports of empirical findings.
difficulties.response: Teach a graded set of inference verbs (suggest, indicate, support, demonstrate) and when each fits; note that 'prove' is appropriate in mathematics and formal logic.

diagnostic.task: Give the argument 'Every participant in this study improved after the training, so the training works for all students' and ask what kind of reasoning it is and how it could fail.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies it as inductive generalisation; notes sample size and representativeness, lack of comparison group and possible counter-cases; proposes a hedged conclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies one weakness but not the inference type, or vice versa.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the conclusion as proven.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, emphasise calibration and hedging rather than terminology. Undergraduate learners meet discipline-specific inference (legal reasoning, hypothesis testing). PGT learners connect inference types to research designs and generalisability; PGR learners, particularly in qualitative fields, may need to articulate abductive reasoning in their methodology.
reviewNotes: 'Abduction' is unfamiliar to many disciplinary tutors; 'inference to the best explanation' may be a more transparent label in teaching materials.

records.summary: Treat this as statistical literacy with a strong linguistic dimension. Gal's model of adult statistical literacy pairs knowledge of how data are produced with critical 'worry questions' about design and interpretation, and Creswell and Creswell's account of experimental, quasi-experimental and correlational designs gives learners a vocabulary for judging which claims a design supports. Linking the concept directly to causal verbs and hedges (cause, lead to, is associated with, may contribute to) turns a reading insight into a writing habit.

activities.title: Find the third variable
learnerActions: Examine a deliberately spurious correlation (e.g. ice-cream sales and drowning) and identify the confounder
Repeat with two realistic findings from education or health research
Propose a design that could test whether the relationship is causal
activities.intendedInsight: A correlation leaves several explanations open; design choices are what narrow them down.
activities.rationale: Gal argues that statistically literate adults need critical questions about how data were produced before accepting conclusions drawn from them.

activities.title: From paper to press release
learnerActions: Compare the abstract of a correlational study with a news report of it
Highlight every causal verb or phrase in both
Rewrite the news headline so that it matches what the study design supports
activities.intendedInsight: Causal language often inflates as findings are reported second-hand, and the writer is responsible for calibrating it.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell's distinction between experimental and non-experimental designs provides the criterion for deciding which causal wording is justified.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study found a significant relationship, so X causes Y.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Causal verbs used to report correlational findings in summaries and literature reviews.
difficulties.response: Practise matching claim wording to design; ask 'What design was this?' before every causal verb.

difficulties.pattern: 'Correlation tells us nothing about causes.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissing all observational evidence after instruction on confounding.
difficulties.response: Discuss how converging observational evidence, dose–response patterns and natural experiments can support causal conclusions even without randomised trials.

difficulties.pattern: Defaulting to 'cause' or 'effect' because few alternative causal expressions are available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate understanding in discussion but repetitive, overstrong causal wording in writing.
difficulties.response: Teach a graded repertoire of causal and associative expressions and practise choosing among them; avoid simply correcting 'cause' without offering alternatives.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Countries with more universities have higher average incomes. Would building more universities raise incomes?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes possible confounding and reverse causation and suggests what kind of evidence or design could test the causal claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says 'not necessarily' but cannot name a mechanism for the alternative explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the causal reading without qualification.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners apply the topic to news and source reading. Undergraduates in social, health and life sciences need it for module reading; PGT learners for research-methods modules and critical appraisal; PGR learners for framing their own causal claims and limitations.
reviewNotes: Formal causal-inference frameworks (e.g. counterfactual and directed acyclic graph approaches) are beyond general EAP scope but may matter for PGR learners in quantitative fields.

records.summary: Follow Walton's dialectical approach, in which a fallacy is an argumentation scheme used in a way that blocks or distorts reasonable dialogue; many patterns that appear on fallacy lists (appeal to expertise, argument from consequences, attacks on credibility) are often reasonable in context. Johnson and Blair's tradition of teaching fallacies alongside criteria of relevance, sufficiency and acceptability keeps the focus on why an argument fails. In EAP, the most useful fallacies are those that occur in students' own source use: straw-man summaries, hasty generalisation from single studies and false dilemmas in thesis statements.

activities.title: Legitimate or fallacious?
learnerActions: Examine pairs of near-identical arguments, one reasonable and one fallacious
Decide which is fallacious and state the feature of the context that decides it
Write a rule of thumb for when that pattern is acceptable
activities.intendedInsight: Context and relevance, not surface form, determine whether an argument is fallacious.
activities.rationale: Walton treats fallacies as context-dependent misuses of argumentation schemes rather than as intrinsically invalid forms.

activities.title: Straw-man audit
learnerActions: Compare their summary of a source's argument with the original
Check whether the version they rebut is the one the source actually holds
Ask a partner to verify and suggest a fairer formulation
activities.intendedInsight: Fallacies are not only something others commit; misrepresenting sources is a common fallacy in student writing.
activities.rationale: Johnson and Blair's criteria of relevance and acceptability provide a practical test for whether a rebuttal engages the real position.

difficulties.pattern: 'That's ad hominem!' — applied to any comment about a person.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mislabelling relevant credibility concerns as fallacies; labels given without explanation.
difficulties.response: Require an explanation of why the move is irrelevant to the claim; use paired legitimate and fallacious examples.

difficulties.pattern: 'I couldn't find any fallacies, so the argument is strong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations that consist only of fallacy-hunting, ignoring evidence quality and warrants.
difficulties.response: Present fallacy recognition as one part of argument evaluation alongside judging evidence and reasoning; return to the structure of the argument.

diagnostic.task: Present the thesis 'Either universities ban AI writing tools completely or academic integrity will collapse' and ask what is wrong with it and how to repair it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies a false dilemma (and possibly slippery slope), proposes intermediate options and rewrites a qualified thesis.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes that it is exaggerated but does not identify the structure or offer a repair.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the thesis or simply disagrees with its conclusion.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners meet fallacies mainly through argumentative essays and source summaries. Undergraduates use them in debate and critical reviews; PGT learners in evaluating policy and practice literature, where false dilemmas and hasty generalisations are common.
reviewNotes: Fallacy taxonomies vary across textbooks; teach a small, high-yield set rather than an exhaustive list.

records.summary: Nickerson's review shows confirmation bias operating across many contexts — in how people seek, interpret and remember evidence — and Kahneman's dual-process account explains why fast, intuitive judgement produces predictable errors. Kahneman himself notes that knowing about biases offers limited protection against them, so teaching should centre on procedures embedded in reading and research tasks rather than on memorising lists of named biases. Link the topic to searching and synthesis, where confirmation bias does its most consequential damage in student work.

activities.title: Search for the opposite
learnerActions: Rerun the search behind a current assignment and note the terms used
Design and run a search intended to find evidence against the thesis
Compare the two result sets and decide whether the thesis needs qualifying
activities.intendedInsight: Search terms often presuppose conclusions; deliberately seeking disconfirming evidence changes what one finds.
activities.rationale: Nickerson documents confirmation bias in the way people seek evidence, which a counter-search procedure directly addresses.

activities.title: Criteria before reading
learnerActions: Before reading a set of abstracts, write down criteria for 'strong evidence'
Rate each abstract against the criteria
Compare ratings given to congenial and uncongenial findings and discuss any differences
activities.intendedInsight: People tend to apply looser standards to evidence they agree with; fixing criteria in advance reduces this.
activities.rationale: Kahneman's account suggests that structured procedures are more reliable than intention for checking intuitive judgement.

difficulties.pattern: 'I know about my biases, so I am objective.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims of neutrality alongside one-sided source selection.
difficulties.response: Emphasise procedures over awareness; have peers review each other's source lists for missing counter-positions.

difficulties.pattern: Calling any source one disagrees with 'biased'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissive evaluations with no evidence of distortion.
difficulties.response: Distinguish cognitive bias in reasoning from a source's perspective or interests, and require evidence of actual skew before the label is used.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how confirmation bias might affect a literature review and what they would do about it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes effects at search, selection and interpretation stages and proposes at least one concrete safeguard.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an accurate definition but no application or safeguard.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Confuses confirmation bias with prejudice against groups or with a source's political stance.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, introduce biases through source selection in the extended writing project. Undergraduates apply them in projects and dissertations; PGT learners in literature reviews and research design; PGR learners in systematic searching, analysis and, where relevant, pre-registration.
reviewNotes: Some studies reported in Kahneman (2011), particularly on behavioural priming, have not replicated well; avoid those examples.
Evidence that general debiasing training transfers to new contexts is limited; activities are proposed as task-embedded routines.

records.summary: Kuhn's interviews found that many adults struggled to generate alternative theories or counter-arguments to their own views, suggesting that perspective-taking needs explicit practice rather than being assumed. Facione's consensus lists fair-mindedness among critical-thinking dispositions, and Andrews shows that much argument in higher education proceeds by weighing positions rather than simply defending one. Teach representation (accurate, charitable, attributed) and weighing (criteria-based) as separate steps, because learners often list views without evaluating them.

activities.title: Steel-manning
learnerActions: Write the strongest version of a view they reject
Ask a partner who holds or role-plays that view to rate its fairness
Revise the summary until the partner accepts it, then write a response to it
activities.intendedInsight: Fair representation takes deliberate effort and makes subsequent rebuttal more credible.
activities.rationale: Kuhn found counter-argument and alternative-theory generation to be weak argument skills, which suggests deliberate practice is needed.

activities.title: Perspective grid
learnerActions: Complete a grid of stakeholders or disciplines against their claims, underlying values and evidence, using course readings
Choose one criterion (e.g. effectiveness, equity) for weighing the perspectives
Write a paragraph that weighs two perspectives against that criterion
activities.intendedInsight: Perspectives differ in values as well as evidence, and naming a criterion makes it possible to weigh them.
activities.rationale: The activity combines Facione's fair-mindedness disposition with the weighing of positions that Andrews identifies in academic argument.

difficulties.pattern: 'Some people think A. Others think B. There are advantages and disadvantages.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion essays that list views and end without a judgement.
difficulties.response: Require a criterion and a reasoned judgement after each comparison. Do not simply tell learners to 'add your opinion'; teach them to weigh.

difficulties.pattern: Summarising opposing views in loaded terms ('this naive claim').
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluative adjectives inside summaries; selective quotation.
difficulties.response: Separate representation from evaluation: summarise first in neutral reporting language, then evaluate in a separate sentence; check summaries against the source.

difficulties.pattern: 'A good essay is balanced and does not take sides.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Refusal to reach a conclusion even when the task asks 'to what extent', often after school or test discussion-essay formats that reward listing both sides.
difficulties.response: Show that in many English-medium university genres (check local criteria) balanced consideration is expected to lead to a reasoned position; contrast discussion and argumentative tasks.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner for the strongest argument against a view they have just stated.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a substantive, accurately characterised counter-position with its rationale.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a weak or token objection that is easy to dismiss.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot produce one, or caricatures the opposing view.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, use everyday issues and stakeholder role-play. The topic is core on UG pre-sessional courses, where discussion essays and seminars assess fair representation; PG pre-sessional learners develop it through literature-based tasks. Undergraduates engage with disciplinary debates; PGT and PGR learners revisit it as they position their own work among competing theoretical, policy and methodological schools.

records.summary: Perry's scheme, derived from interviews with Harvard undergraduates, and Kuhn's absolutist–multiplist–evaluativist sequence describe a broad movement from seeing knowledge as certain and authority-given, through seeing it as mere opinion, to seeing it as constructed yet open to reasoned evaluation; Hofer and Pintrich's review recasts this as several dimensions (certainty, simplicity, source and justification of knowledge) that may develop unevenly. These models describe tendencies, not fixed stages, and were developed largely in particular educational systems, so they should be used to make expectations discussable rather than to classify learners. The multiplist 'it's all opinion' position is often a productive transitional step that teaching should build on, not punish.

activities.title: When sources disagree
learnerActions: Read two abstracts that reach conflicting conclusions
In groups, decide how to judge between them and list the criteria used
Compare criteria across groups and classify them (authority, recency, design, sample, context)
activities.intendedInsight: Disagreement in the literature is normal and can be adjudicated by evaluating evidence, not only by deferring to authority or calling it opinion.
activities.rationale: Kuhn's work characterises evaluativist thinking as weighing competing claims by the quality of their support.

activities.title: How knowledge changed
learnerActions: Trace how a claim or guideline in their field changed over time
Identify what new evidence or argument prompted the change
Discuss what this implies for how current knowledge should be worded in their own writing
activities.intendedInsight: Knowledge is provisional, which is why academic writers hedge and attribute.
activities.rationale: Hofer and Pintrich identify certainty of knowledge as one dimension of epistemic belief; historical cases make it concrete.

difficulties.pattern: 'What answer is the tutor actually looking for?' — treating an open question as if it had a hidden correct answer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for model answers, frustration with open questions and reproduction of lecture content as the answer, typically after assessment regimes with fixed mark schemes that reward a single correct answer.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that exam systems in many countries, including the UK's school-leaving examinations, reward correct answers, and that first-year students from all backgrounds meet this shift. Show explicitly, with marked exemplars, how university tasks reward reasoned evaluation. Do not attribute the expectation to national culture or treat it as a lower developmental stage.

difficulties.pattern: 'Everything is subjective, so my opinion is as good as any study.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Unsupported opinions presented as conclusions; dismissal of evidence as 'just one view'.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a transitional position and introduce criteria for comparing support. Do not shut it down by reasserting authority, which pushes learners back towards absolutism.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Two experts disagree about the effect of a policy. What does that tell you, and what would you do?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Considers differences in evidence, method or values and proposes how to reach a provisional, reasoned judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says one must be wrong or that it is a matter of opinion, but mentions some relevant criterion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Defers entirely to the more senior expert or concludes that no judgement is possible.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, tutors should frame open questions explicitly and reassure learners that there is no single expected answer. UG pre-sessional courses often manage the shift from test preparation; PG pre-sessional courses can introduce contested literatures and research paradigms. Undergraduate first-year transition is a key point; PGT learners meet contested literatures immediately; PGR learners articulate epistemological positions (paradigms) in their methodology.
reviewNotes: Perry's original sample (largely male Harvard undergraduates in the 1950s–60s) limits generalisation; later research suggests that epistemic beliefs are partly domain-specific.

records.summary: Kuhn's research on argument skill shows how often reasoners fail to keep theory and evidence distinct — treating the plausibility of an explanation as if it were evidence for it — which is precisely the distinction needed to evaluate theories. Criteria for evaluation are partly disciplinary: Becher and Trowler's account of hard/soft and pure/applied knowledge cultures suggests why predictive accuracy dominates in some fields and interpretive richness or critical purchase in others. Wallace and Wray's guidance for postgraduates on scrutinising theoretical literature offers practical question frames.

activities.title: Criteria matrix
learnerActions: Build a matrix of two rival models from their discipline against criteria such as scope, evidence, coherence and usefulness
Fill each cell with evidence or examples rather than ticks
Write a comparison paragraph that reaches a qualified judgement for a stated purpose
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating a theory is a judgement relative to explicit criteria and purposes, which vary by discipline.
activities.rationale: Becher and Trowler show that disciplines differ in what they value in knowledge claims, so criteria should be made explicit and field-appropriate.

activities.title: What would challenge it?
learnerActions: State a model's key claims or predictions
Specify what evidence would count against each
Search for such evidence and report what was found
activities.intendedInsight: Separating a theory from its evidence is the basis for evaluating it.
activities.rationale: Kuhn identifies the coordination of theory and evidence as a core and often weak argument skill.

difficulties.pattern: 'This theory is from the 1970s, so it is out of date.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissing foundational frameworks by date alone.
difficulties.response: Point out that age is not an evaluative criterion; ask what evidence or developments have challenged the theory.

difficulties.pattern: Reporting a widely cited theory as established fact beyond evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Theories presented with boosters ('X proved that…') and no limitations, often reflecting textbook or lecture presentations of theories as settled.
difficulties.response: Show published critiques and model mitigated evaluative language; reinforce that frameworks are provisional tools.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner why they chose the framework in their current assignment over an alternative.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Compares the two on explicit criteria and relates the choice to the purpose of the assignment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the chosen framework's features without comparison.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites only that the lecturer recommended it or that it is well known.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduates usually meet this in later-year essays that evaluate models. PGT learners need it for selecting frameworks in assignments and dissertations; PGR learners for theoretical framework chapters and for claiming a contribution to theory.
reviewNotes: Evaluation criteria for theory differ sharply between, for example, physics, economics and cultural studies; disciplinary tutors should validate the criteria taught.

records.summary: Gardner and Nesi's classification of university assignment genres shows how many assessed tasks — case studies, explanations, problem questions, design specifications — require applying disciplinary concepts to particulars. Maton's notion of semantic waves offers a useful lens: successful analytical writing moves repeatedly between abstract, condensed concepts and concrete, context-dependent detail, whereas weaker writing stays at one level (theory summary or case retelling). Teaching should therefore model the 'wave' at paragraph level, not only at text level.

activities.title: Tracing semantic waves
learnerActions: Mark where an exemplar analytical paragraph moves up to concepts and down to case detail
Draw the resulting 'wave' and compare it with a weaker paragraph that stays flat
Revise the weaker paragraph to create movement between levels
activities.intendedInsight: Application means repeated movement between concept and case within paragraphs.
activities.rationale: Maton argues that cumulative knowledge-building depends on movement between abstract and concrete meanings, which this activity makes visible.

activities.title: Model-to-case mapping table
learnerActions: Complete a three-column table: model component, specific case evidence, what this shows
Add a row for a feature of the case the model does not explain
Convert the table into an analytical paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Application requires specific evidence for each component and an inference drawn from it, including where the fit is poor.
activities.rationale: Case-study and explanation genre families in Gardner and Nesi's classification require this mapping of concepts onto particulars.

difficulties.pattern: Describing the theory at length and then retelling the case, with no connection between them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Two-block structure: a theory section followed by a case section.
difficulties.response: Use the mapping table and paragraph-level wave tracing. Do not respond by removing theory, which is needed for analysis.

difficulties.pattern: Forcing every detail of the case to fit the model.
difficulties.revealedBy: No limitations of fit noted; strained interpretations of case evidence.
difficulties.response: Require one 'poor fit' observation in every application and discuss what it implies for the model or the case.

difficulties.pattern: Using the everyday meaning of a theoretical term (e.g. 'power', 'culture', 'stakeholder').
difficulties.revealedBy: Applications that rely on general rather than technical senses of key concepts.
difficulties.response: Return to the formal definition and its distinguishing features before mapping it to the case.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how one concept from their current module applies to a recent news event.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Makes specific concept–evidence links and notes one limitation of fit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Makes a general link without specific evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the event or defines the concept without connecting them.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level, use simple models (e.g. SWOT, supply and demand) with structured tables; pre-sessional learners on subject-specific UG and PG pathways practise case-based writing. The topic is core for undergraduates, who apply concepts in case studies and problem questions; PGT learners extend it in consultancy-style reports and assignments; PGR learners revisit it when using analytical frameworks in data-analysis chapters.

records.summary: Hoey's situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern gives a textual model of the reasoning process and links problem-solving to the structure of problem–solution essays, reports and case analyses. Facione's consensus statement presents critical-thinking skills such as analysis, evaluation and inference as the means of reasoned problem-solving and decision-making. Separating option generation from option evaluation, and making evaluation criteria explicit, are, in practitioner experience, the two moves most likely to improve student work; neither cited source tests this.

activities.title: Symptom or cause?
learnerActions: Sort statements about a case into symptoms and possible causes
Rewrite the problem statement so that it names a cause
Check whether the proposed solutions address the cause or only the symptoms
activities.intendedInsight: Responses should target causes, and a problem statement that names only symptoms leads to weak solutions.
activities.rationale: Hoey's problem–solution pattern separates the problem from the response, which this activity uses to sharpen problem definition.

activities.title: Criteria-weighted options
learnerActions: In groups, generate at least three options for a problem before discussing any
Agree and define weighted criteria
Score the options, then present a recommendation with its trade-offs
activities.intendedInsight: A recommendation is a judgement under explicit criteria, and its trade-offs should be stated.
activities.rationale: Facione's account treats evaluation and inference as the core skills applied in problem-solving and decision-making.

difficulties.pattern: Jumping to a single solution as soon as the problem is stated.
difficulties.revealedBy: Problem–solution essays with one option and no comparison.
difficulties.response: Build in a compulsory option-generation stage before evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Criteria such as 'good' or 'effective' used without definition, or applied inconsistently across options.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations that cannot be compared because the criteria shift.
difficulties.response: Require operational definitions of each criterion and evidence for each judgement.

diagnostic.task: Give a brief scenario and ask for a problem definition and two possible solutions with a reason for preferring one.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Cause-focused definition, two genuinely different options and an explicit criterion for the preference.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Symptom-focused definition or very similar options; preference stated without a criterion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A single fix with no definition of the problem or criteria.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners on STEM and business pathways meet problem-solving tasks early. Pre-sessional courses use problem–solution essays and group projects. Undergraduates apply the process in case studies and design work; PGT learners in business, policy and professional reports.
reviewNotes: Problem-solving processes differ substantially between, for example, engineering design and policy analysis; discipline-specific versions belong in the Disciplinary Literacies strand.

records.summary: Reflexivity builds on evaluativist beliefs about knowledge: if knowledge is constructed, the knower's position matters. Creswell and Creswell present researcher reflexivity as a standard component of qualitative research, and Finlay's analysis distinguishes several forms of reflexivity while warning against self-indulgent confession that displaces the research itself. For multilingual learners, positionality also includes language — translating participants' words or researching one's own community are reflexive issues in their own right.

activities.title: Same data, different researchers
learnerActions: Read a short interview extract
Interpret it from two assigned researcher positions (e.g. insider and outsider, different disciplinary backgrounds)
Discuss which interpretive differences arise from position and how a researcher could account for them
activities.intendedInsight: Interpretation is positioned, and accounting for position strengthens rather than weakens research claims.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell describe reflexivity as the researcher's account of how background and experience shape interpretation.

activities.title: Reflexive memo or confession?
learnerActions: Compare two positionality paragraphs: one linked to research decisions, one autobiographical
Identify which sentences do analytical work
Revise a draft of their own so that each statement of position is linked to a decision and a safeguard
activities.intendedInsight: Reflexive writing is useful when it connects position to specific research decisions.
activities.rationale: Finlay cautions that reflexivity can slide into self-absorption; linking position to decisions keeps it purposeful.

difficulties.pattern: 'Good research is objective, so I should not mention myself.'
difficulties.revealedBy: No reflexive commentary in qualitative projects; discomfort with first-person writing about the research process.
difficulties.response: Explain that expectations depend on paradigm and genre, and that the belief is reasonable in some research traditions; show disciplinary exemplars, noting that some quantitative genres legitimately include little reflexive commentary.

difficulties.pattern: Positionality statements that list identity categories without linking them to the research.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic lists of personal characteristics with no stated effect on design or interpretation.
difficulties.response: Provide a frame such as 'Because I…, I may… ; to address this I…'.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to disclose personal information in assessed writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of positionality sections or very vague statements.
difficulties.response: Emphasise that learners choose what to disclose and that only research-relevant aspects of position are needed. Do not require disclosure of sensitive identities.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'How might your position affect your project, and what will you do about it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific aspect of position, a plausible effect on the research and a concrete practice to examine it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names an aspect of position without an effect or practice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Claims complete objectivity or lists identity categories only.

records.contextNotes: Undergraduates meet reflexivity mainly in reflective writing and final-year projects. PGT learners in social sciences, education and health need it for dissertations. The topic is core for PGR learners, especially in qualitative and practice-based fields, who need it for methodology chapters, ethics applications and likely viva questions; in some quantitative fields it is limited to a brief statement of the researcher's role.
reviewNotes: Expectations of reflexive writing vary greatly by paradigm and discipline; this topic should be paired with discipline-specific exemplars.

records.summary: Wingate's study found that students' understanding of 'argument' was often limited and that tutors' feedback used the term without explaining it; she proposes teaching argument as three components: the writer's position, the coherent presentation of that position, and its development through analysis and evaluation of knowledge and sources. Andrews stresses that argument in higher education takes discipline-specific forms, and Hirvela argues that L2 writing instruction has given argumentation less attention than its centrality warrants. Start by making explicit that most assessed writing is argumentative even when the task word is 'discuss' or 'explain'.

activities.title: Argument or not?
learnerActions: Sort short texts (news report, encyclopaedia entry, opinion blog, academic paragraph) into those that do and do not contain an argument
Justify each decision by pointing to a position and its support, or their absence
Draft a working definition of academic argument and test it on a new text
activities.intendedInsight: An argument needs a contestable position with support; accurate information alone is not an argument.
activities.rationale: Wingate's three-component model gives learners a concrete basis for recognising argument.

activities.title: Translating 'argument' in feedback
learnerActions: Examine tutor comments that use the word 'argument' on sample essays
Decide whether each comment concerns the position, its presentation or its development
Rewrite each comment as a specific revision action
activities.intendedInsight: 'Argument' in feedback refers to identifiable features that can be revised.
activities.rationale: Wingate found that feedback on argument was often too general for students to act on, and Andrews notes that tutors' expectations of argument vary across disciplines.

difficulties.pattern: 'An argument is a fight — it would be rude to argue in an essay.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of any stance; essays that report sources accurately but never commit to an answer.
difficulties.response: Contrast everyday and academic senses of 'argument'; show measured, hedged arguments in exemplars.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I include all the relevant information, I have answered the question.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehensive, well-organised but descriptive essays, often shaped by knowledge-display exams.
difficulties.response: Use exemplars to show that the question demands a position; have learners state their answer before planning content.

difficulties.pattern: 'Argument is only for argumentative essays, not for reports or lab write-ups.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion sections that restate results without interpretation.
difficulties.response: Show the argument in a discussion section or a case report: the interpretation is a claim supported by results.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state the argument of their most recent essay in one sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A specific, contestable position that answers the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A topic statement such as 'This essay discusses the advantages and disadvantages of…'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot answer, or restates the essay title.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and UG pre-sessional courses, where the topic is core, should establish the concept early and return to it in every writing task; PG pre-sessional courses can move quickly from the concept to its realisation in longer source-based assignments. In undergraduate in-sessional settings, revisit the concept by showing what argument looks like in each discipline's genres, including reports and lab write-ups. PGT learners usually control the concept and need only brief recalibration for dissertations; PGR provision assumes it.

records.summary: The classical stasis tradition, adapted for composition teaching by Fahnestock and Secor, sorts claims into fact, definition, cause, value and policy, each with typical lines of support. Walton's argumentation schemes offer a complementary view: argument from verbal classification supports definitional claims, causal schemes support causal claims, and practical reasoning supports policy claims, each with its own critical questions. Teach claim types as a planning tool tied to assignment questions rather than as classification for its own sake.

activities.title: From question to claim type
learnerActions: Analyse six real assignment questions and identify the claim type or types each demands
List the kinds of support each claim type will need
Compare analyses and resolve disagreements
activities.intendedInsight: The type of claim a question invites predicts the kind of evidence and reasoning the answer needs.
activities.rationale: Fahnestock and Secor's stasis-based categories link claim types to characteristic forms of support.

activities.title: Unpacking a policy claim
learnerActions: Take a policy claim and list the factual, causal and value claims it presupposes
Order those claims so that each depends only on earlier ones
Turn the ordered list into an essay plan
activities.intendedInsight: Policy claims rest on chains of other claims that must be established first.
activities.rationale: Walton's account of practical reasoning shows that arguments for action depend on goals, means and consequences, each open to critical questions.

difficulties.pattern: Supporting a value claim ('X is the best approach') with description alone.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluative theses followed by paragraphs of description with no criteria.
difficulties.response: Require explicit criteria for every value claim and evidence against each criterion.

difficulties.pattern: 'According to the Oxford Dictionary, X means…' used to settle a contested concept.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dictionary definitions opening essays on contested disciplinary concepts, a move often taught as a standard essay opening at school.
difficulties.response: Show competing scholarly definitions and treat choosing a definition as a claim that needs justification.

diagnostic.task: Give the claim 'Social media should be regulated in the same way as tobacco' and ask what other claims must be established first.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies claims about harm (fact/cause), comparability with tobacco (definition/analogy), values and feasibility.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies harm only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates agreement or disagreement with the claim.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use simplified claim types when planning short essays. Pre-sessional learners apply them to analysing essay questions. Undergraduates meet discipline-specific claim types (e.g. interpretive claims in the humanities); PGT learners in management, policy and health need policy and value claims in particular.
reviewNotes: The five-type taxonomy is a teaching heuristic from rhetoric and composition; real academic claims often combine types.

records.summary: Toulmin proposed his layout as a field-dependent alternative to formal logic, describing how practical arguments move from data to claim through warrants that may themselves need backing and that are limited by qualifiers and rebuttal conditions. Qin and Karabacak's study of argumentative essays by EFL undergraduates at one Chinese university used a modified Toulmin scheme and found that counter-argument and rebuttal elements were relatively infrequent but associated with higher-rated essays; Wingate (2012) similarly reports that students at a UK university were often unclear about what argument requires, so the pattern reflects novice status and instruction, not nationality. Andrews cautions that the model analyses individual arguments rather than whole texts, so use it diagnostically and keep the terminology light at lower levels.

activities.title: Unpacking an argument
learnerActions: Label the elements of three short arguments taken from texts in their discipline
Reconstruct each implicit warrant in a sentence
Compare reconstructions across groups and discuss which warrants are contestable
activities.intendedInsight: Warrants are usually implicit and are often the point at which an argument can be challenged.
activities.rationale: Toulmin's model was designed to expose the warrant that licenses the move from data to claim.

activities.title: Finding the rebuttals
learnerActions: Code two student essays for claims, data, counter-arguments and rebuttals using a simplified scheme
Compare the higher-rated and lower-rated essays
Identify where a counter-argument and rebuttal could be added to the weaker essay
activities.intendedInsight: Higher-rated essays tend to acknowledge and respond to opposition rather than only stating claims and data.
activities.rationale: Qin and Karabacak found counter-argument and rebuttal elements associated with essay quality in their sample.

difficulties.pattern: Labelling the evidence itself as the warrant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statistics or quotations identified as warrants in analysis tasks.
difficulties.response: Present the warrant as a general 'since…' or 'if…then…' principle connecting any such data to such a claim.

difficulties.pattern: 'My claim is… My data is… My warrant is…' — using the model as a paragraph template.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic paragraphs that name the elements explicitly.
difficulties.response: Stress that the model is analytical; show how expert texts realise elements implicitly and in varied orders.

difficulties.pattern: Qualifiers limited to 'maybe' or 'I think'.
difficulties.revealedBy: A narrow hedging repertoire in analysis and writing.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of hedging devices and match them to the strength of data and warrant.

diagnostic.task: Give a short paragraph and ask the learner to identify its claim and the assumption that links its evidence to that claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurately states the implicit warrant and notes whether it is contestable.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies claim and data but restates the data as the warrant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify the claim.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, use a simplified version (claim, reason, evidence, objection, response). Undergraduates can use the full model to analyse readings and write critiques; PGT learners use it to examine research arguments, particularly in discussion sections.
reviewNotes: Evidence on the effect of explicit Toulmin instruction on L2 writing quality is mixed and context-specific; the model is presented as an analytical tool, not a proven intervention.

records.summary: Kuhn found that many people offered 'pseudoevidence' — plausible scenarios illustrating how something might happen — in place of evidence bearing on whether it is true; making this distinction explicit is central to teaching support. Wingate's account of argument places the development of a position through analysis of knowledge and sources at the centre of essay writing. At lower levels, paragraph scaffolds such as point–evidence–explanation can help, provided learners see that the explanation step does the argumentative work.

activities.title: Evidence or scenario?
learnerActions: Sort support items into research evidence, illustrative example and hypothetical scenario
Discuss what each can and cannot show
Rewrite a paragraph, replacing a scenario with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A plausible story about how something could happen is not evidence that it does happen.
activities.rationale: Kuhn identified pseudoevidence as a common substitute for genuine evidence in everyday argument.

activities.title: Highlight the link
learnerActions: Highlight claim, evidence and explanation in their own paragraph in three colours
Identify any evidence that has no explanation next to it
Add or revise the explanation so that the link to the claim is explicit
activities.intendedInsight: Support requires an explicit link between evidence and claim.
activities.rationale: Wingate presents the development of a position through analysis of sources as a core component of argument.

difficulties.pattern: 'The quotation speaks for itself.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotations dropped into paragraphs without comment.
difficulties.response: Require a comment sentence after every quotation explaining its relevance. Do not ban quotation; teach integration.

difficulties.pattern: 'In my experience…' or 'Everyone knows…' used as the main support.
difficulties.revealedBy: Personal experience and general knowledge used where research evidence is expected, often carried over from timed test essays that invite examples from the writer's own knowledge or experience.
difficulties.response: Show where personal experience is acceptable (e.g. reflective genres) and where research evidence is expected; practise locating sources for claims first supported by experience.

difficulties.pattern: Piling up citations without showing how each relates to the claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of parenthetical citations after general statements.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state what each source contributes; reduce citations to those that do distinct work.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to support the claim 'Online learning can widen access to higher education' in three sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific type of evidence, explains how it supports the claim and adds a qualification.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an example or general statement without explaining the link.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the claim in different words.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and UG pre-sessional learners, for whom the topic is core, benefit from point–evidence–explanation scaffolds and source-based practice. PG pre-sessional learners extend this to research evidence. Undergraduate in-sessional and PGT learners revisit it as evidence density and disciplinary norms increase; PGR learners revisit it when supporting original claims with their own data.

records.summary: In Toulmin's terms, warrants license the step from data to claim and may themselves require backing; writers often omit them because they seem obvious from their own perspective. Walton's argumentation schemes, each paired with critical questions, give learners a repertoire of common warrant types (from expert opinion, from cause to effect, from analogy, from consequences) and a way to anticipate where readers will push back. The writing goal is not to state every warrant, but to state those a reader in the discipline would not supply unaided.

activities.title: Same evidence, different claims
learnerActions: Examine one dataset and two opposing claims based on it
Write the warrant each claim needs
Decide which warrant is more defensible and explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence does not speak for itself; the warrant determines what it supports.
activities.rationale: Toulmin shows that the same data can support different claims depending on the warrant invoked.

activities.title: Schemes and critical questions
learnerActions: Identify the argumentation scheme in a source argument (e.g. analogy, expert opinion)
Apply the scheme's critical questions
Add a warrant and backing to a paragraph of their own that uses the same scheme
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing the scheme predicts the objections a reader will raise and so which warrants need stating.
activities.rationale: Walton pairs each scheme with critical questions that expose its typical points of weakness.

difficulties.pattern: Leaving the link between evidence and claim implicit because it seems obvious to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'So what?' or 'How does this support your point?' comments; claims and evidence placed side by side.
difficulties.response: Ask a peer reader to mark every point where they cannot follow the reasoning; revise by adding warrants there.

difficulties.pattern: Explaining reasoning that expert readers already share.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-explained, patronising passages after instruction on warrants, wasting word count.
difficulties.response: Calibrate with disciplinary exemplars: which links do expert writers leave implicit for their readers?

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with one missing warrant and ask the learner to find where a reader would ask 'Why does that follow?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the gap and supplies a plausible warrant, with backing if contestable.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Locates the gap but cannot articulate the warrant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no gap.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners can begin with simple 'this shows that… because…' frames. Undergraduates learn discipline-specific warrants. PGT learners writing for expert readers need to judge which warrants to state; PGR learners must defend conceptual and methodological warrants to examiners and reviewers.

records.summary: Kuhn's interviews showed that generating counter-arguments and alternative theories was among the weakest argument skills across age groups, which suggests it requires explicit teaching. Qin and Karabacak found counter-argument and rebuttal elements uncommon in their sample of EFL university essays but associated with higher quality, supporting deliberate attention. Effective practice separates generating strong objections — often by searching sources — from responding to them, which is taught next.

activities.title: Devil's advocate pairs
learnerActions: State a thesis to a partner
Listen while the partner raises the strongest objections they can
Record the objections, then swap roles
activities.intendedInsight: Others can see objections that writers miss in their own arguments.
activities.rationale: Kuhn's findings suggest that people seldom generate counter-arguments to their own views unprompted.

activities.title: Counter-source search
learnerActions: Search specifically for published sources that disagree with their thesis
Summarise the strongest counter-position fairly
Decide whether it must be addressed in the essay and where
activities.intendedInsight: Published counter-positions exist and readers will expect them to be engaged.
activities.rationale: Qin and Karabacak's results link the presence of counter-argument elements to higher-rated essays.

difficulties.pattern: 'Including counter-arguments will weaken my essay.'
difficulties.revealedBy: One-sided essays with no acknowledgement of other views.
difficulties.response: Show that addressing objections strengthens credibility, using higher-graded exemplars.

difficulties.pattern: 'Some people may say it is expensive, but this is not true.' — token objections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weak, unsourced objections dismissed in a sentence.
difficulties.response: Require at least one sourced objection and ask peers to rate how damaging it is.

difficulties.pattern: A fixed 'Some people believe… However, I believe…' paragraph before the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic counter-argument paragraphs learned from test-preparation templates.
difficulties.response: Show how expert writers raise objections at the point where they are most relevant.

diagnostic.task: Give a thesis and ask for the strongest objection to it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A substantive objection grounded in evidence or reasoning.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A plausible but weak or vague objection.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No objection, or a restatement of the thesis.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners can practise simple objection generation orally. The topic is core on UG and PG pre-sessional courses, in argumentative essays and seminars. Undergraduates use it in critiques; PGT learners in literature reviews and discussion sections; PGR learners revisit it when anticipating examiner and reviewer questions.

records.summary: Martin and White's engagement system describes how writers counter and concede in order to contract or expand dialogic space, and Lancaster's analysis of upper-level student writing found that highly valued papers combined concession with counter-moves, acknowledging alternatives while asserting a position. Qin and Karabacak's findings link rebuttal elements to higher-rated EFL essays. Teach the moves and their language together, and check that concessions have consequences for the claim rather than being ritual.

activities.title: Concession sequences in expert texts
learnerActions: Find concede–counter patterns in a disciplinary article
Classify them (concede then counter, deny, qualify the claim)
Write two sentences of their own imitating the most useful pattern
activities.intendedInsight: Expert writers concede strategically and then reassert their position.
activities.rationale: Martin and White's engagement categories and Lancaster's findings on valued student writing both highlight concession followed by counter-assertion.

activities.title: Matching the response to the objection
learnerActions: Read objections of varying strength to the same thesis
Choose for each whether to refute, partially concede or modify the claim
Write the responses and have peers judge their credibility
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate response depends on how strong the objection is.
activities.rationale: Qin and Karabacak associate rebuttal elements with essay quality; varying the response type develops judgement rather than formula.

difficulties.pattern: The concession takes over and the writer seems to change sides.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end on the opposing point; unclear final stance.
difficulties.response: Teach that the conceded point goes in the subordinate clause and the writer's point in the main clause, and that paragraphs should end on the writer's position.

difficulties.pattern: Rebuttal by assertion: 'This is not true.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Denials of objections with no evidence or reasoning.
difficulties.response: Require that every rebuttal cite evidence or give a reason; model with examples.

difficulties.pattern: 'On the other hand' used for every concession.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated, sometimes inaccurate, use of one contrastive phrase.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of concessive resources and the logical differences between them.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to respond in two sentences to the objection 'Your proposal is too expensive.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Concedes the cost, rebuts with evidence of benefit or alternatives, and maintains or qualifies the position.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Concedes without rebutting, or denies without evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Abandons the position or ignores the objection.

records.contextNotes: UG pre-sessional learners practise these moves in essays and seminars; on PG pre-sessional courses the topic is core because critiques and literature-based assignments depend on it. Undergraduates use the moves in critiques; PGT learners in discussion sections and literature reviews; PGR learners revisit them when responding to examiners and journal reviewers.

records.summary: Wingate identifies the writer's position as the first component of argument and found that many students did not realise that essays require one. Lancaster's study of valued stance patterns suggests that strong positions in upper-level student writing are typically asserted with calibrated hedging and concession rather than with categorical boosting. Teach position-taking as reaching a judgement from evidence, and make clear that a qualified or conditional position ('largely', 'under these conditions') is still a position.

activities.title: Position spectrum
learnerActions: Place sample thesis statements on a line from 'no position' to 'overstated'
Identify the defensible zone for the given evidence
Write their own thesis within that zone
activities.intendedInsight: A position can be qualified and still clear and committed.
activities.rationale: Lancaster's findings suggest that valued student writing combines commitment with calibrated hedging and concession.

activities.title: Skeleton read
learnerActions: Give a partner only the introduction, the conclusion and the first sentence of each body paragraph
Ask the partner to state the position they perceive
Compare it with the intended position and revise where they differ
activities.intendedInsight: A position must be visible in the structure of a text, not only stated once.
activities.rationale: Wingate distinguishes the presentation of a position across a text from simply having one.

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic writing must be objective, so I should not take a side.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that survey views but reach no judgement, even for 'to what extent' questions, sometimes following advice that academic writing must be 'objective'.
difficulties.response: Distinguish objectivity (fair use of evidence) from neutrality (no judgement); show position statements in exemplars.

difficulties.pattern: The conclusion argues something different from the introduction.
difficulties.revealedBy: Position drift as the writer discovers their view while drafting.
difficulties.response: Treat drift as a normal outcome of drafting that calls for global revision of the introduction; do not penalise it in exploratory drafts.

difficulties.pattern: 'This essay will prove that X is completely wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Overstated positions, often carried over from test genres that reward strong opinion.
difficulties.response: Practise matching position strength to evidence and introduce qualified forms.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In one sentence, what is your answer to the essay question?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: A specific, qualified position that answers the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A vague or topic-only statement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: 'It depends', with no further judgement, or no answer.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners work towards a clear thesis. The topic is core on UG and PG pre-sessional courses, where sustaining a position across extended source-based essays is usually assessed for progression. Undergraduates adapt positions to disciplinary genres; PGT learners sustain positions in dissertations; PGR learners articulate the position of a whole thesis.
reviewNotes: Conventions differ on where and how explicitly a position is stated (for example delayed or emergent theses in some humanities writing and in some other writing traditions); the added mastery statement carries the argument-structure point from idn.intercultural-rhetoric (R1-11).

records.summary: Andrews emphasises that argument in higher education operates at the level of whole texts as well as individual claims, and that its structure varies by discipline. Wingate's model identifies the coherent presentation of a position as a distinct component that students often find difficult. Argument maps can expose dependence among sub-claims before drafting, and claim-based reverse outlining exposes topic-led structures afterwards.

activities.title: Map before drafting
learnerActions: Map the main claim, sub-claims, evidence and anticipated objections for a planned assignment
Decide which sub-claims depend on others
Sequence sections according to these dependencies
activities.intendedInsight: The order of an extended argument should follow logical dependence, not the order in which sources were read.
activities.rationale: Andrews treats argument as a whole-text structure; mapping makes that structure visible before drafting.

activities.title: Claim-based reverse outline
learnerActions: Write the claim of each section of a draft in one sentence
Test each with the question 'How does this advance my position?'
Merge, cut or reorder sections that fail the test
activities.intendedInsight: Topics are not claims; each section must advance the argument.
activities.rationale: Wingate's 'presentation of position' component concerns exactly this organisation of the whole argument.

difficulties.pattern: Sections organised source by source or topic by topic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Headings or paragraph openings naming authors or topics; no cumulative logic.
difficulties.response: Use claim-based outlines and require each section opening to state a claim.

difficulties.pattern: All counter-arguments placed in a single paragraph before the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: A detached 'counter-argument' section, often learned from five-paragraph templates.
difficulties.response: Show how objections are addressed where they bear on a specific sub-claim.

difficulties.pattern: Losing the thread of the argument in long texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Later sections that no longer connect to the main position.
difficulties.response: Keep an updated argument map beside the draft and add brief metatext at section openings.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain why the sections of their plan are in that order.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains the order through logical dependence between sub-claims.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains it chronologically or by importance without logical links.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives no rationale.

records.contextNotes: UG and PG pre-sessional extended essays and projects (2,000–4,000 words) are often learners' first experience of extended argument. The topic is core where long assessed texts dominate: undergraduate long essays and dissertations, PGT dissertations and PGR theses, where an argument must be sustained across chapters.

records.summary: Hyland's account of metadiscourse explicitly links interactional resources to the classical appeals: writers build credibility through hedges, self-mention and citation, engage readers through reader pronouns and appeals to shared knowledge, and support rational appeals through transitions and code glosses. His stance and engagement model shows that academic persuasion is interpersonal even when it appears impersonal. The teaching point is not that academic writing avoids ethos and pathos, but that it realises them in restrained, discipline-specific ways.

activities.title: Appeals across genres
learnerActions: Analyse an academic abstract, an opinion article and a charity appeal on the same issue
Tabulate the appeals used and the linguistic features that realise them
Discuss which features would transfer to academic writing
activities.intendedInsight: Academic texts use all three appeals, but realise them differently from popular persuasive genres.
activities.rationale: Hyland relates metadiscourse resources directly to rational, credibility and affective appeals.

activities.title: Credibility audit
learnerActions: Mark features in their own draft that build or damage credibility (citation accuracy, hedging, unsupported boosters, emotive language)
Revise three features that damage credibility
activities.intendedInsight: Credibility in academic writing is constructed linguistically, sentence by sentence.
activities.rationale: Hyland's stance and engagement model identifies the resources through which writers project authority and engage readers.

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic writing must have no emotion or values.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Inability to state why a problem matters; flat introductions.
difficulties.response: Show restrained value appeals in research introductions (significance, consequences) and practise writing them.

difficulties.pattern: Emotive, exaggerated language ('a shocking and devastating crisis').
difficulties.revealedBy: Language carried over from persuasive school genres, including rhetorical questions and intensifiers.
difficulties.response: Compare register choices across genres and revise towards evidence-based significance statements.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how an academic article persuades readers to trust its findings.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names methodological transparency, citation and hedging as ways of building credibility, with examples.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says only that it 'uses evidence'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Says it is trustworthy because it is published.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners use the appeals as a lens for critical reading of media and persuasive texts. Undergraduates connect them to stance and credibility in their own writing; PGT learners also adapt arguments for policy and public audiences.
reviewNotes: Hyland's mapping of metadiscourse onto the classical appeals is one interpretive framework; other accounts treat ethos more broadly as authorial identity.

records.summary: Van Gelder argues, drawing on cognitive science and his own computer-supported courses, that critical thinking improves through extensive deliberate practice and that argument mapping makes reasoning structure visible in ways that prose does not. Walton uses argument diagramming as a core tool for identifying premises and conclusions and for distinguishing linked from convergent support. Mapping can be done on paper or with software; its value lies in the analytical decisions it forces, so begin with short, clearly structured texts.

activities.title: Map a source
learnerActions: In pairs, map the argument of a short opinion article or abstract
Compare the map with another pair's
