Discuss the points where the maps differ and what this reveals about the text
activities.intendedInsight: Disagreements about structure reveal ambiguity or unstated premises in the source.
activities.rationale: Walton treats diagramming as a means of making premises and their relations explicit for evaluation.

activities.title: Map the plan
learnerActions: Map their planned argument for an assignment
Ask a peer to mark any claim without support
Revise the plan before drafting
activities.intendedInsight: Maps expose gaps in reasoning before they become gaps in a draft.
activities.rationale: Van Gelder argues that mapping externalises reasoning and supports deliberate practice.

difficulties.pattern: Maps that reproduce the order of sentences rather than their logical relations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Linear chains of boxes following the text.
difficulties.response: Start from the main claim and ask 'Why should we believe this?' to build downward.

difficulties.pattern: Spending more effort on the software than on the reasoning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Elaborate visual maps with little analytical content.
difficulties.response: Begin on paper with minimal conventions; introduce software only once the reasoning is secure.

diagnostic.task: Give a three-sentence argument with an implicit premise and ask for a map.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct structure with the implicit premise added.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct structure but the implicit premise is missing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A linear chain that follows sentence order.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use simple claim–reason maps. Pre-sessional learners use mapping to plan reading-into-writing tasks. Undergraduates use it for critiques; PGT learners for literature reviews; PGR learners for planning chapters and the overall thesis argument.
reviewNotes: Reported gains from argument-mapping courses come largely from studies associated with developers of mapping software; independent replications are fewer.

records.summary: Basturkmen's analysis of seminar-type discussion shows that ideas are negotiated across extended exchanges rather than delivered in single turns, so learners need resources for reformulating, challenging and building on others' points. Ferris and Tagg's survey of subject instructors found that expectations for oral participation vary across disciplines but commonly include class discussion and responding to questions. Morita's study of graduate students shows that oral academic activities are also sites of socialisation in which participation and positioning are negotiated.

activities.title: Challenge rounds
learnerActions: In threes, one learner states a position, a second challenges it with a counter-example, and a third records the response move (clarify, defend, concede, refine)
Rotate roles
Discuss which response moves were most effective
activities.intendedInsight: Responding to a challenge involves a repertoire of moves, not only defence.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen shows that meaning in discussion is negotiated across turns, which requires flexible response moves.

activities.title: Evidence in discussion
learnerActions: Prepare two source-based points for a seminar on a shared reading
Practise referring to the source orally
Use the points in discussion and note how others respond
activities.intendedInsight: Oral arguments are strengthened by reference to shared readings and data.
activities.rationale: Ferris and Tagg found that subject instructors expect students to participate in discussion, which in many disciplines centres on assigned readings.

difficulties.pattern: Waiting, then delivering a long prepared monologue unconnected to the previous turn.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contributions that do not refer to what others have said.
difficulties.response: Practise short linked turns that begin by referring to the previous speaker. Do not force spontaneous turns on anxious learners first; stage preparation.

difficulties.pattern: Disagreement that sounds blunt, or so heavily mitigated that the position disappears.
difficulties.revealedBy: Peers' reactions; listeners unsure what the speaker thinks.
difficulties.response: Teach a graded set of mitigation and stance expressions and practise firm but polite disagreement.

difficulties.pattern: 'If someone challenges me, it means I have failed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Withdrawal or abandonment of a position after the first challenge.
difficulties.response: Normalise challenge as part of academic talk; show tutors revising views in discussion.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state a view on a reading, then respond with 'But what about…?' and a counter-example.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Acknowledges the point, gives a reason or evidence, and maintains or refines the position.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Repeats the original point without engaging the counter-example.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Abandons the position or cannot respond.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses often assess seminar participation. Undergraduates argue orally in seminars and tutorials; PGT learners in discussion-heavy modules. The topic is core for PGR learners, who must defend arguments in supervision, conference Q&A and the viva. Accept prepared and written contributions (for example posting a position in an online forum before discussion) as ways of showing the skill, since real-time turns are harder for some learners, including some autistic, anxious or hearing-impaired students.

records.summary: Walton distinguishes types of dialogue — including persuasion, inquiry and deliberation — each with different goals and norms, which explains why the same move can be appropriate in one context and inappropriate in another. Andrews highlights the place of exploratory, dialogic argument in higher education alongside more adversarial forms. Learners often arrive with one dominant model, frequently the debate or the timed test essay, so explicit contrast helps them read task expectations.

activities.title: Sorting tasks by orientation
learnerActions: Sort task descriptions (debate, seminar, literature review, policy brief, discussion essay, research proposal) by orientation
Justify each placement
Discuss tasks that combine both orientations
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate orientation depends on the task and its purpose.
activities.rationale: Walton's dialogue types provide criteria for distinguishing inquiry from persuasion.

activities.title: Reframing a text
learnerActions: Rewrite a persuasive paragraph as an exploratory one
Note changes in framing, hedging and treatment of alternatives
Compare versions with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Exploratory and adversarial argument are realised by different linguistic choices.
activities.rationale: Andrews describes exploratory argument as a valued mode in higher education that students may not recognise.

difficulties.pattern: Treating every task as a debate to be won.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissive treatment of sources in literature reviews and an adversarial tone in seminars, often carried over from debate formats or test essays that reward persuasive advocacy.
difficulties.response: Contrast orientations explicitly with exemplars from both.

difficulties.pattern: 'Exploratory means I don't have to conclude anything.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion essays and reviews that end without any judgement.
difficulties.response: Show that exploratory argument still reaches a provisional, reasoned judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how the aims of a seminar discussion differ from those of a formal debate.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Contrasts inquiry with advocacy and notes differences in norms (building on others, conceding).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes format differences only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no difference.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can contrast debate and seminar formats directly. Undergraduates need the distinction for discussion essays and seminars; PGT learners for literature reviews; PGR learners for supervisory dialogue and for framing a thesis as a contribution to ongoing inquiry.
reviewNotes: The terms 'exploratory' and 'adversarial' are used variously in the literature; the distinction here follows dialogue-type theory rather than a single source's terminology.

records.summary: Johnson and Blair's criteria of relevance, sufficiency and acceptability provide a portable framework for appraising premises and their support, while Walton's critical questions provide scheme-specific tests. Van Gelder suggests that mapping an argument before evaluating it helps reasoners separate its structure from their agreement with its conclusion. In EAP, evaluation must also be expressed: learners need evaluative lexis and mitigation to write critiques that are firm but fair.

activities.title: Relevance, sufficiency, acceptability
learnerActions: Map a short argument
Rate each premise for relevance, sufficiency and acceptability
Identify the weakest link and explain its effect on the conclusion
activities.intendedInsight: Systematic criteria reveal where an argument is weakest.
activities.rationale: Johnson and Blair's criteria and van Gelder's case for mapping together support structured evaluation.

activities.title: Agree but weak, disagree but strong
learnerActions: Evaluate a poorly argued case for a conclusion they agree with
Evaluate a well-argued case for a conclusion they reject
Discuss why the quality of an argument and agreement with its conclusion can come apart
activities.intendedInsight: Argument quality is independent of whether one agrees with the conclusion.
activities.rationale: Walton's critical questions provide criteria that apply regardless of the evaluator's view.

difficulties.pattern: 'This argument is weak because I disagree with it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations that attack conclusions rather than support.
difficulties.response: Use the 'agree but weak' activity and require evaluation to name a criterion.

difficulties.pattern: Listing every minor flaw without weighing which matters most.
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques that catalogue limitations of equal weight.
difficulties.response: Require identification of the single most consequential weakness and its effect on the conclusion.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluative language pitched at the wrong strength: either sweeping dismissal ('This study is useless') or praise and hedging so heavy that no judgement is visible.
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques whose conclusions do not match the weaknesses identified, or that identify weaknesses without ever stating how much they matter; common among novice writers of all language backgrounds.
difficulties.response: Teach evaluative patterns that pair acknowledgement with critique ('While X offers…, it does not…') and have learners match the strength of each evaluative phrase to the seriousness of the weakness they have identified.

diagnostic.task: Give a flawed argument for a conclusion that happens to be true and ask the learner to evaluate it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the flaw and notes that the conclusion may still be true on other grounds.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the flaw but rejects the conclusion because of it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts the argument as strong because the conclusion is true.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners (UG and PG) evaluate arguments in critical reading tasks. The topic is core for undergraduates writing critiques of single texts and for PGT learners evaluating arguments across literatures and in critical appraisal; PGR learners develop it further as peer reviewers and in anticipating evaluation of their own work.

records.summary: Introduce genre through contrasting texts before definitions, so that learners see purpose and readership motivating structure and wording, which is the core of Swales's (1990) account of genre and discourse community. Teachers should know the three traditions Hyon (1996) describes (ESP move analysis, Sydney School systemic functional pedagogy and New Rhetoric's emphasis on social action and context) because they imply different classroom emphases, from textual form to situated purpose; most EAP courses blend them. Bruce's (2008) distinction between social genres (the essay, the report) and cognitive genres or text types (explanation, discussion) helps learners see why a 'report' in one module may be argued like an essay. Present conventions as typified, flexible and locally negotiated rather than as templates (Johns, 1997).

activities.title: Same topic, different genres
learnerActions: Read three short texts on one topic, for example an encyclopaedia entry, a lab report introduction and a student essay paragraph
For each, note who writes it, who reads it, why, and what the reader will do with it
Underline two language features in each text that serve that purpose
In pairs, write one sentence per text linking a feature to its purpose ('The report uses ... because its reader needs ...')
activities.intendedInsight: Textual features are motivated by purpose and readership; 'academic style' is not a single fixed register.
activities.rationale: Holding the topic constant isolates purpose and audience as the variables, reflecting Swales's (1990) definition of genre by communicative purpose and Johns's (1997) emphasis on text, role and context.

activities.title: Genre inventory for my programme
learnerActions: List the genres you expect to read and write in your target programme (for example lecture handouts, lab reports, case analyses, emails to tutors)
For two of them, note who reads them, what the reader does with them and what counts as a good text
Compare with a partner from a different discipline and identify one genre whose conventions differ between your fields
Note where you could find authentic evidence for each genre: exemplars, briefs, marking criteria or a tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Each genre answers to particular readers and purposes, and learners can investigate those expectations rather than wait to be told.
activities.rationale: Positions learners as investigators of the genres in their own contexts, a central principle of Johns's (1997) socioliterate approach; the questions follow Swales's (1990) definition of genre by communicative purpose. The discourse-community analysis itself is left to acu.discourse-communities.

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic writing has one correct structure; my teacher just needs to tell me the rules.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for a single template; transfer of a five-paragraph or test-essay structure to every assignment regardless of brief.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that templates have served learners well in test preparation, then show two high-graded texts of the same nominal genre from different modules that are organised differently. Do not replace one template with another; teach learners to ask what the purpose and reader require.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing genre with topic or with text type ('This is a business essay'; 'Discussion is a genre').
difficulties.revealedBy: Texts labelled by subject matter or rhetorical function rather than by social purpose; inability to say why a case study is not an essay.
difficulties.response: Use Bruce's social-versus-cognitive genre distinction explicitly and have learners label texts at both levels (social genre: report; dominant text type: explanation).

difficulties.pattern: Treating genre conventions as fixed and rejecting legitimate variation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners reject a valid exemplar because it lacks a taught heading or move, or 'correct' an expert text towards a class model.
difficulties.response: Present conventions as tendencies with rationales, and set tasks in which learners find and justify a deviation in a high-graded or published text. Avoid presenting move models as obligatory checklists.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a short assignment brief and ask: what kind of text is this asking for, who will read it, and how might it differ from an essay?
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the genre, identifies the marker as an expert reader assessing stated outcomes, links at least two expected features (for example headings, recommendations) to purpose, and notes what to check locally (exemplars, criteria).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the genre and lists features but cannot explain why they exist, or treats the features as universal.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes only the topic, or assumes the task is 'an essay' without considering purpose or reader.

records.contextNotes: At foundation level keep the concept practical (purpose, reader, stages) and use familiar contrasts. On pre-sessional courses, both undergraduate and postgraduate, it frames the move from test writing to university genres. In-sessional undergraduate and taught postgraduate learners usually need only a brief revisit applied to their own modules' assignment types. For doctoral researchers, revisit it in relation to research genres and publishing, where it supports independent genre analysis.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-28): discourse community is now left to acu.discourse-communities. The recommended hard edge is added as soft, because acu.discourse-communities starts at B2 and is not taught at foundation, where this topic is introduced; a hard edge would block foundation pathways.

records.summary: Treat learners as researchers of genre (Johns, 1997): the teacher models a move analysis, then progressively hands over the analytic questions. Swales's (1990) move analysis supplies the method; Cheng (2018) argues that graduate writers benefit when they analyse disciplinary exemplars themselves and articulate the rhetorical reasons for what they notice, and Tardy (2009) shows that genre knowledge combines formal, rhetorical, process and subject-matter dimensions that develop over repeated encounters. Yasuda (2011) reported gains in genre awareness and linguistic choices among EFL university writers after genre-based tasks. Always pair exemplars with the brief and criteria, and use more than one exemplar so that learners do not over-generalise from a single text.

activities.title: Move-labelling with a widening lens
learnerActions: With the teacher, label the first two stages of a model text by their function
In pairs, label the remaining stages and agree a function label for each
Highlight the language that signals each move (tense, reporting verbs, hedges, frame markers)
Read a second exemplar of the same genre and record what is shared and what differs
activities.intendedInsight: Moves are recognised by function and signalling language, and comparing exemplars separates conventions from individual choices.
activities.rationale: Applies Swales's (1990) move analysis as a learner procedure; the gradual handover follows the deconstruction stage of the teaching–learning cycle (Rose & Martin, 2012).

activities.title: Genre analysis log for a real assignment
learnerActions: Collect the brief, marking criteria and, where permitted, one or two exemplars for an upcoming assignment
Complete a log: purpose, reader, stages, typical language, what the criteria reward
Note one question the materials do not answer and ask the module tutor
After receiving feedback, record what you would change in your analysis next time
activities.intendedInsight: Local materials and tutors are the authority on local genres, and analysis is a reusable strategy rather than a one-off class exercise.
activities.rationale: Cheng (2018) and Tardy (2009) both emphasise learner-led, recurring engagement with disciplinary genres; the log makes the strategy portable beyond the EAP course.

difficulties.pattern: 'The model text is the answer; I will copy its structure and phrases.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts that reproduce the exemplar section by section, including topic-specific content and phrasing.
difficulties.response: Use at least two exemplars and ask learners to account for the differences; set analysis tasks that require function labels, not content summaries. Do not withhold exemplars altogether: the remedy is comparative analysis, not avoidance.

difficulties.pattern: Labelling stages by topic rather than function ('this paragraph is about the history').
difficulties.revealedBy: Move labels that name content; inability to say what a section does for the reader.
difficulties.response: Provide a bank of function verbs (introduces, justifies, concedes, evaluates, recommends) and ask 'What does this do for the reader?' rather than 'What is it about?'.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the EAP class model as more authoritative than departmental practice.
difficulties.revealedBy: A learner insists on an EAP-taught structure that conflicts with the module brief or exemplars, often because EAP materials presented the model as the correct form.
difficulties.response: EAP teachers and course designers should present models as starting hypotheses to test against local evidence, and make the brief and local criteria the first source in every analysis; where possible, agree with subject staff which exemplars learners may analyse.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a 200–300-word exemplar from a genre the class has not studied and five minutes to label its moves and one language feature per move.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Functional labels with plausible boundaries, accurate language observations linked to moves, and an explicit caution about generalising from one text.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A mix of functional and topical labels; language features noticed but not linked to moves.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A paragraph-by-paragraph summary of the content.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: highly guided analysis of short texts with given move labels. Pre-sessional UG: analysis of the genres in the progression assessment. Pre-sessional PG: independent analysis of exemplars from the target master's programme and of research articles in the learner's field, a core transferable skill. In-sessional undergraduate and taught postgraduate: analysis of real module briefs and exemplars, ideally with subject staff. PGR: independent analysis of research articles, theses and reviews in the field, extending to corpus-assisted analysis.
reviewNotes: Access to authentic exemplars is often restricted by departmental policy. Where they are unavailable, analysis can use published models, past EAP student texts used with permission, or texts from openly available corpora of proficient student writing such as BAWE.

records.summary: Use Gardner and Nesi's (2013) classification, derived from the BAWE corpus of highly rated undergraduate and master's assignments, to show learners thirteen genre families grouped by five social purposes, and the essay subtypes within the essay family (such as exposition, discussion, factorial and challenge essays). Nesi and Gardner (2012) show that the essay predominates in arts, humanities and social sciences but much less so in the sciences and engineering, where methodology recounts, explanations, exercises and design specifications are common; Horowitz's (1986) earlier survey of the tasks university teachers set makes a similar point about diversity. Moore and Morton (2005) found that proficiency-test essays differ from university assignments, notably in drawing on personal knowledge and opinion rather than sources. Teach essay types as purposes rather than formulas, stress that textbook and handbook labels vary, and aim for a usable mental map and the habit of asking what a brief requires, not memorisation of a taxonomy.

activities.title: Sort the briefs
learnerActions: In groups, read 10–12 anonymised assignment briefs from several disciplines
Sort them into families and name the social purpose of each
Compare your groupings with the Gardner and Nesi families and discuss mismatches
Identify the families you are most likely to meet in your own programme
activities.intendedInsight: University assessment uses many genres; the essay is one family among several and dominant mainly in some disciplines.
activities.rationale: Grounded in Gardner and Nesi's (2013) corpus-based classification, which was built from real assessed writing rather than textbook categories.

activities.title: Same topic, different essay type
learnerActions: Read four essay questions on one topic that ask for different things (explain, compare, evaluate responses, argue a position)
Identify the type and purpose each implies
Write a thesis for each and compare how they differ
Find one question that blends types and sketch a plan that serves both purposes
activities.intendedInsight: The essay type determines what the thesis has to do, and real questions often blend types.
activities.rationale: Holding the topic constant isolates the effect of purpose, using the essay subtypes identified by Gardner and Nesi (2013).

activities.title: Test task versus university task
learnerActions: Compare a proficiency-test essay prompt with a first-year assignment brief on a related topic
List differences in sources, reader, length, structure and what counts as evidence
Decide which skills from test preparation transfer and which need to be developed
activities.intendedInsight: Test essays and university genres differ in source use and purpose; test success does not guarantee readiness for assessed genres.
activities.rationale: Moore and Morton (2005) identified systematic differences between IELTS Task 2 and university writing tasks, particularly in the use of sources and the kinds of entities writers deal with.

difficulties.pattern: 'All university writing is an essay, and an essay is the five-paragraph opinion essay I practised for the test.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Essay-style responses to report, case-study or lab tasks; opinion essays with no sources; a pattern reinforced by school-leaving and proficiency-test preparation that practises one essay format.
difficulties.response: Show high-graded examples from non-essay families in the learner's discipline, compare the briefs and criteria that produced them, and compare test and university essays explicitly. Acknowledge that the test format served its purpose; the aim is to add genres, not to discredit prior learning.

difficulties.pattern: Mapping command words mechanically to templates ('discuss means both sides with no view'; 'compare means describe A, then B').
difficulties.revealedBy: Near-identical outlines for differently focused questions; discussion essays that end without a judgement.
difficulties.response: Treat command words as one clue among several, alongside the focus of the question and the criteria, and show high-graded essays in which the same command word leads to different structures.

difficulties.pattern: Taking the assignment label at face value.
difficulties.revealedBy: A learner treats every task called 'report' or 'essay' identically, regardless of what the brief and criteria ask for.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to read the brief's purpose, reader and criteria as stronger evidence than the label, and to ask the tutor when they conflict; departmental labels are not used consistently.

diagnostic.task: Give three essay questions on one topic and ask the learner to name the type each implies and outline its structure in three lines; then ask them to name two kinds of writing, other than essays, that students in their subject are assessed on, and what each is for.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Types identified with reference to purpose, outlines that differ appropriately, any blended question recognised, and plausible non-essay genres for the discipline with accurate purposes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Types identified from command words with near-identical outlines, or non-essay genres named without their purposes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The same five-paragraph outline for all three questions, and no genres beyond the essay and the exam.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: build the map with the main essay types and the report, linked to the learners' subject pathways. Pre-sessional UG: a core element that addresses test-essay habits and previews the genre families of year one. Pre-sessional PG: the same map with attention to the professional and research-oriented families of the target master's programme. In-sessional undergraduate: revisit with real module briefs and disciplinary essay types such as legal essays (dlw.legal-essays) and interpretive essays (dhu.interpretive-argument). Taught postgraduate: many learners meet unfamiliar families (reflective, professional, design) for the first time within a compressed year.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-16): the former essay-types topic is absorbed here, so the topic now covers both the genre families and the essay types within the essay family; production of individual essay types is covered by the GES genre topics.

records.summary: Wingate (2012) found that many students do not understand what 'argument' means in essays, and proposes making three components explicit: developing a position by evaluating evidence, presenting that position, and structuring the text to support it. Andrews (2010) shows that argument is central to higher education but realised differently across disciplines, so any generic model should be tested against target-department exemplars. Martin and Rose's (2008) exposition and challenge genres give a useful staging vocabulary, and the university essay usually adds explicit engagement with counter-positions. Pre-sessional teachers should address Moore and Morton's (2005) finding that test essays draw on personal knowledge and opinion, whereas university essays build positions from sources.

activities.title: From topics to reasons
learnerActions: Read a weak essay plan whose body paragraphs are topics ('Economic factors', 'Social factors')
Rewrite each as a claim that supports the thesis ('Economic incentives explain most of the rise because ...')
Test each topic sentence by asking what it contributes to the thesis
Reorder the claims to build a cumulative case and justify the order
activities.intendedInsight: The body of an argumentative essay is a sequence of reasons, not a set of topics.
activities.rationale: Addresses the gap Wingate (2012) identifies between students' view of essays as displays of information and tutors' expectation of a position built through the text.

activities.title: Joint construction of a counter-argument paragraph
learnerActions: Analyse a model paragraph that concedes and counters an objection, labelling the concession, the counter and the evidence
As a class, jointly construct a parallel paragraph for a different objection, with the teacher scribing and prompting
Individually write a paragraph addressing an objection to your own thesis
Peer-check whether the objection is stated fairly and answered with a reason
activities.intendedInsight: Engaging opposing views strengthens a position when the objection is fairly stated and answered with reasons.
activities.rationale: Joint construction follows the teaching–learning cycle (Rose & Martin, 2012). Qin and Karabacak (2010) found counter-argument and rebuttal elements relatively infrequent in a corpus of EFL university argumentative essays, suggesting explicit instruction in this stage is worthwhile.

difficulties.pattern: 'Argument means listing advantages and disadvantages and giving my opinion at the end.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The position appears only in the conclusion; body paragraphs are balanced but uncommitted; 'In my opinion' arrives late. The pattern is rewarded by some test-preparation templates for advantages-and-disadvantages essays.
difficulties.response: Show that the position should be visible from the introduction and shape every paragraph; have learners draft the thesis first and test each paragraph against it. Do not ban balanced treatment: the issue is that the evaluation must lead somewhere.

difficulties.pattern: Claims supported by personal experience or general knowledge rather than sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Few or no citations; support such as 'everyone knows' or a personal anecdote; test-style responses to source-based tasks, reflecting proficiency-test essays that are written without sources.
difficulties.response: Contrast a test response with a source-based university paragraph and require each body paragraph to introduce, cite and comment on at least one source.

difficulties.pattern: Counter-arguments are straw men or dismissed in a sentence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weak objections followed by 'but this is wrong'; no concession of anything valid.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state the strongest objection a knowledgeable critic would make, and to concede what is valid in it before countering.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a 400-word student essay and ask them to underline the thesis, number the reasons and mark where an alternative view is addressed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the thesis, recognises whether paragraphs are reasons or topics, and evaluates how well counter-views are handled.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds the thesis but treats topical paragraphs as reasons, or overlooks the absence of counter-views.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a position, or equates an opinion in the conclusion with the thesis.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: one-sided expositions with a clear thesis and two or three reasons, introducing source support. Pre-sessional UG and PG: a core progression genre marking the transition from test-style opinion essays to source-based argument with counter-argument; postgraduate cohorts are usually expected to argue from a wider and more evaluated source base. In-sessional undergraduate: disciplinary argument (interpretive in the humanities, evidential in the social sciences) linked to marking criteria. Taught postgraduate: argument integrated with critical evaluation of literature and theory, usually revisited briefly rather than retaught.
reviewNotes: 'Argumentative essay' is an EAP label; departments rarely use it, but many 'critically evaluate' and 'to what extent' essays are argued in this way.

records.summary: Martin and Rose (2008) distinguish discussion (weighing two or more positions) from exposition (arguing for one), which helps learners see the discussion essay as having its own evaluative stage. The pedagogical challenge is that stage: Wingate (2012) shows students often understand 'discuss' as 'describe both sides', while tutors expect a reasoned position, and Lea and Street (1998) found that tutors' expectations about notions such as argument are frequently tacit. Teach balance as fair representation rather than neutrality, and make the criteria for judgement explicit.

activities.title: Weighing the views
learnerActions: Read two short sources with opposing views and note each view's main claim and evidence
Agree three criteria for judging the issue, such as strength of evidence, cost or fairness
Rate each view against each criterion in a grid, with a brief reason
Write a conclusion stating which view is stronger and under what conditions
activities.intendedInsight: A discussion is resolved by explicit criteria, and the conclusion follows from the weighing.
activities.rationale: Makes the evaluative stage visible, addressing the description-heavy pattern Wingate (2012) reports.

activities.title: Block or point by point?
learnerActions: Compare two model discussion essays on the same question, one organised in blocks and one point by point
Mark where evaluation appears in each
Decide which organisation suits your own question and justify the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Organisation should serve evaluation; point-by-point structures often make it easier to keep evaluating throughout.
activities.rationale: Staging analysis based on Martin and Rose's (2008) description of the discussion genre.

difficulties.pattern: 'A discussion essay should be neutral; I shouldn't give my opinion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions such as 'there are both advantages and disadvantages'; little or no evaluative language.
difficulties.response: Distinguish fair representation from neutrality and show high-graded discussion essays that reach a qualified judgement. Check the local brief, since a few tasks do ask only for an account of views.

difficulties.pattern: Reported views and the writer's view blur together.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed claims the marker cannot assign to a source or to the writer; apparent shifts of position from paragraph to paragraph.
difficulties.response: Have learners highlight attributed and averred sentences in two colours, then revisit how fair representation of a view differs from endorsing it; teach signal phrases and stance markers that mark the move to the writer's own evaluation (see sta.averral-attribution).

diagnostic.task: Give learners a discussion essay plan and ask them to write its concluding paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Weighs the views and reaches a qualified judgement with reasons and conditions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reaches a judgement that is unrelated to the body or unsupported.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises both sides without any judgement.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: a core entry genre; keep to two perspectives with a short source pack. Pre-sessional UG and PG: often folded into source-based argument, with emphasis on source-based perspectives and early signalling of position. In-sessional undergraduate: revisit through 'discuss' and 'to what extent' questions in modules and departmental expectations, which differ in how explicitly a position must be stated.
reviewNotes: EAP materials often treat discussion and argumentative essays as distinct genres; in departmental practice they blur, and the distinction is better taught as a continuum of how early and how strongly the position is stated.

records.summary: Exam essays are a high-stakes genre that is largely absent from corpora of assessed coursework, so teaching should be built on local past papers, examiners' comments and departmental guidance. Horowitz's (1986) analysis of essay examination prompts suggests that exam questions typically ask writers to select and organise known content in response to specific demands, which makes question analysis and selective use of revised material central. Weigle (2002) discusses how timed, impromptu writing constrains planning and revision; practice should therefore build fast planning routines, not only language. Make clear that university exam essays differ from proficiency-test essays: they are judged mainly on disciplinary content and its use, not on language display.

activities.title: Five-minute plans
learnerActions: Read three past-paper questions
For each, spend five minutes writing only a thesis and a three-point plan
Swap plans and judge whether each point answers the question as set
Choose one plan and write its introduction in eight minutes
activities.intendedInsight: Many marks are won or lost in planning and relevance rather than in language.
activities.rationale: Builds the fast planning routines that timed conditions constrain (Weigle, 2002).

activities.title: Revise for questions, not topics
learnerActions: Take a set of revision notes on one topic
Write four different exam questions that could be set on that topic
For each question, mark which notes are relevant and which are not
Write one paragraph for one question using only relevant notes
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting and reorganising content for the question is the core exam-essay skill; reproducing everything learned is not.
activities.rationale: Responds to the content-selection demands identified in Horowitz's (1986) analysis of essay examination prompts.

difficulties.pattern: 'I will write down everything I memorised about the topic.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Long descriptive answers loosely related to the question; a prepared essay adapted awkwardly to a different question, a strategy that assessment systems rewarding reproduction of memorised content can encourage.
difficulties.response: Practise answering differently worded questions on the same topic, spending the first minutes on question analysis and a plan, and mark for relevance first. Avoid encouraging memorised model essays as the main revision strategy.

difficulties.pattern: Running out of time and leaving answers unfinished.
difficulties.revealedBy: A long first answer and incomplete final answers.
difficulties.response: Practise time allocation under realistic conditions and teach a fallback of bullet-point conclusions when time runs out. Do not focus only on shortening introductions; uneven allocation and skipped planning are usually the cause.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety leading to blanking or loss of planned structure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report blanking; answers that start well and then lose direction.
difficulties.response: Rehearse a plan-first routine under realistic conditions so that it becomes automatic, and signpost anxiety-management strategies and support services.

diagnostic.task: Give a past-paper question and ask the learner to write only the plan and introduction in ten minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The introduction answers the question directly and the plan's points are relevant and logically ordered.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The plan is relevant but the introduction is generic or defers the answer.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic-focused plan that does not address the question's demand.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: many foundation programmes assess subject content through exams, so focus on question analysis and timed planning. Pre-sessional UG and PG: timed writing appears in some progression assessments but differs from disciplinary exams; make the distinction explicit. In-sessional undergraduate: a core focus, with subject-specific practice on past papers, ideally with subject staff. Taught postgraduate: exams are less frequent but often require application to cases, and some programmes use seen or open-book formats. Learners with approved exam adjustments (extra time, rest breaks, assistive technology) should practise under those conditions.
reviewNotes: Corpora of proficient student writing such as BAWE consist mainly of coursework, so genre-analytic evidence on exam essays is thin.

records.summary: Short answers serve the purpose of demonstrating knowledge and understanding that Gardner and Nesi (2013) associate with the Exercise and Explanation genre families. The main transfer problem is essay habits (introductions, restating the question, elaboration) that cost time and earn no marks. Teach command words and mark allocation, model formal definitions of the term–class–distinguishing-feature type described in rhetorical analyses of scientific English (Trimble, 1985), and use subject-specific past papers, because what counts as a complete answer is disciplinary.

activities.title: Marks to points
learnerActions: Read short-answer questions with their mark allocations
Predict how many distinct points each requires
Compare your predictions with a marking scheme or teacher model
Rewrite a padded answer so that it fits the marks available
activities.intendedInsight: Mark allocation signals expected content; length should follow content, not effort.
activities.rationale: Makes the economy of knowledge-display genres explicit (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: Definition upgrade
learnerActions: Read a set of informal definitions ('Osmosis is when water moves')
Rewrite each as term + class + distinguishing features
Add an example only where it would earn credit
Check accuracy against a subject glossary with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Formal definitions are compact and precise, and are often exactly what the marks are for.
activities.rationale: Uses the definitional pattern described in rhetorical analyses of scientific and technical English (Trimble, 1985).

difficulties.pattern: Writing a mini-essay with an introduction and conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Restated questions, background sentences and time overruns on short items.
difficulties.response: Show marking schemes and practise first-sentence answers. Do not present this as 'style does not matter': accuracy and terminology still carry the marks.

difficulties.pattern: Identifying without explaining in 'explain' questions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that name a factor but give no reason or mechanism.
difficulties.response: Contrast 'state' and 'explain' answers to the same item and teach extensions such as 'because ...' and 'which means that ...'.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer 'Define X and explain why it matters (4 marks)' on a familiar topic.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate formal definition and two developed points, with no padding.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate definition with an undeveloped explanation, or a padded answer.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A vague or circular definition.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: highly relevant because subject modules often use short-answer tests; link closely to content teaching. In-sessional undergraduate: support for first-year science, health and social science assessments, ideally agreeing with subject tutors what counts as a full answer.
reviewNotes: There is little EAP genre research on short-answer responses as such; this guidance extrapolates from work on definitions and on knowledge-display genres.

records.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) place the Critique family among genres whose purpose is developing independent reasoning, and Swales and Feak (2012) treat critiques as a core graduate writing task in which evaluation must be grounded and appropriately mitigated. Wallace and Wray (2016) offer critical questions about a text's claims, evidence and contribution that learners can turn into explicit evaluation criteria. Teach the balance between summary and evaluation explicitly, because briefs vary (some want very little summary), and check the local brief for required criteria or headings.

activities.title: Criteria before reading
learnerActions: Before reading, agree evaluation criteria suited to the text type (empirical, review or theoretical)
Read and note evidence for each criterion with page references
Classify each note as a strength or limitation, and as minor or major
Write one judgement sentence that weighs the major points
activities.intendedInsight: Critique is criterion-based judgement, not personal agreement.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the critical-questions approach of Wallace and Wray (2016).

activities.title: Mitigating criticism
learnerActions: Read a set of blunt evaluative sentences ('The study is useless because the sample is small')
Rewrite them using hedging, praise–criticism pairs and specific consequences for the claims
Compare your versions with evaluative sentences in published reviews
activities.intendedInsight: Academic critique is specific, reasoned and courteous, and mitigation adds to rather than weakens the critic's credibility.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak (2012) address evaluative language in critiques, and Hyland's (2004) analysis of reviews shows how academic critics typically temper criticism.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means finding faults.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviews that list only weaknesses, often in a dismissive tone.
difficulties.response: Show that evaluation weighs strengths and limitations relative to the text's purpose, and require at least one justified strength.

difficulties.pattern: Criticism that could apply to any study ('the sample is small'; 'more research is needed') rather than to this text's design and claims.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic limitations that recur across different critiques, with no account of how the limitation affects the authors' conclusions.
difficulties.response: After each evaluative point ask 'so what does this mean for the authors' claim?', and have learners link each limitation to a specific claim and say whether it weakens, qualifies or leaves it intact. Do not supply a checklist of stock limitations: that reinforces the pattern.

difficulties.pattern: Summary takes up most of the word count.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluation confined to a final short paragraph.
difficulties.response: Set word budgets from the brief and practise 100-word summaries of the same article.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a 150-word critique paragraph and ask them to identify its criterion, its evidence and its judgement.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies all three and comments on whether the evidence justifies the judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the judgement but not the criterion or evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the paragraph as a summary.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG: an introduction to evaluating a single text, using accessible articles and shared criteria. Pre-sessional PG: a core genre, often the first assessed evaluation of an empirical article in the learner's field. In-sessional undergraduate: article critiques are common in psychology, health, education and the social sciences, and criteria are disciplinary (for example validity in psychology). Taught postgraduate: critiques of empirical studies prepare for literature reviews and dissertation methodology, and expectations of methodological critique rise.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-01): the reluctance-to-criticise pattern has been replaced with a difficulty specific to this genre; the deference pattern is kept only in a few anchor topics elsewhere.

records.summary: Hyland's (2004) study of published book reviews shows that reviewers commonly temper criticism, for example by pairing it with praise or hedging it, and that evaluative practices differ across disciplines. Swales and Feak (2012) treat reviews as a form of critique with particular audience demands. For student assignments, clarify whether the task is a disciplinary book review or a book-length critique; for doctoral researchers a published book review is a common first publication and an introduction to their field's review practices, so analysing recent reviews in a target journal is the best preparation.

activities.title: Anatomy of a review
learnerActions: Read two reviews from a journal in your field
Label the stages: bibliographic details, context, description, evaluation, recommendation
Highlight praise in one colour and criticism in another, and note how criticism is softened
Write a short style sheet for reviews in that journal
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews have recognisable stages and evaluative conventions that vary by venue and discipline.
activities.rationale: Learner-led analysis that tests Hyland's (2004) observations about praise and criticism in learners' own fields.

activities.title: Writing for readers
learnerActions: Identify two possible readerships for a book (for example specialists and new postgraduates)
Write a short recommendation for each
Discuss how evaluation and terminology change between the two
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews are written for readers deciding whether to read; evaluation is tied to readership.
activities.rationale: Applies the audience orientation that Swales and Feak (2012) emphasise in evaluative genres.

difficulties.pattern: Chapter-by-chapter summary with a brief evaluation at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Description dominates and evaluation is confined to the last paragraph.
difficulties.response: Require evaluative comment within descriptive sections and set a word budget for description.

difficulties.pattern: A tone that is either harsh or wholly deferential.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmitigated criticism, or unreserved praise with no limitations noted.
difficulties.response: Compare hedged and unhedged versions of the same evaluation and analyse how published reviewers in the field calibrate theirs.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to write two sentences evaluating a book they know, one on a strength and one on a limitation, for a stated reader.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specific, mitigated and oriented to the stated reader.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Specific but unmitigated, or mitigated but vague.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Expresses personal liking or disliking.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: book reviews occur mainly in the humanities and some social sciences, often as a first exercise in a published evaluative genre. Taught postgraduate: reviews of key texts on programme reading lists. PGR: published book reviews are a common early publication, and venue conventions and editors' expectations are the priority.
reviewNotes: Tagged EGAP because its features are shared across fields, but book reviews are concentrated in the humanities and social sciences and rare in science and engineering coursework; designers may treat it as ESAP for those programmes.

records.summary: Reflective writing draws on Schön's (1983) account of the reflective practitioner and is commonly scaffolded with models such as Gibbs's (1988) reflective cycle. Moon (2004) distinguishes descriptive writing from progressively deeper levels of reflection, which helps make markers' expectations explicit. Ryan (2011) argues that reflective writing must be taught as an academic genre with specific linguistic resources, for example the shift from past-tense reporting to present-tense reasoning and future-oriented reconstruction, rather than assumed to come naturally. Because reflective conventions range from personal journals to formal assignments with citations, the brief and local exemplars must guide the form.

activities.title: Depth ladder
learnerActions: Read four extracts reflecting on the same incident at different depths
Rank them and agree what distinguishes each level
Highlight language that signals analysis ('this may have been because', 'in light of')
Rewrite a descriptive extract so that it reaches the next level
activities.intendedInsight: Depth comes from interpretation, questioning and links to theory, not from more detail or stronger emotion.
activities.rationale: Based on Moon's (2004) distinction between descriptive writing and deeper levels of reflection; it makes tacit criteria visible.

activities.title: Mapping reflective language by stage
learnerActions: Analyse a model reflection and label its reporting and responding, relating, reasoning and reconstructing stages
Note tense, pronoun and modal choices in each stage
Draft your own reflection stage by stage with a language bank
Peer-check that each stage does its job
activities.intendedInsight: Each reflective stage has typical language; reflection is a learnable academic genre.
activities.rationale: Applies Ryan's (2011) social semiotic account of reflective writing and the 4Rs scaffold she adapted from earlier work by Bain and colleagues.

difficulties.pattern: 'Reflection is just describing what happened and how I felt.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Narrative-dominated texts with little analysis; feelings reported without interpretation.
difficulties.response: Use word budgets per stage and the depth ladder. Do not respond by discouraging feelings altogether: feelings are data to be analysed.

difficulties.pattern: Discomfort with the first person and with personal disclosure in assessed writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Impersonal reflections that avoid 'I', often reflecting earlier instruction that treated 'never use I' as a rule, or, conversely, disclosure beyond what the task needs.
difficulties.response: Explain that the first person is expected here and that 'never use I' is not a rule of academic writing; discuss what to disclose, and how to protect privacy and confidentiality.

difficulties.pattern: Mechanical use of a reflective cycle as a set of headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Six headings with one short paragraph each and a superficial action plan.
difficulties.response: Present models as thinking tools, compare formulaic and integrated reflections, and check the brief on whether headings are expected.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to spend ten minutes reflecting in writing on a recent learning experience in the course.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Brief description, analysis with reasons, a link to a concept or source, and a specific future action.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some analysis but no link to theory, or a vague action ('I will work harder').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Narrative and feelings only.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional (UG and PG): reflective learning logs and reflective commentaries on the extended project build the genre's language. In-sessional undergraduate: a core genre in education, nursing, business and engineering placements, where models and criteria differ. Taught postgraduate: reflective components of professional master's programmes usually require explicit links to theory; see also the professional practice portfolio. Accept alternative modes (audio or video reflection, structured templates) where the brief allows, as they can suit learners with dyslexia or other learning differences.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice (health-specific) and lrn.reflective-logs; this topic covers the general assessed genre.

records.summary: Horowitz (1986) found annotated bibliographies among the writing tasks university teachers actually set, and Gardner and Nesi (2013) place them in the Literature Survey family, whose purpose is building research skills. The genre is a useful scaffold because it isolates three skills (summarising, evaluating and judging relevance) that literature reviews later integrate. Briefs vary considerably (descriptive or evaluative annotations, word limits, ordering), so analyse the local brief first. Johns and Mayes (1990) found that less proficient summarisers relied more heavily on copying from the source, a risk that is acute when annotations are written from abstracts.

activities.title: Three-layer annotation
learnerActions: Read an article and write one sentence on its purpose and approach and two on its findings
Add one or two evaluative sentences that use explicit criteria
Add one sentence on relevance to your project
Colour-code the three layers and check that the evaluation is not disguised description
activities.intendedInsight: Annotations combine summary, evaluation and relevance, each with its own language.
activities.rationale: Separating the layers mirrors the main variations in annotated-bibliography briefs and prepares for later synthesis in literature reviews (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: An abstract is not an annotation
learnerActions: Compare a source's abstract with a model annotation of the same source
Identify what the annotation adds and what it leaves out
Rewrite an annotation that was copied from an abstract
activities.intendedInsight: Annotations are written for a different purpose and reader from an abstract.
activities.rationale: Targets the reliance on source wording that Johns and Mayes (1990) observed in less proficient summary writers.

difficulties.pattern: Annotations that paraphrase the abstract.
difficulties.revealedBy: Close textual similarity to abstracts; no evaluation or relevance comment.
difficulties.response: Ask for annotations written from notes on the full text, and show that evaluation and relevance require the writer's own judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluation based on surface features ('a good article because it is recent and long').
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic evaluative comments that could apply to any source.
difficulties.response: Provide evaluation criteria tied to source type, such as sample and design for empirical studies or scope and currency for reviews.

diagnostic.task: Give learners an annotation containing summary, evaluation and relevance sentences and ask them to label each sentence's function.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels every sentence correctly and comments on the adequacy of the evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the summary but confuses evaluation with relevance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish summary from evaluation.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: annotated bibliographies scaffold the extended project, often with tutor-approved sources. Pre-sessional UG and PG: a core staged assessment within the extended project, with PG cohorts expected to evaluate empirical sources more closely. In-sessional undergraduate: often a preparatory assessment before a dissertation or major essay. Taught postgraduate: usually assumed, and revisited where it precedes a literature review.

records.summary: Feak and Swales (2009) present the literature review as telling a research story, with attention to organisation, citation choices and the writer's stance towards the literature. Wallace and Wray (2016) provide a framework for critical engagement with literature that makes evaluation explicit. Coursework literature reviews belong to Gardner and Nesi's (2013) Literature Survey family, whose purpose is building research skills; they differ from review sections in research articles and theses (res.literature-review) because the gap often serves a coursework question rather than justifying the writer's own study. Emphasise synthesis over serial summary, and analyse local exemplars, because expectations range from narrative reviews to systematic-style reviews with documented searches.

activities.title: From list to synthesis
learnerActions: Read a source-by-source review extract
Use a synthesis matrix to regroup its sources by theme
Rewrite one paragraph led by a thematic topic sentence in your own voice, with sources in dialogue
Compare the two versions for voice and evaluation
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews are organised by ideas, and sources serve the writer's points.
activities.rationale: Targets the serial-summary pattern and the questions of organisation and stance discussed by Feak and Swales (2009).

activities.title: Critical questions for the review
learnerActions: For your review question, list what is known, how it is known and what is disputed
Apply critical questions about claims, evidence and warrants to three key sources
Write a paragraph that evaluates the evidence base for one theme
activities.intendedInsight: A literature review evaluates the evidence base rather than simply reporting it.
activities.rationale: Uses Wallace and Wray's (2016) critical reading framework as a writing scaffold.

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source summaries ('Smith (2019) found ... Jones (2020) argued ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs beginning with author names; few comparative or evaluative statements.
difficulties.response: Require thematic topic sentences in the writer's voice and use synthesis matrices. Do not ban integral citation; teach when author prominence is rhetorically useful.

difficulties.pattern: Unsupported or absolute gap claims ('no research has been done on this').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged gap statements, or gaps unrelated to the literature reviewed.
difficulties.response: Teach hedged gap language and require that every gap claim follows from the reviewed literature.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about what to include and how much is enough.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-inclusive reviews that cover everything found; anxiety about missing sources.
difficulties.response: Agree scope criteria tied to the question and keep a search record; explain that coverage depends on the review's purpose.

diagnostic.task: Show two paragraphs reviewing the same three sources, one serial and one synthesised, and ask which is stronger and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Prefers the synthesised paragraph and explains its use of voice, comparison and evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Prefers the synthesised paragraph but cannot say why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Prefers the serial version as clearer.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional PG: a short review section within the extended project, often with provided or tutor-approved sources. In-sessional undergraduate: reviews in second and final years, frequently preparing for dissertations. Taught postgraduate: a core genre, set as stand-alone reviews and as preparation for the dissertation, with rising expectations of critical evaluation and justified scope. The stage boundary with res.literature-review is functional: once the review must justify the writer's own study in a dissertation, thesis or article, teach it through that topic.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-15): the stage boundary with res.literature-review is now stated in the description; this topic has no pgr role and no undergraduate pre-sessional role.

records.summary: Horowitz (1986) found summary of, and reaction to, reading among the tasks university teachers set, and Hirvela (2004) argues that connecting reading and writing, with summary and response at its centre, is fundamental to L2 writing instruction. Leki and Carson (1997) contrasted EAP writing that could draw on personal knowledge with content-course writing that held students responsible for source texts; summary–response builds that text-responsible stance. Grabe and Zhang (2013) argue that reading and writing should be taught together, with explicit attention to summarising and responding.

activities.title: Two-colour paper
learnerActions: Read a model summary–response
Highlight summary sentences in one colour and response sentences in another
Note the signal phrases and reporting verbs at the boundary
Find any sentence that mixes the two and rewrite it
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to know whose idea is whose, and the boundary is marked linguistically.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the text-responsible stance described by Leki and Carson (1997).

activities.title: Respond to a claim, not a topic
learnerActions: Identify the source's three main claims
Choose one and draft agree, disagree and qualify responses, each with a reason
Select the strongest and develop it with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A response must engage the source's argument rather than the general topic.
activities.rationale: Applies the reading–writing integration Hirvela (2004) advocates.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluation leaking into the summary ('The author wrongly claims ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Loaded reporting verbs and evaluative adjectives in the summary section.
difficulties.response: Contrast neutral and evaluative reporting verbs and reserve evaluation for the response.

difficulties.pattern: The response addresses the general topic rather than the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion essays only loosely connected to the source's argument.
difficulties.response: Require the response to quote or paraphrase the specific claim it answers.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to write a three-sentence summary and a two-sentence response to a short argumentative paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate, attributed summary and a response that engages a specific claim with a reason.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate summary followed by a generic response.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies the source, or gives an opinion without a summary.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: a core entry genre into source-based writing. Pre-sessional UG: frequent in early weeks and closely related to integrated reading-into-writing tasks. Pre-sessional PG: usually assumed and revisited quickly before critique. In-sessional undergraduate: appears as reading responses and seminar papers, particularly in the humanities and social sciences and in North American-style curricula.
reviewNotes: The summary–response paper is mainly a North American composition genre; in UK contexts it is more often an EAP or foundation teaching genre than a departmental assessment.

records.summary: Treat explanation, comparison and problem–solution as patterns that organise essays and essay sections rather than as separate genres: Gardner and Nesi (2013) place factorial and consequential essays within the essay family and show that such patterns also run through explanations, case studies and reports. Martin and Rose (2008) distinguish sequential, factorial and consequential explanations, giving learners a principled choice of structure depending on whether a question asks how something happens, why it happens or what it leads to. Hoey's (2001) situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern shows that a response is complete only once it is evaluated, and Carrell (1985) found that explicit teaching of top-level text structures, comparison among them, helped L2 readers, an awareness that can be carried into writing through exemplar analysis. The common teaching challenge across all three patterns is moving from listing (causes, features, solutions) to explaining, judging significance and calibrating certainty, and avoiding coursebook templates that departments do not recognise.

activities.title: One topic, three patterns
learnerActions: Sort six essay and exam questions on one topic by whether they ask mainly for explanation, comparison or problem–solution, or a mix
Choose an organising pattern for each (by factor, consequence, sequence, criterion or problem–response–evaluation)
Write a thesis for two of the questions that states what the essay will show
Plan one essay in full, justifying the order of the body sections
activities.intendedInsight: The question's purpose determines the pattern, and each pattern still needs a claim that says what it shows.
activities.rationale: Applies Martin and Rose's (2008) explanation types and Hoey's (2001) problem–solution pattern as planning choices rather than fixed templates.

activities.title: From list to analysis
learnerActions: Read three short paragraphs: one lists causes, one describes item A then item B, one names solutions
For the first, add the mechanism by which one cause produces the effect, with source evidence
For the second, rewrite it point by point around one criterion and add a sentence on what the difference means
For the third, evaluate one solution against two explicit criteria and acknowledge a trade-off
activities.intendedInsight: Each pattern becomes analytical at the same point: when the writer explains why, why it matters or how well it works.
activities.rationale: Targets the listing tendency common to all three patterns and makes the evaluative element of the problem–solution pattern explicit (Hoey, 2001); comparison as a text structure follows Carrell (1985).

activities.title: Criteria before judgement
learnerActions: From a source pack, list the items, causes or responses relevant to a question
Agree three or four criteria that matter to the question (for example strength of evidence, cost, feasibility, fairness)
Rate each item against the criteria in a grid, citing the evidence
Write a concluding paragraph whose judgement follows from the grid
activities.intendedInsight: Comparisons, explanations and recommendations persuade when the criteria for judgement are explicit.
activities.rationale: Makes criterion-based evaluation, shared by all three patterns, into a reusable procedure that transfers to case-study and report genres (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

difficulties.pattern: Listing causes without explaining how they operate ('Another reason is …').
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of one claim plus one example; repeated additive connectors.
difficulties.response: Prompt with 'How exactly does this lead to …?' and model mechanism sentences. Do not respond by supplying more connectors: the gap is explanatory content, not linking.

difficulties.pattern: 'Compare means describe A, then describe B.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Two descriptive halves with comparison appearing only in the conclusion, and no statement of what the comparison shows.
difficulties.response: Require a cross-referencing sentence in each paragraph and teach point-by-point organisation first. Do not forbid block organisation: it is acceptable when each block makes the comparison explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Describing the problem at length and listing solutions, or recommending them as unconditional commands ('The government must ban …'), without evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Most of the word count on background; responses named but not evaluated; strong modals with no criteria, feasibility or trade-offs.
difficulties.response: Set word budgets for each stage, require an evaluation for every response proposed, and contrast hortatory statements with justified, hedged recommendations.

difficulties.pattern: Overstating causation ('X causes Y') on the basis of correlational evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged causal verbs attached to survey or correlational findings.
difficulties.response: Review correlation and causation using examples from the learners' own sources, then practise rewording with calibrated causal language ('is associated with', 'may contribute to').

diagnostic.task: Give three questions on one topic that call for different patterns and ask the learner to name the pattern each needs, write a one-sentence thesis for each and outline one in three lines.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Patterns identified from the purpose of each question, theses that state an outcome, and an outline organised by factor, criterion or problem–response–evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Patterns identified correctly but theses that announce topics, or outlines that list without an evaluative stage.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The same descriptive outline offered for all three questions.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: a core genre set; use familiar phenomena, items and problems with short source packs, closely linked to subject-content modules. Pre-sessional UG: source-based explanation, comparison of models or policies, and problem–solution essays as preparation for argumentative and report writing. Pre-sessional PG: usually revisited within source-based argument rather than taught separately. In-sessional undergraduate: these patterns appear inside discipline-specific essays, exam answers and reports (historical causation, comparing theoretical approaches, problem–solution in engineering, environmental and health subjects), where the criteria and norms for causal argument come from the module.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-16): the former compare-and-contrast and problem–solution essay topics are absorbed here, and the former explanation-essay topic is renamed; the topic now treats the three as rhetorical patterns within the essay family.

There is little genre-analytic research on compare-and-contrast or problem–solution essays as distinct student genres; this guidance draws on research on explanation genres, text patterns and text structure.

records.summary: The extended project answers Moore and Morton's (2005) finding that proficiency-test writing differs from university tasks, and Leki and Carson's (1997) contrast between EAP writing that draws on personal knowledge and content-course writing that holds students responsible for source texts: it is the pre-degree task closest to that text-responsible coursework. Because it is staged, it assesses process as well as product; Carless and Boud (2018) argue that students need help to appreciate feedback, make judgements, manage the feelings it provokes and take action, so tutorials should be built around the learner's own questions and followed by visible revision. Teach topic narrowing, source management and global revision explicitly, use exemplars from earlier cohorts with permission, and keep the scope modest so that the project rewards control of sources and argument rather than coverage.

activities.title: From topic to question
learnerActions: List three topics related to your intended degree
For one, write three increasingly narrow questions (by context, population, period or aspect)
Run a quick library search for each question and note whether you find too many, too few or a manageable set of relevant sources
Agree a final question with your tutor and record why it is answerable within the word limit
activities.intendedInsight: A good project question is narrow enough to answer with the sources and words available, and testing it with a search shows this early.
activities.rationale: Makes feasibility concrete before learners invest in reading, and turns the topic plan into a reasoned decision rather than an expression of interest; it applies the search skills the project depends on.

activities.title: Source map before drafting
learnerActions: Enter 8–12 sources in a grid against the sub-questions of your project
Mark where sources agree, disagree or add a qualification
Use the grid to decide the order of your sections and the point each will make
Write one topic sentence per section in your own voice before drafting
activities.intendedInsight: Sections are organised around the writer's points, with sources in dialogue, rather than around individual sources.
activities.rationale: Supports the text-responsible use of sources that Leki and Carson (1997) found content courses demand, and guards against source-by-source reporting across a long text.

activities.title: Tutorial preparation and feedback log
learnerActions: Before each tutorial, write two specific questions about your draft
After the tutorial, log each feedback point, your decision (act, clarify or not act, with a reason) and the change you made
Before submission, check that every logged decision has been carried out
Use the log as evidence in your reflective commentary
activities.intendedInsight: Feedback becomes useful when the writer judges it, decides what to do and can show the result.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the appreciating, judging, managing affect and taking action elements of feedback literacy described by Carless and Boud (2018); the log also documents the learner's process.

difficulties.pattern: Choosing a topic that is too broad or too far from accessible sources ('The impact of technology on education').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unfocused plans, drafts that survey a whole field, and reliance on general web sources because scholarly sources on the topic as stated are unmanageable.
difficulties.response: Narrow by context, population, period or aspect, and test the question with a short search before approving it. Do not simply assign a topic: the narrowing decision is part of what the project develops.

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source reporting across the whole project, with the writer's own line of argument appearing only in the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sections or paragraphs that begin with author names; a reverse outline that lists sources rather than points.
difficulties.response: Have learners reverse-outline the draft by points, rebuild sections around the source map, and write section topic sentences in their own voice. Do not ban integral citation; teach when author prominence is useful.

difficulties.pattern: Revising only surface errors between drafts, or treating tutorial comments as corrections to accept or ignore without judgement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Second drafts with corrected grammar but unchanged structure and argument; feedback points neither acted on nor discussed. The pattern is common where earlier writing was assessed as single, unrevised products such as timed test essays.
difficulties.response: Model a substantive revision of a sample draft, use the feedback log, and ask learners to explain one structural change at each tutorial.

difficulties.pattern: Marked improvement between drafts, or a detector score, is treated as a sign that the learner did not write the project.
