difficulties.revealedBy: Integrity queries based on a change in style or an AI-detection or similarity score, without other evidence.
difficulties.response: Institutions should not treat detector scores or a change in style as evidence of misconduct: the burden of proof lies with the institution, and multilingual writers are disproportionately misclassified by detectors. Course teams should set clear rules on AI and proofreading in the brief, and staged drafts, notes, search records and version histories give learners a natural record of their process without requiring them to prove their innocence.

diagnostic.task: At topic-plan stage, ask the learner to state their question, name three sources they intend to use and say how each will help to answer the question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A focused, answerable question and sources of suitable types, each with a distinct role such as background, evidence or a counter-view.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A reasonably focused question, but sources that are only topically related or whose roles are unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic rather than a question, with no identified or suitable sources.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: a shorter, more scaffolded project with tutor-approved topics and sometimes provided source packs, often linked to the learner's subject pathway. Pre-sessional UG: a source-based essay or report related to the intended degree, usually assessed for progression alongside other components; the topic plan is a short agreement with a tutor, not a research proposal. Pre-sessional PG: topics close to the learner's master's field, with a short review of literature and higher expectations of source evaluation; some programmes include small-scale primary data (grp.empirical-project-report). Lengths, the number of drafts and whether a reflective commentary is required vary with course length and institution, and in EMI and transnational programmes the project may be assessed jointly with subject staff. Offer tutorials and feedback in more than one mode (written, recorded or face to face) and plan deadlines with reasonable adjustments in mind.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-20): added as the pre-sessional and foundation capstone genre and linked to INF, SYN, SRC, CIT, WPR and EDT prerequisites. The 2,000–4,000-word range reflects typical UK provision and varies elsewhere.

There is little published genre analysis of the pre-sessional extended project itself; this guidance draws on research on source-based writing, task differences between tests and university study, and feedback literacy.

records.summary: Nesi and Gardner (2012) show that 'report' is a label applied to several distinct genre families (methodology recounts, research reports, design specifications and case studies among them), so report conventions should be taught as a family resemblance rather than a single template. Gardner and Nesi's (2013) classification helps learners locate the report they have been set. Bruce's (2008) distinction between social genres and the cognitive genres within them shows learners that a report may contain explanation, discussion or recount. Contrast essay and report on the same content, emphasise the reader who reads selectively and acts on findings, and always check the brief and templates.

activities.title: Essay to report
learnerActions: Read a short essay and the brief for a report on the same topic
Identify the report's reader and what decision or understanding they need
Restructure the essay into headed sections
Write informative headings and decide where a table would serve better than prose
activities.intendedInsight: Report structure serves a reader who reads selectively and needs findings and recommendations.
activities.rationale: Holding content constant while changing the genre isolates purpose and reader, the factors that distinguish the report families described by Nesi and Gardner (2012).

activities.title: Which report is this?
learnerActions: Examine extracts from a lab report, a business report and a design report
Compare their sections, headings and use of visuals
Agree which features are shared and which are specific to each
activities.intendedInsight: 'Report' covers several genres, and the shared features are fewer than learners expect.
activities.rationale: Based on Gardner and Nesi's (2013) classification of genre families in student writing.

difficulties.pattern: 'A report is an essay with headings.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Headings inserted into continuous argumentative prose; no separation of findings from recommendations.
difficulties.response: Show reports in which sections do different jobs and ask what the reader of each section needs. Do not imply that reports contain no argument: analysis and justification remain central.

difficulties.pattern: Uninformative or generic headings ('Part 1', 'Main body').
difficulties.revealedBy: Headings that do not tell the reader what a section contains.
difficulties.response: Practise writing headings a reader could navigate by, and check them against the template.

difficulties.pattern: Visuals inserted without number, caption or reference in the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Figures that the text never mentions or explains.
difficulties.response: Teach captioning and in-text reference together, and require every visual to be cited and commented on.

diagnostic.task: Ask: what are three differences between an essay and a report?
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions purpose and reader, selective reading supported by headings, separation of findings from conclusions or recommendations, and integrated visuals.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions headings only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot name a difference.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: a core topic, introduced through simple reports in subject modules. Pre-sessional UG and PG: needed where the progression project takes report form, and in subject-specific strands. In-sessional undergraduate: reports in science, engineering, business and social science differ substantially, so work from departmental templates. Taught postgraduate: usually assumed, and revisited for professional report formats.

records.summary: Parkinson (2017) characterises the student laboratory report as a genre in its own right that differs from the research article it superficially resembles, notably because it is written to demonstrate understanding of established theory and procedure rather than to claim a new contribution. Gardner and Nesi (2013) classify lab reports with Methodology Recounts. Teach section by section with the department's lab manual, attending to data commentary (Swales & Feak, 2012) and to the discussion of error, which students frequently reduce to generic statements. Conventions such as passive or active voice, and whether results and discussion are combined, vary by discipline and lab manual and should be checked locally.

activities.title: Results or discussion?
learnerActions: Sort sentences from a lab report into results (what was found) and discussion (what it means)
Identify the language that distinguishes them, such as tense, hedging and comparison with theory
Rewrite a mixed paragraph as separate results and discussion paragraphs
activities.intendedInsight: Results report and highlight; discussion interprets and evaluates.
activities.rationale: Builds awareness of section functions as described in genre analysis of student lab reports (Parkinson, 2017).

activities.title: Beyond 'human error'
learnerActions: List possible sources of error in a familiar experiment
Classify them as systematic or random, procedural or instrumental
Estimate the direction and approximate size of each one's effect on the result
Write an evaluation paragraph that ends with a specific improvement
activities.intendedInsight: Error analysis is reasoning about specific effects on results, not a ritual admission of imperfection.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the evaluative expectations of the discussion section, which generic error statements do not meet; the activity draws on data commentary principles (Swales & Feak, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Method written as instructions copied from the lab manual ('Add 5 ml of ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Imperative sentences in the method section.
difficulties.response: Contrast manual instructions with a report method and practise converting them to past-tense description, passive or active according to the local convention. Do not teach that the passive is always required.

difficulties.pattern: Results described vaguely, without values or figure references, or mixed with interpretation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'the graph goes up' and explanations embedded in the results.
difficulties.response: Teach location and highlighting statements that cite values and figure numbers, and move interpretation to the discussion.

difficulties.pattern: Introduction written as a general history of the topic or as a research-gap argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long background with no link between theory and the aim of the experiment.
difficulties.response: Analyse departmental exemplar introductions and focus on the theory needed to interpret this experiment.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a short results table and ask for two sentences of results and two of discussion.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Results sentences cite values and the table; discussion sentences interpret them against theory.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Cites values but mixes interpretation into the results.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the whole table without selecting what matters.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: science foundation students write lab reports early, usually with structured templates. Pre-sessional UG and PG: taught in science, engineering and health subject strands, where a short practical report may be assessed. In-sessional undergraduate: discipline-specific support, ideally embedded with lab staff, since conventions differ between chemistry, physics, biology and engineering. Taught postgraduate: lab-based MSc students may need support in moving towards research-article conventions for project reports.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-35): pre-sessional roles added as develop for subject-strand pre-sessionals. Claims about Parkinson (2017) are stated at a general level; specific move findings should be checked in the article before adding detail.

records.summary: Nesi and Gardner (2012) identify the Research Report as a genre family in which students report their own investigations, usually later in a programme. Swales and Feak (2012) give accessible, move-based treatments of research-reporting sections, and Creswell and Creswell (2018) offer frameworks for aligning questions, design and reporting across quantitative, qualitative and mixed approaches. Emphasise alignment between questions, methods, findings and conclusions, and proportionate claims from small samples. On pre-sessionals the project is also a vehicle for academic socialisation, so keep its scope modest and its process visible.

activities.title: Alignment audit
learnerActions: Write your research questions at the top of a page
For each question, note the method, data and finding that address it
Mark any finding not linked to a question and any question without a finding
Revise the questions or the conclusions to restore alignment
activities.intendedInsight: Coherence in a report comes from alignment between questions, methods, findings and conclusions.
activities.rationale: Applies the design alignment emphasised by Creswell and Creswell (2018) to the student's own report.

activities.title: Claims sized to data
learnerActions: Read conclusions from three student projects
Rate the strength of each claim against the sample size and design
Rewrite overclaims with hedges and explicit scope limits
activities.intendedInsight: Small-scale studies support modest, bounded claims, and stating limits strengthens credibility.
activities.rationale: Builds claim calibration in the context where learners most often overclaim: reporting their own first research.

difficulties.pattern: Generalising from small samples ('This proves that students prefer ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged generalisations beyond the participants studied.
difficulties.response: Teach scope language and the limitations section together. Do not discourage claims altogether; the aim is claims that the data can bear.

difficulties.pattern: Literature review and discussion disconnected from each other.
difficulties.revealedBy: A discussion that never returns to the sources reviewed.
difficulties.response: Require each discussion paragraph to relate a finding to at least one reviewed source.

difficulties.pattern: Research questions too broad to answer with the data available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions such as 'What is the impact of social media on society?'
difficulties.response: Narrow by population, context and variable or phenomenon, check feasibility before data collection, and pilot survey or interview questions with a few people like the intended participants.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a research question and ask what data could answer it and what claims would then be possible.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Proposes feasible data and states bounded claims.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Proposes feasible data but overclaims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Proposes unfeasible or misaligned data.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional PG: some programmes include a small empirical project, often with secondary data or a short survey, where process and alignment matter more than results; most pre-sessional projects are source-based instead (ges.extended-source-based-project). In-sessional undergraduate: research methods modules and final-year projects, with disciplinary conventions for quantitative and qualitative reporting. Taught postgraduate: projects that prepare for or form part of the dissertation.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-20, R1-26): the undergraduate pre-sessional role is removed because most pre-sessional projects are source-based, and a soft link to res.instrument-wording now covers question design for survey and interview projects.

records.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) classify case studies among genres that prepare students for professional practice, and Horowitz (1986) found case studies among the tasks university teachers set. Nathan's (2013) analysis of the business case report describes a problem-oriented genre organised around analysis and recommendations and distinct from the essay. The central challenge is analytical application: frameworks and theories must be used to explain the case, not summarised. Because the genre varies so much across fields (a nursing case study differs markedly from a business case report), analyse departmental exemplars and briefs.

activities.title: Facts, inferences, assumptions
learnerActions: Read a short case and list its facts
List the inferences you draw and the evidence for each
Identify assumptions that would need checking
Write a short statement of the main issue grounded in the facts
activities.intendedInsight: Analysis rests on distinguishing what the case states from what the analyst infers.
activities.rationale: Supports the analytical stance expected in professional-practice genres (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: Framework as lens, not list
learnerActions: Compare two paragraphs applying the same framework to a case, one descriptive and one analytical
Identify how the analytical paragraph uses case evidence and draws implications
Rewrite a descriptive paragraph analytically
activities.intendedInsight: Frameworks earn credit when they reveal something about the case.
activities.rationale: Reflects the analysis-and-recommendation focus Nathan (2013) describes in business case reports.

difficulties.pattern: Retelling the case.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long summaries of the case at the expense of analysis.
difficulties.response: Tell learners to assume the marker knows the case, and set a small word budget for the overview.

difficulties.pattern: Describing a framework or theory at length without applying it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that define a model or list its components with little reference to the case, a habit encouraged where earlier assessment rewarded accurate reproduction of models.
difficulties.response: Require every analytical paragraph to contain case evidence and an implication for the issue.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations not linked to the analysis, or not feasible.
difficulties.revealedBy: New ideas appearing for the first time in the recommendations.
difficulties.response: Have learners trace each recommendation back to an issue and forward to feasibility and risk.

diagnostic.task: Give a mini-case and ask for the most important issue and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a prioritised issue with supporting case evidence and an implication.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names an issue without justification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Retells the case.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: business and other pathways introduce short cases with guided frameworks. Pre-sessional UG and PG: taught in business, health and law subject strands, often as a short case analysis. In-sessional undergraduate: discipline-specific case studies in business, health, law, education and engineering, ideally co-taught with subject staff. Taught postgraduate: professional master's programmes rely heavily on case analysis, often with complex cases and group work.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-35): pre-sessional roles added as develop for subject-strand pre-sessionals.

records.summary: Nathan (2013) shows that business school case report writing is problem-oriented and recommendation-driven and argues for making its structure and expectations explicit to students. Zhu's (2004) analysis of writing assignments in business courses found case-based and professional genres such as case analyses and business reports rather than essays alone, which is why business pre-sessional and in-sessional provision teaches the report early. Bhatia (1993) offers a framework for analysing professional genres through the communicative purposes of their users, which suits reports written for simulated clients and managers. Teach the findings–conclusions–recommendations chain, the role of the executive summary and analytical use of frameworks, and check local templates because business schools differ.

activities.title: Findings, conclusions, recommendations
learnerActions: Given a set of findings, write a conclusion for each
Derive a recommendation from each conclusion
Prioritise the recommendations by impact and feasibility
Check that no recommendation lacks a supporting finding
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations persuade when they can be traced back to findings.
activities.rationale: Reflects the recommendation-driven structure of business case genres (Nathan, 2013).

activities.title: Writing for a busy manager
learnerActions: Read two versions of a report introduction, one front-loaded and one background-heavy
Decide which better supports a decision and why
Rewrite a background-heavy section so that the key message comes first
activities.intendedInsight: Professional readers prioritise purpose, conclusions and actions.
activities.rationale: Communicative purpose shapes the structure of professional genres (Bhatia, 1993).

difficulties.pattern: Essay-like discussion with vague or missing recommendations.
difficulties.revealedBy: A final section that summarises rather than recommends.
difficulties.response: Use the findings–conclusions–recommendations chain and require a recommendations section mapped to the conclusions.

difficulties.pattern: Management frameworks used as checklists.
difficulties.revealedBy: Bulleted framework lists with no prioritisation or implications, a habit encouraged where earlier courses assessed recall of framework components.
difficulties.response: Require learners to prioritise framework items and state the implication of each for the problem.

difficulties.pattern: Bullet points used for analysis, or avoided where they would help.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analysis fragmented into bullets, or long recommendations buried in prose.
difficulties.response: Use bullets for parallel items such as recommendations and continuous prose for analysis and justification, following the brief.

diagnostic.task: Ask: what is the difference between a conclusion and a recommendation in a business report?
diagnostic.strongResponse: A conclusion is a judgement drawn from findings; a recommendation proposes an action that follows from a conclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vague or partly correct distinction.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats them as the same.

records.contextNotes: Foundation: simple reports in business pathways. Pre-sessional UG and PG: business-specific pre-sessionals often use report assessments, with PG cohorts writing for simulated clients. In-sessional undergraduate: business, management and accounting reports. Taught postgraduate: MBA and management master's reports, often for simulated clients and with group authorship.

records.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) identify Design Specification as a genre family that prepares students for professional practice, particularly in engineering. Trimble's (1985) rhetorical approach to scientific and technical English highlights the description, definition, classification and visual–verbal relationships on which technical reports depend. Prioritise justification of decisions against requirements and integration of visuals, and consult departmental templates, professional-body expectations and module briefs, because formats differ between engineering branches, computing and product design.

activities.title: Requirements to criteria
learnerActions: Extract requirements and constraints from a design brief
Rewrite vague requirements as measurable ones
Use them as criteria in a decision matrix for two options
Write a selection paragraph that refers to the matrix
activities.intendedInsight: Design decisions are justified by explicit, measurable criteria.
activities.rationale: Supports the justificatory purpose of the Design Specification family (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: Text and diagram together
learnerActions: Describe a component using a labelled diagram
Write a paragraph that refers to the diagram and explains each part's function
Ask a partner to identify the parts from your text alone
activities.intendedInsight: Technical description depends on precise integration of text and visuals.
activities.rationale: Trimble (1985) treats visual–verbal relationships as a core rhetorical feature of technical writing.

difficulties.pattern: Narrating what the team did chronologically instead of justifying decisions.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'First we ..., then we ...' structures with little evaluation.
difficulties.response: Restructure sections around decisions, options and criteria, keeping chronology for logs or appendices.

difficulties.pattern: Imprecise requirements and evaluations ('the design is efficient and good').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmeasurable claims without values or units.
difficulties.response: Require quantification with units and tolerances, and link each evaluative claim to a requirement.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to justify, in three sentences, choosing one of two familiar products for a stated purpose.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names explicit criteria, compares the options on them with values where possible, and acknowledges a trade-off.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives criteria but no comparison, or comparison without criteria.
diagnostic.gapResponse: States a preference without reasons.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: engineering, computing and design programmes, best embedded in project modules with subject staff. Taught postgraduate: MSc engineering and computing projects, where professional standards and group-authored reports are common.

records.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) include proposals among genres preparing students for professional and research practice. Creswell and Creswell (2018) provide widely used proposal structures for quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods studies that emphasise alignment between purpose, questions and methods, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss the proposal as a persuasive text addressed to supervisors and committees. Connor and Mauranen's (1999) move analysis of research grant proposals identifies persuasive moves (such as territory, gap, goal, means and benefits) that can be adapted to student proposals, which are far less competitive. Departmental templates differ substantially and must guide the structure.

activities.title: Proposal skeleton from the template
learnerActions: Collect your department's proposal template and assessment criteria
Write one sentence for each section
Check alignment: does each question have a method and a data source?
Ask a peer to review feasibility within the time available
activities.intendedInsight: A convincing proposal is aligned, feasible and shaped by the local template.
activities.rationale: Applies the alignment of purpose, questions and methods emphasised by Creswell and Creswell (2018).

activities.title: Persuasive moves
learnerActions: Label the moves in a model proposal rationale (territory, gap, aim, method, benefit)
Identify the language that persuades the reader of significance and feasibility
Draft your own rationale paragraph using the moves
activities.intendedInsight: A proposal is an argument for the project, not a description of it.
activities.rationale: Adapts Connor and Mauranen's (1999) analysis of grant proposal moves to student proposals.

difficulties.pattern: Over-ambitious scope for the time and resources available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Multiple broad questions, large samples or several methods in a short project.
difficulties.response: Narrow the questions and test feasibility against the timeline and access, with supervisor input.

difficulties.pattern: A rationale based only on personal interest ('I have always been interested in ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Significance argued from the writer's biography rather than from literature or need.
difficulties.response: Allow a brief note of motivation where the brief permits, but require significance to be argued from the literature, a gap or a practical need.

difficulties.pattern: Ethics treated as a formality.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic statements ('there are no ethical issues') for projects involving people or data.
difficulties.response: Discuss consent, confidentiality, data management and risk for the specific project and link to the institution's ethics process.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state their project aim, one research question and the data that will answer it in three sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A focused aim, an answerable question and feasible, aligned data.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A focused aim but a misaligned or unfeasible data source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic rather than an aim or question.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional PG: some programmes assess a short dissertation-style proposal for a project in the learner's field; on undergraduate pre-sessionals the topic plan belongs to the extended project instead. In-sessional undergraduate: final-year project and dissertation proposals. Taught postgraduate: a core genre, since dissertation proposals are frequently assessed and are followed by ethics applications, often within weeks. The stage boundary with res.research-proposal is functional: proposals that must argue for an original contribution to a doctoral panel or funder belong there.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-15): the stage boundary with res.research-proposal is now stated in the description; this topic has no pgr role, and research-writing proposals belong to pre-sessional PG, not UG.

records.summary: Executive summaries are professional rather than research genres: Bhatia (1993) argues that professional genres are best understood through the communicative purposes of their users, here a reader deciding whether and how to act. They share with abstracts the demand for a stand-alone condensation of a longer text (Swales & Feak, 2009) but prioritise findings and recommendations over method. Teach by comparing an abstract, an introduction and an executive summary for the same report, and have learners write for a named reader facing a specific decision.

activities.title: Three openings compared
learnerActions: Read an abstract, an introduction and an executive summary written for the same report
List what each includes and omits and in what order
Identify the reader and purpose of each
Write a rule of thumb for each text type in one sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Different reader purposes produce different selections and orderings of the same content.
activities.rationale: Comparison by purpose follows Bhatia's (1993) approach to professional genres; the abstract provides a familiar point of contrast (Swales & Feak, 2009).

activities.title: Two sentences first
learnerActions: State the report's main finding and main recommendation in two sentences
Test them on a partner who has not read the report: could they act on them?
Expand to the required length, adding supporting findings in order of importance
Check that nothing appears that is not in the report
activities.intendedInsight: The executive summary is built outward from the key message rather than compiled section by section.
activities.rationale: Front-loading serves the decision-making reader that defines the genre's purpose (Bhatia, 1993).

difficulties.pattern: The summary is written as an introduction, describing background and what the report will do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Phrases such as 'This report will examine ...' and no findings or recommendations.
difficulties.response: Contrast introduction and executive summary directly, and require findings and recommendations in the first paragraph.

difficulties.pattern: One sentence copied or paraphrased from each section in report order.
difficulties.revealedBy: A summary that mirrors the report's table of contents and gives method as much space as findings.
difficulties.response: Have learners rank content by importance to the reader before drafting, and allow the order to depart from the report's.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in two or three sentences, how an executive summary differs from an abstract.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes the decision-making reader, the emphasis on findings and recommendations over method, and stand-alone use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says it is 'a longer abstract' or notes only position in the document.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats it as an introduction.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: business, engineering and some social science reports require executive summaries, often as a separately marked element. Taught postgraduate: management, public policy and public health programmes use them routinely, and they recur in professional practice.
reviewNotes: No item in the closed bibliography analyses executive summaries directly; the citations support only the general claims about professional genres and abstracts.

records.summary: Treat the policy brief as a professional genre whose structure follows its users' purposes (Bhatia, 1993): busy readers need key messages first, a clear problem, a fair account of evidence and actionable options. A recurrent challenge is presenting evidence accessibly without distortion; Gigerenzer et al. (2007) show that statistical information is better understood when presented as absolute risks and natural frequencies rather than relative risks alone, which is directly relevant to briefs on health, education or social policy. Analyse briefs from the organisations learners might write for, as templates and expectations vary.

activities.title: Key messages from research
learnerActions: Read the abstract and findings of a policy-relevant study
Draft three key messages for a named policy reader
Check each against the evidence for overstatement
Rewrite any statistics as absolute figures or natural frequencies where helpful
activities.intendedInsight: Policy messages must be both actionable and faithful to the strength of the evidence.
activities.rationale: Applies Gigerenzer et al.'s (2007) principles for transparent risk communication to the genre's central move.

activities.title: Brief anatomy
learnerActions: Compare two published policy briefs from different organisations
Label their sections and identify how evidence and recommendations are presented
Note how visuals and headings serve a skimming reader
Draft a template for a brief in your field
activities.intendedInsight: Policy briefs share a purpose-driven logic but differ in template by organisation.
activities.rationale: Analysing professional genres through their purposes and users follows Bhatia (1993).

difficulties.pattern: Writing an academic literature review with recommendations added at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long background, dense citation and recommendations only in the final paragraph.
difficulties.response: Insist on key messages first and a strict page limit; move citations to endnotes or links where the template allows.

difficulties.pattern: Overstating certainty or causal effects to make recommendations persuasive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unqualified claims ('X will reduce Y') from observational or limited evidence.
difficulties.response: Teach plain-language ways of signalling evidence strength ('strong evidence suggests', 'early findings indicate') and check each message against its source.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations that are vague or addressed to no one ('More should be done').
difficulties.revealedBy: Recommendations without an actor, action or time frame.
difficulties.response: Require each recommendation to name who should do what, by when, and at roughly what cost or risk.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a research finding and ask for one recommendation for a named policy actor.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A specific, feasible action for a named actor, worded within the strength of the evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A specific action that overstates the evidence, or a cautious but vague action.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A general statement with no actor or action.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: occasional assessments in politics, development, public health and environmental studies. Taught postgraduate: common in public policy, international development, public health and education master's programmes. PGR: briefs are a route to research impact and engagement, often written with institutional policy or knowledge-exchange teams.
reviewNotes: The bibliography contains no genre analysis of policy briefs; a source on policy-brief writing would strengthen this topic. Overlaps with dss.policy-analysis.

records.summary: Portfolios operationalise Schön's (1983) idea of the reflective practitioner in assessed form, typically combining logs, reflective accounts and evidence mapped to competencies. Moon (2004) shows that reflective writing ranges from description to deeper, critical reflection, and Ryan (2011) argues that the language of reflection must be taught explicitly; both apply to the reflective components of portfolios. The less-discussed demands are documentary: concise factual logging, selection and annotation of evidence against standards, and confidentiality. Work from the specific professional standards and templates learners must use, ideally with placement tutors.

activities.title: Evidence to competency
learnerActions: Take one competency statement from your professional standards
Collect three possible pieces of evidence from your practice
Rank them by how directly they demonstrate the competency
Write an annotation for the best one explaining what it shows and what it does not
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence must be selected and explicitly argued to meet a standard; inclusion alone does not demonstrate competence.
activities.rationale: Connects reflective practice (Schön, 1983) to the argumentative work of evidencing competence.

activities.title: From log entry to reflective account
learnerActions: Read a factual log entry about a placement incident
Identify what in it is worth reflecting on and why
Write a short reflective account using the language of reasoning and reconstruction
Link it to one theory or standard
activities.intendedInsight: Logs record; reflective accounts interpret and plan, and each has its own language.
activities.rationale: Applies Ryan's (2011) reflective language resources and Moon's (2004) levels of reflection to portfolio components.

difficulties.pattern: Including everything rather than selecting and annotating evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large portfolios with unannotated certificates, notes and documents.
difficulties.response: Limit evidence per competency and require an annotation for every item.

difficulties.pattern: Breaching confidentiality through identifiable details about patients, pupils, clients or colleagues.
difficulties.revealedBy: Names, locations or distinctive details in logs and reflections.
difficulties.response: Teach anonymisation conventions of the relevant profession and review drafts before submission.

difficulties.pattern: Reflection reduced to descriptive logging.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts that list activities without interpretation or learning.
difficulties.response: Return to reflective writing models and require an explicit link to theory or a standard in each account.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to annotate one piece of evidence against a given competency in 80–100 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explicitly maps the evidence to the competency, specifies what it demonstrates and notes its limits.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the evidence without explicit mapping.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the competency or the evidence title.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: nursing, midwifery, allied health, teacher education, social work and engineering placements, where professional bodies define standards. Taught postgraduate: professional master's and conversion programmes, often with e-portfolio platforms and tight placement schedules.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice and mmd.digital-assessments (e-portfolios).

records.summary: Public-facing writing intensifies the engagement resources Hyland (2005) describes for academic discourse, and Hyland (2010) compares how popular and professional science texts construct proximity to their readers, which gives learners a principled basis for adapting their writing. Mewburn and Thomson (2013) analysed academic blogs and found a range of audiences and purposes, so 'blog' is not a single genre. Teach learners to adapt their own academic texts for a named public, to keep fidelity to the evidence, and to consider their public academic identity.

activities.title: Same finding, two readers
learnerActions: Compare a research article's abstract with a blog post or news piece on the same study
List changes in structure, voice, engagement and treatment of uncertainty
Identify any place where the public version distorts or overstates the finding
Rewrite one paragraph of your own assignment for a public reader
activities.intendedInsight: Adapting for the public changes structure and voice but should not change what the evidence shows.
activities.rationale: Draws on Hyland's (2010) comparison of popular and professional science and on Hyland's (2005) account of engagement resources.

activities.title: Purpose and platform
learnerActions: Read three academic blog posts with different purposes (explaining research, commenting on policy, reflecting on academic life)
Identify each post's likely audience and how it addresses them
Plan a post for one purpose and audience relevant to your field
activities.intendedInsight: Academic blogs serve varied purposes and audiences, and these shape their style.
activities.rationale: Reflects Mewburn and Thomson's (2013) finding that academic blogs vary in audience and purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a shortened academic paper, dense with terminology and citations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unexplained jargon, formal citations and a slow build-up to the main point.
difficulties.response: Have learners state the main point in one plain sentence first, then test drafts on a non-specialist reader.

difficulties.pattern: Overcorrecting into hype or oversimplification.
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims such as 'scientists prove' or 'breakthrough' for tentative findings.
difficulties.response: Practise plain-language signals of uncertainty and compare drafts with the source's own claims.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety about public visibility or criticism online.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to publish, or extreme hedging and impersonality in public drafts.
difficulties.response: Discuss platform choice, moderation and institutional support; start with internal or departmental outlets.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a key finding from their field to a non-specialist in three sentences in writing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate, jargon-free, leads with significance and signals uncertainty appropriately.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate but jargon-heavy, or accessible but overstated.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Inaccurate or incomprehensible to a lay reader.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: blog and opinion-piece assessments are increasingly common in media, politics and science communication modules. Taught postgraduate: public-facing assessments in policy, development and communication programmes. PGR: blogs and outreach writing as part of research engagement and impact, often supported by institutional communications teams.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with pub.research-engagement, which covers engagement strategy and channels; this topic covers the writing of specific public genres.

records.summary: Paltridge (2002) identified several macrostructures for theses and dissertations (traditional simple, traditional complex, topic-based and compilation) and showed that published advice under-represents this variety; Paltridge and Starfield (2020) offer practical guidance for second-language writers and their supervisors. Research on master's dissertations shows where high- and low-rated work differ, for example in the range of rhetorical functions of citation (Petrić, 2007), and Hopkins and Dudley-Evans (1988) analysed the moves of discussion sections in MSc dissertations. Use departmental handbooks and past dissertations as primary sources, and present the dissertation as one argument developed across chapters.

activities.title: Past dissertation analysis
learnerActions: With departmental permission, examine two high-graded dissertations from your programme
Map each chapter's function and its share of the total word count
Compare the maps with the handbook's guidance and with each other
Draft your own chapter plan with functions and word allocations
activities.intendedInsight: Dissertation structures vary within a department; functions and proportions matter more than chapter names.
activities.rationale: Paltridge (2002) shows that actual practice is more varied than published advice suggests, so local examples are essential.

activities.title: What citation is doing
learnerActions: Classify the citations in two pages of a dissertation by function (attribution, support, comparison, evaluation, establishing links)
Compare the distribution with a page of your own draft
Revise one paragraph to use citation for comparison or evaluation rather than attribution alone
activities.intendedInsight: Higher-rated work uses citation to do more rhetorical work than attribution.
activities.rationale: Based on Petrić's (2007) comparison of citation functions in high- and low-rated master's theses.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the dissertation as a long essay or as a set of separate assignments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chapters that do not refer to each other; research questions that disappear after the introduction.
difficulties.response: Have learners write chapter introductions and conclusions that state each chapter's contribution to answering the questions.

difficulties.pattern: A thin discussion that restates findings without interpreting them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion chapters that repeat results and add little reference to literature.
difficulties.response: Analyse discussion moves in local exemplars and require each finding to be interpreted against the literature.

difficulties.pattern: A literature review disconnected from the study.
difficulties.revealedBy: A broad review that does not lead to the research questions or return in the discussion.
difficulties.response: Require the review's final section to justify the research questions and the discussion to revisit the review's key themes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe, in five bullet points, what each chapter of their planned dissertation will do.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Functional descriptions linked to the research questions, with a coherent through-line.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate chapter names with topical rather than functional descriptions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot outline a structure or lists generic headings.

records.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: a core focus for final-year dissertations and projects, whose length, format and empirical expectations vary greatly between disciplines. Taught postgraduate: a core focus, since the dissertation is often written over a compressed summer period, carries heavy credit weighting and may be the learner's first extended research text, so early planning support is especially valuable. Doctoral thesis structures are taught through res.thesis-macrostructure.

records.summary: Teach IMRaD as a conventional answer to a reader's questions (why, how, what was found, what it means) and as a hypothesis to test against the learner's own disciplinary exemplars, not as a template. Move studies show both a stable core and real variation: Kanoksilapatham (2005) describes a predictable move structure across sections of biochemistry articles, whereas Yang and Allison (2003) show that in applied linguistics the functions of results, discussion and conclusion overlap across section boundaries. Rhetorical consciousness-raising with discipline-specific exemplars (Swales 1990; Cheng 2018) lets mixed-discipline groups compare findings productively.

activities.title: Headings-stripped sorting
learnerActions: Take an article from your own field with headings and section breaks removed
Mark where you think each section begins and write a one-line function label for it
Compare your segmentation with the original and with a partner from a different discipline
Record one convention of your field that differs from canonical IMRaD and suggest why
activities.intendedInsight: Section boundaries are signalled by rhetorical function and by language such as tense, citation density and hedging, and the conventional order varies by field.
activities.rationale: Genre-based consciousness-raising asks learners to notice function–form relations in authentic exemplars; cross-disciplinary comparison guards against generalising one model (Swales 1990; Cheng 2018).

activities.title: Reader-question mapping
learnerActions: List the questions a reader in your field brings to a research article
Map each question to the section that answers it in two field-specific articles
Identify any question answered in an unexpected place, for example limitations in Methods
Discuss why that placement might suit the field or the journal
activities.intendedInsight: Macrostructure is a contract with the reader; variants arise when fields ask different questions or build knowledge differently.
activities.rationale: A functional framing supports transfer to non-IMRaD genres and discourages template-driven writing; Yang and Allison (2003) document functions spreading across section boundaries.

difficulties.pattern: Every research paper must have these four sections, so my history or design project is wrong if it doesn't.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners in humanities, theoretical or practice-based fields force IMRaD headings onto argument-led work, or describe published papers from their field as badly structured.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars from the learner's field and ask what organising principle they use (argument, chronology, case, theme). Present IMRaD as one family of structures tied to empirical reporting, not as the academic norm.

difficulties.pattern: Interpretation and comparison with the literature are placed in Results, leaving the Discussion to restate findings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts with heavily evaluative results and short, repetitive discussions containing few explanations or comparisons with prior work.
difficulties.response: Have learners colour-code a draft by function (report, comment, interpret, compare) and check the distribution against field exemplars. Do not impose a ban on commentary in Results, because the acceptable level of commentary varies by field; the aim is a fit with field norms.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to bring one recent article from their target journal or field and explain, in three minutes, where its argument is made and why it is organised as it is.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the structure accurately, names at least one field-specific variant and explains it in terms of what the field counts as evidence or how readers use the article.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the sections correctly but treats variation as error, or cannot say why the field departs from IMRaD.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify section functions or assumes all academic texts follow essay structure.

records.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals IMRaD is mainly a reading tool for navigating articles before an extended project. At UG and PGT it becomes a writing frame for project reports and dissertations, where departmental handbooks may impose headings. At PGR the emphasis shifts to variants such as article-based theses, theory chapters and merged results and discussion, and to the writer's informed choices within field norms.

records.summary: Use the Create-a-Research-Space model (Swales 1990, revised in Swales 2004) as an analytical lens and planning tool for introductions, while making disciplinary variation explicit. Samraj (2002) found background material and recursive move cycles in some fields that the original model did not anticipate, and Bunton (2002) describes additional steps in PhD thesis introductions, such as outlining the thesis structure and defining terms. Genre analysis of the learner's own exemplars, followed by drafting and move-annotated peer review, is the core sequence.

activities.title: Move-annotate and reconstruct
learnerActions: Annotate an introduction from your field sentence by sentence for moves and steps
Note where moves recur in cycles and where optional steps such as summarising findings appear
Reconstruct a jumbled introduction from a different field and compare its structure with yours
Write a move outline for your own introduction before drafting
activities.intendedInsight: The CARS moves are a recognisable logic that fields realise differently, and outlining by move separates rhetorical planning from sentence-level drafting.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of authentic exemplars is the established genre-based method for research writing (Swales 1990, 2004), and cross-field comparison exposes variation such as that reported by Samraj (2002).

activities.title: Article versus thesis introduction
learnerActions: Compare an article introduction and a PhD or master's thesis introduction from your field
List the steps the thesis introduction adds (for example scope, definitions, chapter outline)
Decide which of these your own text needs and draft them
activities.intendedInsight: Thesis introductions carry additional reader-orientation work because of their length and their examiner audience.
activities.rationale: Bunton (2002) shows that PhD introductions extend the CARS moves with thesis-orientation steps.

difficulties.pattern: I start with the history of the topic from ancient times and get to my study on page five.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, unfocused Move 1 with generic centrality claims ('since the dawn of time', 'in today's world') and a late or missing niche, often modelled on the broad-to-narrow introductions taught for school and test essays.
difficulties.response: Have the learner count sentences per move and compare with exemplars, then compress Move 1 to what the niche needs. Avoid banning background outright, since some fields use substantial background.

difficulties.pattern: The CARS model is a formula, so every introduction should have exactly these three moves in order.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mechanical introductions with one sentence per step and phrasebank formulae, regardless of field.
difficulties.response: Return to field exemplars showing cycling and optional steps, and ask the learner to justify each choice by what readers in their field expect.

difficulties.pattern: Move 3 announces the topic but not the questions, so readers cannot see what the study will answer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Announcements such as 'This study will look at…' with no aims, questions or hypotheses.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to insert their research questions verbatim into Move 3 and check that they answer the niche.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to annotate their own draft introduction by move in the margin and to explain one optional step they included or omitted.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Annotation is accurate, the niche follows from the reviewed work, Move 3 answers the niche and optional steps are justified by field convention.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Moves are present, but Move 1 is overlong or generic, or the link between niche and announcement is weak.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify moves in their own text, or the introduction lacks a niche or an announcement of the study.

records.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals the focus is a short, complete CARS introduction for the extended project. UG and PGT learners apply it to dissertation introductions, often with departmental templates. PGR learners need thesis-level introductions and article introductions written for different readers, and attention to disciplinary variation.

records.summary: Teach the research literature review as an argument about the state of knowledge that makes room for the writer's study. Kwan (2006) found an introduction–body–conclusion structure in applied linguistics doctoral reviews, with the body cycling through moves that establish territory and create niches, although writers did not always relate the literature to their own research. Feak and Swales (2009) frame the review as a 'research story' with deliberate choices of citation form, metadiscourse and stance. Petrić (2007) found that higher-rated master's theses used citation for a wider range of functions, notably application and comparison, which can be made explicit in teaching. Kamler and Thomson (2014) also treat the review as identity work: writers must position themselves with authority among established scholars.

activities.title: Paragraph function audit
learnerActions: Number the paragraphs of your draft review
Write beside each one the claim it makes and how it serves your study (justifies a question, a concept or a design choice)
Highlight sentences that only report a source and those that evaluate, compare or apply it
Revise two report-only paragraphs so that they make a positioning claim
activities.intendedInsight: Every paragraph of a research review should do positioning work, and evaluation and application of sources are what make the writer's voice visible.
activities.rationale: Petrić's (2007) finding on citation functions in higher- and lower-rated theses, and Kwan's (2006) observation that writers do not always connect literature to their own study, suggest these are the points to make explicit.

activities.title: From matrix to story
learnerActions: Build a synthesis matrix of your key sources by theme, finding and method
Identify two or three tensions or trends across the matrix
Sequence these as a 'research story' leading to your niche
Draft topic sentences that state the story's claims before adding the sources
activities.intendedInsight: Organisation should come from the argument about the field, not from the order in which sources were read.
activities.rationale: Feak and Swales (2009) treat the review as a narrative with a purpose; planning claims before sources counters source-by-source organisation.

difficulties.pattern: Smith (2015) found…; Jones (2017) found…; Lee (2019) found… — one paragraph per source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Integral citations opening most sentences, a list-like structure and little evaluative language.
difficulties.response: Have the learner rewrite one paragraph with a topic sentence that makes a claim about the group of studies and uses non-integral citation for support. Do not simply ban integral citation, which is valuable for foregrounding key scholars and contrasting positions.

difficulties.pattern: I must include everything ever written on my topic to show the examiner I have read widely.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long reviews covering loosely related literature, with no criteria for inclusion and no links to the study.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to justify each section by reference to a research question or a design decision, and to cut or condense what cannot be justified.

difficulties.pattern: I am only a student, so I cannot judge published work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviews in which every study is presented neutrally or approvingly and no tensions or weaknesses are named.
difficulties.response: Present evaluation as a disciplinary expectation that novice writers of all backgrounds find difficult, model mitigated evaluation from published reviews and discuss authorial identity explicitly (Kamler & Thomson 2014). Show how a niche can be built from tensions between studies, which makes evaluation a structural need rather than a personal judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to give a two-minute oral summary of their literature review without notes, then to say how it leads to their research questions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Summarises the review as a small number of claims about the field, with tensions and a gap, and links these explicitly to the questions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Summarises themes accurately but cannot say how they justify the study, or lists authors rather than claims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Recounts sources one by one with no organising claim or link to the study.

records.contextNotes: At PGT, the review is typically a dissertation chapter, marked for criticality and relevance to the study. At PGR, the review may be distributed across chapters or articles, must demonstrate command of the field and is revisited throughout the project, including updating before submission. Undergraduate dissertations and coursework reviews use the student literature review genre instead.

records.summary: Methods sections are more rhetorical than they look: Cotos, Huffman and Link (2017) describe moves for contextualising the study's methods, describing the study and establishing credibility, and Lim (2006) showed management writers justifying sampling and procedures, not only describing them. Kanoksilapatham (2005) found the methods moves of biochemistry articles centred on describing materials and procedures, so the degree of justification varies by field. Teach learners to analyse exemplars from their own journals or departments and to check completeness against reporting guidelines, while treating voice and tense as field choices rather than fixed rules.

activities.title: Describe versus justify
learnerActions: Highlight descriptive statements in one colour and justifying statements in another in two field exemplars
Note which decisions are justified and how (rationale, precedent citation, reference to the research questions)
Apply the same highlighting to your own draft
Add justification for the two decisions a sceptical reader would question most
activities.intendedInsight: Credibility comes from justified choices; a methods section that only describes leaves readers to doubt the design.
activities.rationale: The credibility-establishing move identified by Cotos et al. (2017) and the justification steps in Lim (2006) give learners named targets for revision.

activities.title: Replication check
learnerActions: Exchange methods drafts with a peer in a related field
Try to write a step-by-step protocol from the peer's text
Note every point where you had to guess
Return the list and revise your own draft
activities.intendedInsight: Experts underestimate the detail readers need, and gaps become visible only when someone tries to follow the procedure.
activities.rationale: Peer reconstruction makes the reader's needs concrete; the activity is a proposal adapted from replication logic, not a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: The passive is more objective, so I must never write 'we' or 'I' in methods.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strained agentless passives, dangling modifiers ('After collecting the data, it was analysed') or inconsistency with the learner's target journal.
difficulties.response: Show the variation in voice in the learner's target journals and discuss when an agent matters. Present voice as a field and journal choice, not a rule about objectivity.

difficulties.pattern: Methods are just a list of what I did, in the order I did it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chronological narratives including irrelevant steps, missing analysis procedures and no justification.
difficulties.response: Return to the function of methods within the macrostructure and reorganise by conventional sub-sections. Ask what the reader needs in order to trust and evaluate the findings.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to identify the riskiest decision in their design and show where their methods section justifies it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a consequential decision, points to a justification using rationale or precedent, and notes any limitation it creates.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a decision but the text describes it without justification, or justifies a trivial decision only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a design decision that needs justification, or the methods section is purely narrative.

records.contextNotes: UG project reports often follow departmental templates and lab-report conventions. PGT dissertations in the social sciences may require a separate methodology chapter with paradigm discussion, which overlaps with methods writing. PGR learners writing articles must compress methods to journal norms and use supplementary materials, while thesis methods chapters are often extensive.
reviewNotes: dss.methodology-justification now depends on this topic: this topic covers the description and local justification of procedures in a methods section, and the DSS topic covers paradigm-level methodology chapters.

records.summary: Results writing extends data commentary to a whole section organised around research questions. Yang and Allison (2003) found results sections in applied linguistics that included comment on results as well as reporting, and Basturkmen (2009) found that published research articles developed commentary more extensively than master's dissertations did. Swales and Feak (2012) provide accessible practice in location, highlighting and comment. Teach the field's tolerance for commentary explicitly, using exemplars, and pair it with selectivity: what to say in prose and what to leave in visuals.

activities.title: Select, don't recite
learnerActions: Take a table from your own data and list every pattern it shows
Rank the patterns by relevance to your research questions
Write a results paragraph using only the top two or three patterns
Compare it with an earlier draft that reported every value
activities.intendedInsight: Results prose selects and interprets for the reader; repeating the table adds length without adding meaning.
activities.rationale: Location–highlighting–comment sequences in data commentary (Swales & Feak 2012) give a structure for selection.

activities.title: How much comment here?
learnerActions: Mark the comment statements (explanation, comparison, evaluation) in three results sections from your field
Estimate the proportion of comment to report in each
Decide what level of commentary your own results section should include and check it with your supervisor
activities.intendedInsight: The boundary between Results and Discussion is a field convention that writers can observe and match.
activities.rationale: Yang and Allison (2003) and Basturkmen (2009) show that commentary in results varies across writers and genres, so learners need to calibrate to their own field.

difficulties.pattern: Every number in the table is important, so I describe them all.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs listing values in table order, with no highlighting or link to the research questions.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner what the reader should remember from the table and build the paragraph around that. Do not simply impose a word limit; teach selection criteria.

difficulties.pattern: Findings are stated as facts about the world ('Students prefer online learning') rather than as findings of this study.
difficulties.revealedBy: Present-tense generalisations in results without reference to the sample or data, and unhedged comments.
difficulties.response: Contrast 'participants in this study reported…' with general claims, and practise tense and hedging choices that keep the scope of results claims explicit.

diagnostic.task: Give a two-variable table and one research question; ask for a short results paragraph in ten minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the table, highlights the patterns relevant to the question, uses tense consistently and adds proportionate comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reports accurately but lists too many values or omits the link to the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the table in prose, misreads values or presents results as general truths.

records.contextNotes: UG lab and project reports often require strict separation of results and discussion. PGT dissertations vary, and qualitative dissertations frequently merge findings and discussion. PGR writers must match target-journal conventions and handle multiple results chapters in a thesis.

records.summary: Discussion sections have been modelled as cycles of moves: Hopkins and Dudley-Evans (1988) identified a sequence including statement of result, (un)expected outcome, reference to previous research, explanation, deduction and recommendation, recurring for each finding, and Yang and Allison (2003) described related moves in applied linguistics. Basturkmen (2009) found that published articles developed commentary on results more extensively than master's dissertations, for instance by offering and evaluating alternative explanations, which identifies a concrete target for postgraduate teaching. Swales and Feak (2012) provide practice in calibrating claims at the level of generality the data support.

activities.title: Cycle mapping
learnerActions: Annotate a discussion from your field for statement, comparison with literature, explanation and implication
Draw the cycles as a flow diagram
Draft your own discussion as a sequence of cycles, one per key finding
activities.intendedInsight: Discussions are built from repeated, finding-led cycles rather than from a single summary followed by implications.
activities.rationale: The cyclical move structure described by Hopkins and Dudley-Evans (1988) is a usable planning device.

activities.title: Alternative explanations
learnerActions: Choose one unexpected finding from your study
List at least three possible explanations, including methodological ones
Write a paragraph that weighs them using evidence and hedging
Compare your paragraph with an expert example that evaluates alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Considering and weighing alternatives makes interpretation more credible than asserting a single explanation.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen (2009) identifies the development of alternative explanations as a difference between expert and student commentary.

difficulties.pattern: My discussion repeats my results and then says what future research should do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussions with few citations, no explanations of findings and generic implications.
difficulties.response: Use cycle mapping and require each finding to be compared with at least one previous study and explained. Do not respond by asking for a longer discussion; the issue is function, not length.

difficulties.pattern: My findings prove that the theory is correct.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boosted claims, generalisation beyond the sample and no mention of alternative explanations or limitations.
difficulties.response: Work through claim calibration with the learner's own sentences: what does the design allow, for whom, under what conditions? Avoid over-correcting into hedging every clause.

difficulties.pattern: Unexpected results are mistakes, so I mention them briefly or leave them out.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unexpected findings are omitted, apologised for or explained away without evidence.
difficulties.response: Present unexpected findings as a legitimate and often valuable part of discussions, and model language for treating them as findings to explain.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to pick their most important finding and say, in two minutes, how it relates to previous research and why it might have occurred.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Relates the finding to specific previous studies, proposes and weighs explanations, and states a calibrated implication.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Relates the finding to previous research but offers one explanation only, or makes uncalibrated claims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the finding without comparison or explanation.

records.contextNotes: UG reports often need a short discussion with comparison to the literature and limitations. PGT dissertations are frequently weakest in the discussion, so it deserves sustained attention. PGR writers handle multiple findings, theoretical contributions and examiners' expectations of originality, and may write a separate general discussion chapter.

records.summary: Conclusions in research writing do more than summarise. Yang and Allison (2003) describe conclusion moves in applied linguistics articles including summarising the study, evaluating it and deducing from the research, such as recommending further research and drawing pedagogic implications. For theses, Bunton (2005) distinguishes conclusions focused on the thesis itself from those oriented to the field. Teach learners to answer their research questions, articulate contribution and derive implications explicitly from findings, with genre-appropriate length.

activities.title: Question-answer check
learnerActions: Copy your research questions to the top of your draft conclusion
Highlight the sentence that answers each one
Add answers for any question not addressed, using the same key terms
Remove chapter-by-chapter summary that does not contribute to an answer
activities.intendedInsight: A conclusion is judged by whether it answers the questions the text set out to address.
activities.rationale: Summarising and evaluating moves (Yang & Allison 2003) work only when tied to the study's stated aims.

activities.title: Implication tracing
learnerActions: List each implication and recommendation in your conclusion
Draw an arrow from each to the finding that supports it
Rewrite or delete implications with no supporting finding
Make each future-research recommendation specific about focus, population or design
activities.intendedInsight: Implications must be grounded in findings, and recommendations for research are more convincing when specific.
activities.rationale: Thesis conclusions vary in orientation (Bunton 2005); tracing ensures that whatever the orientation, claims remain grounded.

difficulties.pattern: My conclusion repeats my abstract and ends with 'more research is needed'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions with no explicit answers, contribution or specific implications.
difficulties.response: Use the question–answer check and implication tracing. Do not just ask for more content; ask for the functional moves that are missing.

difficulties.pattern: New ideas and new literature appear for the first time in the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions introducing new findings, concepts or citations not discussed earlier.
difficulties.response: Help the learner move new material into the discussion or remove it, and reserve the conclusion for consolidating what has been established.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read their conclusion and say which sentences answer which research questions and which state the contribution.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Points to explicit answers for every question, a contribution statement and implications linked to findings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers some questions but implications are generic or the contribution is implicit.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The conclusion summarises content without answers, contribution or implications.

records.contextNotes: Many UG reports merge conclusions with the discussion. PGT dissertations usually have a separate conclusion chapter with recommendations. PGR thesis conclusions must synthesise across chapters, articulate contribution to knowledge and anticipate examiners' questions, and article conclusions follow journal norms that may omit a separate section.

records.summary: Abstracts are highly conventional and highly visible. Santos (1996) described a five-move structure for applied linguistics article abstracts (situating the research, presenting it, describing the methodology, summarising results and discussing the research), and Swales and Feak (2009) offer graded tasks across abstract types, including the distinction between informative and indicative abstracts. Student abstracts use similar moves but are read by markers checking that the writer can represent the work accurately and concisely, whereas research abstracts are also promotional texts in which writers present themselves as credible insiders, with disciplinary variation in which moves are included (Hyland 2004). Kamler and Thomson (2014) use abstract writing as a 'tiny text' that helps doctoral writers clarify their argument. Teach abstracts both as a genre, calibrated to local exemplars, and as a thinking tool.

activities.title: Move census
learnerActions: Collect eight to ten abstracts from your department, programme or target journal
Label each sentence by move and note which moves are present, absent or combined
Note tense, voice and the specificity of results statements
Draft your abstract to match the most common pattern, then justify any deviation
activities.intendedInsight: Abstract conventions are specific to journals and fields, and results are usually stated concretely.
activities.rationale: Move analysis (Santos 1996; Swales & Feak 2009) and disciplinary variation (Hyland 2004) suggest calibrating to a local corpus rather than a generic template.

activities.title: From indicative to informative
learnerActions: Read an abstract that says what the report 'will discuss' without stating results
Rewrite it so that it states the actual findings and conclusion
Compare which version better serves a marker, an examiner or a reader deciding whether to read on
activities.intendedInsight: Informative abstracts state findings; indicative abstracts only describe topics.
activities.rationale: The distinction between informative and indicative abstracts is a standard element of abstract instruction (Swales & Feak 2009).

activities.title: Abstract as argument test
learnerActions: Write a short abstract for your project early in the writing process
Exchange with a peer who states, in one sentence, what they think your argument is
Revise the abstract until the peer's sentence matches your intention
Revisit the abstract each time a chapter is completed
activities.intendedInsight: If the argument cannot be stated in an abstract, the text's argument may not yet be clear.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) use abstract writing as a tool for doctoral writers to articulate their argument and contribution.

difficulties.pattern: The results will be discussed and implications will be considered.
difficulties.revealedBy: Indicative abstracts that describe content, or read like an introduction or table of contents, without stating findings or conclusions.
difficulties.response: Contrast indicative and informative abstracts and require at least one specific results statement. Avoid generalising: some genres, such as some humanities abstracts and conference proposals, legitimately differ.

difficulties.pattern: Half the abstract is background, and the method and results are squeezed into one sentence at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Disproportionate Move 1, often copied from the introduction.
difficulties.response: Have the learner allocate word counts per move before drafting, using exemplars as a guide.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent or unmotivated tense shifts between moves.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods in the present and conclusions in the past, or random alternation within a move.
difficulties.response: Show the typical tense pattern by move and the reasons for it, noting that local conventions differ. Do not present one pattern as a rule for every field.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 100-word abstract of a short article they have read, in ten minutes, without looking back at the original abstract.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Includes purpose, method, specific findings and a conclusion in proportion, with appropriate tense.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes most moves but results are vague or background is disproportionate.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes an introduction-like summary of the topic with no findings.

records.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, abstracts are written for extended projects and posters; undergraduate-entry courses that set an abstract can use the same core moves without the research-article emphasis. In-sessional UG learners write abstracts for final-year projects, lab reports and posters, often after drafting the full text. PGT learners write dissertation abstracts, sometimes structured, and abstracts for student conferences. PGR learners write thesis abstracts within institutional word limits and article abstracts that must match journal formats, including structured abstracts in health and some social sciences.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-15 merged grp.student-abstract into this topic. Its moves, tense guidance, indicative-versus-informative activity and student contexts are incorporated here, and the range is widened to B2–C1.
