records.summary: Limitations writing is an exercise in calibrated evaluation, not confession. Yang and Allison (2003) identify an evaluating-the-study move, covering limitations and significance, in the closing sections of applied linguistics articles, and Swales and Feak (2012) treat limitation statements as part of positioning a study's claims. Hyland (1998) shows how hedging allows writers to qualify commitment while protecting their claims. Teach learners to select consequential limitations, to state their effects and to frame them with concessive moves that keep the contribution intact.

activities.title: Limitation, effect, response
learnerActions: List every limitation of your study you can think of
Keep only those that affect how a reader should interpret your findings
For each, write one sentence on its likely effect and one on mitigation or future work
Compare your version with the limitation statements of two published studies in your field
activities.intendedInsight: Useful limitations are specific to the study and tell the reader how to read the findings.
activities.rationale: The evaluating-the-study move (Yang & Allison 2003) combines limitation with significance; structuring each limitation as effect plus response operationalises this.

activities.title: Tone calibration
learnerActions: Read three versions of the same limitation: apologetic, dismissive and calibrated
Identify the language that creates each tone (apology, minimisers, concessive structures, hedges)
Rewrite one of your own limitation statements in the calibrated style
activities.intendedInsight: Language choices determine whether a limitation weakens the study or demonstrates the writer's command of it.
activities.rationale: Hedging and concession shape commitment without retraction (Hyland 1998); contrasting versions makes the effect noticeable.

difficulties.pattern: This study has many limitations. The sample was small. The time was short. I apologise for these weaknesses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, generic, apologetic lists, often unconnected to the specific findings.
difficulties.response: Reframe limitations as evidence of methodological awareness, not as admissions of failure, and ask for the effect of each one on interpretation. Avoid telling the learner to omit limitations; examiners expect them.

difficulties.pattern: If I mention limitations, examiners will mark me down, so I add one sentence at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missing or token limitations sections, even where a design has obvious constraints.
difficulties.response: Show marking criteria and examiners' reports that reward critical evaluation of one's own study, and discuss how unacknowledged limitations invite criticism.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to name the single most important limitation of their study and explain how it affects one specific finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a consequential limitation, explains its likely effect on a specific finding and suggests a mitigation or future direction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a relevant limitation but cannot say how it affects the findings, or names only a generic one.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a limitation, or lists generic weaknesses unrelated to the design.

records.contextNotes: UG report criteria often require limitations explicitly, and short generic statements are common. At PGT, limitations are part of demonstrating criticality in the discussion. At PGR, limitations are scrutinised in the viva and by reviewers, and they must be consistent across thesis chapters and derived articles.

records.summary: Treat research questions as the hinge between the gap and the design: they should follow from the literature and determine what data and analysis are needed. Creswell and Creswell (2018) offer scripts for purpose statements, questions and hypotheses across qualitative, quantitative and mixed designs, and Bunton (2002) shows that statements of purpose and questions are a recurrent element of PhD thesis introductions. A practitioner proposal, not a tested one, is to revise the learner's own questions repeatedly against their methods rather than to rely on generic question-writing exercises.

activities.title: Alignment table
learnerActions: Write your aim and each research question in the first column of a table
In further columns, record for each question the data source, the analysis and the kind of answer it will produce
Mark any question whose row cannot be completed, or whose answer is yes or no
Revise or remove those questions and explain the changes to a peer
activities.intendedInsight: A research question is only as good as its fit with the data and analysis that will answer it.
activities.rationale: Making alignment explicit turns an abstract quality criterion into a checkable procedure and mirrors how examiners read across chapters (Paltridge & Starfield 2020).

activities.title: Question form by design
learnerActions: Sort a set of published research questions and hypotheses into exploratory, descriptive, explanatory and confirmatory types
Note the grammatical forms each type uses (wh-questions, 'to what extent', directional hypotheses)
Rewrite one of your questions in the form suited to your design
activities.intendedInsight: Question form signals the design and the type of claim the study will be able to make.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) link the wording of purpose statements and questions to the design tradition, which gives learners a principled basis for choosing a form.

difficulties.pattern: My question is 'What is the impact of social media on students?' which covers everything I am interested in.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions that name a broad topic with no population, context, construct or type of answer, and methods that could not possibly answer them.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to say what a satisfying answer would look like and what data would produce it, then narrow the question until it can be answered. Avoid supplying a rewritten question, since ownership of the question matters at PGT and PGR level.

difficulties.pattern: Questions drift: the introduction asks one thing, the methods measure another and the discussion answers a third.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent wording of aims across chapters, or findings reported for questions never posed.
difficulties.response: Have the learner paste the exact wording of each question into the opening of the methods, results and discussion and reconcile any differences. Do not treat this as a language error; it is usually the result of the project evolving, so the fix is to update the questions or to signal the change.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read out their research questions and say, for each, what data will answer it and what form the answer will take.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Each question is scoped and answerable, its data and analysis are named without hesitation, and hypothesis language, if used, matches the design.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Questions are answerable but at least one is too broad, is a yes/no question or is only loosely linked to the data.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Questions restate the topic, or the learner cannot link them to any data or analysis.

records.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessional projects need modest, answerable questions within weeks. UG and PGT dissertations often require supervisor approval of questions early, so formulation and alignment checks are most useful at proposal stage. At PGR, questions are expected to evolve, and the focus moves to tracking and justifying that evolution, including in progression reviews.

records.summary: The niche is the pivot of a research introduction. Swales (1990) described niche-establishing options as counter-claiming, indicating a gap, question-raising and continuing a tradition, and Swales (2004) revised Move 2 to centre on indicating a gap or adding to what is known, with an optional positive justification. Samraj (2002) shows disciplinary variation in how and where niches are established, and Kwan (2006) found niche-creating moves recurring through the bodies of doctoral literature reviews. Teach learners to analyse niche language in field exemplars and to ground every gap claim in cited work, with calibrated scope.

activities.title: Niche-type hunt
learnerActions: Collect the niche sentences from eight introductions in your field
Classify each as counter-claim, gap, question, continuation or extension
Underline the signalling resources (contrastive connectors, negative quantifiers, evaluative adjectives, present perfect)
Compare frequencies with a partner from a different discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Fields favour different niche types; a gentle 'extension' niche may be more persuasive in some fields than a direct counter-claim.
activities.rationale: Swales' (1990, 2004) move model and Samraj's (2002) disciplinary findings give learners categories to test against their own field's texts.

activities.title: Stress-testing the gap
learnerActions: Write your niche statement
Swap with a peer, who tries to find one study that falsifies it
Narrow or rephrase the statement so that it survives, for example by naming population, setting, method or time-scale
Check that the revised gap still leads to your aims
activities.intendedInsight: A precise, bounded gap is more defensible and more persuasive than a sweeping one.
activities.rationale: Reviewers and examiners routinely challenge overstated gap claims; peer challenge rehearses this and links niche construction to claim calibration.

difficulties.pattern: No research has ever been done on this topic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Absolute gap claims with no supporting citations, often contradicted by sources the learner has already cited.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to evidence the gap with the closest existing studies and to state precisely what those studies do not do. Do not simply replace 'no' with 'little'; the problem is the unsupported scope of the claim, not its wording.

difficulties.pattern: My gap is that this has not been studied in my country, so the study is justified.
difficulties.revealedBy: Niches that rest only on a new location, population or period, with no argument for why the difference matters.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to explain what might be different in the new context and why that matters for theory or practice, and show niches that justify a contextual extension. Do not dismiss contextual gaps; they are legitimate when their significance is argued.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a four-study review paragraph and a one-sentence aim; ask them to write the two sentences that connect them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a niche that is traceable to the cited studies, bounded in scope, uses evaluative and contrastive resources and leads directly to the aim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Signals a gap with appropriate language but the gap is generic, or does not connect clearly to the aim.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Omits the niche, makes an unsupported absolute claim or restates the aim.

records.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessional and UG learners usually meet gap language through short introductions to projects. At PGT the gap justifies the dissertation and is often examined explicitly in marking criteria. At PGR, niches must survive expert scrutiny, recur across chapters and connect to a claimed contribution.

records.summary: Claiming contribution combines promotion with calibration. Hyland (2001) found that self-mention in research articles is concentrated where writers make claims and present their own contribution, and that it is more frequent in the humanities and social sciences than in the sciences, while Hyland (2005) describes how stance resources position claims relative to readers. Kamler and Thomson (2014) and W. L. Belcher (2019) both press novice writers to state the 'so what' of their work explicitly. Teach contribution statements as short, revisable texts that are linked to the niche and calibrated to the evidence.

activities.title: Contribution sentence drafting
learnerActions: Write one sentence stating what your study adds and one stating why it matters
Label the contribution type (empirical, methodological, theoretical, contextual or practical)
Check it against your niche statement and revise until they match
Test the sentences on a peer from outside your field
activities.intendedInsight: A contribution is only convincing if it answers the niche and can be stated plainly.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) and W. L. Belcher (2019) both treat explicit articulation of the argument and its significance as central to successful research writing.

activities.title: Self-mention and stance survey
learnerActions: Collect contribution statements from ten articles in your target journals
Note the use of self-mention, boosters, hedges and evaluative adjectives
Decide what level of promotion is conventional in your field and revise your statement accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: Fields differ in how openly writers promote their contribution; matching the convention avoids both arrogance and invisibility.
activities.rationale: Hyland's (2001, 2005) findings on disciplinary variation in self-mention and stance support a field-specific approach.

difficulties.pattern: This is the first study ever to investigate this important topic, and it will revolutionise the field.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unsupported 'first', 'novel' and 'revolutionary' claims, boosted language and contributions disconnected from evidence.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to point to the evidence for each element of the claim, then rewrite it in bounded terms. Do not ban promotional language altogether; teach calibrated promotion.

difficulties.pattern: It is not my place to say my work is original; the examiners will decide.
difficulties.revealedBy: No explicit contribution statement anywhere, or one hidden in heavy hedges and impersonal constructions.
difficulties.response: Explain that examiners and reviewers expect writers to state their contribution, and show examples of confident but measured statements. Discuss self-mention as a disciplinary choice rather than arrogance; reluctance to claim originality is common among novice writers of all backgrounds.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner: 'In two sentences, what does your thesis add that we did not know before?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a specific, typed contribution, links it to a gap in the field and calibrates its scope.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a topic-level contribution ('it adds to our understanding of X') or overstates its novelty.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes what the study did rather than what it adds, or cannot answer.

records.contextNotes: At PGT, the contribution may be modest and contextual, and the main need is to state it at all. At PGR, originality is an explicit examination criterion and must be argued throughout the thesis, in articles and in the viva.

records.summary: Paltridge (2002) identified four broad thesis types, traditional simple, traditional complex, topic-based and compilations of research papers, and found that published advice to thesis writers often described only the traditional simple type. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) extend this to guidance on choosing and planning structures, including publication-based theses, and Swales (2004) discusses the PhD dissertation as a research genre whose form has changed over time. Teaching should start from departmental theses and regulations, making the range of legitimate structures visible and linking the choice to the research design.

activities.title: Thesis repository survey
learnerActions: Download the tables of contents of five recent theses from your department
Classify each by macrostructure type
Note chapter titles, relative lengths and where literature and theory appear
Present to a mixed-discipline group and compare
activities.intendedInsight: There are several legitimate thesis structures, and the department's own practice is the most relevant guide.
activities.rationale: Paltridge's (2002) finding that published advice under-represents actual variety supports analysis of local theses rather than reliance on generic guides.

activities.title: Chapter purpose map
learnerActions: Draft a chapter plan listing each chapter's purpose and main claim
Show how each chapter connects to the research questions
For a publication-based thesis, plan the framing and linking chapters
Review the plan with your supervisor against the regulations
activities.intendedInsight: The macrostructure should express the thesis argument, not only the sequence of research activities.
activities.rationale: Paltridge and Starfield (2020) recommend planning chapters around the overall argument and the examiner's reading of the whole thesis.

difficulties.pattern: A thesis is just a very long dissertation with the same chapters.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans that copy a master's dissertation structure regardless of whether the research has several studies or is theory-led.
difficulties.response: Show alternative structures from the department and ask the learner to justify their choice by the shape of the research.

difficulties.pattern: My chapters follow the order in which I did the work, so the argument only becomes clear at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chapter plans organised by the chronology of fieldwork or experiments, with key concepts introduced late and conclusions that surprise the reader.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write the thesis argument in five sentences and to reorder chapters so that each sentence has a home. Keep chronology where it serves the argument.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe their thesis structure and explain why it suits their research.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a recognised structure, explains how it fits the design and argument, and shows awareness of regulations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has a reasonable plan but cannot justify it beyond 'this is the usual structure'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no plan or applies an unsuitable structure without awareness of alternatives.

records.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic: master's dissertation structures are usually prescribed by the programme and are covered by the dissertation topic in Academic Genres. At PGR, learners may choose among structures; publication-based theses are increasingly common in some countries and fields, with institution-specific rules, and practice-based and professional doctorates have their own formats.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-15 retagged this topic to PGR only, and R6-22 softened its dependency on IMRaD. Detailed guidance on integrating papers has moved to res.publication-based-thesis.

records.summary: In long texts, metatext operates above the paragraph: Bunton (1999) describes higher-level metatext in PhD theses that refers to chapters and to the thesis as a whole, and Hyland (2005) places frame markers, endophoric markers and code glosses within the interactive resources writers use to guide readers. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss chapter introductions and conclusions as structural signposts. Teach metatext as reader guidance that should be accurate, proportionate and revised as the thesis changes.

activities.title: Skeleton read-through
learnerActions: Extract all chapter introductions and conclusions from a model thesis
Read them in sequence and summarise the thesis argument
Repeat the exercise with your own draft
Identify where the argument breaks down and revise the metatext
activities.intendedInsight: Chapter openings and closings carry the thesis argument for readers who navigate rather than read straight through.
activities.rationale: Higher-level metatext guides readers across the thesis (Bunton 1999; Hyland 2005); reading it alone tests whether it does that job.

activities.title: Metatext density check
learnerActions: Highlight all metatext in one chapter
Count instances per page and compare with a model thesis in your field
Remove redundant previews and repetitive formulae
Check every cross-reference against the current chapter numbering
activities.intendedInsight: Too little metatext leaves readers lost, while too much pads the text and can read as uncertain.
activities.rationale: Metadiscourse varies across fields and genres (Hyland 2005), so a local comparison is a better guide than a fixed rule.

difficulties.pattern: Every chapter begins 'In this chapter, I will…' followed by a list of section headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic previews that duplicate the table of contents and do not state purpose or relation to the argument.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to state why the chapter is there before what it contains, and to vary language. Avoid forbidding previews, which are conventional and useful.

difficulties.pattern: Previews and cross-references refer to chapters that have since moved or been cut.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inaccurate 'see Chapter 4' references and previews that no longer match content.
difficulties.response: Recommend automatic cross-referencing in word processors and a final metatext check as a distinct editing pass.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud the first and last paragraphs of one chapter and say how they connect to the chapters before and after.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Paragraphs state the chapter's purpose and contribution and link explicitly to adjacent chapters and the research questions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Paragraphs preview or summarise content but do not link to the wider argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No chapter introduction or conclusion, or paragraphs that are unrelated to the thesis argument.

records.contextNotes: PGT dissertations benefit from chapter introductions and conclusions but on a smaller scale. At PGR, metatext is essential to readability and is often added or revised in the final stages, and publication-based theses need linking text between papers.

records.summary: Frameworks are a common source of difficulty because their form and even their existence vary by field: social science and education theses typically expect an explicit framework, whereas many experimental papers embed theory in the introduction. Creswell and Creswell (2018) distinguish how theory is used deductively in quantitative work and more variably in qualitative and mixed designs, which helps learners decide where and how the framework should appear. Teaching should centre on tracing concepts forward into methods and analysis, so that the framework does visible work, and on discussing field exemplars, including the variation that Paltridge and Starfield (2020) note in how theses handle theory.

activities.title: Concept tracing
learnerActions: List the three to five key concepts of your framework
For each, find where it appears in your methods (instrument, coding frame, variable) and in your findings
Mark concepts that never reappear after the framework chapter
Either connect them to the analysis or remove them, and revise the framework section accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: A framework is justified by what it does in the analysis; concepts that do no work weaken the thesis.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) present theory as something that shapes questions, data and interpretation; tracing makes this relationship checkable.

activities.title: Framework exemplar comparison
learnerActions: Read framework sections from two theses in your field
Identify how each defines constructs, justifies its theory choice and anticipates the analysis
Note what the writers say about alternatives they did not adopt
Draft a justification paragraph for your own framework that names one alternative
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a framework involves showing that alternatives were considered, not only that the chosen theory is well known.
activities.rationale: Analysing successful theses is a core strategy recommended for thesis writers by Paltridge and Starfield (2020).

difficulties.pattern: My framework chapter summarises Bourdieu's theory in detail, but I don't refer to it again.
difficulties.revealedBy: Framework chapters that read as textbook summaries, and findings chapters with no theoretical vocabulary.
difficulties.response: Use concept tracing and ask the learner to rewrite the chapter around the concepts they actually apply. Avoid requiring more theory; the issue is application, not coverage.

difficulties.pattern: Theoretical framework, conceptual framework and literature review are the same thing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners are unsure what to include, duplicate content across chapters or follow supervisors' conflicting terminology.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that the terms are used inconsistently across fields and supervisors. Help the learner agree working definitions with their supervisor and check them against departmental theses.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner why they chose their framework rather than one named alternative, and where its concepts appear in their analysis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a reasoned justification tied to the research questions, names the alternative's limitations for this study and points to specific analytic uses.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Justifies the choice in general terms (it is widely used, my supervisor suggested it) or can point to only one analytic use.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot explain the choice or link the framework to the analysis.

records.contextNotes: At PGT, frameworks are expected mainly in social science, education and business dissertations, and may be brief. At PGR the framework is often a chapter or a major section that examiners scrutinise closely and that may be revised late as the analysis matures. Learners in experimental sciences may need only to recognise the concept.
reviewNotes: Disciplinary practice on whether a separate framework section is expected varies widely; check with departmental exemplars before teaching it as a requirement.

records.summary: Qualitative findings are persuasive when themes are presented as analytic claims that extracts illustrate and evidence, not as collections of quotations. Braun and Clarke (2006) caution that themes should be analytic constructions rather than summaries of what participants said, and that extracts need analytic narrative around them; their later account of reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke 2019) stresses that themes are generated by the researcher rather than 'emerging', and that coding-agreement statistics do not fit reflexive designs, points that examiners and reviewers now often raise. The APA's qualitative reporting standards (APA 2020) and Creswell and Creswell (2018) describe expectations about transparency, reflexivity and evidence. EAP teaching can focus on the language of the claim–extract–commentary unit and on keeping analyst and participant voices distinct.

activities.title: Claim–extract–comment frames
learnerActions: Identify the claim, extract and commentary in three findings paragraphs from published qualitative studies in your field
Note the language used to introduce extracts and to return to the analyst's voice
Rewrite one of your own quotation-heavy paragraphs into claim–extract–comment units
activities.intendedInsight: Extracts serve the analytic claim; the commentary after an extract is where interpretation happens.
activities.rationale: Braun and Clarke (2006) emphasise analytic narrative around extracts; making the unit explicit gives learners a revisable structure.

activities.title: Prevalence without pseudo-counting
learnerActions: Collect expressions used in your field's qualitative papers to indicate how widespread a pattern is (most, several, two participants, only one)
Discuss when numbers help and when they mislead
Revise your own findings to signal prevalence and divergence consistently
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to know how typical a pattern is, but counts should be used in ways consistent with the methodology.
activities.rationale: Transparency about the basis of claims is a common expectation in qualitative reporting standards (APA 2020); the specific practice of signalling prevalence varies by tradition.

difficulties.pattern: The quotations speak for themselves.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs consisting of a theme label followed by several long extracts with little or no commentary.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write what each extract shows before including it, and to cut extracts that do not support a stated claim. Avoid simply asking for fewer quotations without teaching the claim–commentary structure.

difficulties.pattern: It is unclear whether a statement is the participant's view or the researcher's interpretation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed paraphrases of participants presented as findings, and reporting verbs that blur the two voices.
difficulties.response: Practise attribution (participants described…, as Ana put it…) and averral (this suggests…) and have learners colour-code voices in a draft.

difficulties.pattern: Three themes emerged from the data, and two coders agreed on most codes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analysis accounts in which themes appear to form by themselves, or that combine reflexive thematic analysis with inter-rater agreement figures without justification.
difficulties.response: Discuss how the chosen version of thematic analysis positions the researcher, and ask learners to describe their analytic decisions actively. Do not ban agreement measures; they suit coding-reliability approaches but not reflexive ones (Braun & Clarke 2019).

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to talk through one findings paragraph and explain why they chose each extract and what their commentary adds.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Each extract is chosen to evidence a stated claim, commentary interprets rather than repeats, and divergent cases are mentioned.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Claims are present but commentary mostly paraphrases the extracts, or extract choice is not explained.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Extracts are presented without claims or commentary, or the learner cannot explain their selection.

records.contextNotes: UG qualitative projects tend to be small and may focus on presenting a few themes clearly. PGT dissertations in education, health and social sciences frequently use thematic analysis and merge findings with discussion. PGR writers must align reporting with a specific methodology, which may be phenomenological, ethnographic or discourse-analytic, and handle longer findings chapters.

records.summary: Statistical reporting combines formatting conventions, which can be taught through style guides such as the APA Publication Manual (APA 2020), with interpretive language that demands statistical literacy (Gal 2002). The ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016) gives an authoritative basis for teaching learners not to equate p < .05 with importance or truth and to report effect sizes and uncertainty. EAP teachers need not teach statistics, but they can require every statistic to be accompanied by an accurate plain-language interpretation and can target the formulaic misstatements that reviewers flag.

activities.title: Output to prose
learnerActions: Take software output for one test from your own analysis
Write the reporting sentence in your target style, checking symbols, italics, decimals and exact p-values against the style guide
Add a sentence saying what the result means for your research question, including the size of the effect
Swap with a peer who checks the format and challenges the interpretation
activities.intendedInsight: A statistic in the text needs both conventional form and an interpretation that a reader can evaluate.
activities.rationale: Style-guide formats (APA 2020) are learnable rules; pairing them with interpretation addresses the literacy gap described by Gal (2002).

activities.title: Misstatement clinic
learnerActions: Read a set of reporting sentences containing common errors (proof language, 'trend towards significance', non-significance as no difference)
Identify the error in each and explain why it misleads
Rewrite each sentence accurately
activities.intendedInsight: Some familiar phrases in published papers misrepresent what p-values show.
activities.rationale: The ASA statement (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016) sets out principles for p-value interpretation that can be applied directly to sentence revision.

difficulties.pattern: The result was significant, so the intervention clearly works.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boosted claims attached to p-values, no effect sizes, and 'significant' used in both its statistical and everyday senses.
difficulties.response: Separate statistical significance, effect size and practical importance in the learner's sentences, and reserve 'significant' for its statistical sense in results. Refer statistical misunderstandings to supervisors or statistics support rather than correcting the analysis yourself.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent formatting: p = 0.000, mixed decimal places, values duplicated in tables and text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Surface inconsistencies that reviewers and examiners notice quickly.
difficulties.response: Provide a style-guide checklist and ask learners to run it as a separate editing pass. Do not spend class time on rules the checklist covers; reserve discussion for interpretation.

diagnostic.task: Give the output of a non-significant comparison with a moderate effect size and a wide confidence interval; ask for a two-sentence report and interpretation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports in correct format with effect size and interval, and interprets the result as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no difference.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Formats correctly but omits the effect size, or interprets non-significance as 'no difference'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misformats the statistic and misinterprets it, for example as proof or as 'nearly significant'.

records.contextNotes: UG reports usually require basic descriptive and inferential reporting. PGT dissertations in the social and health sciences often involve the first independent statistical reporting. PGR writers face journal-specific requirements and reporting guidelines and often reviewer demands for effect sizes and confidence intervals.

records.summary: Proposals are persuasive, promissory genres read by evaluators under time pressure. Connor and Mauranen (1999) analysed EU research grant proposals and identified moves such as territory, gap, goal, means, reporting previous research, achievements, benefits, importance and competence claims, showing that proposals combine research-article moves with promotional ones; doctoral proposals share many of these moves, with more emphasis on design and feasibility. Creswell and Creswell (2018) give templates for qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods proposals, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) address doctoral proposals. Teach learners to analyse the specific template and criteria they face and to make alignment and feasibility visible.

activities.title: Criteria mapping
learnerActions: Obtain the assessment criteria for your proposal (admission, confirmation or funder)
Map each criterion to the section of your draft that addresses it
Identify criteria addressed weakly or not at all
Revise those sections and ask a peer to score the draft against the criteria
activities.intendedInsight: Proposals are evaluated against explicit criteria, and writers should address these visibly.
activities.rationale: Connor and Mauranen (1999) show that proposals include moves such as benefits and competence claims that respond to evaluators' needs rather than to purely academic conventions.

activities.title: Promissory language workshop
learnerActions: Collect future and conditional forms from funded proposals (will, aims to, is expected to, would enable)
Compare with language from completed-research articles
Revise your proposal to commit clearly to actions while hedging expected outcomes
activities.intendedInsight: Proposals commit firmly to what the researcher will do but calibrate claims about what will be found.
activities.rationale: Proposal templates (Creswell & Creswell 2018) separate planned procedures from anticipated outcomes, which calls for different degrees of commitment.

difficulties.pattern: My proposal explains the topic in depth but the methods are a paragraph and there is no timeline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposals that resemble essays, with extensive background and little design or feasibility detail.
difficulties.response: Use the criteria map to show reviewers' priorities, and ask for a Gantt-style timeline and a risk table.

difficulties.pattern: My study will prove that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Predetermined conclusions and boosted claims about outcomes of research not yet done.
difficulties.response: Distinguish what the researcher will do from what they expect to find, and practise hypothesis and expectation language.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to give a 90-second pitch of their proposal covering the problem, aims, approach, feasibility and significance.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Covers all elements concisely, with aims and approach clearly aligned and significance tailored to the audience.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers problem and aims well but is vague on approach or feasibility.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic without stating aims, approach or significance.

records.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, prospective doctoral students draft or revise the proposal on which admission or supervision depends; prospective master's students usually write the student project proposal instead. PGT learners applying for doctoral study write admission proposals. At PGR, the proposal is revised during the first year and then feeds the confirmation or progression report and, later, funding applications, which have their own topics.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-15 asks for a stage boundary with grp.project-proposal; the description now states it, and pre-sessional use is limited to the postgraduate stage for prospective doctoral students. Confirmation reports and grant applications have moved to res.progression-review and pub.funding-applications.

records.summary: Ethics documentation joins research integrity to plain-language writing. Creswell and Creswell (2018) set out ethical issues to anticipate at each stage of research, which can structure an application, and the Vitae RDF places ethics and research integrity within the professional conduct sub-domain (C1). For participant documents, the main EAP task is adapting register for a lay reader while preserving accuracy, which is mediation across audiences. Institutional templates take precedence and should be the starting point.

activities.title: Two-audience rewrite
learnerActions: Take a paragraph from your ethics application describing what participants will do
Rewrite it for a participant information sheet using plain language and direct address
Ask a peer outside your field to explain back what taking part involves
Revise any part they misunderstood
activities.intendedInsight: The same procedure must be described differently for a committee and for a participant, without loss of accuracy.
activities.rationale: Adapting register for a non-specialist audience is a mediation skill; comprehension checks with lay readers make clarity testable.

activities.title: Consistency audit
learnerActions: Place your methods description, ethics application and participant documents side by side
Check that sample, procedures, data storage and withdrawal arrangements match
Record and correct any discrepancies
activities.intendedInsight: Inconsistencies between documents can delay approval and raise integrity concerns later.
activities.rationale: Integrity requires that research is conducted as approved, which depends on consistent documentation (Vitae 2010, sub-domain C1).

difficulties.pattern: Participants will be informed that their data will be pseudonymised and stored in accordance with GDPR-compliant protocols.
difficulties.revealedBy: Participant sheets written in committee or legal register, with long sentences and technical terms.
difficulties.response: Model plain-language equivalents and use readability checks as a prompt for revision, not as a target. Keep required legal elements but explain them.

difficulties.pattern: Ethics is a bureaucratic hurdle, so I copy someone else's form and change the title.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applications that do not describe the actual study, and mismatched risks and procedures.
difficulties.response: Discuss the purpose of ethics review and the integrity implications of inaccurate applications.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain to you, as if you were a potential participant, what taking part in their study would involve and what happens to your data.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains clearly and accurately in plain language, including voluntariness, withdrawal and data handling.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains procedures but omits withdrawal or data use, or slips into technical language.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot give a clear account, or relies on jargon.

records.contextNotes: UG dissertations involving human participants usually require departmental ethics approval with simplified forms. PGT dissertations often involve first full applications. PGR applications may be complex, multi-site or international and may involve translated participant documents.
reviewNotes: No source in the current bibliography addresses the readability of participant information sheets directly; a reference from research-ethics or health-communication literature would strengthen this topic.

records.summary: Supervision is a relationship mediated by talk and text, and it is often where tacit disciplinary expectations become visible. Belcher (1994) studied three advisor–student pairs and linked the more successful relationship to a more reciprocal, collaborative stance and shared understanding of the target discourse community. Kamler and Thomson (2014) and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) treat supervision as a site of writing pedagogy, and Carless and Boud (2018) show that taking up feedback requires appreciating it, making judgements, managing affect and acting. Teach explicit expectation-setting and feedback negotiation, and treat indirectness in supervisor comments as a pragmatic issue.

activities.title: Expectation-setting conversation
learnerActions: Complete an expectations checklist covering meeting frequency, draft turnaround, feedback type and communication channels
Discuss it with your supervisor and agree a short written summary
Review the summary at an agreed point
activities.intendedInsight: Making expectations explicit reduces misunderstandings that might otherwise be attributed to language or personality.
activities.rationale: Belcher (1994) shows that mismatched understandings can undermine supervisory relationships; making them explicit is a practical response.

activities.title: Decoding feedback comments
learnerActions: Collect anonymised supervisor comments from your drafts
Classify each as directive, suggestion, question or praise, and rate how indirect it is
Write a response log stating what you changed for each comment or why you did not
Discuss any comments you were unsure about at the next meeting
activities.intendedInsight: Hedged comments are usually requests, and a response log makes engagement with feedback visible.
activities.rationale: Carless and Boud (2018) identify making judgements and taking action as components of feedback literacy; a response log operationalises both.

difficulties.pattern: My supervisor said 'you might want to think about' restructuring, so it's optional.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hedged suggestions left unaddressed and surprise when the supervisor repeats them more forcefully.
difficulties.response: Discuss how indirectness in English academic feedback often encodes requests, and practise clarifying ('Would you like me to restructure this before the next draft?'). Note that this varies by individual supervisor and that many first-language English students misread hedged advice too; clarity is a shared responsibility, so where possible encourage supervisors to mark which suggestions are requirements.

difficulties.pattern: I send my supervisor a whole chapter with no note and then wait for weeks without asking when to expect comments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback that does not address the learner's priorities, long waits and frustration on both sides.
difficulties.response: Practise covering notes that state the stage of the draft, two or three specific questions and a requested timescale, and agree expectations about turnaround early. Recognise that delays can have institutional causes such as supervisors' workloads, and make sure learners know the routes for raising concerns.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to draft the email they would send with their next chapter draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the draft's stage, asks two or three specific questions, proposes a meeting and uses an appropriate register.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sends the draft politely but with no specific questions or stage information.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sends the draft with no context or with an inappropriate register or demand.

records.contextNotes: UG dissertation supervision is usually brief and structured. PGT supervision is time-limited, so efficient agendas and specific requests matter. At PGR, supervision is a multi-year relationship, often with co-supervisors and formal progress reviews, and expectations differ by country and institution.

records.summary: Kamler and Thomson (2014) reject the idea of 'writing up' at the end of research and treat writing as a way of doing research and of forming a scholarly identity, which supports writing from the start of a project. Self-regulation research (Zimmerman 2002) provides a cycle of forethought, performance and self-reflection that maps onto writing goals, monitoring and adjustment. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss practical strategies for managing thesis writing. Writing groups and retreats are widely used in doctoral education; present them as options to try and evaluate, not as proven interventions.

activities.title: Writing log cycle
learnerActions: Set a weekly writing goal in terms of specific text
Log each session's time, output and obstacles
Review the log at the end of the week and adjust the next goal and strategy
Share one insight with a writing partner
activities.intendedInsight: Monitoring actual writing behaviour reveals patterns that intentions hide.
activities.rationale: The forethought–performance–reflection cycle of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002) applied to writing.

activities.title: Writing group trial
learnerActions: Join or form a writing group that meets regularly for focused writing time
State a session goal at the start and report progress at the end
After four sessions, evaluate whether the group helps and adjust the format
activities.intendedInsight: Social structures can make writing regular and less isolating.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) argue for social and pedagogical structures around doctoral writing; the specific format here is a proposal to test locally.

difficulties.pattern: I will start writing when I have finished reading and collecting data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long periods with no written output and a last-minute writing crisis.
difficulties.response: Present writing as part of thinking and research (memos, draft sections, notes towards chapters). Avoid shaming; many writers have been taught that writing comes last.

difficulties.pattern: I keep rewriting the first chapter and never move on.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated versions of one section with little overall progress.
difficulties.response: Encourage separating generative drafting from revision, and set goals for new text. Refer to wellbeing services where anxiety is significant.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe a typical writing week and what they produced last week.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a regular routine, text-specific goals and at least one support structure, and can name what was produced.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes regularly but with vague goals, or relies only on bursts before deadlines.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no routine or output and is postponing writing to a later stage.

records.contextNotes: PGT dissertation writing is compressed into a few months, so planning and routines matter most. PGR writing spans years, and sustained productivity, wellbeing and recovery from setbacks become central, often with institutional writing retreats and groups.

records.summary: Positionality writing draws on work on writer identity and self-mention. Ivanič (1998) distinguishes the autobiographical self, the discoursal self and the self as author, which helps writers separate useful reflexivity from personal narrative, and Tang and John (1999) and Hyland (2002) describe the roles authors take through first-person reference. Creswell and Creswell (2018) present reflexivity as a component of qualitative research reporting. Teach positionality statements as analytic, study-specific and linked to methodological decisions.

activities.title: From identity list to analytic statement
learnerActions: List aspects of your position relevant to the study (relationship to participants, language, professional role, theoretical commitments)
For each, write how it may have shaped access, data or interpretation
Note what you did about it
Draft a statement that keeps only the aspects that had consequences
activities.intendedInsight: Positionality is valuable when it explains effects and responses, not when it lists identity categories.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) frame reflexivity in terms of how researcher background shapes interpretation, which this sequence makes explicit.

activities.title: First-person roles
learnerActions: Collect first-person uses from methodology and reflexivity sections in your field
Classify them by authorial role (representative, guide, recounter of procedures, opinion-holder, originator)
Check your own statement for the range of roles you use
activities.intendedInsight: First-person reference can perform different roles, and reflexive writing needs the more committed ones.
activities.rationale: Tang and John's (1999) typology of 'I' roles and Hyland's (2002) work on authorial identity support a role-based analysis.

difficulties.pattern: I was taught never to use 'I' in academic writing, so I write 'the researcher' throughout my positionality statement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward third-person self-reference in sections where first person is conventional.
difficulties.response: Show field exemplars using 'I' in reflexive sections and discuss the myth of the absolute rule. Respect institutional or supervisory requirements where they genuinely differ.

difficulties.pattern: My positionality statement describes my life story and why I care about the topic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Biographical narratives with no link to methodological decisions or interpretation.
difficulties.response: Ask for each sentence 'So what for the study?' and cut or develop accordingly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how one aspect of their position might have affected one specific finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific aspect, explains a plausible effect on a specific finding and describes what was done about it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a relevant aspect but the effect is general or no response is described.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists identity categories or describes personal motivation without consequences.

records.contextNotes: At PGT, positionality statements are mainly required in qualitative dissertations in education, health and social sciences. At PGR they are often integrated throughout the methodology and discussion and are probed in the viva. In many quantitative and experimental fields they are not expected.

records.summary: Hyland's (2004) analysis of dissertation acknowledgements identified a three-tier structure (reflecting, thanking and announcing moves) and showed the genre's role in self-presentation and academic networking. Article acknowledgements serve additional functions: disclosing funding and recognising contributors who do not meet authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025; Brand et al., 2015). Teaching should combine move analysis with institutional and journal requirements and attention to confidentiality.

activities.title: Move analysis of acknowledgements
learnerActions: Analyse several thesis or dissertation acknowledgements from their field
Identify the moves and their order
Note variation in register and length
Draft their own acknowledgement
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgements follow recognisable conventions while allowing personal expression.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2004) identifies the moves of dissertation acknowledgements, providing a basis for analysis.

activities.title: Who goes where?
learnerActions: Sort a list of contributors into authors, acknowledged contributors and those not acknowledged
Justify decisions using ICMJE criteria or CRediT roles
Draft a funding statement
Compare decisions with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgement and authorship are distinct, with ethical implications.
activities.rationale: Authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025) and contributor role taxonomies (Brand et al., 2015) define who is acknowledged rather than listed as an author.

difficulties.pattern: Naming participants or organisations that were promised anonymity.
difficulties.revealedBy: Acknowledgements that identify research sites or participants by name.
difficulties.response: Check the consent and ethics documentation before naming anyone, and thank participants collectively where anonymity was promised.

difficulties.pattern: Register that is either extremely effusive or perfunctory.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long, emotional acknowledgements or a single generic line.
difficulties.response: Show a range of models from the learner's field and institution and discuss audience.

difficulties.pattern: Offering authorship as a form of thanks, or acknowledging someone whose contribution merits authorship.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposed author lists that include people who only provided resources, or acknowledgements of substantial intellectual contributors.
difficulties.response: Revisit authorship criteria and discuss with supervisors.

diagnostic.task: Give a list of contributors and ask the learner to decide who is acknowledged, who might be an author and how anonymous participants are thanked.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correctly distinguishes authors and acknowledged contributors, includes funding details and protects anonymity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but omits funding or names an anonymous participant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Confuses authorship and acknowledgement or omits required elements.

records.contextNotes: UG and PGT dissertation acknowledgements are usually short and optional. PGR thesis acknowledgements are longer and more personal, and in theses by publication they sit alongside contribution statements for each paper. Article acknowledgements are formulaic and often accompany required funding and competing-interest statements. Conventions on how personal thesis acknowledgements may be vary across countries and institutions.
reviewNotes: Review response: R1-33 moved this topic from Academic Pragmatics (prg.acknowledgements) to Research Writing; it now links to ethics documentation and authorship as part of the thesis and article apparatus.

records.summary: Progression reviews are often the first formal assessment of a doctoral researcher's writing and of their ability to defend a design orally, but their form is set by local regulations rather than by a shared genre model, so teaching starts from the institution's documentation, criteria and, with permission, past reports. Kamler and Thomson (2014) treat early doctoral texts as both text work and identity work, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) address the doctoral proposal from which these reports develop; together they support treating the report as an argued account of a developing project rather than a list of activities. The Vitae Researcher Development Framework (Vitae 2010) places project planning and risk management under research management (C2), which gives panels' feasibility questions a recognisable basis. Rehearsing the oral component with probing follow-up questions is a practitioner proposal, and anxiety about a high-stakes milestone should be acknowledged rather than dismissed.

activities.title: What has changed and why
learnerActions: List the differences between your original proposal and your current project: questions, design, sample, scope and timeline
For each change, write one or two sentences giving the reason and the evidence that prompted it
Draft the report's progress-and-revisions section from these notes
Ask a peer from another field whether each change reads as a reasoned decision or as drift
activities.intendedInsight: Panels expect projects to change; they assess whether changes are reasoned, evidenced and coherent with the aims.
activities.rationale: Presenting a revised design as argued development rather than as failure reflects the view of doctoral writing as ongoing text and identity work (Kamler & Thomson 2014); the activity is a practical proposal.

activities.title: Mock panel with follow-ups
learnerActions: Exchange reports in groups of three and prepare two feasibility questions and one design question for each other
Run ten-minute panels in which every first answer receives at least one follow-up question
Note which answers referred to specific evidence in the plan and which stayed general
Revise the timeline or risk table in response to the hardest question
activities.intendedInsight: Feasibility is shown through specific plans, contingencies and evidence, and panel questions are a resource for improving the plan.
activities.rationale: Panels typically probe research management, which the Vitae RDF describes in terms of project planning, delivery and risk (Vitae 2010); follow-up questions bring the rehearsal closer to the real event. This is a practitioner proposal, not a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: My report lists everything I did this year — courses, conferences, reading — so the panel can see I have worked hard.
difficulties.revealedBy: Activity-log reports with little about questions, design or findings and no argument that the project is on track.
difficulties.response: Show that panels judge the coherence and feasibility of the project, not effort. Ask the learner to open each section with a claim about the project and to use activities only as evidence; training records usually belong in a separate form or appendix.

difficulties.pattern: Changing my research questions will look like failure, so I keep the original ones even though my data no longer fit them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions that no longer match the design or preliminary findings, and evasive answers when the panel asks about the mismatch.
difficulties.response: Present revision as an expected part of doctoral research and model sentences that report a change with its reason. Do not push changes for their own sake; the aim is alignment between questions, design and data.

difficulties.pattern: The criteria, length and the panel's role differ from what other students told me, and nobody explained what the possible outcomes mean.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports written to the wrong length or template, and candidates surprised by outcomes such as a deferred decision or a second review.
difficulties.response: Teachers should work from the current regulations and criteria with the learner, and graduate schools should publish exemplars and descriptions of outcomes. Learners can ask the supervisor or panel chair in writing what will be assessed. Candidates who need adjustments to the oral component, such as questions in advance or rest breaks, should arrange them through the institution's normal processes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in two minutes what has changed in their project since the proposal and why, then ask one follow-up question about feasibility.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific changes with reasons grounded in the work, links them to the aims and answers the follow-up with concrete evidence such as dates, access arrangements or pilot results.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes changes accurately but gives reasons only in general terms, or answers the follow-up with reassurance rather than evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists activities without identifying changes, or cannot connect the plan to the remaining time and resources.

records.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic, best taught in the months before the first formal review. UK institutions commonly hold a confirmation or upgrade review in the first year or so and annual reviews after that; Australian universities typically have a confirmation of candidature; in North America the comparable hurdles are usually qualifying or comprehensive examinations and a prospectus or proposal defence; in many continental European systems a first-year evaluation or individual study plan serves a similar purpose. Part-time, professional-doctorate and publication-based candidates often have different timings and components.
reviewNotes: No genre analysis of confirmation or progression reports is in the bibliography; the guidance relies on doctoral-writing handbooks and the Vitae RDF and should be checked against local regulations.

records.summary: Paltridge (2002) identified compilations of research papers as one of four broad thesis types and found that published advice for thesis writers seldom described them, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss how publication-based theses are framed and integrated. The integrative chapters must carry the argument of the whole thesis across papers written for different journals and readerships, so teaching concentrates on framing, linking and cross-paper synthesis, and on contribution statements that make the candidate's responsibility for co-authored work visible. Contributor-role taxonomies such as CRediT (Brand et al. 2015) can structure these statements, although institutions usually prescribe their own forms.

activities.title: Thread map
learnerActions: List your papers and write the one question each answers
Draw the relations between them (extends, tests, applies, explains) and name the overarching problem they share
Draft the paragraph of your introduction that explains this structure to an examiner
Check that your concluding chapter answers the overarching problem, not only each paper's question
activities.intendedInsight: The integrating argument has to be made explicit because the papers were written to stand alone.
activities.rationale: Paltridge and Starfield (2020) stress that a publication-based thesis must still read as a coherent whole; mapping the relations between papers makes that argument plannable. The activity is a practical proposal.

activities.title: Contribution statements
learnerActions: Collect contribution statements from theses by publication in your institution
List each author's contributions to one of your papers using CRediT roles
Draft your contribution statement in the institution's required form
Check the statement with your co-authors
activities.intendedInsight: Contribution statements must be accurate, agreed with co-authors and specific enough for examiners to judge the candidate's own work.
activities.rationale: CRediT (Brand et al. 2015) provides a shared vocabulary for contributor roles, which helps make individual contributions explicit.

difficulties.pattern: In a thesis by publication, I just staple my papers together.
difficulties.revealedBy: Minimal introductory and concluding chapters, literature reviews repeated across papers and no linking text.
difficulties.response: Discuss examiners' expectations of coherence across the whole thesis and the institution's rules on framing chapters. Ask for a written account of how the papers relate before any integrative text is drafted.

difficulties.pattern: My concluding chapter summarises paper 1, then paper 2, then paper 3.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions made of paper-by-paper summaries, with no cross-paper synthesis and no statement of the thesis's overall contribution.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write three claims that can only be supported by combining papers, then build the conclusion around them. Do not insist on removing all summary; brief reminders help examiners.

difficulties.pattern: The rules on co-authored papers, the status of submitted papers and reproducing published text are unclear, and my supervisors disagree.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late discovery that a paper does not count, that a publisher's permission is needed or that contribution forms are required.
difficulties.response: Point learners to the current regulations and publishers' author-reuse policies early, and encourage graduate schools to publish clear guidance and exemplars. Learners should record decisions about paper status and co-authorship with their supervisors in writing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in under two minutes, how their papers together answer one overarching research problem.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a single problem, names the role of each paper in addressing it and identifies a contribution that emerges only from the set.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes each paper clearly but links them chronologically or by topic without an overarching argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot state a shared problem, or describes the papers as independent projects.

records.contextNotes: This is a PGR topic. Theses by publication are common in the Nordic countries, the Netherlands and Australia and in many science, health and engineering fields, and are increasingly offered elsewhere, including in the social sciences; some systems require papers to be published, others accept submitted or publishable papers. Professional doctorates and retrospective PhDs by published works have their own requirements, and candidates should find out how examiners are briefed to judge coherence.

records.summary: PRISMA 2020 (Page et al. 2021) sets out the items a systematic review report should contain, including full search strategies, a flow diagram of study selection and the methods used to assess risk of bias and certainty, and many journals and examiners use it as a checklist. Arksey and O'Malley (2005) proposed a framework for scoping studies that map the extent and nature of research rather than appraising and pooling it, which changes what the report must say. Greenhalgh (2019) explains how health readers appraise systematic reviews, which helps writers anticipate what a critical reader will check. EAP teaching concentrates on the reporting language (precise past-tense procedure, transparent numbers, cross-study synthesis and calibrated conclusions) and on matching the review type to the question; review methods themselves are taught by subject specialists and librarians.

activities.title: Checklist-led reverse engineering
learnerActions: Choose a published review in your field that reports following PRISMA 2020 or one of its extensions
Locate where each checklist item for the methods and results is reported
Mark the sentence patterns used to report searches, selection and appraisal
Draft the same sections for your own review protocol
activities.intendedInsight: Reporting guidelines specify content; published reviews show how that content is phrased and placed.
activities.rationale: Page et al. (2021) present PRISMA 2020 as reporting guidance; analysing exemplars against it connects the checklist to the language that realises it.

activities.title: From study-by-study to synthesis
learnerActions: Take a results draft that summarises included studies one at a time
Group the findings by outcome, theme or direction of effect in a table
Rewrite one paragraph so that it opens with a claim about the body of evidence and cites studies in support
Add a sentence on the quality or consistency of that evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A review synthesis makes claims about a body of evidence, qualified by its quality, rather than describing studies in turn.
activities.rationale: Synthesis across studies and calibration to the certainty of evidence are central reporting items in PRISMA 2020 (Page et al. 2021); the activity is a practitioner proposal adapted from teaching synthesis paragraphs.

difficulties.pattern: A systematic review is just a literature review with more sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Protocols with no explicit eligibility criteria or search strategy, and reports that select studies to support a position.
difficulties.response: Contrast the purposes and reporting requirements of narrative, scoping and systematic reviews using one example of each from the learner's field. Do not present the systematic review as superior; the right type depends on the question.

difficulties.pattern: Study A found…; Study B found…; Study C found…, followed by a one-line conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Results organised study by study, with appraisal reported separately and not used in the synthesis.
difficulties.response: Use a findings-by-study matrix to plan claims across studies, and require each synthesis paragraph to say how strong the evidence behind its claim is.

difficulties.pattern: My supervisor asked for a 'systematic review', but there is no time or second reviewer for screening.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviews labelled systematic that lack the procedures the label implies, and examiners questioning the method.
difficulties.response: Help the learner and supervisor agree an honest label, such as a scoping or rapid review or a review with a systematic search, and report the procedures actually used. Programmes that set review-based dissertations should state which review type and procedures they expect.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three sentences reporting a database search and its results for a review they are planning or have read.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names databases and dates, says where the full strategy is available and gives the numbers retrieved, screened and included, in precise past-tense prose.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives sources and numbers but omits dates or the screening procedure, or reports the procedure vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic of the search without details that would allow it to be repeated.

records.contextNotes: At PGT, review-based dissertations are common in health, education, psychology and management, often as scoping or rapid reviews with limited resources, so honesty about the review type matters more than full systematic procedures. At PGR, a systematic or scoping review is often the first paper or chapter, with a registered protocol (for example on PROSPERO or the Open Science Framework) and full reporting to a guideline. Fields differ: software engineering has its own guidelines for systematic literature reviews, and qualitative evidence syntheses have specific reporting standards.
reviewNotes: Review response: R6-02 also asks for dhl.critical-appraisal to be narrowed to single-study appraisal and its PRISMA material moved here; that edit belongs to the Disciplinary Literacies group. This topic depends softly on dhl.critical-appraisal.

records.summary: Creswell and Creswell (2018) treat instrument design as part of research design, linking items to variables and research questions and recommending piloting. Item-writing guidelines developed for tests (Haladyna et al. 2002) share several principles that carry over to questionnaires, such as keeping each item focused, using vocabulary suited to the respondents and avoiding negative wording, although they were written for multiple-choice assessment rather than surveys. For EAP the topic is a language problem as much as a methods one: precision, neutrality, presupposition and register decide whether participants answer the question the researcher intended. Teach it through diagnosis and rewriting of flawed items and through think-aloud piloting, in which a few people like the participants say how they understand each item.

activities.title: Item clinic
learnerActions: Sort a set of flawed items by problem: double-barrelled, leading, presupposing, negative, vague quantifier or jargon
Rewrite each item and compare rewrites in pairs
Check each rewrite against the research question it is meant to serve
Apply the same checks to your own draft instrument
activities.intendedInsight: Most item problems are visible in the wording and can be fixed before data collection.
activities.rationale: Guidance on focused, positively worded items (Haladyna et al. 2002) and on aligning instruments with variables (Creswell & Creswell 2018) can be turned into a checklist; the activity is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Think-aloud pilot
learnerActions: Recruit two or three people similar to your participants
Ask them to read each item aloud and say what they think it asks and how they would answer
Record misunderstandings and hesitations
Revise the items and note the changes for your methods section
activities.intendedInsight: Researchers cannot judge clarity from their own reading; participants' interpretations reveal ambiguity.
activities.rationale: Piloting is a standard recommendation in research design texts (Creswell & Creswell 2018); asking pilot participants to say how they read each item makes ambiguity visible.

difficulties.pattern: Do you agree that the new library services are useful and easy to access?
difficulties.revealedBy: Items that ask two things at once, presuppose an answer or invite agreement.
difficulties.response: Teach the checks one at a time and have learners mark each item against them. Do not ban agree–disagree formats; teach when they suit the construct and how to balance them.

difficulties.pattern: My participants are students like me, so they will understand my questions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Items that use disciplinary terms or the researcher's own concepts, and no pilot reported.
difficulties.response: Require a pilot with at least two people outside the research team and a short record of what changed. Where participants will answer in another language, plan translation and checking with a fluent speaker.

difficulties.pattern: Some of my items do not measure anything my research questions ask about, and one construct has no items at all.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questionnaires with items that cannot be traced to any construct, and constructs with no items.
difficulties.response: Have the learner build an alignment table running from research question to construct to items before revising any wording.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write one questionnaire item and one interview prompt for a stated research question and to say who will answer them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The item is single-focus, neutral and in the participants' language with suitable response options; the prompt is open with a planned probe; both are clearly linked to the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One of the two is well formed, but the other leads, asks two things or uses jargon.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Both are leading or yes/no and cannot be traced to the research question.

records.contextNotes: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, short questionnaire or interview projects make this topic useful when an instrument forms part of the assessed project; undergraduate-entry courses with survey projects can use a simplified version of the item checks. UG and PGT dissertations in the social sciences, education, business and health often rely on self-designed instruments with limited piloting. At PGR, wording interacts with validated scales, translation and adaptation across languages, and ethics committee review of instruments.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no dedicated source on questionnaire or interview design; haladyna2002 is cited only for item-writing principles that carry over from test design.

records.summary: Research on international teaching assistants shows that students' comprehension judgements depend on more than the speaker's language: Rubin (1992) found that undergraduates who believed a recorded lecture was given by an Asian instructor rated the speaker as more accented and scored lower on comprehension than those who heard the same recording attributed to a white instructor. Pickering (2001) found differences in tone choice between international and US teaching assistants that affected how information and rapport were signalled in class. Written feedback on student work can be framed by principles of good feedback practice (Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick 2006), such as clarifying what good performance is and giving information students can act on. The Vitae Researcher Development Framework (Vitae 2010) places teaching within engagement and impact. Teach explanation, questioning and feedback language explicitly, and address listener expectations and institutional support alongside the teaching assistant's own speech.

activities.title: Micro-teach with checks
learnerActions: Choose a concept or procedure that first-year students often find difficult
Plan a three-part explanation: link to what students know, explain with an example, then check understanding with a question that requires students to use the idea rather than 'Is that clear?'
Deliver it to peers and receive feedback on organisation, examples and checking
Teach it again with one change
activities.intendedInsight: Clear teaching talk depends on organisation and checking as much as on pronunciation.
activities.rationale: Rubin (1992) and Pickering (2001) suggest that comprehension in international teaching assistants' classes depends on listener expectations and on discourse-level features such as tone choice, not only on individual sounds; micro-teaching targets the features the teaching assistant controls. This is a practitioner proposal.

activities.title: Feedback calibration
learnerActions: Mark the same anonymised student answer independently using the module criteria
Compare marks and written comments in a group
Rewrite comments so that each refers to a criterion and suggests a next step
Agree how to phrase a comment on a serious weakness respectfully
activities.intendedInsight: Useful feedback is criterion-referenced, prioritised and actionable, and markers' comments vary more than they expect.
activities.rationale: Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) argue that good feedback clarifies what good performance is and gives students information they can use; calibrating comments against criteria applies this to marking by teaching assistants.

difficulties.pattern: Students say they can't understand me, so my accent must be the problem.
difficulties.revealedBy: Teaching assistants avoiding interaction or over-scripting sessions, and module evaluations that comment on accent.
