diagnostic.task: Ask: 'When will you start revising for your next exam, and what will a typical session look like?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Starts weeks ahead, revisits topics, uses retrieval and past papers, and adjusts according to results.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Starts early but plans to reread, or uses retrieval but only in the final days.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans to start in the final week by reading notes.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners preparing for their first subject exams need explicit planning support. In-sessional UG and PGT learners benefit from short sessions before exam seasons, ideally with subject past papers. Pre-sessional courses rarely include content exams, so the topic is not listed there.

records.summary: Ellis and Yuan (2004) found that pre-task planning increased the fluency and syntactic complexity of L2 writing, while unpressured on-line planning favoured accuracy, which suggests a trade-off that timed conditions make acute. Weigle (2002) discusses timed impromptu writing as an assessment format, including its limitations as a measure of academic writing. Under time pressure writers may revert to knowledge telling (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987). Teach a short, routine planning phase, disciplined time allocation and targeted final checking, and present timed writing as a distinct performance rather than a compressed version of coursework writing.

activities.title: Short plan drill
learnerActions: Read an unseen question and give yourself a few minutes only to write a position and three to four points
Write the answer within the remaining time
Compare your plan with the finished script: did you follow it?
Repeat weekly with new questions and track whether your plans become quicker and more usable
activities.intendedInsight: A brief plan keeps a timed answer focused and does not waste time.
activities.rationale: Ellis and Yuan (2004) found benefits of pre-task planning for fluency and complexity; the drill makes short planning automatic.

activities.title: Graduated time compression
learnerActions: Write an answer with generous time
Write an answer to a similar question with less time, then with exam-length time
Compare the three scripts and note what was lost (accuracy, development, conclusion)
Decide what to protect under pressure and plan your checking routine accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing what slips under time pressure lets you decide in advance what to protect.
activities.rationale: Weigle (2002) notes that timed writing captures a particular kind of performance; experiencing the effect of time limits helps learners manage it deliberately.

difficulties.pattern: 'There's no time to plan.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Scripts that wander, change position midway or stop without a conclusion.
difficulties.response: Show planned and unplanned scripts side by side. Do not demand elaborate plans: a position and a few points are enough.

difficulties.pattern: Reproducing a memorised essay that does not fit the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent, accurate scripts that are off-question; identical openings across scripts.
difficulties.response: Use questions that require adapting known content, and give feedback specifically on relevance.

difficulties.pattern: Accuracy declines sharply under time pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: More errors in timed scripts than in coursework from the same learner.
difficulties.response: Teach a short final check for the learner's most frequent error types. Do not expect error-free timed writing or penalise it as though it were edited coursework.

difficulties.pattern: Timed formats disadvantage candidates whose processing, handwriting or typing speed is affected by a disability or specific learning difference (for example dyslexia or dyspraxia) when agreed adjustments are not in place.
difficulties.revealedBy: Scripts that are well planned but unfinished or hard to read; learners who do not know they can apply for extra time, rest breaks or a word processor.
difficulties.response: Tell learners early how to apply for exam adjustments and assistive technology (see dig.assistive-technology), and let them practise with the same adjustments. Programmes should apply agreed adjustments to timed progression tasks as well as to degree exams. Do not read slower completion as a language weakness without checking.

diagnostic.task: Set a short timed question and look at the plan and script together.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A brief plan with a position, followed by a script that answers the question directly, develops the planned points and finishes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A plan exists but is abandoned, or the script is relevant but unfinished.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No plan; a script that drifts or does not address the question.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and in-sessional UG learners use this for subject exam essays and short answers, increasingly typed in online exams. On UG-route pre-sessionals timed writing is often part of progression; on PG-route pre-sessionals it matters where the progression assessment includes a timed task, though coursework often carries more weight. PGT learners meet timed writing less often, so it is revisited where modules use exams. Practise under the conditions learners will face (handwritten or typed, with any agreed adjustments).
reviewNotes: Ellis and Yuan's study used narrative writing with planning-time manipulations; extending its findings to argumentative exam essays is an inference.

records.summary: Practice testing, including with objective formats, is itself a high-utility learning technique (Dunlosky et al., 2013), so preparation and test performance reinforce each other. Item-writing guidance advises against negatively worded stems and absolute terms (Haladyna et al., 2002), which suggests that well-constructed university items may be less vulnerable to cue-based 'test-wise' strategies than learners believe. For L2 readers the main difficulties are often linguistic (negatives, qualifiers, dense stems), so emphasise precise reading and knowledge over tricks.

activities.title: Qualifier spotting
learnerActions: Read a set of stems and options and underline every negative, absolute and qualifier
Rephrase each stem in plain English
Explain how each underlined word changes which option is correct
activities.intendedInsight: Small words such as 'not', 'always' and 'usually' can decide the answer.
activities.rationale: Qualifiers and negatives are a known source of misreading, and item-writing guidance treats them as potential problems (Haladyna et al., 2002).

activities.title: Cover the options
learnerActions: Cover the options and answer the stem from knowledge
Uncover the options and look for your answer
If it is not there, eliminate options with stated reasons
Review which items you could answer before seeing options
activities.intendedInsight: Answering from knowledge first reduces the pull of plausible-looking distractors.
activities.rationale: Generating an answer before reading options is a form of retrieval practice (Dunlosky et al., 2013) and reduces reliance on recognising familiar wording.

difficulties.pattern: Missing 'NOT' or 'EXCEPT' in a stem.
difficulties.revealedBy: Choosing a true statement when asked for the false one.
difficulties.response: Train a habit of marking negatives before reading options.

difficulties.pattern: Choosing the option whose wording is most familiar from lectures.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors on application items where a distractor reuses lecture phrasing.
difficulties.response: Practise items where the correct answer is paraphrased and the distractor uses familiar wording.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on cue-based tricks such as 'choose the longest answer'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report rules of thumb in place of reasoning.
difficulties.response: Show that well-written items avoid such cues and redirect effort to knowledge and precise reading.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer one 'NOT' item and one qualifier item aloud.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notices the negative and qualifier, reasons about each option and selects correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Selects correctly but cannot explain, or notices the negative only when prompted.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misses the negative or qualifier.

records.contextNotes: Foundation learners often meet objective tests in science, business and health modules. In-sessional UG and PGT learners meet them in quantitative and professional programmes. Pre-sessional courses rarely use subject objective tests, although proficiency tests use selected-response formats.
reviewNotes: No bibliography source directly addresses L2 learners' performance on content multiple-choice items; Haladyna et al. (2002) concerns item writing rather than test taking, so claims drawn from it are framed as implications.

records.summary: Open-book, take-home and online time-windowed exams shift the demand from recall to application, analysis and synthesis, and increase the importance of organised materials and integrity awareness. The Handbook of Academic Integrity (Bretag, 2016) covers the forms of misconduct, including collusion and contract cheating, that unsupervised formats can make more tempting, and Pecorari (2013) emphasises teaching good source use rather than only policing it. Teach learners to prepare indexed materials, to write answers that apply rather than transcribe, to plan within the window, and to check paper-specific rules on collaboration, resources and AI use, which vary and change.

activities.title: Index your resources
learnerActions: Organise your notes for one module into a structure with tabs or a contents page
Create a one-page index of key concepts, cases or formulae with locations
Test it by finding five items against a timer
Revise the index where retrieval was slow
activities.intendedInsight: In open-book exams, the speed of finding information depends on preparation done beforehand.
activities.rationale: Searching unorganised materials takes time away from analysis, which is what these formats reward; this is practitioner reasoning rather than a tested finding.

activities.title: Reproduction versus application
learnerActions: Compare two answers to a take-home question: one assembled from notes and one that applies concepts to the question
Identify which parts of each answer the question actually asked for
Rewrite a paragraph of the first answer so that it applies rather than reproduces
activities.intendedInsight: Having access to notes does not mean copying them; the marks are for using them.
activities.rationale: Pecorari (2013) argues for teaching purposeful source use; open-book answers are a case in which source material must be transformed to serve a new purpose.

difficulties.pattern: 'Open-book is easier, so I'll revise less.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Little preparation; answers that reproduce notes.
difficulties.response: Show the higher-order demands of open-book questions and the time cost of searching.

difficulties.pattern: Copying from notes, slides or sources without attribution under time pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed strings matching lecture slides or readings in submitted answers.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to prepare notes that already separate quotation, paraphrase and own words, and clarify the paper's citation expectations.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a take-home or online exam like coursework: discussing answers with peers or using AI tools that the paper does not permit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Similar answers from students who studied together; questions after the exam about whether a tool was allowed.
difficulties.response: Make each paper's collaboration and AI rules explicit, show learners where they are stated, and discuss why the boundaries are drawn where they are. Where the rules are unclear, learners should ask before the exam, not after.

difficulties.pattern: 'A 24-hour window means 24 hours of writing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers far beyond the expected length; exhaustion; uploads in the final minutes.
difficulties.response: Point to the expected working time where the paper states one, plan a schedule with breaks inside the window, and submit well before the deadline. Do not assume that everyone can use the whole window: caring, work and time-zone constraints differ.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In your next take-home exam, what are you allowed to use and do, and how will you prepare your materials?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the rules accurately (sources, collaboration, AI), describes organised and indexed materials, and plans to apply rather than reproduce.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows some rules but has no preparation plan, or prepares but is unsure of the rules.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know the rules and plans minimal preparation.

records.contextNotes: Foundation programmes increasingly use open-book, take-home or online formats in subject modules, and some pre-sessional programmes run timed progression tasks online within a fixed window. In-sessional UG and PGT learners meet these formats across disciplines, with PGT take-home exams often resembling short essays. Rules on AI use, permitted resources and remote invigilation vary by paper and change often; similarity and AI-detection scores do not by themselves establish misconduct, and detection tools have been found unreliable (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023). Remote invigilation can create barriers for some disabled learners and for those without a quiet private space, so learners should know how to request alternative arrangements.
reviewNotes: Rules on take-home exams, especially on generative AI, vary widely and are changing rapidly; teach learners to check paper-specific rules rather than presenting general rules.
No bibliography source specifically evaluates open-book exam preparation; guidance here is practitioner-based.

records.summary: Oral assessments in higher education vary along several dimensions, including what is assessed, how interactive the event is and how structured it is (Joughin, 1998), so preparation must start from the specific format. Horwitz et al. (1986) identified fear of negative evaluation and communication apprehension as components of foreign language anxiety, which oral exams can intensify. Teach learners to anticipate question types, use a direct-answer structure, ask for clarification and recover from breakdowns, and rehearse with realistic follow-up questions rather than memorised scripts.

activities.title: Mock oral with question types
learnerActions: List likely question types for your oral assessment (clarification, justification, challenge, extension)
Prepare flexible bullet-point answers, not scripts
Take part in a mock oral in which a peer or tutor asks one question of each type
Review a recording and identify one strength and one change
activities.intendedInsight: Preparing for types of question is more robust than preparing scripted answers to predicted questions.
activities.rationale: Oral formats vary in structure and interaction (Joughin, 1998), so rehearsal should include unscripted follow-up.

activities.title: Clarify and hold
learnerActions: Collect your own phrases for asking for repetition, checking meaning and gaining a few seconds of thinking time
Practise them in rapid question rounds with a partner
Discuss when each phrase is appropriate and when it might sound evasive
activities.intendedInsight: Asking for clarification and taking thinking time are legitimate moves, not signs of weakness.
activities.rationale: Having routines for these moves reduces the risk that fear of negative evaluation (Horwitz et al., 1986) leads to silence or guessing.

difficulties.pattern: Memorised scripts break down when the question is unexpected.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent openings followed by long pauses or irrelevant answers to follow-ups.
difficulties.response: Rehearse with unpredictable follow-ups and flexible outlines. Do not ban preparation; change its form.

difficulties.pattern: Freezing or long silence under questioning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence, very short answers, visible distress in mock orals.
difficulties.response: Normalise the experience, rehearse holding and clarification phrases, and use graded practice from low to higher stakes.

difficulties.pattern: Answering a question that has only been partly understood rather than asking for it to be repeated, because asking seems to risk losing marks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that address a misinterpreted question.
difficulties.response: Make explicit that examiners generally expect and accept clarification requests, check whether the format limits them (some test speaking tasks do), and model them. This hesitation is common among novice candidates of all backgrounds.

diagnostic.task: Ask one ambiguous question about the learner's own work and one follow-up challenge.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Asks for clarification of the ambiguous question, answers directly with justification, and handles the challenge by acknowledging and responding.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers the ambiguous question without clarifying, or handles the challenge with long hesitation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot respond to the challenge or answers a different question.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners meet oral assessment in presentations with questions, seminars and speaking assessments; PG-route pre-sessionals often include questioning on the learner's own project. In-sessional UG learners meet orals in language, professional and some science programmes, and PGT learners revisit them where modules use them. The doctoral viva is treated separately (pub.viva). Learners who stammer, are deaf or hard of hearing, or are autistic may need adjustments such as extra time, written questions or a different format; these should be arranged in advance and the assessment should not penalise fluency features unrelated to the construct.
reviewNotes: Oral assessment conventions (permitted notes, whether questions may be repeated, length) differ between formats and institutions; learners should check the rules for each assessment.

records.summary: Putwain (2008) conceptualises test anxiety as multidimensional, involving worry and physical and emotional components that arise when evaluative situations are appraised as threatening. Horwitz et al. (1986) identified test anxiety as one component of foreign language anxiety, alongside communication apprehension and fear of negative evaluation, so L2 learners in high-stakes language or content exams may face compounded pressure. Ramirez and Beilock (2011) found that brief expressive writing about test worries before an exam improved anxious students' performance. Present anxiety management as a normal skill, combine it with preparation, and refer severe cases to appropriate services.

activities.title: Worry writing before a mock test
learnerActions: Before a mock test, spend a few minutes writing freely about any worries you have about it
Take the mock test
Afterwards, note whether the writing changed how you felt or performed
Decide whether to use the technique before a real exam
activities.intendedInsight: Putting worries on paper may free attention for the task.
activities.rationale: Ramirez and Beilock (2011) reported benefits of expressive writing for anxious test takers; this classroom version is a proposal to try, not a guaranteed intervention.

activities.title: Realistic rehearsal
learnerActions: Take at least one full practice paper under exam conditions (timing, room, no notes)
Note moments of rising anxiety and what triggered them
Plan a response for each trigger, such as starting with a question you are confident about
activities.intendedInsight: Familiarity with exam conditions reduces uncertainty, and planned responses make anxious moments manageable.
activities.rationale: Putwain (2008) links test anxiety to the appraisal of evaluative situations; rehearsal and planned responses address both uncertainty and the sense of being unprepared.

difficulties.pattern: 'Feeling anxious means I'm not ready or not capable.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Catastrophic statements before exams; avoidance of mock tests.
difficulties.response: Normalise anxiety, separate the feeling from evidence of preparation, and discuss reinterpreting arousal as readiness.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding mock exams to escape the feeling.
difficulties.revealedBy: Absence from practice tests; no timed practice in revision plans.
difficulties.response: Offer graded exposure, starting with short, low-stakes timed tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Going blank on first reading the paper.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports of losing the first minutes; slow starts.
difficulties.response: Teach a first-minutes routine: breathe, read all questions, start with the one you are most confident about. Do not simply advise learners to 'relax', which gives no actionable step.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What do you do when you feel anxious during an exam?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific techniques used before and during exams and knows where to seek support if needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes a general approach ('try to calm down') without specific steps.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no strategy or describes only avoidance.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners face high-stakes progression decisions and often recent proficiency tests. Foundation learners face their first university exams. In-sessional UG learners benefit from short sessions before exam seasons, linked to wellbeing services and to the institution's process for exam adjustments; PGT learners revisit the topic where exams are used. Speaking-specific anxiety is treated in sem.speaking-anxiety.
reviewNotes: Evidence for brief expressive writing comes mainly from Ramirez and Beilock's (2011) studies; it is presented as something to try, and evidence from other contexts should be checked before stronger claims are made.
Severe anxiety is a matter for wellbeing or disability services; this topic is not clinical guidance.

records.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) frame assessment as a chain from performance to interpretation to decision, which shows learners that a score matters because of the decision it supports. The CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001) distinguishes types of assessment, including achievement and proficiency assessment, and Murray (2016) discusses post-entry language assessment as a separate purpose from entry testing. Teach purposes through the assessments learners actually face, and address common misconceptions, such as treating a diagnostic task as a test to be gamed.

activities.title: Purpose–decision map
learnerActions: List every language assessment you have taken or will take this year
For each, note its purpose, who uses the result and what decision it affects
Compare maps in groups and identify any assessment whose purpose was unclear
activities.intendedInsight: Each assessment exists to support a particular decision, which affects how you should approach it.
activities.rationale: Bachman and Palmer's assessment use argument links scores to decisions; mapping makes that link concrete for learners.

activities.title: Same score, different decisions
learnerActions: Consider a borderline score and discuss what decisions different users (a university, a placement coordinator, a teacher) might make with it
Discuss why a small score difference may not reflect a real difference in ability
Agree what other evidence could inform each decision
activities.intendedInsight: Scores are evidence with limits, and decisions should take those limits into account.
activities.rationale: Measurement error and the uses made of scores are central concerns in Bachman and Palmer's framework.

difficulties.pattern: 'My score is my level, permanently.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners describe themselves by a score; discouragement or complacency based on a single result.
difficulties.response: Discuss scores as a snapshot with error, and point to development since the test.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a post-entry diagnostic task as high-stakes and preparing to 'pass' it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memorised essays in diagnostic writing; anxiety about results that only guide support.
difficulties.response: Explain the purpose and use of diagnostic results and stress that accurate results lead to more useful support.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting the course achievement mark to equal a proficiency score.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions such as 'What IELTS score is this mark?'
difficulties.response: Explain the difference between what was taught and assessed on a course and general proficiency, and refer to how the institution expresses equivalence where it does.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is the difference between the test you took to apply and the assessments on this course?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes the purposes (general proficiency for admission versus achievement and progression on a course) and the decisions each supports.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes differences in format but not in purpose.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no difference, or describes both simply as 'English tests'.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners face several assessments with different purposes in a short period. In-sessional UG and PGT learners may meet post-entry diagnostic assessment and need to revisit its supportive purpose.

records.summary: The CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001, 2020) is a descriptive framework of communicative ability, not a test; the Companion Volume refines and extends the illustrative scales, including plus levels and mediation. North (2014) explains that relating an examination to the CEFR requires specific procedures and expert judgement, so test-to-CEFR alignments are claims made by test owners, not exact conversions. As a UK example, at the time of writing the Student route requires English at CEFR B2 for degree-level study (B1 below degree level), shown through a Home Office-approved secure English language test or, for degree-level study at higher education providers with a track record of compliance, the provider's own assessment, with some nationality and qualification exemptions (UK Visas and Immigration, 2025). Both the requirements and the approved-test arrangements change, so they must be checked at source and visa questions referred to qualified advisers. Arkoudis et al. (2012) argue that meeting entry standards is the start of language development, not its end.

activities.title: Read the requirement
learnerActions: Find the English language requirement for your intended programme
Identify the overall score and any minimum per skill
Check three sample score profiles against it
Note where the institution says its requirement comes from and when it was last updated
activities.intendedInsight: Requirements have several parts, and missing one component minimum can matter as much as the overall score.
activities.rationale: Accurate reading of requirements prevents costly misunderstandings; component minimums reflect the CEFR's recognition that profiles differ across skills.

activities.title: Where is the official rule?
learnerActions: Find the official government guidance on the English requirement for your visa route
Compare it with what an agent website or forum says
Note differences and the date of each source
activities.intendedInsight: Official current sources are the only reliable basis for decisions about requirements.
activities.rationale: Visa requirements change; learning to check the official source is more durable than learning a specific rule.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a test score as an exact CEFR level ('6.5 is C1') or assuming scores convert directly between tests.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners quoting conversion tables as exact; surprise when institutions accept different scores from different tests.
difficulties.response: Explain that alignments are approximate claims by test owners and that institutions set their own requirements. Do not supply a single conversion table as authoritative.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I meet the entry requirement, my English is good enough for my degree.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to engage with in-sessional support after admission.
difficulties.response: Show the language demands of the degree that entry tests do not measure directly, such as extended source-based writing.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on outdated or unofficial information about requirements.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners citing rules that have changed, or advice from agents and social media.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to check dates and official sources, and model doing so.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What English level do you need for your programme, and how do you know?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the requirement including component minimums, names the official source and acknowledges that rules can change.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States the overall requirement but not the component minimums, or cites an unofficial source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Is unsure of the requirement or confuses institutional and visa rules.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners are often under direct pressure from entry and visa requirements, so accuracy and up-to-date sources are essential; reading individual score reports against requirements is treated in tst.score-reports. Teachers should avoid giving visa advice and refer learners to official guidance and institutional advisers.
reviewNotes: Visa rules and accepted tests change; the UKVI reference is dated 2025 and content must be reviewed at each release.
No test-to-CEFR concordance is stated, by design.

records.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) describe how task characteristics shape what an assessment measures, which is why preparation should target the constructs behind task types rather than surface tricks. Washback, the influence of tests on teaching and learning, is more complex than often assumed and has to be demonstrated rather than presumed (Alderson & Wall, 1993), and Green's (2007) study of IELTS preparation documents how test-focused preparation can narrow attention to test task types. Teach formats at the level of task types and constructs, using official current sample materials and public criteria, and do not reproduce test content. Formats and timings change, so learners should check the test owner's current information.

activities.title: Construct mapping
learnerActions: Using official sample tasks, list each task type in your test
For each, write what skill or ability you think it is trying to measure
Discuss which university activities draw on the same ability
activities.intendedInsight: Each task measures something, and preparing for that ability is more useful than preparing for the task's surface.
activities.rationale: Focusing on constructs rather than task tricks reflects Bachman and Palmer's account of task characteristics and may reduce the narrowing effects of washback that Green (2007) describes.

activities.title: Criterion paraphrase
learnerActions: Find the public names of the scoring criteria for the writing or speaking tasks
Explain each criterion in your own words
Identify which criterion your recent practice responses meet least well
activities.intendedInsight: Scores for productive tasks rest on several criteria, so preparation should address all of them.
activities.rationale: Knowing the criteria directs preparation towards what is assessed; criterion names are public, but descriptor text should not be reproduced in class materials.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on unofficial templates and 'tricks' learned from preparation materials.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memorised phrases and structures; claims about secret rules for scoring.
difficulties.response: Compare the tricks with official criteria and samples, and show their limits. Do not ridicule the learner's preparation; it often reflects the market they had access to.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming all academic tests have the same format.
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparing for one test with another's materials.
difficulties.response: Compare task types across two tests at the level of constructs.

difficulties.pattern: Using outdated information about formats.
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparing for tasks or timings that no longer apply.
difficulties.response: Direct learners to the test owner's current official information.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe the speaking section of the test they will take and what it scores.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes task types accurately, names the scoring criteria and explains them.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes tasks accurately but not the criteria, or vice versa.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives an inaccurate or trick-based description.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners may be preparing for, or have recently taken, a test. Emphasise constructs and official sources, and connect test preparation to broader academic literacy development rather than replacing it. Task types, timings, delivery modes and score scales change (several major tests have been redesigned in recent years), so check the test owner's current task list before teaching any task-specific strategy, including for integrated tasks (see syn.integrated-tasks).
reviewNotes: Test formats, timings and delivery modes change; this topic deliberately avoids specific timings, item counts and named task lists.
IELTS criterion links were removed so that the topic does not imply a preferred test (R6-11).

records.summary: Moore and Morton (2005) compared IELTS Task 2 prompts with university writing assignments and found that university writing typically draws on sources and spans varied genres, whereas the test task relies on prior knowledge and opinion and more closely resembles certain public, non-academic genres. Horowitz (1986) found that university tasks mostly require selecting and reorganising material from sources. Green (2007) documents how test-focused preparation can narrow attention to test task types. Make the differences explicit so that learners can set aside test habits that do not serve them, without dismissing the test skills that transfer.

activities.title: Two-task comparison grid
learnerActions: Place a test writing prompt and a university assignment brief side by side
Compare them on length, sources, audience, genre, time and criteria
Identify which test skills transfer (for example, paragraph organisation) and which do not (for example, unsupported opinion)
activities.intendedInsight: Some test skills transfer, but university writing makes different demands, above all for using sources.
activities.rationale: The grid operationalises the dimensions of difference identified by Moore and Morton (2005).

activities.title: Template audit
learnerActions: Highlight memorised phrases and structures from test preparation in one of your recent texts
Decide for each whether it suits an academic text in your field
Replace those that do not with alternatives found in disciplinary texts
activities.intendedInsight: Phrases that score well in a test can sound formulaic or out of place in university writing.
activities.rationale: Green (2007) shows how test preparation shapes learners' language and attention; auditing makes these effects visible and revisable.

difficulties.pattern: Using memorised test templates (for example, a fixed introduction formula) in university assignments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Identical openings across assignments; formulaic linking.
difficulties.response: Compare templated and disciplinary introductions and discuss their effect on readers. Do not ban formulaic language, which has legitimate uses; ask whether each phrase does its job.

difficulties.pattern: Writing opinion without sources ('In my opinion…') in assignments that require evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unsupported claims; feedback asking for evidence.
difficulties.response: Show the function of sources in university writing and practise supporting claims with them.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting university criteria to resemble generic test criteria.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners look for criteria such as 'lexical resource' in university rubrics.
difficulties.response: Compare a test criterion list with a disciplinary rubric, and link to genre families.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What did you do in your test essay that you should not do in a university essay, and why?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific habits (opinion without sources, templates, general topics) and explains the difference in task demands.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names one difference in general terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no difference or says only that university writing is longer.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses are the main sites for this topic, and it is core on both UG- and PG-route pre-sessionals; PG-route learners compare test tasks with master's assignments in their field. In-sessional UG and PGT learners who entered directly with a test score may need it in their first weeks, especially PGT learners with only a year to adjust.
reviewNotes: Moore and Morton's study concerns IELTS; other tests include integrated, source-based tasks, so the contrast is less sharp for them.
The IELTS Task 2 link was removed because the topic contrasts test tasks with university tasks (R6-11).

records.summary: Weigle (2002) discusses alternatives to timed impromptu writing, including portfolio and process-based assessment, which allow writing to be judged under conditions closer to academic practice; many pre-sessional programmes assess progression in this way through extended writing, projects and presentations. Bachman and Palmer (2010) highlight the consequences of assessment decisions for test takers, which are particularly significant in progression. Make components, weightings, criteria, thresholds and integrity rules explicit early, and build the course around formative stages.

activities.title: Progression map
learnerActions: Using your programme handbook, list each assessed component, its weighting and its criteria
Identify how results combine into the progression decision, including any minimum per skill
Mark the formative stages before each summative submission
Compare maps with a partner and check any uncertainty with your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Progression depends on several components and thresholds, and formative stages are the opportunities to improve.
activities.rationale: Making the assessment design visible lets learners plan effort and use formative feedback, which is how portfolio and process-based assessment is intended to work (Weigle, 2002).

activities.title: Draft-to-final tracker
learnerActions: Record the feedback you receive at each formative stage
Note the action you took on each comment
Before final submission, check that every priority comment has been addressed
activities.intendedInsight: Final performance in coursework-based progression depends heavily on how formative feedback is used.
activities.rationale: Process-based assessment rewards revision; tracking actions links progression assessment to feedback literacy.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the pre-sessional as test preparation and waiting for a final exam.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low engagement with drafts; questions about when 'the test' is.
difficulties.response: Explain the coursework-based design early and show how formative stages count towards the outcome.

difficulties.pattern: Over-investing in one component and neglecting others with minimum thresholds.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong essay, weak presentation or speaking result.
difficulties.response: Review the progression map at mid-course and rebalance effort.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about what help is permitted with drafts (peers, proofreaders, translation and AI tools).
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about using translation or AI tools, proofreaders or friends' help with drafts.
difficulties.response: Make the programme's integrity rules explicit with examples of permitted and non-permitted help, and ask learners to keep notes and drafts as a record of their process. A change of style between drafts is not evidence of misconduct on its own.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'How will your progression decision be made, and what is your weakest component?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes components, weightings and thresholds accurately and has a plan for the weakest component.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows the components but not the thresholds, or names a weak component with no plan.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know how progression is decided.

records.contextNotes: This is central on pre-sessional programmes. On UG-route courses, the extended project (see ges.extended-source-based-project) is often shorter and more scaffolded, and a timed integrated task is common; on PG-route courses, learners often choose a focus in their own field and present it orally. It is also relevant to foundation and pathway programmes with similar progression arrangements, and to bridging and direct-entry programmes outside the UK. Arrangements vary considerably between institutions.
reviewNotes: Progression arrangements vary widely; institutions that accept their own pre-sessional outcomes in place of a test for immigration purposes do so under specific regulatory conditions that change.

Review response: R1-02 proposed teachingTime and assessedIn fields and a pathways layer with task anchors. These are not in the current schema (the validator rejects extra fields), so they are not added here; the description now names the typical assessed-task anchors (extended source-based project, seminar or presentation, reflective portfolio, timed integrated task) so that a pathways layer can map to them.

records.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) treat a score as evidence for a particular interpretation and use, which explains why the same report can satisfy one receiving body and not another: each institution or authority decides which tests, delivery modes, component profiles and test dates it accepts. Arkoudis et al. (2012) argue that entry standards mark the start of language development rather than its end, so test choice should also consider what the preparation will build. Rules on retakes, combined sittings, validity periods and at-home or remotely proctored versions differ between tests and receiving bodies and change often, and a visa route may set conditions different from a university's admission rules (for example, the UK Student route; UK Visas and Immigration, 2025). Teach learners to read a report against each condition and to verify every rule at source, not to memorise current rules.

activities.title: Report against requirement
learnerActions: Read a sample score report and note the overall score, each component score and the test date
Read a programme's English requirement page and list each condition (overall score, component minimums, accepted tests and delivery modes, validity, retake or combination rules)
Decide whether the report meets each condition on the programme's start date
Note which conditions you had to confirm in another official source, and which source
activities.intendedInsight: A score meets a requirement only if every condition is met, not just the overall score.
activities.rationale: A requirement is a decision rule applied to score evidence (Bachman & Palmer, 2010); checking each condition separately mirrors how receiving bodies apply it.

activities.title: Choosing a test from official sources
learnerActions: List the institutions, and any visa route, that will receive your score

For two tests you could take, collect from official pages only: acceptance by each receiving body, delivery modes, validity, retake and combination rules, cost and dates, noting the date you accessed each page
Compare the tests with your own skill profile and choose one, justifying the choice in three sentences
Check with a partner whether any part of your choice rests on an unofficial source
activities.intendedInsight: Test choice depends on what your receiving bodies accept now, which their official pages state and agents or forums may not.
activities.rationale: Score-use rules differ between receiving bodies and change; checking current official sources is more durable than learning specific rules, as visa guidance itself shows by being revised over time.

difficulties.pattern: 'My overall score is above the requirement, so I've met it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans or applications that overlook a component below the minimum.
difficulties.response: Work through profiles that pass overall but miss a component minimum, and have learners check each condition separately.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that a single-skill retake, a result combined from two sittings or an at-home version is accepted everywhere because the test owner offers it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners booking a format or retake without checking the receiving body's rules.
difficulties.response: Distinguish what a test owner offers from what each receiving body accepts, and require evidence from the receiving body's own page before booking.

difficulties.pattern: Requirement pages, agents and test owners give inconsistent or outdated information.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners citing conflicting rules, or rules that have since changed.
difficulties.response: Institutions should keep requirement pages dated, consistent and clear about which body's rule governs. Learners should record the date and source of each rule and, where sources conflict, ask the admissions office in writing before booking or submitting.

difficulties.pattern: Treating remote-proctoring and test-day rules (identity checks, room scans, no notes or second screens) as formalities.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about keeping notes nearby or using another device during an at-home test.
difficulties.response: Walk through the test owner's official candidate rules and the possible consequences, such as scores being withheld or cancelled. Learners who need adjustments (extra time, breaks, assistive technology) should request them through the test owner's process well in advance.

diagnostic.task: Give a programme requirement and a score report whose overall score meets it but which misses one component minimum and will be outside the stated validity period on the start date. Ask: 'Can this applicant use this score?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies both problems, names the official sources to check (the receiving body and the test owner) and suggests options, such as a retake if the receiving body accepts one.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Spots one problem, or spots both but would rely on an agent's advice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges by the overall score alone.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners use this when applying, when meeting conditional offers and when deciding between retesting and a longer pre-sessional; PG applicants more often hold older scores and need validity checks. Teach the process of reading and checking, and refer specific admissions or visa questions to the receiving body or qualified advisers rather than giving rules from memory. In EMI and TNE settings, local institutional tests or national examinations may stand in for international tests, so the receiving body's own list is the reference.
reviewNotes: Score-use rules (retakes, combined sittings, validity periods, accepted delivery modes) differ by test and receiving body and change often; the topic deliberately states no specific rule and should be reviewed at each release.

records.summary: Teach organisational knowledge through tasks that require it, such as finding the right contact in a real handbook or tracing how module marks feed progression, rather than through induction talks; this follows Wingate's (2006) argument that study-related knowledge is better embedded in authentic activity than delivered as decontextualised 'study skills'. Use the learner's actual or destination institution wherever possible, because titles, structures and processes vary widely. Treat comparison with previous institutions as a resource for noticing, not a ranking.

activities.title: Handbook search with consequences
learnerActions: Work in pairs with a real programme handbook and VLE site, answering scenario questions (who approves an extension; what happens if a module is failed)
Record the page or link where each answer was found
Compare answers across pairs and resolve disagreements by returning to the source or asking the programme office
Produce a one-page personal 'who to contact for what' map
activities.intendedInsight: Institutional information is distributed across documents and roles; locating it is a skill that saves time and prevents misdirected requests.
activities.rationale: Locating information in genuine institutional texts for a realistic purpose embeds orientation knowledge in use rather than presenting it as content to memorise (Wingate, 2006).

activities.title: Two systems side by side
learnerActions: Sketch how a previous school or university was organised: units, roles, who set and confirmed marks
Sketch the equivalent for the current institution from the handbook
Annotate differences that might affect help-seeking or how decisions are interpreted
Share one difference that surprised them and one prior practice that still applies
activities.intendedInsight: Structures differ, and the new one is easier to understand when prior knowledge is made explicit rather than ignored.
activities.rationale: Building explicitly on learners' existing institutional knowledge treats prior experience as a resource. This is a practice-based proposal; its effect on help-seeking has not been tested.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll email the professor about everything; they are in charge.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Administrative queries (timetables, extensions, enrolment) sent to module leaders or senior academics; slow replies and redirections.
difficulties.response: Show the division of labour between academic and professional services roles with real examples, and practise routing scenarios. Explain that routing a query correctly is seen as competent, not disrespectful. Do not present the learner's expectation as wrong in itself: in some systems academic staff do handle such matters.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that 'course', 'module', 'programme' or 'tutor' mean the same as in a previous institution or another university's materials.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion between programme and module requirements; uncertainty about who the personal tutor is or what they do.
difficulties.response: Gloss key terms from the institution's own glossary and contrast common alternative uses (for example 'course' meaning a whole degree in some systems and a single unit in others). Have learners verify terms against local documents.

difficulties.pattern: Little is retained from orientation week because everything is presented at once.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot name key contacts or processes some weeks after induction.
difficulties.response: Revisit structures at the point of need, for example just before the first deadline or the first marks release. Do not rely on a single front-loaded session.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'If you were ill during the week of an assessment deadline, what would you do and whom would you contact?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the relevant procedure (extension or extenuating circumstances), where to find it, the responsible role or office, and the likely evidence required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows to contact someone but names a general or senior academic and does not mention a procedure.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would wait until after the deadline, would contact nobody, or does not know that a procedure exists.

records.contextNotes: On foundation programmes, orientation is broad and revisited at points of need. Pre-sessional courses can use the destination institution's documents so that learners arrive informed; postgraduate entrants often know one system well and benefit from explicit comparison. In-sessional UG and PGT work revisits specific processes (progression, extensions, representation) as they arise, early for one-year PGT programmes. In TNE programmes, learners need to tell local campus structures apart from the awarding institution's regulations and boards; in EMI programmes, some governance documents may exist only in the local language. Part-time, mature and commuting students may miss induction events, so information should also be available asynchronously.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography researches the teaching of institutional structures directly; this guidance is practice-based and should be checked against local induction evaluations.

Review response (R1-06): pgr removed. Doctoral researchers' orientation to graduate school structures, supervisory teams and progression reviews is covered by res.supervision and acu.hidden-curriculum.

records.summary: Ferris and Tagg (1996) found that subject instructors' oral requirements vary with discipline, class size and level, and Biber (2006) documents distinct language across university registers including classroom teaching, labs, office hours and study groups. Teaching should therefore move from a generic lecture/seminar contrast to the learner's actual timetable and clarify what preparation and participation each format assumes. Blended provision and lecture capture (Lynch, 2011) add decisions about how to use VLE materials alongside attendance.

activities.title: Timetable decoding
learnerActions: List each session type in one week of their own or a sample timetable
Predict each session's purpose and what students do before, during and after it
Check predictions against module VLE pages or by asking a current student or tutor
Revise a personal weekly plan to include preparation and follow-up for each session
activities.intendedInsight: Each format implies different preparation and participation, and contact hours are only part of the workload.
activities.rationale: Starting from the learner's real timetable ties format knowledge to immediate action; expectations vary across disciplines and classes (Ferris & Tagg, 1996).

activities.title: Who talks, and how?
learnerActions: Watch a recorded lecture extract and a seminar or tutorial extract from the same discipline
Note who talks, for how long, and what kinds of contribution are made
Compare the language of the two (extended explanation versus questions, responses and building on others)
Discuss what a student would need to do to participate well in each
activities.intendedInsight: Formats differ in interaction patterns and language, not only in size.
activities.rationale: Comparing spoken university registers makes their structural and linguistic differences noticeable (Biber, 2006).

difficulties.pattern: 'The lecture is where the real learning happens; the seminar is optional discussion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Missed or unprepared seminar attendance; surprise at participation-related marks or comments.
difficulties.response: Show how seminars and tutorials relate to the specific module's outcomes and assessment, and make preparation tasks explicit. Avoid implying that lecture-centred prior schooling was inferior; it was organised around different assumptions.

difficulties.pattern: Equating timetabled contact hours with the whole workload.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weekly plans with no time for reading or assignment work; reports of being overwhelmed mid-term.
difficulties.response: Have learners estimate notional study hours from credit values using the conventions of their target context (for example, one UK credit commonly represents about ten notional hours and one ECTS credit about 25–30) and distribute them across the week.

difficulties.pattern: Treating recorded lectures as a full substitute for attending.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low attendance combined with passive or postponed viewing of recordings.
difficulties.response: Discuss what live sessions offer (questions, interaction, peer contact) and how recordings can be used for targeted review. Recognise that for some disabled, commuting, working or caring students recordings are a legitimate primary mode of access. Do not moralise about attendance; focus on effective use.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would prepare differently for a lecture, a seminar and a lab session in the same week.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes previewing for the lecture, preparing positions and questions for the seminar, and reading the protocol and safety information for the lab, and mentions follow-up work.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises differences in size or setting but describes the same preparation for each.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no need for preparation beyond attending.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit most, particularly where prior schooling was organised differently; pre-sessional PG work should stress the shift to seminar-based teaching and independent study. In-sessional UG work can address discipline-specific formats such as studios, crits or clinical skills labs. PGT students meet compressed timetables and more seminar-based teaching and need early re-orientation. In many EMI programmes, large lecture classes dominate and seminar culture is limited, so lecture listening and self-directed study matter more than discussion formats; online and distance learners need the same analysis applied to synchronous and asynchronous VLE formats.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-25, R3-01): removed the soft edge from acu.university-structures and the soft edge from this topic to acu.academic-expectations, so that orientation topics no longer chain into language and critical-thinking topics. Recommended for the owning groups: remove voc.university-terminology <- acu.teaching-formats (the two are taught together, not in sequence) and reconsider lis.lecture-structure <- acu.teaching-formats, since knowing what lectures are for is not a prerequisite for recognising their structure.

records.summary: Expectations such as independence, criticality and participation are usually stated abstractly and treated as self-evident; teaching should translate them into concrete practices in specific modules (Wingate, 2015). Present them as situated institutional practices rather than personal or cultural traits: Atkinson (1997) argued that critical thinking is a socially embedded practice, and Leki and Carson (1997) found that students experienced EAP writing and subject-course writing as making quite different demands, especially about accountability to source content. Many learners already practise criticality and independence in forms that a new context may not recognise.

activities.title: From outcome to action
learnerActions: Take one learning outcome or graduate attribute (for example 'demonstrate independent critical judgement')
List what a student would observably do in this module to meet it
Compare lists with peers and with a tutor's interpretation or a high-graded exemplar
Choose one action to adopt in the coming week and report back
activities.intendedInsight: Abstract expectations become manageable when translated into specific practices that can be checked.
activities.rationale: Making expectations explicit and concrete is central to inclusive approaches to academic literacy (Wingate, 2015).

activities.title: Two task briefs compared
learnerActions: Read two short task briefs, one from an EAP course and one from a subject module
Identify what each expects regarding source use, personal opinion and independence
Discuss where the expectations differ and why
Note what this implies for transferring EAP practice to their subject
activities.intendedInsight: Expectations vary across courses even within one institution, so transfer has to be checked rather than assumed.
activities.rationale: Leki and Carson (1997) found differences between EAP and subject writing demands, particularly in how far writing had to be accountable to source texts.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means finding something wrong with what I read.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Unsupported negative evaluations, or summaries that report sources without any evaluation.
difficulties.response: Model criticality as judging claims against evidence and purpose, including recognising strengths, using discipline-specific examples. Do not attribute either pattern to a learner's national or cultural background.

difficulties.pattern: 'Independent study means I should not ask for help.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners struggle without asking, skip office hours and avoid clarification questions.
difficulties.response: Present help-seeking (office hours, feedback requests, support services) as part of independent learning, and normalise it with accounts from current students.

difficulties.pattern: Expectations expressed as traits ('be proactive', 'show initiative') produce anxiety rather than action.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report feeling they are failing vague standards and cannot say what to change.
difficulties.response: Break each expectation into small, observable steps. Avoid presenting expectations as tests of personality or as signs of fitting in.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your module handbook says students should be independent learners. What will you do this week that shows that?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives specific actions tied to the module, such as following up a reference from the lecture, preparing seminar questions, or scheduling reading hours.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives general intentions such as 'study more' or 'read widely'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Interprets independence as working alone without guidance, or cannot answer.

records.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need expectations made concrete across the board, with explicit attention to what changes at postgraduate level on pre-sessional PG courses. In-sessional UG work should connect to specific modules and levels, since first-year and final-year expectations differ; first-generation and mature students may meet these expectations for the first time alongside international students. PGT students face greater autonomy within compressed timelines. In EMI programmes, stated expectations may come from an international policy while teaching remains lecture-based, so learners need to read what is actually rewarded. Doctoral expectations are handled under acu.hidden-curriculum and res.supervision.
reviewNotes: This topic overlaps with lrn.independent-study and crt.concept; cross-reference rather than duplicate content.

Review response (R1-06): pgr removed; doctoral expectations of independence are covered by acu.hidden-curriculum and res.supervision. The soft edge from acu.teaching-formats was removed (R1-25), so the topic is now an entry point.

records.summary: Swales (1990) characterised a discourse community by shared public goals, mechanisms of intercommunication, participatory use of those mechanisms, owned genres, specific lexis and a threshold of expert members, and Hyland (2004) shows how disciplinary communities are realised in members' textual choices. Teach the concept through learners' own fields and present membership as developing through participation (Duff, 2010). Johns (1997) stresses that students move between several communities with different demands, so the concept is most useful as a heuristic rather than a fixed taxonomy.

activities.title: Profile your community
learnerActions: Use Swales's criteria as prompts to profile their target discipline
Find a concrete example for each criterion (a genre, a channel, a specialist term, a gatekeeper)
Present the profile to peers from other fields
Identify similarities and differences across the profiles
activities.intendedInsight: Academic conventions serve particular communities and vary between them.
activities.rationale: Applying Swales's (1990) criteria to a familiar field turns an abstract concept into a reusable analytic tool.

activities.title: Membership trajectories
learnerActions: Interview, or read an account by, a more advanced student or academic in their field about how they learned its practices
Identify turning points in that person's participation
Map their own current position and plausible next steps
Reflect on what helps or hinders newcomers' participation
activities.intendedInsight: Membership is achieved through participation over time, not conferred by enrolment.
activities.rationale: Language socialisation research shows newcomers learning academic discourse through interaction with more expert members (Duff, 2010).

difficulties.pattern: 'Academic English is one set of rules for everyone.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Advice from one field (for example about first-person use or passive voice) applied universally.
difficulties.response: Contrast short texts from different fields to show disciplinary variation in textual features (Hyland, 2004), and ask learners to collect evidence from their own field.

difficulties.pattern: Seeing the community as a closed club that one either belongs to or not.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners describe themselves as outsiders without a legitimate voice and hold back contributions.
difficulties.response: Present peripheral participation as legitimate and emphasise internal variation and debate within communities. Avoid implying that newcomers must wait for full membership before contributing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to name two genres in their field and explain what each does for the community.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names field-specific genres (for example a case report or a design brief) and links each to a community purpose.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names generic genres (essay, article) with vague purposes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot name genres beyond the essay or relate any genre to a purpose.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce the concept through mixed-discipline groups comparing fields. In-sessional UG and PGT work applies it to the learner's own discipline, ideally with subject input. For PGR, the focus is the research community of a specialism (journals, conferences, networks) and the researcher's developing role in it.
reviewNotes: Swales's later revisions of the discourse community concept are not in the closed bibliography; the 1990 criteria are presented as a heuristic, and the description acknowledges internal diversity and contested boundaries.
Recommended for the GES group (R1-28): add ges.genre-concept <- acu.discourse-communities (hard), now that ges.genre-concept has been narrowed to genre and leaves discourse community to this topic.

records.summary: Biglan's (1973) dimensions (hard/soft, pure/applied, life/non-life) and Becher and Trowler's (2001) account of disciplinary 'tribes and territories' give learners a vocabulary for epistemological difference, and Hyland (2004) shows how such differences surface in citation, hedging and self-mention. Use the typologies heuristically and invite critique, since interdisciplinary and professional fields often fit poorly. Threshold concepts (Meyer & Land, 2005) help learners name the troublesome ways of thinking that mark entry to a discipline, and Maton's (2013) semantic waves offer a lens on how disciplinary texts move between abstract theory and concrete cases.

activities.title: Same topic, two disciplines
learnerActions: Read two short extracts on one topic (for example obesity) from contrasting disciplines
Identify what evidence each uses and how claims are justified
Locate textual features that signal certainty, attribution and author presence
Explain the differences with reference to each field's knowledge-making
activities.intendedInsight: Textual conventions follow from how fields build and warrant knowledge.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2004) links disciplinary differences in textual features to underlying epistemological and social practices.

activities.title: Placing your field
learnerActions: Place their field on Biglan's dimensions and discuss the placement with peers
Identify where the typology fits poorly, such as interdisciplinary or practice-based fields
Name a concept in their field that was difficult and changed how they saw the subject
Discuss what that concept implies for how they should read and write in the field
activities.intendedInsight: Typologies are useful starting points but must be tested against one's own field.
activities.rationale: Biglan (1973) and Becher and Trowler (2001) offer comparative frames, and the threshold concepts framework (Meyer & Land, 2005) gives learners language for disciplinary ways of thinking.

difficulties.pattern: 'Science is objective; the humanities are just opinion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissal of interpretive argument; treating numbers as proof in themselves.
difficulties.response: Show that every field has standards of warrant, illustrate interpretive rigour with examples, and show uncertainty and argument in scientific writing.

difficulties.pattern: Forcing an interdisciplinary or professional programme into a single typology category.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot classify their field or produce strained classifications.
difficulties.response: Treat typologies as heuristics and ask learners to analyse actual texts and assessments from their programme instead.

difficulties.pattern: Carrying the conventions of a first-degree discipline unchanged into a new field at master's level.
difficulties.revealedBy: PGT students changing field reproduce genres and argument styles from their previous discipline.
difficulties.response: Compare old and new fields' expectations explicitly in the first weeks, using assessed genres from the new programme.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In your field, how would you convince a sceptical colleague that a claim is true?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the field's typical evidence and reasoning (for example replication, archival interpretation, case analysis) and acknowledges their limits.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a general answer ('use evidence', 'cite sources') without field specificity.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot describe how claims are justified, or appeals only to authority.

records.contextNotes: In pre-sessional courses for postgraduates, comparison across mixed-discipline groups works well. In-sessional UG support should tie this to the learner's modules. PGT students changing field need explicit comparison of the old and new disciplines. For PGR, it connects to methodology, theoretical frameworks and positioning within debates.
reviewNotes: Biglan's typology derives from 1970s US academics' judgements of subject similarity; present it as a heuristic for contemporary and interdisciplinary fields.

Specificity changed from ESAP (listed only for the sciences) to EGAP: the topic compares knowledge-making across disciplines and is usually taught to mixed-discipline groups; discipline-specific epistemology is handled in the Disciplinary Literacies strand.

records.summary: Lea and Street (1998) found that tutors and students held different, unarticulated understandings of terms such as 'argument' and 'structure', and Lillis (2001) described the resulting 'institutional practice of mystery', which particularly disadvantages students unfamiliar with essayist conventions. Teaching should surface tacit expectations through exemplars, analysis of feedback and dialogue with subject staff, and ideally prompt the institution to state its expectations more clearly (Wingate, 2015; Bond, 2020). Learners also need strategies for uncovering expectations themselves, not just a list of rules.

activities.title: Feedback lexicon
learnerActions: Collect anonymised feedback comments (their own or supplied) and highlight evaluative terms
Group the terms and hypothesise what each means in practice
Test the hypotheses against marked exemplars at different grades
Formulate questions to ask a tutor about any remaining ambiguity
activities.intendedInsight: Feedback language encodes tacit expectations that can be partly decoded, and some ambiguity can only be resolved by asking.
activities.rationale: Lea and Street (1998) found that feedback terms were interpreted differently by tutors and students; making the terms an object of study addresses that gap directly.

activities.title: Unwritten rules from exemplars
learnerActions: Compare two anonymised assignments on the same task that received different grades
List differences that the published criteria do not mention
Write these as explicit 'unwritten rules'
Check the list with a subject tutor or against further exemplars
activities.intendedInsight: Some valued features are absent from the written criteria but can be inferred and then checked.
activities.rationale: Comparing exemplars to make implicit criteria explicit is consistent with inclusive approaches to academic literacy instruction (Wingate, 2015).

difficulties.pattern: 'If I just improve my grammar, my marks will go up.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Low marks attributed to language when feedback actually concerns argument, structure or use of sources.
difficulties.response: Sort feedback comments into categories (language, argument, sources, task fulfilment) and show that many concern genre and disciplinary expectations. Acknowledge genuine language concerns while widening the frame; avoid reinforcing the belief that all difficulty is linguistic.

difficulties.pattern: 'My tutor said this once, so all tutors want it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Rigid application of one tutor's preferences (for example about headings or first-person use) across modules.
difficulties.response: Show variation between tutors and modules with real examples, and teach learners to check expectations for each module rather than treating any one preference as universal.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to ask a tutor what a comment means, for fear of seeming incapable or disrespectful.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback not acted on; no clarification requests even when comments are ambiguous.
difficulties.response: Model and rehearse brief, specific clarification requests, and present asking as expected practice. Link this to office-hours and email work.

difficulties.pattern: Criteria and feedback use evaluative terms that markers themselves interpret differently, so the same choice is praised by one tutor and criticised by another.
difficulties.revealedBy: Contradictory feedback across modules or markers on the same feature; learners conclude that marking is arbitrary.
difficulties.response: With subject staff, build a shared glossary of evaluative terms illustrated with annotated exemplars, and raise inconsistencies through module teams rather than leaving students to reconcile them. Show learners how to ask a module leader which interpretation applies.

diagnostic.task: Give the comment 'This is too descriptive' with the paragraph it refers to, and ask what the tutor wants.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Recognises that the paragraph reports without interpreting or evaluating, proposes adding analysis, significance or comparison, and notes the option of confirming with the tutor.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Suggests adding more sources or detail, which would increase description.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the comment as a language error or cannot interpret it.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, focus on decoding task and feedback language. In-sessional UG work is most effective when co-designed with subject staff, and serves first-generation, mature and returning home students as well as international students, since tacit expectations follow prior schooling and family experience rather than nationality. PGT students meet new disciplinary norms quickly and benefit from exemplar analysis in the first weeks. For PGR, tacit expectations concern supervision, progression reviews, thesis conventions and the viva, and can vary between supervisors and examiners; this is the main PGR entry to the domain. In TNE programmes, tacit expectations may differ between local tutors and the awarding institution's moderators.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-06): pgr kept because doctoral tacit expectations (supervision, progression reviews, the viva) differ materially from taught-programme expectations.

Recommended for the FBK group (R5-02, so that socialisation topics feed later work): add fbk.marking-criteria <- acu.hidden-curriculum (soft) and fbk.feedback-literacy <- acu.hidden-curriculum (soft), since both build on recognising that criteria and feedback carry unstated expectations.

records.summary: This record is a teacher-facing principle. Lea and Street (1998) distinguished study skills, academic socialisation and academic literacies models of student writing, the last treating literacy as social practice involving identity, power and institutional epistemologies. Ivanič (1998) and Lillis (2001), whose studies were largely with mature and non-traditional home students, show how writers' identities and desires are at stake in academic writing, and Lillis and Scott (2007) characterise the approach as transformative rather than normative. In teaching, the principle supports dialogue about meaning-making; Wingate (2012) argues that it can be combined with genre-based instruction so that critique does not leave students without access to valued forms.

activities.title: Three lenses on one difficulty
learnerActions: Read a short case of a student repeatedly told their work 'lacks argument'
Explain the difficulty through a study skills lens, a socialisation lens and an academic literacies lens
Discuss what support each lens would recommend and who is expected to change
Decide what combination would help the student most
activities.intendedInsight: How a difficulty is explained shapes what support is offered and where responsibility is placed.
activities.rationale: Lea and Street's (1998) three models give a clear frame for comparing explanations of student writing difficulties.

activities.title: Writing and identity talkback
learnerActions: Choose a passage of their own writing where the voice felt constrained, or a published account by another writer if they prefer not to use their own
Describe the identity the writer wanted to project and the conventions that pulled against it
Discuss with a peer or tutor how the tension might be negotiated
Revise the passage, or propose a revision, and reflect on the outcome
activities.intendedInsight: Writers make identity choices within conventions, and those choices can be discussed and negotiated.
activities.rationale: Ivanič (1998) shows that academic writing constructs writer identity, and Lillis (2001) argues for dialogic 'talkback' about meaning-making rather than one-way feedback.

difficulties.pattern: 'This means I don't have to follow the conventions.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback dismissed as mere institutional power; conventions ignored without a considered rationale.
difficulties.response: Distinguish understanding conventions as contingent from ignoring them, discuss consequences, and pair the perspective with explicit teaching of valued genres (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: The perspective is felt to be abstract theory irrelevant to getting good marks.
