activities.intendedInsight: Goals describe what will change for the patient, and must be measurable so that evaluation is possible.
activities.rationale: Goal-writing is where the logic of a plan most often breaks; making the outcome orientation explicit connects each goal to its evaluation and to the case-study purpose of applying knowledge to a particular patient.

activities.title: Linking need to intervention
learnerActions: Read a care plan with goals and interventions but no rationales
Add an evidence-based rationale for each intervention, citing a source or guideline
Write an evaluation criterion for each goal and check that it measures the goal as worded
activities.intendedInsight: A care plan is an argument from assessed need to intervention to evaluation, and every link needs justification.
activities.rationale: Making rationales explicit connects care planning to evidence-based practice, in which interventions are justified by evidence, expertise and the patient’s circumstances.

difficulties.pattern: Writing goals as things the nurse will do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Goals such as 'to monitor blood pressure', and evaluation sections that report actions taken rather than outcomes achieved.
difficulties.response: Use the tasks-or-outcomes activity and a sentence frame for patient-centred goals. Do not simply give a SMART acronym; check that each goal can actually be evaluated.

difficulties.pattern: Using a care-plan format or abbreviations from a previous hospital, country or textbook.
difficulties.revealedBy: Templates, headings or abbreviations that do not match the programme's model or the local approved list.
difficulties.response: Treat the programme's model and approved-abbreviation list as the reference, and discuss differences from learners' previous practice as professional variation, not error.

difficulties.pattern: Labelling the patient by their condition or behaviour ('the diabetic', 'non-compliant').
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback on language that is not person-centred, often in otherwise sound plans.
difficulties.response: Teach person-centred alternatives and the reasons for them, following the programme's guidance, and note that preferred terms differ between communities and change over time.

diagnostic.task: Give an assessment summary and a care-plan row with a weak goal and no rationale, and ask the learner to improve it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Rewrites the goal as a measurable patient outcome with a timescale, adds an evidenced rationale and an evaluation criterion that matches the goal.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves the goal but leaves the rationale generic, or writes an evaluation that does not measure the goal.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Changes wording only, leaving a task-based goal and no rationale.

records.contextNotes: UG nursing students write care plans from the first year, often within case-study assignments and alongside placement documentation; embed support with clinical educators and the programme’s template. On pre-registration master’s programmes and some advanced-practice modules, care planning is assessed with more emphasis on evidence, risk and interprofessional context. Documentation standards and nursing models differ between countries and institutions, so learners who trained elsewhere may bring a different but valid model.
reviewNotes: Nursing models (for example activities-of-living models) and documentation standards vary by programme and country; no specific model is cited, and teachers should use the programme’s own.
Care plans in clinical records follow legal and organisational documentation rules that differ from those of academic care-planning assignments.

records.summary: Nathan's (2013) genre analysis of the business case report describes a problem-oriented structure that differs from the essay: the writer identifies a problem, analyses it, evaluates alternatives and makes recommendations for an organisational reader. Zhu (2004) found that business courses assign a range of such case-based and professional tasks requiring skills beyond the essay. Teaching should start from exemplars and briefs in the student's own school, because schools vary in how far they expect headings, theory and personal recommendation, and should involve subject staff in setting and reviewing tasks.

activities.title: Problem or symptom?
learnerActions: Read a short case and list everything that is going wrong
Sort the list into symptoms and underlying problems, using arrows to show which causes which
Write a one-sentence problem statement and compare it with other groups
activities.intendedInsight: A strong case analysis is built on a well-defined problem, which is usually a cause rather than the most visible symptom.
activities.rationale: Problem identification is the opening move of the business case report as described by Nathan, and sorting symptoms from causes makes that move explicit.

activities.title: Options against criteria
learnerActions: Generate three options for the problem identified
Agree four criteria (for example cost, time, risk, strategic fit) and score each option in a decision matrix
Write the evaluation and recommendation section from the matrix, then compare with a high-scoring exemplar
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations are persuasive when they follow visibly from an evaluation against criteria.
activities.rationale: Making evaluation criteria explicit supports the option-evaluation and recommendation stages that distinguish case reports from discussion essays.

difficulties.pattern: Retelling the case in detail before any analysis, as if the marker had not read it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Case reports in which a third or more of the word count summarises the case narrative.
difficulties.response: Clarify that the reader knows the case and wants analysis. Set a strict limit for background and show exemplars. Do not ban background entirely; a short framing of the problem is expected.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations that do not follow from the analysis, or that are generic (improve marketing, train staff).
difficulties.revealedBy: Recommendation sections that introduce new ideas or could apply to any company.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to link each recommendation to a numbered finding and to add who, what, when and cost. Use the decision matrix to make the link visible.

diagnostic.task: Give a one-page case and ask for an outline of a case report: problem statement, three analytic points with evidence, two options and a recommendation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines a causal problem, supports analysis with case data, evaluates options against criteria and recommends one with implementation notes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a problem and recommends a solution but the analysis is a list of facts or the options are not evaluated.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the case and offers general opinions.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional business pathways, use short cases and contrast the case report with the essay; UG entrants need the basic problem–analysis–recommendation pattern, while PG entrants should practise it under time pressure. In UG in-sessional work, use the module’s own case and brief. PGT students on intensive programmes meet many cases quickly, so focus on efficient problem definition and recommendation writing.
reviewNotes: The overlap with grp.case-study is handled by treating that topic as the general genre and this one as its business-school realisation.

records.summary: McCloskey (1998) argued that economics is rhetorical: it persuades through models, metaphors and stylised assumptions as well as through data, which makes the language of models a legitimate object of teaching. For learners, the key resources are conditional and ceteris paribus structures, comparative statics, the precise description of diagrams and the positive–normative distinction. Because economics varies from highly mathematical to more discursive (for example in political economy), the teacher should check with lecturers which kind of writing the module expects.

activities.title: Holding everything else constant
learnerActions: Read three short predictions from an economics textbook and underline the assumptions, conditions and ceteris paribus clauses
Rewrite each prediction without its assumptions and discuss what claim it now makes
Write your own prediction about a change in one variable, stating assumptions explicitly
activities.intendedInsight: Economic predictions are conditional on stated assumptions, and dropping them changes the claim.
activities.rationale: Making the assumptions and conditions of model-based argument explicit reflects McCloskey's account of economic reasoning as built from models with stylised assumptions.

activities.title: Diagram to prose
learnerActions: Work in pairs: one student describes a change in a supply-and-demand or cost diagram while the other draws it without seeing the original
Compare drawings and identify which words caused errors (shift, movement along, increase in demand, increase in quantity demanded)
Write a short paragraph explaining the change and its effect on equilibrium
activities.intendedInsight: Precise distinctions such as shift versus movement along encode different economic events.
activities.rationale: Information-gap description exposes ambiguity in the learner's language through a listener's misunderstanding.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing normative judgements into positive analysis ('The government should not tax this because demand will fall').
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers to explain-type questions that drift into opinion, with feedback about relevance or objectivity.
difficulties.response: Classify sentences as positive or normative and discuss where each belongs in an answer. Normative argument is legitimate when the question asks for evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Treating model predictions as unconditional facts about the real economy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'Price will rise' with no assumptions or conditions, or confusion when real data diverge from the model.
difficulties.response: Have learners add the assumptions and conditions to each prediction and discuss what happens when they do not hold.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'cause' or 'lead to' for relationships found only in correlational data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Empirical essays that overclaim causation from regression results or descriptive statistics.
difficulties.response: Contrast sentences that report association and causation, and connect this to what research designs can support.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in writing the effect of a fall in consumer income on the market for a normal good, using a diagram.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the assumption of a normal good, shows a shift of the demand curve, explains the effects on price and quantity with ceteris paribus, and avoids normative comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the correct direction of change but confuses shift and movement along, or omits conditions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a general opinion about recession without model-based reasoning.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional economics pathways, focus on basic model language and diagram description for UG entrants and on reading empirical economics for PG entrants. In UG in-sessional work, link the topic to essay and exam answers. At PGT, the emphasis shifts to empirical claims, econometric reporting and the hedging of causal claims.
reviewNotes: ESP research on economics discourse could support this topic further; the guidance currently draws mainly on McCloskey (1998) and general work on causal and conditional language.

records.summary: Bhatia (1993) shows how professional genres such as promotional and business letters are shaped by communicative purpose and by the relationship between writer and reader, and Zhu (2004) found that business courses assign memos, letters, reports and similar tasks that mimic workplace writing. Teaching should therefore contrast these genres with the essay: the main point first, organisation for a decision-maker, and tone fitted to role relationships. Because company and school templates differ, learners should analyse the specific brief, template and exemplars.

activities.title: Essay to memo
learnerActions: Read a short academic answer to a business question
Identify the recommendation and the two strongest reasons
Rewrite the content as a memo to a named manager, with the recommendation in the first sentence, and compare tone across the class
activities.intendedInsight: The same content is reorganised and re-voiced when the reader changes from marker to decision-maker.
activities.rationale: Rewriting across genres highlights how purpose and reader shape structure, as genre analysis of professional writing predicts.

activities.title: Pitch in three minutes
learnerActions: Analyse a recorded or transcribed pitch for its stages (problem, solution, benefits, evidence, request)
Plan a three-minute pitch for a product or project from your module using the same stages
Deliver the pitch and receive peer feedback on clarity of the request and evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A pitch is a persuasive genre with a predictable structure that ends in a specific request.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of a model before production applies genre pedagogy to a spoken professional genre that business schools assess.

difficulties.pattern: Writing memos and briefing notes as essays, with background first and the recommendation in the last paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memos marked down for structure or for burying the main point.
difficulties.response: Contrast reader needs in each genre and practise front-loading. Do not suggest that the essay structure is wrong; it suits a different purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Being very indirect or very blunt with a senior reader in a simulated workplace task.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memos that are either heavily mitigated and unclear or directive in a way that suits a superior rather than a subordinate.
difficulties.response: Discuss the role relationship in the brief and model wording at different levels of directness. Treat expectations as local business conventions, not universal norms.

diagnostic.task: Give a 300-word essay paragraph on a business issue and ask for a 120-word memo to a line manager recommending action.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Opens with purpose and recommendation, gives concise reasons, closes with a next step, and uses a tone suitable for a manager.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Shortens the text but keeps the essay order or an unsuitable tone.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the paragraph without a clear recommendation or reader orientation.

records.contextNotes: UG business students meet these genres in modules on management and communication. PGT students, especially on MBA-type programmes, are often assessed through reports, pitches and briefing papers, and some will already know workplace conventions from experience that may differ from the school's expectations.
reviewNotes: 'Bottom line up front' ordering is a widely taught convention, but expectations vary between organisations, sectors and countries; it is presented as typical for assessed business-school memos.

Review response (R1-34): the topic is kept as one topic for memos, briefing notes, management reports and pitches, which share a reader-first, decision-oriented logic and are usually taught together; the consultancy report and accounting and finance genres are now separate topics (dbe.consultancy-report, dbe.accounting-finance-discourse).

records.summary: Management frameworks are useful prompts, but Hill and Westbrook (1997), studying SWOT use in companies, found that outputs tended to be long, unprioritised lists that were rarely used in later strategy work. That is the same pattern markers criticise in student work. Teaching should frame each framework as a means to an analytic end: select, evidence, prioritise and draw implications. Nathan (2013) shows that the analysis stage of the business case report is where such frameworks are expected to do this work.

activities.title: From list to analysis
learnerActions: Take an unprioritised SWOT or PESTLE table for a familiar company
Delete factors that lack evidence and rank the remainder by likely impact
Write a paragraph on the two most significant factors, explaining their implications and how internal and external factors interact
activities.intendedInsight: A framework produces analysis only when its contents are evidenced, prioritised and connected to a decision.
activities.rationale: Hill and Westbrook's finding that SWOT outputs are rarely prioritised or used shows why the move from list to implication is the teaching target.

activities.title: Choosing the right tool
learnerActions: Read three short case questions (for example entering a new market, improving internal efficiency, responding to a new competitor)
Decide which framework fits each question best and why
Write one sentence for each acknowledging what the chosen framework cannot capture
activities.intendedInsight: Frameworks answer different questions, and choosing one is itself an analytical decision with limitations.
activities.rationale: Justifying framework choice and limits reflects the evaluative use of frameworks expected in the analysis stage of case reports.

difficulties.pattern: Including every framework taught in the module to show knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports with several framework tables but little analysis, and feedback such as 'descriptive' or 'lacks depth'.
difficulties.response: Show markers' criteria and high-scoring exemplars that use one or two frameworks in depth. Discuss depth versus breadth.

difficulties.pattern: Listing factors as bullet points without evidence or implications.
difficulties.revealedBy: Framework tables with generic entries that could apply to any company.
difficulties.response: Require each factor to have a piece of evidence from the case and a 'so what' sentence. Avoid simply asking for more factors.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 150-word PESTLE-based paragraph on one external factor affecting a company described in a short case.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects a significant factor, supports it with case evidence and explains its implication for the company's decision.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a relevant factor but gives generic evidence or no implication.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists several PESTLE categories with one-line entries and no analysis.

records.contextNotes: Pre-sessional business pathways should introduce the analytical use of frameworks early, with short cases. UG students meet many frameworks across modules and need help to use them selectively. PGT management students, some of whom have used frameworks at work, are assessed heavily on them and need to adjust to academic expectations of critique, evidence and prioritisation.

records.summary: Accounting and finance students write about numbers for readers who will act on them: investors, managers, auditors or lenders. Zhu (2004) found that business-course assignments often simulate professional genres written for business readers, and the commentary genres of finance follow the general pattern of data commentary while adding evaluation of performance and hedged projection. Corporate narratives are a reading as well as a writing challenge: research on impression management (Merkl-Davies & Brennan, 2007) shows that narrative disclosures can present results selectively and favourably, so students need to test evaluative claims against the figures. Appraisal theory (Martin & White, 2005) gives teachers tools for showing how evaluation is built into apparently neutral financial prose.

activities.title: From figures to judgement
learnerActions: Read a table of two years’ results and write three sentences that only describe changes
Add a sentence to each that explains a likely driver, hedged appropriately
Add a final sentence evaluating what the results mean for a named reader, such as a lender or shareholder
activities.intendedInsight: Financial commentary moves from accurate description to explanation and evaluation for a particular user.
activities.rationale: Commentary that only restates figures is a frequent criticism; building the explanation and evaluation layers separately makes the expected moves visible and keeps the professional reader in view.

activities.title: Testing the narrative
learnerActions: Highlight the evaluative words in a chair's or chief executive's statement (for example strong, resilient, challenging)
Check each evaluative claim against the financial statements and note whether the figures support it
Rewrite one paragraph as a neutral analyst's commentary
activities.intendedInsight: Corporate narratives evaluate as well as inform, and an analyst's commentary tests those evaluations against evidence.
activities.rationale: Research on impression management in corporate narratives, and appraisal analysis of evaluative language, both suggest that critical reading of disclosure language is a distinct skill worth teaching.

difficulties.pattern: Listing every figure and change without saying which ones matter.
difficulties.revealedBy: Commentaries that restate tables line by line, with feedback asking for analysis.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to choose the three most significant changes for the named reader and to justify the choice. Do not simply ask for more ratios.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing percentage and percentage-point change, or stating forecasts as facts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Numerical errors in commentary and unhedged statements such as 'the share price will rise'.
difficulties.response: Use short accuracy drills with real figures and a checklist of the assumptions behind every forecast.

difficulties.pattern: The terms I learned in my previous accounting course are different here.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixed terminology (for example turnover and revenue, stock and inventory) and uncertainty about which reporting framework a module assumes.
difficulties.response: Treat terminology from other frameworks and varieties as a resource and build a comparison glossary. Module teams should state which reporting framework and terminology an assignment assumes, since briefs often leave this implicit.

diagnostic.task: Give a small table of results and ask for a three-sentence commentary for a shareholder.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects the most significant change, reports it accurately, explains a plausible driver with a hedge and evaluates the implication for the shareholder.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reports changes accurately but only describes them, or evaluates without supporting figures.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates figures without selection, or makes errors in calculating or describing changes.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional pathways for finance and accounting master’s programmes, introduce the commentary pattern and accurate number language using real annual reports. UG accounting and finance students meet these genres in financial reporting, analysis and audit modules alongside numerical examinations. On MSc Finance and Accounting programmes, which recruit large international cohorts, commentary, valuation reports and analyses of disclosures are central to coursework and dissertations, and some students already hold professional qualifications whose terminology differs from the module’s.
reviewNotes: Reporting frameworks (for example IFRS and national standards) and terminology differ between jurisdictions; teachers should confirm which the programme uses.
The EAP research base on student accounting and finance writing is small; the guidance draws on business-writing and corporate-disclosure research and should be checked against local exemplars.

records.summary: Consultancy projects, live or simulated, are now common capstones on business master’s programmes and some UG degrees, and they combine a professional report genre with academic assessment. Nathan (2013) shows that the business case report is problem- and decision-oriented, and the consultancy report extends this to a real reader whose priorities, vocabulary and time shape the text. Bhatia’s (1993) analysis of professional genres supports teaching the report through its communicative purpose and readers, and Zhu (2004) shows that business-course assignments draw on professional as well as academic conventions. The main teaching challenge is the dual readership: what persuades a client and what earns marks are related but not identical.

activities.title: Two readers, one recommendation
learnerActions: Take one recommendation from a project and write it twice: once for the client's managing director and once for the module marker
Compare length, order, terminology and the role of theory and citation in the two versions
Agree as a team where each version belongs in the submission
activities.intendedInsight: The client wants actionable advice; the marker wants to see how analysis and theory support it.
activities.rationale: Contrasting the same content for two readers makes the genre’s dual purpose explicit, in line with genre analysis that starts from communicative purpose.

activities.title: Making recommendations actionable
learnerActions: Review the recommendations in a past or draft report
Add who, what, when, cost and risk to each recommendation
Rank the recommendations by impact and feasibility and justify the order in one sentence each
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations are judged on feasibility and priority as well as on their link to evidence.
activities.rationale: Business case reports are judged on recommendations that follow from the analysis and can be implemented; adding implementation detail tests both.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the client report like an academic essay, with theory first and recommendations at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Client feedback that the report is hard to use, and long literature sections in client-facing text.
difficulties.response: Show model client reports and the module's guidance on where theory belongs. Do not tell learners to remove theory altogether; it often belongs in a separate academic section or appendix.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting everything the client asks for, or never questioning the brief.
difficulties.revealedBy: Scope creep, unclear objectives and reports that do not answer the agreed question.
difficulties.response: Practise scoping meetings and written confirmation of the brief, including polite language for negotiating scope. Supervisors should model how to renegotiate a brief, since students often lack authority with real clients.

difficulties.pattern: Some team members' contributions disappear from the final report.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uneven sections, complaints about workload and reflective accounts that describe conflict.
difficulties.response: Agree roles and drafting and editing processes early, and give everyone a visible section or task. Module teams should design peer assessment and contribution statements that do not penalise quieter members or those writing in an additional language.

diagnostic.task: Give a client brief and one paragraph of findings, and ask for a three-sentence recommendation for the client.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Leads with a specific, feasible action, links it to the findings and gives responsibility, timescale or cost in plain language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Links the recommendation to the findings but is vague about implementation, or uses an academic register and citations unsuited to the client.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the findings or gives a generic recommendation not grounded in them.

records.contextNotes: In UG business programmes, consultancy-style projects usually appear in the final year, often in teams with simulated clients. On PGT programmes such as MSc Management and the MBA, live consultancy projects often replace or sit alongside the dissertation, so support should begin with scoping the brief and continue through the report and the reflective account. Requirements for confidentiality, client sign-off and the balance between client report and academic reflection differ between schools, so the module handbook is the reference.
reviewNotes: No EAP study of student consultancy reports is in the bibliography; the guidance extends research on business case reports and professional genres and should be checked with module leaders.

records.summary: Bhatia (1993) shows that features often criticised as obscure in legal English, such as complex qualifications in legislative sentences, serve the drafter's aim of precision and all-inclusiveness. Mertz (2007) describes legal education as a linguistic reorientation in which students learn to read texts for legal categories and authority rather than for moral or narrative meaning. Teaching should therefore explain the functions of legal features, distinguish what learners need to recognise from what they should produce, and emphasise that legal terms belong to a specific legal system.

activities.title: Same word, different law
learnerActions: Collect five words from a case you are reading that have both everyday and legal meanings
Write the everyday meaning and the legal meaning side by side, using a legal dictionary to check
Write one sentence in your own words using each word in its legal sense
activities.intendedInsight: Many difficult legal words look familiar, and the familiar meaning can lead to a wrong reading.
activities.rationale: Reading for legal rather than everyday meaning is the reorientation Mertz describes as central to legal education.

activities.title: Why is it written like this?
learnerActions: Read a short statutory provision and a plain-language version of it
Identify what the original says that the plain version leaves out or makes less precise
Discuss which features of the original you should recognise when reading and which you should avoid in your own analytical writing
activities.intendedInsight: Legal drafting features serve precision and inclusiveness, but student analysis is expected to be clear rather than imitative.
activities.rationale: Bhatia's analysis of legislative writing shows how its complexity follows from its purpose, which helps learners read it without imitating it.

difficulties.pattern: Translating legal terms through a bilingual dictionary or assuming they mean what the closest term means in the legal system I studied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misuse of concepts such as consideration, equity or trust, which have no direct equivalent in many civil-law systems.
difficulties.response: Treat legal terms as system-specific concepts. Use an English legal dictionary and the cases that define them, and note differences from the learner's home legal system as a comparative resource.

difficulties.pattern: Imitating archaic drafting in my essays (hereinafter, the said party, aforementioned) because it sounds legal.
difficulties.revealedBy: Student essays and problem answers with drafting formulas that markers mark as unclear or inappropriate.
difficulties.response: Distinguish reading legal drafting from writing legal analysis, and show model answers in clear academic prose.

diagnostic.task: Give six sentences from judgments and statutes, each with a highlighted word, and ask the learner to explain the meaning of each in context.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives the legal meaning for all items and explains how the everyday sense would mislead for at least two.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises some legal senses but defaults to everyday meanings for less familiar words.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives everyday meanings throughout.

records.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional law pathways, focus on recognition and on frequently confused legal senses. UG students need terminology tied to core modules. LLM students often know legal concepts in their own system well, so comparative discussion is valuable, alongside explicit warning about false equivalents.
reviewNotes: The topic assumes common-law, primarily English, legal English; programmes in other jurisdictions should adapt examples.

records.summary: Bhatia (1993) describes legal cases as a genre with recognisable moves (identifying the case, establishing the facts, arguing the case, pronouncing judgment), which gives learners a map for reading. Twining and Miers (2010) treat reading cases and extracting the ratio as an interpretive skill, noting that the ratio is not stated in the judgment and that its formulation can be contested. Mertz (2007) shows that law students learn to read cases for legal authority and procedure rather than for the human story. Teaching should model the process of briefing, practise it with real judgments, and discuss competing formulations of the ratio.

activities.title: Map the judgment
learnerActions: Skim a short judgment and mark where the facts, procedural history, arguments, reasoning and decision appear
Highlight the sentences that state the legal principle the decision depends on
Compare the headnote with your reading and note anything the headnote simplifies
activities.intendedInsight: Judgments have a recognisable structure, and the headnote is a guide to them, not a substitute.
activities.rationale: Genre awareness of the moves in a legal case supports strategic reading of long judgments.

activities.title: How wide is the ratio?
learnerActions: Write the ratio of a case in one sentence
Compare formulations across the group, from very narrow (tied to the exact facts) to very broad
Discuss which formulation the material facts justify, and identify one obiter statement and why it is not binding
activities.intendedInsight: Formulating the ratio is an interpretive act, and its level of generality matters for later cases.
activities.rationale: Twining and Miers present the ratio as something readers construct from the judgment, which group comparison makes visible.

difficulties.pattern: Reading the judgment from start to finish and summarising everything, or relying only on the headnote.
difficulties.revealedBy: Case briefs that retell the facts at length, or that reproduce headnote wording without the reasoning.
difficulties.response: Teach strategic reading with the case structure and set a strict length for briefs. Explain that the headnote is not authority.

difficulties.pattern: Treating everything a senior judge says as binding law.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays and problem answers that cite obiter remarks as if they were the ratio, or dissenting judgments as authority.
difficulties.response: Practise separating ratio, obiter and dissent, and explain precedential weight with the court hierarchy.

diagnostic.task: Give a 500-word extract from a judgment and ask the learner to identify the issue, the decision, the ratio in one sentence and any obiter remark.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the issue as a legal question, formulates a ratio grounded in material facts and correctly identifies obiter remarks.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies issue and decision but gives a ratio that restates the outcome or confuses it with obiter.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the facts without identifying the legal principle.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, use short, accessible judgments; UG entrants need the basic structure of a judgment, while LLM entrants need explicit work on precedent. First-year LLB students need briefing practice early, coordinated with their legal method modules. LLM students from civil-law systems may be used to codes and academic doctrine as primary sources and need explicit work on precedent and on extracting the ratio.
reviewNotes: Mertz's study concerns US law schools; its relevance to UK legal education is by analogy.

The four-move description of judgments follows Bhatia's (1993) analysis of legal cases; judgments of some courts and jurisdictions do not follow it closely, so it is offered as a reading map rather than a fixed structure.

records.summary: Problem questions test the application of legal rules to facts, which Twining and Miers (2010) treat as a core interpretive skill of legal method. Scaffolds such as IRAC help novices organise answers, but they are contested: lecturers vary in whether they recommend them, and applied mechanically they lead to rule-stating with little application. Teaching should use IRAC-type structures as a starting point, foreground application to facts and the handling of ambiguity, and follow the conventions of the specific law school, including OSCOLA footnoting (Goudkamp, 2026).

activities.title: Issue spotting
learnerActions: Read a problem scenario and underline every fact that may have legal significance
Group the facts into legal issues and decide the order in which to address them
Compare your list with a lecturer's model issue list and discuss any issues you missed
activities.intendedInsight: Each significant fact is usually there for a reason, and missing an issue costs more than imperfect expression.
activities.rationale: Issue identification is the first step of applying rules to facts and a common source of lost marks.

activities.title: Apply, don't recite
learnerActions: Read two answers to the same issue: one that states the law at length and one that applies it closely to the facts
Highlight sentences that mention the specific facts of the scenario
Rewrite a rule-heavy paragraph so that at least half of it applies the rule to the facts, using analogy with or distinction from a decided case
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are earned mainly in application: connecting the rule to these facts through comparison with decided cases.
activities.rationale: Comparing answers makes the balance between rule statement and application visible, addressing a known weakness of mechanical IRAC use.

difficulties.pattern: Writing everything I know about the area of law and then giving a one-line conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that resemble essays on the topic, with little reference to the parties or facts.
difficulties.response: Show the marking criteria for application and require each paragraph to mention a fact from the scenario. Avoid presenting IRAC as a formula to fill.

difficulties.pattern: Giving certain conclusions ('X will definitely win') or refusing to conclude because the law is uncertain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions that overstate certainty or leave the client without advice.
difficulties.response: Teach language for calibrated advice (is likely to, has a strong argument that, may be able to) and show how lawyers advise despite uncertainty.

difficulties.pattern: Inventing facts to resolve ambiguity in the scenario.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that assume facts not stated, such as what a party intended.
difficulties.response: Model conditional analysis that addresses each possibility (if X intended…, if, however,…). Explain that examiners include ambiguity on purpose.

diagnostic.task: Give a short problem scenario raising one main issue and one ambiguous fact, and ask for a 250-word answer advising one party.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the issue, gives the rule with authority, applies it closely with an analogy or distinction, addresses the ambiguous fact conditionally and concludes with calibrated advice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the issue and rule correctly but applies them thinly or ignores the ambiguity.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Discusses the area of law generally without applying it or advising the party.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, introduce the genre with short scenarios. First-year LLB students need support as they meet problem questions in exams and coursework. LLM students may not have met problem questions in their prior legal education, which often used other assessment forms.
reviewNotes: Critiques of IRAC are widespread among legal educators but are not documented by a source in the bibliography; they are presented here as a matter of practitioner debate.
Some UK law schools discourage IRAC labels and others teach them explicitly; check local practice.

records.summary: Bhatia (1993) analyses legislative provisions as sentences in which qualifications are inserted at points of potential ambiguity to make the provision precise and all-inclusive, which explains much of their reading difficulty. Twining and Miers (2010) treat statutory interpretation as reasoning about rules and their purposes, not only as the parsing of text. Teaching should combine structural parsing (main rule, conditions, exceptions, definitions) with awareness of how courts approach interpretation.

activities.title: Statute to flowchart
learnerActions: Read a statutory subsection and identify the main rule
Mark each condition, exception and cross-reference
Draw a flowchart or decision tree showing when the rule applies, then test it against two short fact scenarios
activities.intendedInsight: A long provision becomes manageable when its rule, conditions and exceptions are separated.
activities.rationale: Bhatia's account of qualificational insertion explains where the complexity lies, and visualising the structure supports accurate reading.

activities.title: Same words, different readings
learnerActions: Read a short provision with a known interpretive problem
In groups, argue for a literal reading and for a purposive reading
Write one paragraph explaining which reading you prefer and why, referring to the purpose of the Act
activities.intendedInsight: Reading legislation involves interpretive choices that courts justify by reference to the text and its purpose.
activities.rationale: Treating interpretation as reasoning about rules follows Twining and Miers' approach to statutory interpretation.

difficulties.pattern: Reading 'and' and 'or' between conditions loosely, so that cumulative conditions become alternatives or vice versa.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that apply a provision when only one of several cumulative conditions is met.
difficulties.response: Practise marking conjunctions in provisions and converting them into lists and flowcharts. Slow, structural reading is expected here.

difficulties.pattern: Ignoring the definitions section and reading defined terms in their ordinary sense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misapplication of provisions in which a term has a specific statutory meaning.
difficulties.response: Make checking the interpretation section a routine step and show cases where a definition changed the outcome.

diagnostic.task: Give a 70-word statutory provision with two cumulative conditions and an exception, plus two short scenarios. Ask whether the provision applies in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Applies the provision correctly to both scenarios and explains the conditions and the exception.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the main rule but misreads a condition or the exception.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Answers from general fairness without reference to the provision's structure.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, use short provisions to build structural reading. UG students meet statutes in public, criminal and contract law. LLM students need efficient navigation of long Acts and secondary legislation, and may compare common-law statutory interpretation with civil-law code interpretation.

records.summary: Legal essays combine accurate exposition of the law with argument about it, and students often over-describe cases at the expense of evaluation. Mertz (2007) shows that legal reading attends to the authority and procedural position of texts, which in essays becomes a hierarchy of sources and reporting verbs with legal meanings. OSCOLA (Goudkamp, 2026) specifies footnote referencing for UK law schools. Teaching should use the school's exemplars, model how case discussion is subordinated to a thesis, and make legal reporting conventions explicit.

activities.title: From case list to argument
learnerActions: Read a paragraph that summarises three cases in turn
Decide what claim the three cases could support together
Rewrite the paragraph with the claim first and each case used as evidence, with OSCOLA footnotes
activities.intendedInsight: Cases are evidence for an argument about the law, not the content of the essay in themselves.
activities.rationale: Reordering source-by-source paragraphs into claim-led ones targets the most common weakness in legal essays.

activities.title: Who said what, with what authority?
learnerActions: Collect reporting verbs from a model essay and sort them by who they report (court, judge, counsel, commentator, Law Commission)
Discuss why 'held' is reserved for the court's decision and what 'observed' or 'suggested' signals
Correct the reporting verbs in a short student paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: In legal writing, reporting verbs signal legal authority as well as stance.
activities.rationale: Making legal reporting conventions explicit connects general reporting-verb knowledge to the authority structure Mertz describes.

difficulties.pattern: Describing the facts of every case at length.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays in which case narratives dominate, with feedback such as 'too descriptive' or 'what is your argument?'.
difficulties.response: Limit facts to those needed for the point and require a claim sentence at the start of each paragraph. Do not ban case facts; select them.

difficulties.pattern: Citing textbooks for propositions of law instead of the primary authority.
difficulties.revealedBy: Footnotes to textbooks where the marker expects a case or statute.
difficulties.response: Explain the hierarchy of authority and the role of secondary sources in legal argument, and practise tracing a textbook statement to its primary source.

diagnostic.task: Give a 'To what extent…' legal essay question and ask the learner for a thesis statement and one body paragraph with footnotes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Takes a clear position, uses cases as evidence for a claim, evaluates against a criterion and footnotes correctly in OSCOLA.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a position but the paragraph describes cases with little evaluation, or references are inconsistent.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the law without a position and without legal referencing.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, contrast legal essays with general argumentative essays. UG students need early support with OSCOLA and with using cases as evidence. LLM essays expect more theoretical and comparative depth, and LLM students may bring different conventions for referencing and for the role of academic doctrine.
reviewNotes: Some institutions use OSCOLA variants or other legal citation guides; check local requirements.

records.summary: A moot is a simulated appellate hearing in which students argue a point of law before a judge, usually in pairs against an opposing team. It combines written preparation (the skeleton argument and bundle of authorities) with oral delivery and live interaction, and judges commonly assess the ability to respond to questions from the bench. Twining and Miers (2010) treat legal argument as the interpretation of rules and their application to facts, which supplies the content of each ground, while Joughin (1998) shows that oral assessments differ in how interactive they are and in what they reward, which helps teachers and students see what is being judged. Teaching should rehearse interventions, not only prepared speeches.

activities.title: Interrupt me, please
learnerActions: Prepare a two-minute submission on one ground with two authorities
Deliver it while a peer acting as judge interrupts with prepared questions
After each answer, practise a bridging phrase that returns to your submission, then discuss which answers were direct
activities.intendedInsight: Responding to the bench is part of the argument, not an interruption of it.
activities.rationale: Interactive oral assessment rewards responsiveness; rehearsing interruptions is intended to prepare learners for a feature that a prepared script does not address.

activities.title: From written answer to skeleton argument
learnerActions: Take a written answer to a problem question and reduce one issue to a skeleton argument of grounds and authorities
Compare it with a model skeleton argument for length and structure
Practise citing each authority aloud in the spoken form expected in court
activities.intendedInsight: Oral argument is built from the same legal analysis as written work but is selected, ordered and cited differently.
activities.rationale: Building the skeleton from a written answer makes the dependence on problem-question analysis, and on applying rules to facts, explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a prepared script and losing my place when the judge asks a question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent delivery that breaks down at interventions, and little contact with the bench.
difficulties.response: Rehearse with frequent interruptions using short notes rather than full scripts, and normalise asking the judge to repeat a question. Assessors should be clear about how interventions are marked; learners who stammer, are autistic or experience anxiety may need agreed adjustments to format or timing.

difficulties.pattern: Reading out full written citations, or using conversational forms of address.
difficulties.revealedBy: Submissions slowed by citations read in full, and judges' comments on register.
difficulties.response: Model the spoken form of citation and the forms of address for the relevant court, and practise them as fixed expressions.

difficulties.pattern: Refusing to concede anything, because conceding feels like losing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Persisting with an untenable point under questioning and losing credibility and time.
difficulties.response: Show how strategic concession and distinguishing protect the stronger grounds, using model recordings or transcripts.

diagnostic.task: Ask a question from the bench during a short prepared submission.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Answers directly, cites or distinguishes an authority if relevant, and returns to the submission with a signposting phrase.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers, but at length or indirectly, or does not return to the structure of the submission.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores or misunderstands the question, or carries on reading from the script.

records.contextNotes: On LLB programmes, mooting is usually introduced in the first or second year, sometimes as an assessed part of legal skills modules and sometimes as an extracurricular competition; support should focus on skeleton arguments, oral citation and interventions. LLM students may meet moots in international or commercial law modules and competitions, and those trained in systems with less adversarial oral procedure may find the format unfamiliar. Forms of address and citation differ between jurisdictions and courts, so follow the moot rules provided.
reviewNotes: No applied linguistic study of mooting is in the bibliography; the guidance is based on legal-skills practice and general research on oral assessment and should be reviewed with law staff.
Conventions here follow the appellate model of England and Wales; other jurisdictions and international moot competitions have their own rules.

records.summary: Law dissertations are a particular challenge for writers trained on general research-writing models, because doctrinal legal research analyses authoritative texts to establish, explain and critique the law rather than reporting empirical data. Hutchinson and Duncan (2012) describe doctrinal research as a method with its own rigour that is often left implicit, while socio-legal, comparative and theoretical approaches import methods from other disciplines and need their own justification. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) show that thesis structures vary and that students benefit from analysing theses in their own field. EAP support should help students state their method explicitly, design chapters around an argument and manage authority and referencing over a long text.

activities.title: From topic to legal problem
learnerActions: Write your dissertation topic as a phrase (for example, liability for autonomous vehicles)
Rewrite it as a question that identifies a gap, conflict or uncertainty in the law
Identify the method the question calls for and write two sentences justifying it
activities.intendedInsight: A legal research question names a problem in the law, and the method follows from the kind of problem.
activities.rationale: Doctrinal method is often left implicit; making the question and the method explicit responds to the expectation, set out by Hutchinson and Duncan, that legal researchers can describe what they do.

activities.title: Chapter functions
learnerActions: Analyse the contents pages and chapter introductions of two law theses or LLM dissertations
Label each chapter by its function in the argument (establishing the law, critique, comparison, proposal)
Draft your own chapter plan with a one-sentence function statement for each chapter
activities.intendedInsight: Each chapter of a legal dissertation should advance the argument, not survey an area.
activities.rationale: Analysing local exemplars of thesis structure helps writers see how general macrostructures are adapted in law.

difficulties.pattern: Writing chapters that describe the law in an area without a question driving them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Supervisor feedback such as 'too descriptive' or 'what is your argument?', and conclusions that summarise rather than answer.
difficulties.response: Require a chapter-level claim and a link back to the research question at the start and end of each chapter. Do not ask for more coverage; ask for selection.

difficulties.pattern: Copying an empirical methodology chapter from another discipline, or leaving out method because doctrinal research 'has no method'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methodology sections that discuss sampling and data collection irrelevant to doctrinal work, or no account of method at all.
difficulties.response: Show how doctrinal and socio-legal dissertations state their methods, and agree with supervisors what is expected locally.

difficulties.pattern: Losing control of footnotes and authorities across a long text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent citation forms, missing pinpoints and tables of authorities that do not match the text.
difficulties.response: Introduce reference-management and checking routines early; formatting is a late-stage task, but time for it should be scheduled.

diagnostic.task: Ask for a one-paragraph statement of the dissertation’s research question and method.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a legal problem, names the method with a reason and indicates the expected contribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a topic or question but leaves the method implicit or unjustified.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes an area of law without a question or method.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional programmes for LLM entrants, introduce legal method and research questions through short proposals. LLB students who choose a dissertation option need early help with question design. LLM dissertations are short and written under time pressure, so support focuses on the question, the method statement and the chapter plan. Doctoral law researchers write theses on a different scale, often combining doctrinal and socio-legal work, and need support with sustained argument, contribution and publication. Expectations about method chapters differ between law schools and jurisdictions.
reviewNotes: Legal research methods are debated, including the status of doctrinal research as a method; the topic presents the main approaches without ranking them.
The topic assumes common-law legal research; comparative and civil-law dissertations may follow other structures.

records.summary: Gallie (1956) argued that some concepts, especially evaluative social and political ones, are 'essentially contested': their proper use is permanently disputed. This makes explicit definition and justification an expected move in social science writing. In empirical work, Creswell and Creswell (2018) describe how constructs become variables and measures in quantitative designs, while qualitative research treats concepts as open to participants' meanings. Teaching should help learners show contestation, choose a definition for a reason and carry it consistently through a text.

activities.title: One word, three definitions
learnerActions: Find three definitions of a key concept in your module from different authors or traditions
Tabulate what each includes and excludes and which theoretical position it reflects
Write a paragraph that presents the contestation briefly and adopts one definition with a reason linked to your assignment question
activities.intendedInsight: In the social sciences, defining a concept is an argued choice, not a dictionary look-up.
activities.rationale: Gallie's account of essentially contested concepts explains why markers expect definitions to be positioned and justified.

activities.title: From concept to indicator
learnerActions: Take a concept from your field and propose three indicators or survey items that could measure it
Discuss with a partner what each indicator captures and misses
Write two sentences justifying your indicators and acknowledging one limitation
activities.intendedInsight: Operationalisation narrows a concept, and the narrowing needs to be justified and its limits acknowledged.
activities.rationale: Moving from construct to measure is a standard step in quantitative design, and discussing what is lost develops the critical stance markers value.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with a dictionary definition ('The Oxford Dictionary defines globalisation as…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Introductions that cite general dictionaries for key concepts, with marker comments asking for academic sources.
difficulties.response: Show model introductions that define concepts through the literature, and explain why dictionaries rarely capture disciplinary meanings. Treat dictionary definitions as a starting point for the writer, not for the text.

difficulties.pattern: Shifting between different meanings of a key term across an essay.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays where, for example, 'culture' means nationality in one section and organisational practice in another.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to track every use of the key term in a draft and check it against their stated definition.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a short paragraph defining a contested concept from their field for a specified assignment question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Shows contestation with sources, adopts a definition for a reason linked to the question and signals how it will be used.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Cites an academic definition but does not acknowledge alternatives or justify the choice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a dictionary or common-sense definition.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional social science pathways, introduce contestation and justified definition. UG students meet these demands in essays. At PGT and PGR, operationalisation and conceptual frameworks become central to dissertations and theses.

records.summary: Qualitative research depends on texts that readers rarely see: field notes, analytic memos and records of analytic decisions. Emerson et al. (2011) describe field notes as written constructions that combine description with in-process analysis and recommend keeping the two distinguishable. Braun and Clarke (2006) set out phases of thematic analysis and warn against describing themes as simply emerging, and their later account of reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2019) stresses that themes are actively constructed by the researcher, which affects how analysis should be reported. Teaching should treat these process texts as writing that can be practised and connect them to the transparent account of analysis that examiners expect.

activities.title: From memo to meaning
learnerActions: Code a short interview extract in pairs
Write a five-minute analytic memo on one code: what it might mean, how it relates to other codes and what you are unsure about
Exchange memos and identify one interpretation that could become a theme and one alternative reading
activities.intendedInsight: Analytic memos are where interpretation is developed in writing, and they leave a trail that an account of the analysis can draw on.
activities.rationale: Reflexive thematic analysis treats themes as constructed through the researcher’s interpretive work; memo writing makes that work visible and open to revision.

activities.title: Observation versus interpretation in field notes
learnerActions: Watch a short video of a classroom or public setting and write field notes
Highlight words that interpret rather than describe (bored, aggressive, confused)
Rewrite the interpretive phrases as observable description and move interpretations to a separate analytic memo
activities.intendedInsight: Field notes are more useful for analysis when description and interpretation are kept distinguishable.
activities.rationale: Emerson et al. treat field notes as written constructions in which description and analytic commentary have different functions.

difficulties.pattern: Field notes full of judgements such as 'the students were bored'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes that cannot be re-analysed because the observation behind each judgement was not recorded.
difficulties.response: Ask what was seen or heard that led to the judgement, record that, and move the interpretation to a memo. Do not ban interpretation from notes; mark it as such.

difficulties.pattern: Writing that themes 'emerged from the data' and giving no account of how analysis was done.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods sections with one sentence on analysis and passive constructions that hide analytic decisions.
difficulties.response: Discuss the researcher's active role in analysis and ask learners to describe coding and theme development step by step.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing reflexive thematic analysis with coding-reliability procedures, for example reporting inter-rater agreement in a reflexive design.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts of analysis that combine incompatible procedures or terms, and examiners’ questions about coherence.
difficulties.response: Discuss the different assumptions of approaches to thematic analysis and help learners describe the one they used consistently. Treat this as a debated area; supervisors and fields differ.

diagnostic.task: Give a short video or transcript and ask for field notes and a brief analytic memo.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The notes record observable detail with interpretations marked; the memo develops a tentative interpretation tied to specific observations and notes an alternative reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The notes mix description and interpretation, or the memo summarises rather than interprets.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The notes are mostly evaluative impressions and the memo shows no analytic development.

records.contextNotes: UG students may meet field notes in ethnographic or observational modules and final-year projects. PGT dissertation students in education, the social sciences and health often conduct interviews or observations for the first time and need support with memos and with describing their analysis in the methods chapter. PGR researchers keep extended field and analytic records and must account for their analysis in detail, often in a methodology chapter examined for coherence and reflexivity.
reviewNotes: Findings writing, including the use of participant extracts, belongs to res.qualitative-reporting (R1-29); this topic covers field notes, memos and accounts of analysis.

Approaches to thematic analysis are debated, and fields differ on whether they expect coding-reliability or reflexive approaches; the topic presents reflexive thematic analysis as one widely cited approach, not the only one.

records.summary: Policy analysis assignments draw on two broad traditions: problem-solving approaches that appraise options against criteria, and critical approaches such as Bacchi's (2009) 'What's the problem represented to be?', which question how policies construct the problems they address. Both are organised around a problem–response–evaluation structure, which Hoey (1983) describes as a common text pattern. Teaching should clarify which tradition an assignment expects, and should distinguish academic policy analysis from the shorter policy brief written for policy-makers.

activities.title: What is the problem represented to be?
learnerActions: Read a short policy summary and underline how it describes the problem
Discuss what this representation assumes and leaves out, and who it treats as responsible
Write a paragraph comparing the policy's framing with an alternative framing and its implications
activities.intendedInsight: How a problem is framed shapes which solutions seem reasonable, so framing is part of the analysis.
activities.rationale: Bacchi's approach gives learners explicit questions for examining problem representation in policy texts.

activities.title: Options against criteria
learnerActions: Identify two or three policy options for a problem from your field
Agree criteria such as effectiveness, equity, cost and feasibility, and assess each option against them using evidence
Write an evaluation section that leads to a recommendation and acknowledges trade-offs
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations are credible when they follow from transparent comparison against criteria.
activities.rationale: Building the analysis on the problem–response–evaluation pattern makes the structure of policy argument explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Describing what a policy does and when it was introduced, with little analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments dominated by policy history and content, with feedback asking for critical analysis.
difficulties.response: Provide a set of analytical questions (problem framing, evidence, stakeholders, options) and require each section to answer one.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting the policy's own account of the problem as fact.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analyses that adopt government definitions uncritically and evaluate only implementation.
difficulties.response: Practise identifying assumptions in policy texts and comparing framings from different stakeholders.

diagnostic.task: Give a short policy summary and ask the learner to identify how it frames the problem, one stakeholder whose view differs, and one piece of evidence they would need to evaluate it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the framing and its assumptions, a relevant stakeholder perspective and evidence that would test the policy's claims.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies stakeholders and evidence but treats the framing as given.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the policy or gives an unsupported opinion.

records.contextNotes: UG social policy, politics and education students meet policy analysis in coursework. PGT programmes in public policy, international development and education often assess it extensively, sometimes alongside policy briefs (grp.policy-brief).
reviewNotes: Overlap with grp.policy-brief: the brief is treated as a short professional genre, this topic as the academic analysis that may underpin it.

records.summary: Creswell and Creswell (2018) frame research design as a set of connected choices about philosophical worldview, approach and methods, which gives learners a vocabulary for justification. Move analyses of methods sections (Cotos et al., 2017; Lim, 2006) show that expert writers do more than describe procedures: they justify choices to establish rigour and credibility. Teaching should focus on the language of rationale, the coherence between questions and design, and the honest treatment of trade-offs, and should check with supervisors how much paradigm discussion the field expects.

activities.title: Description or justification?
learnerActions: Read a methodology section from a dissertation in your field
Label each sentence as procedure, justification or limitation
Add justification sentences to a procedure-only paragraph, linking each choice to the research questions
activities.intendedInsight: Methodology writing argues for the design; procedure alone does not show why it is appropriate.
activities.rationale: Move analyses show that justifying procedures is a recognised step in methods sections across disciplines.

activities.title: Paradigm to procedure
learnerActions: Choose a research question in your field
In groups, design two contrasting studies that answer different versions of it from different paradigms
Write a short paragraph explaining what each design can and cannot claim
activities.intendedInsight: Paradigm, design and the type of claim a study can make are linked.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell present design as following from worldview and questions, which contrasting designs make concrete.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a long general account of positivism and interpretivism that is not connected to my study.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methodology chapters with textbook-like paradigm sections and feedback asking 'how does this relate to your study?'.
difficulties.response: Require every paradigm statement to be linked to a decision in the study. Check with supervisors how much paradigm discussion is expected, since it varies by field.

difficulties.pattern: Claiming the chosen method is the best or only way to answer the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Justifications without acknowledged trade-offs or alternatives.
difficulties.response: Practise language that acknowledges alternatives and limitations while defending the choice.

diagnostic.task: Give a research question and a two-sentence design description and ask the learner to write a justification paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Connects design to question and paradigm, justifies key choices with reasons and acknowledges a trade-off.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Justifies some choices but in general terms, or omits limitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the procedure or asserts that the design is appropriate without reasons.

records.contextNotes: UG final-year project students need a brief, proportionate justification. PGT dissertation students, often new to social research, need explicit work on paradigm vocabulary and coherence from the start of the programme, building on methods-section writing. PGR researchers write full methodology chapters examined for coherence and reflexivity.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with res.methods, which is treated as the general prerequisite; this topic adds paradigm-level justification typical of social science and education.

records.summary: The psychology report is a closely conventionalised genre: the APA Publication Manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) specifies its structure, statistical reporting and bias-free language, and departments usually add their own guide. Beyond format, the genre carries the discipline’s view of evidence: hypotheses are derived from theory, results are reported so that effect sizes and uncertainty are visible, and conclusions are calibrated to the data. Cumming (2014) argues for estimation with effect sizes and confidence intervals, and the ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) sets out common misinterpretations of significance testing; markers increasingly expect students to interpret results in these terms. Teaching is likely to be most useful when it draws on departmental exemplars and the module’s own statistics output.

activities.title: From output to sentence
learnerActions: Take a statistics output table from a practical class
Identify the values that must be reported (test statistic, degrees of freedom, p, effect size, confidence interval)
Write the results sentence in APA format, then add a plain-language sentence saying what the result means for the hypothesis
activities.intendedInsight: A results sentence turns software output into a conventional, interpretable claim.
activities.rationale: Reporting effect sizes and intervals, not only p values, reflects the estimation approach Cumming recommends.

activities.title: From hypothesis to discussion
learnerActions: Highlight each hypothesis in an exemplar introduction
Find where each hypothesis is tested in the results and discussed in the discussion
Draft a discussion paragraph for a non-significant result that does not claim the hypothesis was disproved
activities.intendedInsight: The report is organised around its hypotheses, and each must be followed through to the discussion.
activities.rationale: Tracing hypotheses through an exemplar makes the genre’s logic visible, and the non-significant case addresses misreadings of p values that the ASA statement warns against.

difficulties.pattern: Copying p = .000 from the software output, or reporting only whether a result was significant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Results without effect sizes, or with impossible exact p values.
difficulties.response: Teach the convention explicitly (p < .001) and show why effect sizes and intervals are expected. Avoid treating this as carelessness; it follows from how software displays output.

difficulties.pattern: A non-significant result means there is no effect, so my study failed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussions claiming that the null hypothesis was proved, or apologetic discussions of 'failed' studies.
difficulties.response: Discuss what non-significance does and does not show, including statistical power and confidence intervals, and model neutral discussion language.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the introduction as a general literature review that does not lead to the hypotheses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypotheses that appear without a rationale, and markers' comments on the structure of the introduction.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to write the hypotheses first and then check that each paragraph of the introduction contributes to the rationale for one of them.

diagnostic.task: Give a statistics output and a hypothesis, and ask for a results sentence and a one-sentence interpretation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports the statistic, degrees of freedom, p, effect size and interval in APA format and relates the result to the hypothesis with calibrated language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Formats the statistic correctly but omits the effect size, or misstates the relation to the hypothesis.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reports only significant or non-significant, or copies output values without interpretation.

records.contextNotes: UG psychology students write reports from the first year, and in accredited programmes the empirical project is a substantial final-year requirement; embed support in research-methods modules. Conversion master’s students may come from other disciplines and need a rapid induction into the genre and its statistics. Preregistration and other open-research practices increasingly shape method and results sections at PGT level and beyond (see pub.open-research). Qualitative psychology reports follow different conventions, partly covered by res.qualitative-reporting.
reviewNotes: Departmental conventions vary (for example on stating hypotheses and on report length); the department’s guide takes precedence over general APA advice.
The topic follows the 7th edition of the APA Publication Manual; APA style is revised periodically.

records.summary: Education and TESOL practice genres sit between professional documents and academic writing: a lesson plan is a working document, but its rationale is an academic argument, and a teaching-practice reflection is assessed for analysis, not narration. Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner and Moon’s (2004) account of reflective learning underpin much teacher-education assessment, while classroom research reports adapt general research design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018) to practitioner enquiry. Many MA TESOL students are experienced teachers whose expertise is a resource; the writing challenge is to connect it explicitly to literature and evidence. Programme templates and exemplars are essential, as genres and criteria differ widely.

activities.title: Why this stage?
learnerActions: Read a lesson plan and annotate each stage with the questions 'why here?' and 'why this?'
Write a rationale sentence for each stage that refers to the learners and to a principle or study
Compare rationales with a partner and identify any that rely only on personal preference
activities.intendedInsight: A lesson-plan rationale is an argument that justifies decisions by the learners’ needs and by theory.
activities.rationale: Making the reasoning behind planning explicit reflects the reflective-practitioner view that professional knowledge can be articulated and examined.

activities.title: From description to analysis in teaching-practice reflection
learnerActions: Read two reflections on the same observed lesson, one mainly descriptive and one analytic
Identify the sentences that link classroom evidence to principles and propose changes
Rewrite a descriptive paragraph from your own reflection using that pattern
activities.intendedInsight: Teaching-practice reflections are assessed on analysis and action, not on the account of what happened.
activities.rationale: Moon distinguishes descriptive writing from deeper reflection; comparing the two side by side makes the expected depth visible.

difficulties.pattern: My teaching experience is evidence enough, so I do not need to cite literature.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rationales and reflections built on anecdote, with feedback asking for engagement with the literature.
difficulties.response: Value experience explicitly and show how to pair each experiential claim with a source that supports, qualifies or challenges it. Do not imply that experienced teachers’ knowledge is invalid.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluating materials by whether I liked them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Materials evaluations without criteria, or with criteria that are not justified.
difficulties.response: Build or adopt a set of criteria with learners and require each judgement to cite a criterion and evidence from the materials.

difficulties.pattern: Generalising from one class to all learners of a nationality or level ('learners from my country prefer…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Classroom research reports that make claims about whole groups from a single class.
difficulties.response: Practise scoping claims to the context and discuss what practitioner research can and cannot claim. Address essentialising language explicitly and respectfully.

diagnostic.task: Give one stage of a short lesson plan and ask for a two-sentence rationale.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Justifies the stage by the learners’ needs and a named principle or study, and anticipates a likely issue.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a plausible reason but without reference to the learners or the literature.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes what happens in the stage rather than why.

records.contextNotes: On pre-sessional programmes for education and TESOL master’s entrants, introduce the rationale and reflective genres through short tasks that build on participants’ teaching experience.
